title: Lemma 10.79.1
section: 10.79 Integral periods, Picard tori and Albanese maps
text: Lemma 10.79.1 . 1B257374E593 The fundamental group of a connected compact smooth manifold is finitely generated. Its abelianization has the form $\mathbb Z^ b\oplus T$ with $T$ finite. Proof. A smooth positive metric exists by partitions of unity. Its path distance induces the topology: on a relatively compact coordinate ball, metric lengths and Euclidean lengths are bounded above and below by positive constant multiples; a path leaving a smaller concentric ball has a positive lower length bound. The triangle inequality and these local bounds prove that the path distance is a metric with the original topology. Connectedness implies path connectedness since coordinate balls are path connected. Take a finite cover by coordinate balls whose coordinate images are convex. By compactness choose $\epsilon >0$ such that every metric ball of radius $10\epsilon $ lies in one of them. Take a finite $\epsilon $-net of points, including a base point $a$. Join two net points by one fixed path of length less than $4\epsilon $ whenever their distance is less than $3\epsilon $. These finitely many edges form a graph mapped to the manifold. A based loop can be subdivided into segments of image diameter less than $\epsilon $; replace each division point by a net point at distance less than $\epsilon $, keeping $a$ at both ends. Consecutive net points are joined by an edge. Join each original division point to its net point by a path of length less than $2\epsilon $. Each resulting quadrilateral, including the original short segment and the fixed edge, lies in a ball of radius $6\epsilon $ about its first original point. It contracts in a convex coordinate ball. The loop is therefore homotopic, with base point fixed, to the graph's edge loop. The same construction on paths shows the graph component containing $a$ contains all net vertices. Choose a finite spanning tree. The loops consisting of a tree path, a non-tree edge and a return tree path generate every edge loop by cancellation of tree paths. Their images generate the fundamental group. In dimension zero the manifold is a point and the assertion is immediate. Here are the needed integral algebra details. A subgroup of $\mathbb Z^ r$ is free and finitely generated: project onto the last coordinate, whose image is $d\mathbb Z$; if $d>0$ choose an element mapping to $d$, and split off its cyclic group. The kernel is a subgroup of $\mathbb Z^{r-1}$, so induction applies. Write the abelianization as $G=\mathbb Z^ r/L$ and put $L_ s=(\operatorname {span}_{\mathbb Q}L)\cap \mathbb Z^ r$. If $l_1,\ldots ,l_ s$ is a basis of $L$, a nonzero $s$-row minor of their coordinate matrix has some integer determinant $d\ne 0$. Cramer's rule shows $dL_ s\subset L$. Thus $L_ s/L$ is finite, since $L_ s/dL_ s$ is finite by the subgroup result. It is exactly the torsion subgroup $T$ of $G$. The quotient $G/T$ injects into the rational vector space $\mathbb Q^ r/\operatorname {span}_{\mathbb Q}L$. Choose a rational basis there and clear the finitely many denominators of the images of the original generators. This embeds $G/T$ in a finite-rank free integer group. The subgroup result makes it free; lifting its basis splits $G\cong \mathbb Z^ b\oplus T$. The case $L=0$ has $T=0$ and needs no minor. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.79.2
section: 10.79 Integral periods, Picard tori and Albanese maps
text: Theorem 10.79.2 . F90F5D542AFB Let $M$ be a connected compact smooth manifold and $a\in M$. For every abelian group $A$ there is a natural isomorphism 6D4EC61A4B96 10.79.3 \begin{equation}  H^1(M,\underline A)\cong \operatorname {Hom}(\pi _1(M,a),A). \end{equation} For $A=\mathbb R$, the de Rham comparison identifies it with $[\alpha ]\mapsto (\gamma \mapsto \int _\gamma \alpha )$. Consequently $H^1(M,\underline{\mathbb Z})\cong \mathbb Z^ b$, its map to $H^1_{\rm dR}(M,\mathbb R)$ is injective with full lattice image, and the image consists exactly of the classes with integer periods. The image of $H^1(M,\underline{\mathbb Q})$ is the rational span of that lattice. If $G=\pi _1(M,a)_{\rm ab}$, the evaluation map induces \[  G/\operatorname {Tor}G \cong \operatorname {Hom}(H^1(M,\underline{\mathbb Z}),\mathbb Z).  \] Proof. By lemma 10.40.1 , degree-one sheaf classes are represented by locally constant Čech cocycles $c_{ij}$ on open covers. They satisfy $c_{ij}+c_{jk}=c_{ik}$. Glue $U_ i\times A$ by the coordinate changes $t_ j=t_ i-c_{ij}$. Since these changes are locally constant, the result is a covering space locally of the form $U_ i\times A$, with a free transitive $A$-action on each fiber. It has path lifting: subdivide a path into finitely many pieces in such trivializations and keep its fiber coordinate constant on each piece. Uniqueness on overlapping intervals gives uniqueness of the lift. Subdividing a homotopy square into small trivialized rectangles shows that continuation along homotopic paths with fixed endpoints is equal. Thus continuation around a based loop is translation by an element of $A$, and gives a homomorphism $\chi :\pi _1(M,a)\to A$. A coboundary changes fiber origins and not this translation. If $\chi =0$, continuation of one chosen origin along paths gives a global section of this covering: path independence follows by closing two paths to a loop, and local trivializations give continuity. Its local coordinates show that $c_{ij}$ is a coboundary. Conversely choose a coordinate-ball cover, and for each ball choose a path from $a$ to its center, followed by the straight coordinate path to a varying point $x$ of the ball. Call the resulting path $\lambda _ i(x)$. Given $\chi $, set \[  c_{ij}(x)=\chi ([\lambda _ j(x)*\lambda _ i(x)^{-1}]).  \] Here $*$ means concatenation in the written order. On a small neighborhood of any overlap point the displayed loop class is constant, by contracting inside the two coordinate balls. The cocycle identity holds after applying the abelian homomorphism $\chi $. Its glued covering has monodromy $\chi $: along each coordinate segment the paths $\lambda _ i$ vary by that segment, and the changes $t_ j=t_ i-c_{ij}$ cancel the chosen access paths. This also proves compatibility with refinements and coefficient homomorphisms. The constructions are additive and inverse, proving ( 10.79.3 ). For a closed real one-form choose local primitives $f_ i$. The de Rham resolution sends it to the cocycle $f_ j-f_ i$, by the positive connecting convention already checked in lemma 10.40.1 . With the gluing rule above, a telescoping sum along a subdivided loop gives monodromy $\int _\gamma \alpha $: it is minus the sum of the successive $f_ j-f_ i$ at switching points. This proves the asserted de Rham compatibility, including its sign. Use lemma 10.79.1 to write $G=\mathbb Z^ b\oplus T$. Homomorphisms from $T$ to $\mathbb Z,\mathbb Q,\mathbb R$ vanish, so the three groups in question identify naturally with $\mathbb Z^ b,\mathbb Q^ b, \mathbb R^ b$, and coefficient inclusions give the usual inclusions. The integer subgroup is discrete and spans the real space; its fundamental parallelotope is compact, proving that it is a full lattice. Evaluation of $G$ on its integer characters is the ordinary evaluation of $\mathbb Z^ b$ on its dual, with kernel exactly $T$. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.79.4
section: 10.79 Integral periods, Picard tori and Albanese maps
text: Theorem 10.79.4 . C1FB3F157E12 Let $X$ be a connected compact Kähler manifold and $q=h^{0,1}(X)$. The coefficient map \[  H^1(X,\underline{\mathbb Z})\longrightarrow H^1(X,\mathcal O_ X)  \] is injective with full lattice image $\Lambda _ X$ of rank $2q$. The complex torus \[  J(X)=H^1(X,\mathcal O_ X)/\Lambda _ X  \] is naturally the subgroup $\operatorname {Pic}^0(X)$ of holomorphic line bundles whose integer-sheaf Chern class is zero. Its elements are exactly the topologically trivial smooth line bundles equipped with these holomorphic structures. There is an exact sequence \[  0\to J(X)\to \operatorname {Pic}(X) \xrightarrow {c_1^{\mathbb Z}}\mathrm{NS}(X)\to 0, \qquad \mathrm{NS}(X)=\ker \bigl (H^2(X,\underline{\mathbb Z}) \to H^2(X,\mathcal O_ X)\bigr ).  \] This assertion does not require discarding integer classes with zero real image or presuppose any finiteness theorem for $\mathrm{NS}(X)$. Proof. The compact Kähler Hodge decomposition theorem 10.47.13 gives \[  H^1_{\rm dR}(X,\mathbb C)=H^{1,0}(X)\oplus H^{0,1}(X), \qquad \overline{H^{1,0}(X)}=H^{0,1}(X).  \] Projection from the real part to $H^{0,1}$ is a real-linear isomorphism: a real class is determined by this component, and an arbitrary $\eta \in H^{0,1}$ comes from $\eta +\bar\eta $. By proposition 10.40.7 , this is exactly the coefficient map to $H^1(\mathcal O_ X)$ under the canonical comparisons. The preceding full-lattice theorem proves the first assertion. If $q=0$ the quotient is a point. Otherwise translations by a full real lattice in a complex vector space act discretely; balls smaller than half the shortest nonzero lattice distance give holomorphic quotient charts. A fundamental parallelotope proves compactness of the quotient. The remaining assertions follow from the exact exponential sequence and smooth-line classification in theorem 10.40.2 . In particular its kernel at the Picard group is exactly this quotient; zero integer class is equivalent to a trivial underlying smooth line bundle. No replacement of the integer class by its real image is made. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.79.5
section: 10.79 Integral periods, Picard tori and Albanese maps
text: Theorem 10.79.5 . 99C9CC069FA0 For a connected compact Kähler manifold put $V=H^0(X,\Omega _ X^1)$ and \[  \Gamma _ X=\left\{ u\longmapsto \int _\gamma u: [\gamma ]\in \pi _1(X,a)\right\} \subset V^*.  \] This is a full lattice of rank $2\dim _{\mathbb C}V$ in $V^*$. The period torus $A(X)=V^*/\Gamma _ X$ is therefore a compact complex torus. The map 43EBBCC4E992 10.79.6 \begin{equation}  \alpha _ a:X\longrightarrow A(X),\qquad x\longmapsto \left(u\longmapsto \int _ a^ x u\right)\bmod \Gamma _ X \end{equation} is well defined and holomorphic, with differential $d\alpha _ a(v)(u)=u(v)$. Every holomorphic map to a complex torus which takes $a$ to zero factors uniquely through $\alpha _ a$ by a homomorphism induced by a complex-linear map of the covering vector spaces. Proof. Holomorphic one-forms are harmonic on a compact Kähler manifold: they are $\bar\partial $-closed and their $\bar\partial $ adjoint has out-of-range antiholomorphic degree. The proved identity $\Delta _ d=2\square $ makes them $d$-closed. Hodge decomposition shows that $u\mapsto [\operatorname {Re}u]$ is a real-linear isomorphism from $V$ to $H^1_{\rm dR}(X,\mathbb R)$. Under this isomorphism a complex-linear functional $\ell \in V^*$ corresponds to the real functional $[\operatorname {Re}u]\mapsto \operatorname {Re}\ell (u)$. This identifies the underlying real vector space of $V^*$ with the real dual of $H^1_{\rm dR}(X,\mathbb R)$: a real functional $b$ on $V$ determines the complex-linear functional $u\mapsto b(u)-\mathrm i b(\mathrm i u)$. Under it the period of a loop is precisely evaluation of real cohomology on that loop. The final evaluation assertion of theorem 10.79.2 identifies these evaluations with the full dual lattice of $H^1(X,\underline{\mathbb Z})$. This proves the lattice assertion, including the possible finite torsion kernel of the loop period map. Two paths from $a$ to $x$ differ by a loop period. Local closed holomorphic one-forms have holomorphic primitives: the radial Poincaré primitive in a coordinate ball has differential $u$, so its $\bar\partial $ is zero. These primitives give local holomorphic lifts of ( 10.79.6 ) and its stated differential. Let $f:X\to W/L$ be a holomorphic map to a complex torus with $f(a)=0$, where $L$ is a full lattice in the complex vector space $W$. Constant covectors on $W$ descend to holomorphic one-forms. Their pullbacks define a complex-linear map $W^*\to V$; let $B:V^*\to W$ be its dual. Integrating along a loop, local lifts of $f$ change by an element of $L$, so $B\Gamma _ X\subset L$. It induces a homomorphism $\bar B:A(X)\to W/L$. The maps $f$ and $\bar B\alpha _ a$ have identical differentials and agree at $a$; their difference has locally constant lifts, so connectedness gives equality. For uniqueness, the complex span of all $d\alpha _ a(T_ xX)$ is $V^*$: an element of its annihilator would be a holomorphic one-form vanishing at every point. Thus two covering linear maps inducing the same factorization have equal differentials and are equal. A holomorphic group homomorphism between complex tori is of this linear type: its differential is translation invariant by the group law. On the covering vector space subtract the map induced by its differential at zero; the difference has zero differential, hence is constant and zero. Evaluating at lattice points gives the required compatibility of the covering linear map with both lattices. $\square$

title: Lemma 10.79.7
section: 10.79 Integral periods, Picard tori and Albanese maps
text: Lemma 10.79.7 . 1CADB2D45709 On a connected compact curve, every degree-zero line bundle lies in $\operatorname {Pic}^0(X)$. For a fixed $a\in X$, the map \[  \Phi _ a:X\longrightarrow J(X),\qquad x\longmapsto \mathcal O_ X([x]-[a])  \] is well defined and holomorphic. Moreover 58128D058B3D 10.79.8 \begin{equation}  H^2(X,\underline{\mathbb Z})\cong \mathbb Z, \qquad c_1^{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal O_ X([a]))\longmapsto 1, \end{equation} The real coefficient map is injective, and the $\Psi _2^{-1}$ image of this generator has integral one. Proof. First take $x$ near $a$ in a coordinate disk, writing $z(a)=0$ and $z(x)=t$. Choose nested disks $D_ r\Subset D_ R$ about zero, with $|t|<r/2$, and the cover $U_1=D_ R$, $U_2=X\setminus \overline D_ r$. Local meromorphic equations for $[x]-[a]$ are $f_1=(z-t)/z$ and $f_2=1$. The canonical frames $e_ i=1/f_ i$ have transition $g_{12}=f_2/f_1=z/(z-t)$; this is the frame, rather than fiber-coordinate, convention. On their annular overlap it has the holomorphic logarithm E6A14AA9C835 10.79.9 \begin{equation}  c_ t(z)=\frac1{2\pi \mathrm i}\log \frac z{z-t} =-\frac1{2\pi \mathrm i}\log (1-t/z),\qquad c_0=0. \end{equation} Thus the line bundle is in the exponential image of $H^1(\mathcal O_ X)$. We check holomorphic parameter dependence without an assumed theorem on analytic families of line bundles. Let $\chi $ be a smooth cutoff equal to one near $\overline D_ r$ and supported in $D_ R$. The smooth cochain $b_1=-(1-\chi )c_ t$, $b_2=\chi c_ t$, extended by zero where necessary, satisfies $b_2-b_1=c_ t$. Its Dolbeault representative is the global smooth form F6740EF6A319 10.79.10 \begin{equation}  \eta _ t=\bar\partial \chi \, c_ t, \end{equation} supported on a fixed compact subannulus. This is the positive connecting convention, since $\bar\partial b_ i=\eta _ t$. The power series in $t/z$ converges with all $z$ derivatives on that support uniformly for $t$ in smaller parameter disks. Projection onto the finite harmonic space is continuous linear by theorem 10.46.6 . Therefore $t\mapsto [\eta _ t]\in H^1(\mathcal O_ X)$ is holomorphic, as is its quotient in $J(X)$. The same local construction about every point shows that the coset of $\mathcal O_ X([x]-[a])$ modulo $\operatorname {Pic}^0(X)$ is locally constant: near $x_0$ its difference from the value at $x_0$ is $\mathcal O_ X([x]-[x_0])$, just treated. Connectedness makes it the zero coset everywhere. The same local logarithmic lifts prove global holomorphicity of $\Phi _ a$. Every line bundle is $\mathcal O_ X(D)$ by lemma 10.78.1 . If $\deg D=0$, write it as the tensor product of $\mathcal O_ X([x]-[a])^{m_ x}$, because $\sum m_ x=0$. It lies in $\operatorname {Pic}^0$. Conversely zero integer Chern class has zero real curvature class, so has degree zero. Since $\deg \mathcal O_ X([a])=1$, degree gives an isomorphism $\operatorname {Pic}(X)/\operatorname {Pic}^0(X)\cong \mathbb Z$. Finally $H^2(X,\mathcal O_ X)=0$ by the one-dimensional Dolbeault resolution, so the exponential sequence identifies this quotient with $H^2(X,\underline{\mathbb Z})$. The Chern/curvature comparison and divisor degree give the stated positive real image, which is injective since its generator has nonzero integral. $\square$

title: Lemma 10.79.11
section: 10.79 Integral periods, Picard tori and Albanese maps
text: Lemma 10.79.11 . 6D7C5C5A2C24 Let $X$ be a connected compact curve, let $V=H^0(X,K_ X)$, and use \[  \mathcal S:H^1(X,\mathcal O_ X)\longrightarrow V^*, \qquad \mathcal S([\eta ])(u)=\int _ Xu\wedge \eta .  \] This Serre isomorphism maps $\Lambda _ X$ onto $\Gamma _ X$. Moreover $\pi _1(X)_{\rm ab}$ is free of rank $2g$, and integration currents give an isomorphism \[  \pi _1(X)_{\rm ab}\longrightarrow H^1(X,\underline{\mathbb Z})  \] whose real image is the de Rham class of the loop current, with the complex orientation of $X$. Proof. We first justify the regular-value assertion used below. A smooth real function on a surface has critical values of measure zero. At a critical point where some second derivative is nonzero, the zero set of a suitable first derivative is a smooth curve by the inverse function theorem. Its critical subset maps into the critical values of the restricted one-variable function. Those values have measure zero: on the open set $|f'|<\delta $, disjoint intervals cover the compact critical set, and their image lengths total at most $\delta $ times the total domain length; then let $\delta \to 0$. Use countably many such curve neighborhoods. On the remaining critical set both first and second derivatives vanish. In a compact coordinate rectangle with bounded third derivatives, a square of side $r$ meeting that set has image of that set in an interval of length at most $Cr^3$, by Taylor's formula at a point of the set in the square. At most $C'r^{-2}$ squares are needed. Letting $r\to 0$ gives measure zero there too. Countable compact subrectangles and target coordinate intervals prove the assertion also for a smooth map to $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$. Every class of $H^1(X,\underline{\mathbb Z})$ is the connecting class of a smooth circle-valued function $f$. Indeed the exact sequence $0\to \underline{\mathbb Z}\to \mathcal A_{\mathbb R} \xrightarrow {\exp (2\pi \mathrm i\, \cdot )}\mathcal T\to 1$ has acyclic additive middle sheaf. Locally write $f=\exp (2\pi \mathrm i t_ i)$. Its real de Rham image is $\beta =dt_ i=f^*(dt)$, by the same connecting/sign calculation as in theorem 10.79.2 . Choose a regular value of $f$. Its fiber $C$ is a compact oriented one-manifold, hence a finite union of circles. Orient it by requiring $dt$ followed by its orientation to give the orientation of $X$. On a small band of regular values, the vector field $\nabla t/|dt|^2$ gives a product $C\times (-\delta ,\delta )$: its flow changes $t$ at unit rate, and compactness of a slightly larger closed band ensures existence for these short times. Choose a one-form $\chi (t)dt$ of integral one supported in that band. On the circle it differs from $dt$ by an exact form, since the integral of the difference is zero and its primitive is periodic. Thus $\beta $ is cohomologous to $f^*(\chi (t)dt)$. For any closed one-form $u$, Stokes on the intervening cylinders makes $\int _{C_ t}u$ independent of $t$. Fubini in the product band therefore gives 853E7016EF11 10.79.12 \begin{equation}  \int _ X\beta \wedge u=\int _ Cu. \end{equation} An empty regular fiber gives zero and causes no exception. For a holomorphic $u$, the $(1,0)$ part of $\beta $ wedges with $u$ to zero. Hence $\mathcal S$ of its $(0,1)$ class is minus the period along $C$, which lies in $\Gamma _ X$. Joining the components to a base point changes no closed-form integral. This proves $\mathcal S\Lambda _ X\subset \Gamma _ X$. Conversely any piecewise smooth loop on an oriented surface splits, after small homotopies in coordinate disks, into finitely many embedded oriented circles: choose finitely many coordinate arcs in transverse position, split at their finitely many double crossings and round the corners. The general coordinate-arc construction in the proof of lemma 10.77.6 justifies these operations; it precedes and does not use that lemma's cohomology hypothesis. Local primitives preserve all closed-form periods. An embedded circle has a two-sided collar, with normal coordinate $t$. The closed form $\beta =\chi (t)dt$, of normal integral one, extends smoothly by zero off the collar. Its periods on all loops are integers: put a loop in transverse position to the collar center and use on the complement of the center the primitives obtained by integrating from the two outer ends. A crossing contributes its sign, and all other increments cancel. The integral-period characterization in theorem 10.79.2 puts its class in $H^1(X,\underline{\mathbb Z})$. Orient the normal coordinate so that $dt$ followed by the given circle orientation is positive. As in ( 10.79.12 ), $\int _ X\beta \wedge u=\int _ Cu$; using $-\beta $ under $\mathcal S$ realizes the positive period of $C$. Summing over the split loop proves $\Gamma _ X\subset \mathcal S\Lambda _ X$. It remains to check the integral torsion assertion, rather than assume it from an integral duality theorem. The constant coefficient sequence $0\to \mathbb Z\to \mathbb R\to \mathbb R/\mathbb Z\to 0$ gives \[  H^1(X,\underline{\mathbb R})\to H^1(X,\underline{\mathbb R/\mathbb Z})\to H^2(X,\underline{\mathbb Z})\to H^2(X,\underline{\mathbb R}).  \] The last arrow is injective by lemma 10.79.7 , so the first arrow is onto. By the coefficient/monodromy theorem this means that every character of $G=\pi _1(X)_{\rm ab}$ into $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ lifts to a real character. If the finite torsion subgroup $T$ of $G=\mathbb Z^{2g}\oplus T$ were nonzero, it would have a nonzero character into $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$: quotient by a maximal proper subgroup gives a cyclic group of prime order, and embed that group as the corresponding roots of unity. Extend the character by zero on the free summand. No real character can lift it, since real characters kill torsion. Thus $T=0$. Finally a loop's integration current is closed and has real de Rham class represented by the sum of its collar forms $\beta $ above. Indeed their integrals against every closed one-form coincide; corollary 10.43.11 and the perfect de Rham Hodge pairing of corollary 10.46.10 identify these classes. Its restriction to real forms is perfect: the real Laplacian commutes with conjugation and a real harmonic form pairs with its real Hodge star to give its positive squared norm. This gives a well-defined integral class: integer $H^1$ injects into real $H^1$, so it is independent of the chosen splitting or collars. Under $\mathcal S$ it maps to minus the loop's period. The period map is an isomorphism from $G$ onto $\Gamma _ X$, by the evaluation theorem and $T=0$. The equality of lattices just proved makes the loop-current map an isomorphism onto $H^1(X,\underline{\mathbb Z})$. It is natural under orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms, by the integration-current characterization. Through isothermal coordinates the conclusion applies to every connected compact oriented smooth real surface by theorem 10.77.1 , not just one with a previously chosen complex atlas. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.79.13
section: 10.79 Integral periods, Picard tori and Albanese maps
text: Theorem 10.79.13 . 06A0A5883E2F For a connected compact curve the map $\mathcal S$ induces an isomorphism $J(X)\cong A(X)$ of complex tori, and under it \[  \Phi _ a(x)=\mathcal O_ X([x]-[a])=\alpha _ a(x).  \] If $g\geq 1$, this is an embedding and the global holomorphic one-forms do not all vanish at any point. If $g=1$, it is a biholomorphism onto $J(X)$, so $X$ is a complex torus of dimension one. If $g=0$, $X$ is biholomorphic to $\mathbb P^1$. Proof. The equality of the two full lattices in the preceding lemma gives the torus isomorphism. We compute the map with all signs fixed. In ( 10.79.9 ), $\partial _ t c_ t=1/(2\pi \mathrm i(z-t))$. For $u=U(z)\, dz$, ( 10.79.10 ) gives \[  \partial _ t\mathcal S([\eta _ t])(u) =-\frac1{2\pi \mathrm i} \int \frac{\bar\partial \chi }{z-t}\wedge U(z)\, dz =U(t).  \] The last equality is ordinary Stokes on the punctured disk: the outer boundary is zero because $\chi $ has compact support, and the inner boundary has negative orientation, so $\int \bar\partial \chi \wedge U(z)dz/(z-t)=-2\pi \mathrm iU(t)$ by Cauchy's formula. Thus there is no identification of a scalar distribution with a wrongly graded current. At $t=0$ the class is zero, so $\mathcal S([\eta _ t])(u)=\int _0^ t u$. The same calculation near every point, translated by its fixed base-point value, gives identical differentials for $\Phi _ a$ and $\alpha _ a$. Their difference is locally constant and vanishes at $a$, proving the global equality. We use the simple-pole criterion in an explicit form. A meromorphic function with just one simple pole defines a biholomorphism to $\mathbb P^1$: for every finite $c$, Poincaré–Lelong and Stokes give total zero order one for $f-c$, so every fiber is one simple point, including the pole over infinity. The local holomorphic inverse theorem finishes. On $\mathbb P^1$, a holomorphic one-form is $F(z)dz$ with $F$ entire and $F(z)=O(|z|^{-2})$ at infinity; Cauchy's estimate makes $F=0$. Hence its genus is zero by Serre. Conversely if $g=0$, the prescribed-point principal-part lemma for $E=\mathcal O_ X$, $m=1$ supplies such a simple pole. These arguments also give the complete equivalence between genus zero, one simple pole and $X\cong \mathbb P^1$. Suppose now $g\geq 1$. If $\Phi _ a(x)=\Phi _ a(y)$ with $x\ne y$, the line $\mathcal O_ X([x]-[y])$ is trivial. The exact sequence theorem 10.78.5 supplies a meromorphic function with divisor $[x]-[y]$. The simple-pole criterion would make the genus zero, a contradiction. This proves injectivity. There is likewise no nonconstant function with only a simple pole at any $x$, so $h^0(\mathcal O_ X([x]))=1$. The formula in corollary 10.78.11 gives $h^0(K_ X(-[x]))=g-1<h^0(K_ X)=g$. Some holomorphic one-form is nonzero at $x$. The differential formula for $\alpha _ a$ therefore makes its one-dimensional complex differential injective. Locally a target coordinate with nonzero derivative gives a graph by the inverse function theorem, so this is an immersion. Compactness and injectivity make it a homeomorphism onto its image, hence an embedding. If $g=1$, target and source have dimension one, so its image is open as well as compact and closed in the connected torus. It is the whole torus, with holomorphic inverse locally and globally. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.79.14
section: 10.79 Integral periods, Picard tori and Albanese maps
text: Corollary 10.79.14 . 7DB1B17F312B For $n\geq 1$, every holomorphic line bundle on $\mathbb P^ n$ is uniquely $\mathcal O(k)$ for an integer $k$. Moreover $H^2(\mathbb P^ n,\underline{\mathbb Z})\cong \mathbb Z$ with generator $c_1^{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal O(1))$, positive under the curvature comparison $\Psi _2^{-1}$. For $n=0$ both the Picard group and this cohomology group are zero. Proof. We first verify simple connectivity without an integral cell calculation. The map $S^{2n+1}\to \mathbb P^ n$ taking a unit vector to its complex line has local sections in each affine chart, obtained by normalizing the vector whose chosen coordinate is one. Thus paths lift by subdividing into those charts. A lifted loop has endpoints differing by a phase $e^{\mathrm i\theta }$; multiplying its lift by $e^{-\mathrm i t\theta }$ closes it without changing its projection. Loops can be replaced by finitely many smooth coordinate arcs, via fixed-endpoint homotopies in convex charts. Every piecewise smooth loop in $S^ m$, $m\geq 2$, misses a point: subdividing its parameter into intervals of length $1/N$ covers its image by $O(N)$ coordinate balls of radius $C/N$, whose total $m$-dimensional volume tends to zero. A flat unitary line connection has local parallel unit frames: its imaginary connection form is closed, so is locally $\mathrm i\, d\varphi $ by the real Poincaré lemma; multiplication by $e^{-\mathrm i\varphi }$ makes the connection zero. Transition functions between these frames are constant. Continuing a frame along paths is homotopy independent by subdividing a homotopy square into these flat charts. Simple connectivity gives a global parallel frame. For the Chern connection its $(0,1)$ part is the holomorphic $\bar\partial $ operator, so that frame is holomorphic. Consequently $F$ is trivial and $L\cong \mathcal O(k)$; uniqueness follows by restriction and degree. Finally the projective Hodge computation and sheaf comparison give $H^1(\mathcal O)=H^2(\mathcal O)=0$. The exponential sequence makes $c_1^{\mathbb Z}$ an isomorphism from this Picard group onto $H^2(\underline{\mathbb Z})$, with the stated generator and real sign. A point has only a trivial line and acyclic constant sheaves, giving the last assertion. $\square$

section: 9.43 Coherent products and nuclear analytic modules
text: Analytic spaces are Hausdorff and have countable bases, and may be nonreduced. Their coherent section spaces carry the intrinsic nuclear Fréchet topologies of theorem 9.51.5 , corollary 9.51.6 . Every tensor without a subscript is the completed projective tensor over $\mathbb C$; on nuclear Fréchet spaces it also has the injective topology. Algebraic cokernels below mean quotients by the actual image, not its closure. Proposition 9.43.1 . BDBDC4F6CABA Analytic products and coherent external products exist in the nonreduced category. External product is right exact in each coherent variable. For coherent $\mathcal F,\mathcal G$ on $X,Y$ there is a natural topological isomorphism \[  \mathcal F(X)\widehat\otimes \mathcal G(Y) \simeq (\mathcal F\boxtimes \mathcal G)(X\times Y).  \] All local presentation and acyclic-rectangle hypotheses of proposition 9.42.2 , corollary 9.42.4 are satisfied by the analytic category, using countable strict-PSH presentation patches. Proof. In local embeddings $X\subset D\subset \mathbb C^ n$ and $Y\subset D'\subset \mathbb C^ m$, with ideals $\mathcal J, \mathcal K$, give the product support its structure \[  \mathcal O_{D\times D'}/ (\mathcal J(z)\mathcal O_{D\times D'}+ \mathcal K(w)\mathcal O_{D\times D'}).  \] These ideals are generated by their local finite generators, so are coherent by Oka and coherent-sheaf algebra. Coordinate changes on either factor extend locally holomorphically to its ambient space and take its defining ideal into the other defining ideal. Taking their products gives compatible changes of these quotient rings. Opposite coordinate changes compose to the identity modulo the defining ideals, so the quotient ringed patches glue. This also proves the product universal property: a pair of analytic maps pulls back convergent germs in $(z,w)$ by substitution, and the two ideals vanish. Uniqueness is local substitution in these coordinates. No ideal is replaced by its radical. For a morphism $p$ define analytic pullback by $p^*\mathcal F=\mathcal O\otimes _{p^{-1}\mathcal O_ X} p^{-1}\mathcal F$, and put $\mathcal F\boxtimes \mathcal G=p_ X^*\mathcal F \otimes _{\mathcal O_{X\times Y}}p_ Y^*\mathcal G$. Ordinary module tensor product is right exact: a presentation of a quotient gives precisely the quotient of the tensor by the images of its relations, as follows directly from bilinear balanced maps. Apply this on each stalk. A finite local presentation pulls back to the same finite matrix with pulled-back entries, so its cokernel is coherent by Oka. Tensoring two finite presentations gives a finite presentation with the relations from both matrices; this also proves coherence of the external product and right exactness in either variable. No assertion of left exactness or flatness is used. Choose small polydiscs on which the ambient direct images of the coherent sheaves have finite presentations $\mathcal O_ D^ r\to \mathcal O_ D^ s\to i_*\mathcal F\to 0$, and similarly on $D'$. Their product presentations are the same finite matrices in $z$, and then in $w$, on $D\times D'$. Their coherent relation kernels have zero first cohomology there by theorem 9.51.13 , since the sum of strict-PSH polydisc exhaustions is a strict-PSH exhaustion. Consequently these presentations remain right exact on sections, with their actual closed quotient kernels and open section surjections. A closed embedding does not change sections or their intrinsic topology, by the checked closed-embedding comparison. These are exactly the previously explicit analytic presentation hypotheses; the complete quotient/tensor/gluing proof of proposition 9.42.2 therefore gives the displayed natural isomorphism, first locally and then by countable overlap-refined gluing. It applies on arbitrary $X,Y$, without global finite presentations. Finite products of strict-PSH spaces have strict-PSH exhaustions by summing nonnegative exhaustions. Their analytic closed subspaces inherit such exhaustions, and finite intersections of the chosen patches do so as in the coherent-section theorem. Thus the required product rectangles are acyclic for every coherent external product, by the already proved coherent vanishing theorem. This verifies the remaining acyclic-cover hypotheses of the completed cohomology comparison without assuming that cohomology commutes with tensor completion. $\square$ Proposition 9.43.2 . 3D82D215FD97 For a continuous map $p:X\to Y$ and a sheaf $\mathcal S$ of complex vector spaces, $R^ qp_*\mathcal S$ is the sheafification of $U\mapsto H^ q(p^{-1}U,\mathcal S)$, when both are defined by the checked Godement/flabby resolution. In particular the relative tensor conclusions of corollary 9.42.5 hold on a basis of strict-PSH analytic spaces, with the precise Hausdorff or finite-dimensional cohomology hypotheses stated there. Proof. Let $\mathcal I^\bullet $ be the Godement resolution. Its restriction to every $p^{-1}U$ is a flabby resolution, so $H^ q(p^{-1}U,\mathcal S)$ is the cohomology of $\mathcal I^\bullet (p^{-1}U)$. At $y\in Y$ the stalk of $p_*\mathcal I^ j$ is the filtered limit of these sections as $U$ shrinks to $y$. Filtered limits of vector spaces are exact: a kernel equality, a lift, or a vanishing class is witnessed at one sufficiently small common index for the finitely many elements involved. They therefore commute with kernels, images and cohomology. The stalk of the cohomology sheaf is consequently $\varinjlim _{U\ni y}H^ q(p^{-1}U,\mathcal S)$, which is exactly the stalk of the asserted sheafification. The maps are natural under restriction, proving the sheaf identity. The preceding proposition, coherent vanishing on strict-PSH rectangles, and this identification verify all the analytic inputs in the cited relative argument. This conclusion does not identify a stalkwise analytic fibre with a completed section tensor or impose an unstated flatness hypothesis. $\square$ Lemma 9.43.3 . CE08E5D64C0A The section algebra $\mathcal O(X)$ is a unital commutative nuclear Fréchet algebra; $\mathcal F(X)$ is a nuclear Fréchet module with jointly continuous multiplication. Restriction $\mathcal F(U)\to \mathcal F(U')$ for $U'\Subset U$ is a complex-nuclear map. Proof. On a distinguished ambient patch the action is induced by multiplication on finite free holomorphic sections. The surjective presentation maps are open, so their product map is an open quotient; the continuous bilinear action descends. Countable local gluing then proves joint continuity on every open, since each target seminorm depends on finitely many local seminorms. Nuclearity is already proved. For the last assertion, compact coherent restriction maps one neighborhood into a bounded set. If a continuous map $u:E\to F$ between Fréchet spaces has this property, take a continuous source seminorm $p$ whose unit ball maps to a bounded set. For every target seminorm $q$ one has $q(ux)\leq C_ qp(x)$; scaling and the $p(x)=0$ case prove this inequality for all $x$. Hence $u$ factors through the Banach completion $E_ p$, since $F$ is complete. For nuclear $E$ such a factorization is nuclear by the Banach-link criterion proved with theorem 2.13.3 . Apply it to the compact restriction from the coherent-section theorem. $\square$

title: 9.44 Balanced tensors and the standard resolution

section: 9.44 Balanced tensors and the standard resolution
text: Let $A$ be a unital commutative nuclear Fréchet algebra. An $A$-module means a nuclear Fréchet space with a jointly continuous unital action. The completed balanced tensor is 095A4D1A198E 9.44.1 \begin{equation}  E\widehat\otimes _ A F= (E\widehat\otimes F)/\operatorname {im}\delta _ A, \quad \delta _ A(x\otimes a\otimes y)=ax\otimes y-x\otimes ay, \end{equation} with its quotient topology. It need not be Hausdorff. If it is Hausdorff, its relation image is closed and the quotient is nuclear Fréchet. We never complete or Hausdorffize this quotient unless this has been proved. Continuous module maps induce quotient maps because they carry the actual completed relation image into the corresponding relation image. A nuclearly free module is $A\widehat\otimes V$ for a nuclear Fréchet space $V$, with action on the first factor. Proposition 9.44.2 . 32299AAD67C6 Every nuclear $A$-module $F$ has a nuclearly free resolution $L_ q=A^{\widehat\otimes (q+1)}\widehat\otimes F$, $q\geq 0$, with augmentation $d_0(a\otimes y)=ay$ and \[  d_ q(a_0\otimes \cdots \otimes a_ q\otimes y) =\sum _{i<q}(-1)^ i a_0\otimes \cdots \otimes a_ i a_{i+1}\otimes \cdots \otimes a_ q\otimes y +(-1)^ q a_0\otimes \cdots \otimes a_{q-1}\otimes a_ qy.  \] It is split exact as a complex of topological vector spaces, with no requirement that its splitting be $A$-linear. Moreover \[  (A\widehat\otimes V)\widehat\otimes _ A F \simeq V\widehat\otimes F  \] topologically; in particular this balanced tensor is Hausdorff. Proof. All displayed maps extend continuously to the completions by joint continuity of multiplication/action and the projective tensor universal property. Adjacent multiplication terms cancel in pairs in $d_{q-1}d_ q$, including the last action terms by associativity. Inserting a first factor1, $h_ q(t)=1\otimes t$ and $h_{-1}(y)=1\otimes y$, gives $d_{q+1}h_ q+h_{q-1}d_ q=I$. The first term removes the inserted1; all other terms cancel with the second summand. These identities hold on the full completions by continuity into Hausdorff spaces and density of algebraic tensors. Thus the image in each degree is the closed kernel of the next map, and $d_{q+1}h_ q$ is a continuous projection onto that kernel. This proves the asserted direct splitting. Flip the first two free factors and consider $m:V\widehat\otimes A\widehat\otimes F\to V\widehat\otimes F$, $m(v\otimes a\otimes y)=v\otimes ay$, with section $i(v\otimes y)=v\otimes 1\otimes y$. The continuous map $s(v\otimes a\otimes y)= v\otimes 1\otimes a\otimes y$ satisfies $\delta _ As=I-im$, while $m\delta _ A=0$. Hence the relation image is exactly the closed kernel of $m$, not merely dense in it. The split quotient gives the asserted homeomorphism. This free-factor argument also works for a continuous homomorphism from $A$ into any unital Fréchet algebra $B$: $B\widehat\otimes _ A(A\widehat\otimes V) \simeq B\widehat\otimes V$, without nuclearity of $B$. $\square$ Theorem 9.44.3 . C8C2118EE2C8 Define $\widehat{\operatorname {Tor}}^ A_ q(E,F)$ as the homology of the Fréchet complex \[  C_ q(E,F)=E\widehat\otimes A^{\widehat\otimes q} \widehat\otimes F,  \] with differential \[  \begin{aligned} & d_ q(x\otimes a_1\otimes \cdots \otimes a_ q\otimes y)\\ & \quad =a_1x\otimes a_2\otimes \cdots \otimes a_ q\otimes y\\ & \qquad +\sum _{1\leq i<q}(-1)^ i x\otimes \cdots \otimes a_ i a_{i+1}\otimes \cdots \otimes y\\ & \qquad +(-1)^ q x\otimes a_1\otimes \cdots \otimes a_{q-1}\otimes a_ qy. \end{aligned}  \] Its degree-zero homology is the actual balanced tensor above. These topological homology spaces are symmetric in $E,F$, vanish in positive degrees if either factor is nuclearly free, and have a continuous algebraically exact long sequence for every short exact sequence of nuclear modules. For every nuclearly free resolution $P_\bullet \to F$, not necessarily split, there is a canonical topological isomorphism \[  \widehat{\operatorname {Tor}}^ A_ q(E,F) \simeq H_ q(E\widehat\otimes _ A P_\bullet ).  \] No Hausdorffness of these homology quotients is assumed. Proof. The free-factor identification applied to the standard resolution is precisely the displayed complex, and $d_1$ is $\delta _ A$. Symmetry is the continuous reversal \[  x\otimes a_1\otimes \cdots \otimes a_ q\otimes y \longmapsto (-1)^{q(q+1)/2} y\otimes a_ q\otimes \cdots \otimes a_1\otimes x.  \] Reversal interchanges the $i$th and $(q-i)$th boundary terms, whose signs differ by $(-1)^ q$; the displayed prefactors make this a chain isomorphism in all degrees. For a free factor the complex is a tensor of the split standard resolution with its nuclear free vector-space factor; tensor its explicit contracting homotopy. This proves positive-degree vanishing and the degree-zero formula. A short exact sequence of nuclear Fréchet modules is strict by open mapping and its closed kernel. Ordinary tensor with the fixed nuclear factors $A^{\widehat\otimes q} \widehat\otimes F$ preserves strict exactness by theorem 2.13.5 . We obtain a degreewise strict short exact sequence of Fréchet complexes. The ordinary cycle-lifting proof gives the algebraic long homology sequence. Its connecting maps are continuous by the closed-cycle-preimage/open-lift construction of section 9.41 , with homological indices reversed. Symmetry gives the long sequence in the second variable as well. For resolution independence take the first-quadrant homological array $C_{p,q}=E\widehat\otimes A^{\widehat\otimes p} \widehat\otimes P_ q$, with bar differential in $p$ and $(-1)^ p$ times the resolution differential in $q$. The augmentations in $q$ are exact because the resolution is exact with closed images and the other tensor factors are nuclear. The augmentations in $p$ are exact in positive degrees since each $P_ q$ is nuclearly free; their degree-zero terms are $E\widehat\otimes _ A P_ q$, themselves Hausdorff Fréchet by the free-factor formula. Finite-diagonal comparison therefore gives continuous cohomology bijections from this total complex to both $C_\bullet (E,F)$ and $E\widehat\otimes _ A P_\bullet $. Explicitly, a cycle in an augmented total is reduced by lifting its outermost nonzero component in the exact augmented row or column and subtracting a boundary; successive components run through the finitely many positions on that total diagonal. The same procedure proves injectivity for a total boundary. This is the actual finite-comparison argument of lemma 10.43.15 , with arrows reversed. Its finite diagonals are unchanged. Both induced bijections are topological by cohomological openness for Fréchet complexes. Their augmentations are natural, so the resulting isomorphism is canonical and natural for resolution maps; no projectivity or unproved continuous module lifting theorem is needed. $\square$

title: 9.45 Transversality and analytic restriction
text: Two nuclear $A$-modules are transverse if their balanced tensor is Hausdorff and their positive Tor groups vanish. Theorem 9.45.1 . ED1150490F04 The following assertions hold with actual quotient topologies. In a short exact sequence $0\to E_1\to E_2\to E_3\to 0$, if $E_2,E_3$ are transverse to $M$, so is $E_1$, and $0\to M\widehat\otimes _ A E_1\to M\widehat\otimes _ A E_2 \to M\widehat\otimes _ A E_3\to 0$ is strictly exact. Let $A\to B\to C$ be continuous unital homomorphisms of nuclear Fréchet algebras. If $B$ is transverse to $E$ over $A$, then \[  \widehat{\operatorname {Tor}}^ B_ q (C,B\widehat\otimes _ A E) \simeq \widehat{\operatorname {Tor}}^ A_ q(C,E).  \] If $C$ is also transverse to $E$ over $A$, then $C$ is transverse to $B\widehat\otimes _ A E$ over $B$. Let $E^\bullet $ be bounded above and consist of modules transverse to $M$. If it is acyclic in degrees at least $k$, then $M\widehat\otimes _ A E^\bullet $ is acyclic there. If $f:E^\bullet \to F^\bullet $ is a map of bounded-above complexes whose terms are transverse to $M$, and $H^ j(f)$ is bijective for $j\geq k$ and onto for $j=k-1$, then $H^ j(M\widehat\otimes _ A f)$ has the same properties. Proof. The Tor long sequence proves positive-degree vanishing for $E_1$ and an exact sequence of the three balanced tensors. The first balanced tensor continuously injects into the Hausdorff middle one, so is Hausdorff. It is consequently a nuclear Fréchet quotient, and its image is the closed kernel of the last map. Open mapping gives the asserted strictness. This proves(1). We spell out the balanced associativity needed for(2). If $H=B\widehat\otimes _ A E$ is Hausdorff, then E40E41A27BB9 9.45.2 \begin{equation}  C\widehat\otimes _ B H\simeq C\widehat\otimes _ A E \end{equation} as actual quotient spaces, whether or not the two final quotients are Hausdorff. In fact $B\widehat\otimes E\to H$ is strict with closed kernel equal to the image of the completed relation map. Tensor it with $C$ using strict ordinary nuclear exactness. Its kernel is exactly the image of the tensor of that relation map: factor the original map through its closed image and use ordinary tensor surjectivity. The free-factor collapse $C\widehat\otimes _ B(B\widehat\otimes E) \simeq C\widehat\otimes E$ is the explicit unit-insertion identity proved above. Under that collapse the additional $A$-relations become precisely $ca\otimes x-c\otimes ax$. Thus successive quotients are quotients by the same actual linear image sum, with the same quotient topology. This proves the formula without an inference from separated continuous functionals on a non-Hausdorff quotient. Take a nuclearly free resolution $P_\bullet \to E$ over $A$. By transversality and the proved resolution computation, $B\widehat\otimes _ A P_\bullet \to H$ is an exact nuclearly free resolution over $B$, all terms and $H$ being Fréchet. Apply the resolution theorem over $B$. Term by term its tensor with $C$ is the tensor of $P_\bullet $ with $C$ over $A$, by the free-factor formula. The differentials agree on dense elementary tensors. Resolution computation over $A$ gives(2), including degree zero and Hausdorffness when $C$ is transverse to $E$. For(3), write $Z^ j=\ker d^ j$. Starting above the last nonzero term, use the strict exact sequences $0\to Z^ j\to E^ j\to Z^{j+1}\to 0$ for $j\geq k-1$. They are exact because acyclicity is known at degree $j+1$, and closedness follows from the next differential's kernel. Backward induction and(1) show that every $Z^ j$ in this range is transverse to $M$, and that their balanced-tensored short sequences are exact. They identify boundaries and cycles in degrees $j\geq k$, proving(3). The exact sequence $0\to F[-1]\to C(f)\to E\to 0$ has connecting map $+H(f)$, as the lift $(x,0)$ has second differential component $fx$. Consequently $H^ j(C(f))=0$ exactly when $H^ j(f)$ is injective and $H^{j-1}(f)$ is onto. Finite sums preserve transversality, as the bar complex and actual balanced quotient split accordingly. Thus(3) makes the balanced tensor of this cone acyclic in degrees at least $k$. Balanced tensor commutes with finite sums, so that complex is the same corrected cone of the tensor map. In particular the plus/minus signs in the cone, its shifted differential and its connecting map are checked together. $\square$ Proposition 9.45.4 . 8308DB03978F Let $X,Y$ have smooth strict-PSH exhaustions. Let $U'\subset U\Subset X$ and $V\Subset Y$ be open sets which themselves have such exhaustions. If $\mathcal F$ is coherent on $X\times Y$, then $\mathcal O(U')$ and $\mathcal F(U\times V)$ are transverse over $\mathcal O(U)$, and naturally \[  \mathcal O(U')\widehat\otimes _{\mathcal O(U)} \mathcal F(U\times V)\simeq \mathcal F(U'\times V).  \] The isomorphism is topological; it is analytic restriction, not a claim about arbitrary fibres or arbitrary algebra maps. Proof. The product $X\times Y$ has a strict-PSH exhaustion. The proved global-generation consequence of coherent vanishing supplies finitely many global sections generating $\mathcal F$ near each point. Finitely many such families cover the compact $\overline U\times \overline V$, giving a finite global free map onto $\mathcal F$ on a neighborhood of this compact set. Its coherent kernel is defined on all of $X\times Y$ even where the map need not be onto. Apply the same argument to that kernel, and repeat. This produces a free resolution on $U\times V$ of arbitrary infinite length with finite rank in every degree: no common shrinking is required because at every step global sections generate on the same fixed compact set. The restriction to $U'\times V$ remains exact. All coherent relation kernels on these two domains have vanishing first cohomology, so both section sequences are exact with closed images. Each free section term on $U\times V$ is a finite sum of $\mathcal O(U)\widehat\otimes \mathcal O(V)$ by the external-product theorem, hence is nuclearly free over $\mathcal O(U)$. Its balanced tensor with $\mathcal O(U')$ is the corresponding free section term on $U'\times V$. The matrices and augmentation become their restrictions; this equality follows on elementary sections and extends by continuity into the Hausdorff free spaces. Resolution computation of Tor now gives zero in positive degrees and in degree zero the quotient $\mathcal F(U'\times V)$, with its actual Fréchet section topology. In particular the balanced tensor is Hausdorff, proving transversality. $\square$
