title: 9.46 Relative nuclearity and perturbation
text: For Fréchet modules over any unital Fréchet algebra $A$, a map is $A$-nuclear if it has a series \[  u(x)=\sum _ j\lambda _ j\xi _ j(x)y_ j,\qquad \sum _ j|\lambda _ j|<\infty ,  \] where the $A$-linear maps $\xi _ j:E\to A$ form an equicontinuous family and $(y_ j)$ is bounded. It is $A$-subnuclear if it becomes $A$-nuclear after a continuous open module surjection from a Fréchet module; if the source is nuclear this covering module is required nuclear. These definitions do not require a Banach algebra to be nuclear as a complex vector space. Proposition 9.46.1 . 4BBFDD591C1E Within nuclear Fréchet modules, relative nuclear and subnuclear maps are preserved by continuous module precomposition and postcomposition. If $v:V\to W$ is complex-nuclear, then $I_ A\widehat\otimes v:A\widehat\otimes V\to A\widehat\otimes W$ is $A$-nuclear. In the analytic setting of the preceding proposition, restriction $\mathcal F(S\times U)\to \mathcal F(S\times U')$ is $\mathcal O(S)$-subnuclear when $S\Subset X$ and $U'\Subset U\Subset Y$ are strict-PSH open sets. For the structure sheaf it is $\mathcal O(S)$-nuclear. Moreover let $A,B$ be nuclear Fréchet algebras, $\rho :A\to B$ a complex-nuclear homomorphism, $E,F$ nuclear $A$-modules and $F_1\subset F$ a closed $A$-submodule. Suppose $B$ is transverse over $A$ to $E,F,F/F_1$. If $u:E\to F$ is $A$-subnuclear with image in $F_1$, then the induced map $B\widehat\otimes _ A E\to B\widehat\otimes _ A F_1$ is $B$-subnuclear. Proof. Postcomposition sends the bounded vectors to bounded vectors; precomposition sends the coefficient family to an equicontinuous family. For subnuclear precomposition along $v:S\to E$, pull the chosen open cover $M\to E$ back to $S$. The closed pullback in $S\times M$ is Fréchet, maps onto $S$ openly, and is nuclear if $S,M$ are nuclear. The lifted map is a restriction of a nuclear composition. Finite direct sums use the direct sums of the covering modules and the concatenated finite list of summable series; coefficient maps project to their source summand. This proves the ideal and finite-direct-sum assertions. For the tensor assertion extend the coefficients $\eta _ j:V\to \mathbb C$ of a nuclear series to $I_ A\widehat\otimes \eta _ j$ with target $A$, and take vectors $1\otimes w_ j$. Their equicontinuity follows from the projective seminorm bounds and their boundedness from continuity of tensor insertion. Compact coherent restrictions are complex-nuclear by lemma 9.43.3 . The structure sheaf formula follows by the external-product isomorphism. For $\mathcal F$ choose finitely many global generators near the compact $\overline S\times \overline U$ exactly as above. Coherent vanishing on $S\times U$ makes the free section map onto $\mathcal F(S\times U)$ an open surjection. In the restriction square the free vertical map is $\mathcal O(S)$-nuclear and the lower quotient map is continuous. This is the required subnuclear covering. For the last assertion write first $u$ as $A$-nuclear and $\rho (a)=\sum _ k\mu _ k\eta _ k(a)b_ k$ complex-nuclear. The map $E\to B\widehat\otimes _ A F$, $x\mapsto 1\otimes u(x)$, is complex-nuclear, with the actual series \[  \sum _{j,k}\lambda _ j\mu _ k (\eta _ k\circ \xi _ j)(x)[b_ k\otimes y_ j].  \] The scalar coefficients form an equicontinuous family and the bracketed vectors a bounded family. Absolute convergence in every target seminorm proves the equality by the balanced relation. By transversality and(1) of the preceding calculus theorem, $B\widehat\otimes _ A F_1$ is a closed subspace of $B\widehat\otimes _ A F$. Nuclear maps from nuclear Fréchet sources remain nuclear when their range is regarded in a closed target subspace, by the proved Banach-factor range criterion of theorem 2.13.3 . If $u$ was only subnuclear, do this on its nuclear covering module and descend through the closed kernel using the same Banach-factor quotient criterion. Thus $j:E\to B\widehat\otimes _ A F_1$, $j(x)=1\otimes u(x)$, is complex-nuclear in either case. The map $I_ B\widehat\otimes j$ is then $B$-nuclear. Compose with the action $B\widehat\otimes (B\widehat\otimes _ A F_1) \to B\widehat\otimes _ A F_1$. It factors through the open surjection $B\widehat\otimes E\to B\widehat\otimes _ A E$ and gives the required base-changed map. The covering space $B\widehat\otimes E$ is nuclear, as required. $\square$ Lemma 9.46.2 . 627F10C620CF Let $A\to B$ be a homomorphism of nuclear Fréchet algebras and let $B$ be transverse to the nuclear modules $E,F$. An $A$-subnuclear $u:E\to F$ induces a $B$-subnuclear map $u_ B:E_ B\to F_ B$, where $E_ B=B\widehat\otimes _ A E$. It can be tested on a nuclearly free covering of $E_ B$. Proof. Take the nuclear covering $M\to E$ in the definition and compose it with the action $P=A\widehat\otimes M\to M$. This gives an open surjection $p:P\to E$ with $P$ nuclearly free and $up$ $A$-nuclear. Its closed kernel is transverse to $B$ by the transversality calculus, so $P_ B\to E_ B$ is an open surjection. Write $P=A\widehat\otimes M$. For an equicontinuous family $\xi _ j:P\to A$, the formulas \[  \xi _{j,B}(b\otimes m)=b\rho (\xi _ j(1\otimes m))  \] form an equicontinuous family $B\widehat\otimes M\to B$. Indeed each target seminorm is bounded using continuity of multiplication by one product of a $B$-seminorm and a common $M$-seminorm; the latter comes from equicontinuity of the original family. The bounded vectors of the nuclear series remain bounded under $F\to F_ B$. The same series is thus $B$-nuclear on $P_ B$, and proves the claim. This argument also gives the nuclear series on a free base change to an arbitrary Banach algebra $B$, whenever the target free base change is being used. $\square$ Lemma 9.46.3 . 5C1AB5BDC27C Let $B$ be a unital Banach algebra, $S$ a Fréchet $B$-module and $v:S\to S$ a $B$-nuclear map. Then $\operatorname {coker}(I-v)$ is finitely generated as an algebraic $B$-module. More strongly, for every continuous unital map $B\to C$ to a complete Fréchet algebra, the actual balanced quotient $S_ C=C\widehat\otimes _ B S$ satisfies \[  \operatorname {coker}(I-v_ C)\text{ is finitely generated over }C.  \] Neither cokernel nor $S_ C$ is required Hausdorff in this assertion. Here the unbalanced tensors use the projective topology, and the balanced quotient uses the actual image. Proof. Write $v(x)=\sum _ j\lambda _ j\xi _ j(x)y_ j$. The maps \[  \alpha :S\to \ell ^1(B),\quad \alpha (x)=(\lambda _ j\xi _ j(x))_ j, \qquad \beta :\ell ^1(B)\to S,\quad \beta ((b_ j))=\sum _ jb_ jy_ j  \] are continuous $B$-linear. Equicontinuity bounds $\alpha $ by one source seminorm. For every seminorm $q$ of $S$, joint continuity of its action gives $q(by)\leq K_ q\| b\| r_ q(y)$ for a source seminorm $r_ q$; boundedness of $(y_ j)$ then proves convergence and continuity of $\beta $. We have $v=\beta \alpha $ and $w=\alpha \beta $ is $B$-nuclear on the Banach module $L=\ell ^1(B)$, with coefficient maps $\xi _ j\beta $ and vectors the standard unit vectors $e_ j$. Split $w=w'+w''$ at a large finite index $N$. On the Banach space $L$, equicontinuity of the coefficient maps is a uniform operator norm bound, so $\| w''\| <1$ for large $N$. The Neumann series makes $T=I-w''$ a continuous $B$-linear automorphism with continuous inverse. Write $w'=J\Lambda $, where $J:B^ N\to L$ inserts the first $N$ vectors and $\Lambda :L\to B^ N$ is the finite list of coefficient maps including the $\lambda _ j$. The exact continuous identity 08CCD417EB8B 9.46.4 \begin{equation}  I=(I-w)T^{-1}+J\Lambda T^{-1} \end{equation} proves finite generation of its cokernel. The maps $\alpha ,\beta $ induce inverse algebraic cokernel isomorphisms for $I-v$ and $I-w$: they intertwine the two operators, and their compositions $v,w$ act as the identity modulo the respective actual images. Retain this identity before passing to any cokernel. Every continuous $B$-linear map and each of its inverse identities induces a map on the actual balanced quotient with $C$. The free-factor formula gives $C\widehat\otimes _ B B^ N=C^ N$. Thus the induced identity is \[  I=(I-w_ C)(T^{-1})_ C+J_ C\Lambda _ C(T^{-1})_ C.  \] For precision this equality is not inferred merely by continuity from a dense subset of a non-Hausdorff target. The original operator identity is first tensored as an identity on the Hausdorff unbalanced completion $C\widehat\otimes L$, where it holds by density. The factorization through $C^ N$ then follows from the exact balanced relation: for a continuous $B$-linear coefficient $\ell :L\to B$, the difference between $c\otimes \ell (x)e_ j$ and $c\rho (\ell (x))\otimes e_ j$ is the image of the completed relation map applied to $c\otimes \ell (x)\otimes e_ j$. This formula is an identity of continuous maps before quotienting. Hence the residual summand really has image in the module generated by the finitely many classes $[1\otimes e_ j]$. The induced $\alpha _ C,\beta _ C$ still intertwine and have the same composition identities, giving the cokernel isomorphism with $I-v_ C$. This proves the stronger assertion without tensoring a possibly non-Hausdorff cokernel. $\square$ A fully nuclear algebra is a unital Fréchet algebra $A$ whose topology is defined by increasing multiplicative seminorms $p_ t$, $0<t<1$, with nuclear Banach links $A_{p_{t'}}\to A_{p_ t}$ whenever $t<t'$. A countable cofinal set of indices defines the same topology. Let $A_ t$ be the Hausdorff completion for $\{ p_{\lambda t}:0<\lambda <1\} $, where $0<t\leq 1$; thus $A_1=A$. This is again fully nuclear, $(A_ t)_ s=A_{st}$, and $A_{t'}\to A_ t$ is complex-nuclear for $t<t'$. Indeed choose $t<u<u'<t'$ and factor that map through the nuclear Banach link $A_{p_{u'}}\to A_{p_ u}$; all maps to and from these completions are bounded by their indicated seminorms. A nuclear $A$-module is fully $A$-transverse if it is transverse to every $A_ t$. Put $E_ t=A_ t\widehat\otimes _ A E$. The transversality calculus and the free-resolution associativity show that $E_ t$ is fully $A_ t$-transverse and $(E_ t)_ s=E_{st}$. All these identifications are topological and use a Hausdorff intermediate quotient. Theorem 9.46.5 . 741AFF17E7BD Let $A$ be fully nuclear, $E,F$ fully $A$-transverse nuclear modules, $f:E\to F$ an open surjective module map and $u:E\to F$ $A$-subnuclear. Then for every $t<1$ \[  \operatorname {coker}(f_ t-u_ t) \text{ is a finitely generated algebraic }A_ t\text{-module}.  \] No Hausdorffness of this cokernel is asserted. Proof. Use the preceding free-cover construction to replace the source by a nuclearly free $P=A\widehat\otimes M$, so that $u$ becomes $A$-nuclear and $f$ is still onto. The kernel of the cover is fully transverse by applying (1) of the calculus theorem to every $A_ t$; hence the cover remains onto after each base change. Proving finite generation for the replaced source therefore proves it for the original map. In an $A$-nuclear series for $u$ arrange $y_ j\to 0$. To do so choose $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$ slowly enough that $\sum _ j|\lambda _ j|/\varepsilon _ j<\infty $, replace $y_ j$ by $\varepsilon _ jy_ j$ and $\lambda _ j$ by $\lambda _ j/\varepsilon _ j$. Boundedness of the old vectors proves convergence of the new vectors to zero in every seminorm. Open surjectivity of $f$ gives lifts $x_ j\to 0$ with $f(x_ j)=y_ j$: a decreasing countable zero-neighborhood basis has open images, and successively late terms $y_ j$ can be lifted in successively small such neighborhoods. Then $v(x)=\sum _ j\lambda _ j\xi _ j(x)x_ j$ is an $A$-nuclear endomorphism of $P$ and $u=fv$. The kernel of $f:P\to F$ is fully transverse, so $f_ t$ remains onto. Thus the cokernel of $f_ t-u_ t=f_ t(I-v_ t)$ is an algebraic quotient of that of $I-v_ t$. Fix $t<1$ and let $B=A_{p_ t}$, a Banach algebra. There is a continuous homomorphism $B\to A_ t$ because each $p_{\lambda t}\leq p_ t$. Free base change identifies $P_ B=B\widehat\otimes M$ and makes $v_ B$ $B$-nuclear: its coefficient maps are $b\otimes m\mapsto b\rho (\xi _ j(1\otimes m))$, uniformly bounded by a projective seminorm, and its vectors are the bounded images of $x_ j$. Apply the strengthened Banach perturbation lemma with $C=A_ t$. Its free-factor collapse identifies $A_ t\widehat\otimes _ B(B\widehat\otimes M) =A_ t\widehat\otimes M=P_ t$. Both iterated base changes of $v$ agree on elementary free tensors and hence on this Hausdorff completion. The lemma therefore proves finite generation of $\operatorname {coker}(I-v_ t)$ and then of the desired cokernel. At no point is a non-Hausdorff cokernel placed in the nuclear Fréchet tensor category. $\square$ Proposition 9.46.6 . 06B015B619A5 Let $X$ be a closed analytic subspace of an open $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, with any coherent defining ideal $\mathcal J$, and $D=D(a,R)\Subset \Omega $ a polydisc. Put $U=X\cap D$ and $U_ t=X\cap D(a,tR)$. The quotient seminorms on $A=\mathcal O(U)$ of $p_ t(f)=\sup _{\overline{D(a,tR)}}|f|$ make $A$ fully nuclear, and $A_ t=\mathcal O(U_ t)$ topologically. If $Y$ has a strict-PSH exhaustion, $V\Subset Y$ is a strict-PSH open and $\mathcal F$ is coherent on $X\times Y$, then $\mathcal F(U\times V)$ is fully $A$-transverse and its $t$th base change is $\mathcal F(U_ t\times V)$. Proof. Coherent vanishing gives an open algebra quotient $\mathcal O(D)\to \mathcal O(U)$ with closed kernel $\mathcal J(D)$. Its quotient seminorms are multiplicative: take holomorphic lifts of two classes, multiply them and take the infimum of their norm products. They define its quotient Fréchet topology. For $t<t'$ insert one radius $s$ strictly between them. The two Banach polydisc restriction links at $t'>s>t$ in the direction from larger to smaller radii are nuclear by the explicit polydisc series. After projecting the target to its quotient by the closed ideal image, their composition vanishes on the closed source ideal image. The proved two-Banach-link quotient criterion in theorem 2.13.3 makes the descended map between the two quotient Banach completions nuclear. These completions are precisely those for the quotient seminorms. Thus every indicated link is nuclear. For clarity about the intermediate completions, the restriction $\mathcal J(D)\to \mathcal J(D(a,tR))$ has dense image by the full coherent $1$-Runge theorem: concentric smaller polydiscs are $1$-Runge complete. For a compact $L$ in a smaller polydisc choose $r<s<t$ containing $L$ in the radius-$r$ polydisc. For large $m$, $\sum _ i|(z_ i-a_ i)/R_ i|^{2m}$ is less than $s^{2m}$ on $L$ and its $s^{2m}$-sublevel is inside the radius-$s$ polydisc. Add a sufficiently small positive multiple of a nonnegative strict-PSH exhaustion of $D$. This preserves the strict margin on $L$ and makes that sublevel relatively compact inside the radius-$t$ polydisc. The completion of $\mathcal O(D)$ for the seminorms with indices below $t$ is $\mathcal O(D(a,tR))$ by Taylor density. Its closed ideal is therefore the closure of the image of $\mathcal J(D)$. Taking the quotient commutes with this completion in this specific situation. Indeed each quotient seminorm is the infimum over that ideal; taking its closure does not change the infimum, and the closed quotient is Fréchet complete with the original quotient image dense. This proves the claimed completion identity, including nonreduced ideals and components missed by a smaller sublevel. Choose a slightly larger concentric polydisc $D^+$ with $\overline D\subset D^+\Subset \Omega $; compactness of $\overline D$ inside $\Omega $ permits this enlargement. Then $X\cap D^+$ is a closed analytic subspace of a strict-PSH polydisc and inherits its exhaustion. Restrict $\mathcal F$ to this space times $Y$ and apply proposition 9.45.4 to $U_ t\subset U\Subset X\cap D^+$ for $t<1$. It gives all positive Tor vanishings, Hausdorffness and the claimed section identification. For $t=1$ it is the free identity $A\widehat\otimes _ A E=E$. This is full transversality in the stated nonreduced category. $\square$ Theorem 9.46.7 . 71936EFE5494 Let $A$ be fully nuclear and $E^\bullet ,F^\bullet $ bounded-above complexes of fully $A$-transverse nuclear modules. Suppose a continuous $A$-linear chain map $f:E\to F$ is subnuclear in each degree and induces cohomology isomorphisms in all degrees. For every $t<1$ there is a bounded-above complex $L^\bullet $ of finite-rank free $A_ t$-modules and a continuous chain map $h:L\to E_ t$ inducing all cohomology isomorphisms. No closedness of the original cohomology boundary images is required or asserted. Proof. We first prove a top-degree finite-generation statement. Suppose $E,F$ are acyclic above degree $q$. For every $s<1$, $H^ q(E_ s)\simeq H^ q(F_ s)$ is finitely generated over $A_ s$. To see this choose $s<r<1$. Backward transversality induction shows that $Z^ j(E)$ and $Z^ j(F)$ are fully transverse for $j\geq q$: use the strict sequences $0\to Z^ j\to E^ j\to Z^{j+1}\to 0$, beginning above the last nonzero term. Their base changes identify $(Z^ j)_ r=Z^ j(E_ r)$ and the corresponding $F$ cycles. The quotient $F^ q/Z^ q(F)=Z^{q+1}(F)$ is fully transverse. The map $f^ q$ restricted to $Z^ q(E)$ is subnuclear into $F^ q$ and has image in $Z^ q(F)$. Since $A\to A_ r$ is complex-nuclear, the closed-range relative nuclearity proposition makes its induced map into $Z^ q(F_ r)$ $A_ r$-subnuclear. Base change preserves the quasi-isomorphism by the transversality calculus, applied in every degree. Hence \[  d_ F^{q-1}\oplus f_ r^ q: F_ r^{q-1}\oplus Z^ q(E_ r)\longrightarrow Z^ q(F_ r)  \] is onto. Both source and target are fully $A_ r$-transverse, and $0\oplus f_ r^ q$ is $A_ r$-subnuclear. Apply the perturbation theorem with scale $s/r<1$. The perturbed map is $d_ F^{q-1}\oplus 0$, whose actual cokernel is $H^ q(F_ s)$. This proves the finite-generation statement, including when that cokernel is non-Hausdorff. Choose $N$ with $E^ j=F^ j=0$ for $j>N$, and numbers $t<t_ q<t_{q+1}<1$ for $q\leq N+1$, tending to $t$ as $q\to -\infty $. For example take $t_ q=t+(1-t)2^{q-N-2}$. Start with no free terms in degrees at least $N+1$. Its corrected cone into $E$ is $E[-1]$ and is acyclic in degrees greater than $N+1$. Inductively suppose a finite tail $L^{\geq q}$ and a map into $E_{t_ q}$ have been constructed whose cone $M_ q$ is acyclic in degrees greater than $q$. Form also the cone $N_ q$ of its composite into $F_{t_ q}$. The map $M_ q\to N_ q$ is $I_ L\oplus f_{t_ q}$. Every term is fully $A_{t_ q}$-transverse. Its maps are $A_{t_ q}$-subnuclear: identity on a finite free module is a finite nuclear series, and the remaining summand is subnuclear by the free-cover base-change lemma. It is a quasi-isomorphism, by the natural long exact cone sequences and the quasi-isomorphism of $f_{t_ q}$; the elementary kernel/image chase in these two exact sequences gives injectivity and surjectivity of the middle cohomology map. Thus $N_ q$ too is acyclic above $q$. The just proved statement, applied over $A_{t_ q}$ and shrunk to $t_{q-1}$, makes $H^ q((M_ q)_{t_{q-1}})$ finitely generated. Choose cycle representatives of finitely many module generators, defining a continuous $A_{t_{q-1}}$-linear map \[  (a,b):L^{q-1}\longrightarrow L^ q_{t_{q-1}}\oplus E_{t_{q-1}}^{q-1} =(M_ q)_{t_{q-1}}^ q  \] from a finite free module. Being cycles says exactly $d_ La=0$ and $ha-d_ Eb=0$. Set the new differential $d_ L^{q-1}=a$ and the new chain-map component $h^{q-1}=b$. The new cone has the same cycles and boundaries above $q$; in degree $q$ its boundaries additionally include these representatives, so its cohomology is zero there. It is therefore acyclic above $q-1$, completing induction. Finally base change every constructed finite tail to $A_ t$. The tails agree in their overlapping degrees by construction, and define a bounded-above complex of finite free modules and a chain map $h:L\to E_ t$. Every cone tail stays acyclic in its proved degree range by the transversality calculus, since its terms are fully transverse and $t<t_ q$. For any fixed degree $j$ choose a tail starting below $j-1$. Its cone agrees with the full cone in degrees $j-1,j,j+1$, so the full cone is acyclic in degree $j$. The corrected cone criterion implies $H^ j(h)$ bijective in every degree. Only these finite neighboring degrees were used; no inverse limit of cones, completion of a spectral page, or infinite total diagonal is involved. $\square$

title: Proposition 9.46.1
text: Proposition 9.46.1 . 4BBFDD591C1E Within nuclear Fréchet modules, relative nuclear and subnuclear maps are preserved by continuous module precomposition and postcomposition. If $v:V\to W$ is complex-nuclear, then $I_ A\widehat\otimes v:A\widehat\otimes V\to A\widehat\otimes W$ is $A$-nuclear. In the analytic setting of the preceding proposition, restriction $\mathcal F(S\times U)\to \mathcal F(S\times U')$ is $\mathcal O(S)$-subnuclear when $S\Subset X$ and $U'\Subset U\Subset Y$ are strict-PSH open sets. For the structure sheaf it is $\mathcal O(S)$-nuclear. Moreover let $A,B$ be nuclear Fréchet algebras, $\rho :A\to B$ a complex-nuclear homomorphism, $E,F$ nuclear $A$-modules and $F_1\subset F$ a closed $A$-submodule. Suppose $B$ is transverse over $A$ to $E,F,F/F_1$. If $u:E\to F$ is $A$-subnuclear with image in $F_1$, then the induced map $B\widehat\otimes _ A E\to B\widehat\otimes _ A F_1$ is $B$-subnuclear. Proof. Postcomposition sends the bounded vectors to bounded vectors; precomposition sends the coefficient family to an equicontinuous family. For subnuclear precomposition along $v:S\to E$, pull the chosen open cover $M\to E$ back to $S$. The closed pullback in $S\times M$ is Fréchet, maps onto $S$ openly, and is nuclear if $S,M$ are nuclear. The lifted map is a restriction of a nuclear composition. Finite direct sums use the direct sums of the covering modules and the concatenated finite list of summable series; coefficient maps project to their source summand. This proves the ideal and finite-direct-sum assertions. For the tensor assertion extend the coefficients $\eta _ j:V\to \mathbb C$ of a nuclear series to $I_ A\widehat\otimes \eta _ j$ with target $A$, and take vectors $1\otimes w_ j$. Their equicontinuity follows from the projective seminorm bounds and their boundedness from continuity of tensor insertion. Compact coherent restrictions are complex-nuclear by lemma 9.43.3 . The structure sheaf formula follows by the external-product isomorphism. For $\mathcal F$ choose finitely many global generators near the compact $\overline S\times \overline U$ exactly as above. Coherent vanishing on $S\times U$ makes the free section map onto $\mathcal F(S\times U)$ an open surjection. In the restriction square the free vertical map is $\mathcal O(S)$-nuclear and the lower quotient map is continuous. This is the required subnuclear covering. For the last assertion write first $u$ as $A$-nuclear and $\rho (a)=\sum _ k\mu _ k\eta _ k(a)b_ k$ complex-nuclear. The map $E\to B\widehat\otimes _ A F$, $x\mapsto 1\otimes u(x)$, is complex-nuclear, with the actual series \[  \sum _{j,k}\lambda _ j\mu _ k (\eta _ k\circ \xi _ j)(x)[b_ k\otimes y_ j].  \] The scalar coefficients form an equicontinuous family and the bracketed vectors a bounded family. Absolute convergence in every target seminorm proves the equality by the balanced relation. By transversality and(1) of the preceding calculus theorem, $B\widehat\otimes _ A F_1$ is a closed subspace of $B\widehat\otimes _ A F$. Nuclear maps from nuclear Fréchet sources remain nuclear when their range is regarded in a closed target subspace, by the proved Banach-factor range criterion of theorem 2.13.3 . If $u$ was only subnuclear, do this on its nuclear covering module and descend through the closed kernel using the same Banach-factor quotient criterion. Thus $j:E\to B\widehat\otimes _ A F_1$, $j(x)=1\otimes u(x)$, is complex-nuclear in either case. The map $I_ B\widehat\otimes j$ is then $B$-nuclear. Compose with the action $B\widehat\otimes (B\widehat\otimes _ A F_1) \to B\widehat\otimes _ A F_1$. It factors through the open surjection $B\widehat\otimes E\to B\widehat\otimes _ A E$ and gives the required base-changed map. The covering space $B\widehat\otimes E$ is nuclear, as required. $\square$

title: Lemma 9.46.2
text: Lemma 9.46.2 . 627F10C620CF Let $A\to B$ be a homomorphism of nuclear Fréchet algebras and let $B$ be transverse to the nuclear modules $E,F$. An $A$-subnuclear $u:E\to F$ induces a $B$-subnuclear map $u_ B:E_ B\to F_ B$, where $E_ B=B\widehat\otimes _ A E$. It can be tested on a nuclearly free covering of $E_ B$. Proof. Take the nuclear covering $M\to E$ in the definition and compose it with the action $P=A\widehat\otimes M\to M$. This gives an open surjection $p:P\to E$ with $P$ nuclearly free and $up$ $A$-nuclear. Its closed kernel is transverse to $B$ by the transversality calculus, so $P_ B\to E_ B$ is an open surjection. Write $P=A\widehat\otimes M$. For an equicontinuous family $\xi _ j:P\to A$, the formulas \[  \xi _{j,B}(b\otimes m)=b\rho (\xi _ j(1\otimes m))  \] form an equicontinuous family $B\widehat\otimes M\to B$. Indeed each target seminorm is bounded using continuity of multiplication by one product of a $B$-seminorm and a common $M$-seminorm; the latter comes from equicontinuity of the original family. The bounded vectors of the nuclear series remain bounded under $F\to F_ B$. The same series is thus $B$-nuclear on $P_ B$, and proves the claim. This argument also gives the nuclear series on a free base change to an arbitrary Banach algebra $B$, whenever the target free base change is being used. $\square$

title: Lemma 9.46.3
search_title: Banach module perturbation with base change
text: Lemma 9.46.3 . 5C1AB5BDC27C Let $B$ be a unital Banach algebra, $S$ a Fréchet $B$-module and $v:S\to S$ a $B$-nuclear map. Then $\operatorname {coker}(I-v)$ is finitely generated as an algebraic $B$-module. More strongly, for every continuous unital map $B\to C$ to a complete Fréchet algebra, the actual balanced quotient $S_ C=C\widehat\otimes _ B S$ satisfies \[  \operatorname {coker}(I-v_ C)\text{ is finitely generated over }C.  \] Neither cokernel nor $S_ C$ is required Hausdorff in this assertion. Here the unbalanced tensors use the projective topology, and the balanced quotient uses the actual image. Proof. Write $v(x)=\sum _ j\lambda _ j\xi _ j(x)y_ j$. The maps \[  \alpha :S\to \ell ^1(B),\quad \alpha (x)=(\lambda _ j\xi _ j(x))_ j, \qquad \beta :\ell ^1(B)\to S,\quad \beta ((b_ j))=\sum _ jb_ jy_ j  \] are continuous $B$-linear. Equicontinuity bounds $\alpha $ by one source seminorm. For every seminorm $q$ of $S$, joint continuity of its action gives $q(by)\leq K_ q\| b\| r_ q(y)$ for a source seminorm $r_ q$; boundedness of $(y_ j)$ then proves convergence and continuity of $\beta $. We have $v=\beta \alpha $ and $w=\alpha \beta $ is $B$-nuclear on the Banach module $L=\ell ^1(B)$, with coefficient maps $\xi _ j\beta $ and vectors the standard unit vectors $e_ j$. Split $w=w'+w''$ at a large finite index $N$. On the Banach space $L$, equicontinuity of the coefficient maps is a uniform operator norm bound, so $\| w''\| <1$ for large $N$. The Neumann series makes $T=I-w''$ a continuous $B$-linear automorphism with continuous inverse. Write $w'=J\Lambda $, where $J:B^ N\to L$ inserts the first $N$ vectors and $\Lambda :L\to B^ N$ is the finite list of coefficient maps including the $\lambda _ j$. The exact continuous identity 08CCD417EB8B 9.46.4 \begin{equation}  I=(I-w)T^{-1}+J\Lambda T^{-1} \end{equation} proves finite generation of its cokernel. The maps $\alpha ,\beta $ induce inverse algebraic cokernel isomorphisms for $I-v$ and $I-w$: they intertwine the two operators, and their compositions $v,w$ act as the identity modulo the respective actual images. Retain this identity before passing to any cokernel. Every continuous $B$-linear map and each of its inverse identities induces a map on the actual balanced quotient with $C$. The free-factor formula gives $C\widehat\otimes _ B B^ N=C^ N$. Thus the induced identity is \[  I=(I-w_ C)(T^{-1})_ C+J_ C\Lambda _ C(T^{-1})_ C.  \] For precision this equality is not inferred merely by continuity from a dense subset of a non-Hausdorff target. The original operator identity is first tensored as an identity on the Hausdorff unbalanced completion $C\widehat\otimes L$, where it holds by density. The factorization through $C^ N$ then follows from the exact balanced relation: for a continuous $B$-linear coefficient $\ell :L\to B$, the difference between $c\otimes \ell (x)e_ j$ and $c\rho (\ell (x))\otimes e_ j$ is the image of the completed relation map applied to $c\otimes \ell (x)\otimes e_ j$. This formula is an identity of continuous maps before quotienting. Hence the residual summand really has image in the module generated by the finitely many classes $[1\otimes e_ j]$. The induced $\alpha _ C,\beta _ C$ still intertwine and have the same composition identities, giving the cokernel isomorphism with $I-v_ C$. This proves the stronger assertion without tensoring a possibly non-Hausdorff cokernel. $\square$

title: Equation 9.46.4
text: 08CCD417EB8B 9.46.4 \begin{equation}  I=(I-w)T^{-1}+J\Lambda T^{-1} \end{equation}

title: Theorem 9.46.5
text: Theorem 9.46.5 . 741AFF17E7BD Let $A$ be fully nuclear, $E,F$ fully $A$-transverse nuclear modules, $f:E\to F$ an open surjective module map and $u:E\to F$ $A$-subnuclear. Then for every $t<1$ \[  \operatorname {coker}(f_ t-u_ t) \text{ is a finitely generated algebraic }A_ t\text{-module}.  \] No Hausdorffness of this cokernel is asserted. Proof. Use the preceding free-cover construction to replace the source by a nuclearly free $P=A\widehat\otimes M$, so that $u$ becomes $A$-nuclear and $f$ is still onto. The kernel of the cover is fully transverse by applying (1) of the calculus theorem to every $A_ t$; hence the cover remains onto after each base change. Proving finite generation for the replaced source therefore proves it for the original map. In an $A$-nuclear series for $u$ arrange $y_ j\to 0$. To do so choose $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$ slowly enough that $\sum _ j|\lambda _ j|/\varepsilon _ j<\infty $, replace $y_ j$ by $\varepsilon _ jy_ j$ and $\lambda _ j$ by $\lambda _ j/\varepsilon _ j$. Boundedness of the old vectors proves convergence of the new vectors to zero in every seminorm. Open surjectivity of $f$ gives lifts $x_ j\to 0$ with $f(x_ j)=y_ j$: a decreasing countable zero-neighborhood basis has open images, and successively late terms $y_ j$ can be lifted in successively small such neighborhoods. Then $v(x)=\sum _ j\lambda _ j\xi _ j(x)x_ j$ is an $A$-nuclear endomorphism of $P$ and $u=fv$. The kernel of $f:P\to F$ is fully transverse, so $f_ t$ remains onto. Thus the cokernel of $f_ t-u_ t=f_ t(I-v_ t)$ is an algebraic quotient of that of $I-v_ t$. Fix $t<1$ and let $B=A_{p_ t}$, a Banach algebra. There is a continuous homomorphism $B\to A_ t$ because each $p_{\lambda t}\leq p_ t$. Free base change identifies $P_ B=B\widehat\otimes M$ and makes $v_ B$ $B$-nuclear: its coefficient maps are $b\otimes m\mapsto b\rho (\xi _ j(1\otimes m))$, uniformly bounded by a projective seminorm, and its vectors are the bounded images of $x_ j$. Apply the strengthened Banach perturbation lemma with $C=A_ t$. Its free-factor collapse identifies $A_ t\widehat\otimes _ B(B\widehat\otimes M) =A_ t\widehat\otimes M=P_ t$. Both iterated base changes of $v$ agree on elementary free tensors and hence on this Hausdorff completion. The lemma therefore proves finite generation of $\operatorname {coker}(I-v_ t)$ and then of the desired cokernel. At no point is a non-Hausdorff cokernel placed in the nuclear Fréchet tensor category. $\square$

title: Proposition 9.46.6
text: Proposition 9.46.6 . 06B015B619A5 Let $X$ be a closed analytic subspace of an open $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, with any coherent defining ideal $\mathcal J$, and $D=D(a,R)\Subset \Omega $ a polydisc. Put $U=X\cap D$ and $U_ t=X\cap D(a,tR)$. The quotient seminorms on $A=\mathcal O(U)$ of $p_ t(f)=\sup _{\overline{D(a,tR)}}|f|$ make $A$ fully nuclear, and $A_ t=\mathcal O(U_ t)$ topologically. If $Y$ has a strict-PSH exhaustion, $V\Subset Y$ is a strict-PSH open and $\mathcal F$ is coherent on $X\times Y$, then $\mathcal F(U\times V)$ is fully $A$-transverse and its $t$th base change is $\mathcal F(U_ t\times V)$. Proof. Coherent vanishing gives an open algebra quotient $\mathcal O(D)\to \mathcal O(U)$ with closed kernel $\mathcal J(D)$. Its quotient seminorms are multiplicative: take holomorphic lifts of two classes, multiply them and take the infimum of their norm products. They define its quotient Fréchet topology. For $t<t'$ insert one radius $s$ strictly between them. The two Banach polydisc restriction links at $t'>s>t$ in the direction from larger to smaller radii are nuclear by the explicit polydisc series. After projecting the target to its quotient by the closed ideal image, their composition vanishes on the closed source ideal image. The proved two-Banach-link quotient criterion in theorem 2.13.3 makes the descended map between the two quotient Banach completions nuclear. These completions are precisely those for the quotient seminorms. Thus every indicated link is nuclear. For clarity about the intermediate completions, the restriction $\mathcal J(D)\to \mathcal J(D(a,tR))$ has dense image by the full coherent $1$-Runge theorem: concentric smaller polydiscs are $1$-Runge complete. For a compact $L$ in a smaller polydisc choose $r<s<t$ containing $L$ in the radius-$r$ polydisc. For large $m$, $\sum _ i|(z_ i-a_ i)/R_ i|^{2m}$ is less than $s^{2m}$ on $L$ and its $s^{2m}$-sublevel is inside the radius-$s$ polydisc. Add a sufficiently small positive multiple of a nonnegative strict-PSH exhaustion of $D$. This preserves the strict margin on $L$ and makes that sublevel relatively compact inside the radius-$t$ polydisc. The completion of $\mathcal O(D)$ for the seminorms with indices below $t$ is $\mathcal O(D(a,tR))$ by Taylor density. Its closed ideal is therefore the closure of the image of $\mathcal J(D)$. Taking the quotient commutes with this completion in this specific situation. Indeed each quotient seminorm is the infimum over that ideal; taking its closure does not change the infimum, and the closed quotient is Fréchet complete with the original quotient image dense. This proves the claimed completion identity, including nonreduced ideals and components missed by a smaller sublevel. Choose a slightly larger concentric polydisc $D^+$ with $\overline D\subset D^+\Subset \Omega $; compactness of $\overline D$ inside $\Omega $ permits this enlargement. Then $X\cap D^+$ is a closed analytic subspace of a strict-PSH polydisc and inherits its exhaustion. Restrict $\mathcal F$ to this space times $Y$ and apply proposition 9.45.4 to $U_ t\subset U\Subset X\cap D^+$ for $t<1$. It gives all positive Tor vanishings, Hausdorffness and the claimed section identification. For $t=1$ it is the free identity $A\widehat\otimes _ A E=E$. This is full transversality in the stated nonreduced category. $\square$

title: 9.53.1 Formal complex structures and complex coordinates

section: 9.53 Formal integrability and smooth complex coordinates
text: Let $M$ be a smooth real manifold of dimension $2n$, $n\geq 1$, and let $J^2=-1$ be a smooth endomorphism of its tangent bundle. In dimension zero the manifold is discrete and already has its unique complex atlas, so that case requires no construction. All manifolds are Hausdorff and second countable. Complex differential forms below are smooth unless a distributional domain is specified. Write $\mathcal H(f)=\mathrm i d'd''f$; this is the unscaled Levi form. No complex atlas is assumed in the definitions or arguments below. Proposition 9.53.2 . 7D9D38C5DA0E The projections $(1-\mathrm iJ)/2$ and $(1+\mathrm iJ)/2$ split $T_{\mathbb C}M=T^{1,0}\oplus T^{0,1}$ into conjugate rank-$n$ bundles and induce the type decomposition of exterior forms. For $(1,0)$ vector fields define $\vartheta (X,Y)=[X,Y]^{0,1}$. This is a tensor in $\Lambda ^{2,0}T^*M\otimes T^{0,1}M$. If $\vartheta =\sum _ j\alpha _ j\otimes \bar\xi _ j$ in a local frame, put \[  \vartheta ' u=\sum _ j\alpha _ j\wedge \iota _{\bar\xi _ j}u, \qquad \vartheta ''u=\sum _ j\bar\alpha _ j\wedge \iota _{\xi _ j}u.  \] These intrinsic derivations have types $(2,-1)$ and $(-1,2)$. Let $d'$ and $d''$ be the components of $d$ of bidegrees $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$. Then A64B66D1EDF0 9.53.3 \begin{equation}  d=d'+d''-\vartheta '-\vartheta ''. \end{equation} In particular $\vartheta =0$ if and only if $d=d'+d''$. In this case 3BE881B07623 9.53.4 \begin{equation}  (d')^2=(d'')^2=0,\qquad d'd''+d''d'=0. \end{equation} We call this condition formal integrability. Proof. The displayed projections are complementary idempotents, with the asserted images and conjugation. Their ranks are $n$: a real basis $(e_1,Je_1,\ldots ,e_ n,Je_ n)$ gives the corresponding eigenbases. The bracket formula $[fX,gY]=fg[X,Y]+f(Xg)Y-g(Yf)X$ proves tensoriality after projecting to $T^{0,1}$. Tensor contraction makes the two ensuing operators frame-independent. Since contraction is an odd derivation and each $\alpha _ j$ has degree two, their signed product rule is that of $d$. The type projections of the product rule for $d$ give the same rule for $d'$ and $d''$. It is enough to check ( 9.53.3 ) on functions and one-forms, which locally generate the exterior algebra. For a function it is its type decomposition. For a $(0,1)$ one-form $u$ and $(1,0)$ fields $X,Y$, \[  du(X,Y)=X(u(Y))-Y(u(X))-u([X,Y])=-u(\vartheta (X,Y)).  \] Thus $(du)^{2,0}=-\vartheta 'u$; its other components are the two specified type derivatives. Conjugation handles $(1,0)$ one-forms. If $d=d'+d''$, the same formula detects every component of $\vartheta $ by pairing with $(0,1)$ covectors. Finally the distinct types in $d^2=0$ give ( 9.53.4 ). $\square$ Lemma 9.53.5 . 30126C7FDE2C Suppose $J$ is formally integrable. At every $a\in M$, for every integer $s\geq 1$, there are smooth complex-valued real coordinates $z=(z_1,\ldots ,z_ n)$ centered at $a$ with 1F71301249BA 9.53.6 \begin{equation}  d''z_ j=O(|z|^ s),\qquad 1\leq j\leq n. \end{equation} Here an estimate for a smooth coefficient also says that all its Taylor terms of smaller degree vanish. Proof. Choose real linear coordinates so that $dz_ j(a)$ are a basis of $(T^{1,0}_ a)^*$. This gives $s=1$, with invertible real differential. Assume the assertion at order $s$. The coframe $d''\bar z_ k$ is invertible near $a$, and Taylor expansion gives \[  d''z_ j=\sum _ k P_{jk}(z,\bar z)d''\bar z_ k+O(|z|^{s+1}),  \] where each $P_{jk}$ is homogeneous of total degree $s$. The identity $(d'')^2z_ j=0$ implies $\partial _{\bar z_ l}P_{jk}=\partial _{\bar z_ k}P_{jl}$. Indeed these are the coefficients of degree $s-1$ of its two-form: terms involving $d''z_ l$ have order at least $2s-1\geq s$, and $d''d''\bar z_ k=0$; differentiating the remainder gives order $s$. The chain rule now gives $d''(z_ j-Q_ j)=O(|z|^{s+1})$: its uncancelled term $\sum _ k(\partial _{z_ k}Q_ j)d''z_ k$ has order $2s\geq s+1$. The differential of this change at $a$ is the identity, so it is a real coordinate change. Norms and orders are preserved under that change, completing the induction. $\square$ Lemma 9.53.7 . 53F867AC87E1 On a formally integrable almost complex manifold, let $z$ be real coordinates satisfying ( 9.53.6 ) with $s\geq 3$. Put $r=|z|$ and $\psi =r^2$. On one sufficiently small coordinate ball, independent of $0<\epsilon \leq 1$, \[  \mathcal H(\psi )>0,\qquad \mathcal H\bigl (\psi +\log (\psi +\epsilon ^2)\bigr )>0.  \] These forms are closed. On that ball $\mathcal H(\log (\psi +\epsilon ^2))\geq -\mathcal H(\psi )$. Proof. Use the coframe $\zeta _ j=d'z_ j$, whose conjugate is $d''\bar z_ j$. Differentiating smooth Taylor remainders lowers their order by at most one. The product rule and $d'd''z_ j=-d''d'z_ j$ therefore give \[  \mathcal H(\psi )=\mathrm i\sum _ j\zeta _ j\wedge \bar\zeta _ j +O(r^ s),\qquad d'\psi =\sum _ j\bar z_ j\zeta _ j+O(r^{s+1}).  \] For example the error $z_ jd'd''\bar z_ j$ has order $s$, and the term $d'\bar z_ j\wedge d''z_ j$ has order $2s$. With $t=r^2+\epsilon ^2$ the chain rule yields \begin{align*}  \mathcal H(\psi +\log t) & =\mathcal H(\psi )+\mathrm i \frac{t\sum _ j\zeta _ j\wedge \bar\zeta _ j -(\sum _ j\bar z_ j\zeta _ j)\wedge (\sum _ k z_ k\bar\zeta _ k)}{t^2}\\ & \hspace{8mm}+O(r^ s/t)+O(r^{s+2}/t^2). \end{align*} The fraction is semipositive by Cauchy–Schwarz. For $r>0$ the error norm is at most $Cr^{s-2}$, uniformly in $\epsilon $; at $r=0$ the errors vanish. The first Levi form has a fixed positive lower bound after shrinking, so the assertions follow. Closedness is a consequence of ( 9.53.4 ) and $d=d'+d''$. Subtracting $\mathcal H(\psi )$ from the positive second form proves the last inequality. $\square$ We next justify the analytic identity needed before constructing a complex atlas. A positive real $(1,1)$ form $\gamma $ with $d\gamma =0$ will be called a formally Kähler metric. It induces the usual pointwise form norms, real metric and volume $dV_\gamma =\gamma ^ n/n!$. The notation in the next lemma describes smooth bundles and differential operators, not presumed holomorphic trivializations. Lemma 9.53.8 . 7B10208C6D56 Let $J$ be formally integrable and let $\gamma $ be formally Kähler. Let $K=\Lambda ^{n,0}T^*M$. The operator $d''$ on sections of $K$ defines a partial connection with square zero. Its dual on $K^{-1}$ and the induced metric define a smooth Hermitian connection whose curvature is of type $(1,1)$. Denote its real unscaled curvature by $\operatorname {Ric}(\gamma )$. For a smooth real weight $\phi $, if 68B288E2D6BF 9.53.9 \begin{equation}  \mathcal H(\phi )+\operatorname {Ric}(\gamma )\geq \gamma , \end{equation} then every compactly supported smooth $(0,1)$ form $v$ satisfies B23883666796 9.53.10 \begin{equation}  \int _ M|v|_\gamma ^2e^{-\phi }\, dV_\gamma \leq \| d''v\| _\phi ^2+\| \delta _\phi ''v\| _\phi ^2. \end{equation} Here $\delta _\phi ''$ is the formal adjoint with the displayed smooth weight. If $\gamma $ is complete, every distributionally closed $g\in L^2_{0,1}(e^{-\phi },\gamma )$ has a solution 1BE0D874AB82 9.53.11 \begin{equation}  d''u=g,\qquad \int _ M|u|^2e^{-\phi }\, dV_\gamma \leq \int _ M|g|_\gamma ^2e^{-\phi }\, dV_\gamma . \end{equation} Proof. The product rule on $(n,0)$ forms gives the partial connection on $K$, and $(d'')^2=0$ gives its square zero. For clarity, a smooth line frame with squared norm $H$ and partial-connection form $a''$ has unique metric connection with $a'=H^{-1}d'H-\overline{a''}$ and $(0,1)$ part $a''$. This formula transforms as a connection and verifies compatibility by differentiating $H$. Its $(0,2)$ curvature is zero by the partial connection equation, and its $(2,0)$ part is zero by compatibility and conjugation. For $E=K^{-1}$ equipped with its induced metric times $e^{-\phi }$, its real curvature is consequently $\operatorname {Ric}(\gamma )+\mathcal H(\phi )$. Here is a pointwise justification of the Kähler identity for this connection, including the jets which are needed. At any point use lemma 9.53.5 with $s=5$. In these real coordinates $J-J_{\rm std}=O(r^5)$: the $(0,1)$ projection of each $dz_ j$ is $O(r^5)$ and its conjugate has the same property, which determines the matrix of $J$. The degree-two real Taylor polynomial $\gamma _2$ of $\gamma $ is a standard type $(1,1)$ form, and is closed. Indeed all its non-$(1,1)$ coefficients have zero Taylor polynomial through degree two, and $d\gamma _2$ is the degree-one Taylor polynomial of $d\gamma =0$. It is positive on a smaller ball. Thus $\gamma _2$ is an actual standard Kähler metric there and has exactly the same two-jet as $\gamma $ at the point. The smooth frame $\eta =d'z_1\wedge \cdots \wedge d'z_ n$ of $K$ satisfies $d''\eta =O(r^4)$, since $d''d'z_ j=-d'd''z_ j$. Hence its partial-connection coefficients and their derivatives through order two vanish at the point. The metric of $\eta ^{-1}$ is the reciprocal of the squared norm of $\eta $, so it agrees through order two with the metric of the standard inverse canonical frame for $\gamma _2$. Use also the degree-two Taylor polynomial of $\phi $. The connection just defined, the exterior operators, their adjoints and Laplacians, and their curvature operators therefore have exactly the same pointwise coefficients as in that genuine Kähler model. Exterior operators use first jets, adjoints use first metric jets, and their second-order compositions and curvature use at most second jets; the type projections also have matching jets. Coefficients of a test form can be given the same two-jet in the two frames. Apply the already proved local identity theorem 10.33.2 in the genuine model. Equality of these coefficients proves the same identity for $E$ at the chosen point, hence everywhere. This uses the proof of that local differential-operator identity, without presuming the existence of any holomorphic coordinates for $J$. There is a global isometry from scalar $(0,q)$ forms to $E$-valued $(n,q)$ forms, given in a local frame by $v\mapsto (-1)^{nq}\eta \wedge v\otimes \eta ^{-1}$. The connection terms on $\eta $ and its dual cancel, and the indicated sign makes this commute with $d''$ in consecutive degrees. Adjoints commute as well. On $(n,1)$ forms the curvature operator is precisely the Hermitian form of $\mathcal H(\phi )+\operatorname {Ric}(\gamma )$, by the coefficient formula in proposition 10.33.6 . Its lower bound is the identity under ( 9.53.9 ). The integrated Kähler identity now gives ( 9.53.10 ). The complete-domain argument requires no complex coordinate charts. They are closed and densely defined, and $ST=0$. The smooth complete gradient cutoffs of lemma 6.26.1 have the product rules \[  d''(\chi v)=\chi d''v+d''\chi \wedge v, \quad \delta _\phi ''(\chi v)=\chi \delta _\phi ''v -(d''\chi \wedge )^*v.  \] Their errors are bounded by $C\| v\| _\phi /R$. Near zero $g_ j=O(r^ s)$; away from zero their support is compact. Consequently \[  I_ j=\int _\Omega |g_ j|_\gamma ^2 e^{-b(\rho )} \psi ^{-n-1}\, dV_\gamma <\infty :  \] near zero the radial bound is $C r^{2s-3}\, dr$, and $s\geq 2$ is enough. On two such neighborhoods the transition has complex-linear differential, so satisfies the ordinary Cauchy–Riemann equations. The canonical local Cauchy theorem makes it holomorphic, with the convergent local expansion holomorphic power series and Cauchy bounds . text: Proposition 9.53.2 . 7D9D38C5DA0E The projections $(1-\mathrm iJ)/2$ and $(1+\mathrm iJ)/2$ split $T_{\mathbb C}M=T^{1,0}\oplus T^{0,1}$ into conjugate rank-$n$ bundles and induce the type decomposition of exterior forms. Then A64B66D1EDF0 9.53.3 \begin{equation}  d=d'+d''-\vartheta '-\vartheta ''. \end{equation} In particular $\vartheta =0$ if and only if $d=d'+d''$. For a function it is its type decomposition. Finally the distinct types in $d^2=0$ give ( 9.53.4 ). $\square$

This uses the proof of that local differential-operator identity, without presuming the existence of any holomorphic coordinates for $J$. There is a global isometry from scalar $(0,q)$ forms to $E$-valued $(n,q)$ forms, given in a local frame by $v\mapsto (-1)^{nq}\eta \wedge v\otimes \eta ^{-1}$. The connection terms on $\eta $ and its dual cancel, and the indicated sign makes this commute with $d''$ in consecutive degrees. Adjoints commute as well. On $(n,1)$ forms the curvature operator is precisely the Hermitian form of $\mathcal H(\phi )+\operatorname {Ric}(\gamma )$, by the coefficient formula in proposition 10.33.6 . text: Lemma 9.53.12 . 515854F40204 For a smooth almost complex structure, if $u\in L^2_{\rm loc}$ and $d''u$ is smooth distributionally, then $u$ is smooth. Formal integrability is not needed for this assertion. Proof. Choose any smooth positive metric and its unweighted local formal adjoint. The operator $P=\delta ''d''$ on functions has principal symbol $|\xi ^{0,1}|^2=|\xi |^2/2$ for real covectors. Thus it is uniformly elliptic on compact coordinate balls, and $Pu=\delta ''(d''u)$ is smooth. We specify the initial regularity step: after a compact cutoff, the right-hand side of the localized equation is in $H^{-1}$, since its commutator with $P$ is first order applied to $u\in L^2$. Conjugate by the smooth square root of the density and coefficient metric. The symmetric principal coefficient matrix is real and uniformly positive; antisymmetric coefficients contribute only first-order terms. In divergence form, ordinary mollification $J_ t$ satisfies $\| [a^{ij}\partial _ j,J_ t]u\| _2\leq C\| u\| _2$ on the fixed compact chart, by graph-norm density by cutoffs and mollification . Consequently $PJ_ tu$ is bounded in $H^{-1}$. The coercive integration-by-parts inequality $\| w\| _{H^1}^2\leq C(|\langle Pw,w\rangle |+\| w\| _2^2)$, followed by duality and Young's inequality, bounds $J_ tu$ in $H^1$. Weak compactness gives $u\in H^1_{\rm loc}$. This is the same local commutator argument as in lemma 6.28.1 , with a smooth source added. The checked divergence-form interior theorem interior regularity for elliptic systems in divergence form now bootstraps on nested balls to every Sobolev order. The local Sobolev embedding Sobolev spaces, duality and local embedding gives smoothness. $\square$

title: Theorem 9.53.13
section: 9.53 Formal integrability and smooth complex coordinates
text: Theorem 9.53.13 . 58DA08F550FB A smooth almost complex structure is induced by a complex analytic atlas if and only if it is formally integrable. That atlas is unique up to compatibility. More precisely, about every point of a formally integrable structure there are smooth complex-valued real coordinates $w_1,\ldots ,w_ n$ satisfying $d''w_ j=0$. Proof. An existing complex atlas gives $\vartheta =0$ by commuting its coordinate fields and tensoriality. For the converse choose the coordinates of lemma 9.53.5 with $s\geq 5$ and shrink to a ball $\Omega =\{ \psi =|z|^2<r_0^2\} $ on which lemma 9.53.7 holds. Here $\psi $ is strictly PSH in the defined formal sense. The function $\rho =(r_0^2-\psi )^{-1}$ is a smooth positive strict-PSH exhaustion. The form $\gamma =\mathcal H(e^\rho )$ is positive and closed, and complete: its rank-one summand gives $|d\rho |_\gamma ^2\leq 2e^{-\rho }\leq 2$. A length-Cauchy sequence has bounded $\rho $ and so lies in a compact sublevel, where the smooth metric and coordinate topologies agree. It therefore converges. This repeats the real-metric proof of lemma 6.26.8 , which uses only the displayed formal product and closedness identities. Choose a smooth convex increasing function $b$ on the range of $\rho $ so fast that AC2A3454F009 9.53.14 \begin{equation}  \mathcal H(b\circ \rho )\geq (n+1)\mathcal H(\psi )-\operatorname {Ric}(\gamma )+\gamma . \end{equation} Here is an explicit existence check. Relative to the positive $\mathcal H(\rho )$, the right side has a finite upper eigenvalue bound on each compact sublevel. Take a nondecreasing positive sequence dominating those bounds on successive sublevels; a locally finite sum of nondecreasing smooth step functions gives a smooth nondecreasing derivative $b'$ dominating the bound on each band. Its integral is convex and increasing. The chain rule $\mathcal H(b\circ \rho )=b'(\rho )\mathcal H(\rho )+ \mathrm i b''(\rho )d'\rho \wedge d''\rho $ proves the inequality. No boundedness of the Ricci form near the boundary is assumed. Put \[  \phi _\epsilon =b(\rho )+(n+1)\log (\psi +\epsilon ^2), \qquad 0<\epsilon \leq 1.  \] The uniform logarithmic-weight lemma and ( 9.53.14 ) give $\mathcal H(\phi _\epsilon )+\operatorname {Ric}(\gamma )\geq \gamma $ for every $\epsilon $. All these weights are smooth on $\Omega $. Take $h\in C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$ equal to one near zero and set $g_ j=d''(hz_ j)$. These are smooth closed $(0,1)$ forms by ( 9.53.4 ). Near zero $g_ j=O(r^ s)$; away from zero their support is compact. Consequently \[  I_ j=\int _\Omega |g_ j|_\gamma ^2 e^{-b(\rho )} \psi ^{-n-1}\, dV_\gamma <\infty :  \] near zero the radial bound is $C r^{2s-3}\, dr$, and $s\geq 2$ is enough. By lemma 9.53.8 there are solutions $u_{j,\epsilon }$ with $d''u_{j,\epsilon }=g_ j$ and $\| u_{j,\epsilon }\| _{\phi _\epsilon }^2\leq I_ j$. For a sequence $\epsilon _ k\downarrow 0$, these bounds give weak compactness in every fixed space $L^2(e^{-\phi _{\epsilon _ l}})$ after discarding $k<l$. A diagonal subsequence has one distributional limit $u_ j$, because the weights and metric have fixed positive lower bounds on compact sets. Weak lower semicontinuity in each fixed space followed by monotone convergence gives 1594A5CCAFB4 9.53.15 \begin{equation}  d''u_ j=g_ j,\qquad \int _\Omega |u_ j|^2 e^{-b(\rho )}\psi ^{-n-1}\, dV_\gamma \leq I_ j. \end{equation} The function $u_ j$ is locally $L^2$, and $g_ j$ is smooth. Hence lemma 9.53.12 proves smoothness using the unweighted smooth elliptic operator. No regularity theorem for a singular weighted adjoint is being invoked. The last integral forces $u_ j(0)=du_ j(0)=0$. Indeed a nonzero constant Taylor term gives radial divergence $\int r^{-3}dr$; if the constant term vanishes and the real linear term is nonzero, it is bounded below by $cr$ on a fixed cone of directions and gives divergence $\int r^{-1}dr$. Smooth positive metric and weight factors near zero do not change either conclusion. Thus $w_ j=hz_ j-u_ j$ satisfies $d''w_ j=0$ and $dw_ j(0)=dz_ j(0)$. The real inverse function theorem makes $w$ a coordinate system on a smaller neighborhood. Its differential intertwines $J$ with the standard structure, since $d''w_ j=0$. On two such neighborhoods the transition has complex-linear differential, so satisfies the ordinary Cauchy–Riemann equations. The canonical local Cauchy theorem makes it holomorphic, with the convergent local expansion holomorphic power series and Cauchy bounds . Conversely any compatible complex atlas has these same local $J$-holomorphic functions, proving uniqueness. $\square$

We use quadratic Hermitian metrics and the normalization $c_1(L,h)=\mathrm i\Theta (L,h)/(2\pi )$. Positivity is unchanged by this positive scalar. All manifolds below are Hausdorff and second countable. A compact manifold has finitely many connected components. The metric construction in Kähler metrics on smooth-center blowups gives the following consequence. If $L$ is positive on a compact complex manifold $X$, $\pi :Y	o X$ is the blowup along a closed smooth center of positive codimension, and $E$ is its inverse-image divisor, there is a metric with curvature $\eta =c_1(\mathcal O_ Y(-E))$ such that \[  \pi ^*c_1(L)+\varepsilon \eta >0 \quad 	ext{for all sufficiently small }\varepsilon >0.  \] Consequently $\mathcal O_ Y(-E)\otimes \pi ^*L^ k$ is positive for every sufficiently large integer $k$, by multiplying this inequality by $k$ and taking $\varepsilon =1/k$. It also proves projectivity of $Y$ by theorem 10.40.10 . Proposition 10.41.1 . A8BE0AECFD69 Let $X$ be a compact complex manifold of pure dimension $n\geq 1$, let $L	o X$ be a positive holomorphic line bundle, and let $\pi :Y	o X$ be the blowup of a finite set of distinct points. Write $E$ for the inverse-image divisor. There is a constant $C>0$ such that, for all integers $m\geq 1$ and $k\geq Cm$, \[  H^1 igl (Y,\mathcal O_ Y(-mE)\otimes \pi ^*L^ k igr )=0.  \] The constant depends on $X,L$, the chosen finite center and fixed metrics, and is independent of $m,k$. The empty center is allowed, with $Y=X$ and $E=0$. Proof. Put $\omega =\mathrm i\Theta (L)>0$ and fix a metric on $K_ X$. By compactness choose $k_0>0$ with $k_0\omega -\mathrm i\Theta (K_ X)>0$ everywhere. The preceding canonical blowup construction, with the unscaled curvature $\eta _0=\mathrm i\Theta (\mathcal O_ Y(-E))$, gives $C_0>0$ such that \[  \eta _0+C_0\pi ^*\omega >0.  \] In particular $Y$ is compact Kähler. If the center is empty this inequality holds with $\eta _0=0$ and any $C_0>0$. The blowup charts smooth-center blowup coordinates have $\det (d\pi )=\pm t^{n-1}$. Pullback of a local canonical form therefore gives a nowhere vanishing bundle isomorphism \[  K_ Y\simeq \pi ^*K_ X\otimes \mathcal O_ Y((n-1)E).  \] Indeed its local zero divisor is $(n-1)E$, and dividing by that local equation makes the local bundle maps invertible and compatible on overlaps. In dimension one the blowup is the identity, the factor is $\mathcal O_ Y$, and the same formula holds. For the empty center it is the identity as well. Let $a=m+n-1\geq 1$ and equip \[  F=K_ Y^{-1}\otimes \mathcal O_ Y(-mE)\otimes \pi ^*L^ k \simeq \mathcal O_ Y(-aE)\otimes \pi ^*(K_ X^{-1}\otimes L^ k)  \] with the corresponding product metric. Its curvature is \[  \mathrm i\Theta (F) =a(\eta _0+C_0\pi ^*\omega ) +\pi ^* igl ((k-C_0a)\omega -\mathrm i\Theta (K_ X) igr ).  \] The first term is positive definite. The second is semipositive when $k\geq k_0+C_0a$, since its form before pullback is positive. Thus $F$ is positive. Because $a\leq nm$ for $m\geq 1$, the choice $C=k_0+nC_0$ ensures this inequality whenever $k\geq Cm$. Apply corollary 10.33.14 to the line bundle $F$ on $Y$. The bundle Dolbeault comparison and the local canonical wedge identification give \[  H^1(Y,\mathcal O_ Y(-mE)\otimes \pi ^*L^ k) \simeq H^{n,1}_{ ar\partial }(Y,F)=0.  \] The identifications use corollary 10.43.11 . AF752427463F A compact complex manifold of pure dimension $n\geq 0$ which admits a holomorphic embedding into some projective space admits one into $\mathbb P^{2n+1}$. Its image is an algebraic submanifold. Iterating these projections gives the stated bound by an actual linear projection. Proof. Regard projective space as lines in $V=\mathbb C^{N+1}$. For $x\in X$, choose a local holomorphic lift $F$ of the inclusion with one homogeneous coordinate equal to one. The vectors $F(x)$ and the image of $dF_ x$ are linearly independent, and define an $(n+1)$-dimensional subspace \[  \widehat T_ xX=\mathbb C F(x)+dF_ x(T_ xX)\subset V.  \] It is independent of the lift, since replacing $F$ by $uF$ changes $dF$ by a multiple of $F$ and a nonzero scalar factor. Define the bad set of centers to be \[  B=X\  \cup \!  igcup _{x
e y\in X}\mathbb P(\mathbb C F(x)+\mathbb C F(y)) \  \cup \!  igcup _{x\in X}\mathbb P(\widehat T_ xX).  \] The secant part is parameterized locally by $(x,y,[a:b])\mapsto [aF(x)+bG(y)]$, for $x
e y$ and local lifts $F,G$. This is a smooth map from a complex manifold of dimension $2n+1$; its denominator never vanishes, since the two projective points are distinct. The tangent part has local parameterization $(x,[a:v])\mapsto [aF(x)+dF_ x(v)]$ with $[a:v]\in \mathbb P^ n$, of complex dimension $2n$. Countably many coordinate pieces cover these parameter spaces, and each is a countable union of compact coordinate cubes on which the map is Lipschitz in target charts. For a converging sequence of secant centers take a subsequence with endpoints $x_ j	o x$ and $y_ j	o y$. If $x
e y$, the limiting center is on the limiting secant line. If $x=y$, use one local lift $F$ and coordinates $z_ j,w_ j	o z$. After a subsequence, \[  v_ j= rac{w_ j-z_ j}{|w_ j-z_ j|}\longrightarrow v,\quad |v|=1, \qquad  rac{F(w_ j)-F(z_ j)}{|w_ j-z_ j|}\longrightarrow dF_ z(v).  \] The last convergence follows by integrating $dF$ along the local straight segment. otin B$ and project by $V	o V/\mathbb Ca$. The projection is defined on $X$. e y$, it is the two independent values; and for $D=2[x]$ it is the one-jet in the local quotient $\mathbb C\{ z\} /(z^2)$. e n-1,\end{cases} \qquad 0\leq q\leq n.  \] Proof. The last group is the already proved theorem 10.50.3 : it is one dimensional exactly when $n-q=1$ and is zero otherwise. Its exact threshold is $\min (n-q+1,r)=2$, so it forces the nonzero group on the left to vanish, a contradiction. This excludes every Hermitian metric on the bundle, rather than just its induced projective metric. For $n=1$ this obstruction does not apply; the induced tangent metric is strictly positive as in example 10.34.10 . $\square$

The two vectors $F(z),dF_ z(v)$ are independent. Thus the secant two-planes converge to their span: their displayed bases converge to an independent pair, so normalized projective coefficients have convergent subsequences. The limiting center belongs to $\mathbb P(\widehat T_ xX)$. When $n=0$, distinct endpoints cannot converge to the same point of the finite set $X$. This proves closedness. Since nonempty open sets in projective space have positive measure, the complement of $B$ is dense open and of full measure. Choose $[a]
otin B$ and project by $V	o V/\mathbb Ca$. The projection is defined on $X$. title: Corollary 10.41.3
section: 10.41 Blowup vanishing and small projective embeddings
text: Corollary 10.41.3 . 4E2A659999BE Every compact Riemann surface is biholomorphic to an algebraic curve in $\mathbb P^3$. More precisely, on a connected compact Riemann surface of genus $g$, every line bundle $L$ with $\deg L\geq 2g+1$ is very ample. Proof. First let $X$ be connected. For any effective divisor $D$ of degree at most two, the degree formula gives \[  \deg (K_ X\otimes L^*\otimes \mathcal O_ X(D)) =2g-2-\deg L+\deg D<0.  \] The degree and Serre assertions in lemma 10.78.7 , theorem 10.78.9 , corollary 10.78.11 therefore give $H^1(X,L(-D))=0$. Apply lemma 10.78.1 with the line bundle $L(-D)$ and divisor $D$. Its quotient is locally the Taylor jets of sections of $L$ modulo the equation of $D$. The exact sequence gives \[  H^0(X,L)\longrightarrow H^0(X,L/L(-D))\longrightarrow 0.  \] For $D=[x]$ this is evaluation in $L_ x$; for $D=[x]+[y]$, $x\ne y$, it is the two independent values; and for $D=2[x]$ it is the one-jet in the local quotient $\mathbb C\{ z\} /(z^2)$. Thus one fixed finite-dimensional section space $H^0(X,L)$ has no base point, separates every pair and separates every tangent vector. Its projective map is injective. At $x$, choose a section nonzero there and another with value zero and nonzero first derivative; the ratio is an affine coordinate of the map with nonzero derivative. The map is an immersion, hence an embedding by compactness and the local argument in the preceding theorem. For existence take any $a\in X$ and $L=\mathcal O_ X((2g+1)[a])$, of degree $2g+1$ by the checked divisor degree formula. Apply theorem 10.41.2 with $n=1$. This proves the claim without an identification of integral or rational degree-two cohomology with topological cycles. If the surface is disconnected, it has finitely many components. Choose these very ample bundles on each component and their union on $X$. Their section spaces form a finite direct sum. Extend a component's sections by zero on the other open and closed components; the resulting projective map embeds the components in disjoint projective linear subspaces. Apply the same projection theorem to this compact curve. The empty case is immediate. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.41.4
section: 10.41 Blowup vanishing and small projective embeddings
text: Corollary 10.41.4 . 94F862F11834 For $n\geq 2$, the holomorphic tangent bundle of $\mathbb P^ n$ has no smooth Hermitian metric whose curvature is nonnegative on all tensors of rank at most two at every point and strictly positive on every nonzero such tensor at one point. In every dimension $n\geq 1$ the underlying cohomology calculation is \[  \dim H^{n,q}_{\bar\partial }(\mathbb P^ n,T\mathbb P^ n) =\begin{cases} 1,& q=n-1,\\ 0,& q\ne n-1,\end{cases} \qquad 0\leq q\leq n.  \] Proof. The exact analytic Serre pairing and the holomorphic identification $(T\mathbb P^ n)^*=\Omega ^1_{\mathbb P^ n}$ give \[  H^{n,q}_{\bar\partial }(\mathbb P^ n,T\mathbb P^ n)^* \simeq H^{0,n-q}_{\bar\partial }(\mathbb P^ n,\Omega ^1) \simeq H^{1,n-q}_{\bar\partial }(\mathbb P^ n,\mathbb C).  \] The second identification uses the coefficientwise Dolbeault complex: a $(0,q)$-form $\alpha $ with a holomorphic cotangent factor $\theta $ maps to $\alpha \wedge \theta $, so it commutes with $\bar\partial $. The last group is the already proved theorem 10.50.3 : it is one dimensional exactly when $n-q=1$ and is zero otherwise. If the asserted metric existed, fix the Fubini–Study Kähler form on the base and apply corollary 10.48.2 with $q=n-1$, $r=n$ and $m=2$. Its exact threshold is $\min (n-q+1,r)=2$, so it forces the nonzero group on the left to vanish, a contradiction. This excludes every Hermitian metric on the bundle, rather than just its induced projective metric. For $n=1$ this obstruction does not apply; the induced tangent metric is strictly positive as in example 10.34.10 . $\square$

title: 10.63 Constant coefficients and integral cohomology lattices
search_title: Constant coefficients and integral cohomology lattices
section: 10.63 Constant coefficients and integral cohomology lattices
text: For an abelian group $A$, let $\underline A$ be the constant sheaf, whose sections are locally constant $A$-valued functions. In degree zero these are arbitrary values on connected components if the components are open; that condition is not automatic on an arbitrary space. For example on $\{ 0\} \cup \{ 1/n:n\ge 1\} $ a locally constant integer function is eventually equal to its value at zero. Smooth manifolds are Hausdorff and without boundary. Except in theorem 10.63.5 , they are second countable. Sheaf cohomology uses the existing Godement convention.

title: 10.63.1 Homotopy invariance without a singular comparison
search_title: Homotopy invariance without a singular comparison
section: 10.63 Constant coefficients and integral cohomology lattices
text: Lemma 10.63.2 . 73465E4FD7CC For every abelian group $A$ and $I=[0,1]$, $H^0(I,\underline A)=A$ and $H^ q(I,\underline A)=0$ for $q>0$. Proof. Use the cofinal interval covers $U_{j,k}=I\cap ((j-1)/k,(j+1)/k)$, $0\le j\le k$, whose cofinality was proved in theorem 10.62.2 . Every nonempty member and consecutive intersection is connected. The alternating constant-sheaf Čech complex is therefore \[  A^{k+1}\longrightarrow A^ k,\qquad (a_0,\ldots ,a_ k)\longmapsto (a_1-a_0,\ldots ,a_ k-a_{k-1}),  \] with no higher terms. The displayed map is onto by successive partial sums, and its kernel consists of constant tuples. The integral alternating comparison and global paracompact comparison in proposition 10.44.14 , theorem 10.44.12 give the result. No acyclicity of these intersections was assumed to compute the direct limit. $\square$ Theorem 10.63.3 . 0FA0E78E20CF For any topological space $X$, projection $\pi :X\times I\to X$ induces an isomorphism on cohomology with constant abelian coefficients. Every slice $i_ t$ induces its inverse. Consequently homotopic maps induce the same map, homotopy equivalences induce inverse isomorphisms, and a nonempty contractible space has no positive constant-sheaf cohomology and has $H^0= A$. Proof. The compact-slice formula proposition 10.61.4 identifies the higher-image stalks with the interval groups just computed. The unit $\underline A\to \pi _*\underline A$ is an isomorphism: on stalks it is $A\to H^0(I,\underline A)=A$, the identity. The positive higher images vanish, and the exact Leray edge of theorem 10.55.6 is precisely $\pi ^*$. Since $\pi i_ t=\operatorname {id}$, every $i_ t^*$ is its inverse. For a homotopy $F:X\times I\to Y$ the maps at its endpoints are $i_0^*F^*=i_1^*F^*$. The remaining assertions follow by composition and the exact cohomology of a point. $\square$

title: 10.63.4 Good covers
section: 10.63 Constant coefficients and integral cohomology lattices
text: Theorem 10.63.5 . 2AA913B1559D Let $M$ be a paracompact smooth manifold of real dimension $n$. Every open cover of $M$ has a locally finite open refinement $(U_\alpha )$ such that every nonempty finite intersection of its members is diffeomorphic to a convex open subset of $\mathbb R^ n$. In particular all such intersections are smoothly contractible. No countability assumption on $M$ is needed. Proof. Paracompactness includes Hausdorffness, as in lemma 10.44.2 . The empty case is immediate. For $n=0$, the manifold is discrete and its singleton cover has all the asserted properties. Suppose $n\geq 1$. First cover $M$ by relatively compact coordinate balls, each contained in a member of the prescribed cover. The closed-refinement and shrinking assertions of lemma 10.44.2 give a locally finite open cover $(V_ l)$, with each $\overline{V_ l}$ contained in one of these coordinate balls, and open sets $V'_ l$ still covering $M$ such that $K_ l=\overline{V'_ l}\subset V_ l$. Each $K_ l$ is compact: it is closed and lies in the compact closure of the corresponding original coordinate ball. Cover each $K_ l$ by finitely many concentric coordinate-ball pairs $\Omega '_ j\Subset \Omega _ j\subset V_ l$. Relabel all the pairs with one index $j$, and write $\phi _ j:\Omega _ j\longrightarrow B_ j\subset \mathbb R^ n$ for their coordinates. Both families are locally finite, because each pair is contained in one $V_ l$ and only finitely many pairs were chosen for each $l$. The smaller sets $\Omega '_ j$ cover $M$, and $\overline{\Omega '_ j}\subset \Omega _ j$. We claim that every point $a$ and every open neighborhood $G$ of $a$ admit a coordinate ball $U\subset G$, containing $a$, with the following properties: 5A887333DA73 10.63.6 \begin{equation}  U\subset \Omega '_ j\text{ for some }j, \qquad U\cap \Omega '_ k\ne \varnothing \  \Longrightarrow  U\subset \Omega _ k\text{ and }\phi _ k(U)\text{ is convex}. \end{equation} Choose $j$ with $a\in \Omega '_ j$. By local finiteness of the closures, there is an open neighborhood $N_0$ of $a$ meeting only finitely many $\overline{\Omega '_ k}$; denote those indices by $J_0$. Put $J=\{ k\in J_0:a\in \overline{\Omega '_ k}\} $. For $k\in J$, one has $a\in \Omega _ k$. Hence \[  N=G\cap N_0\cap \Omega '_ j\cap \bigcap _{k\in J}\Omega _ k \  \setminus \! \bigcup _{k\in J_0\setminus J} \overline{\Omega '_ k}  \] is an open neighborhood of $a$. Every $\Omega '_ k$ meeting $N$ has $k\in J$. This finite exclusion is what also controls charts whose smaller domain meets a ball but does not contain its center. On $\Omega _ j$ put $f(x)=|\phi _ j(x)-\phi _ j(a)|^2$. In $\phi _ k$ coordinates, for $k\in J$, the Hessian of $f$ at $\phi _ k(a)$ is \[  2\bigl (D(\phi _ j\circ \phi _ k^{-1})\bigr )^{\! T} D(\phi _ j\circ \phi _ k^{-1}),  \] which is positive definite. Terms involving second derivatives of the transition map vanish at that point because $\phi _ j(a)-\phi _ j(a)=0$. By continuity, choose a convex Euclidean ball $Q_ k$ about $\phi _ k(a)$ with $\overline{Q_ k}\subset \phi _ k(N)$, on which the Hessian is positive definite. Choose $\varepsilon >0$ so small that the closed coordinate ball \[  \overline U= \phi _ j^{-1}\bigl (\overline{B(\phi _ j(a),\varepsilon )}\bigr ) \subset \bigcap _{k\in J}\phi _ k^{-1}(Q_ k).  \] This is possible because the finite intersection on the right is an open neighborhood of $a$. For each $k\in J$ the inclusion of $U$ in that neighborhood gives the exact identity \[  \phi _ k(U)= \{ z\in Q_ k:f(\phi _ k^{-1}(z))<\varepsilon ^2\} .  \] The right side is convex: along every segment in the convex domain $Q_ k$, its defining function has nonnegative second derivative, so its value is at most the interpolation of the endpoint values. Notice that convexity is proved on the whole domain $Q_ k$, not merely at points of the sublevel set. Since $U\subset N$, every smaller chart meeting $U$ has index in $J$. Thus ( 10.63.6 ) holds, proving the claim. For every $l$ apply the claim with $G=V_ l$ to the points of $K_ l$, and choose finitely many of the resulting balls covering $K_ l$. Their combined family $(U_\alpha )$ is locally finite: a neighborhood meeting only finitely many $V_ l$ meets only finitely many of these balls. It covers $M$ because the $K_ l$ do, and it refines the original prescribed cover because every $V_ l$ does. Finally, let $U_{\alpha _0}\cap \cdots \cap U_{\alpha _ q}$ be nonempty, and choose $j$ with $U_{\alpha _0}\subset \Omega '_ j$ from ( 10.63.6 ). Every $U_{\alpha _ i}$ meets $\Omega '_ j$ at a point of the common intersection. The same condition therefore puts all these balls inside $\Omega _ j$ and makes every $\phi _ j(U_{\alpha _ i})$ convex. The restriction of $\phi _ j$ identifies their intersection with the intersection of these convex open sets, which is convex and open. Straight-line contraction to any one of its points, transported by this diffeomorphism, is smooth. This proves the theorem. $\square$ Lemma 10.63.7 . A49628740AA3 Every compact smooth manifold has arbitrarily fine finite good covers. Here a cover is good if each of its nonempty finite intersections is smoothly contractible. Proof. A compact Hausdorff space is paracompact: every open cover has a finite subcover, which is locally finite. Apply theorem 10.63.5 and retain a finite subcover. Its nonempty finite intersections are smoothly contractible by that theorem. The empty manifold has the empty cover. $\square$

title: 10.64 A finite integer complex and coefficient comparison
search_title: A finite integer complex and coefficient comparison
section: 10.64 A finite integer complex and coefficient comparison
text: Theorem 10.64.1 . F04BCA811EFA For a compact smooth manifold $M$ there is a finite cochain complex $D^\bullet $ of finitely generated free abelian groups with integer differentials, and natural coefficient isomorphisms \[  H^ q(M,\underline A)\simeq H^ q(D^\bullet \otimes _{\mathbb Z}A)  \] for every abelian group $A$. A single chosen finite good cover gives all these isomorphisms compatibly with coefficient homomorphisms; their comparison with sheaf cohomology is the existing natural one. For any Noetherian commutative coefficient ring $R$, $H^ q(M,\underline R)$ is a finitely generated $R$-module. Proof. Choose the finite good cover $(U_ i)_{1\le i\le N}$ of the lemma. Every nonempty finite intersection is contractible, so the homotopy theorem makes it acyclic with every constant coefficient group. Let $D^ q$ have one copy of $\mathbb Z$ for each increasing $(q+1)$-tuple with nonempty intersection, and use the alternating restriction differential. The intersections are connected, so their constant-sheaf sections equal $A$. The alternating Čech complex is exactly $D^\bullet \otimes A$, and is zero above $N-1$. The integral alternating homotopy and the actual acyclic-cover comparison identify its cohomology with sheaf cohomology, naturally in $A$. This uses no singular chain or triangulation theorem. For $A=R$ the complex has finite free $R$-terms. Over a Noetherian ring every submodule of a finite free module is finitely generated: induct on the number of coordinates, projecting to the last coordinate, an ideal, and lifting its finitely many generators. Kernels and their quotients therefore give the claimed finite generation. No such conclusion is asserted for an arbitrary ring. $\square$ Lemma 10.64.2 . 7C6F99D51075 Let $D^\bullet $ be a finite complex of finite free abelian groups. Its cohomology groups are finitely generated. The natural maps \[  H^ q(D)\otimes \mathbb Q\longrightarrow H^ q(D\otimes \mathbb Q), \qquad H^ q(D)\otimes \mathbb R\longrightarrow H^ q(D\otimes \mathbb R)  \] are isomorphisms. The kernel of $H^ q(D)\to H^ q(D\otimes \mathbb R)$ is exactly its finite torsion subgroup, and its image is a full lattice in that finite-dimensional real vector space. The rational image is its rational span and is dense. Proof. A subgroup of $\mathbb Z^ m$ is finite free: project onto the last coordinate, whose image is $d\mathbb Z$; if $d>0$, choose a lift of $d$ and split off its infinite cyclic subgroup, then induct on $m$. If the image is zero just use the kernel. Consequently the cycle group $Z$ and boundary group $B\subset Z$ are finite free. Put $S=(\operatorname {span}_{\mathbb Q}B)\cap Z$. For a basis $b_1,\ldots ,b_ s$ of $B$, choose a nonzero $s$-row minor of its coordinates in a basis of $Z$, with determinant $d\ne 0$. Cramer's rule gives $dS\subset B$, so $S/B$ is finite; it is precisely the torsion subgroup of $Z/B$. If $B=0$, take $S=0$. The quotient $Z/S$ injects into the rational vector space $(Z\otimes \mathbb Q)/(B\otimes \mathbb Q)$. Choose a rational basis there and clear the denominators of the finitely many images of generators of $Z$. This embeds $Z/S$ into some $\mathbb Z^ b$; the subgroup argument makes it free. Its basis lifts split the finitely generated group $Z/B$ as a free group plus its finite torsion. Gaussian elimination with rational row operations shows that the kernel of an integer matrix over $\mathbb R$ is the real span of its rational kernel. Clearing denominators shows the latter is the rational span of its integer kernel. Images have the same span property directly. Thus the cohomology over $\mathbb Q$ or $\mathbb R$ is the corresponding scalar extension of $(Z/B)$. Explicitly a lifted basis of $Z/S$ is a rational basis modulo $B\otimes \mathbb Q$, and remains a real basis: a nonzero rational minor detects the same rank over both fields. Its integral span is exactly the image of $Z/B$, and so is a full lattice. Rational coefficients give its rational span. Rational approximation in each of finitely many basis coordinates proves density. This proves the natural maps stated, not merely equality of their dimensions. $\square$ Theorem 10.64.3 . 04921B659563 For every compact smooth manifold $M$ and every $q$, the natural coefficient maps induce \[  H^ q(M,\underline{\mathbb Z})\otimes \mathbb Q \simeq H^ q(M,\underline{\mathbb Q}),\qquad H^ q(M,\underline{\mathbb Z})\otimes \mathbb R \simeq H^ q(M,\underline{\mathbb R}).  \] Through the existing real de Rham comparison, the integral image $I^ q\subset H^ q_{\rm dR}(M,\mathbb R)$ is a full lattice; its kernel is exactly the finite torsion subgroup. The rational image is the dense rational span of $I^ q$. All statements commute with coefficient maps and smooth pullbacks. In particular real degree-two cohomology has a basis consisting of integral-image classes. Proof. Apply the preceding two results using the same finite cover for all three coefficients. Naturality of the actual Čech-to-Godement maps identifies these scalar-extension maps with the sheaf coefficient maps. Different covers give the same maps by refinement. The existing de Rham resolution comparison is natural in maps and coefficients. Transporting the finite-matrix conclusions through it proves every assertion. Retain the positive connecting normalization of corollary 10.43.11 ; no new sign convention or integral/singular comparison is introduced. $\square$
