Over a Noetherian ring every submodule of a finite free module is finitely generated: induct on the number of coordinates, projecting to the last coordinate, an ideal, and lifting its finitely many generators. Kernels and their quotients therefore give the claimed finite generation. No such conclusion is asserted for an arbitrary ring. $\square$

title: Lemma 10.64.2
section: 10.64 A finite integer complex and coefficient comparison
text: Lemma 10.64.2 . 7C6F99D51075 Let $D^\bullet $ be a finite complex of finite free abelian groups. Its cohomology groups are finitely generated. The natural maps \[  H^ q(D)\otimes \mathbb Q\longrightarrow H^ q(D\otimes \mathbb Q), \qquad H^ q(D)\otimes \mathbb R\longrightarrow H^ q(D\otimes \mathbb R)  \] are isomorphisms. The kernel of $H^ q(D)\to H^ q(D\otimes \mathbb R)$ is exactly its finite torsion subgroup, and its image is a full lattice in that finite-dimensional real vector space. The rational image is its rational span and is dense. Proof. A subgroup of $\mathbb Z^ m$ is finite free: project onto the last coordinate, whose image is $d\mathbb Z$; if $d>0$, choose a lift of $d$ and split off its infinite cyclic subgroup, then induct on $m$. If the image is zero just use the kernel. Consequently the cycle group $Z$ and boundary group $B\subset Z$ are finite free. Put $S=(\operatorname {span}_{\mathbb Q}B)\cap Z$. For a basis $b_1,\ldots ,b_ s$ of $B$, choose a nonzero $s$-row minor of its coordinates in a basis of $Z$, with determinant $d\ne 0$. Cramer's rule gives $dS\subset B$, so $S/B$ is finite; it is precisely the torsion subgroup of $Z/B$. If $B=0$, take $S=0$. The quotient $Z/S$ injects into the rational vector space $(Z\otimes \mathbb Q)/(B\otimes \mathbb Q)$. Choose a rational basis there and clear the denominators of the finitely many images of generators of $Z$. This embeds $Z/S$ into some $\mathbb Z^ b$; the subgroup argument makes it free. Its basis lifts split the finitely generated group $Z/B$ as a free group plus its finite torsion. Gaussian elimination with rational row operations shows that the kernel of an integer matrix over $\mathbb R$ is the real span of its rational kernel. Clearing denominators shows the latter is the rational span of its integer kernel. Images have the same span property directly. Thus the cohomology over $\mathbb Q$ or $\mathbb R$ is the corresponding scalar extension of $(Z/B)$. Explicitly a lifted basis of $Z/S$ is a rational basis modulo $B\otimes \mathbb Q$, and remains a real basis: a nonzero rational minor detects the same rank over both fields. Its integral span is exactly the image of $Z/B$, and so is a full lattice. Rational coefficients give its rational span. Rational approximation in each of finitely many basis coordinates proves density. This proves the natural maps stated, not merely equality of their dimensions. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.64.3
section: 10.64 A finite integer complex and coefficient comparison
text: Theorem 10.64.3 . 04921B659563 For every compact smooth manifold $M$ and every $q$, the natural coefficient maps induce \[  H^ q(M,\underline{\mathbb Z})\otimes \mathbb Q \simeq H^ q(M,\underline{\mathbb Q}),\qquad H^ q(M,\underline{\mathbb Z})\otimes \mathbb R \simeq H^ q(M,\underline{\mathbb R}).  \] Through the existing real de Rham comparison, the integral image $I^ q\subset H^ q_{\rm dR}(M,\mathbb R)$ is a full lattice; its kernel is exactly the finite torsion subgroup. The rational image is the dense rational span of $I^ q$. All statements commute with coefficient maps and smooth pullbacks. In particular real degree-two cohomology has a basis consisting of integral-image classes. Proof. Apply the preceding two results using the same finite cover for all three coefficients. Naturality of the actual Čech-to-Godement maps identifies these scalar-extension maps with the sheaf coefficient maps. Different covers give the same maps by refinement. The existing de Rham resolution comparison is natural in maps and coefficients. Transporting the finite-matrix conclusions through it proves every assertion. Retain the positive connecting normalization of corollary 10.43.11 ; no new sign convention or integral/singular comparison is introduced. $\square$

section: 10.65 Integral two-periods on a real torus
text: Theorem 10.65.1 . 19630A31AE86 Let $T=V/\Gamma $ be a real torus, with lattice basis $\gamma _1,\ldots ,\gamma _ m$ and dual linear coordinates $x_1,\ldots ,x_ m$ on $V$. A constant real two-form \[  \alpha =\sum _{j<k}a_{jk}\, dx_ j\wedge dx_ k  \] has integral de Rham class, in the image $I^2$, if and only if $a_{jk}\in \mathbb Z$ for every $j<k$. Equivalently its alternating period on every lattice parallelogram is an integer. This criterion uses the coefficient/de Rham normalization already fixed for integral first Chern classes. Proof. We first verify necessity without an assumed integral fundamental class or singular-cohomology pairing. By the smooth classification in theorem 10.40.2 , an integral class is $c_1^{\mathbb Z}(L)$ for a smooth Hermitian line bundle. Choose a compatible connection $D$. By theorem 10.40.5 its real image is represented by $\omega =\mathrm i\Theta (D)/(2\pi )$. For any $\gamma ,\eta \in \Gamma $, pull the bundle and connection back by $\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2\to T$, $(s,t)\mapsto s\gamma +t\eta $. Its further pullback to $\mathbb R^2$ is trivial: the latter is contractible by a smooth linear homotopy, so has $H^2(\underline{\mathbb Z})=0$, and the same smooth classification applies. A global unit frame gives an imaginary connection one-form $B$ on $\mathbb R^2$. Its unit frame transformations under the two deck translations are smooth circle-valued functions $g_1,g_2$, with \[  B(s+1,t)-B(s,t)=g_1^{-1}dg_1,\qquad B(s,t+1)-B(s,t)=g_2^{-1}dg_2,  \] and the corner identity \[  g_1(0,1)g_2(0,0)=g_2(1,0)g_1(0,0).  \] Choose real arguments $f_1(t)$ and $f_2(s)$ for $g_1(0,t)$ and $g_2(s,0)$, with exponential $\exp (2\pi \mathrm i f_ l)$. Such arguments on an interval exist explicitly: integrate $g^{-1}g'/(2\pi \mathrm i)$ after choosing the initial argument; the exponential divided by $g$ has derivative zero. Stokes on the square gives \[  \frac1{2\pi \mathrm i}\int _{[0,1]^2}dB =f_1(1)-f_1(0)-f_2(1)+f_2(0)\in \mathbb Z,  \] where integrality is exactly the corner identity. Since $\mathrm i/(2\pi )=-1/(2\pi \mathrm i)$, the normalized curvature period is the negative of this integer. Exact forms integrate to zero on the torus by the existing compact Stokes theorem. Therefore the period of $\alpha $ on this parallelogram is integral as well. For $(\gamma ,\eta )=(\gamma _ j,\gamma _ k)$ it equals $a_{jk}$. For sufficiency identify $V$ with $\mathbb R^ m$ by the lattice basis. For each $j<k$ let $\mathbb Z^ m$ act on $\mathbb R^ m\times \mathbb C$ by \[  \gamma \cdot (x,z)= (x+\gamma ,\exp (2\pi \mathrm i\gamma _ jx_ k)z).  \] The two successive phase factors differ from the factor for their sum by $\exp (2\pi \mathrm i\gamma _ j\eta _ k)=1$; this is an action. Small coordinate neighborhoods with disjoint lattice translates give bundle trivializations of its quotient, a smooth Hermitian line bundle on $T$. For its pullback frame $e(x)=[x,1]$ one has $e(x+\gamma )=\exp (-2\pi \mathrm i\gamma _ jx_ k)e(x)$. The imaginary one-form \[  B=-2\pi \mathrm i x_ j\, dx_ k  \] has exactly the required frame transformation, since its translate differs by $-2\pi \mathrm i\gamma _ jdx_ k$. It defines a compatible connection whose normalized curvature is $dx_ j\wedge dx_ k$. The checked curvature/connecting theorem makes this an integral-image class with this positive sign. Tensor powers, duals and tensor products realize every integer combination of these forms. This proves sufficiency, including $m<2$ where the sum is zero. An arbitrary lattice parallelogram period is an integer combination of the basis entries, proving the equivalent formulation. $\square$ Proposition 10.65.2 . 769E96CD43B2 Every closed smooth real form on a real torus is cohomologous to a unique constant form. On a complex torus averaging preserves type and preserves strict positivity of a real $(1,1)$-form. In particular every Kähler class has a constant positive representative, to which theorem 10.65.1 applies. Proof. Write $\tau _ a$ for translation by $a$, taking representatives $a\in [0,1]^ m$. For its constant vector field $V_ a$, direct coordinate differentiation gives \[  \frac d{dt}\tau _{ta}^*u =d(\tau _{ta}^*\iota _{V_ a}u)+\tau _{ta}^*\iota _{V_ a}(du).  \] Integrating first in $t$ and then in $a$ proves $\overline u-u=dK u+Kdu$, with \[  \overline u=\int _{[0,1]^ m}\tau _ a^*u\, da, \qquad Ku=\int _{[0,1]^ m}\int _0^1 \tau _{ta}^*\iota _{V_ a}u\, dt\, da.  \] All coefficients and derivatives are smooth on compact parameter sets, so these integrations commute with differentiation. The coefficients of $\overline u$ in the frame $dx_ J$ are constant: integrating a periodic function over a full period in each variable is independent of the translate, by the fundamental theorem of calculus or change of variables one coordinate at a time. Conversely a constant exact form $u=dv$ has $u=d\overline v=0$, proving uniqueness. Complex-torus translations are holomorphic, so type is preserved. For every nonzero tangent vector a positive $(1,1)$-form evaluates positively on that vector and its complex partner at every translate, hence its average does also. Closedness follows either from the identity or differentiation under the integral. $\square$

title: 10.66 The sphere calculation
text: Proposition 10.66.1 . 91C788EF5865 For every abelian group $A$ and $n\ge 1$, \[  H^ q(S^ n,\underline A)= \begin{cases} A,& q=0\text{ or }q=n,\\ 0,& \text{otherwise}. \end{cases}  \] Proof. For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, flabbiness of each Godement term gives an exact sequence of complexes \[  0\to C^\bullet A(X)\to C^\bullet A(U)\oplus C^\bullet A(V) \xrightarrow {(u,v)\mapsto v|_{U\cap V}-u|_{U\cap V}} C^\bullet A(U\cap V)\to 0.  \] The kernel assertion is sheaf gluing; surjectivity follows by extending an overlap section to $V$. The existing long exact sequence of complexes supplies ordinary Mayer–Vietoris, since restriction of these terms is still a flabby resolution on the open sets. Remove opposite poles from $S^ n$ to give $U,V$, each homeomorphic to $\mathbb R^ n$ by stereographic projection. For $n=1$ their intersection is two contractible arcs. The degree-zero difference map $A^2\to A^2$ is $(a,b)\mapsto (b-a,b-a)$, with cokernel $A$; all positive groups of these opens and intersections vanish by homotopy invariance. This gives $H^1(S^1)=A$ and no higher groups. For $n\ge 2$ the intersection deformation retracts onto the equator $S^{n-1}$: write a point as $(t,\sqrt{1-t^2}\, v)$ with $-1<t<1$, $v\in S^{n-1}$, and replace $t$ by $(1-s)t$. It is connected, so the degree-zero difference map is onto and $H^1(S^ n)=0$. For $q\ge 2$ the same exact sequence gives $H^ q(S^ n)=H^{q-1}(S^{n-1})$. Induction proves the result; $H^0=A$ follows from connectedness. All maps are the actual coefficient maps, with no homology or singular comparison assumed. $\square$

title: Proposition 6.37.1
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text: Proposition 6.37.1 . 8EFE1AE46FF7 The boundary measure of $\varphi _{a,\lambda }$ at level $r$ is \[  \mu _ r=\Lambda \tau _{a,\lambda ,r}.  \] Consequently every plurisubharmonic function $V$ defined near $Q_{a,\lambda }(r)$ has a finite angular mean $m_ V(r)=\tau _{a,\lambda ,r}(V)$. Proof. Translate $a$ to zero. By corollary 6.36.9 , the actual top Monge–Ampere measure of the weight is $\Lambda \delta _0$. Its boundary measure, from proposition 6.36.1 , is therefore $\mu _ r=(dd^ c\max \{ \varphi _{0,\lambda },r\} )^ n$ and is positive, supported on $\{ \varphi _{0,\lambda }=r\} $, with mass $\Lambda $. At a point of this level outside the distinguished boundary some index $k$ satisfies $\lambda _ k\log |z_ k|^2<r$. In a neighborhood of that point, the truncated potential is \[  \max \{ r,\lambda _ j\log |z_ j|^2:j\ne k\} ,  \] which is continuous, locally bounded and independent of $z_ k$. Regularize it in the other $n-1$ variables on a product neighborhood. The regularizations converge locally uniformly; every smooth $n$th Hessian power is zero by degree. Hence uniform convergence of bounded Bedford–Taylor products makes the original $n$th power zero there. When $n=1$ the potential is the constant $r$. It follows that $\mu _ r$ is supported on the distinguished torus. Independent coordinate rotations preserve the potential and hence its bounded product measure. For a continuous function $f$ on the torus, average $f$ over these rotations with product angular probability. The resulting function is constant, equal to $\tau _{0,\lambda ,r}(f)$; translation of each angular integration variable proves this directly. Invariance and Fubini therefore give \[  \mu _ r(f)=\int \mu _ r(f\circ \mathcal R_\theta ) \frac{d\theta }{(2\pi )^ n} =\Lambda \tau _{0,\lambda ,r}(f).  \] Equality on continuous functions gives equality of the finite Borel measures. Translation proves the assertion at $a$. Finally proposition 6.36.1 gives $\mu _ r$-integrability of every such PSH $V$, including its negative-infinite values. Since $\Lambda >0$, its angular mean is finite as asserted. $\square$

title: Lemma 6.37.2
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text: Lemma 6.37.2 . 8A0C22EC23BC Let $V$ be plurisubharmonic on a neighborhood of the closed polydisc $Q=\{ |z_ j-a_ j|\leq R_ j\} $, where $R_ j>0$. For every interior point $z$, put $w_ j=(z_ j-a_ j)/R_ j$. Then 1A7B33754DD6 6.37.3 \begin{equation}  V(z)\leq \int _{[0,2\pi ]^ n} V(a_1+R_1e^{i\theta _1},\ldots ,a_ n+R_ ne^{i\theta _ n}) \prod _{j=1}^ n\frac{1-|w_ j|^2}{|e^{i\theta _ j}-w_ j|^2} \frac{d\theta }{(2\pi )^ n}. \end{equation} The integral is interpreted as a bounded-above extended integral. In particular, if $V\leq 0$ on $Q$ and $|w_ j|\leq \eta _ j<1$, then E5DFC36BFD39 6.37.4 \begin{equation}  V(z)\leq \left(\prod _ j\frac{1-\eta _ j}{1+\eta _ j}\right) \int _{[0,2\pi ]^ n} V(a_1+R_1e^{i\theta _1},\ldots ,a_ n+R_ ne^{i\theta _ n}) \frac{d\theta }{(2\pi )^ n}. \end{equation} Also $\sup _ QV=\sup _{\partial _{\rm d}Q}V$, where $\partial _{\rm d}Q$ is the distinguished boundary. Proof. We first verify the one-variable Poisson inequality without any boundary continuity assumption on the subharmonic function. For a bounded subharmonic $u$ near a closed disc, take continuous boundary majorants decreasing to its upper semicontinuous boundary values, using decreasing continuous majorants of upper semicontinuous functions . Their Poisson integrals are harmonic with those boundary values by the Dirichlet problem on a ball . Subharmonic comparison subharmonic comparison and mean inequalities bounds $u$ by each of them. Decreasing convergence of these finite integrals gives the desired Poisson bound with $u$'s actual boundary values. The normalized disc kernel is exactly $(1-|w|^2)/|e^{i\theta }-w|^2$. For $V_ N=\max \{ V,-N\} $, the restriction to each coordinate disc is bounded subharmonic. Apply the one-variable inequality in the first coordinate, then to every boundary value in the second, and so on. Positive kernels preserve the inequalities; boundedness and Fubini justify every iterated integral. This proves ( 6.37.3 ) for $V_ N$. A common finite upper bound exists on $Q$. Subtracting from it and using monotone convergence lets $N\to \infty $ and proves the extended inequality for $V$. This includes coordinate slices on which $V$ is identically $-\infty $; their bounded truncations were constant subharmonic functions. For $|w|\leq \eta <1$ the positive normalized kernel satisfies \[  \frac{1-|w|^2}{|e^{i\theta }-w|^2} \geq \frac{1-|w|}{1+|w|} \geq \frac{1-\eta }{1+\eta }.  \] Since $V\leq 0$, multiplication by this lower bound gives the upper bound on its weighted integral in ( 6.37.4 ), with the stated direction. For the supremum assertion apply the product Poisson bound to $V_ N$: its product kernel is probability, so $V_ N(z)\leq \sup _{\partial _{\rm d}Q}V_ N$ at interior points. The same inequality holds on all of $Q$: apply the same argument in the coordinates that are strictly interior, fixing all other coordinates at their boundary values. If no coordinate is interior, the point already belongs to the distinguished boundary. Let $N\to \infty $; since $\sup _{\partial _{\rm d}Q}V_ N= \max \{ \sup _{\partial _{\rm d}Q}V,-N\} $, this gives $V\leq \sup _{\partial _{\rm d}Q}V$ throughout $Q$. The reverse supremum inequality is inclusion. $\square$

title: 10.67 Algebraic tensor products and universal coefficients
search_title: Algebraic tensor products and universal coefficients
section: 10.67 Algebraic tensor products and universal coefficients
text: Until a principal ideal domain is explicitly assumed, $R$ is a commutative ring with identity. Modules are unital. All tensor products in this section are algebraic tensor products over $R$. An arbitrary direct-sum total complex is used: \[  (K\otimes L)^ n=\bigoplus _{p+q=n}K^ p\otimes L^ q, \qquad D(k\otimes l)=d_ Kk\otimes l+(-1)^ p k\otimes d_ Ll.  \] Thus every element has finite support in the bidegrees, even when the complexes are unbounded. There is no topology or completion. A principal ideal domain is, in particular, an integral domain; the zero ring and principal ideal rings with zero divisors are not included in that later hypothesis.

title: 10.67.1 Resolutions, torsion products and principal ideal domains
search_title: Resolutions, torsion products and principal ideal domains
section: 10.67 Algebraic tensor products and universal coefficients
text:
Lemma 10.67.2 . BB113EE3ABCF Tensor product is right exact and commutes with direct sums and filtered direct limits in either variable. Filtered direct limits of modules are exact. A module is projective if and only if it is a direct summand of a free module. Projective modules are flat, and every module has a free resolution in nonnegative homological degrees. Proof. For a submodule $A\subset B$, a balanced bilinear map on $(B/A)\times M$ is precisely a balanced bilinear map on $B\times M$ vanishing on $A\times M$. Consequently \[  (B/A)\otimes M=(B\otimes M)/\operatorname {im}(A\otimes M).  \] The same universal property identifies tensoring a direct sum or a filtered direct limit with the direct sum or direct limit of the tensors. In a filtered limit, an element represented at one stage is zero if it becomes zero at a subsequent stage. More generally, any equality of finitely many representatives holds at a common subsequent stage: the filteredness conditions combine the finitely many indices and equalize the finitely many arrows. Applying this observation to a kernel element in a compatible system of exact sequences proves exactness at the middle term; lifting a representative proves surjectivity at the last term. It also proves that cohomology commutes with filtered limits. Direct sums are exact by the same finite-support argument. Here projective means that every map from the module to the target of a surjection lifts through that surjection. For a free module, lift each basis vector; for a direct summand, restrict such a lift after projecting the free module to its summand. Conversely, a free surjection onto a projective module splits by lifting its identity. Tensoring a free module is a direct sum of copies of the original sequence and therefore preserves injections. The same is true for a direct summand, proving flatness. Finally, take a free surjection $P_0\to A$, then a free surjection onto its kernel, and repeat. The resulting augmented complex $P_\bullet \to A$ is exact, with $P_ q=0$ for $q<0$. $\square$ Proposition 10.67.3 . E5490FB46564 Let $P_\bullet \to A$ and $Q_\bullet \to B$ be projective resolutions. The modules \[  \operatorname {Tor}^ R_ q(A,B)=H_ q(P_\bullet \otimes B) \simeq H_ q\operatorname {Tot}(P_\bullet \otimes Q_\bullet ) \simeq H_ q(A\otimes Q_\bullet )  \] are independent of the resolutions, naturally in both variables. They are also computed by any flat resolution in the resolved variable. They are symmetric, commute with filtered direct limits in either variable, and satisfy $\operatorname {Tor}_0^ R(A,B)=A\otimes B$. Each short exact sequence in either variable gives its natural long exact Tor sequence. A module $B$ is flat if and only if $\operatorname {Tor}_1^ R(A,B)=0$ for every $A$; in this case all positive Tor groups with $B$ vanish. Proof. For a map $a:A\to A'$, a projective resolution $P$ of $A$, and any exact resolution $P'$ of $A'$, lift $a\epsilon :P_0\to A'$ to $P'_0$. If $f_0,\ldots ,f_{q-1}$ have been constructed, $f_{q-1}\partial $ has image in $\ker \partial '_{q-1}=\operatorname {im}\partial '_ q$. Projectivity of $P_ q$ gives $f_ q$. Two such lifts satisfy \[  f_ q-g_ q=\partial '_{q+1}h_ q+h_{q-1}\partial _ q, \qquad h_{-1}=0.  \] Indeed, in degree zero their difference has image in $\ker \epsilon '$, so one chooses $h_0$. Inductively the difference $f_ q-g_ q-h_{q-1}\partial _ q$ has zero differential, by the previous-degree identity, and lifts to $P'_{q+1}$ by projectivity. After tensoring, this remains a homotopy. Lifts of identities and compositions are therefore unique on homology. This proves resolution independence and functoriality for projective resolutions. The differential on the homological double complex is $\partial _ P\otimes 1+(-1)^ p1\otimes \partial _ Q$ on $P_ p\otimes Q_ q$. For fixed $p$, flatness of $P_ p$ gives the augmented exact column $P_ p\otimes Q_\bullet \to P_ p\otimes B$; the analogous augmented rows are exact by flatness of $Q_ q$. The homological version of the finite elimination in lemma 10.43.15 makes both augmentations quasi-isomorphisms. Explicitly, lift a degree-$n$ cycle of $P\otimes B$ to $P_ n\otimes Q_0$. Its horizontal differential has zero augmentation, so exactness of the next column supplies a correction in $P_{n-1}\otimes Q_1$. Continue through $P_{n-2}\otimes Q_2$ down to $P_0\otimes Q_ n$; the vertical sign $(-1)^ p$ is absorbed in each correction. There is no next horizontal term, so the result is a total cycle. For injectivity, subtract a lift of a boundary to make the augmentation of a total cycle zero. Kill its component in $P_ n\otimes Q_0$ by a vertical preimage in $P_ n\otimes Q_1$. The next component is vertically closed by the total cycle equation, so it too has a preimage. Continue down to horizontal degree zero. The sum of these finitely many preimages bounds the original cycle. These constructions are the augmentation maps' surjectivity and injectivity on homology, not choices defining those maps. Only $p,q\geq 0$ occur, so no unbounded convergence is used. The same argument works with an arbitrary flat resolution in place of $P$ or $Q$; it does not require comparison lifts from a flat module. The interchange \[  P_ p\otimes Q_ q\longrightarrow Q_ q\otimes P_ p, \qquad x\otimes y\longmapsto (-1)^{pq}y\otimes x  \] commutes with the differentials and gives the natural symmetry. This fixes the symmetry convention also in positive Tor degree. Right exactness gives the assertion in degree zero. For $0\to A\to A'\to A''\to 0$, the free resolution $Q$ of $B$ gives a short exact sequence \[  0\longrightarrow A\otimes Q_\bullet \longrightarrow A'\otimes Q_\bullet \longrightarrow A''\otimes Q_\bullet \longrightarrow 0.  \] The long exact sequence of lemma 10.43.3 , reindexed homologically, applies. Its connecting map lifts a cycle to the middle complex and takes its differential in the first complex. This description proves naturality and fixes its sign. Symmetry gives the sequence in the other variable. If $B$ is flat, tensoring the augmented resolution $P\to A$ stays exact, giving positive-degree vanishing. Conversely, the part \[  \operatorname {Tor}_1^ R(A'',B)\longrightarrow A\otimes B \longrightarrow A'\otimes B  \] shows that the stated vanishing implies preservation of every injection, hence flatness. Finally compute a filtered limit in the first variable using the fixed free resolution $Q$ of $B$. Tensor and homology commute with that limit by lemma 10.67.2 . Symmetry treats the other variable. No assertion about arbitrary, unfiltered colimits is being made. $\square$ Lemma 10.67.4 . 3F097EB89283 Over a principal ideal domain every submodule of a free module is free, with no finite-generation assumption. Every finitely generated module is a finite direct sum of a free module and cyclic modules $R/aR$ with $a\ne 0$. A module is flat if and only if it is torsion free. A projective module is free, but a flat module need not be free. Proof. Well order a basis $(e_\alpha )_{\alpha <\kappa }$ of a free module $F$, and set \[  F_\alpha =\bigoplus _{\beta <\alpha }Re_\beta , \qquad N_\alpha =N\cap F_\alpha  \] for a submodule $N\subset F$. The $e_\alpha $ coordinate identifies $N_{\alpha +1}/N_\alpha $ with an ideal $I_\alpha $ of $R$. If this ideal is nonzero, choose its generator $a_\alpha $ and a vector $v_\alpha \in N_{\alpha +1}$ with that coordinate. Every element of $N_{\alpha +1}$ differs by a multiple of $v_\alpha $ from one in $N_\alpha $, and the sum is direct because $a_\alpha \ne 0$ in a domain. If $I_\alpha =0$, the two successive submodules agree. At a limit ordinal, $N_\lambda =\bigcup _{\alpha <\lambda }N_\alpha $, because each vector has finite support. Transfinite induction thus gives a basis consisting of the selected $v_\alpha $. For a submodule of $R^ m$ the same proof gives at most $m$ basis vectors. A finitely generated module has a presentation $0\to N\to R^ m\to A\to 0$, and the preceding finite-rank case makes its relation matrix finite. We give the required diagonal reduction over a PID without assuming a Euclidean algorithm. Move a nonzero entry $a$ to the upper-left corner. For another entry $b$ in its column, let $g$ generate $(a,b)$, write $a=ga'$, $b=gb'$, and choose $u,v$ with $ua'+vb'=1$. The invertible row operation with matrix \[  \begin{pmatrix} u

& v

\\ -b'

& a'

\end{pmatrix}  \] replaces the two entries by $g,0$. Column operations do the same for the first row. Whenever an entry was not divisible by the old pivot, its principal ideal strictly increases. An increasing chain of ideals in a PID stabilizes: its union is an ideal $(c)$, and its generator already belongs to one stage. Thus only finitely many such strict increases occur. When all entries in the first row and column are divisible by the pivot, ordinary row and column subtractions clear them. If a remaining entry $b$ is not divisible by the pivot, add its row to the first row and repeat the Bezout operation; this again strictly increases the pivot ideal. Eventually the pivot divides every entry and the first row and column are cleared. Repeat on the remaining smaller matrix. All of its entries remain divisible by the first pivot, so the successive nonzero diagonal entries can be taken to satisfy $a_1\mid a_2\mid \cdots $. The cokernel is the asserted direct sum; unit entries give zero summands. The inclusion matrix has independent columns over the fraction field, so its diagonal has no zero relation column. If a finitely generated module is torsion free, all its nonzero cyclic torsion summands vanish, and it is free. Every torsion-free module is the filtered union of its finitely generated submodules, which are consequently free. Exactness of filtered limits and tensor shows that it is flat. Conversely, tensor the injection $R\xrightarrow {a}R$ for every $a\ne 0$ with a flat module: multiplication by $a$ remains injective, proving torsion-freeness. A projective module is a submodule of a free module and hence free. For the distinction from flatness, $\mathbb Q$ is a flat $\mathbb Z$-module, but is not free: every nonzero free abelian group has a basis vector not divisible by $2$, whereas every element of $\mathbb Q$ is divisible by $2$. $\square$ Corollary 10.67.5 . 9E1649673CCE Over a principal ideal domain, $\operatorname {Tor}_ q^ R(A,B)=0$ for $q\geq 2$. Write $A\star B=\operatorname {Tor}_1^ R(A,B)$ and $B[a]=\{ b\in B:ab=0\} $. For $a\ne 0$ one has \[  (R/aR)\star B=B[a].  \] If $a,b\ne 0$ and $g$ generates $(a,b)$, then \[  (R/aR)\star (R/bR)\simeq R/gR.  \] If either $a=0$ or $b=0$, the latter torsion product is zero, since that factor is free. In contrast, $(R/aR)\otimes (R/bR)=R/(a,b)$ holds also with zero parameters. Every short exact sequence gives the six-term sequence \[  \begin{aligned}  0\longrightarrow A\star B\longrightarrow A'\star B & \longrightarrow A''\star B\longrightarrow A\otimes B\\ & \longrightarrow A'\otimes B\longrightarrow A''\otimes B \longrightarrow 0. \end{aligned}  \] Proof. The kernel of a free surjection onto $A$ is free by lemma 10.67.4 , so $A$ has a free resolution of length one. This proves the vanishing and truncates the long exact sequence. For $a\ne 0$ use the resolution $0\to R\xrightarrow {a}R\to R/aR\to 0$. If $a=ga'$, $b=gb'$ with $(a',b')=R$, the condition $ax\in bR$ is equivalent to $x\in b'R$: Bezout's identity for $a',b'$ proves the nontrivial implication. The map $R\to (R/bR)[a]$, $r\mapsto b'r\bmod bR$, is onto with kernel $gR$. This proves the cyclic formula and specifies its dependence on chosen generators. The tensor formula is right exactness applied to the same quotient presentation. The case $a=0$ uses the free module $R$, not the displayed length-one resolution with a zero, noninjective first map. $\square$

title: Lemma 10.67.4
section: 10.67 Algebraic tensor products and universal coefficients
text:
Lemma 10.67.4 . 3F097EB89283 Over a principal ideal domain every submodule of a free module is free, with no finite-generation assumption. Every finitely generated module is a finite direct sum of a free module and cyclic modules $R/aR$ with $a\ne 0$. A module is flat if and only if it is torsion free. A projective module is free, but a flat module need not be free. Proof. Well order a basis $(e_\alpha )_{\alpha <\kappa }$ of a free module $F$, and set \[  F_\alpha =\bigoplus _{\beta <\alpha }Re_\beta , \qquad N_\alpha =N\cap F_\alpha  \] for a submodule $N\subset F$. The $e_\alpha $ coordinate identifies $N_{\alpha +1}/N_\alpha $ with an ideal $I_\alpha $ of $R$. If this ideal is nonzero, choose its generator $a_\alpha $ and a vector $v_\alpha \in N_{\alpha +1}$ with that coordinate. Every element of $N_{\alpha +1}$ differs by a multiple of $v_\alpha $ from one in $N_\alpha $, and the sum is direct because $a_\alpha \ne 0$ in a domain. If $I_\alpha =0$, the two successive submodules agree. At a limit ordinal, $N_\lambda =\bigcup _{\alpha <\lambda }N_\alpha $, because each vector has finite support. Transfinite induction thus gives a basis consisting of the selected $v_\alpha $. For a submodule of $R^ m$ the same proof gives at most $m$ basis vectors. A finitely generated module has a presentation $0\to N\to R^ m\to A\to 0$, and the preceding finite-rank case makes its relation matrix finite. We give the required diagonal reduction over a PID without assuming a Euclidean algorithm. Move a nonzero entry $a$ to the upper-left corner. For another entry $b$ in its column, let $g$ generate $(a,b)$, write $a=ga'$, $b=gb'$, and choose $u,v$ with $ua'+vb'=1$. The invertible row operation with matrix \[  \begin{pmatrix} u

& v

\\ -b'

& a'

\end{pmatrix}  \] replaces the two entries by $g,0$. Column operations do the same for the first row. Whenever an entry was not divisible by the old pivot, its principal ideal strictly increases. An increasing chain of ideals in a PID stabilizes: its union is an ideal $(c)$, and its generator already belongs to one stage. Thus only finitely many such strict increases occur. When all entries in the first row and column are divisible by the pivot, ordinary row and column subtractions clear them. If a remaining entry $b$ is not divisible by the pivot, add its row to the first row and repeat the Bezout operation; this again strictly increases the pivot ideal. Eventually the pivot divides every entry and the first row and column are cleared. Repeat on the remaining smaller matrix. All of its entries remain divisible by the first pivot, so the successive nonzero diagonal entries can be taken to satisfy $a_1\mid a_2\mid \cdots $. The cokernel is the asserted direct sum; unit entries give zero summands. The inclusion matrix has independent columns over the fraction field, so its diagonal has no zero relation column. If a finitely generated module is torsion free, all its nonzero cyclic torsion summands vanish, and it is free. Every torsion-free module is the filtered union of its finitely generated submodules, which are consequently free. Exactness of filtered limits and tensor shows that it is flat. Conversely, tensor the injection $R\xrightarrow {a}R$ for every $a\ne 0$ with a flat module: multiplication by $a$ remains injective, proving torsion-freeness. A projective module is a submodule of a free module and hence free. For the distinction from flatness, $\mathbb Q$ is a flat $\mathbb Z$-module, but is not free: every nonzero free abelian group has a basis vector not divisible by $2$, whereas every element of $\mathbb Q$ is divisible by $2$. $\square$

Theorem 10.67.7 . 669128A0733C Let $R$ be a principal ideal domain and let $K,L$ be complexes of $R$-modules. Suppose that every term of at least one complex is torsion free. There is a natural short exact sequence ADD4029A2513 10.67.8  egin{equation}   egin{aligned}  0\longrightarrow  igoplus _{p+q=n}H^ p(K)\otimes H^ q(L) & \xrightarrow {\  \mu \  } H^ n(K\otimes L)\ & \xrightarrow {\  
u \  }  igoplus _{p+q=n+1}H^ p(K)\star H^ q(L)\longrightarrow 0, \end{aligned} \end{equation} where $\mu ([k]\otimes [l])=[k\otimes l]$. This assertion uses direct-sum totalization and needs no boundedness or finite-type assumption. The exact sequence splits as a sequence of modules; a natural choice of splitting is not part of the assertion. Proof. We first prove exactness when the terms of $K$ are flat, leaving the splitting and full functorial normalization to the end of the proof. Write $Z^ p=\ker d_ K^ p$ and $B^ p=\operatorname {im}d_ K^{p-1}$. These submodules of torsion-free modules are torsion free, hence flat. Give $Z$ and $Q=K/Z$ zero differentials. The differential of $K$ identifies $Q^ p$ with $B^{p+1}$, so $Q^ p$ is flat. Consequently \[  0\longrightarrow Z\otimes L\longrightarrow K\otimes L \longrightarrow Q\otimes L\longrightarrow 0  \] is an exact sequence of total complexes. Indeed, flatness of $Q^ p$ makes the original short exact sequence stay exact after tensoring by any $L^ q$, and direct sums preserve exactness. Flatness also identifies \[   egin{aligned}  H^ n(Z\otimes L)& = igoplus _{p+q=n}Z^ p\otimes H^ q(L),\  H^{n-1}(Q\otimes L)& = igoplus _{p+q=n}B^ p\otimes H^ q(L). \end{aligned}  \] For this computation, each $Z^ p\otimes L$ is simply a shifted complex with differential $(-1)^ p d_ L$; its cycles and boundaries are the corresponding tensors, by exactness of $Z^ p\otimes -$. Cohomology commutes with the direct sum. Under these identifications, the connecting map from the second displayed group to the first is induced by $B^ p\hookrightarrow Z^ p$, with sign $+1$. To check it, a product class represented by $b\otimes l$ lifts to $k\otimes l$ with $d_ Kk=b$ and $d_ Ll=0$, and $D(k\otimes l)=b\otimes l$. Such classes generate the entire group, because $Q^ p$ is flat. The long exact sequence therefore identifies the kernel and cokernel needed for $H^ n(K\otimes L)$ with the kernel and cokernel of these inclusion maps in degrees $n+1$ and $n$, respectively. The flat presentation $0	o B^ p	o Z^ p	o H^ p(K)	o 0$ gives \[   egin{aligned}  0\longrightarrow H^ p(K)\star H^ q(L) \longrightarrow B^ p\otimes H^ q(L) \longrightarrow Z^ p\otimes H^ q(L)\  \longrightarrow H^ p(K)\otimes H^ q(L)\longrightarrow 0. \end{aligned}  \] This proves the exact sequence and its asserted product map when $K$ is termwise flat. Changing the representative $k$ by $d_ Ka$ changes the product by $D(a\otimes l)$; changing $l$ by $d_ Lb$ changes it by $(-1)^ pD(k\otimes b)$. Thus the map is precisely the canonical cross product. If $L$ is termwise flat, the chain isomorphism $k\otimes l\mapsto (-1)^{pq}l\otimes k$ gives exactness with the roles reversed. Two consequences of this exactness will be used before any splitting is claimed. If a termwise flat complex is acyclic, its tensor with every complex is acyclic. Also, tensoring an arbitrary acyclic complex with a termwise flat complex is acyclic. Both follow immediately because the two outer terms in the already proved sequence vanish. Hence tensoring a quasi-isomorphism between termwise flat complexes with any complex preserves quasi-isomorphisms; likewise tensoring any quasi-isomorphism with a termwise flat complex preserves it. For the first assertion use its acyclic, termwise flat cone. For the second use its acyclic cone and the other flat factor. With the convention \[  \operatorname {Cone}(f)^ j=D^ j\oplus C^{j+1},\qquad d(y,x)=(d_ Dy+fx,-d_ Cx),  \] the identity of the two displayed summands identifies $\operatorname {Cone}(f)\otimes L$ with $\operatorname {Cone}(f\otimes 1)$; the vertical differential on the shifted component has exactly the required minus sign. The long exact cone sequence gives the usual acyclicity criterion. This argument covers unbounded direct sums and uses no spectral sequence. For precision about naturality, there is a functorial, termwise free replacement $\epsilon _ C:P(C)	o C$ over a PID. For every $x\in C^ j$ take a copy of the disk complex $R\xrightarrow {1}R$ in degrees $j,j+1$, mapping its generators to $x,d_ Cx$. Their direct sum is a termwise free complex $F(C)$ with a degreewise surjection $F(C)	o C$. The kernel $N(C)$ is termwise free by lemma 10.67.4 . Put \[  P(C)=\operatorname {Cone} igl (N(C)\hookrightarrow F(C) igr ), \qquad \epsilon _ C(f,n)=\epsilon (f).  \] Its kernel is $\operatorname {Cone}(1_{N(C)})$, which is contractible: $h(a,b)=(0,a)$ satisfies $dh+hd=1$. Thus $\epsilon _ C$ is a quasi-isomorphism and a degreewise surjection. A map $C	o C'$ sends the disk indexed by $x$ to that indexed by its image, giving functorial maps on $F,N,P$ and a natural augmentation. No basis of $N(C)$ is chosen to define these maps; only its freeness is used. Set $P=P(K)$ and $T=P(L)$. The natural map $P\otimes T	o K\otimes L$ is a quasi-isomorphism under the theorem's hypotheses. For example, when $K$ is termwise flat, factor it as $P\otimes T	o P\otimes L	o K\otimes L$. The first arrow uses flatness of $P$ and the acyclic cone of $T	o L$; the second uses that $P	o K$ is a quasi-isomorphism between termwise flat complexes. If $L$ is flat, use the factorization through $K\otimes T$ instead. Transport the exact sequence already constructed for $P,T$ through this natural isomorphism, identifying their cohomologies with those of $K,L$. This specifies $
u $ naturally for all pairs in the theorem. When $K$ is flat it agrees with the preceding cycle–boundary construction, by its naturality under the two comparison maps. In particular it never requires natural choices of cycle complements. Finally, in every free complex $P$ the sequence $0	o Z^ p(P)	o P^ p	o B^{p+1}(P)	o 0$ splits since its last term is free. Choose such complements and define \[  e_ P:P\longrightarrow H(P),\qquad e_ P(z+s)=[z],  \] where the target has zero differential. This is a chain map: $d_ P(z+s)=d_ Ps$ is a boundary and is sent to zero. Define $e_ T$ in the same way. The actual chain map $e_ P\otimes e_ T:P\otimes T	o H(P)\otimes H(T)$ induces a retraction of its cross-product map, since it sends a product of cycle classes to that same tensor. Transport this retraction through the natural comparison just proved. An exact sequence $0	o A\xrightarrow {\mu }E\xrightarrow {
u }B 	o 0$ with a retraction $r:E	o A$ splits: for $b\in B$ choose any lift $x$ and set $s(b)=x-\mu r(x)$. This is independent of the lift and is an $R$-linear section. e 0$ in the theorem. For the second assertion, a torsion-free cohomology factor is flat, so every Tor term vanishes. For an integer $m\geq 2$ take $K^0=\mathbb Z^2$, $K^1=\mathbb Z$, $d(u,v)=mv$, and $M=\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z$. The degree-zero coefficient sequence is \[  0\longrightarrow M\xrightarrow {u\mapsto (u,0)}M^2 \xrightarrow {(u,v)\mapsto v}M\longrightarrow 0.  \] The chain automorphism $(u,v)\mapsto (u+v,v)$, with the identity in degree one, induces the identity on $H(K)$ but the displayed shear on $H^0(K\otimes M)$. A section would have to send $1$ to $(a,1)$; this vector is never fixed by the shear. Hence no section natural under all chain maps can exist. A projection of graded modules $P	o Z(P)$ is not itself a chain map to the zero-differential cycle complex. For $P^0\xrightarrow {1}P^1$ with both terms $R$, the cycles are $Z^0=0$, $Z^1=R$, and the projection $\pi $ satisfies $\pi ^1d^0=1$ but $d_ Z^0\pi ^0=0$. It therefore gives no cohomology arrow $H(P\otimes L)	o H(Z(P)\otimes L)$. The map $e_ P:P	o H(P)$ used in the theorem is valid because it additionally kills boundaries; the retraction uses this map for both free replacements. Proposition 10.67.11 . 64AD0CD558E6 Let $R$ be a principal ideal domain, let $K$ be termwise torsion free, and filter $K\otimes L$ by the $K$ degree. The spectral sequence obtained by first taking $L$ cohomology has \[  E_1^{p,q}=K^ p\otimes H^ q(L),\qquad E_2^{p,q}=H^ p igl (K\otimes H^ q(L) igr ),  \] and all differentials $d_ r$ for $r\geq 2$ vanish. Choose complements $P^ p=Z^ p\oplus S^ p$. As a complex, $P$ is the direct sum, over $a$, of the two-term complexes \[  S^{a-1}\xrightarrow {\  d\  }Z^ a  \] in degrees $a-1,a$. This is an actual decomposition of complexes; the displayed differential has image $B^ a$ and is injective on $S^{a-1}$. After tensoring with $L$, each summand has just these two adjacent $K$ columns. Every $d_ r$ with bidegree $(r,1-r)$ and $r\geq 2$ is therefore zero on that summand. The finite-filtration convergence statement is exactly the filtered-complex construction already established in theorem 10.54.3 ; it is not inferred from an abstract, unfiltered direct-sum isomorphism. $\square$

Its degree-zero cohomology becomes $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$, although $H(K)=0$. Nor is the splitting generally natural in the complexes. The degree-zero coefficient sequence is \[  0\longrightarrow M\xrightarrow {u\mapsto (u,0)}M^2 \xrightarrow {(u,v)\mapsto v}M\longrightarrow 0.  \] The chain automorphism $(u,v)\mapsto (u+v,v)$, with the identity in degree one, induces the identity on $H(K)$ but the displayed shear on $H^0(K\otimes M)$. A section would have to send $1$ to $(a,1)$; this vector is never fixed by the shear. Hence no section natural under all chain maps can exist. A projection of graded modules $P\to Z(P)$ is not itself a chain map to the zero-differential cycle complex. For $P^0\xrightarrow {1}P^1$ with both terms $R$, the cycles are $Z^0=0$, $Z^1=R$, and the projection $\pi $ satisfies $\pi ^1d^0=1$ but $d_ Z^0\pi ^0=0$. It therefore gives no cohomology arrow $H(P\otimes L)\to H(Z(P)\otimes L)$. The map $e_ P:P\to H(P)$ used in the theorem is valid because it additionally kills boundaries; the retraction uses this map for both free replacements.

title: Proposition 10.67.11
section: 10.67 Algebraic tensor products and universal coefficients
text: Proposition 10.67.11 . 64AD0CD558E6 Let $R$ be a principal ideal domain, let $K$ be termwise torsion free, and filter $K\otimes L$ by the $K$ degree. The spectral sequence obtained by first taking $L$ cohomology has \[  E_1^{p,q}=K^ p\otimes H^ q(L),\qquad E_2^{p,q}=H^ p\bigl (K\otimes H^ q(L)\bigr ),  \] and all differentials $d_ r$ for $r\geq 2$ vanish. Whenever the filtration is finite in each relevant total degree, for example when $K$ and $L$ are bounded below, it converges to the associated graded of total cohomology. No general convergence conclusion for an unbounded filtration is included in this statement. Proof. Use the filtered map $P(K)\otimes L\to K\otimes L$ from the theorem. On $E_2$ it is the map $H^ p(P(K)\otimes H^ q(L))\to H^ p(K\otimes H^ q(L))$, which is an isomorphism by the already proved preservation of quasi-isomorphisms between termwise flat complexes. Choose complements $P^ p=Z^ p\oplus S^ p$. As a complex, $P$ is the direct sum, over $a$, of the two-term complexes \[  S^{a-1}\xrightarrow {\  d\  }Z^ a  \] in degrees $a-1,a$. This is an actual decomposition of complexes; the displayed differential has image $B^ a$ and is injective on $S^{a-1}$. After tensoring with $L$, each summand has just these two adjacent $K$ columns. Every $d_ r$ with bidegree $(r,1-r)$ and $r\geq 2$ is therefore zero on that summand. Kernels, images and quotients commute with direct sums of module complexes, so every page and differential of the full filtered complex is the direct sum of those of these summands. The filtered comparison is an isomorphism from $E_2$ onward, giving the asserted vanishing for $K\otimes L$. The finite-filtration convergence statement is exactly the filtered-complex construction already established in theorem 10.54.3 ; it is not inferred from an abstract, unfiltered direct-sum isomorphism. $\square$

title: 10.68 Injective modules and extension modules

A map on a quotient is a map on the middle module annihilating the submodule. A module $I$ is injective if every map $A	o I$ extends across every injection $A\hookrightarrow B$. Proposition 10.68.1 . 4C5B1C59E318 Over a principal ideal domain, a module is injective if and only if it is divisible: for every $a
e 0$, multiplication by $a$ is surjective on the module. In particular, quotients of injective modules are injective over a PID. Proof. For injective $I$, extend the map $aR	o I$ taking $a$ to any prescribed $x\in I$ across $aR\hookrightarrow R$. The image of $1$ is a solution to $ay=x$. Conversely let $I$ be divisible, let $A\subset B$, and let $f:A	o I$. Order its extensions to intermediate submodules by extension of both the domain and map. The union along any chain is a well-defined extension, so Zorn's lemma gives a maximal one, $\widetilde f:\widetilde A	o I$. If $x\in B\setminus \widetilde A$, the set \[  J=\{ r\in R:rx\in \widetilde A\}   \] is an ideal. Write $J=aR$. For $a
e 0$ choose $y\in I$ with $ay=\widetilde f(ax)$; for $a=0$ choose any $y$. Define an extension on $\widetilde A+Rx$ by $\widetilde f(b+rx)=\widetilde f(b)+ry$. If $b+rx=b'+r'x$, then $r-r'=at$ and $\widetilde f((r-r')x)=t\widetilde f(ax)=(r-r')y$. This proves well-definedness, including $a=0$, and contradicts maximality. Hence $\widetilde A=B$. Finally a quotient of a divisible module is divisible: solve the multiplication equation for a representative before taking the quotient. Apply the equivalence just proved. $\square$ Proposition 10.68.2 . 9253F65EBAE8 For every commutative ring $R$, every $R$-module embeds in an injective module and has an injective resolution in nonnegative cohomological degrees. Over a PID such a resolution can be chosen to have length one. Proof. The abelian group $\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ is divisible and hence injective by proposition 10.68.1 for $R=\mathbb Z$. It separates points of every abelian group $A$. Indeed, for $x
e 0$ of order $m<\infty $, send $x$ in its cyclic subgroup to $1/m mod \mathbb Z$; for $x$ of infinite order send it to $1/2 mod \mathbb Z$. In either case extend that homomorphism to $A$ using injectivity. Put $S=\operatorname {Hom}_{\mathbb Z} (A,\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$. The evaluation map \[  e:A\longrightarrow E=(\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)^ S, \qquad e(a)=(\chi (a))_{\chi \in S},  \] is therefore injective. The product $E$ is injective as an abelian group: extend each coordinate homomorphism. It is the full product that is used here; no injectivity of the subgroup of additive characters on $S$ is needed. For an $R$-module $A$, apply this construction to its underlying abelian group and set $J=\operatorname {Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(R,E)$, with $(r\varphi )(s)=\varphi (rs)$. The map \[  A\longrightarrow J,\qquad a\longmapsto (r\mapsto e(ra))  \] is $R$-linear and injective, as evaluation at $r=1$ shows. There is an explicit adjunction \[  \operatorname {Hom}_ R(N,J) \simeq \operatorname {Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(N,E).  \] It sends $u$ to $n\mapsto u(n)(1)$; its inverse sends $v$ to $n\mapsto (r\mapsto v(rn))$. Since every abelian homomorphism to $E$ extends across an injection, this adjunction proves injectivity of $J$ over $R$. Embed the successive cokernels in injective modules to obtain an injective resolution. Over a PID the first quotient $J/A$ is already injective by proposition 10.68.1 , so $0	o A	o J	o J/A	o 0$ has the required length. $\square$ Proposition 10.68.3 . E2AECDB17A12 For a projective resolution $P_ ullet 	o A$ and an injective resolution $B	o I^ ullet $, define \[  \operatorname {Ext}^ q_ R(A,B) =H^ q\operatorname {Hom}_ R(P_ ullet ,B).  \] There are natural resolution-independent identifications \[   egin{aligned}  \operatorname {Ext}^ q_ R(A,B) & \simeq H^ q\operatorname {Tot} \operatorname {Hom}_ R(P_ ullet ,I^ ullet )\ & \simeq H^ q\operatorname {Hom}_ R(A,I^ ullet ). \end{aligned}  \] In particular $\operatorname {Ext}^0_ R(A,B)= \operatorname {Hom}_ R(A,B)$. Short exact sequences in the first variable give the contravariant long exact Ext sequence; those in the second give the covariant long exact Ext sequence. A module $A$ is projective if and only if $\operatorname {Ext}^1_ R(A,B)=0$ for all $B$; a module $B$ is injective if and only if $\operatorname {Ext}^1_ R(A,B)=0$ for all $A$. Proof. Projective resolution comparison and homotopy were proved in proposition 10.67.3 ; applying $\operatorname {Hom}(-,B)$ to its explicit homotopy gives the same independence assertion here. We also give the injective comparison, to fix the needed resolution maps. For $b:B	o B'$ and injective resolutions $I,J$, extend $B	o B'	o J^0$ across $B\hookrightarrow I^0$ to $f^0$. The map $d_ Jf^0$ vanishes on $B$, so factors through $\operatorname {im}d_ I^0\subset I^1$ and extends to a map $f^1:I^1	o J^1$ by injectivity. Inductively, $d_ Jf^ q$ vanishes on $\ker d_ I^ q=\operatorname {im}d_ I^{q-1}$ and the same extension defines $f^{q+1}$. If $f,g$ lift the same $b$, construct $h^ q:I^ q	o J^{q-1}$ so that \[  f^ q-g^ q=d_ Jh^ q+h^{q+1}d_ I^ q,\qquad h^0=0.  \] For $q=0$, the difference vanishes on $B$, factors through $\operatorname {im}d_ I^0$, and extends to $I^1$ because $J^0$ is injective. At the next step subtract $d_ Jh^ q$; the preceding identity makes the residual vanish on $\ker d_ I^ q$, so it again factors through $\operatorname {im}d_ I^ q$ and extends to $I^{q+1}$. On bidegree $(p,q)$ put \[  C^{p,q}=\operatorname {Hom}_ R(P_ q,I^ p),\qquad Df=d_ If+(-1)^ p f\partial _ P.  \] The two mixed terms in $D^2$ cancel, since the $I$ differential changes $p$ by one; the two unmixed terms are zero. Both indices are nonnegative. For fixed $p$, injectivity of $I^ p$ makes the horizontal cohomology $\operatorname {Hom}_ R(A,I^ p)$ in degree zero and zero in positive degrees. The actual finite-diagonal comparison of lemma 10.43.15 gives the two asserted total cohomology isomorphisms. Their naturality follows from the comparison maps and homotopies just constructed. A surviving first-page row or column still has its Hom differential; it is the second page that has zero later differentials. For example, with $A=B=\mathbb Z$ and injective resolution $\mathbb Z	o \mathbb Q	o \mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$, that first-page differential is the nonzero surjection $\mathbb Q	o \mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$. Conversely, if $\operatorname {Ext}^1(A,B)=0$ for all $B$, any surjection $E	o A$ with kernel $B$ gives a surjection $\operatorname {Hom}(A,E)	o \operatorname {Hom}(A,A)$. Lifting the identity splits every such surjection, and a free surjection proves that $A$ is projective. If $\operatorname {Ext}^1(C,B)=0$ for all $C$, the first variable sequence for $0	o A	o E	o C	o 0$ makes $\operatorname {Hom}(E,B)	o \operatorname {Hom}(A,B)$ surjective. This is the extension definition of injectivity. $\square$ Corollary 10.68.4 . 7E187B2EFD5F Over a PID, $\operatorname {Ext}^ q_ R(A,B)=0$ for $q\geq 2$. Write $\operatorname {Ext}_ R(A,B)=\operatorname {Ext}^1_ R(A,B)$. For $a
e 0$, \[  \operatorname {Ext}_ R(R/aR,B)=B/aB.  \] For $a=0$ that Ext module is zero, since $R/aR=R$ is projective. If $A\simeq R^ r\oplus  igoplus _{i=1}^ sR/a_ iR$ is a finite-generation decomposition with $a_ i
e 0$, then \[  \operatorname {Ext}_ R(A,B) \simeq  igoplus _{i=1}^ s B/a_ iB.  \] Proof. Use either the length-one free resolution of $A$ or the length-one injective resolution of $B$. For a nonzero $a$, applying $\operatorname {Hom}_ R(-,B)$ to $R\xrightarrow {a}R$ gives $B\xrightarrow {a}B$; its first cohomology is the stated quotient. Finite direct sums of resolutions compute the last formula, since Hom takes a finite direct sum to a finite product, which is the same finite direct sum. This finite-generation calculation does not assert a cyclic decomposition of arbitrary modules or that Ext commutes with filtered direct limits. $\square$

A module $A$ is projective if and only if $\operatorname {Ext}^1_ R(A,B)=0$ for all $B$; a module $B$ is injective if and only if $\operatorname {Ext}^1_ R(A,B)=0$ for all $A$. Proof. Projective resolution comparison and homotopy were proved in proposition 10.67.3 ; applying $\operatorname {Hom}(-,B)$ to its explicit homotopy gives the same independence assertion here. If $f,g$ lift the same $b$, construct $h^ q:I^ q\to J^{q-1}$ so that \[  f^ q-g^ q=d_ Jh^ q+h^{q+1}d_ I^ q,\qquad h^0=0.  \] For $q=0$, the difference vanishes on $B$, factors through $\operatorname {im}d_ I^0$, and extends to $I^1$ because $J^0$ is injective. At the next step subtract $d_ Jh^ q$; the preceding identity makes the residual vanish on $\ker d_ I^ q$, so it again factors through $\operatorname {im}d_ I^ q$ and extends to $I^{q+1}$. On bidegree $(p,q)$ put \[  C^{p,q}=\operatorname {Hom}_ R(P_ q,I^ p),\qquad Df=d_ If+(-1)^ p f\partial _ P.  \] The two mixed terms in $D^2$ cancel, since the $I$ differential changes $p$ by one; the two unmixed terms are zero. For fixed $q$, projectivity of $P_ q$ makes the vertical cohomology $\operatorname {Hom}_ R(P_ q,B)$ in degree zero and zero in positive degrees. The actual finite-diagonal comparison of lemma 10.43.15 gives the two asserted total cohomology isomorphisms. Their naturality follows from the comparison maps and homotopies just constructed. A surviving first-page row or column still has its Hom differential; it is the second page that has zero later differentials. For example, with $A=B=\mathbb Z$ and injective resolution $\mathbb Z\to \mathbb Q\to \mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$, that first-page differential is the nonzero surjection $\mathbb Q\to \mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$. For a short exact sequence in $A$, apply $\operatorname {Hom}_ R(-,I^ p)$ degreewise. This gives the short exact sequence of complexes in the reversed direction and hence the long exact sequence beginning \[  \begin{aligned}  0\longrightarrow \operatorname {Hom}(A'',B) \longrightarrow \operatorname {Hom}(A',B) \longrightarrow \operatorname {Hom}(A,B)\\  \longrightarrow \operatorname {Ext}^1(A'',B) \longrightarrow \operatorname {Ext}^1(A',B)\longrightarrow \cdots . \end{aligned}  \] For a short exact sequence in $B$, apply $\operatorname {Hom}_ R(P_ q,-)$ degreewise and use the covariant long exact sequence. title: Corollary 10.68.4
text: Corollary 10.68.4 . 7E187B2EFD5F Over a PID, $\operatorname {Ext}^ q_ R(A,B)=0$ for $q\geq 2$. Write $\operatorname {Ext}_ R(A,B)=\operatorname {Ext}^1_ R(A,B)$. For $a\ne 0$, \[  \operatorname {Ext}_ R(R/aR,B)=B/aB.  \] For $a=0$ that Ext module is zero, since $R/aR=R$ is projective. If $A\simeq R^ r\oplus \bigoplus _{i=1}^ sR/a_ iR$ is a finite-generation decomposition with $a_ i\ne 0$, then \[  \operatorname {Ext}_ R(A,B) \simeq \bigoplus _{i=1}^ s B/a_ iB.  \] Proof. For a nonzero $a$, applying $\operatorname {Hom}_ R(-,B)$ to $R\xrightarrow {a}R$ gives $B\xrightarrow {a}B$; its first cohomology is the stated quotient. title: 10.68.5 Derived Hom and the coefficient sequence
search_title: Derived Hom and the coefficient sequence
text: Theorem 10.68.6 . 04CB406A4809 Let $R$ be a principal ideal domain, let $K_\bullet $ be a homological complex, and let $M\to I^\bullet $ be an injective resolution in degrees $p\geq 0$. Put \[  L^ n=\bigoplus _{p+q=n}\operatorname {Hom}_ R(K_ q,I^ p), \qquad Df=d_ If+(-1)^ p f\partial _ K.  \] There is a natural short exact sequence F019AD1FFDA1 10.68.7 \begin{equation}  0\longrightarrow \operatorname {Ext}_ R(H_{n-1}(K),M) \xrightarrow {\  j\  }H^ n(L) \xrightarrow {\  \rho \  }\operatorname {Hom}_ R(H_ n(K),M) \longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} The middle functor is independent of the injective resolution. The sequence splits as modules, generally without a natural choice of splitting. No finite-type condition is required, and $K$ may be unbounded with the displayed direct-sum convention. Proof. Choose first a length-one injective resolution $0\to M\to I^0\xrightarrow {\delta }I^1\to 0$, which exists by proposition 10.68.2 . The total complex has only two summands in each degree, regardless of the bounds on $K$: \[  L^ n=\operatorname {Hom}(K_ n,I^0) \oplus \operatorname {Hom}(K_{n-1},I^1).  \] A pair $(f,g)$ is a cocycle exactly when \[  f\partial _{n+1}=0,\qquad \delta f=g\partial _ n.  \] Its coboundaries have the form BC6133A80BC8 10.68.8 \begin{equation}  (a\partial _ n,\  \delta a-b\partial _{n-1}), \quad a:K_{n-1}\to I^0,\quad b:K_{n-2}\to I^1. \end{equation} These formulas follow directly from the specified total differential. Write $Z_ q=\ker \partial _ q$, $B_ q=\operatorname {im}\partial _{q+1}$. For a cocycle, $f|_{Z_ n}$ has values in $\ker \delta =M$ and vanishes on $B_ n$. Define $\rho [f,g]$ by this map $H_ n(K)\to M$. Every coboundary has zero restriction to $Z_ n$, so $\rho $ is well defined. For surjectivity, start with $h:H_ n(K)\to M$. Its composition $Z_ n\to M\hookrightarrow I^0$ extends to $f:K_ n\to I^0$. The map $\delta f$ vanishes on $Z_ n$, hence factors through $B_{n-1}=K_ n/Z_ n$. Extend that factor to $g:K_{n-1}\to I^1$ by injectivity. Then $(f,g)$ is a cocycle with $\rho [f,g]=h$. The injective resolution identifies \[  \operatorname {Ext}(H_{n-1}(K),M) =\frac{\operatorname {Hom}(H_{n-1}(K),I^1)}{\delta \operatorname {Hom}(H_{n-1}(K),I^0)}.  \] For a representative $c:H_{n-1}(K)\to I^1$, extend it across $H_{n-1}(K)=Z_{n-1}/B_{n-1}\subset K_{n-1}/B_{n-1}$ to $v$, using injectivity of $I^1$. Set $j[c]=[0,v]$, composing $v$ with the quotient of $K_{n-1}$. This is a cocycle because $v$ kills $B_{n-1}$. If two such extensions differ by $w$, then $w$ vanishes on $Z_{n-1}$ and factors through $B_{n-2}$. Extend this factor to $b:K_{n-2}\to I^1$; the difference $(0,w)$ is the boundary $D(0,-b)$. If $c$ is changed by $\delta a_0$ with $a_0:H_{n-1}(K)\to I^0$, extend $a_0$ to $K_{n-1}/B_{n-1}$ by injectivity of $I^0$. The corresponding change is the boundary $D(a,0)$, because $a\partial _ n=0$. Thus $j$ is well defined. If $[0,v]=D(a,b)$, its first component says $a\partial _ n=0$, so $a$ kills $B_{n-1}$. Restriction of its second component to $Z_{n-1}/B_{n-1}$ is $\delta (a|_{Z_{n-1}/B_{n-1}})$; hence $[c]=0$. This proves injectivity of $j$. Its image plainly lies in $\ker \rho $. Conversely, if $\rho [f,g]=0$, $f$ vanishes on $Z_ n$ and factors through $B_{n-1}$. Extend that factor to $a:K_{n-1}\to I^0$ and subtract $D(a,0)$. The result is $(0,g-\delta a)$, whose second component kills $B_{n-1}$ by the cocycle equation. Restrict it to $Z_{n-1}/B_{n-1}$ to obtain $c$. The preceding construction gives exactly $[f,g]=j[c]$. This proves the full exact sequence. Every extension choice was eliminated by an explicit coboundary. The constructions therefore commute with chain maps in $K$ and with comparison maps of injective resolutions for maps of coefficients. For a different, possibly longer injective resolution, proposition 10.68.3 supplies comparison maps to and from this length-one resolution whose composites are homotopic to the identity. These homotopies remain total Hom homotopies for arbitrary $K$: if $h:I^ p\to J^{p-1}$, define $H(f)=hf$ on $\operatorname {Hom}(K_ q,I^ p)$. In $DH+HD$ the terms involving $\partial _ K$ cancel, with signs $(-1)^{p-1}$ and $(-1)^ p$, leaving the coefficient homotopy identity. Each map and homotopy sends a finite-support element to a finite-support element. This proves the claimed resolution independence without any infinite-diagonal convergence inference, and transports the natural sequence to the stated $I$. It remains to split it. Reverse the cohomological indices in the functorial free replacement constructed in theorem 10.67.7 . This gives a termwise free homological complex $P\to K$ which is degreewise onto and has a contractible kernel $E$. Complex spaces are Hausdorff and have a countable basis. Their dimension is that of their reduction. Smooth functions and strong $q$-convexity, $q\geq 1$, have the local ambient-extension meaning of lemma 9.49.1 ; thus the geometric assertions also apply to nonreduced spaces. An exhaustion has compact closed sublevels. On a Hermitian manifold put $L_\omega f=\operatorname {Tr}_\omega (\mathrm i\partial  ar\partial f)$. This is a real elliptic operator with no zeroth-order term. In holomorphic real coordinates it has the form $\sum a^{ij}(x)\partial _ i\partial _ j$ with symmetric positive definite real matrix $a$. In particular $L_\omega f>0$ implies strong $n$-convexity in complex dimension $n$. Lemma 9.52.1 . 88C2BC468CBC Let $U,W$ be open in a Hermitian manifold. Suppose every component $U_ s$ of $U$ meets a component $W_{t(s)}$ of $W$ for which 2A3AB1116C31 9.52.2  egin{equation}  W_{t(s)}\setminus \overline U
e \varnothing . \end{equation} There is a smooth nonnegative $v$, zero outside $U\cup W$, such that $v>0$ and $L_\omega v>0$ on $U$, and $L_\omega v\geq 0$ off $W$. If $U$ has finitely many components, the set where $L_\omega v<0$ has closure in a compact subset of $W\setminus \overline U$. In all cases $\operatorname {supp}v\subset \overline U\cup \overline W$. Proof. The case $U=\varnothing $ has the solution $v=0$. Here is a local construction allowing arbitrarily thin cylinders. Normalize the metric at the center of a holomorphic chart and use a unitary rotation to put the chosen real direction on its first axis. On a sufficiently small chart there are constants $c_0,C_0>0$ such that $a^{11}\geq c_0$, the transverse quadratic form is at least $c_0|\xi '|^2$, and $\sum _{j>1}a^{jj}\leq C_0$. We may also require $|(a^{12},\ldots ,a^{1,2n})|\leq c_0/12$: these mixed coefficients vanish at the center and are continuous. Choose a longitudinal half-length $\ell $ and a transverse radius $ho $ inside this chart, put $u=x_1+\ell $ and $T=ho ^2-|x'|^2$, and on $|x_1|<\ell $, $|x'|<ho $ set $v=\chi _ A(u)e^{-1/T}$, where $\chi _ A(u)=u e^{-A/u^2}$ for $u>0$ and is zero for $u\leq 0$. Multiply its continuation in $x_1$ by a nonnegative smooth cutoff equal to one for $x_1\leq \ell $ and zero before $x_1=\ell +\epsilon $. Extend by zero across the transverse boundary. The flat exponential factors make all these extensions smooth, and any negative Laplacian outside the main cylinder is confined to the exit cap $\ell <x_1<\ell +\epsilon $, $|x'|<ho $. Direct differentiation on the main cylinder gives \[   rac{\chi _ A'}{\chi _ A}=u^{-1}+2Au^{-3},\quad  rac{\chi _ A''}{\chi _ A}=4A^2u^{-6}-2Au^{-4},\quad  rac{\partial _ j e^{-1/T}}{e^{-1/T}}=-2x_ jT^{-2},  \] and, for $j,k>1$, \[   rac{\partial _{jk}e^{-1/T}}{e^{-1/T}} =(4-8T)x_ jx_ kT^{-4}-2\delta _{jk}T^{-2}.  \] The mixed sum in $L_\omega v/v$ is $-4\sum _{j>1}a^{1j}(u^{-1}+2Au^{-3})x_ jT^{-2}$. Take $A\geq (2\ell )^2$ and $ho ^2\leq 1/4$. Then $\chi _ A'/\chi _ A\leq 3Au^{-3}$, $\chi _ A''/\chi _ A\geq 2A^2u^{-6}$ and $4-8T\geq 2$. The absolute value of the mixed sum is at most $c_0Au^{-3}|x'|T^{-2}$, hence at most $	frac 12c_0(A^2u^{-6}+|x'|^2T^{-4})$. We obtain, with $c=c_0$ and $C=2C_0$, EE28C5815630 9.52.3  egin{equation}  L_\omega v/v\geq c A^2u^{-6}+c|x'|^2T^{-4}-C T^{-2}. \end{equation} Where $|x'|^2\geq 2CT^2/c$, the last two terms are nonnegative. Else $|x'|^2\leq (2C/c)ho ^4$, so $T\geq ho ^2/2$ if $ho ^2\leq c/(4C)$. The negative part is then at most $4Cho ^{-4}$. Choose $A$ still larger so that $cA^2(2\ell )^{-6}>4Cho ^{-4}$. This proves $L_\omega v>0$ on the cylinder, for arbitrarily small $ho $ relative to the fixed short longitudinal segment and with any prescribed small exit cap. Setting $A=1$ in the differentiation formulas also gives the corrected original longitudinal factors. Fix a small ball $B\Subset W_{t(s)}\setminus \overline U$ and a point $p\in U_ s$. A path in $U_ s\cup W_{t(s)}$ joins $p$ to $B$. It can be taken piecewise straight in finitely many holomorphic charts, with all exit junctions different from $p$. Indeed join successive points in overlapping coordinate balls and, after leaving a small ball about $p$, use that a connected real manifold of dimension at least two remains path connected after one point is removed. This last fact follows by replacing passages through that point by arcs in a punctured coordinate ball. Subdivide the compact path into sufficiently short chart segments. Working backwards, the thin-cylinder construction gives finitely many bumps $b_0,\ldots ,b_ N$ with main cylinders $D_ j$ and exit caps $E_ j$ such that \[  p\in D_0,\qquad \overline E_ j\subset D_{j+1},\qquad \overline E_ N\subset B.  \] All cylinder closures lie in $U_ s\cup W_{t(s)}$; their closed exit caps avoid $p$. Backwards choice is possible since the next main cylinder contains its junction as an interior point, and the preceding exit cap can have arbitrarily small transverse radius. Each $b_ j$ has positive Laplacian on $D_ j$, and its negative Laplacian is confined to $E_ j$. Inductively choose positive coefficients so that $w_ p=b_0+C_1b_1+\cdots +C_ Nb_ N$ has nonnegative Laplacian off $E_ N$ and strictly positive Laplacian near $p$. At each step the previous possible negative part lies on the compact $\overline E_{j-1}$, where $L_\omega b_ j$ has a positive minimum, so a finite coefficient suffices. Previously nonnegative points outside the new exit cap stay nonnegative; near $p$ every new Laplacian is nonnegative. Also $w_ p>0$ near $p$, and it has compact support in $U_ s\cup W_{t(s)}$. For each $s$ use one fixed sink ball $B_ s$ as above. Choose countably many of these positive neighborhoods covering $U_ s$. Take a positive linear combination of their $w_ p$'s converging with every derivative on compact subsets of the entire manifold. All sinks lie outside $\overline U$, so terms from other components have nonnegative Laplacian on $U$; this proves the assertion on the entire $U$. If there are finitely many components the finite union of sink closures is compact inside $W\setminus \overline U$. $\square$ Example 9.52.4 . On $M=\mathbb P^1$ with its Fubini–Study metric, take $U=\mathbb P^1\setminus \{ |z|=1\} $ and $W=M$. Its two components both meet $W$ and each has proper closure. Use lemma 9.52.9 to get a nonnegative exhaustion $f$ strongly $n$-convex near $Y$. On $N$ any smooth function is strongly $(n+1)$-convex, since its dimension is $n$; the embedding-independent convention then proves the first assertion on all $X$. For item1, the components $N_ j$ of $N$ have closures equal to the $n$-dimensional irreducible components $Z_ j$ of $X$, by global irreducible analytic components . They are noncompact by hypothesis. On a neighborhood of $Y$ the function $f$ has at least one positive Levi eigenvalue along $N$. Apply lemma 9.50.1 there with $q=n$ and $(n-1)\varepsilon <1$ to give its Levi form positive trace. Choose a smooth cutoff on $X$ equal to one on a smaller neighborhood $V$ of $Y$ and supported where this metric is defined on $N$. A convex combination of this inverse metric and an arbitrary smooth inverse metric on $N$ is positive definite and smooth. On $V\cap N$ it is the constructed inverse metric, so $L_\omega f>0$ there. Apply corollary 9.52.7 on each $Z_ j$, with analytic set $Y\cap Z_ j$ and neighborhood $V\cap Z_ j$. The analytic set is nowhere dense in this irreducible component and contains its singular locus, and its complement is $N_ j$. Apply lemma 9.52.1 to consecutive open sets to obtain $v_{j,
u }$, supported in $\overline{U_{j,
u }}\cup \overline{U_{j,
u +1}}$ and with all negative Laplacian in a compact subset of $U_{j,
u +1}$. Each compactly supported smooth regular-locus bump extends by zero to a smooth function on $X$: its support is compact and avoids $Y$, and near it $X$ is the smooth manifold $N_ j$. The supports form a locally finite family in $X$. Within $Z_ j$ this is the properness argument in the preceding corollary; a compact set in $X$ meets only finitely many of its locally finite irreducible components. On each $N_ j$ repeat the coefficient construction of theorem 9.52.8 , using the compact targets $C_{j,
u }$ outside $V$ and the preceding compact negative locus $S_{j,
u -1}$. Add all these nonnegative bumps to $f$. Their sum $\psi $ is smooth on $X$, exhaustive and unchanged near each point of $Y$, since their supports are locally finite and disjoint from $Y$. On $N$ the last-negative-summand argument gives $L_\omega \psi >0$: outside $V$ use its covered compact target; inside $V$ the initial trace is positive unless a negative summand occurs, whose last occurrence is corrected at the next step. Thus $\psi $ is strongly $n$-convex both near $Y$ and on $N$, proving item1. This also completes the induction. For item2 let $B$ be the union of $Y$ and all the noncompact $n$-dimensional components of $X$. This is closed analytic by local finiteness; it has no compact irreducible component of dimension $n$. The closed complement $X\setminus O$ is contained in the finite union of compact top components, so is compact. This proves item2 without the false assertion that $B$ must have dimension less than $n$. $\square$ Lemma 9.52.11 . 90D581391F17 If $F$ is closed in a locally compact Hausdorff space and $T$ is a compact connected component of $F$, there is a compact neighborhood $Q$ of $T$ with $\partial Q\cap F=\varnothing $. Proof. Choose a compact neighborhood $D$ of $T$. In the compact Hausdorff space $H=F\cap D$, the component containing $T$ is still $T$: any connected enlargement in $H$ would enlarge it in $F$. We show that $T$ has a clopen neighborhood in $H$ avoiding $F\cap \partial D$. Let $J$ be the intersection of all clopen neighborhoods of $T$ in $H$. If $J$ were separated into two nonempty compact parts $J_1,J_2$, its connected subset $T$ would lie in one, say $J_1$. Choose disjoint open neighborhoods of $J_1,J_2$. Finitely many clopen neighborhoods of $T$ exclude the compact set outside their union. Their intersection is clopen and splits into two clopen parts inside those open neighborhoods. Its first part is a clopen neighborhood of $T$ excluding $J_2$, a contradiction to the definition of $J$. Thus $J$ is connected and equals $T$. Compactness now supplies a finite intersection $E$ of such clopen neighborhoods disjoint from $F\cap \partial D$. The set $E$ is compact, lies in $\operatorname {int}D$ and is open in $F$, so $F\setminus E$ is closed in the ambient space. By local compactness and regularity, finitely many relatively compact open sets cover $E$ with closures disjoint from $F\setminus E$. Their union $B$ has compact closure, contains $E$, and satisfies $\overline B\cap F\subset E\subset B$. Therefore $\partial \overline B\cap F=\varnothing $, and $Q=\overline B$ is the required compact neighborhood of $T$. $\square$ Proposition 9.52.12 . 5366BBA720F6 Let $M$ be a connected noncompact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, and $U\subset M$ open. The following are equivalent: For every compact $K\subset U$ some smooth strongly $n$-convex exhaustion $\psi $ of $M$ has $K\subset \{ \psi <b\} \Subset U$. $M\setminus U$ has no compact connected component. In particular this is precisely the top-degree Runge-complete condition. Proof. If $T$ is a compact component of the closed complement, use lemma 9.52.11 to choose a compact neighborhood $Q$ of it with $\partial Q\subset U$. A strongly $n$-convex function has no local maximum, because a negative-semidefinite Levi form cannot have a positive eigenvalue. Its maximum on $Q$ must therefore occur on $\partial Q$. A sublevel containing that compact boundary contains $Q$, contradicting its containment in $U$. Conversely, if $K=\varnothing $, use any strongly $n$-convex exhaustion and a level below its infimum. Suppose now that $K\subset U$ is nonempty and compact, and take a strictly $\omega $-subharmonic exhaustion $f$ supplied by theorem 9.52.8 . Choose $b>\max _ K f$, with a positive margin, and put $P=(M\setminus U)\cap \{ f\leq b\} $. It is compact. Every component $T$ of the complement is closed and noncompact, so $f$ is unbounded on it. A point $x\in P\cap T$ and a point $y\in T$ with $f(y)>b+2$ lie in the same component of the open manifold $M\setminus K$: connectedness of $T$ is enough, and the containing open component is path connected. A thin connected relatively compact path neighborhood $D_ x\Subset M\setminus K$ thus connects $x$ to $W=\{ f>b+1\} $. Finitely many such $D_ x$ cover $P$. Their union $D$ has finitely many components and compact closure disjoint from $K$. Every component of $D$ meets $W$. Each component of $W$ has noncompact closure. Otherwise $f$ would attain a maximum greater than $b+1$ in its interior, since its boundary has value $b+1$, contradicting strict subharmonicity. Thus each component of $W$ meeting $D$ contains a point outside $\overline D$. The whole-open sink lemma gives $v\geq 0$, positive on $P$, with $L_\omega v\geq 0$ off a compact $S\subset W\setminus \overline D$. It vanishes on a neighborhood of $K$, since both $\overline D$ and $\overline W$ avoid $K$. Choose $C$ so that $f+Cv>b+1$ on $P$, a strict margin. Choose a smooth convex increasing $\chi \geq 0$, zero for $t\leq b+1/2$, whose derivative for $t\geq b+1$ is large enough that $\chi '(f)L_\omega f$ dominates $C|L_\omega v|$ on the compact $S$. Such a function is an integral of a smooth nondecreasing step times a sufficiently large constant; $\min _ S L_\omega f>0$ when $S$ is nonempty. If $S=\varnothing $, take $\chi =0$. The chain rule gives \[  \psi =f+Cv+\chi (f),\qquad L_\omega \psi >0.  \] It is exhaustive since $\psi \geq f$, and $\psi =f$ on $K$. On the complement of $U$, points with $f\leq b$ belong to $P$ and have $\psi >b+1$, and other points have $\psi \geq f>b$. Hence $\{ \psi \leq b\} \subset U$. This is compact, so $K\subset \{ \psi <b\} \Subset U$ as claimed. If $P$ is empty the same conclusion holds with $v=\chi =0$. $\square$ Corollary 9.52.13 . 0AD84DC1EF06 Let $\mathcal F$ be coherent on a countable-basis complex space $X$, possibly nonreduced, with $\dim X\leq n$ for an integer $n\geq 0$. Then $H^ k(X,\mathcal F)=0$ for $k\geq n+1$. If $X$ has no compact irreducible component of dimension $n$, then $H^ n(X,\mathcal F)=0$. If it has only finitely many such compact components, then $H^ n(X,\mathcal F)$ is Hausdorff and finite dimensional. Proof. For $n\geq 1$ apply the complete vanishing and compact-exceptional finiteness theorem 9.51.13 to theorem 9.52.10 , with $q=n+1$ or $q=n$. If $\dim X<n$, its strongly $(\dim X+1)$-complete exhaustion already gives the degree-$n$ vanishing. For $n=0$ the first assertion uses strong1-completeness. The second says $X$ is empty. In the last, $X$ is a finite set and hence compact; apply theorem 9.51.10 also in degree zero. This retains the full nonreduced coherent module, not just its values on the reduction. $\square$ Corollary 9.52.14 . DBA14B44B8CF Let $\mathcal F$ be coherent on a connected noncompact complex $n$-manifold $M$, where $n\geq 1$, and let $U\subset M$ be open. If $M\setminus U$ has no compact connected component, restriction \[  H^{n-1}(M,\mathcal F)\longrightarrow H^{n-1}(U,\mathcal F)  \] has dense image for the intrinsic quotient cohomology topologies. Proof. The manifold is strongly $n$-complete by theorem 9.52.8 . The preceding Runge-complete proposition gives, for every compact subset of $U$, a globally strongly $n$-convex exhaustion with the required relatively compact sublevel. This satisfies all hypotheses of the degree $q-1$ density assertion in theorem 9.51.13 , for $q=n$. Its topology is exactly the intrinsic cohomology topology constructed there, including degree zero when $n=1$. $\square$
