text: Lemma 9.52.1 . 88C2BC468CBC Let $U,W$ be open in a Hermitian manifold. Suppose every component $U_ s$ of $U$ meets a component $W_{t(s)}$ of $W$ for which 2A3AB1116C31 9.52.2 \begin{equation}  W_{t(s)}\setminus \overline U\ne \varnothing . \end{equation} There is a smooth nonnegative $v$, zero outside $U\cup W$, such that $v>0$ and $L_\omega v>0$ on $U$, and $L_\omega v\geq 0$ off $W$. If $U$ has finitely many components, the set where $L_\omega v<0$ has closure in a compact subset of $W\setminus \overline U$. In all cases $\operatorname {supp}v\subset \overline U\cup \overline W$. Proof. The case $U=\varnothing $ has the solution $v=0$. Here is a local construction allowing arbitrarily thin cylinders. Normalize the metric at the center of a holomorphic chart and use a unitary rotation to put the chosen real direction on its first axis. On a sufficiently small chart there are constants $c_0,C_0>0$ such that $a^{11}\geq c_0$, the transverse quadratic form is at least $c_0|\xi '|^2$, and $\sum _{j>1}a^{jj}\leq C_0$. We may also require $|(a^{12},\ldots ,a^{1,2n})|\leq c_0/12$: these mixed coefficients vanish at the center and are continuous. Choose a longitudinal half-length $\ell $ and a transverse radius $\rho $ inside this chart, put $u=x_1+\ell $ and $T=\rho ^2-|x'|^2$, and on $|x_1|<\ell $, $|x'|<\rho $ set $v=\chi _ A(u)e^{-1/T}$, where $\chi _ A(u)=u e^{-A/u^2}$ for $u>0$ and is zero for $u\leq 0$. Multiply its continuation in $x_1$ by a nonnegative smooth cutoff equal to one for $x_1\leq \ell $ and zero before $x_1=\ell +\epsilon $. Extend by zero across the transverse boundary. The flat exponential factors make all these extensions smooth, and any negative Laplacian outside the main cylinder is confined to the exit cap $\ell <x_1<\ell +\epsilon $, $|x'|<\rho $. Direct differentiation on the main cylinder gives \[  \frac{\chi _ A'}{\chi _ A}=u^{-1}+2Au^{-3},\quad \frac{\chi _ A''}{\chi _ A}=4A^2u^{-6}-2Au^{-4},\quad \frac{\partial _ j e^{-1/T}}{e^{-1/T}}=-2x_ jT^{-2},  \] and, for $j,k>1$, \[  \frac{\partial _{jk}e^{-1/T}}{e^{-1/T}} =(4-8T)x_ jx_ kT^{-4}-2\delta _{jk}T^{-2}.  \] The mixed sum in $L_\omega v/v$ is $-4\sum _{j>1}a^{1j}(u^{-1}+2Au^{-3})x_ jT^{-2}$. Take $A\geq (2\ell )^2$ and $\rho ^2\leq 1/4$. Then $\chi _ A'/\chi _ A\leq 3Au^{-3}$, $\chi _ A''/\chi _ A\geq 2A^2u^{-6}$ and $4-8T\geq 2$. The absolute value of the mixed sum is at most $c_0Au^{-3}|x'|T^{-2}$, hence at most $\tfrac 12c_0(A^2u^{-6}+|x'|^2T^{-4})$. We obtain, with $c=c_0$ and $C=2C_0$, EE28C5815630 9.52.3 \begin{equation}  L_\omega v/v\geq c A^2u^{-6}+c|x'|^2T^{-4}-C T^{-2}. \end{equation} Where $|x'|^2\geq 2CT^2/c$, the last two terms are nonnegative. Else $|x'|^2\leq (2C/c)\rho ^4$, so $T\geq \rho ^2/2$ if $\rho ^2\leq c/(4C)$. The negative part is then at most $4C\rho ^{-4}$. Choose $A$ still larger so that $cA^2(2\ell )^{-6}>4C\rho ^{-4}$. This proves $L_\omega v>0$ on the cylinder, for arbitrarily small $\rho $ relative to the fixed short longitudinal segment and with any prescribed small exit cap. Setting $A=1$ in the differentiation formulas also gives the corrected original longitudinal factors. Fix a small ball $B\Subset W_{t(s)}\setminus \overline U$ and a point $p\in U_ s$. A path in $U_ s\cup W_{t(s)}$ joins $p$ to $B$. It can be taken piecewise straight in finitely many holomorphic charts, with all exit junctions different from $p$. Indeed join successive points in overlapping coordinate balls and, after leaving a small ball about $p$, use that a connected real manifold of dimension at least two remains path connected after one point is removed. This last fact follows by replacing passages through that point by arcs in a punctured coordinate ball. Subdivide the compact path into sufficiently short chart segments. Working backwards, the thin-cylinder construction gives finitely many bumps $b_0,\ldots ,b_ N$ with main cylinders $D_ j$ and exit caps $E_ j$ such that \[  p\in D_0,\qquad \overline E_ j\subset D_{j+1},\qquad \overline E_ N\subset B.  \] All cylinder closures lie in $U_ s\cup W_{t(s)}$; their closed exit caps avoid $p$. Backwards choice is possible since the next main cylinder contains its junction as an interior point, and the preceding exit cap can have arbitrarily small transverse radius. Each $b_ j$ has positive Laplacian on $D_ j$, and its negative Laplacian is confined to $E_ j$. Inductively choose positive coefficients so that $w_ p=b_0+C_1b_1+\cdots +C_ Nb_ N$ has nonnegative Laplacian off $E_ N$ and strictly positive Laplacian near $p$. At each step the previous possible negative part lies on the compact $\overline E_{j-1}$, where $L_\omega b_ j$ has a positive minimum, so a finite coefficient suffices. Previously nonnegative points outside the new exit cap stay nonnegative; near $p$ every new Laplacian is nonnegative. Also $w_ p>0$ near $p$, and it has compact support in $U_ s\cup W_{t(s)}$. For each $s$ use one fixed sink ball $B_ s$ as above. Choose countably many of these positive neighborhoods covering $U_ s$. Take a positive linear combination of their $w_ p$'s converging with every derivative on compact subsets of the entire manifold. Explicitly, for a compact exhaustion $K_ l$, make the $j$th coefficient at most $2^{-j}/(1+\max _{l,k\leq j}\| w_{p_ j}\| _{C^ k(K_ l)})$. The sum is globally smooth, nonnegative, positive and strictly subharmonic on $U_ s$, and its negative Laplacian is confined to $\overline B_ s$. Sum in the same way over components. All sinks lie outside $\overline U$, so terms from other components have nonnegative Laplacian on $U$; this proves the assertion on the entire $U$. If there are finitely many components the finite union of sink closures is compact inside $W\setminus \overline U$. $\square$

text: Example 9.52.4 . E0D7BF24D793 In the preceding lemma one cannot replace $\overline U$ in ( 9.52.2 ) by $\overline{U_ s}$. On $M=\mathbb P^1$ with its Fubini–Study metric, take $U=\mathbb P^1\setminus \{ |z|=1\} $ and $W=M$. Its two components both meet $W$ and each has proper closure. Yet a smooth function with $L_\omega v>0$ on the dense open set $U$ would have $L_\omega v\geq 0$ everywhere and a strictly positive integral. Stokes gives $\int _ M L_\omega v\, dV_\omega =0$, a contradiction.

section: 9.52 Convexity and cohomology in the top degrees
text:
Lemma 9.52.5 . 4A19B00897C5 Let $Z$ be connected, locally connected, locally compact and Hausdorff. If $O\Subset Z$ is open, adjoining all compact connected components of $Z\setminus O$ gives an open relatively compact set whose complement has finitely many components, all noncompact. If $K\subset Z$ is compact, adjoining all relatively compact components of the open set $Z\setminus K$ gives a compact set $\widehat K$; every component of $Z\setminus \widehat K$ has noncompact closure. If $K$ is connected, so is $\widehat K$. If in addition $Z$ has a countable basis and is noncompact, there are connected compact sets $K_
u \subset \operatorname {int}K_{
u +1}$ exhausting $Z$, with all complementary open components having noncompact closure. Proof. Every compact set is contained in a connected relatively compact open set $V$. Cover it by finitely many connected relatively compact neighborhoods and connect them by finite chains of such neighborhoods. The set of points accessible by these chains from one neighborhood is both open and closed, hence all of the connected space. The finite union used for the compact set is the desired $V$. Choose such a $V$ containing $\overline O$. Every component $T$ of the closed set $Z\setminus O$, when $O$ is nonempty, meets $\partial O$: otherwise its points have connected open neighborhoods disjoint from $\overline O$, so $T$ would be open and closed in $Z$. Every $T$ not contained in $\overline V$ consequently meets $\partial V$. A finite cover of the compact $\partial V$ by connected neighborhoods disjoint from $\overline O$ shows that there are only finitely many such $T$. Every noncompact $T$ is among them. The compact components not among them lie in $\overline V$; adding the finitely many other compact components still gives a relatively compact set. Its complement is a finite union of closed noncompact components, hence is closed. This proves the first assertion. The empty $O$ case is immediate. For compact $K$ the components $G$ of $Z\setminus K$ are open, and $\partial G\subset K$. If $K$ is nonempty each $\overline G$ meets $K$, or $G$ would be open and closed in $Z$. A connected relatively compact neighborhood $V$ of $K$ and the same finite boundary cover show that only finitely many $G$ extend outside $\overline V$. Thus all the relatively compact $G$ together with $K$ lie in a compact set. Their union with $K$ is closed, since its complement is the union of the remaining open components, and is therefore compact. Adjoining connected sets whose closures touch a connected $K$ preserves connectedness. Start with larger and larger connected compact closures of relatively compact open neighborhoods of a countable compact exhaustion, including the preceding $K_
u $ in their interiors, and fill them by this operation. This proves the last assertion. Empty $K$ causes no exception. $\square$

text: Lemma 9.52.9 . 61FD8A8E66FF If a closed analytic $Y\subset X$ is strongly $q$-complete, there is a nonnegative smooth exhaustion $f$ on $X$ which is strongly $q$-convex on a neighborhood of $Y$. Proof. If $Y=\varnothing $, take any nonnegative smooth exhaustion of $X$. Assume henceforth that $Y$ is nonempty. Use proposition 9.49.4 to extend its exhaustion approximately, with error less than one, to a strongly $q$-convex $f_0$ on a neighborhood $W$. Shift it so that $f_0\geq 1$ on $Y$. Its restriction to $Y$ still has compact closed sublevels. Let $r$ be a nonnegative smooth exhaustion of $X$. The quantities $\sup _{Y\cap \{ f_0\leq j\} }r$ are finite; choose a continuous increasing function $a:\mathbb R\to (0,\infty )$ majorizing them strictly on the preceding integer bands, assigning zero to an empty supremum. For example prescribe $a(j)>1+ \sup _{Y\cap \{ f_0\leq j+1\} }r$ for $j\geq 0$ and interpolate increasingly. Then $r<a(f_0)$ on $Y$. Shrink $W$ to the open neighborhood where $f_0>0$ and $r<a(f_0)$, and choose a closed neighborhood $D\subset W$ of $Y$, using the locally finite smooth partitions of lemma 9.49.1 . On $D$, every closed $f_0$ sublevel is closed in $X$ and lies in a compact $r$ sublevel, so is compact. Take a smooth cutoff $0\leq \eta \leq 1$ equal to one on a smaller neighborhood of $Y$ and supported in the interior of $D$, and set $f=\eta f_0+(1-\eta )r$. It is smooth, nonnegative and agrees with $f_0$ near $Y$. A sublevel $f\leq c$ lies in the union of the compact sets $D\cap \{ f_0\leq 2c\} $ and $\{ r\leq 2c\} $, according as $\eta \geq 1/2$ or $\eta <1/2$. It is closed there, hence compact. $\square$

title: Theorem 9.52.10
section: 9.52 Convexity and cohomology in the top degrees
text:
Theorem 9.52.10 . E86D84BDEFC8 Let $X$ be a complex space, possibly nonreduced, of dimension at most an integer $n\geq 0$. It is strongly $(n+1)$-complete. For $n\geq 1$: If $X$ has no compact irreducible component of dimension $n$, then it is strongly $n$-complete. If it has only finitely many compact irreducible components of dimension $n$, then it has a smooth exhaustion strongly $n$-convex outside a compact set. Only compact top-dimensional components are counted in the last hypothesis; there can be infinitely many noncompact ones. Proof. The geometric statements depend only on the reduction. We prove the first assertion and item1 by dimension induction. A zero-dimensional space is discrete, with a smooth exhaustion; in a zero-dimensional local model the strong1 condition is vacuous. Suppose the assertions below dimension $n$ are known. The dimension filtration of lemma 9.49.3 supplies a closed analytic $Y$ with $\dim Y\leq n-1$ and smooth pure $n$-dimensional complement $N$. If $\dim X<n$, the inductive assertion and monotonicity in $q$ already give the required conclusions. Otherwise $Y$ is strongly $n$-complete by induction. Use lemma 9.52.9 to get a nonnegative exhaustion $f$ strongly $n$-convex near $Y$. On $N$ any smooth function is strongly $(n+1)$-convex, since its dimension is $n$; the embedding-independent convention then proves the first assertion on all $X$. For item1, the components $N_ j$ of $N$ have closures equal to the $n$-dimensional irreducible components $Z_ j$ of $X$, by global irreducible analytic components . They are noncompact by hypothesis. On a neighborhood of $Y$ the function $f$ has at least one positive Levi eigenvalue along $N$. Apply lemma 9.50.1 there with $q=n$ and $(n-1)\varepsilon <1$ to give its Levi form positive trace. Choose a smooth cutoff on $X$ equal to one on a smaller neighborhood $V$ of $Y$ and supported where this metric is defined on $N$. A convex combination of this inverse metric and an arbitrary smooth inverse metric on $N$ is positive definite and smooth. On $V\cap N$ it is the constructed inverse metric, so $L_\omega f>0$ there. Apply corollary 9.52.7 on each $Z_ j$, with analytic set $Y\cap Z_ j$ and neighborhood $V\cap Z_ j$. The analytic set is nowhere dense in this irreducible component and contains its singular locus, and its complement is $N_ j$. Apply lemma 9.52.1 to consecutive open sets to obtain $v_{j,
u }$, supported in $\overline{U_{j,
u }}\cup \overline{U_{j,
u +1}}$ and with all negative Laplacian in a compact subset of $U_{j,
u +1}$. Each compactly supported smooth regular-locus bump extends by zero to a smooth function on $X$: its support is compact and avoids $Y$, and near it $X$ is the smooth manifold $N_ j$. The supports form a locally finite family in $X$. Within $Z_ j$ this is the properness argument in the preceding corollary; a compact set in $X$ meets only finitely many of its locally finite irreducible components. On each $N_ j$ repeat the coefficient construction of theorem 9.52.8 , using the compact targets $C_{j,
u }$ outside $V$ and the preceding compact negative locus $S_{j,
u -1}$. Add all these nonnegative bumps to $f$. Their sum $\psi $ is smooth on $X$, exhaustive and unchanged near each point of $Y$, since their supports are locally finite and disjoint from $Y$. On $N$ the last-negative-summand argument gives $L_\omega \psi >0$: outside $V$ use its covered compact target; inside $V$ the initial trace is positive unless a negative summand occurs, whose last occurrence is corrected at the next step. Thus $\psi $ is strongly $n$-convex both near $Y$ and on $N$, proving item1. This also completes the induction. For item2 let $B$ be the union of $Y$ and all the noncompact $n$-dimensional components of $X$. This is closed analytic by local finiteness; it has no compact irreducible component of dimension $n$. Item1, including its lower-dimensional case, makes $B$ strongly $n$-complete. The preceding proper extension lemma gives an exhaustion strongly $n$-convex on an open neighborhood $O$ of $B$. The closed complement $X\setminus O$ is contained in the finite union of compact top components, so is compact. This proves item2 without the false assertion that $B$ must have dimension less than $n$. $\square$

title: Lemma 9.52.11
section: 9.52 Convexity and cohomology in the top degrees
text: Lemma 9.52.11 . 90D581391F17 If $F$ is closed in a locally compact Hausdorff space and $T$ is a compact connected component of $F$, there is a compact neighborhood $Q$ of $T$ with $\partial Q\cap F=\varnothing $. Proof. Choose a compact neighborhood $D$ of $T$. In the compact Hausdorff space $H=F\cap D$, the component containing $T$ is still $T$: any connected enlargement in $H$ would enlarge it in $F$. We show that $T$ has a clopen neighborhood in $H$ avoiding $F\cap \partial D$. Let $J$ be the intersection of all clopen neighborhoods of $T$ in $H$. If $J$ were separated into two nonempty compact parts $J_1,J_2$, its connected subset $T$ would lie in one, say $J_1$. Choose disjoint open neighborhoods of $J_1,J_2$. Finitely many clopen neighborhoods of $T$ exclude the compact set outside their union. Their intersection is clopen and splits into two clopen parts inside those open neighborhoods. Its first part is a clopen neighborhood of $T$ excluding $J_2$, a contradiction to the definition of $J$. Thus $J$ is connected and equals $T$. Compactness now supplies a finite intersection $E$ of such clopen neighborhoods disjoint from $F\cap \partial D$. The set $E$ is compact, lies in $\operatorname {int}D$ and is open in $F$, so $F\setminus E$ is closed in the ambient space. By local compactness and regularity, finitely many relatively compact open sets cover $E$ with closures disjoint from $F\setminus E$. Their union $B$ has compact closure, contains $E$, and satisfies $\overline B\cap F\subset E\subset B$. Therefore $\partial \overline B\cap F=\varnothing $, and $Q=\overline B$ is the required compact neighborhood of $T$. $\square$

title: Proposition 9.52.12
section: 9.52 Convexity and cohomology in the top degrees
text: Proposition 9.52.12 . 5366BBA720F6 Let $M$ be a connected noncompact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, and $U\subset M$ open. The following are equivalent: For every compact $K\subset U$ some smooth strongly $n$-convex exhaustion $\psi $ of $M$ has $K\subset \{ \psi <b\} \Subset U$. $M\setminus U$ has no compact connected component. In particular this is precisely the top-degree Runge-complete condition. Proof. If $T$ is a compact component of the closed complement, use lemma 9.52.11 to choose a compact neighborhood $Q$ of it with $\partial Q\subset U$. A strongly $n$-convex function has no local maximum, because a negative-semidefinite Levi form cannot have a positive eigenvalue. Its maximum on $Q$ must therefore occur on $\partial Q$. A sublevel containing that compact boundary contains $Q$, contradicting its containment in $U$. Conversely, if $K=\varnothing $, use any strongly $n$-convex exhaustion and a level below its infimum. Suppose now that $K\subset U$ is nonempty and compact, and take a strictly $\omega $-subharmonic exhaustion $f$ supplied by theorem 9.52.8 . Choose $b>\max _ K f$, with a positive margin, and put $P=(M\setminus U)\cap \{ f\leq b\} $. It is compact. Every component $T$ of the complement is closed and noncompact, so $f$ is unbounded on it. A point $x\in P\cap T$ and a point $y\in T$ with $f(y)>b+2$ lie in the same component of the open manifold $M\setminus K$: connectedness of $T$ is enough, and the containing open component is path connected. A thin connected relatively compact path neighborhood $D_ x\Subset M\setminus K$ thus connects $x$ to $W=\{ f>b+1\} $. Finitely many such $D_ x$ cover $P$. Their union $D$ has finitely many components and compact closure disjoint from $K$. Every component of $D$ meets $W$. Each component of $W$ has noncompact closure. Otherwise $f$ would attain a maximum greater than $b+1$ in its interior, since its boundary has value $b+1$, contradicting strict subharmonicity. Thus each component of $W$ meeting $D$ contains a point outside $\overline D$. The whole-open sink lemma gives $v\geq 0$, positive on $P$, with $L_\omega v\geq 0$ off a compact $S\subset W\setminus \overline D$. It vanishes on a neighborhood of $K$, since both $\overline D$ and $\overline W$ avoid $K$. Choose $C$ so that $f+Cv>b+1$ on $P$, a strict margin. Choose a smooth convex increasing $\chi \geq 0$, zero for $t\leq b+1/2$, whose derivative for $t\geq b+1$ is large enough that $\chi '(f)L_\omega f$ dominates $C|L_\omega v|$ on the compact $S$. Such a function is an integral of a smooth nondecreasing step times a sufficiently large constant; $\min _ S L_\omega f>0$ when $S$ is nonempty. If $S=\varnothing $, take $\chi =0$. The chain rule gives \[  \psi =f+Cv+\chi (f),\qquad L_\omega \psi >0.  \] It is exhaustive since $\psi \geq f$, and $\psi =f$ on $K$. On the complement of $U$, points with $f\leq b$ belong to $P$ and have $\psi >b+1$, and other points have $\psi \geq f>b$. Hence $\{ \psi \leq b\} \subset U$. This is compact, so $K\subset \{ \psi <b\} \Subset U$ as claimed. If $P$ is empty the same conclusion holds with $v=\chi =0$. $\square$

title: Corollary 9.52.13
section: 9.52 Convexity and cohomology in the top degrees
text: Corollary 9.52.13 . 0AD84DC1EF06 Let $\mathcal F$ be coherent on a countable-basis complex space $X$, possibly nonreduced, with $\dim X\leq n$ for an integer $n\geq 0$. Then $H^ k(X,\mathcal F)=0$ for $k\geq n+1$. If $X$ has no compact irreducible component of dimension $n$, then $H^ n(X,\mathcal F)=0$. If it has only finitely many such compact components, then $H^ n(X,\mathcal F)$ is Hausdorff and finite dimensional. Proof. For $n\geq 1$ apply the complete vanishing and compact-exceptional finiteness theorem 9.51.13 to theorem 9.52.10 , with $q=n+1$ or $q=n$. If $\dim X<n$, its strongly $(\dim X+1)$-complete exhaustion already gives the degree-$n$ vanishing. For $n=0$ the first assertion uses strong1-completeness. The second says $X$ is empty. In the last, $X$ is a finite set and hence compact; apply theorem 9.51.10 also in degree zero. This retains the full nonreduced coherent module, not just its values on the reduction. $\square$

title: Corollary 9.52.14
section: 9.52 Convexity and cohomology in the top degrees
text: Corollary 9.52.14 . DBA14B44B8CF Let $\mathcal F$ be coherent on a connected noncompact complex $n$-manifold $M$, where $n\geq 1$, and let $U\subset M$ be open. If $M\setminus U$ has no compact connected component, restriction \[  H^{n-1}(M,\mathcal F)\longrightarrow H^{n-1}(U,\mathcal F)  \] has dense image for the intrinsic quotient cohomology topologies. Proof. The manifold is strongly $n$-complete by theorem 9.52.8 . The preceding Runge-complete proposition gives, for every compact subset of $U$, a globally strongly $n$-convex exhaustion with the required relatively compact sublevel. This satisfies all hypotheses of the degree $q-1$ density assertion in theorem 9.51.13 , for $q=n$. Its topology is exactly the intrinsic cohomology topology constructed there, including degree zero when $n=1$. $\square$

title: 10.36 Smooth bundles, connections and holomorphic extensions

section: 10.36 Smooth bundles, connections and holomorphic extensions
text:
Manifolds are Hausdorff and second countable. Write $\mathcal A^ k(E)=C^\infty (M,\Lambda ^ kT^*M\otimes E)$, with complex coefficients when $E$ is complex. Matrix products of forms include wedge product in the displayed order. Definition 10.36.1 . 50F3CC97C433 A smooth vector bundle of rank $r$ over $M$, over $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, is a smooth projection $\pi :E\to M$ with $\mathbb K$-vector-space fibers and local trivializations $\theta _ i:E|_{U_ i}\to U_ i\times \mathbb K^ r$ whose restrictions to the fibers are linear isomorphisms. A $C^ k$ section over $U$ is a $C^ k$ map $s:U\to E$ with $\pi \circ s=\operatorname {id}_ U$, where $0\leq k\leq \infty $. A frame is a tuple of sections forming a fiber basis at every point. A sheaf of modules is locally free of rank $r$ if it is locally isomorphic to the direct sum of $r$ copies of its ring sheaf. Ranks may vary between connected components, and rank zero is allowed. Proposition 10.93.1 . 24324B70E319 Smooth real or complex vector bundles are equivalent to locally free finite-rank modules over the corresponding sheaf of smooth functions. Holomorphic vector bundles are similarly equivalent to locally free $\mathcal O_ X$-modules. Bundle morphisms correspond to module morphisms. Proof. On a trivializing cover coefficient columns of a section satisfy $s_ i=g_{ij}s_ j$, where $g_{ij}g_{jk}=g_{ik}$ and the matrices are invertible and smooth, or holomorphic in the holomorphic case. Conversely glue $U_ i\times \mathbb K^ r$ by $(x,v)_ j\sim (x,g_{ij}(x)v)_ i$. The cocycle identity makes these identifications consistent, and each inverse image of $U_ i$ is exactly $U_ i\times \mathbb K^ r$. Points with different base points are separated on the base; points over the same base point are separated in such a product chart. A countable trivializing subcover gives a countable atlas. Thus the glued total space is a Hausdorff second-countable smooth or complex manifold with the required vector-bundle charts. A morphism between free sheaf modules is a matrix of functions: its columns are the images of the constant basis sections, and linearity determines every other section. Applying this to local bases of a locally free module gives the preceding invertible transition matrices. The reconstructed bundle's section sheaf is the original module by these same local identifications. Morphisms glue by the same matrix rule, proving full faithfulness as well as existence. In particular sections are $C^ k$ exactly when their coefficient columns are $C^ k$. For the trivial bundle these are arbitrary $C^ k$ maps to $\mathbb K^ r$. In a coordinate chart $x:U\to \mathbb R^ m$, the tangent trivialization is $v\mapsto (\pi (v),dx(v))$. Its transitions are the coordinate Jacobians, and the chain rule is exactly their cocycle identity. Dual and exterior powers give the cotangent and differential-form bundles; their sections have the usual coordinate coefficients. In the holomorphic case the same constructions use holomorphic frames and give the existing sheaf $\mathcal O(E)$. $\square$ Definition 10.36.2 . 7346D78B2C78 A connection on $E$ is a $\mathbb K$-linear operator $D:\mathcal A^\bullet (E)\to \mathcal A^{\bullet +1}(E)$ satisfying \[  D(\alpha \wedge s)=d\alpha \wedge s+(-1)^ p\alpha \wedge Ds \quad \text{for }\alpha \in \mathcal A^ p(M,\mathbb K).  \] Its covariant derivative along a real vector field $\xi $ is $D_\xi s=(Ds)(\xi )$ for sections $s$. Its curvature is the endomorphism-valued two-form representing $D^2$, as established below. A connection is flat if this curvature is zero. Proposition 10.36.3 . 090E2091E078 Every smooth bundle has a connection; its connections form an affine space over $\mathcal A^1(\operatorname {End}E)$. A connection is locally $D=d+A\wedge $ and has curvature $F_ D=dA+A\wedge A$. It induces connections on sums, tensors, duals, Hom and exterior powers, and on smooth pullbacks. For a Hom-valued $k$-form $B:E\to F$ the induced differential is EB79762053F3 10.36.4 \begin{equation}  D_{\operatorname {Hom}(E,F)}B =dB+A_ F\wedge B-(-1)^ k B\wedge A_ E. \end{equation} One has the Bianchi and covariant-derivative identities \[  D_{\operatorname {End}E}F_ D=0,\qquad [D_\xi ,D_\eta ]-D_{[\xi ,\eta ]}=F_ D(\xi ,\eta ).  \] Proof. The Leibniz rule makes $D$ local. If a section vanishes near $x$, multiply it by a smooth cutoff supported in that neighborhood and equal to one near $x$; applying the rule shows $Ds(x)=0$. The graded Leibniz rule gives $D=d+A\wedge $ from its values on a local frame. If new columns are $\widetilde s=gs$, compatibility gives $\widetilde A=gAg^{-1}-(dg)g^{-1}$. Squaring and using $d(A\wedge s)=dA\wedge s-A\wedge ds$ gives $D^2s=F_ D\wedge s$. It follows either from this equality or the transformation law that $\widetilde F_ D=gF_ Dg^{-1}$. In rank one $A\wedge A=0$; $F_ D=dA$ is a globally defined closed scalar two-form. The matrix $A$ itself is defined only on the chosen frame domain. For existence, take trivial connections $d_ i$ on a trivializing cover and a subordinate smooth partition $(\chi _ i)$, as in proposition 10.43.10 . The locally finite sum $D=\sum _ i\chi _ i d_ i$, each summand extended by zero where necessary, is smooth and has the required Leibniz rule because $\sum _ i\chi _ i=1$. The difference of two connections is linear over smooth functions on sections, hence is an endomorphism-valued one-form. Its action in higher degrees is left wedge multiplication by that form, by the graded rule. Conversely adding any such form gives a connection. The transition matrices for tensor, dual and exterior bundles are $g_ E\otimes g_ F$, $(g_ E^{-1})^{\mathsf T}$ and $\Lambda ^ kg_ E$. For a direct sum use block diagonal matrices and the componentwise connection. On tensor-valued forms the defining identity is $D(s\otimes t)=Ds\otimes t+(-1)^{\deg s}s\otimes Dt$, where the form factors are wedged in that order. The induced connection forms are respectively $A_ E\otimes I+I\otimes A_ F$, $-A_ E^{\mathsf T}$ and the derivation of $A_ E$ on the exterior factors. The local graded product rule verifies that they glue and uniquely determines them. Their curvatures are respectively \[  F_{E\otimes F}=F_ E\otimes I+I\otimes F_ F, \qquad F_{E^*}=-F_ E^{\mathsf T},\qquad F_{\det E}=\operatorname {tr}F_ E.  \] The exterior curvature acts by the sum of its actions on each factor; there are no extra signs because curvature has even degree. Applying the product rule to $B s$ proves ( 10.36.4 ), and gives $F_{\operatorname {Hom}(E,F)}B=F_ FB-BF_ E$ for zero-form $B$. For $F_ D=dA+A\wedge A$, direct expansion yields $dF_ D=dA\wedge A-A\wedge dA$ and $A\wedge F_ D-F_ D\wedge A=A\wedge dA-dA\wedge A$. This proves Bianchi by ( 10.36.4 ). Finally $D_\xi =\xi +A(\xi )$, so subtracting $D_{[\xi ,\eta ]}$ from the commutator gives \[  \xi (A(\eta ))-\eta (A(\xi ))-A([\xi ,\eta ]) +[A(\xi ),A(\eta )]=F_ D(\xi ,\eta ),  \] with the indicated sign on the derivative term. For a smooth map $f:N\to M$, the fiber product $f^*E=\{ (y,v):f(y)=\pi (v)\} $ has charts $(y,v)\mapsto (y,\operatorname {pr}_2\theta _ i(v))$ over $f^{-1}U_ i$. The first coordinate is $y$, not $f(y)$. Its transitions are $g_{ij}\circ f$ and its connection forms are $f^*A_ i$; the gauge rule verifies their compatibility. The pullback identities for $d$ and wedge products give $D_{f^*E}f^*s=f^*D_ Es$ and $F_{f^*E}=f^*F_ E$. No immersion assumption on $f$ is required. $\square$ Lemma 10.36.5 . 6DF73544DD2F A smooth connection has unique invertible parallel transport along piecewise smooth paths: a starting vector extends uniquely to a section $u$ along the path with $D_ tu=0$. Transport respects concatenation and reversal and depends smoothly on smooth finite-dimensional families of paths, piecewise on a fixed finite subdivision near each parameter value. Proof. In a local frame the equation is $U'=-B(t,z)U$, $U(0,z)=I$, with \[  B(t,z)=A_{\gamma _ z(t)}(\dot\gamma _ z(t)).  \] On a compact interval and compact parameter set the iterated integral series \[  U(t,z)=I+\sum _{k\geq 1}(-1)^ k \int _{0<t_ k<\cdots <t_1<t} B(t_1,z)\cdots B(t_ k,z)\, dt_ k\cdots dt_1  \] converges uniformly: the kth norm is at most $(Mt)^ k/k!$. It satisfies the integral equation and hence the differential equation. After any fixed number $a$ of parameter derivatives, the kth term is bounded by $C_ a^ k(1+k)^ a t^ k/k!$, after increasing $C_ a$ to bound all coefficient derivatives of order at most $a$. Thus those derivatives also converge uniformly. Time derivatives follow from the equation, proving smooth parameter dependence. The same construction solves $V'=VB$, $V(0)=I$; differentiating $VU$ proves $VU=I$. For uniqueness the difference of two solutions with zero initial value satisfies its homogeneous integral equation. Iterating it bounds the difference by $(Mt)^ k/k!$ times its bounded supremum, which tends to zero. Initial values enter linearly. A compact path is subdivided into finitely many frame neighborhoods. Gauge transformations take the local equations to each other, so uniqueness glues the solutions. The same finite subdivision works near any fixed member of a smooth path family, proving the assertion for global families as well. Concatenation and reversal follow from uniqueness and the chain rule. The argument also works over the reals and on reversed time intervals. $\square$ Inner products on complex bundles are linear in the first argument. A smooth Hermitian metric is a smoothly varying positive definite Hermitian form on the fibers. A connection is metric-compatible when \[  d\langle u,v\rangle =\langle Du,v\rangle +\langle u,Dv\rangle  \] for sections. On bundle-valued forms the pairing wedges the first coefficient with the conjugate of the second, and the corresponding rule has the sign $(-1)^{\deg u}$ before the second term. For line bundles this is the quadratic metric of quadratic Hermitian metrics on line bundles ; its squared norms, rather than their square roots, occur in curvature weights. Theorem 10.36.6 . 08655B144691 A smooth connection is flat exactly when it has parallel frames locally. For a flat connection, parallel transport depends only on the endpoint-preserving continuous homotopy class of a path. It has a parallel frame on every connected simply connected open set. On a connected base, rank-$r$ flat bundles with connection correspond to representations of $\pi _1(M,a)$ on $\mathbb K^ r$, up to conjugacy. A Hermitian bundle with a flat metric-compatible connection corresponds to a unitary representation, with unitary conjugacy for isometric connection isomorphisms. Proof. In real dimension zero each component is a point and every assertion is immediate. To obtain local parallel frames from $F_ D=0$ otherwise, work in a coordinate box and solve $\partial _1G=-A_1G$, $G(0,x')=I$. The lemma makes $G$ smooth and invertible. Replace a frame $e$ by $eG$, so new coefficient columns are $G^{-1}$ times the old ones. In this new frame the first connection coefficient is zero. The $(1,j)$ flat-curvature equation then gives $\partial _1\widetilde A_ j=0$. On the hyperplane $x_1=0$ repeat in the remaining variables; the residual connection is flat there and the resulting frame change is independent of $x_1$. Induction makes every coefficient zero. Conversely a parallel frame has $A=0$ and therefore $F_ D=0$. Two parallel frames differ by a matrix $g$ satisfying $dg=0$, so their transition is locally constant. In these frames transport extends even to continuous paths: keep the coefficient vector constant on each subpath in a frame neighborhood. Refining the finite subdivision changes nothing, because the overlap transitions are locally constant along that subpath. It agrees with ODE transport on piecewise smooth paths. For a continuous homotopy, subdivide its compact square sufficiently finely that each small rectangle maps into a single frame neighborhood. Transport around its boundary is the identity. Replace two consecutive edges of a rectangle by its other two edges and sweep through the grid. Each replacement preserves transport; interior backtracks cancel by reversal, and the fixed endpoint edges have identity transport. This proves invariance along the two paths. Paths can also be replaced by piecewise smooth ones by such coordinate subdivisions. On a simply connected open set, transport of one fiber basis is consequently independent of path and gives a smooth parallel frame, as is visible in the local parallel frames just constructed. We give the covering construction to specify the representation convention. Multiply based loops by composition: $\gamma \delta $ means first $\delta $, then $\gamma $. The set $\widetilde M$ of endpoint-preserving homotopy classes of paths $p$ starting at $a$ is covered by endpoint charts over simply connected coordinate balls: append any path inside the ball. Such appended paths are equivalent exactly when their endpoints agree. The charts are compatible by locally constant changes of sheet. They make the endpoint map a covering; distinct points over one endpoint are separated by disjoint sheets. They give a smooth Hausdorff manifold. It is second countable: choose a countable coordinate-ball cover. Components of its pairwise intersections are open and hence at most countable; subdivision of paths shows that a sheet is specified by a finite word of these chart and intersection choices. Indeed, in each ball two intervening paths with the same endpoints contract, and moving a crossing point inside its intersection component does not change the sheet. There are countably many such words and endpoint charts. This cover is connected, since a defining path lifts from the identity sheet to its own class. A loop there projects to a null-homotopic loop: its class must be the identity because its lift closes at the identity sheet. Lifting a contracting homotopy, by subdivision into covering charts, contracts the original loop. Thus this is the universal cover, with the usual equivalent base points handled by conjugating paths. There is a right action $p\cdot \gamma =p\circ \gamma $ of $\pi _1(M,a)$ on $\widetilde M$, free and transitive on every endpoint fiber. Set $\rho (\gamma )=T_\gamma $. The concatenation identity makes $\rho $ a representation. The map $(p,v)\mapsto T_ pv$ identifies $E$ with the quotient by the right action \[  (p,v)\cdot \gamma =(p\circ \gamma ,\rho (\gamma )^{-1}v).  \] It is invariant by the transport rule. In each sheet chart it is a smooth fiberwise isomorphism, and its local frames are parallel. Conversely for any representation this quotient is a smooth vector bundle: the sheet charts have locally constant transition matrices. Their trivial connections glue, are flat, and have the prescribed monodromy. A connection isomorphism conjugates the representations by its value at $a$; conversely such a fiber intertwiner extends by transport to an isomorphism. These constructions are inverse. For a metric-compatible connection and sections $u,v$ along a smooth path, \[  \frac d{dt}h(u,v)=h(D_ tu,v)+h(u,D_ tv).  \] Thus parallel transport is isometric. The flat frames may be chosen orthonormal at one point and are then orthonormal everywhere, with unitary constant transitions. Conversely unitary transitions glue the fixed fiber metric and its trivial compatible connection. The quotient construction and its isomorphisms are then unitary exactly as asserted. The real Euclidean version has orthogonal transitions. $\square$ Over a complex manifold set $\mathcal A^{p,q}(E)=C^\infty (X,\Lambda ^{p,q}T^*X\otimes E)$. Projection onto types gives a unique decomposition $D=D'+D''$, where $D'$ raises $p$ and $D''$ raises $q$. Each satisfies the graded Leibniz rule with $d$ replaced by $\partial $ or $\bar\partial $. Conversely any two operators of these types and with these rules sum to a connection. Locally they are $\partial +A'\wedge $ and $\bar\partial +A''\wedge $, respectively. Proposition 10.36.7 . CCF7A9609341 For every smooth Hermitian bundle over a complex manifold and every prescribed $(0,1)$-connection $D''$, there is a unique compatible connection having that $(0,1)$ part. No integrability of $D''$ is required. On a real base a connection is compatible precisely when its one-form matrix in a unitary frame is skew Hermitian. Compatible connections exist, and their differences are exactly the skew-Hermitian endomorphism-valued one-forms. Proof. Differentiating the inner product in a unitary frame gives compatibility exactly when $A+A^*=0$, where adjoint conjugates the one-form as well as transposing its matrix. This test on sections gives the full graded metric product rule on forms by the ordinary graded Leibniz rule. On a complex base write the prescribed part in such a frame as $\bar\partial +B$. The unique skew-adjoint matrix with $(0,1)$ part $B$ is $A=B-B^*$, its $(1,0)$ part being $-B^*$. This local construction glues: on an overlap the transformed compatible connection has the same prescribed $(0,1)$ part, and local uniqueness applies. This proves existence and uniqueness. Local unitary frames exist by smooth Gram–Schmidt. Smooth metrics exist by summing local Euclidean metrics with a smooth partition of unity, exactly as in the line case smooth line-bundle metrics and curvature changes . Over a real base the partition is supplied by proposition 10.43.10 . Averaging the trivial connections in unitary frames by that partition gives a compatible connection, since their metric product rules sum with coefficients whose sum is one. The difference assertion follows from the unitary-frame test and the preceding affine-space description. Compatibility also makes $F_ D$ skew Hermitian, by applying $d^2$ to the metric product rule. In rank one a unitary frame has imaginary $A$ and real $\mathrm iF_ D$. On a simply connected open set a unitary gauge $g$ has a smooth real phase $g=e^{\mathrm i\varphi }$: its local phases have the same closed differential $-\mathrm i g^{-1}dg$, whose path integrals are independent of path by the coordinate-square homotopy argument above. Adjust the additive constant to recover $g$. The gauge rule is then $A=\widetilde A+\mathrm i\, d\varphi $. For a holomorphic bundle the prescribed canonical coefficientwise $\bar\partial $ gives precisely its already-defined Chern connection. Its curvature has type $(1,1)$: the $(0,2)$ part is $(D'')^2=\bar\partial ^2=0$, and skew-adjointness makes the $(2,0)$ part zero as well. $\square$ Corollary 10.36.8 . DD24E61268DB A Hermitian holomorphic bundle has zero Chern curvature if and only if it has orthonormal holomorphic frames locally. On a connected simply connected open set, zero Chern curvature gives a single such frame. On a connected manifold these bundles correspond to unitary representations of its fundamental group, up to unitary conjugacy for isometric holomorphic isomorphisms. Proof. If the Chern curvature vanishes, the parallel frames of theorem 10.36.6 can be chosen orthonormal. Their sections are holomorphic because their Chern $(0,1)$ derivative is zero. Conversely the trivial connection in an orthonormal holomorphic frame is compatible and has canonical $(0,1)$ part; uniqueness in proposition 10.36.7 makes it the Chern connection, so its curvature vanishes. An isometric holomorphic isomorphism preserves that unique connection. Conversely unitary locally constant transition matrices are holomorphic and give this Chern connection. The representation statement therefore follows from the same flat-bundle correspondence. $\square$ Remark 10.36.9 . 597030C175B7 For a holomorphic bundle $E$, the canonical coefficientwise $\bar\partial $ is independent of holomorphic frame, since its transition matrices are holomorphic. It squares to zero. Its cohomology on global $(p,q)$-forms is denoted $H^{p,q}(X,E)$. Write $\Omega _ X^ p$ for the holomorphic bundle $\Lambda ^ pT^{1,0*}X$ or its sheaf of holomorphic sections, according to context. The existing differential-resolution comparison corollary 10.43.11 is precisely \[  H^{p,q}(X,E)=H^ q(X,\Omega _ X^ p\otimes \mathcal O(E));  \] in particular $H^{p,0}(X,E)$ is the space of holomorphic sections of $\Lambda ^ pT^{1,0*}X\otimes E$. This notation does not impose a metric, positivity or compactness condition. Theorem 10.36.10 . B7A8F8D8A536 Let $L$ be a smooth complex line bundle on an oriented real manifold $M$, and let $s$ be a smooth section transverse to the zero section. Then $Z=s^{-1}(0)$ is a closed smooth submanifold of real codimension two, with its normal orientation induced by the complex line $L$. Orient $Z$ so that the oriented normal plane followed by $TZ$ gives the orientation of $TM$. For any connection $D$ on $L$, the one-form $u=s^{-1}Ds$ off $Z$ extends with locally integrable coefficients, and as complex currents on $M$ 3E0F17FBE3F5 10.36.11 \begin{equation}  du=2\pi \mathrm i[Z]+F_ D. \end{equation} If $D$ is compatible with a smooth Hermitian metric, the real locally integrable form $\alpha =(2\pi )^{-1}\operatorname {Im}u$ satisfies \[  d\alpha =[Z]-\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }F_ D.  \] Consequently $[Z]$ represents the real image of $c_1(L)\in H^2(M,\mathbb Z)$ under the de Rham comparison. No compactness is required. Proof. Write $s=fe$ in a smooth complex frame, and $D=d+A$ there. At a zero, $Ds=df\otimes e$, independently of the connection. Transversality says that $(\operatorname {Re}f,\operatorname {Im}f)$ has rank two there. The real inverse function theorem, applied after completing these two differentials to a basis, gives local coordinates $(x,y,t)$ with $f=x+\mathrm iy$. The orientation rule makes $dx\wedge dy$ followed by the orientation of the $t$ coordinates the positive orientation of $M$; in dimension two the latter factor is the signed orientation of a point. A change of frame multiplies the normal derivative by a nonzero complex scalar at a zero, whose real determinant is positive; hence this normal and induced orientation is intrinsic. These charts also prove that $Z$ is a closed embedded submanifold and its integration current has locally finite mass. On the complement of $Z$, \[  u=\frac{df}{f}+A.  \] In the coordinates just chosen, $df/f=(dx+\mathrm i\, dy)/(x+\mathrm iy)$ has coefficients bounded by a constant times $(x^2+y^2)^{-1/2}$. They are locally integrable in the two normal variables, hence also in all variables by Fubini. Thus $u$ defines an intrinsic locally integrable current: its expressions agree off $Z$, and $Z$ has Lebesgue measure zero. We check the distributional derivative, including its orientation. On the plane let $z=x+\mathrm iy$ and let $\varphi $ be a smooth compactly supported test function. With the convention $T_\eta (\psi )=\int \eta \wedge \psi $, the derivative of a one-current satisfies $dT_\eta (\varphi )=T_\eta (d\varphi )$. On a punctured disc containing the support, $d(dz/z)=0$ classically, so Stokes' formula Stokes' formula on compact domains with corners gives \[  \left\langle d\left(\frac{dz}{z}\right),\varphi \right\rangle =\lim _{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \int _{|z|>\varepsilon }\frac{dz}{z}\wedge d\varphi =\lim _{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \int _{|z|=\varepsilon }^{\rm counterclockwise}\varphi \frac{dz}{z} =2\pi \mathrm i\, \varphi (0).  \] The boundary sign is positive because the inner boundary of the punctured disc is clockwise, whereas $d(\varphi \, dz/z)=-dz/z\wedge d\varphi $. The last equality follows by setting $z=\varepsilon e^{\mathrm i\theta }$; the integrand converges uniformly to $\mathrm i\varphi (0)\, d\theta $. The first limit is justified by the local integrability just proved. In the product coordinates $(x,y,t)$ the coefficients are independent of $t$, so all their distributional $t$ derivatives vanish, by integration by parts in those variables. Applying the plane identity to the coefficient of a test form containing only the $t$ differentials and using Fubini gives $d(df/f)=2\pi \mathrm i[\{ x=y=0\} ]$, with exactly the specified orientation: if the coordinate orientation differs from that of $M$, both this integral and the induced integral over $Z$ acquire the same sign. All other components of a test form contain $dx$ or $dy$ and contribute zero. Since $F_ D=dA$ for a line connection, this proves ( 10.36.11 ) near $Z$; off $Z$ it is the ordinary identity $du=dA$. Equality of currents is local, so the formula holds on all of $M$. Choose a compatible connection, which exists by proposition 10.36.7 . Its scalar curvature is imaginary. Taking imaginary parts and dividing by $2\pi $ gives the formula for $d\alpha $, because $\operatorname {Im}F_ D=-\mathrm iF_ D$. The current and smooth-form de Rham comparison of corollary 10.43.11 , and the integral comparison theorem 10.40.5 , give the asserted class. If $Z$ is empty, $u$ is smooth globally and the same proof applies. In real dimension less than two transversality forces $Z$ to be empty, and all two-forms and two-currents vanish, so the statement still holds. $\square$ Proposition 10.36.12 . 84111D436822 For a holomorphic exact sequence $0\to S\xrightarrow jE \xrightarrow gQ\to 0$, give $S,Q$ the induced and quotient metrics. Use the smooth orthogonal identification $E=S\oplus Q$. Let $\beta \in \mathcal A^{1,0}(\operatorname {Hom}(S,Q))$ be the second fundamental form, so that the established block connection is $D_ E=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}D_ S& -\beta ^*\\ \beta & D_ Q\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. Put $b=\beta ^*$. The full map derivative identities are \[  \begin{array}{ll} D'j=g^*\beta ,& \bar\partial j=0,\\  D'g=-\beta j^*,& \bar\partial g=0,\\  D'j^*=0,& \bar\partial j^*=b g,\\  D'g^*=0,& \bar\partial g^*=-j b. \end{array}  \] Here each operator is the induced Hom connection. Moreover $\bar\partial _{\operatorname {Hom}(Q,S)}b=0$ and \[  F_ E=\begin{pmatrix}  F_ S-b\wedge \beta 

& -D'_{\operatorname {Hom}(Q,S)}b

\\  \bar\partial _{\operatorname {Hom}(S,Q)}\beta 

& F_ Q-\beta \wedge b 

\end{pmatrix}.  \] The orthogonal splitting is holomorphic exactly when $\beta =0$. Proof. The block connection and diagonal curvature identities are those already proved in proposition 10.34.9 ; their proof imposes no positivity condition. Here $j$ and $g$ and their adjoints are the constant inclusion and projection matrices. Apply ( 10.36.4 ) in degree zero to each. The four results are respectively $(0,\beta )^{\mathsf T}$, $(-\beta ,0)$, $(0,b)$ and $(-b,0)^{\mathsf T}$, proving all types and signs displayed above. Squaring the block connection gives upper-right entry $-D_{\operatorname {Hom}(Q,S)}b$ and lower-left entry $D_{\operatorname {Hom}(S,Q)}\beta $ by the degree-one formula. Chern curvature has type $(1,1)$; its $(0,2)$ upper-right part forces $\bar\partial b=0$, and its $(2,0)$ lower-left part forces $D'\beta =0$. This proves the matrix, including the minus sign in its upper-right entry. Finally $\bar\partial g^*=-jb$ vanishes exactly when $b=0$, since $j$ is injective. This is exactly when the orthogonal right inverse is holomorphic. $\square$ Theorem 10.36.13 . 304DF496E0BF With $S,Q$ fixed, isomorphism classes of holomorphic extension diagrams $0\to S\to E\to Q\to 0$, with identity maps on their ends, are in bijection with $H^{0,1}_{\bar\partial }(X,\operatorname {Hom}(Q,S))$, and hence with $H^1(X,\mathcal O(\operatorname {Hom}(Q,S)))$. The class is $[\beta ^*]$. It is independent of all metrics and vanishes exactly for a holomorphically split extension. Proof. A smooth right inverse $h$ exists by orthogonal splitting. For the orthogonal one the preceding proposition says $\bar\partial h=-jb$, with $b=\beta ^*$ closed. For any smooth right inverse define $b=-j^{-1}\bar\partial h$: the expression lies in $S$ because $g\bar\partial h=\bar\partial (gh)=0$. Any other right inverse is $h+jv$, with a global smooth $v:Q\to S$, so its form is $b-\bar\partial v$. This proves independence of splitting and metric. Transporting a splitting under an extension isomorphism proves invariance as well. In the splitting coordinates the Dolbeault operator is $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\bar\partial _ S& -b\\ 0& \bar\partial _ Q\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. A smooth extension isomorphism inducing the identity on the ends has the form $\Psi =\left(\begin{smallmatrix}I& v\\ 0& I\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. From the coefficient product rule it is holomorphic from $E_ b$ to $E_ c$ precisely when \[  \bar\partial v-c+b=0.  \] Thus equal Dolbeault classes give isomorphic diagrams, and a split diagram has class zero. This also proves the converse splitting claim. For surjectivity take any closed smooth $b$. On the smooth bundle $S\oplus Q$ use the displayed operator. It squares to zero because $\bar\partial b=0$. More concretely, in local holomorphic frames the local complex exactness local Dolbeault exactness for forms and currents gives $b=\bar\partial v_ i$. The matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}I& -v_ i\\ 0& I\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ intertwines this operator with the usual one on the local split bundle, by the same calculation. On overlaps these trivializations differ by holomorphic upper-triangular matrices, since $\bar\partial (v_ i-v_ j)=0$. They therefore define a holomorphic structure, with holomorphic inclusion and projection, and with the prescribed class $[b]$. This is an explicit triangular construction; no general integrable-connection theorem is needed. The final sheaf identification is corollary 10.43.11 . Zero ranks give the unique trivial extension and zero cohomology. $\square$ Proposition 10.36.14 . 732A25F31FC3 Extension diagrams with fixed end bundles $S,Q$, allowing arbitrary holomorphic automorphisms on both ends, are classified by the orbits \[  H^1(X,\mathcal O(\operatorname {Hom}(Q,S))) /(\operatorname {Aut}(S)\times \operatorname {Aut}(Q)), \qquad (u,v)[b]=[u b v^{-1}].  \] This gives a surjection onto the isomorphism classes of their abstract middle bundles, which need not be injective. For line bundles on a compact connected complex manifold the diagram orbit set is $\{ 0\} \sqcup \mathbb P(H^1(X,\mathcal O(\operatorname {Hom}(Q,S))))$, where the first element is the split diagram. Proof. A diagram map with end automorphisms $u,v$ has smooth block matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}u& w\\ 0& v\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. It is holomorphic exactly when $\bar\partial w-cv+ub=0$. Since $u,v$ are holomorphic and invertible, this is equivalent to $[c]=[ubv^{-1}]$, and the equation constructs the isomorphism whenever that class equality holds. Forgetting the inclusion and projection gives the asserted surjection. For line bundles each end automorphism is a nowhere vanishing holomorphic function; on a compact connected manifold it is a nonzero constant by the local maximum principle. Its action is scalar multiplication, whose orbits are zero and the projective lines of nonzero classes. If the cohomology vanishes its projective space is empty. Here is a counterexample to injectivity after forgetting the diagram. On $\mathbb P^1$ let $S=\mathcal O(-2)$ and use the two maps into $E=\mathcal O^2$ given in homogeneous coordinates by \[  j_1=(x^2,y^2)^{\mathsf T},\qquad j_2=(x^2,y^2+xy)^{\mathsf T}.  \] Each pair has no common zero and hence is a subbundle inclusion: locally one entry is a unit, and an invertible two-by-two matrix completes it to a frame. Each quotient is a line bundle with $Q\simeq \det E\otimes S^{-1}\simeq \mathcal O(2)$; this determinant isomorphism follows locally by wedging a frame of $S$ with any quotient lift. Choose such an identification for each quotient. Every automorphism of $\mathcal O^2$ is a constant invertible matrix, since its entries are global holomorphic functions on $\mathbb P^1$. It and a scalar automorphism of $S$ preserve the span of the two quadratic components of an injection. But \[  \operatorname {span}\{ x^2,y^2\}  \ne \operatorname {span}\{ x^2,y^2+xy\} ,  \] by independence of the homogeneous monomials. Thus the diagrams lie in distinct diagram orbits while their middle bundles are identical. Both are nonsplit: a right inverse from $\mathcal O(2)$ to $\mathcal O^2$ would have components in $H^0(\mathbb P^1,\mathcal O(-2))=0$, by proposition 10.51.5 . This counterexample also concerns nonzero extension classes. $\square$

title: Definition 10.36.1
section: 10.36 Smooth bundles, connections and holomorphic extensions
text: Definition 10.36.1 . 50F3CC97C433 A smooth vector bundle of rank $r$ over $M$, over $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, is a smooth projection $\pi :E\to M$ with $\mathbb K$-vector-space fibers and local trivializations $\theta _ i:E|_{U_ i}\to U_ i\times \mathbb K^ r$ whose restrictions to the fibers are linear isomorphisms. A $C^ k$ section over $U$ is a $C^ k$ map $s:U\to E$ with $\pi \circ s=\operatorname {id}_ U$, where $0\leq k\leq \infty $. A frame is a tuple of sections forming a fiber basis at every point. A sheaf of modules is locally free of rank $r$ if it is locally isomorphic to the direct sum of $r$ copies of its ring sheaf. Ranks may vary between connected components, and rank zero is allowed.

title: Proposition 10.93.1
search_title: Vector bundles and locally free function-sheaf modules
text: Proposition 10.93.1 . 24324B70E319 Let $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $X$ be a topological space, and let $\mathcal A$ be a subsheaf of the sheaf of continuous $\mathbb K$-valued functions containing the locally constant functions. Locally free $\mathcal A$-modules of rank $r$ correspond to topological vector bundles with an $\mathcal A$-atlas, meaning trivializations whose transition matrices and their inverses have entries in $\mathcal A$. The correspondence identifies the module with the sections whose coefficient functions belong to $\mathcal A$, and identifies module morphisms with bundle morphisms having such coefficient matrices. No locality assumption on the rings $\mathcal A_ x$ is necessary. Proof. Evaluation $\mathcal A_ x\to \mathbb K$ is onto, since constants are present; denote its maximal kernel by $\mathfrak m_ x$. For a locally free module $\mathcal M$ put $E_ x=\mathcal M_ x/\mathfrak m_ x\mathcal M_ x$ and $E=\coprod _ xE_ x$. A local module basis identifies these fibers with $\mathbb K^ r$. Between two bases the coefficient columns obey $v_ i=g_{ij}v_ j$, where $g_{ij}$ and $g_{ji}$ are matrices of $\mathcal A$-sections and $g_{ij}g_{jk}=g_{ik}$. Their evaluated matrices are continuous and invertible. Give $E$ the topology of the glued charts $U_ i\times \mathbb K^ r$ with these identifications. Every product chart is open and homeomorphic to its corresponding part of $E$, so this is a topological vector bundle. If $X$ is Hausdorff, so is $E$: different base points are separated on $X$, and points in a common fiber are separated in one product chart. Local module sections give exactly the coefficient functions just specified. This description is injective, since a section with all fiber values zero has all its local coefficient functions zero. It is surjective by the sheaf gluing axiom. Conversely an $\mathcal A$-atlas glues copies of $\mathcal A^ r$ with the same matrices, giving a locally free module and recovering the original bundle and atlas. A module morphism is locally multiplication by the matrix of the images of its basis sections. These matrices obey the bundle transition rules, and conversely such matrices give a module morphism. This proves both constructions are inverse on objects and morphisms. With continuous, $C^ k$ or holomorphic coefficient sheaves the same charts give respectively continuous, $C^ k$ or holomorphic bundles and morphisms; in the latter two cases their coordinate changes have exactly that regularity. Taking smooth or holomorphic coefficient sheaves gives the corresponding smooth or holomorphic equivalence as a special case. $\square$ Proposition 10.93.1 . 24324B70E319 Smooth real or complex vector bundles are equivalent to locally free finite-rank modules over the corresponding sheaf of smooth functions. Holomorphic vector bundles are similarly equivalent to locally free $\mathcal O_ X$-modules. Bundle morphisms correspond to module morphisms. Proof. On a trivializing cover coefficient columns of a section satisfy $s_ i=g_{ij}s_ j$, where $g_{ij}g_{jk}=g_{ik}$ and the matrices are invertible and smooth, or holomorphic in the holomorphic case. Conversely glue $U_ i\times \mathbb K^ r$ by $(x,v)_ j\sim (x,g_{ij}(x)v)_ i$. The cocycle identity makes these identifications consistent, and each inverse image of $U_ i$ is exactly $U_ i\times \mathbb K^ r$. Points with different base points are separated on the base; points over the same base point are separated in such a product chart. A countable trivializing subcover gives a countable atlas. Thus the glued total space is a Hausdorff second-countable smooth or complex manifold with the required vector-bundle charts. A morphism between free sheaf modules is a matrix of functions: its columns are the images of the constant basis sections, and linearity determines every other section. Applying this to local bases of a locally free module gives the preceding invertible transition matrices. The reconstructed bundle's section sheaf is the original module by these same local identifications. Morphisms glue by the same matrix rule, proving full faithfulness as well as existence. In particular sections are $C^ k$ exactly when their coefficient columns are $C^ k$. For the trivial bundle these are arbitrary $C^ k$ maps to $\mathbb K^ r$. In a coordinate chart $x:U\to \mathbb R^ m$, the tangent trivialization is $v\mapsto (\pi (v),dx(v))$. Its transitions are the coordinate Jacobians, and the chain rule is exactly their cocycle identity. Dual and exterior powers give the cotangent and differential-form bundles; their sections have the usual coordinate coefficients. In the holomorphic case the same constructions use holomorphic frames and give the existing sheaf $\mathcal O(E)$. $\square$

title: Definition 10.36.2
section: 10.36 Smooth bundles, connections and holomorphic extensions
text: Definition 10.36.2 . 7346D78B2C78 A connection on $E$ is a $\mathbb K$-linear operator $D:\mathcal A^\bullet (E)\to \mathcal A^{\bullet +1}(E)$ satisfying \[  D(\alpha \wedge s)=d\alpha \wedge s+(-1)^ p\alpha \wedge Ds \quad \text{for }\alpha \in \mathcal A^ p(M,\mathbb K).  \] Its covariant derivative along a real vector field $\xi $ is $D_\xi s=(Ds)(\xi )$ for sections $s$. Its curvature is the endomorphism-valued two-form representing $D^2$, as established below. A connection is flat if this curvature is zero.

title: Proposition 10.36.3
section: 10.36 Smooth bundles, connections and holomorphic extensions
text: Proposition 10.36.3 . 090E2091E078 Every smooth bundle has a connection; its connections form an affine space over $\mathcal A^1(\operatorname {End}E)$. A connection is locally $D=d+A\wedge $ and has curvature $F_ D=dA+A\wedge A$. It induces connections on sums, tensors, duals, Hom and exterior powers, and on smooth pullbacks. For a Hom-valued $k$-form $B:E\to F$ the induced differential is EB79762053F3 10.36.4 \begin{equation}  D_{\operatorname {Hom}(E,F)}B =dB+A_ F\wedge B-(-1)^ k B\wedge A_ E. \end{equation} One has the Bianchi and covariant-derivative identities \[  D_{\operatorname {End}E}F_ D=0,\qquad [D_\xi ,D_\eta ]-D_{[\xi ,\eta ]}=F_ D(\xi ,\eta ).  \] Proof. The Leibniz rule makes $D$ local. If a section vanishes near $x$, multiply it by a smooth cutoff supported in that neighborhood and equal to one near $x$; applying the rule shows $Ds(x)=0$. The graded Leibniz rule gives $D=d+A\wedge $ from its values on a local frame. If new columns are $\widetilde s=gs$, compatibility gives $\widetilde A=gAg^{-1}-(dg)g^{-1}$. Squaring and using $d(A\wedge s)=dA\wedge s-A\wedge ds$ gives $D^2s=F_ D\wedge s$. It follows either from this equality or the transformation law that $\widetilde F_ D=gF_ Dg^{-1}$. In rank one $A\wedge A=0$; $F_ D=dA$ is a globally defined closed scalar two-form. The matrix $A$ itself is defined only on the chosen frame domain. For existence, take trivial connections $d_ i$ on a trivializing cover and a subordinate smooth partition $(\chi _ i)$, as in proposition 10.43.10 . The locally finite sum $D=\sum _ i\chi _ i d_ i$, each summand extended by zero where necessary, is smooth and has the required Leibniz rule because $\sum _ i\chi _ i=1$. The difference of two connections is linear over smooth functions on sections, hence is an endomorphism-valued one-form. Its action in higher degrees is left wedge multiplication by that form, by the graded rule. Conversely adding any such form gives a connection. The transition matrices for tensor, dual and exterior bundles are $g_ E\otimes g_ F$, $(g_ E^{-1})^{\mathsf T}$ and $\Lambda ^ kg_ E$. For a direct sum use block diagonal matrices and the componentwise connection. On tensor-valued forms the defining identity is $D(s\otimes t)=Ds\otimes t+(-1)^{\deg s}s\otimes Dt$, where the form factors are wedged in that order. The induced connection forms are respectively $A_ E\otimes I+I\otimes A_ F$, $-A_ E^{\mathsf T}$ and the derivation of $A_ E$ on the exterior factors. The local graded product rule verifies that they glue and uniquely determines them. Their curvatures are respectively \[  F_{E\otimes F}=F_ E\otimes I+I\otimes F_ F, \qquad F_{E^*}=-F_ E^{\mathsf T},\qquad F_{\det E}=\operatorname {tr}F_ E.  \] The exterior curvature acts by the sum of its actions on each factor; there are no extra signs because curvature has even degree. Applying the product rule to $B s$ proves ( 10.36.4 ), and gives $F_{\operatorname {Hom}(E,F)}B=F_ FB-BF_ E$ for zero-form $B$. For $F_ D=dA+A\wedge A$, direct expansion yields $dF_ D=dA\wedge A-A\wedge dA$ and $A\wedge F_ D-F_ D\wedge A=A\wedge dA-dA\wedge A$. This proves Bianchi by ( 10.36.4 ). Finally $D_\xi =\xi +A(\xi )$, so subtracting $D_{[\xi ,\eta ]}$ from the commutator gives \[  \xi (A(\eta ))-\eta (A(\xi ))-A([\xi ,\eta ]) +[A(\xi ),A(\eta )]=F_ D(\xi ,\eta ),  \] with the indicated sign on the derivative term. For a smooth map $f:N\to M$, the fiber product $f^*E=\{ (y,v):f(y)=\pi (v)\} $ has charts $(y,v)\mapsto (y,\operatorname {pr}_2\theta _ i(v))$ over $f^{-1}U_ i$. The first coordinate is $y$, not $f(y)$. Its transitions are $g_{ij}\circ f$ and its connection forms are $f^*A_ i$; the gauge rule verifies their compatibility. The pullback identities for $d$ and wedge products give $D_{f^*E}f^*s=f^*D_ Es$ and $F_{f^*E}=f^*F_ E$. No immersion assumption on $f$ is required. $\square$
