title: Lemma 10.36.5
section: 10.36 Smooth bundles, connections and holomorphic extensions
text: Lemma 10.36.5 . 6DF73544DD2F A smooth connection has unique invertible parallel transport along piecewise smooth paths: a starting vector extends uniquely to a section $u$ along the path with $D_ tu=0$. Transport respects concatenation and reversal and depends smoothly on smooth finite-dimensional families of paths, piecewise on a fixed finite subdivision near each parameter value. Proof. In a local frame the equation is $U'=-B(t,z)U$, $U(0,z)=I$, with \[  B(t,z)=A_{\gamma _ z(t)}(\dot\gamma _ z(t)).  \] On a compact interval and compact parameter set the iterated integral series \[  U(t,z)=I+\sum _{k\geq 1}(-1)^ k \int _{0<t_ k<\cdots <t_1<t} B(t_1,z)\cdots B(t_ k,z)\, dt_ k\cdots dt_1  \] converges uniformly: the kth norm is at most $(Mt)^ k/k!$. It satisfies the integral equation and hence the differential equation. After any fixed number $a$ of parameter derivatives, the kth term is bounded by $C_ a^ k(1+k)^ a t^ k/k!$, after increasing $C_ a$ to bound all coefficient derivatives of order at most $a$. Thus those derivatives also converge uniformly. Time derivatives follow from the equation, proving smooth parameter dependence. The same construction solves $V'=VB$, $V(0)=I$; differentiating $VU$ proves $VU=I$. For uniqueness the difference of two solutions with zero initial value satisfies its homogeneous integral equation. Iterating it bounds the difference by $(Mt)^ k/k!$ times its bounded supremum, which tends to zero. Initial values enter linearly. A compact path is subdivided into finitely many frame neighborhoods. Gauge transformations take the local equations to each other, so uniqueness glues the solutions. The same finite subdivision works near any fixed member of a smooth path family, proving the assertion for global families as well. Concatenation and reversal follow from uniqueness and the chain rule. The argument also works over the reals and on reversed time intervals. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.36.6
section: 10.36 Smooth bundles, connections and holomorphic extensions
text: Theorem 10.36.6 . 08655B144691 A smooth connection is flat exactly when it has parallel frames locally. For a flat connection, parallel transport depends only on the endpoint-preserving continuous homotopy class of a path. It has a parallel frame on every connected simply connected open set. On a connected base, rank-$r$ flat bundles with connection correspond to representations of $\pi _1(M,a)$ on $\mathbb K^ r$, up to conjugacy. A Hermitian bundle with a flat metric-compatible connection corresponds to a unitary representation, with unitary conjugacy for isometric connection isomorphisms. Proof. In real dimension zero each component is a point and every assertion is immediate. To obtain local parallel frames from $F_ D=0$ otherwise, work in a coordinate box and solve $\partial _1G=-A_1G$, $G(0,x')=I$. The lemma makes $G$ smooth and invertible. Replace a frame $e$ by $eG$, so new coefficient columns are $G^{-1}$ times the old ones. In this new frame the first connection coefficient is zero. The $(1,j)$ flat-curvature equation then gives $\partial _1\widetilde A_ j=0$. On the hyperplane $x_1=0$ repeat in the remaining variables; the residual connection is flat there and the resulting frame change is independent of $x_1$. Induction makes every coefficient zero. Conversely a parallel frame has $A=0$ and therefore $F_ D=0$. Two parallel frames differ by a matrix $g$ satisfying $dg=0$, so their transition is locally constant. In these frames transport extends even to continuous paths: keep the coefficient vector constant on each subpath in a frame neighborhood. Refining the finite subdivision changes nothing, because the overlap transitions are locally constant along that subpath. It agrees with ODE transport on piecewise smooth paths. For a continuous homotopy, subdivide its compact square sufficiently finely that each small rectangle maps into a single frame neighborhood. Transport around its boundary is the identity. Replace two consecutive edges of a rectangle by its other two edges and sweep through the grid. Each replacement preserves transport; interior backtracks cancel by reversal, and the fixed endpoint edges have identity transport. This proves invariance along the two paths. Paths can also be replaced by piecewise smooth ones by such coordinate subdivisions. On a simply connected open set, transport of one fiber basis is consequently independent of path and gives a smooth parallel frame, as is visible in the local parallel frames just constructed. We give the covering construction to specify the representation convention. Multiply based loops by composition: $\gamma \delta $ means first $\delta $, then $\gamma $. The set $\widetilde M$ of endpoint-preserving homotopy classes of paths $p$ starting at $a$ is covered by endpoint charts over simply connected coordinate balls: append any path inside the ball. Such appended paths are equivalent exactly when their endpoints agree. The charts are compatible by locally constant changes of sheet. They make the endpoint map a covering; distinct points over one endpoint are separated by disjoint sheets. They give a smooth Hausdorff manifold. It is second countable: choose a countable coordinate-ball cover. Components of its pairwise intersections are open and hence at most countable; subdivision of paths shows that a sheet is specified by a finite word of these chart and intersection choices. Indeed, in each ball two intervening paths with the same endpoints contract, and moving a crossing point inside its intersection component does not change the sheet. There are countably many such words and endpoint charts. This cover is connected, since a defining path lifts from the identity sheet to its own class. A loop there projects to a null-homotopic loop: its class must be the identity because its lift closes at the identity sheet. Lifting a contracting homotopy, by subdivision into covering charts, contracts the original loop. Thus this is the universal cover, with the usual equivalent base points handled by conjugating paths. There is a right action $p\cdot \gamma =p\circ \gamma $ of $\pi _1(M,a)$ on $\widetilde M$, free and transitive on every endpoint fiber. Set $\rho (\gamma )=T_\gamma $. The concatenation identity makes $\rho $ a representation. The map $(p,v)\mapsto T_ pv$ identifies $E$ with the quotient by the right action \[  (p,v)\cdot \gamma =(p\circ \gamma ,\rho (\gamma )^{-1}v).  \] It is invariant by the transport rule. In each sheet chart it is a smooth fiberwise isomorphism, and its local frames are parallel. Conversely for any representation this quotient is a smooth vector bundle: the sheet charts have locally constant transition matrices. Their trivial connections glue, are flat, and have the prescribed monodromy. A connection isomorphism conjugates the representations by its value at $a$; conversely such a fiber intertwiner extends by transport to an isomorphism. These constructions are inverse. For a metric-compatible connection and sections $u,v$ along a smooth path, \[  \frac d{dt}h(u,v)=h(D_ tu,v)+h(u,D_ tv).  \] Thus parallel transport is isometric. The flat frames may be chosen orthonormal at one point and are then orthonormal everywhere, with unitary constant transitions. Conversely unitary transitions glue the fixed fiber metric and its trivial compatible connection. The quotient construction and its isomorphisms are then unitary exactly as asserted. The real Euclidean version has orthogonal transitions. $\square$

title: Proposition 10.36.7
section: 10.36 Smooth bundles, connections and holomorphic extensions
text: Proposition 10.36.7 . CCF7A9609341 For every smooth Hermitian bundle over a complex manifold and every prescribed $(0,1)$-connection $D''$, there is a unique compatible connection having that $(0,1)$ part. No integrability of $D''$ is required. On a real base a connection is compatible precisely when its one-form matrix in a unitary frame is skew Hermitian. Compatible connections exist, and their differences are exactly the skew-Hermitian endomorphism-valued one-forms. Proof. Differentiating the inner product in a unitary frame gives compatibility exactly when $A+A^*=0$, where adjoint conjugates the one-form as well as transposing its matrix. This test on sections gives the full graded metric product rule on forms by the ordinary graded Leibniz rule. On a complex base write the prescribed part in such a frame as $\bar\partial +B$. The unique skew-adjoint matrix with $(0,1)$ part $B$ is $A=B-B^*$, its $(1,0)$ part being $-B^*$. This local construction glues: on an overlap the transformed compatible connection has the same prescribed $(0,1)$ part, and local uniqueness applies. This proves existence and uniqueness. Local unitary frames exist by smooth Gram–Schmidt. Smooth metrics exist by summing local Euclidean metrics with a smooth partition of unity, exactly as in the line case smooth line-bundle metrics and curvature changes . Over a real base the partition is supplied by proposition 10.43.10 . Averaging the trivial connections in unitary frames by that partition gives a compatible connection, since their metric product rules sum with coefficients whose sum is one. The difference assertion follows from the unitary-frame test and the preceding affine-space description. Compatibility also makes $F_ D$ skew Hermitian, by applying $d^2$ to the metric product rule. In rank one a unitary frame has imaginary $A$ and real $\mathrm iF_ D$. On a simply connected open set a unitary gauge $g$ has a smooth real phase $g=e^{\mathrm i\varphi }$: its local phases have the same closed differential $-\mathrm i g^{-1}dg$, whose path integrals are independent of path by the coordinate-square homotopy argument above. Adjust the additive constant to recover $g$. The gauge rule is then $A=\widetilde A+\mathrm i\, d\varphi $. For a holomorphic bundle the prescribed canonical coefficientwise $\bar\partial $ gives precisely its already-defined Chern connection. Its curvature has type $(1,1)$: the $(0,2)$ part is $(D'')^2=\bar\partial ^2=0$, and skew-adjointness makes the $(2,0)$ part zero as well. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.36.8
section: 10.36 Smooth bundles, connections and holomorphic extensions
text: Corollary 10.36.8 . DD24E61268DB A Hermitian holomorphic bundle has zero Chern curvature if and only if it has orthonormal holomorphic frames locally. On a connected simply connected open set, zero Chern curvature gives a single such frame. On a connected manifold these bundles correspond to unitary representations of its fundamental group, up to unitary conjugacy for isometric holomorphic isomorphisms. Proof. If the Chern curvature vanishes, the parallel frames of theorem 10.36.6 can be chosen orthonormal. Their sections are holomorphic because their Chern $(0,1)$ derivative is zero. Conversely the trivial connection in an orthonormal holomorphic frame is compatible and has canonical $(0,1)$ part; uniqueness in proposition 10.36.7 makes it the Chern connection, so its curvature vanishes. An isometric holomorphic isomorphism preserves that unique connection. Conversely unitary locally constant transition matrices are holomorphic and give this Chern connection. The representation statement therefore follows from the same flat-bundle correspondence. $\square$

title: Remark 10.36.9
section: 10.36 Smooth bundles, connections and holomorphic extensions
text: Remark 10.36.9 . 597030C175B7 For a holomorphic bundle $E$, the canonical coefficientwise $\bar\partial $ is independent of holomorphic frame, since its transition matrices are holomorphic. It squares to zero. Its cohomology on global $(p,q)$-forms is denoted $H^{p,q}(X,E)$. Write $\Omega _ X^ p$ for the holomorphic bundle $\Lambda ^ pT^{1,0*}X$ or its sheaf of holomorphic sections, according to context. The existing differential-resolution comparison corollary 10.43.11 is precisely \[  H^{p,q}(X,E)=H^ q(X,\Omega _ X^ p\otimes \mathcal O(E));  \] in particular $H^{p,0}(X,E)$ is the space of holomorphic sections of $\Lambda ^ pT^{1,0*}X\otimes E$. This notation does not impose a metric, positivity or compactness condition.

title: Theorem 10.36.10
section: 10.36 Smooth bundles, connections and holomorphic extensions
text: Theorem 10.36.10 . B7A8F8D8A536 Let $L$ be a smooth complex line bundle on an oriented real manifold $M$, and let $s$ be a smooth section transverse to the zero section. Then $Z=s^{-1}(0)$ is a closed smooth submanifold of real codimension two, with its normal orientation induced by the complex line $L$. Orient $Z$ so that the oriented normal plane followed by $TZ$ gives the orientation of $TM$. For any connection $D$ on $L$, the one-form $u=s^{-1}Ds$ off $Z$ extends with locally integrable coefficients, and as complex currents on $M$ 3E0F17FBE3F5 10.36.11 \begin{equation}  du=2\pi \mathrm i[Z]+F_ D. \end{equation} If $D$ is compatible with a smooth Hermitian metric, the real locally integrable form $\alpha =(2\pi )^{-1}\operatorname {Im}u$ satisfies \[  d\alpha =[Z]-\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }F_ D.  \] Consequently $[Z]$ represents the real image of $c_1(L)\in H^2(M,\mathbb Z)$ under the de Rham comparison. No compactness is required. Proof. Write $s=fe$ in a smooth complex frame, and $D=d+A$ there. At a zero, $Ds=df\otimes e$, independently of the connection. Transversality says that $(\operatorname {Re}f,\operatorname {Im}f)$ has rank two there. The real inverse function theorem, applied after completing these two differentials to a basis, gives local coordinates $(x,y,t)$ with $f=x+\mathrm iy$. The orientation rule makes $dx\wedge dy$ followed by the orientation of the $t$ coordinates the positive orientation of $M$; in dimension two the latter factor is the signed orientation of a point. A change of frame multiplies the normal derivative by a nonzero complex scalar at a zero, whose real determinant is positive; hence this normal and induced orientation is intrinsic. These charts also prove that $Z$ is a closed embedded submanifold and its integration current has locally finite mass. On the complement of $Z$, \[  u=\frac{df}{f}+A.  \] In the coordinates just chosen, $df/f=(dx+\mathrm i\, dy)/(x+\mathrm iy)$ has coefficients bounded by a constant times $(x^2+y^2)^{-1/2}$. They are locally integrable in the two normal variables, hence also in all variables by Fubini. Thus $u$ defines an intrinsic locally integrable current: its expressions agree off $Z$, and $Z$ has Lebesgue measure zero. We check the distributional derivative, including its orientation. On the plane let $z=x+\mathrm iy$ and let $\varphi $ be a smooth compactly supported test function. With the convention $T_\eta (\psi )=\int \eta \wedge \psi $, the derivative of a one-current satisfies $dT_\eta (\varphi )=T_\eta (d\varphi )$. On a punctured disc containing the support, $d(dz/z)=0$ classically, so Stokes' formula Stokes' formula on compact domains with corners gives \[  \left\langle d\left(\frac{dz}{z}\right),\varphi \right\rangle =\lim _{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \int _{|z|>\varepsilon }\frac{dz}{z}\wedge d\varphi =\lim _{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \int _{|z|=\varepsilon }^{\rm counterclockwise}\varphi \frac{dz}{z} =2\pi \mathrm i\, \varphi (0).  \] The boundary sign is positive because the inner boundary of the punctured disc is clockwise, whereas $d(\varphi \, dz/z)=-dz/z\wedge d\varphi $. The last equality follows by setting $z=\varepsilon e^{\mathrm i\theta }$; the integrand converges uniformly to $\mathrm i\varphi (0)\, d\theta $. The first limit is justified by the local integrability just proved. In the product coordinates $(x,y,t)$ the coefficients are independent of $t$, so all their distributional $t$ derivatives vanish, by integration by parts in those variables. Applying the plane identity to the coefficient of a test form containing only the $t$ differentials and using Fubini gives $d(df/f)=2\pi \mathrm i[\{ x=y=0\} ]$, with exactly the specified orientation: if the coordinate orientation differs from that of $M$, both this integral and the induced integral over $Z$ acquire the same sign. All other components of a test form contain $dx$ or $dy$ and contribute zero. Since $F_ D=dA$ for a line connection, this proves ( 10.36.11 ) near $Z$; off $Z$ it is the ordinary identity $du=dA$. Equality of currents is local, so the formula holds on all of $M$. Choose a compatible connection, which exists by proposition 10.36.7 . Its scalar curvature is imaginary. Taking imaginary parts and dividing by $2\pi $ gives the formula for $d\alpha $, because $\operatorname {Im}F_ D=-\mathrm iF_ D$. The current and smooth-form de Rham comparison of corollary 10.43.11 , and the integral comparison theorem 10.40.5 , give the asserted class. If $Z$ is empty, $u$ is smooth globally and the same proof applies. In real dimension less than two transversality forces $Z$ to be empty, and all two-forms and two-currents vanish, so the statement still holds. $\square$

title: Proposition 10.36.12
section: 10.36 Smooth bundles, connections and holomorphic extensions
text:
Proposition 10.36.12 . 84111D436822 For a holomorphic exact sequence $0\to S\xrightarrow jE \xrightarrow gQ\to 0$, give $S,Q$ the induced and quotient metrics. Use the smooth orthogonal identification $E=S\oplus Q$. Let $\beta \in \mathcal A^{1,0}(\operatorname {Hom}(S,Q))$ be the second fundamental form, so that the established block connection is $D_ E=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}D_ S& -\beta ^*\\ \beta & D_ Q\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. Put $b=\beta ^*$. The full map derivative identities are \[  \begin{array}{ll} D'j=g^*\beta ,& \bar\partial j=0,\\  D'g=-\beta j^*,& \bar\partial g=0,\\  D'j^*=0,& \bar\partial j^*=b g,\\  D'g^*=0,& \bar\partial g^*=-j b. \end{array}  \] Here each operator is the induced Hom connection. Moreover $\bar\partial _{\operatorname {Hom}(Q,S)}b=0$ and \[  F_ E=\begin{pmatrix}  F_ S-b\wedge \beta 

& -D'_{\operatorname {Hom}(Q,S)}b

\\  \bar\partial _{\operatorname {Hom}(S,Q)}\beta 

& F_ Q-\beta \wedge b 

\end{pmatrix}.  \] The orthogonal splitting is holomorphic exactly when $\beta =0$. Proof. The block connection and diagonal curvature identities are those already proved in proposition 10.34.9 ; their proof imposes no positivity condition. Here $j$ and $g$ and their adjoints are the constant inclusion and projection matrices. Apply ( 10.36.4 ) in degree zero to each. The four results are respectively $(0,\beta )^{\mathsf T}$, $(-\beta ,0)$, $(0,b)$ and $(-b,0)^{\mathsf T}$, proving all types and signs displayed above. Squaring the block connection gives upper-right entry $-D_{\operatorname {Hom}(Q,S)}b$ and lower-left entry $D_{\operatorname {Hom}(S,Q)}\beta $ by the degree-one formula. Chern curvature has type $(1,1)$; its $(0,2)$ upper-right part forces $\bar\partial b=0$, and its $(2,0)$ lower-left part forces $D'\beta =0$. This proves the matrix, including the minus sign in its upper-right entry. Finally $\bar\partial g^*=-jb$ vanishes exactly when $b=0$, since $j$ is injective. This is exactly when the orthogonal right inverse is holomorphic. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.36.13
section: 10.36 Smooth bundles, connections and holomorphic extensions
text: Theorem 10.36.13 . 304DF496E0BF With $S,Q$ fixed, isomorphism classes of holomorphic extension diagrams $0\to S\to E\to Q\to 0$, with identity maps on their ends, are in bijection with $H^{0,1}_{\bar\partial }(X,\operatorname {Hom}(Q,S))$, and hence with $H^1(X,\mathcal O(\operatorname {Hom}(Q,S)))$. The class is $[\beta ^*]$. It is independent of all metrics and vanishes exactly for a holomorphically split extension. Proof. A smooth right inverse $h$ exists by orthogonal splitting. For the orthogonal one the preceding proposition says $\bar\partial h=-jb$, with $b=\beta ^*$ closed. For any smooth right inverse define $b=-j^{-1}\bar\partial h$: the expression lies in $S$ because $g\bar\partial h=\bar\partial (gh)=0$. Any other right inverse is $h+jv$, with a global smooth $v:Q\to S$, so its form is $b-\bar\partial v$. This proves independence of splitting and metric. Transporting a splitting under an extension isomorphism proves invariance as well. In the splitting coordinates the Dolbeault operator is $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\bar\partial _ S& -b\\ 0& \bar\partial _ Q\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. A smooth extension isomorphism inducing the identity on the ends has the form $\Psi =\left(\begin{smallmatrix}I& v\\ 0& I\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. From the coefficient product rule it is holomorphic from $E_ b$ to $E_ c$ precisely when \[  \bar\partial v-c+b=0.  \] Thus equal Dolbeault classes give isomorphic diagrams, and a split diagram has class zero. This also proves the converse splitting claim. For surjectivity take any closed smooth $b$. On the smooth bundle $S\oplus Q$ use the displayed operator. It squares to zero because $\bar\partial b=0$. More concretely, in local holomorphic frames the local complex exactness local Dolbeault exactness for forms and currents gives $b=\bar\partial v_ i$. The matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}I& -v_ i\\ 0& I\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ intertwines this operator with the usual one on the local split bundle, by the same calculation. On overlaps these trivializations differ by holomorphic upper-triangular matrices, since $\bar\partial (v_ i-v_ j)=0$. They therefore define a holomorphic structure, with holomorphic inclusion and projection, and with the prescribed class $[b]$. This is an explicit triangular construction; no general integrable-connection theorem is needed. The final sheaf identification is corollary 10.43.11 . Zero ranks give the unique trivial extension and zero cohomology. $\square$

title: Proposition 10.36.14
section: 10.36 Smooth bundles, connections and holomorphic extensions
text: Proposition 10.36.14 . 732A25F31FC3 Extension diagrams with fixed end bundles $S,Q$, allowing arbitrary holomorphic automorphisms on both ends, are classified by the orbits \[  H^1(X,\mathcal O(\operatorname {Hom}(Q,S))) /(\operatorname {Aut}(S)\times \operatorname {Aut}(Q)), \qquad (u,v)[b]=[u b v^{-1}].  \] This gives a surjection onto the isomorphism classes of their abstract middle bundles, which need not be injective. For line bundles on a compact connected complex manifold the diagram orbit set is $\{ 0\} \sqcup \mathbb P(H^1(X,\mathcal O(\operatorname {Hom}(Q,S))))$, where the first element is the split diagram. Proof. A diagram map with end automorphisms $u,v$ has smooth block matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}u& w\\ 0& v\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. It is holomorphic exactly when $\bar\partial w-cv+ub=0$. Since $u,v$ are holomorphic and invertible, this is equivalent to $[c]=[ubv^{-1}]$, and the equation constructs the isomorphism whenever that class equality holds. Forgetting the inclusion and projection gives the asserted surjection. For line bundles each end automorphism is a nowhere vanishing holomorphic function; on a compact connected manifold it is a nonzero constant by the local maximum principle. Its action is scalar multiplication, whose orbits are zero and the projective lines of nonzero classes. If the cohomology vanishes its projective space is empty. Here is a counterexample to injectivity after forgetting the diagram. On $\mathbb P^1$ let $S=\mathcal O(-2)$ and use the two maps into $E=\mathcal O^2$ given in homogeneous coordinates by \[  j_1=(x^2,y^2)^{\mathsf T},\qquad j_2=(x^2,y^2+xy)^{\mathsf T}.  \] Each pair has no common zero and hence is a subbundle inclusion: locally one entry is a unit, and an invertible two-by-two matrix completes it to a frame. Each quotient is a line bundle with $Q\simeq \det E\otimes S^{-1}\simeq \mathcal O(2)$; this determinant isomorphism follows locally by wedging a frame of $S$ with any quotient lift. Choose such an identification for each quotient. Every automorphism of $\mathcal O^2$ is a constant invertible matrix, since its entries are global holomorphic functions on $\mathbb P^1$. It and a scalar automorphism of $S$ preserve the span of the two quadratic components of an injection. But \[  \operatorname {span}\{ x^2,y^2\}  \ne \operatorname {span}\{ x^2,y^2+xy\} ,  \] by independence of the homogeneous monomials. Thus the diagrams lie in distinct diagram orbits while their middle bundles are identical. Both are nonsplit: a right inverse from $\mathcal O(2)$ to $\mathcal O^2$ would have components in $H^0(\mathbb P^1,\mathcal O(-2))=0$, by proposition 10.51.5 . This counterexample also concerns nonzero extension classes. $\square$

title: 20.7.1 Meromorphic bundle sections and divisors
text: Definition 20.7.2 . F9B013D39957 A meromorphic section of a holomorphic vector bundle is given in holomorphic frames by vectors of meromorphic functions, compatible with the frame changes. Here a meromorphic function is locally a quotient of holomorphic functions with nonzero denominator germ. Holomorphic invertible transition matrices preserve such vectors in both directions, so the condition is independent of holomorphic frame. Away from their poles the vectors give an ordinary holomorphic section. No invariance under arbitrary smooth frame changes is claimed. Proposition 20.7.3 . ACC6D09EDDD9 Let $L$ be a holomorphic line bundle, $h$ a smooth quadratic metric, and $s$ a meromorphic section, nonzero on every component. Meromorphic coefficients are taken in holomorphic frames. Then \[  dd^ c\log |s|_ h^2=[\operatorname {div}s]-c_1(L,h), \qquad dd^ c=\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial \bar\partial .  \] In particular the divisor current represents the real image of the integer first Chern class. Every locally finite integral hypersurface divisor $D$ determines a holomorphic line bundle $\mathcal O(D)$, with a canonical meromorphic section of divisor $D$. If $D$ is effective, that section is holomorphic and its zero set is the support of $D$. Moreover $\mathcal O(D_1+D_2)\simeq \mathcal O(D_1)\otimes \mathcal O(D_2)$, and the map $D\mapsto \mathcal O(D)$ has kernel the principal divisors and image the line bundles admitting a componentwise nonzero meromorphic section. Thus $\mathcal O(D_1)\simeq \mathcal O(D_2)$ exactly when $D_2-D_1$ is the divisor of a global meromorphic function, nonzero on every component; these divisors are called linearly equivalent. It is the divisor connecting map in the frame-cocycle convention of theorem 10.40.2 . Proof. In a holomorphic frame $e$, write $s=(a/b)e$, with holomorphic numerator and nonzero denominator germs. Apply the normalized Poincaré–Lelong formula separately to $a,b$, subtract, and use $c_1(L,h)=-dd^ c\log |e|_ h^2$. The local logarithms are integrable and their difference is the global locally integrable norm logarithm. This proves the displayed current identity. The current/smooth de Rham comparison and theorem 10.40.5 give the stated cohomology class. The local equations of local equations and currents of irreducible hypersurfaces give meromorphic local equations $u_ i$ for $D$, by multiplying their integral powers. Their ratios are holomorphic units. Here is the local cancellation argument. If a nonzero holomorphic germ vanishes on an irreducible hypersurface germ, it is divisible by that hypersurface's local equation, since the equation generates its vanishing ideal. Repeatedly divide while a zero hypersurface remains. This terminates: the order of the first nonzero Taylor term at the base point drops by at least one at each division by a nonunit. A remaining nonunit would still have a zero hypersurface by purity of a nontrivial holomorphic zero set , so the final remainder is a unit. At a regular point of each factor outside the others, the equation vanishes to order one; hence its exponent in this factorization is exactly the divisor multiplicity. Applying this factorization to the numerator and denominator cancels equal factors. A quotient of divisor zero is therefore a holomorphic unit, and a meromorphic germ with nonnegative divisor is holomorphic. Thus the meromorphic functions $f$ with $\operatorname {div}f+D\geq 0$ form the locally free sheaf $u_ i^{-1}\mathcal O$ on each such neighborhood. Its local frames $e_ i=1/u_ i$ obey $e_ i=(u_ j/u_ i)e_ j$. Their canonical section one has coefficient $u_ i$, hence divisor $D$. These frame transitions are the reciprocals of the corresponding coefficient transitions. If $D\geq 0$, the local coefficients $u_ i$ are holomorphic by the same cancellation argument and vanish exactly on its support. Multiplying the local equations for two divisors multiplies their frame transitions, proving the tensor-product formula. For the exact sheaf sequence $1\to \mathcal O^*\to \mathcal M^*\xrightarrow {\operatorname {div}} \operatorname {Div}\to 0$, local equations $u_ i$ are local lifts of $D$. The connecting cocycle is $u_ j/u_ i$, by lemma 10.40.1 , precisely the frame cocycle above. Exactness gives the kernel assertion, and applying it to $D_2-D_1$ together with the tensor formula gives linear equivalence. Finally any nonzero meromorphic section $s$ yields an isomorphism $\mathcal O(\operatorname {div}s)\to \mathcal O(L)$ by $f\mapsto fs$: in a local factorization its source generator maps to a holomorphic unit times a frame. Conversely the canonical section of $\mathcal O(D)$ gives such a section for any line bundle in the image. No existence of meromorphic sections for all higher-dimensional line bundles is asserted. $\square$

title: 9.47 Coherence of proper analytic direct images
search_title: Coherence of proper analytic direct images
section: 9.47 Coherence of proper analytic direct images
text: Lemma 9.47.1 . 81A3D17F4D37 Let $X$ be a Hausdorff analytic space, possibly nonreduced, and let finitely many open patches $U_ i$ be closed analytic subspaces of polydiscs $\Omega _ i$. Their intersection $U_ I$ is a closed analytic subspace of $\prod _{i\in I}\Omega _ i$ under the map giving all its coordinate embeddings. If $g:X\to Y\subset W\subset \mathbb C^ m$ is analytic and $D\subset W$ is open, the graph of $g$ on $U_ I\cap g^{-1}D$ is closed analytic in $(\prod _{i\in I}\Omega _ i)\times D$. The direct image of any coherent sheaf under these closed embeddings is coherent, and its section spaces and their intrinsic topologies are unchanged. Proof. A limit in the indicated product of a net of diagonal points has, in every coordinate patch, a limit point $x_ i\in U_ i$, because each $U_ i$ is closed in $\Omega _ i$. The inverse coordinate maps are continuous, so the same net in $X$ converges to every $x_ i$. Hausdorffness makes all these points equal; their common point lies in $U_ I$ and gives the product limit. Thus the diagonal image is closed. At a point of that image choose one patch as coordinates $z$ and extend the other coordinate maps locally holomorphically as $H_ i(z)$. If $\mathcal J(z)$ is the full defining ideal of this first patch, the nonreduced diagonal is locally defined by \[  \mathcal J(z),\qquad w_ i-H_ i(z)\quad (i\ne i_0).  \] The quotient is the original structure ring. The graph assertion follows by adjoining target coordinates $\zeta -g(z)$ with the same substitution calculation. The nonreduced coherent direct-image argument of the local resolution theorem lifts relation generators and adjoins the defining ideal in every coordinate. It proves coherence of the pushed sheaf. Sections under a closed embedding are identical; the intrinsic coherent-section theorem identifies their topologies, including all nilpotent module germs. $\square$ Theorem 9.47.2 (Proper analytic direct images) . 1A9A12704621 Let $g:X\to Y$ be a proper analytic morphism of Hausdorff, countable-basis analytic spaces, possibly nonreduced. For every coherent $\mathcal O_ X$-module $\mathcal S$ and every $q\geq 0$, the analytic higher direct image $R^ qg_*\mathcal S$ is a coherent $\mathcal O_ Y$-module. Proof. Fix $y_0\in Y$ and restrict to an open neighborhood of $y_0$ embedded as a closed analytic subspace of $W\subset \mathbb C^ m$. Properness is preserved by this open restriction: the preimage of each compact subset of the restricted target is the same compact set as before. Choose polydiscs $D\Subset D_0\Subset W$ centered at $y_0$. The set \[  K=g^{-1}(Y\cap \overline{D_0})  \] is compact because the target intersection is compact and $g$ is proper. If it is empty, all these preimages and the resulting cohomology sheaves are zero near $y_0$, so the assertion holds. Otherwise choose finitely many patches $U_ a^0\subset g^{-1}(Y\cap W)$ closed analytic in polydiscs $\Omega _ a^0$, and concentric smaller polydiscs \[  \Omega '_ a\Subset \Omega _ a\Subset \Omega _ a^0, \qquad U_ a=U_ a^0\cap \Omega _ a,\quad U'_ a=U_ a^0\cap \Omega '_ a,  \] such that the $U'_ a$ cover $K$. Thus both larger and smaller families cover $g^{-1}(Y\cap B)$ for every open $B\subset D_0$. This fixed compact preimage and its fixed finite cover will be used for every subsequent shrinking of the base. For each nonempty increasing tuple $I$ of patch indices put $\Omega _ I^0=\prod _{a\in I}\Omega _ a^0$ and similarly $\Omega _ I,\Omega '_ I$. Put $U_ I^0=\bigcap _{a\in I}U_ a^0$. For every open $B\subset D_0$ the actual section identifications are 6DBD55D2F0A7 9.47.3 \begin{equation}  \begin{aligned}  \mathcal S(U_ I\cap g^{-1}B)& =\mathcal S_ I(\Omega _ I\times B),\\  \mathcal S(U'_ I\cap g^{-1}B)& =\mathcal S_ I(\Omega '_ I\times B). \end{aligned} \end{equation} They are topological module identifications, and restriction between them is ordinary restriction in the $\Omega _ I$ variable. There is no assertion that an arbitrary ambient intersection of polydiscs is pseudoconvex; the overlap is instead the explicitly proved closed diagonal subspace of a product of polydiscs. If $B$ is a polydisc, each intersection on the left is closed analytic in the strict-PSH space $\Omega _ I\times B$ or $\Omega '_ I\times B$ through its graph. Restrict the sum of nonnegative strict-PSH exhaustions to this closed analytic subspace. It remains proper and strongly1-complete, including at singular and nonreduced points by the analytic ambient convention. The coherent vanishing theorem therefore makes both finite covers acyclic, with all finite intersections acyclic. Let $A=\mathcal O(D)$ and $D_ t$ denote the concentric polydisc of radius $t$ times that of $D$. Form the alternating Čech complexes \[  E^ p=\bigoplus _{|I|=p+1}\mathcal S_ I(\Omega _ I\times D), \qquad F^ p=\bigoplus _{|I|=p+1}\mathcal S_ I(\Omega '_ I\times D).  \] There are finitely many increasing tuples. These complexes are zero in negative degrees and above one less than the number of patches. The checked integral alternating/full Čech homotopy identifies their cohomology with that of the ordinary acyclic-cover complexes, naturally and $A$-linearly. Consequently the restriction chain map $r:E\to F$ induces the canonical identity on $H^ q(g^{-1}(Y\cap D),\mathcal S)$ in every degree. All cochain restrictions and differentials are continuous. title: 6.38 Analytic multiplicity and ordinary density
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text:
Use $dd^ c= rac{i}{2\pi }\partial  ar\partial $. For a reduced pure $p$-dimensional analytic set $A$ write $[A]$ for its positive closed integration current of theorem 5.61.2 . All assertions below are local at the indicated point. Lemma 6.38.1 . A7BC2FB7F1C6 Let $(A,0)\subset (\mathbb C^ n,0)$ be reduced and pure of dimension $p$. The linear coordinate systems $z=(z',z'')$, with $z'\in \mathbb C^ p$, for which CD38640A3802 6.38.2  egin{equation}  |z''|\leq C|z'|\quad 	ext{on }A	ext{ near }0 \end{equation} for some finite $C$ form an open dense subset of the invertible linear coordinate systems. For any such system, increase $C$ to a positive number if needed. For all sufficiently small $r>0$, the projection \[  \pi :A_ r=A\cap  igl (B_ p(0,r)	imes B_{n-p}(0,Cr) igr ) \longrightarrow B_ p(0,r)  \] is proper with finite fibers and has fiber $\{ 0\} $ over zero. For $1\leq p\leq n$ it is a finite covering with a constant positive integer number of sheets outside a proper analytic subset of the base. For $p=0$ the germ is the reduced point and the projection is the map of that point to $\mathbb C^0$. Proof. There are finitely many irreducible branches, by irreducible analytic branches and prime ideals . Use the triangular-equation construction in the complete proof of finite local parametrization of analytic germs simultaneously on their prime ideals. The simultaneous construction is also used in purity and dimension drop for analytic germs : at each stage finitely many nonzero germs must be distinguished in the last coordinate. Their first nonzero homogeneous parts exclude only the zero set of their nonzero product, so the direction can be chosen arbitrarily close to any prescribed one. The stop dimension of every branch is $p$, by the dimension assertion of that same proposition. Thus these finite successive choices give common coordinates arbitrarily close to any given ones, and the exact monic-root estimate in the parametrization proof gives ( 6.38.2 ) on every branch. Take the maximum of their constants and shrink their common representative. The condition is open as well. In fixed Euclidean coordinates it implies $|z|\leq K|Lz|$ on the germ, where $Lz=z'$ and $K=(1+C^2)^{1/2}$. If $\| \widetilde L-L\| <1/(2K)$, then \[  |\widetilde Lz|\geq |Lz|-\| \widetilde L-L\| \, |z| \geq |z|/(2K)  \] on the same representative. The remaining new linear coordinates are bounded by a constant times $|z|$, proving their cone estimate. This proves openness and the stated precise meaning of genericity. Choose the closed product of balls inside a neighborhood where $A$ is analytic and the estimate holds. For a compact base set $K_0\subset B_ p(0,r)$, choose $t<r$ with $|z'|\leq t$ on $K_0$. All points of its inverse image satisfy $|z''|\leq Ct<Cr$. The inverse image is therefore a closed subset of a compact product strictly inside the coordinate neighborhood, so it is compact. Each fiber is a compact analytic subset of the open vertical ball, hence finite by the maximum principle on analytic branches . The cone estimate gives the single fiber over zero. At every point of $A_ r$ the pure source dimension is $p$ and its fiber is isolated. By proper finite representatives of analytic map germs , projection is locally open there. Its global image in the connected base ball is consequently open, closed by properness, and nonempty; it is the entire ball. For completeness use the exact analytic critical set from the proof of that lemma: let $C_0$ consist of the singular locus and the regular points where $d\pi $ has rank less than $p$. Locally it is the rank-deficient set of the matrix formed by the differentials of generators of the reduced ideal of $A$ and the $p$ coordinate rows of $d\pi $. On the regular locus, maximal minors test full rank on its tangent space; on the singular locus their vanishing is automatic. Thus $C_0$ is analytic. It contains no branch: a smaller maximal rank on a regular open piece would give a positive-dimensional local fiber by the holomorphic constant-rank theorem, contradicting finiteness. The dimension estimates in proper finite representatives of analytic map germs give $\dim C_0\leq p-1$. Its proper image $E=\pi (C_0)$ is analytic by Remmert's proper mapping theorem and has dimension at most $p-1$ by dimension bounds for holomorphic images . Over the connected set $B_ p(0,r)\setminus E$, whose connectedness follows from bounded holomorphic removal and connected complements , projection is a proper local biholomorphism. To see that it is a covering, take the finitely many points of a fiber and disjoint neighborhoods mapped biholomorphically onto neighborhoods of the base point. Properness excludes additional inverse points outside these neighborhoods over all sufficiently close base points: otherwise a sequence of them has a convergent subsequence in the compact inverse image of a compact neighborhood and limits to that fiber. Intersect the finitely many inverse-chart images. This gives an evenly covered neighborhood. The positive finite sheet number is locally constant and hence constant on the connected base complement. When $p=0$, the reduced pure germ is just $\{ 0\} $ and all the claims follow directly. For $p=n$ the zero-dimensional vertical ball is a point; the same proof applies, with no vertical coordinates. $\square$ Theorem 6.38.3 . 673FC5FBB2C8 Let $a\in A$, where $A$ is reduced and pure of dimension $p$ near $a$ in a complex manifold. In any coordinates centered at $a$ satisfying ( 6.38.2 ), let $m$ be the finite sheet number of the preceding projection. Then \[  
u ([A],a)=m.  \] In particular $m$ is independent of the cone-adapted coordinate system, the small representative and its radii. Denote it by $\operatorname {mult}_ a A$, the multiplicity of $A$ at $a$. It is a positive integer. For a reduced isolated point it is one. Proof. Work at $a=0$. If $p=0$, both sides are the mass of the single reduced point, namely one. Suppose $p\geq 1$ and put \[  \varphi (z)=\log |z|^2,\qquad \psi (z)=\log |z'|^2.  \] On $A\setminus \{ 0\} $ the cone estimate gives the actual bound 6576C08255BC 6.38.4  egin{equation}  0\leq \varphi -\psi \leq \log (1+C^2). \end{equation} Both weights have the same point pole on the support of $[A]$. They are semi-exhaustive there on the product representative: small $\varphi $-sublevels lie in a compact ambient ball inside that product, and for $t<r$ the closed $\psi $-sublevel on $A$ with $|z'|\leq t$ has $|z''|\leq Ct<Cr$, hence is compact by the same argument as in the lemma. Thus corollary 6.34.11 gives \[  
u ([A],\varphi )=
u ([A],\psi ).  \] The first side is the ordinary number, by its radial identification in that corollary. The second is $m$ by corollary 6.35.2 , applied to the proper finite projection and its actual covering just proved. That input uses change of variables on the $m$ sheets and zero coefficient mass on the proper analytic discriminant and its inverse image. Thus it is a projection-weight calculation made applicable to the ordinary number by ( 6.38.4 ); finite sheet number alone would not give that identification. The ordinary number is independent of the holomorphic coordinates by theorem 6.33.10 , and depends only on the germ. This proves every asserted independence and positivity. The argument applies to arbitrary, possibly nonlinear, coordinate charts in which the stated cone condition holds. $\square$ Corollary 6.38.5 . CF13884F31CB For an effective integral pure $p$-cycle $Z=\sum _ i c_ i[A_ i]$, \[  
u (Z,a)=\sum _{i:a\in A_ i}c_ i\operatorname {mult}_ a A_ i.  \] In particular a reduced pure germ has multiplicity equal to the sum of the multiplicities of its irreducible local branches. Moreover $\operatorname {mult}_ a A=1$ if and only if $a$ is a regular point of $A$. Proof. The local sum is finite. Distinct pure-dimensional branches meet in smaller-dimensional analytic sets, which give zero coefficient mass to their integration currents; hence the reduced integration current is the sum of the branch currents. Ordinary finite-radius masses and their limits are linear on such finite positive sums. The theorem therefore proves the cycle formula and branch formula. Each branch multiplicity is at least one, since the cone projection on that branch is surjective and has positive sheet number. At a regular point choose submanifold coordinates, so that $A=\{ z''=0\} $ and its projection is one sheet. Conversely, if the reduced multiplicity is one, the cone projection in the lemma has one sheet outside $E$. It is an isomorphism there. The inverse image of $E$ is nowhere dense: projection is locally open on the pure source, so a nonempty source open subset cannot map into the proper analytic set $E$. Thus projection is finite and bimeromorphic onto the base ball, which is normal. By finite bimeromorphic maps to normal spaces it is an isomorphism. Its source is therefore smooth at $a$. For $p=0$ an isolated reduced point is regular and the same conclusion is direct. The case $p=n$ is the local ambient open set, with one sheet and ordinary number one. $\square$

Choose the closed product of balls inside a neighborhood where $A$ is analytic and the estimate holds. For a compact base set $K_0\subset B_ p(0,r)$, choose $t<r$ with $|z'|\leq t$ on $K_0$. All points of its inverse image satisfy $|z''|\leq Ct<Cr$. The inverse image is therefore a closed subset of a compact product strictly inside the coordinate neighborhood, so it is compact. Each fiber is a compact analytic subset of the open vertical ball, hence finite by the maximum principle on analytic branches . The cone estimate gives the single fiber over zero. At every point of $A_ r$ the pure source dimension is $p$ and its fiber is isolated. By proper finite representatives of analytic map germs , projection is locally open there. Its global image in the connected base ball is consequently open, closed by properness, and nonempty; it is the entire ball. For completeness use the exact analytic critical set from the proof of that lemma: let $C_0$ consist of the singular locus and the regular points where $d\pi $ has rank less than $p$. Locally it is the rank-deficient set of the matrix formed by the differentials of generators of the reduced ideal of $A$ and the $p$ coordinate rows of $d\pi $. On the regular locus, maximal minors test full rank on its tangent space; on the singular locus their vanishing is automatic. Thus $C_0$ is analytic. It contains no branch: a smaller maximal rank on a regular open piece would give a positive-dimensional local fiber by the holomorphic constant-rank theorem, contradicting finiteness. The dimension estimates in proper finite representatives of analytic map germs give $\dim C_0\leq p-1$. Its proper image $E=\pi (C_0)$ is analytic by Remmert's proper mapping theorem and has dimension at most $p-1$ by dimension bounds for holomorphic images . Over the connected set $B_ p(0,r)\setminus E$, whose connectedness follows from bounded holomorphic removal and connected complements , projection is a proper local biholomorphism. To see that it is a covering, take the finitely many points of a fiber and disjoint neighborhoods mapped biholomorphically onto neighborhoods of the base point. Properness excludes additional inverse points outside these neighborhoods over all sufficiently close base points: otherwise a sequence of them has a convergent subsequence in the compact inverse image of a compact neighborhood and limits to that fiber. Intersect the finitely many inverse-chart images. This gives an evenly covered neighborhood. The positive finite sheet number is locally constant and hence constant on the connected base complement. When $p=0$, the reduced pure germ is just $\{ 0\} $ and all the claims follow directly. For $p=n$ the zero-dimensional vertical ball is a point; the same proof applies, with no vertical coordinates. $\square$

title: Theorem 6.38.3
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text:
Theorem 6.38.3 . 673FC5FBB2C8 Let $a\in A$, where $A$ is reduced and pure of dimension $p$ near $a$ in a complex manifold. In any coordinates centered at $a$ satisfying ( 6.38.2 ), let $m$ be the finite sheet number of the preceding projection. Then \[  
u ([A],a)=m.  \] In particular $m$ is independent of the cone-adapted coordinate system, the small representative and its radii. Denote it by $\operatorname {mult}_ a A$, the multiplicity of $A$ at $a$. It is a positive integer. For a reduced isolated point it is one. Proof. Work at $a=0$. If $p=0$, both sides are the mass of the single reduced point, namely one. Suppose $p\geq 1$ and put \[  \varphi (z)=\log |z|^2,\qquad \psi (z)=\log |z'|^2.  \] On $A\setminus \{ 0\} $ the cone estimate gives the actual bound 6576C08255BC 6.38.4  egin{equation}  0\leq \varphi -\psi \leq \log (1+C^2). \end{equation} Both weights have the same point pole on the support of $[A]$. They are semi-exhaustive there on the product representative: small $\varphi $-sublevels lie in a compact ambient ball inside that product, and for $t<r$ the closed $\psi $-sublevel on $A$ with $|z'|\leq t$ has $|z''|\leq Ct<Cr$, hence is compact by the same argument as in the lemma. Thus corollary 6.34.11 gives \[  
u ([A],\varphi )=
u ([A],\psi ).  \] The first side is the ordinary number, by its radial identification in that corollary. The second is $m$ by corollary 6.35.2 , applied to the proper finite projection and its actual covering just proved. That input uses change of variables on the $m$ sheets and zero coefficient mass on the proper analytic discriminant and its inverse image. Thus it is a projection-weight calculation made applicable to the ordinary number by ( 6.38.4 ); finite sheet number alone would not give that identification. The ordinary number is independent of the holomorphic coordinates by theorem 6.33.10 , and depends only on the germ. This proves every asserted independence and positivity. The argument applies to arbitrary, possibly nonlinear, coordinate charts in which the stated cone condition holds. $\square$

title: Corollary 6.38.5
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text: Corollary 6.38.5 . CF13884F31CB For an effective integral pure $p$-cycle $Z=\sum _ i c_ i[A_ i]$, \[  \nu (Z,a)=\sum _{i:a\in A_ i}c_ i\operatorname {mult}_ a A_ i.  \] In particular a reduced pure germ has multiplicity equal to the sum of the multiplicities of its irreducible local branches. Moreover $\operatorname {mult}_ a A=1$ if and only if $a$ is a regular point of $A$. Proof. The local sum is finite. Distinct pure-dimensional branches meet in smaller-dimensional analytic sets, which give zero coefficient mass to their integration currents; hence the reduced integration current is the sum of the branch currents. Ordinary finite-radius masses and their limits are linear on such finite positive sums. The theorem therefore proves the cycle formula and branch formula. Each branch multiplicity is at least one, since the cone projection on that branch is surjective and has positive sheet number. At a regular point choose submanifold coordinates, so that $A=\{ z''=0\} $ and its projection is one sheet. Conversely, if the reduced multiplicity is one, the cone projection in the lemma has one sheet outside $E$. It is an isomorphism there. The inverse image of $E$ is nowhere dense: projection is locally open on the pure source, so a nonempty source open subset cannot map into the proper analytic set $E$. Thus projection is finite and bimeromorphic onto the base ball, which is normal. By finite bimeromorphic maps to normal spaces it is an isomorphism. Its source is therefore smooth at $a$. For $p=0$ an isolated reduced point is regular and the same conclusion is direct. The case $p=n$ is the local ambient open set, with one sheet and ordinary number one. $\square$

title: 9.32 Convexity and Stein spaces
text: Complex spaces in this section are Hausdorff and have a countable basis; their structure sheaves may be nonreduced. Scalar smooth functions are understood through ambient extensions, as in lemma 9.49.1 . Fix $q\geq 1$. Besides the strong $q$-convexity convention there, call a $C^ k$ function, $2\leq k\leq \infty $, weakly $q$-convex if locally it has a $C^ k$ ambient extension whose Levi form is nonnegative on a subspace of codimension at most $q-1$. For $q=1$ this is $C^ k$ plurisubharmonicity, with the same ambient convention as ambient plurisubharmonicity on reduced spaces . Levi forms use $\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial $; their signs agree with the normalization of $dd^ c$ used elsewhere.

title: 9.32.1 Weak convexity and intersections
text: Lemma 9.32.2 . 1139FC60D126 Weak $q$-convexity is independent of the local embedding and of the nilpotent structure. It is preserved by restriction to analytic subspaces. If $v_ j$ is weakly $q_ j$-convex and $c_ j>0$, then $\sum _{j=1}^ s c_ jv_ j$ is weakly $q$-convex, where \[  q=1+\sum _{j=1}^ s(q_ j-1).  \] It is strongly $q$-convex wherever one $v_ j$ is strongly $q_ j$-convex. An increasing convex scalar composition preserves weak $q$-convexity; it preserves strong $q$-convexity where its first derivative is positive. These assertions hold in class $C^ k$. Proof. For two embeddings, use holomorphic ambient lifts $H,H'$ of their transition and inverse, as in lemma 9.49.1 . If $f$ is an extension in the first embedding, then \[  f(H'(z'))+|z'-H(H'(z'))|^2  \] extends the same scalar function in the second. Indeed it is the restriction to the graph $z'\mapsto (H'(z'),z')$ of $f(z)+|z'-H(z)|^2$. The holomorphic change of variables $(z,z')\mapsto (z,z'-H(z))$ identifies the latter with $f(z)+|z'|^2$. Its Levi form has a nonnegative subspace of codimension at most $q-1$. Intersecting that subspace with the graph tangent preserves this codimension bound. The same argument with positive subspaces is the strong assertion already used in lemma 9.49.1 , and preserves class $C^ k$. The underlying local analytic subset is the same for a space and its reduction. Restricting an ambient extension proves the subspace assertion, including subspaces with a nonreduced structure. At a point, put the finitely many extensions in one embedding. Intersect their nonnegative subspaces. The resulting codimension is at most $\sum _ j(q_ j-1)$, and the sum of the Levi forms is nonnegative there. It is positive there when a summand has a positive form on its corresponding subspace. For a scalar function $\chi $ the chain rule gives \[  H(\chi (v))=\chi '(v)Hv+\chi ''(v)\partial v\otimes \overline{\partial v}.  \] This proves the composition assertions. If the required positive or nonnegative dimension is nonpositive, the condition is vacuous. $\square$ An exhaustion below is finite and continuous with compact closed sublevels. Such a function is bounded below: otherwise values tending to $-\infty $ would occur in one compact closed sublevel. It may therefore be shifted to be nonnegative. A space is strongly , respectively weakly , $q$-convex if it has a smooth exhaustion with that convexity outside a compact exceptional set. Strong $q$-completeness means that the exceptional set is empty, as in section 9.49 . With the auxiliary convention $q=0$, strong $0$-convexity means compactness, with exceptional set $K=X$: a Levi form cannot have a positive subspace of codimension at most $-1$ at a point outside $K$. Only the empty space can be strongly $0$-complete. This convention is not a degree-zero coherent vanishing assertion. Proposition 9.32.3 . 8B6B09BDCA63 Every weakly $q$-convex space has an everywhere weakly $q$-convex smooth exhaustion. Strong and weak $q$-convexity, and strong $q$-completeness, depend only on the reduction and are inherited by closed analytic subspaces. If $\psi $ is an exhaustion with the specified convexity outside $K$, each sublevel $X_ c=\{ \psi <c\} $ containing $K$ has the same convexity property. For a strongly $q$-complete exhaustion every sublevel is strongly $q$-complete. Proof. Choose $c>\max _ K\psi $ when $K$ is nonempty. Take a smooth convex function $\chi $ which is zero on $(-\infty ,c]$, has positive first derivative on $(c,\infty )$, and tends to infinity. For example, integrate a smooth nondecreasing function which is zero on $(-\infty ,c]$, positive above $c$, and one above $c+1$. Then $\chi (\psi )$ is an exhaustion. It is constant near $K$ and weakly $q$-convex elsewhere by the preceding lemma. For $K$ empty no change is necessary. Reduction invariance and restriction follow from that lemma. Restriction of an exhaustion to a closed subspace is an exhaustion, and its exceptional set is the compact intersection with $K$. On $X_ c$ use $1/(c-\psi )$. This has the required Levi sign off $K$. Its closed $M$-sublevel is empty for $M\leq 0$; for $M>0$ it is a closed subset of the compact set $\{ \psi \leq c-1/M\} $ contained in $X_ c$. Thus it is an exhaustion with the asserted exceptional set. $\square$ Theorem 9.32.4 . B8D34CACDCCC Let $U_ j$ be weakly $q_ j$-convex open subsets of a complex space $X$, $1\leq j\leq s$, with $s\geq 1$. Put $U=\bigcap _ jU_ j$ and $q=1+\sum _ j(q_ j-1)$. Then $U$ is weakly $q$-convex. If one $U_ j$ is strongly $q_ j$-complete, then $U$ is strongly $q$-complete. If instead that $U_ j$ has a strongly $q_ j$-convex exhaustion outside $K_ j$, the same conclusion with “convex” holds provided $K_ j\cap U$ is relatively compact in $U$. Proof. The empty intersection causes no difficulty. Choose nonnegative smooth weakly $q_ j$-convex exhaustions $\psi _ j$ everywhere on the factors, by proposition 9.32.3 . Their sum on $U$ is weakly $q$-convex by lemma 9.32.2 . It is an exhaustion: its closed $M$-sublevel is contained in \[  \bigcap _ j\{ x\in U_ j:\psi _ j(x)\leq M\} .  \] Each set in this finite intersection is compact in the Hausdorff space $X$, and their intersection is contained in $U$. The sublevel is closed there and therefore compact. For a complete factor use its nonnegative strongly $q_ j$-convex exhaustion instead; the sum is strongly $q$-convex everywhere. For the last assertion use the given strongly $q_ j$-convex exhaustion, shifted to be nonnegative, without flattening it. Use everywhere weak exhaustions on the other factors. The sum is strongly $q$-convex outside $K_ j\cap U$ and is still an exhaustion. This exceptional set is closed in $U$, so the relative compactness hypothesis makes it compact in $U$. $\square$ The exceptional-set qualification cannot be omitted. In $X=\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1$, the open set $U_1=X$ is strongly $1$-convex with exceptional set $X$, while $U_2=\mathbb C\times \mathbb P^1$ is weakly $1$-convex with exhaustion $|z|^2$. The intersection $U_2$ is not strongly $1$-convex. For any compact exceptional set, choose $z$ outside its projection to $\mathbb C$. Restriction to the entire compact fiber $\{ z\} \times \mathbb P^1$ would then be strictly plurisubharmonic, contrary to the maximum principle. Recall the $q$-Runge definition in theorem 9.51.13 : each compact $L\subset U$ must lie in a sublevel $X_ b\Subset U$ of a smooth exhaustion which is strongly $q$-convex outside $\overline{X_ b}$. Call $U$ $q$-Runge complete when the exhaustion can be strongly $q$-convex on all of $X$. Thus every sublevel of a strongly $q$-complete exhaustion is $q$-Runge complete. More generally, every sublevel of a strongly $q$-convex exhaustion containing its exceptional set is $q$-Runge. Indeed, choose $b<c$ above the maximum of the exhaustion on $L$ and, in the latter case, above its maximum on the exceptional set. Then $L\subset X_ b\Subset X_ c$ and the required convexity holds outside $\overline{X_ b}$.

title: 9.32.5 Holomorphic powers and ambient sums
text: We use the intrinsic Fréchet topology of theorem 9.51.5 on $\mathcal O_ X(U)$. Choose a countable cover by relatively compact embedded patches $U_ i=A_ i\cap D_ i$, where $D_ i$ is a polydisc and $A_ i$ carries the full analytic subspace structure. The maps \[  Q_ i:\mathcal O(D_ i)\longrightarrow \mathcal O_ X(U_ i)  \] are continuous open surjections by corollary 9.51.14 , applied to the coherent presentation $\mathcal O_{D_ i}\to \mathcal O_{A_ i}$. Fix compact polydiscs $L_{i,n}\Subset D_ i$ increasing to $D_ i$, with every compact subset contained in their interiors eventually. Lemma 9.32.6 . FE34E9B148D1 Let $U=A\cap D\Subset X$ be such a patch and $f\in \mathcal O(X)$. If $|f|\leq \theta <1$ on $\overline U$, then for each continuous seminorm $p$ on $\mathcal O_ X(U)$ and each $r\in (\theta ,1)$ there is a constant $C$ independent of $m$ such that \[  p(f^ m|_ U)\leq Cr^ m\qquad (m\geq 0).  \] In particular $f^ m|_ U\to 0$ in the full intrinsic section topology. Proof. Lift the actual section $f|_ U$ to $F\in \mathcal O(D)$ by the open surjection above, and put $W=\{ z\in D:|F(z)|<r\} $. Its intersection with $A$ is all of $U$, with its original structure. The restriction $Q_ W:\mathcal O(W)\to \mathcal O_ X(U)$ is continuous. One way to see this directly is to apply coherent-morphism continuity in theorem 9.51.5 to $\mathcal O_ W\to i_*\mathcal O_ U$; the topology of the latter's sections is the same intrinsic topology, by the local presentations. Consequently there are a compact $L\Subset W$ and $C>0$ with $p(Q_ W(G))\leq C\sup _ L|G|$ for $G\in \mathcal O(W)$. Use $G=F^ m$ and $|F|<r$ on $W$. The power represents the full section $f^ m$, not merely its reduced point values. This proves the estimate and convergence for every defining seminorm. $\square$ Here is the convergence criterion we will use. Suppose a finite block $(h_{j,l})_{1\leq l\leq N_ j}$ of global holomorphic sections is given for each $j\geq 1$. Suppose that for $i\leq j$ there are lifts $H_{i,j,l}\in \mathcal O(D_ i)$ with 434628413F46 9.32.7 \begin{equation}  Q_ i(H_{i,j,l})=h_{j,l}|_{U_ i},\qquad \sup _{L_{i,j}}|H_{i,j,l}|<2^{-j}/N_ j. \end{equation} Empty blocks are omitted. For $j<i$ choose any lifts by surjectivity. Then \[  \rho =\sum _{j,l}|h_{j,l}|^2  \] has a smooth plurisubharmonic ambient representative on every $U_ i$, namely $\sum _{j,l}|H_{i,j,l}|^2$ on $D_ i$. Indeed, on any smaller compact polydisc the Cauchy estimates, using a fixed larger compact polydisc, bound every differentiated tail by a constant times $\sum _ jN_ j(2^{-j}/N_ j)^2\leq \sum _ j4^{-j}$. This proves convergence of every derivative and the nonnegative Levi form. Equivalently the series $\sum _{j,l}H_{i,j,l}(z)\overline{H_{i,j,l}(\overline w)}$ converges holomorphically on $D_ i\times \overline{D_ i}$, so the representative is even real analytic. No common neighborhood for an arbitrary sequence of unrelated smooth extensions is being assumed. Proposition 9.32.8 . A13AE3DAF423 Every holomorphically convex complex space has a nonnegative smooth plurisubharmonic exhaustion. Here the holomorphic hull is tested by all sections of the full structure sheaf, using their scalar values. Proof. The hull is closed, contains its compact set, and is idempotent, by the same inequalities as in holomorphic hulls and domains of holomorphy . Inductively take hulls of compact neighborhoods to obtain compact holomorphically convex sets $K_ j$, with $K_ j\subset \operatorname {int}K_{j+1}$ and union $X$. At stage $j$ also include $\bigcup _{i\leq j}\overline U_ i$ and the next compact of an ordinary compact exhaustion before taking the hull. Local compactness supplies the compact neighborhoods, and holomorphic convexity makes their hulls compact. For $B_ j=K_{j+2}\setminus \operatorname {int}K_{j+1}$ choose finitely many $g_{j,l}\in \mathcal O(X)$ such that \[  \max _ l|g_{j,l}(x)|>1\quad (x\in B_ j),\qquad \max _ l\sup _{K_ j}|g_{j,l}|<1.  \] This follows from separation from the hull $K_ j$, rescaling, and compactness of $B_ j$. If $B_ j$ is empty take an empty block. For a nonempty block, its first displayed maximum has a minimum strictly greater than one on $B_ j$. For $i\leq j$ the preceding power lemma makes $g_{j,l}^ m|_{U_ i}$ tend to zero intrinsically. The image under $Q_ i$ of $\{ H:\sup _{L_{i,j}}|H|<2^{-j}/N_ j\} $ is an open zero neighborhood. Finitely many such conditions and finitely many $l$ can be met by one sufficiently large exponent $m_ j$. Increase it also so that $\sum _ l|g_{j,l}|^{2m_ j}\geq j$ on $B_ j$. Set $h_{j,l}=g_{j,l}^{m_ j}$. The controlled lifts ( 9.32.7 ) give a smooth nonnegative plurisubharmonic sum $\rho $. It is an exhaustion. A point outside $K_{N+1}$ first belongs to some $K_ m$ with $m\geq N+2$, hence lies in $B_{m-2}$ and has $\rho \geq m-2\geq N$. Thus each closed sublevel is contained in one compact $K_ j$ and is closed there. If the space is compact and the annuli are eventually empty, the same argument applies. $\square$

title: 9.32.9 Local separation and the Stein criterion

text: Global holomorphic sections locally separate points if each $x$ has a neighborhood $V$ such that every $y\in V\setminus \{ x\} $ satisfies $f(y)\ne f(x)$ for some $f\in \mathcal O(X)$. As in theorem 9.26.1 , independent differentials are not part of this hypothesis. Proposition 9.32.10 . 4B62D397B0C6 If global holomorphic sections locally separate points of a complex space $X$, then $X$ has a nonnegative smooth strictly plurisubharmonic function. If $X$ is also holomorphically convex, the function can be chosen to be an exhaustion. Proof. Fix $x$. Choose a local embedding with $x$ at the origin, and a closed unit ambient ball whose intersection with $X$ is compactly contained in a local separation neighborhood and in the patch. At each point of $X\cap \{ |z|=1\} $ choose a global function vanishing at $x$ and, after scaling, having squared modulus greater than two there. A finite selection gives $v=\sum _{l=1}^ N|f_ l|^2$, with $v(x)=0$ and $v>2$ on that compact boundary. If the boundary is empty the selection may be empty. On the relative ball put $b=(1+|z|^2)/3$ and use the normalized regularized maximum from Euclidean Richberg smoothing , with both parameters $\eta \in (0,1/24)$. Define \[  u_ x=M_\eta (v,b)\text{ on the relative ball},\qquad u_ x=v\text{ elsewhere}.  \] The boundary inequality makes these formulas agree on a relative collar by branch deletion. Thus $u_ x$ is globally smooth and nonnegative. Local holomorphic lifts of the $f_ l$ make $v$ ambient plurisubharmonic; the regularized maximum is also so. Near $x$ the maximum is exactly $b$, proving strictness there. These statements remain valid at an isolated point by taking a ball with empty relative boundary. Choose such functions $u_ j$, with neighborhoods covering $X$ on which $u_ j=b_ j>v_ j$ and hence is strict, so that their compact modification supports form a locally finite family. To make this choice, use compact sets $C_ n\subset \operatorname {int}C_{n+1}$ exhausting $X$ as in lemma 9.49.1 . On each compact annulus $C_ n\setminus \operatorname {int}C_{n-1}$ choose finitely many of the strict neighborhoods, with the corresponding closed relative balls inside $\operatorname {int}C_{n+1}\setminus C_{n-2}$; the first missing $C_ n$ are empty. The resulting family is locally finite. Write $v_ j=\sum _ l|f_{j,l}|^2$, so $u_ j=v_ j$ outside its ball. Choose arbitrary lifts $F_{i,j,l}$ of $f_{j,l}|_{U_ i}$ to $D_ i$. For an empty block take any positive $a_ j$. The preceding convergence criterion makes $\sum _ j a_ jv_ j$ smoothly ambient plurisubharmonic. Put \[  u=\sum _ j a_ jv_ j+\sum _ j a_ j(u_ j-v_ j).  \] The second sum is locally finite, so $u$ is smooth and equals the nonnegative sum $\sum _ j a_ ju_ j$ pointwise. To check positivity, fix a point and choose a neighborhood meeting only finitely many modification supports. Remove their finitely many blocks from the ambient square series on a patch $D_ i$ at that point. The remaining series is still smooth plurisubharmonic. C690C430BBD1 Suppose $H^1(X,\mathcal I)=0$ for every coherent ideal sheaf $\mathcal I\subset \mathcal O_ X$. Then $X$ is holomorphically convex, global holomorphic sections separate every pair of points, and finitely many global sections give a closed local embedding near every point. Its points are at most countable, since each can be isolated by a distinct member of a countable basis. Define an ideal sheaf with stalk $\mathfrak m_{x_ j}^{r_ j+1}$ at $x_ j$ and the full local ring off $D$. On a neighborhood containing just one $x_ j$ it is the corresponding power of the point ideal; off $D$ it is the full structure sheaf. The quotient is the sheaf supported on $D$ with these finite jet stalks, so its global sections are the product of all the jet spaces. The cohomology exact sequence gives the surjection \[  \mathcal O(X)\longrightarrow \prod _ j\mathcal O_{X,x_ j}/\mathfrak m_{x_ j}^{r_ j+1}.  \] This establishes the full jets, including nilpotents. title: 10.69 Relative cohomology, external products and integral duality
search_title: Relative cohomology, external products and integral duality
section: 10.69 Relative cohomology, external products and integral duality
text: Cohomology of sheaves uses the functorial Godement complex $C^ qF=G^{q+1}F$, with the alternating coface differential, as in theorem 10.43.5 . Supports are closed supports of germs. The subscript $c$ means compact supports, and extension from an open set always means extension by zero. Throughout, $R$ is a nonzero principal ideal domain; $\operatorname {Ext}$ and $\operatorname {Tor}$ below mean their first algebraic derived functors over $R$. All tensor products are algebraic. Topological manifolds in this section are Hausdorff, paracompact, without boundary and of a fixed finite real dimension $n$. Connectedness and orientability are stated separately. No finite rank or finite generation of a local coefficient module is understood.

title: 10.69.1 Relative groups and the support comparison
search_title: Relative groups and the support comparison
section: 10.69 Relative cohomology, external products and integral duality
text: Lemma 10.69.2 . DEC4F08B6222 For a subspace $i:S\hookrightarrow X$ and a sheaf $A$ on $X$, the functorial restriction \[  r:C_ X^\bullet A(X)\longrightarrow C_ S^\bullet (i^{-1}A)(S)  \] is onto in each degree. Its kernel defines $H^ q(X,S;A)$ and gives the natural long exact sequence of a pair and of a triple. Equivalently, this kernel is quasi-isomorphic to the mapping fiber of $r$. In degree zero it is the module of global sections of $A$ whose restriction to $S$ is zero. For constant coefficients these are locally constant functions vanishing on $S$; arbitrary values on connected components are not asserted when those components are not open. For constant coefficients these groups are the relative Godement, or Alexander–Spanier, groups. Relative pullback is functorial, and constant-coefficient relative groups are invariant under homotopies of pairs. Proof. The restriction map in degree zero of the resolution takes an assignment $(a_ x)_{x\in X}$ to its subassignment on $S$; it is onto. Inductively, a germ at $s\in S$ of an assignment of germs on a relative open neighborhood can be extended to an ambient open neighborhood: lift each of its values by the preceding inductive surjectivity and assign zero away from $S$. This proves that the stalk map $i^{-1}G_ X^ qA\to G_ S^ q i^{-1}A$ is onto, and the outer product over points proves the next degree's surjectivity on sections. These maps commute with cofaces by naturality of augmentation. For a triple, lift a cochain on $S$ that vanishes on $T$ to $X$; its restriction to $T$ is already zero. The kernels therefore form short exact complexes. The long exact sequences, with their positive connecting maps, follow from lemma 10.43.3 . Their degree-zero kernel gives the stated description of sections. For a surjective cochain map the natural map from its kernel to its mapping fiber is a quasi-isomorphism: its quotient is the mapping fiber of the identity of the target, contracted by the identity in the adjacent degree. This observation also shows that replacing both absolute complexes by naturally quasi-isomorphic complexes preserves relative groups. The restriction and inverse-image maps of the Godement construction supply functorial pullback. On a pair, projection to $X$ and to $S$ from their products with $[0,1]$ induces isomorphisms by theorem 10.63.3 . The natural pair sequences and the five lemma give the relative isomorphism. Both endpoint restrictions are its inverse, which proves homotopy invariance for maps of pairs. $\square$ Theorem 10.69.3 . 211571452FE5 If $\overline T\subset \operatorname {int}_ X S$, restriction gives \[  H^ q(X,S;A)\simeq H^ q(X\setminus T,S\setminus T;A).  \] If $S$ is open or strongly paracompact in $X$, there is also a natural isomorphism \[  H^ q(X,S;A)\simeq H^ q_{X\setminus S}(X,A),  \] where the right side allows precisely closed supports contained in $X\setminus S$. If, in addition, $X$ is locally compact Hausdorff, $S$ is closed, and $U=X\setminus S$ has compact closure in $X$, this is $H_ c^ q(U,A|_ U)$. Proof. First, relative groups have Mayer–Vietoris for a cover by two open sets. Apply the absolute Mayer–Vietoris short complexes of theorem 10.43.7 to $X$ and to its induced open cover on $S$ and take mapping fibers. The two term Čech resolutions of flabby Godement terms are exact, so the resulting total complexes compute the relative mapping fibers just proved. This gives the claimed exact sequence, with the restriction maps on all three pair terms. Put $V=\operatorname {int}S$ and $W=X\setminus \overline T$. These are open and cover $X$. In this relative Mayer–Vietoris sequence the pair on $V$ is $(V,V)$ and has zero cohomology; the same is true on $V\cap W$. Thus restriction gives $H^ q(X,S;A)=H^ q(W,S\cap W;A)$. The same argument on $X\setminus T$ uses the open cover by $W$ and $V\setminus T$ and gives the same middle group. The two isomorphisms are the asserted restriction. This proof uses the closure in the hypothesis. For open $S$, restriction of $C_ X^\bullet A$ is exactly the Godement complex on $S$. A section restricting to zero has closed support disjoint from $S$, giving equality of the two kernel complexes. For strongly paracompact $S$, use instead the complex $\Gamma (S,i^{-1}C_ X^\bullet A)$ of germ sections. Each term restricts surjectively from $X$: the closed-section neighborhood extension argument in theorem 10.44.4 extends a germ section to a neighborhood, and flabbiness then extends it to $X$. Its kernel again consists of closed supports disjoint from $S$. The exact proof of theorem 10.60.1 shows that $i^{-1}C_ X^ qA$ is soft and acyclic on $S$; hence this complex computes $H^ q(S,i^{-1}A)$. Its natural map to the intrinsic Godement complex is an acyclic-resolution comparison inducing the identity in degree zero. Comparing the two short exact kernel complexes proves the support assertion. Finally assume the additional hypotheses. A closed support in $X$ contained in $U$ is compact because it lies in $\overline U$. Conversely a compact subset of $U$ is closed in $X$. Restriction and extension by zero identify sections with these supports with compact sections on the open space $U$. The open restriction of a flabby resolution computes both groups, proving the last assertion. The open-complement requirement is essential. For $X=\mathbb R$ and $S=\mathbb R\setminus \{ 0\} $ with integer coefficients, the pair sequence gives $H^0(X,S)=0$, $H^1(X,S)=\mathbb Z$, whereas $H_ c^0(\{ 0\} ,\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$ and $H_ c^1(\{ 0\} ,\mathbb Z)=0$. $\square$ Corollary 10.69.4 . 7B9A12C78AC8 Properly homotopic maps between locally compact Hausdorff spaces induce the same pullback on compactly supported cohomology with constant coefficients. Proof. Write $X^+=X\cup \{ \infty \} $ for the one-point compactification; if $X$ is already compact, the new point is isolated. A proper map $f:X\to Y$ extends continuously to a map $f^+:X^+\to Y^+$ fixing infinity, since inverse images of compact sets are compact. If $H:X\times [0,1]\to Y$ is proper, it extends to $X^+\times [0,1]$ by sending all $(\infty ,t)$ to infinity. Indeed, the projection to $X$ of $H^{-1}(K)$ is compact for every compact $K\subset Y$; outside that projection the extension avoids $K$ uniformly for all $t$. This proves joint continuity at the entire added interval. The preceding theorem gives $H_ c^ q(X,A)=H^ q(X^+,\{ \infty \} ;A)$, and similarly for $Y$. Apply the actual homotopy invariance of pairs. This constructs proper pullback and proves equality of the two endpoint maps. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.69.4

text: Corollary 10.69.4 . 7B9A12C78AC8 Properly homotopic maps between locally compact Hausdorff spaces induce the same pullback on compactly supported cohomology with constant coefficients. Proof. Write $X^+=X\cup \{ \infty \} $ for the one-point compactification; if $X$ is already compact, the new point is isolated. A proper map $f:X\to Y$ extends continuously to a map $f^+:X^+\to Y^+$ fixing infinity, since inverse images of compact sets are compact. If $H:X\times [0,1]\to Y$ is proper, it extends to $X^+\times [0,1]$ by sending all $(\infty ,t)$ to infinity. text: Lemma 10.69.6 . 9BD1AF8701FE Let $B$ be a soft sheaf of $R$-algebras on a compact Hausdorff space $X$, let $F$ be a $B$-module sheaf, and let $N$ be an $R$-module. Suppose either $F$ is stalkwise flat over $R$ or $N$ is flat. Then \[  \Gamma (X,F)\otimes _ RN\  \xrightarrow {\sim } \Gamma (X,F\otimes _ R\underline N).  \] The sheaves $F\otimes _ R\underline N$ are soft. In particular, for a sheaf $A$, the complex $C_ X^\bullet A\otimes _ R\underline N$ is an acyclic resolution of $A\otimes _ R\underline N$ if either $A$ or $N$ is flat. Its section complex is $C_ X^\bullet A(X)\otimes _ RN$. The latter conclusion also holds for arbitrary $X$ when $N$ is finitely generated over a PID. Proof. Every $B$-module sheaf is soft by corollary 10.44.9 . For a free module $P=\bigoplus _ JR$, a section of $F\otimes P=\bigoplus _ JF$ uses only finitely many summands locally. Compactness gives one finite set of summands for the entire section, and therefore $\Gamma (X,F\otimes P)=\Gamma (X,F)\otimes P$. Take a free presentation $0\to P_1\to P_0\to N\to 0$ over the PID. Under either stated flatness assumption its tensor sequence with $F$ is exact. The first term $F\otimes P_1$ is soft, so taking sections preserves this short exact sequence. The free cases and right exactness of tensor give the displayed isomorphism of cokernels. The ring $C_ X^ q\underline R$ is flabby and hence soft. Its module $C_ X^ qA\otimes \underline N$ is therefore acyclic. If $A$ is flat, all $C_ X^ qA$ and their cycle sheaves are flat: products and filtered limits of torsion-free modules are torsion-free, and submodules remain torsion-free. Tensoring the augmented exact resolution remains exact. If $N$ is flat, exactness follows directly. Apply the preceding section comparison term by term and theorem 10.43.8 . For the last assertion use a finite presentation of $N$. Tensoring with a finitely presented module commutes with products and filtered limits: write the tensor as the cokernel of a map between finite powers, and lift coordinates separately to identify product cokernels; filtered limits are exact. Consequently the natural map $C_ X^ qA\otimes \underline N\to C_ X^ q(A\otimes \underline N)$ is an isomorphism, including on sections, by induction on the Godement construction. The latter terms are flabby on every $X$. The preceding exactness argument finishes the proof. $\square$ Theorem 10.69.7 . 77686EA729F2 Let $A$ be a sheaf of modules over a PID $R$ and $N$ an $R$-module, with at least one of $A,N$ flat.
