If $X$ is locally compact Hausdorff, the same statement holds with compact supports and without either finiteness condition. Proof. In the ordinary case the lemma identifies the middle group with the cohomology of the single complex $C_ X^\bullet A(X)\otimes N$. When $A$ is flat its section terms are torsion-free and flat. Apply corollary 10.67.9 . When $N$ is flat, tensor is exact, the Tor term is zero and the left arrow is itself an isomorphism. The maps are the actual coefficient maps of complexes, so the naturality assertion does not depend on the chosen splitting. For compact supports let $U\Subset X$ and $K=\overline U$. The complex $(C_ X^\bullet A)_ U|_ K$ resolves $A_ U|_ K$. Each of its terms is a module over the soft ring $(C_ X^ q\underline R)|_ K$; softness of this restriction follows from the compact strong-paracompactness and neighborhood-extension proof in lemma 10.56.5 . Apply the lemma on $K$. Its section complex is $\Gamma _ c(U,C_ X^\bullet A|_ U)$, as follows by extension by zero. These complexes form a directed union equal to $\Gamma _ c(X,C_ X^\bullet A)$; every compact support is contained in some relatively compact open $U$. The exact compact-neighborhood comparison in theorem 10.56.7 therefore gives the natural quasi-isomorphism \[  \Gamma _ c(X,C_ X^\bullet A)\otimes N \longrightarrow R\Gamma _ c(X,A\otimes \underline N).  \] Here the right side denotes its Godement representative, and the arrow is the usual augmentation comparison, obtained on the compact neighborhoods and then in their directed union. Tensor and cohomology commute with that union. Apply the algebraic theorem to this one compact-section complex. No chosen splitting is passed through a limit. $\square$ Theorem 10.69.8 . 767B8FC48593 Let $A$ and $B$ be sheaves of modules over a PID on $X$ and $Y$, respectively, and put $A\boxtimes B=p_ X^{-1}A\otimes p_ Y^{-1}B$. Suppose $A$ is flat and $Y$ is compact Hausdorff. If $X$ is compact Hausdorff or every $H^ q(Y,B)$ is finitely generated, external cup product is the first map of a natural short exact sequence \[  \begin{aligned}  0\longrightarrow \bigoplus _{p+q=k}H^ p(X,A)\otimes H^ q(Y,B) & \longrightarrow H^ k(X\times Y,A\boxtimes B)\\ & \longrightarrow \bigoplus _{p+q=k+1} \operatorname {Tor}(H^ p(X,A),H^ q(Y,B))\longrightarrow 0. \end{aligned}  \] The sequence splits noncanonically. Resolving each term by its own Godement complex compares their section totals with $K_ K(A_ U|_ K)$ and $K_ L(B_ V|_ L)$ by augmentations. The already proved compact case identifies their external product with cohomology of $(A\boxtimes B)_{U\times V}|_{K\times L}$. The product comparison commutes with these augmentations, since the Godement product does; this is also the acyclic multiplicative comparison of theorem 10.58.9 . Take the directed union over $U,V$. The source becomes $\Gamma _ c(X,C_ X^\bullet A)\otimes \Gamma _ c(Y,C_ Y^\bullet B)$. On the target, compact subsets of $X\times Y$ lie in such rectangles, by their compact projections and relatively compact neighborhoods. The compact-neighborhood theorem therefore identifies the target with compact-support cohomology on the product. All transition maps are extension maps and all product comparisons commute with them. The resulting map of the single tensor complex is a quasi-isomorphism. Its first factor is flat, so the algebraic Künneth theorem proves both the natural exact sequence and its noncanonical splitting. $\square$ Corollary 10.69.9 . D1F14C5698EC In the ordinary theorem, a finite CW complex may be used for the compact factor with constant finitely generated coefficients. When both coefficient sheaves are constant and flat, it is enough that one factor have the homotopy type of a finite CW complex and that the coefficient module on that factor be finitely generated. The coefficient qualification cannot be omitted, even when that factor is a point and both coefficient modules are flat. Proof. Here is the required finiteness argument. For a finite CW complex, its skeletal filtration is finite. A neighborhood of the preceding skeleton inside the next skeleton consists of that skeleton and outer annular collars in the finitely many newly attached disks. Radial motion in each collar, fixed on the attaching boundary, defines a deformation retraction of this neighborhood onto the preceding skeleton, continuously on the attaching quotient. Use two nested collars and relative excision to remove the preceding skeleton and the outer closed collars. This identifies the relative cohomology of successive skeleta with the direct sum, over the new $r$-cells, of the cohomology of a disk relative to its boundary. The contractibility and sphere calculation of theorem 10.63.3 , proposition 10.66.1 and the pair sequence identify that group with one copy of the coefficient module in degree $r$, and zero in other degrees. For $r=0$ these are simply the finitely many point sections. The skeletal pair sequences, by induction, now show that all cohomology modules are finitely generated: kernels and quotients of finitely generated modules over a PID are finitely generated, by lemma 10.67.4 . A finite CW complex is compact Hausdorff: each finite attaching quotient is compact, and the closed equivalence relation in the finite disjoint compact disks gives the Hausdorff quotient. The ordinary theorem applies with this factor. For the homotopy-type version choose a homotopy equivalence of that factor with the finite complex. Product with the identity of the other factor is again a homotopy equivalence. Both external coefficient sheaves are constant, with tensor product the constant sheaf of the tensor module, so constant-sheaf homotopy invariance applies to the factors and the product. Naturality of the actual external cup map transports the short exact sequence. If the compact factor is the first one, interchange factors with the stated Koszul sign; flatness of the other coefficient is exactly what is needed. For the failure without the coefficient qualification take $R=\mathbb Z$, $X=\mathbb N$ discrete, $Y$ a point, $A=\underline{\mathbb Z}$ on $X$ and $B=\mathbb Q$ on $Y$. section: 10.70 Local systems and a singular comparison with supports
text: Proposition 10.70.1 . 3CBF93FB0039 A locally constant sheaf of $R$-modules is equivalently a covering space with discrete module fibers and local trivializations linear on each fiber. On a connected, locally path connected, semilocally simply connected space it is equivalently a module $L$ with a representation of the fundamental group in $\operatorname {Aut}_ R(L)$, up to change of the identification of one fiber with $L$. These hypotheses hold on a connected manifold. Transport is invariant under endpoint-fixed homotopy of paths. For a fixed base, homology is covariant under coefficient homomorphisms; pullback of the coefficient system along a map of bases is a separate, contravariant operation. Proof. Take the disjoint union of the stalks, with the topology whose basic open sets are the germs of a local section. A local constant trivialization identifies this space with $U\times L$, with $L$ discrete. Conversely, sections of such a covering form the required sheaf, and these constructions are inverse on germs and on maps. Subdivide a path into finitely many intervals lying in trivializing opens. Continue a fiber element as a constant local section on each interval. Uniqueness on overlaps proves independence of subdivision and gives inverse transport on the reversed path and composition under concatenation. For a homotopy of paths, subdivide the parameter square into small rectangles each mapped into a trivializing open. Transport around each rectangle is the identity; the interior edges cancel, proving homotopy invariance and the endpoint formula. For completeness the needed universal cover has a direct construction. Fix $x_0$ and take endpoint-fixed homotopy classes $[\gamma ]$ of paths starting there. Over a path connected open $U$ whose loops are nullhomotopic in $X$, extend $\gamma $ by paths in $U$. Their endpoint classes form one sheet mapped bijectively onto $U$. These sheets define a topology: two sheets meeting at a point agree over a smaller such neighborhood, by concatenation and the nullhomotopy condition. They are evenly covered charts. Path lifting is the continuation construction above. A loop in this covering projects to a loop whose path class is trivial, and its nullhomotopy lifts rectangle by rectangle; hence the covering is simply connected. Use path concatenation in the order for which transport is a left representation. A based loop acts on a fiber by its transport. Trivializing a pulled-back local system on the simply connected cover by transport identifies it with the product with $L$. Explicitly, the pair $(\gamma ,l)$ represents $t_\gamma l$ in the endpoint fiber. Two such pairs with the same endpoint represent the same element precisely when $l'=t_{\gamma '}^{-1}t_\gamma l$. This specifies the deck/coefficient quotient without an implicit inverse convention. Conversely, this equivalence relation on path pairs constructs the covering module sheaf from the representation; the evenly covered charts above check it directly and give the prescribed transport. A different identification of the base fiber conjugates the representation, and an isomorphism of sheaves induces exactly such an intertwiner. These statements also apply component by component. Finally a coefficient map acts on the coefficient of each chain in the same direction. A homotopy of base maps gives equality of induced maps only after identifying the pullback systems by its actual path transport; the underlying base homotopy alone does not specify a coefficient map. $\square$ Let $C_ j^{\mathrm{sing}}(U,A)=\bigoplus _{\sigma :\Delta ^ j\to U} A_{\sigma (v_0)}$. A coefficient can equivalently be its unique parallel section on $\Delta ^ j$, since all paths in a simplex between fixed endpoints are homotopic. The boundary is the alternating sum of its restrictions to faces. In initial-vertex notation the face omitting $v_0$ transports the coefficient to $v_1$; the other faces retain it. Cochains $C^ j_{\mathrm{sing}}(U,A)$ assign a coefficient in $A_{\sigma (v_0)}$ to every simplex, with arbitrary, not finite, support. The coboundary is \[  (\delta u)(\sigma )=t_{1,0}u(\sigma [v_1,\ldots ,v_{j+1}]) +\sum _{i=1}^{j+1}(-1)^ i u(\sigma [v_0,\ldots ,\widehat v_ i, \ldots ,v_{j+1}]),  \] where $t_{1,0}$ is transport along the reversed first edge. Commuting restrictions to two faces cancel with opposite signs; the two transports agree because the corresponding paths in the simplex are homotopic. Thus $\partial ^2=\delta ^2=0$. Lemma 10.70.2 . F198D931B2F3 For any open cover $\mathcal U$, the chains whose simplices lie in one cover member form a subcomplex, and its inclusion in the full singular complex is a chain homotopy equivalence. The assertion holds with any local module coefficients, for relative complexes, and for cochains. Singular homology and cohomology consequently have the pair and triple sequences and excision for $\overline T\subset \operatorname {int}S$, and Mayer–Vietoris for open covers. Singular chains commute with directed unions of opens; compact-support singular cohomology is \[  H^ q_{c,\mathrm{sing}}(X,A)= \varinjlim _{K\subset X\  {\rm compact}} H^ q_{\mathrm{sing}}(X,X\setminus K;A).  \] Proof. All constructions can be performed in a simplex, with its pulled-back coefficient system trivialized by its initial vertex; they therefore respect any local coefficients. On affine chains in a convex set, coning to a point $b$ satisfies $\partial b+b\partial =1$ on the augmented complex. Define subdivision on an affine simplex $s$ by $Ss=b_ s(S\partial s)$, where $b_ s$ is its barycenter, starting with the identity in dimension zero. The cone identity gives $\partial Ss=S\partial s$. Define $Ts=b_ s(s-T\partial s)$, starting with zero in augmentation degree. Then \[  \partial Ts=s-T\partial s-b_ s(\partial s-\partial T\partial s) =s-T\partial s-Ss.  \] Pushing these formulas along each singular simplex defines natural carrier-preserving $S,T$ with $\partial T+T\partial =1-S$. A barycentric subsimplex has diameter at most $j/(j+1)$ of the original in dimension $j$: its vertices are barycenters of nested faces; writing a barycenter as the convex combination of a vertex and the opposite face barycenter gives this bound, then induction on faces handles the other pairs of vertices. Iteration and a Lebesgue number of the pulled-back cover make every simplex small. Let $m(\sigma )$ be the least subdivision number for which every geometric subsimplex, before any algebraic cancellation, maps into one cover member. A face has no larger such number. Put $T_ m=\sum _{i=0}^{m-1}TS^ i$, so $\partial T_ m+T_ m\partial =1-S^ m$, and define $D\sigma =T_{m(\sigma )}\sigma $, extended linearly with transported coefficients. Set $\rho =1-\partial D-D\partial $. This is a chain map. Moreover \[  \rho \sigma =S^{m(\sigma )}\sigma + T_{m(\sigma )}\partial \sigma -D\partial \sigma .  \] For a face $\sigma _ j$, the remaining difference is a sum of $TS^ i\sigma _ j$ with $i\ge m(\sigma _ j)$; it is small because $T$ preserves the carrier. Thus $\rho $ has image in small chains. On small simplices $D=0$, whence $\rho $ restricts to the identity. This gives both a retraction and the stated chain homotopy. They preserve every subspace, so pass to relative quotients and, by precomposition, to cochains and their relative kernels. The pair and triple complexes are short exact in every degree; cochain restrictions are onto by assigning zero to all simplices not in the subspace. Their algebraic sequences are therefore exact. For an excisive cover $X=\operatorname {int}S\cup \operatorname {int}B$, the intermediate complex $C(S)+C(B)$ has a homotopy-equivalent inclusion in $C(X)$: the open-cover small complex lies inside it, and both subdivision and its homotopy preserve $S$ and $B$. Its quotient by $C(S)$ is $C(B)/C(S\cap B)$, simplex by simplex. This proves excision, including the stated barred form with $B=X\setminus T$. For two opens the short exact sequence \[  0\to C(U\cap V)\xrightarrow {z\mapsto (z,-z)} C(U)\oplus C(V) \xrightarrow {(a,b)\mapsto a+b} C(U)+C(V)\to 0  \] gives homology Mayer–Vietoris; the analogous cochain kernel and restriction sequence gives cohomology. The same formulas apply to pairs. For finitely many cover members the augmented Čech row is exact: for each small simplex choose one member containing it and prepend its index as the contraction. A homotopy has the prism operator $P\sigma =\sum _{i=0}^ j(-1)^ iH(\sigma \times 1) [v_0,\ldots ,v_ i,w_ i,\ldots ,w_ j]$. Its interior faces cancel, leaving $\partial P+P\partial =H_{1*}-H_{0*}$, with transport along the homotopy on coefficients. This proves homotopy invariance in the form stated above. Finally a chain and a bounding chain use finitely many compact simplices. A compact set in a directed union of opens lies in one of them, proving the chain limit assertion. The last displayed formula follows by taking the directed union of the relative cochain kernels: a cycle or a primitive has its support condition at one compact stage. The condition is vanishing on simplices contained in the complement, not finite support among all singular simplices. $\square$ Theorem 10.70.3 . 9E4C37619D42 On a topological manifold, singular cohomology of a local system agrees naturally with its sheaf cohomology. This comparison commutes with cup product and proper pullback. The augmentation $A\to \mathcal S^\bullet (A)$ is exact. Indeed a coordinate ball trivializes $A$ by path transport; shrinking a germ cycle to a smaller ball and using the prism contraction proves local exactness in positive degree. In degree zero its closed sections are precisely parallel, locally constant sections. This argument requires no acyclicity assertion about the sheaves $\mathcal S^ q$. Form the functorial first-quadrant complex \[  Q^\bullet (U,A)=\operatorname {Tot}_{p,q\ge 0} \Gamma (U,C_ U^ p\mathcal S^ q(A)).  \] There are natural augmentation maps \[  C^\bullet _{\mathrm{sing}}(U,A)\longrightarrow Q^\bullet (U,A) \longleftarrow C_ U^\bullet A(U).  \] The right map is a quasi-isomorphism, since each $\Gamma (U,C_ U^ p-)$ is exact and the vertical augmented sheaf complex is exact. Each term of $Q$ is a finite sum of flabby sheaves before taking sections. On a contractible coordinate ball both sides of the left map have cohomology $A$ in degree zero and zero elsewhere: use the prism contraction for singular cohomology and theorem 10.63.3 for sheaf cohomology. The map on degree zero is the identity. First take an open subset of $\mathbb R^ n$ and cover it by convex balls trivializing the local system. All nonempty finite intersections are convex and have the just computed comparison. The augmented Čech double complex of singular cochains computes global singular cohomology: replace the global cochains by cochains on small chains using the preceding homotopy equivalence, and contract each horizontal row by prepending an index containing the simplex. The corresponding Čech complex of $Q$ computes $Q(U,A)$, since its rows are flabby and Čech acyclic by lemma 10.43.14 . The maps on all intersection complexes are quasi-isomorphisms. The finite-diagonal comparison of lemma 10.43.15 proves the global comparison on this open subset of Euclidean space. Now use any coordinate-ball cover of the manifold. Each finite intersection is an open subset of one coordinate ball, and the preceding paragraph applies there. Repeating the same Čech comparison proves the result on the whole manifold and every open subset. All comparisons came from the displayed functorial maps; changing covers only proves that those same maps are isomorphisms. Thus they commute with restrictions and with coefficient maps. There is no assumed triangulation or unproved global good-cover interface in this argument. For closed $K$, the singular cochain restriction to $X\setminus K$ is onto, and the same is true in every degree of $Q$ by flabbiness. The natural short exact kernel complexes, and the comparison just proved on the two open spaces, identify their kernels by the five lemma. The augmented sheaf total underlying $Q$ is an exact flabby resolution of $A$, so its sections with support in $K$ compute the stated supported sheaf group. Directed union over compact $K$ proves the compact assertion. These constructions also show proper pullback compatibility, since inverse images of compact supports under a proper map remain compact. title: Proposition 10.70.1
section: 10.70 Local systems and a singular comparison with supports
text: Proposition 10.70.1 . 3CBF93FB0039 A locally constant sheaf of $R$-modules is equivalently a covering space with discrete module fibers and local trivializations linear on each fiber. On a connected, locally path connected, semilocally simply connected space it is equivalently a module $L$ with a representation of the fundamental group in $\operatorname {Aut}_ R(L)$, up to change of the identification of one fiber with $L$. These hypotheses hold on a connected manifold. Transport is invariant under endpoint-fixed homotopy of paths. For a fixed base, homology is covariant under coefficient homomorphisms; pullback of the coefficient system along a map of bases is a separate, contravariant operation. Proof. Take the disjoint union of the stalks, with the topology whose basic open sets are the germs of a local section. A local constant trivialization identifies this space with $U\times L$, with $L$ discrete. Conversely, sections of such a covering form the required sheaf, and these constructions are inverse on germs and on maps. Subdivide a path into finitely many intervals lying in trivializing opens. Continue a fiber element as a constant local section on each interval. Uniqueness on overlaps proves independence of subdivision and gives inverse transport on the reversed path and composition under concatenation. For a homotopy of paths, subdivide the parameter square into small rectangles each mapped into a trivializing open. Transport around each rectangle is the identity; the interior edges cancel, proving homotopy invariance and the endpoint formula. For completeness the needed universal cover has a direct construction. Fix $x_0$ and take endpoint-fixed homotopy classes $[\gamma ]$ of paths starting there. Over a path connected open $U$ whose loops are nullhomotopic in $X$, extend $\gamma $ by paths in $U$. Their endpoint classes form one sheet mapped bijectively onto $U$. These sheets define a topology: two sheets meeting at a point agree over a smaller such neighborhood, by concatenation and the nullhomotopy condition. They are evenly covered charts. Path lifting is the continuation construction above. A loop in this covering projects to a loop whose path class is trivial, and its nullhomotopy lifts rectangle by rectangle; hence the covering is simply connected. Use path concatenation in the order for which transport is a left representation. A based loop acts on a fiber by its transport. Trivializing a pulled-back local system on the simply connected cover by transport identifies it with the product with $L$. Explicitly, the pair $(\gamma ,l)$ represents $t_\gamma l$ in the endpoint fiber. Two such pairs with the same endpoint represent the same element precisely when $l'=t_{\gamma '}^{-1}t_\gamma l$. This specifies the deck/coefficient quotient without an implicit inverse convention. Conversely, this equivalence relation on path pairs constructs the covering module sheaf from the representation; the evenly covered charts above check it directly and give the prescribed transport. A different identification of the base fiber conjugates the representation, and an isomorphism of sheaves induces exactly such an intertwiner. These statements also apply component by component. Finally a coefficient map acts on the coefficient of each chain in the same direction. A homotopy of base maps gives equality of induced maps only after identifying the pullback systems by its actual path transport; the underlying base homotopy alone does not specify a coefficient map. $\square$

title: 10.71 Orientation classes and cap duality
text: Lemma 10.71.1 . 603753CCA942 The groups $\tau _{X,x}=H_ n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X,X\setminus \{ x\} ; \mathbb Z)$ form a locally constant sheaf of infinite cyclic groups. There is a canonical identification $\tau _ X\otimes \tau _ X=\underline{\mathbb {Z}}$, sending $o\otimes o$ to $1$ for either local generator. For every compact $K\subset X$ there is a unique class \[  [X]_ K\in H_ n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X,X\setminus K;\tau _ X\otimes R)  \] whose local value at each $x\in K$ is $1$ under this identification. These classes commute with restriction to smaller compact sets and with open excision. For any local module system $A$, $H_ j(X,X\setminus K;A)=0$ for $j>n$, and a class in degree $n$ is determined by all its point restrictions on $K$. Proof. A point has singular homology only in degree zero: the complex for a constant module has differential alternating between the identity and zero in positive degrees. Contracting a ball to a point by the prism gives the same conclusion for balls. The open hemisphere Mayer–Vietoris sequence computes the reduced homology of spheres inductively from $\widetilde H_0(S^0,R)=R$; it is $R$ in the sphere dimension and zero otherwise. Radial retraction of a punctured ball onto a sphere and the pair sequence now give the asserted local infinite cyclic group. In dimension zero the pair is simply a point relative to the empty set. A nonempty compact convex set $K\subset \mathbb R^ n$ has the same relative homology as a point in it. Indeed, with center $x\in K$, choose a sphere of radius greater than every distance from $x$ to $K$. Both $\mathbb R^ n\setminus K$ and $\mathbb R^ n\setminus \{ x\} $ retract radially onto this sphere. The first retraction stays in the complement: a ray from a point of a convex set cannot reenter it after leaving it, and the chosen sphere is beyond the whole set. The retractions commute with the inclusion up to these explicit radial homotopies. The pair sequences therefore give an isomorphism on relative groups, which are the coefficient module in degree $n$ and zero elsewhere. Local systems on the chart are constant by transport. Restriction from a closed ball to every point of its interior consequently supplies compatible local generators. On an overlap two such generators differ by $+1$ or $-1$, locally constantly, since comparison can be made on one smaller closed ball inside the overlap. These are exactly the transition maps defining $\tau _ X$. Their squares are one, proving the canonical tensor identification. We give the compact-set extension argument in detail. For compact $K,L$ the relative Mayer–Vietoris sequence has the segment \[  \begin{aligned}  H_{j+1}(X,X\setminus (K\cap L);A)& \longrightarrow H_ j(X,X\setminus (K\cup L);A)\\ & \longrightarrow H_ j(X,X\setminus K;A)\oplus H_ j(X,X\setminus L;A)\\ & \longrightarrow H_ j(X,X\setminus (K\cap L);A). \end{aligned}  \] It is obtained from the two open complements by the small-chain argument. Thus, if the higher vanishing and local uniqueness hold for $K,L,K\cap L$, they hold for $K\cup L$. Compatible degree-$n$ classes on $K,L$ glue uniquely, since the left group in degree $n$ is zero. Induction proves these assertions for finite unions of compact convex sets in a chart; their finite intersections are again compact convex sets, with the empty case giving zero. For an arbitrary compact $K$ in a chart, let a relative cycle $z$ have boundary disjoint from $K$. Choose finitely many small closed balls centered at points of $K$ whose interiors cover $K$ and whose union $L$ misses that boundary. Then $z$ is already a relative cycle for $L$. Above degree $n$ its class is zero by the preceding finite union case. In degree $n$, if all its point values on $K$ vanish, its restriction to each chosen ball vanishes because it vanishes at that ball's center. Local uniqueness for the finite union makes its class zero on $L$, and hence on $K$. Existence of the canonical class on a compact set in a chart follows by restricting the class of one larger closed ball. The coefficient system $\tau _ X\otimes R$ makes its local value independent of the sign of the chosen coordinate orientation. Finally cover an arbitrary compact $K$ by finitely many compact subsets $K_ i$ contained in coordinate balls; obtain them by shrinking a finite coordinate cover on the compact Hausdorff subspace. The assertions are known for every $K_ i$ and for every intersection with the union of its predecessors, since that intersection is a compact subset of the same chart. The relative Mayer–Vietoris argument proves vanishing, uniqueness and existence successively for their unions. Uniqueness also proves compatibility with smaller compact sets. Open excision has the same point values, so it preserves these classes. This completes the construction, including the integral orientation twist. $\square$ Lemma 10.71.2 . 3C7389B6FCBC The homological orientation system of a smooth manifold agrees with its usual determinant orientation. In particular a smooth coordinate change preserves a local homology generator exactly when its derivative has positive determinant. The group $\operatorname {GL}^+(r,\mathbb R)$ is path connected. Proof. Gram–Schmidt writes a positive-determinant matrix as an orthogonal determinant-one matrix times an upper triangular matrix with positive diagonal. Linear interpolation contracts the latter to the identity through such triangular matrices. For $r\ge 2$, successive plane rotations take the first column of the orthogonal factor to the first coordinate vector, and then act on its orthogonal complement. Induction gives a path to the identity. Rank one is the path of positive scalars; rank zero is immediate. A linear map of positive determinant is thus homotopic through invertible linear maps to the identity, and induces $+1$ on local homology. A reflection in one coordinate induces $-1$. Indeed, it exchanges the two hemispheres of the surrounding sphere and fixes their equator; in the reduced Mayer–Vietoris sequence, exchanging the two summands negates the connecting map. For the zero-sphere this is directly the exchange of its two points in reduced $H_0$. The radial local-homology identification gives the same sign for the reflection. Factoring a negative-determinant matrix as a reflection times a positive-determinant one proves the linear case. Finally let a smooth coordinate change fix the origin, with invertible derivative $T$ there. On a sufficiently small ball write $f(v)=Tv+e(v)$ with $|e(v)|\le \frac12\| T^{-1}\| ^{-1}|v|$. For $0<t\le 1$ set $f_ t(v)=t^{-1}f(tv)$ and set $f_0(v)=Tv$. The first-order remainder estimate makes this a continuous homotopy; the displayed bound makes $f_ t(v)$ nonzero for $v\ne 0$ throughout. It is therefore a homotopy of the punctured-ball pairs defining local homology. The local action of $f$ is the action of $T$, whose sign was just computed. Compatible positive smooth charts and compatible positive homological generators consequently specify the same orientation. $\square$ For a $j$-simplex with a parallel coefficient $e$, and a $p$-cochain $u$, define the cap product by the back face with coefficient transported to the shared vertex: \[  (e\sigma )\frown u= t_{0,p}\bigl (e\otimes u(\sigma [v_0,\ldots ,v_ p])\bigr ) \sigma [v_ p,\ldots ,v_ j].  \] It is zero for $p>j$. Evaluation of a Hom coefficient on $e$ may replace the tensor in this formula. Expanding the two alternating boundaries gives 5E4EEAACF262 10.71.3 \begin{equation}  \partial (c\frown u)=(-1)^ p\bigl ((\partial c)\frown u -c\frown \delta u\bigr ). \end{equation} Indeed faces strictly before the shared vertex cancel against the coboundary sum, faces strictly after it give the boundary of the back face, and the two occurrences of the shared face have opposite signs. All coefficient transports coincide inside the original simplex. The same front/back subdivision gives 6F3FE0A6CE1E 10.71.4 \begin{equation}  \langle c\frown u,v\rangle =\langle c,u\smile v\rangle , \qquad (c\frown u)\frown v=c\frown (u\smile v). \end{equation} These are equalities of coefficients, not just cohomology classes. Cap is natural for maps with the indicated coefficient maps: $f_*(c\frown f^*u)=f_*c\frown u$. Theorem 10.71.5 . 9EC6A8A9270A For every local $R$-module system $A$ on $X$, cap product gives natural isomorphisms \[  D_{X,A}:H_ c^ q(X,A)\xrightarrow {\sim } H_{n-q}^{\mathrm{sing}}(X,\tau _ X\otimes A).  \] There is no torsion-free, finite-generation or orientability hypothesis. The maps commute with open extension and the induced homology maps, and with coefficient maps. On a compact oriented manifold this is cap with the integral fundamental class tensored with the coefficient ring. Proof. Use the supported singular comparison already proved. A cochain $u$ vanishing on $X\setminus K$ is capped with a representative $c$ of $[X]_ K$. Its cap is a cycle by equation 10.71.3 : $\partial c$ lies in the complement where $u$ vanishes. A change by a cochain boundary or by a relative chain boundary changes this cycle by a boundary, by the same identity. Chains in the complement cap to zero. Compatibility of $[X]_ K$ for increasing $K$ proves that this construction defines $D_{X,A}$ on the directed limit. Open excision and the carrier property prove naturality for open extension; no properness of an open inclusion is asserted. On a coordinate ball $\Omega \simeq \mathbb R^ n$, fix a point $x$. Closed Euclidean balls centered there are cofinal among compact subsets. The radial calculation gives $H_ j(\Omega ,\Omega \setminus K;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$ in degree $n$ and zero otherwise, for each such ball $K$ and also for $K=\{ x\} $. The relative homology maps to the point pair preserve the local generator and are isomorphisms. These relative chain complexes are free, being freely spanned by the simplices not lying in the complement. Thus corollary 10.68.9 , over $\mathbb Z$, gives relative cohomology with any constant coefficient module only in degree $n$, where it is that module, compatibly under these maps. The compact-support limit has the same groups. Represent the point-pair local generator by an embedded identity simplex with $x$ in its interior, and its boundary in $\Omega \setminus \{ x\} $. The boundary-sphere computation identifies it as a generator. The same universal coefficient map supplies a relative cocycle with any prescribed value on it. Capping gives that value at the last vertex, hence the corresponding $H_0$ class of $\Omega $. The orientation coefficient makes this independent of the sign used for the local generator. Therefore $D_\Omega $ is an isomorphism. This argument uses only pairs of open manifolds, and does not assume a singular/sheaf comparison on a disk boundary pair. We verify the connecting square required to glue balls. Suppose $X=U\cup V$, $K\subset U$ and $L\subset V$ are compact, and put $P=X\setminus K$, $Q=X\setminus L$. A relative $p$-cocycle $\phi $ vanishing on $P\cap Q$ can be written $\phi =\phi _ P-\phi _ Q$, with $\phi _ P$ vanishing on $P$ and $\phi _ Q$ on $Q$: choose its value simplex by simplex according to whether the simplex is in $P$, in $Q$, or in neither. Then $\delta \phi _ P=\delta \phi _ Q$ vanishes on chains in both $P$ and $Q$, and represents the cohomology Mayer–Vietoris boundary. Replace those complement chains by small chains where necessary; the preceding homotopies justify this replacement on the relative complex as well. Subdivide a representative of $[X]_{K\cup L}$ into $c=c_{U\setminus L}+c_{U\cap V}+c_{V\setminus K}$. These three opens cover $X$. The middle chain represents the class at $K\cap L$, and the sum of the first two represents the class at $K$, by local uniqueness and excision. In particular its boundary lies in $U\setminus K$; this follows also by subtracting the third chain, whose boundary is in $X\setminus K$, from $\partial c$. Cohomology boundary followed by cap gives $[c_{U\cap V}\frown \delta \phi _ P] =[\partial c_{U\cap V}\frown \phi _ P]$ by equation 10.71.3 . Cap followed by homology boundary, using the first summand as the $U$ part, gives \[  [\partial (c_{U\setminus L}\frown \phi )] =(-1)^ p[\partial c_{U\setminus L}\frown \phi _ P] =(-1)^{p+1}[\partial c_{U\cap V}\frown \phi _ P].  \] The omitted $\phi _ Q$ term is zero on $U\setminus L$, and the last equality uses the just established boundary in $U\setminus K$, where $\phi _ P$ is zero. Thus the connecting square commutes with exactly the unit sign $(-1)^{p+1}$. The other two squares follow from restriction and extension on representatives. Taking directed limits over $K,L$ gives the compact-support Mayer–Vietoris diagram. Every compact subset of $U\cup V$ is the union of compact subsets in the two opens, by a finite shrinking; intersections are cofinal for compact subsets of $U\cap V$. The five lemma, adjusting the stated sign, proves duality on a union when it holds on both opens and their intersection. Finite unions of convex balls in $\mathbb R^ n$ now follow by induction: intersection with the last ball is a union of fewer convex opens. Arbitrary Euclidean opens follow by their directed union of such finite unions. On both sides of duality this passage is valid because every compact support, singular cycle and bounding chain is contained in a finite subunion. The same argument for a finite collection of coordinate charts works because every finite intersection is an open subset of the first chart. The manifold is the directed union of finite chart unions. This proves the isomorphism everywhere, with arbitrary local coefficients and with the already defined natural maps. $\square$ Theorem 10.71.6 . 61D073B63D13 For every compact $K\subset X$ and every local system $A$, there is a natural isomorphism \[  D_ K:H^ q(K,A|_ K)\xrightarrow {\sim } H_{n-q}^{\mathrm{sing}}(X,X\setminus K;\tau _ X\otimes A).  \] For $K\subset L$ its restriction map corresponds to the quotient map of relative homology groups. title: Lemma 10.71.1
text: Lemma 10.71.1 . 603753CCA942 The groups $\tau _{X,x}=H_ n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X,X\setminus \{ x\} ; \mathbb Z)$ form a locally constant sheaf of infinite cyclic groups. A nonempty compact convex set $K\subset \mathbb R^ n$ has the same relative homology as a point in it. For an arbitrary compact $K$ in a chart, let a relative cycle $z$ have boundary disjoint from $K$. Choose finitely many small closed balls centered at points of $K$ whose interiors cover $K$ and whose union $L$ misses that boundary. Then $z$ is already a relative cycle for $L$. In degree $n$, if all its point values on $K$ vanish, its restriction to each chosen ball vanishes because it vanishes at that ball's center. title: Lemma 10.71.2
text: Lemma 10.71.2 . 3C7389B6FCBC The homological orientation system of a smooth manifold agrees with its usual determinant orientation. In particular a smooth coordinate change preserves a local homology generator exactly when its derivative has positive determinant. The group $\operatorname {GL}^+(r,\mathbb R)$ is path connected. Proof. Gram–Schmidt writes a positive-determinant matrix as an orthogonal determinant-one matrix times an upper triangular matrix with positive diagonal. Linear interpolation contracts the latter to the identity through such triangular matrices. For $r\ge 2$, successive plane rotations take the first column of the orthogonal factor to the first coordinate vector, and then act on its orthogonal complement. Induction gives a path to the identity. Rank one is the path of positive scalars; rank zero is immediate. A linear map of positive determinant is thus homotopic through invertible linear maps to the identity, and induces $+1$ on local homology. A reflection in one coordinate induces $-1$. Indeed, it exchanges the two hemispheres of the surrounding sphere and fixes their equator; in the reduced Mayer–Vietoris sequence, exchanging the two summands negates the connecting map. For the zero-sphere this is directly the exchange of its two points in reduced $H_0$. The radial local-homology identification gives the same sign for the reflection. Factoring a negative-determinant matrix as a reflection times a positive-determinant one proves the linear case. Finally let a smooth coordinate change fix the origin, with invertible derivative $T$ there. On a sufficiently small ball write $f(v)=Tv+e(v)$ with $|e(v)|\le \frac12\| T^{-1}\| ^{-1}|v|$. For $0<t\le 1$ set $f_ t(v)=t^{-1}f(tv)$ and set $f_0(v)=Tv$. The first-order remainder estimate makes this a continuous homotopy; the displayed bound makes $f_ t(v)$ nonzero for $v\ne 0$ throughout. It is therefore a homotopy of the punctured-ball pairs defining local homology. The local action of $f$ is the action of $T$, whose sign was just computed. Compatible positive smooth charts and compatible positive homological generators consequently specify the same orientation. $\square$

section: 10.72 The dualizing complex and cohomological duality
text: Proposition 10.72.1 . 9E818639205F Let $X$ be locally compact Hausdorff and paracompact, let $A$ be a sheaf of $R$-modules, and suppose $\operatorname {cd}X\le n$. Choose a soft resolution $A\to L^\bullet $ of length $n$ and an injective resolution $0\to M\to I^0\xrightarrow {\delta _ I}I^1\to 0$ over a PID. For $0\le p\le 1$ and $0\le q\le n$ put \[  F^{p,q}(U)=\operatorname {Hom}_ R(\Gamma _ c(U,L^{n-q}),I^ p), \qquad Df=\delta _ If+(-1)^ p f d_ L.  \] These presheaves are flabby sheaves, and their total complex has a natural short exact sequence \[  0\to \operatorname {Ext}(H_ c^{n-q+1}(X,A),M) \to H^ q(\Gamma (X,F^\bullet )) \to \operatorname {Hom}(H_ c^{n-q}(X,A),M)\to 0.  \] It splits noncanonically. The assertions hold on every open subset with the restricted resolution and compact supports there. Proof. We prove the section gluing premise. For a soft sheaf $L$ and two opens $U,V$, extension by zero gives the exact sequence \[  0\to \Gamma _ c(U\cap V,L)\to \Gamma _ c(U,L)\oplus \Gamma _ c(V,L) \to \Gamma _ c(U\cup V,L)\to 0.  \] Only surjectivity needs proof. Extend a compact section $s$ of the union by zero to $X$, and choose a relatively compact open $W$ containing its support. On the closed union $(X\setminus V)\cup (X\setminus U)\cup (X\setminus W)$ prescribe $s$ on the first set and zero on the latter two. These germ sections agree on the intersections, since $s$ is supported in $U\cup V$ and in $W$. Closed pasting and softness extend them to a global section $s_ U$. Its support is contained in $U\cap W$ and is compact; $s-s_ U$ has compact support in $V$. The kernel assertion follows because two opposite extended sections have support in the intersection. For a finite cover, induction gives the cosheaf coequalizer: if $\sum _{i=1}^ rs_ i=0$, the last term lies in the intersection of its open set with the union of the preceding ones. Decompose it there by the just proved finite-cover surjectivity and subtract the resulting pairwise-overlap relations; then apply induction to the first $r-1$ terms. For an arbitrary cover, a compact support has a finite subcover, and an element of the direct sum uses only finitely many terms. Thus \[  \bigoplus _{i,j}\Gamma _ c(U_ i\cap U_ j,L)\longrightarrow \bigoplus _ i\Gamma _ c(U_ i,L)\longrightarrow \Gamma _ c(U,L)\to 0  \] is a coequalizer. Applying $\operatorname {Hom}(-,I)$ gives exactly the sheaf equalizer axiom. Extension by zero from one open to a larger one is injective, so injectivity of $I$ makes restriction of this Hom sheaf onto. It is flabby. Restrictions of a globally soft sheaf to an open set are acyclic for compact supports. Indeed, for $V\Subset U$ the compact closed set $K=\overline V$ has soft restriction $L|_ K$. Extension by zero from the open subset $V$ of $K$ remains soft by proposition 10.56.6 . Its positive cohomology on the compact Hausdorff space $K$ vanishes. The actual compact-neighborhood limit of theorem 10.56.7 , applied to $U$, therefore gives $H_ c^ j(U,L|_ U)=0$ for $j>0$. This argument does not assume that an arbitrary open subset of a paracompact space is paracompact. Hence $\Gamma _ c(U,L^\bullet )$ computes $H_ c^\bullet (U,A)$ by theorem 10.56.3 . Reverse indices to form the homological complex $K_ q=\Gamma _ c(U,L^{n-q})$, with boundary $d_ L$. The displayed differential is precisely that in theorem 10.68.6 ; in particular its two mixed terms have opposite signs, so $D^2=0$. That theorem gives the natural exact sequence and its separately chosen splitting, without finite-type assumptions. All restriction maps are duals of open extension, as required. $\square$ Proposition 10.72.2 . 13DBDC23AA55 On an $n$-manifold and for a local system $A$ of stalk $L$, the preceding complex has cohomology sheaves \[  \mathcal H^0(F)=\tau _ X\otimes \mathcal Hom_ R(A,\underline M), \qquad \mathcal H^1(F)=\tau _ X\otimes \mathcal Ext_ R^1(A,\underline M), \qquad \mathcal H^ q(F)=0\quad (q\ne 0,1).  \] Here the second sheaf is the local system with fiber $\operatorname {Ext}_ R(L,M)$ and its contravariant coefficient transport. In particular \[  \tau _ X(U)=\operatorname {Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(H_ c^ n(U,\mathbb Z),\mathbb Z).  \] The orientation system is constant exactly when $X$ is orientable; a choice of its unit section is the choice of an orientation. If $\operatorname {Ext}_ R(L,M)=0$, the complex $F$ is a flabby resolution of $\tau _ X\otimes \mathcal Hom_ R(A,\underline M)$. Proof. Manifolds have sheaf dimension at most $n$ by the coordinate and local-dimension results used above, so the bounded soft resolution exists. On a ball trivializing $A$, compact cohomology is $L$ in degree $n$ and zero elsewhere. Its Hom sequence therefore gives $H^0(F(U))=\operatorname {Hom}(L,M)$ and $H^1(F(U))=\operatorname {Ext}(L,M)$, with all other groups zero. For nested coordinate balls these identifications are compatible: cap duality identifies the compact top-degree extension with the map on $H_0$ of the balls, carrying the chosen oriented coefficient to the same coefficient. It is an isomorphism. This proves the restriction assertion using open extension, without a deformation retraction onto a proper open subset. Filtered stalk limits are exact, so the preceding calculations compute the cohomology sheaves. Changing a local orientation multiplies them by its sign, and transporting $A$ composes a Hom or Ext class with the inverse coefficient transport. These are exactly the displayed local systems. For $A=M=\mathbb Z$ the Ext fiber vanishes and the degree-zero sheaf is the already constructed $\tau _ X$. Since the complex begins in degree zero, sections of its degree-zero cohomology sheaf are its global zero-cocycles. The preceding natural sequence in degree zero has no Ext term, because $H_ c^{n+1}(U,\mathbb Z)=0$. It gives the displayed identity on every open $U$. A constant unit section chooses compatible local generators, which is precisely orientability. If the Ext fiber is zero, stalkwise exactness makes the augmented complex a flabby resolution, proving the last assertion. $\square$ Theorem 10.72.3 . 3968AEF4C8FE Let $A$ have stalk $L$, let $M$ be a module over a PID, and assume $\operatorname {Ext}_ R(L,M)=0$. There is a natural short exact sequence \[  0\to \operatorname {Ext}(H_ c^{n-q+1}(X,A),M) \to H^ q(X,\tau _ X\otimes \mathcal Hom_ R(A,\underline M)) \xrightarrow {\rho }\operatorname {Hom}(H_ c^{n-q}(X,A),M)\to 0.  \] It splits as modules, without a natural splitting. With cap normalization, $\rho $ is evaluation after the isomorphism $D_{X,A}$. For an oriented connected $X$ this is the compact-first cup product and orientation trace, followed by the coefficient evaluation. If $A=\underline R$ and $M=R$, the twist disappears when $X$ is oriented or when $R$ has characteristic two. Proof. The preceding two propositions already construct such a sequence from a bounded soft resolution. To specify its product normalization and give a second explicit description, set $C_ j=C_ j^{\mathrm{sing}}(X,\tau _ X\otimes A)$. It is a direct sum of modules isomorphic to $L$; the choices of fiber identifications need not be canonical. Taking direct sums of length-one free resolutions and then Hom shows $\operatorname {Ext}(\bigoplus L,M)=\prod \operatorname {Ext}(L,M)=0$. Products are exact, so the augmentation \[  \operatorname {Hom}(C_\bullet ,M)\longrightarrow \operatorname {Tot}\operatorname {Hom}(C_\bullet ,I^\bullet )  \] is a quasi-isomorphism: in each chain degree its coefficient Hom complex has only degree-zero cohomology. This is an actual two-row first-quadrant comparison, not an assumed ordinary Hom exactness. The left complex is canonically the singular cochain complex of $\tau _ X\otimes \mathcal Hom_ R(A,\underline M)$. At a simplex this identifies $\operatorname {Hom}(\tau _ x\otimes A_ x,M)$ with $\tau _ x\otimes \operatorname {Hom}(A_ x,M)$ using $\tau _ x^2=\mathbb Z$; precomposing the chain boundary gives precisely the previously specified transported cochain differential. Apply singular/sheaf comparison, the natural derived Hom sequence of theorem 10.68.6 , and the actual isomorphisms $H_ q(C)=H_ c^{n-q}(X,A)$ supplied by cap duality. This yields the stated sequence with $\rho $ as asserted. Its splitting is the module splitting in that algebraic theorem. Finally equation 10.71.4 identifies evaluation on $D_{X,A}(u)$ with evaluation of the coefficient-contracted cup product $u\smile v$ on the compact fundamental class. This is the orientation trace proved explicitly below. The local coefficient contraction is $A\otimes \mathcal Hom(A,M)\to M$; the two orientation factors cancel. Thus the indicated cup convention gives the stated map. The twist is trivial under the final hypotheses because its transition scalars are $\pm 1$. $\square$ Corollary 10.72.4 . 9C9125F4F2EE For any local system $A$ on a connected manifold, \[  H_ c^ n(X,A)=H_0(X,\tau _ X\otimes A)  \] is the module of coinvariants of the transported fiber $\tau _ x\otimes A_ x$. In particular, for any constant module $L$, \[  H_ c^ n(X,\tau _ X\otimes \underline L)\simeq L, \qquad H_ c^ n(X,\underline L)\simeq L/2L \quad \hbox{if $X$ is nonorientable}.  \] For an oriented connected $X$, the first identity gives the trace $\operatorname {tr}_ X:H_ c^ n(X,\underline L)\to L$. On a disconnected manifold compact top cohomology is the direct sum of its component groups; trace is the sum of the finitely many nonzero component traces. Ordinary cohomology is a product over components. Proof. Cap duality in degree $n$ gives the first equality. In singular $H_0$, the boundary of an edge identifies a coefficient at its first vertex with its transport to the last. Choose paths from a basepoint to all vertices: these relations identify every class with one in the base fiber, and the remaining relations are exactly $\rho (\gamma )a-a$ for based loops. Conversely transport to the coinvariant module kills every edge boundary, proving the asserted presentation. For $\tau \otimes L$, the additional orientation twist squares to the trivial system, so the coinvariants are $L$. For constant $L$ on a nonorientable connected manifold, the orientation character has image $\{ 1,-1\} $, giving precisely the quotient by $2L$. The identification for $\tau \otimes L$ is canonical without an orientation choice. An orientation trivializes $\tau $ in the untwisted case and defines the trace. On a ball it sends the positive compact generator with coefficient $l$ to $l$, and open extension preserves it by cap naturality. Components of a manifold are open. A compact support meets only finitely many of them, whereas an unrestricted section can be chosen on every component. The Godement complexes are consequently the direct sum and the product, respectively, of the component complexes. Both operations are exact for module families, proving the final assertions and the sum trace. $\square$ Proposition 10.72.5 . B7AF8FB473E5 For oriented $X$ and any modules $L,M$, with no Ext hypothesis, \[  H_ c^{n-q}(X,\underline L)\times H^ q(X,\underline M) \longrightarrow L\otimes M, \qquad (u,v)\longmapsto \operatorname {tr}_ X(u\smile v)  \] is a natural bilinear pairing. When the cohomological duality hypothesis $\operatorname {Ext}(L,L\otimes M)=0$ holds, it is its map induced by $M\to \operatorname {Hom}(L,L\otimes M)$ in cap normalization. Reversing the order of the factors multiplies the pairing by $(-1)^{q(n-q)}$ with the corresponding tensor flip. Proof. The supported cup theorem constructs the product with the indicated coefficient and support, and the preceding trace contracts it. The cap evaluation identity proves the comparison under the stated Ext hypothesis. Graded commutativity in theorem 10.58.3 gives the final sign. Thus the pairing exists even when the Ext hypothesis needed for a short exact duality sequence does not hold. One can also check the signs directly in the bounded dualizing resolution. This records a normalization that an unsigned comparison would leave ambiguous. Assume first $X$ connected and take $L=R$. Let $B^\bullet =C_ X^\bullet \underline M$ and $L^ j=C_ X^ j\underline R$ for $j<n$, with $L^ n$ the kernel of its next differential. Embed $E=\Gamma _ c(X,B^ n)/d\Gamma _ c(X,B^{n-1})$ in an injective $I^0$. Its cycle submodule is $H_ c^ n(X,M)=M$ by trace. Hence the induced map $d:E\to \Gamma _ c(X,B^{n+1})$ identifies $E/M$ with its image. The module $I^1=I^0/M$ is injective over a PID, since it is divisible. Extend the inclusion $E/M\to I^1$ from this image to a map $\pi :\Gamma _ c(X,B^{n+1})\to I^1$ by injectivity. Set $\varepsilon _ q=(-1)^{q(q+1)/2}$. A cochain $f\in B^ q(U)$ maps to the following pair of functionals in $F^ q(U)$: \[  f\longmapsto \left( g\longmapsto \varepsilon _ q[f\smile g],\quad h\longmapsto (-1)^ q\varepsilon _ q\pi (f\smile h)\right),  \] where $g\in \Gamma _ c(U,L^{n-q})$ and $h\in \Gamma _ c(U,L^{n-q+1})$; a term outside the bounded resolution is zero. All products extend compactly to $X$ before taking the quotient. Truncate $B$ at its degree-$n$ cycles as well. The first-component chain identity follows from $[df\smile g]=(-1)^{q+1}[f\smile dg]$ in the quotient $E$ and $\varepsilon _{q+1}=(-1)^{q+1}\varepsilon _ q$. For the second component, the relation $\delta _ I[f\smile h]=\pi (d(f\smile h))$ and Leibniz give \[  \varepsilon _ q\pi (df\smile h) +\bigl ((-1)^ q\varepsilon _ q-(-1)^ q\varepsilon _ q\bigr ) \pi (f\smile dh).  \] This is the required second component in the next degree because $(-1)^{q+1}\varepsilon _{q+1}=\varepsilon _ q$. Thus this is an actual morphism of differential sheaves for the specified $D$. In degree zero it induces the identity on $M$ by the chosen trace, so it is the identity-augmenting resolution comparison. Its edge functional is $\varepsilon _ q\operatorname {tr}_ X(f\smile g)$, or $\varepsilon _ q(-1)^{q(n-q)}\operatorname {tr}_ X(g\smile f)$. This explains explicitly the unit signs relating that dualizing complex convention to the compact-first cap normalization; changing a convention does not change the short exact sequence or its nonnatural splitting. Componentwise construction gives the same conclusion without connectedness. $\square$

text: Here $\Theta _ q$ denotes the multiplicative augmentation comparison from constant-sheaf cohomology to differential forms. With the positive connecting comparison $\Psi _ q$ one has $\Theta _ q^{-1}=(-1)^{q(q+1)/2}\Psi _ q$, as proved in theorem 10.58.9 . Thus on a compact curve $C$, for the frame-exponential class of a line bundle, $\deg L=-\operatorname {tr}_{\rm cap,C}(c_1^{\mathbb Z}(L))$. The curve loop-current map $[I_\gamma ]\mapsto \Psi _1[I_\gamma ]$ is likewise the negative of cap Poincaré duality after real coefficients. The integral lattice sets are unchanged by this sign; the individual comparison maps differ. Theorem 10.73.1 . 7ECFE434A83A On an oriented smooth $n$-manifold the trace of a compact top-degree real de Rham class is its integral, using the multiplicative augmentation comparison of corollary 10.58.11 . Consequently the pairing \[  H_ c^{n-q}(X,\mathbb R)\times H^ q(X,\mathbb R)\longrightarrow \mathbb R, \qquad ([\alpha ],[\beta ])\longmapsto \int _ X\alpha \wedge \beta  \] identifies $H^ q(X,\mathbb R)$ with the full algebraic dual of $H_ c^{n-q}(X,\mathbb R)$. No finite-dimensionality or closed-range hypothesis is needed for this assertion. Proof. We fix the local sign explicitly. On the oriented real line use $U_ k=(k-1,k+1)$ and only finite-index-support alternating Čech cochains. Every nonempty intersection is contractible. In the finite-support Godement double complex of theorem 10.56.9 , the vertical augmented columns are therefore exact as well. Thus this fixed cover computes compact cohomology. The integral sorting homotopy of proposition 10.44.14 preserves finite support here: any additional index must meet the compact closure of an active cover member, and local finiteness leaves only finitely many such indices. The complex in degrees zero and one is \[  \bigoplus _{k\in \mathbb Z}\mathbb Z \xrightarrow {(a_ k)\mapsto (a_{k+1}-a_ k)} \bigoplus _{k\in \mathbb Z}\mathbb Z.  \] Its kernel is zero and its image is precisely the sequences of sum zero. For the converse assertion, finite partial sums of a sequence of sum zero give a finitely supported primitive. Thus the single edge cochain $c_{01}=1$ is a generator. With unrestricted products the difference map would be onto and would not compute compact cohomology. This is the positive generator in the cap convention. To verify it, let $f$ be the zero-cochain that is zero on the left of a point in $(0,1)$ and one on its right. Its singular coboundary vanishes on simplices avoiding that point and evaluates to $1$ on an increasing crossing interval. Hence its cap trace is $1$. On each $U_ k$ subtract from $f$ the constant $0$ for $k\le 0$ and $1$ for $k\ge 1$. These local primitives have only two possibly nonzero members. Their Čech difference is $-c$, and in the total complex $D=\delta _{\check C}+(-1)^ a\delta _{\rm sing}$ their differential is $-c+\delta _{\rm sing}f$. Thus the supported comparison identifies $c$ with that positive singular class. For a smooth subordinate partition $(\psi _ k)$, the partition formula of proposition 10.58.13 sends this class in the multiplicative augmentation convention to \[  -\psi _1\, d\psi _0+\psi _0\, d\psi _1=-d\psi _0 \quad \hbox{on }(0,1),  \] and to zero elsewhere. Its integral is $1$, since $\psi _0$ goes from $1$ to $0$ across this overlap. The opposite partition convention in that result differs in degree one by a minus sign; it is not silently substituted here. On an oriented coordinate cube the external product of these $n$ positive interval classes has trace $1$. One can check the normalization without a product homology theorem: triangulate the cube by the $n!$ orders of its coordinate increments, assigning each simplex the sign of its order. Internal faces cancel and its relative class is the oriented cube class. Evaluation of the front/back product of the coordinate step coboundaries is zero on every order except the increasing order, where it is $1$. This gives trace $1$. The multiplicative de Rham comparison sends it to the product compact form of integral $1$. The compact top cohomology of the coordinate ball is one-dimensional, so integration and trace agree there. In dimension zero they both evaluate a coefficient at the positively oriented point. Integration annihilates compact top-degree boundaries by Stokes' formula and homotopy conventions , Stokes' formula on compact domains with corners . A compact top form on $X$ is a finite sum of forms supported in oriented coordinate balls, by a subordinate smooth partition of unity. Each summand is closed by degree. The multiplicative comparison and the trace calculation identify it with the compact-first cup pairing. It gives exactly the full algebraic dual, for arbitrary dimension of the groups. On disconnected spaces the dual of the compact direct sum is the ordinary product, as required. $\square$

Lemma 10.74.1 . 53C4601E9CF2 For any path connected space with basepoint $a$, loops as singular cycles induce an isomorphism $\pi _1(X,a)^{m ab}\simeq H_1^{\mathrm{sing}}(X,\mathbb Z)$. On a smooth manifold every such class has a piecewise smooth loop representative. For a closed smooth one-form $\alpha $, its singular cohomology evaluation on that class is $\int _\gamma \alpha $ under the proved sheaf/de Rham comparisons. Proof. A constant path is the boundary of its constant two-simplex. A homotopy of paths, subdivided into two triangles per prism, shows that homotopic paths have the same homology class; constant end edges contribute boundaries. The singular two-simplex obtained by collapsing a triangle onto the concatenated path has boundary $g-(f*g)+f$. Consequently concatenation is addition in homology, and path reversal is negation. This gives the homomorphism from the abelianized fundamental group. Choose a path $\eta _ x$ from $a$ to each point $x$, with $\eta _ a$ constant. Send a one-cycle $z=\sum n_\sigma \sigma $ to \[  \sum n_\sigma [\eta _{\sigma (v_0)}*\sigma * \eta _{\sigma (v_1)}^{-1}] \quad \hbox{in }\pi _1(X,a)^{m ab}.  \] The boundary of a two-simplex maps to zero: its three based edge loops combine to the boundary loop of that simplex, conjugated by the path to its initial vertex, and that loop contracts in the simplex. Thus this map descends to $H_1$. On a based loop it is the identity. In the other direction the added paths cancel in a cycle, because the coefficient of every endpoint in $\partial z$ is zero. The concatenation identity then gives back $[z]$. This proves both inverse identities without invoking a higher Hurewicz theorem. A continuous path on a smooth manifold can be subdivided into finitely many arcs lying in coordinate balls. Replace each arc by the coordinate line segment between its endpoints. Coordinate straight-line homotopy stays inside the ball, and the pieces agree at the fixed endpoints. This proves the piecewise smooth assertion. For the last assertion, choose local primitives of $\alpha $ on coordinate balls, using the local de Rham homotopy. For any continuous path define its period as the sum of the changes of these primitives on a subordinate subdivision. On the connected overlap used by an arc, changing a primitive adds a constant and does not change that sum; refinement also leaves it unchanged. A subdivided parameter square proves homotopy invariance by cancellation of interior edges, so this defines a singular one-cocycle. On each ball it is the coboundary of the same primitive whose differential is $\alpha $. The natural Čech comparison of these primitives therefore identifies this cocycle with the de Rham class, with the same positive differential. For a piecewise smooth path the fundamental theorem of calculus identifies the sum with its usual integral. $\square$ Lemma 10.74.2 . 67B6FD6C1574 An oriented smooth embedded circle in an oriented smooth manifold has a trivial oriented normal bundle and an open tubular neighborhood diffeomorphic to $S^1	imes \mathbb R^{m-1}$. One may choose either the tangent-first or the normal-first orientation convention, but must keep that choice when specifying its transverse generator. Proof. First, an oriented rank-$r$ bundle on a circle is trivial. Cut the circle inside a trivializing arc. On the resulting interval extend a frame successively through finitely many trivializing intervals: on an overlap express it in the next frame and extend that transition matrix by freezing its parameter before the overlap ends. This gives a frame on the interval, with a transition in $\operatorname {GL}^+(r, \mathbb R)$ at the cut. This group is path connected by lemma 10.71.2 . A path, made constant near its endpoints by a smooth reparameterization, corrects the transition. Using the given frame on the short arc at the cut ensures agreement on neighborhoods of both endpoints, not merely at the endpoints. The corrected frame consequently descends smoothly to the circle. For rank zero the assertion is immediate. Here is an explicit neighborhood construction. Choose an inner product on $TX$ along the circle by a finite partition of unity, and identify the normal bundle with its orthogonal complement to the tangent. Choose finitely many coordinate charts $\phi _ i$ near the circle and a smooth partition $(\psi _ i)$ on the circle with compact support in those charts. For a small normal vector $v$ at $p$, start at $x_0=p$ and successively set \[  x_ i=\phi _ i^{-1} igl (\phi _ i(x_{i-1})+ \psi _ i(p)(d\phi _ i)_ p v igr )  \] where $\psi _ i(p)$ is supported, and use $x_ i=x_{i-1}$ elsewhere. The supports have compact buffers inside their charts, so for uniformly small $v$ all these expressions are defined. They extend smoothly across the zero parts of $\psi _ i$. The resulting map $F(p,v)=x_ N$ satisfies $F(p,0)=p$ and has vertical derivative $\sum _ i\psi _ i(p)v=v$. Its differential on the zero section is therefore the isomorphism $T_ pS^1\oplus N_ p	o T_ pX$. Here the required inverse-function assertion follows directly in coordinates. Normalize a smooth map $f$ by $f(0)=0$, $df_0=1$, and choose a closed ball of radius $a$ with $\| df-1\| \le 1/2$. For $|y|<a/2$, the map $z\mapsto z-f(z)+y$ maps this ball into itself and contracts distances by at most $1/2$. Its successive iterates are Cauchy, with a geometric bound on the tails, and have a unique fixed point $z(y)$. The same estimate gives $|z(y)-z(y')|\le 2|y-y'|$. Differentiating the difference identity $f(z(y'))-f(z(y))=y'-y$ by the first-order remainder estimate gives $dz_ y=(df_{z(y)})^{-1}$. These matrices are invertible by the convergent geometric series for $1-df$; matrix inversion is smooth, so induction on derivatives makes $z$ smooth. The estimate also makes $f$ injective on the ball. This proves the local smooth inverse needed here, and makes $F$ a local diffeomorphism near the zero section. Compactness supplies a uniform disk radius on which that differential is invertible. It also supplies global injectivity after shrinking: otherwise two distinct points of disk bundles of radii tending to zero would have the same image. Subsequence limits of their basepoints would coincide on the circle, so both points would eventually lie in one inverse-function neighborhood of the same zero vector, a contradiction. Thus $F$ is a diffeomorphism of a small open disk bundle onto an open neighborhood. Use the frame already constructed and the orientation-preserving radial diffeomorphism between an open disk and $\mathbb R^ r$ to obtain the stated tube. It is not a covariant-to-contravariant naturality assertion for arbitrary continuous maps. With the current convention $T_\eta (\alpha )=\int _ X\eta \wedge \alpha $, the real image of $\operatorname {PD}_ X[\gamma ]$ is the de Rham class of the integration current $I_\gamma (\alpha )=\int _\gamma \alpha $. If $\gamma $ is embedded, choose its tube $\phi :S^1	imes \mathbb R^{m-1}\xrightarrow {\sim }V$ and let $j:V\hookrightarrow X$. If this chart uses tangent followed by normal orientation, its integral class is \[  (-1)^{m-1}\, j_!(\phi ^{-1})^*(1	imes 
u ), \qquad 
u \in H_ c^{m-1}(\mathbb R^{m-1},\mathbb Z), \quad \operatorname {tr}(
u )=1.  \] If the normal bundle is oriented before the tangent, the same formula has no extra sign. Cap duality on the compact manifold gives the isomorphism in all degrees; take degree $m-1$. The preceding degree-one lemma identifies its domain with abelianized loops on each component. There are only finitely many components by compactness. Orientation-preserving change of variables carries the compact fundamental class to the one on the target, and the chain cap naturality formula gives the stated diffeomorphism identity. This proves the integral assertion before any passage to real coefficients. A piecewise smooth loop defines a closed degree-$(m-1)$ current: testing its differential on a zero-form gives the sum of the endpoint differences on its arcs, which is zero. The current comparison in corollary 10.43.11 , corollary 10.57.1 provides a smooth de Rham representative $\eta $ of its class. If $\alpha $ is any closed smooth one-form, the exact-current difference pairs to zero with $\alpha $ by the current differential and Stokes. Hence $\int \eta \wedge \alpha =I_\gamma (\alpha )$. On the other hand, cap evaluation and the just proved degree-one period comparison give \[  \int _ X\operatorname {PD}_ X[\gamma ]_{\mathbb R}\wedge \alpha =\langle [\gamma ],[\alpha ]angle =\int _\gamma \alpha .  \] The de Rham duality theorem proved above separates the compact $(m-1)$-classes: every nonzero vector has a nonzero algebraic dual functional, and all those functionals are represented by $H^1$. Thus the two real cohomology classes agree. This argument applies to every homology class using piecewise smooth representatives and requires no embedded-loop generation theorem. For an embedded loop use its framed tube and the preceding external Künneth theorem. The class $1	imes 
u $ generates $H_ c^{m-1}(S^1	imes \mathbb R^{m-1},\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$. Its cap on the tangent-first oriented product equals $(-1)^{m-1}[S^1]$. The trace calculation proves that this is the value of cap evaluation. The tube retracts onto the circle, whose $H_1=\mathbb Z$ was computed by the sphere sequence. Thus that value determines its integral class. Open naturality of cap and the tube diffeomorphism therefore give exactly the displayed integral Thom formula, even when its image in global homology is torsion. Reversing the order used to orient the normal changes the transverse generator by $(-1)^{m-1}$ and removes the extra sign. The transverse real class can equally be represented by the Dirac current at zero. Indeed compact top-degree current cohomology agrees with the compact de Rham group. Evaluation of a compact top current on the constant function one, defined with a cutoff equal to one near its support, vanishes on boundaries and agrees with integration on forms. The Dirac current has this value one, so is the image of $
u $. With the indicated orientation and sign its product along the circle acts on a one-form by evaluation at the zero normal coordinate followed by integration on the circle. Its image is precisely $I_\gamma $. The cap proof, not this real description, establishes well-definedness of the integral class under all choices. For $m=0$ both groups in the first display are zero; for $m=1$ the normal rank is zero and the same formulas have sign one. $\square$

Thus that value determines its integral class. Open naturality of cap and the tube diffeomorphism therefore give exactly the displayed integral Thom formula, even when its image in global homology is torsion. Reversing the order used to orient the normal changes the transverse generator by $(-1)^{m-1}$ and removes the extra sign. The transverse real class can equally be represented by the Dirac current at zero. Indeed compact top-degree current cohomology agrees with the compact de Rham group. Evaluation of a compact top current on the constant function one, defined with a cutoff equal to one near its support, vanishes on boundaries and agrees with integration on forms. The Dirac current has this value one, so is the image of $
u $. With the indicated orientation and sign its product along the circle acts on a one-form by evaluation at the zero normal coordinate followed by integration on the circle. Its image is precisely $I_\gamma $. The cap proof, not this real description, establishes well-definedness of the integral class under all choices. For $m=0$ both groups in the first display are zero; for $m=1$ the normal rank is zero and the same formulas have sign one. $\square$
