title: 10.80 Projectivity and integral periods
text: Integral classes mean the image of constant-sheaf integer cohomology under the fixed real de Rham comparison. In particular no singular cohomology identification or integral Poincaré duality is implicit. Hermitian forms are linear in the first argument. A complex torus is called an abelian variety here when it is projective. Corollary 10.80.1 . 167D644EB419 A compact Kähler manifold $X$ with $H^2(X,\mathcal O_ X)=0$ is projective. Proof. Work on a connected component. The zero-dimensional case is a point. In positive dimension, the sheaf/Dolbeault comparison and the Kähler Hodge decomposition give $H^{0,2}=H^{2,0}=0$. Hence all real degree-two cohomology is of type $(1,1)$. By theorem 10.64.3 , it has a finite real basis of integral-image classes. Let $\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ b$ be their real harmonic representatives for a fixed Kähler form $\omega $. They are of type $(1,1)$ by theorem 10.47.13 . The form $\omega $ itself is harmonic: its Hodge star is a constant multiple of $\omega ^{n-1}$ and is closed. Thus equality of harmonic representatives gives \[  \omega =\sum _{j=1}^ b\lambda _ j\alpha _ j,\qquad \lambda _ j\in \mathbb R.  \] If $b=0$ this contradicts positive definiteness, so that case cannot occur in positive dimension. Let $C_ j$ bound the operator norm of $\alpha _ j$ relative to $\omega $; these constants are finite by compactness. Choose rational $\mu _ j$ with $\sum _ jC_ j|\mu _ j-\lambda _ j|<1/2$. Then \[  \omega '=\sum _ j\mu _ j\alpha _ j\geq \tfrac 12\omega >0.  \] It is a closed real $(1,1)$-form. A common positive integer denominator $m$ makes $[m\omega ']$ integral. The already proved theorem 10.40.10 gives projectivity. A compact manifold has finitely many components, so these conclusions combine, including any point components. $\square$ Theorem 10.80.2 . 826013CCAFEC Let $T=V/\Gamma $ be a complex torus, with $\dim _{\mathbb C}V=n$. It is projective if and only if $V$ has a positive definite Hermitian form $h$ such that \[  \operatorname {Im}h(\gamma ,\delta )\in \mathbb Z \qquad (\gamma ,\delta \in \Gamma ).  \] For such a form the associated Kähler form is $\omega =-\operatorname {Im}h$ on the underlying real vector space. For every ordered real lattice basis $a_1,\ldots ,a_{2n}$ one has \[  \int _{T_{jk}}\omega =\omega (a_ j,a_ k) =-\operatorname {Im}h(a_ j,a_ k),\qquad 1\leq j<k\leq 2n,  \] where $T_{jk}$ is the oriented lattice parallelogram torus. Proof. Let $J$ be multiplication by $\mathrm i$ on $V$. For a Hermitian $h$ linear in its first argument, $\omega =-\operatorname {Im}h$ is alternating, $J$-invariant and satisfies $\omega (v,Jv)=h(v,v)>0$ for nonzero $v$. It is constant, hence closed, and descends to a Kähler form. The displayed parallelogram formula follows by pulling back to $(s,t)\mapsto sa_ j+ta_ k$. The exact integral two-period criterion theorem 10.65.1 makes its class integral. Then theorem 10.40.10 proves projectivity. Conversely projectivity supplies an integral Kähler form. By proposition 10.65.2 , its average is a constant positive real $(1,1)$-form $\omega $ in the same integral class. Set \[  h(v,w)=\omega (v,Jw)-\mathrm i\omega (v,w).  \] $J$-invariance and alternation make its real part symmetric and its imaginary part skew. Directly $h(Jv,w)=\mathrm i h(v,w)$ and $h(v,Jw)=-\mathrm i h(v,w)$, so it is Hermitian with the specified convention; $h(v,v)=\omega (v,Jv)>0$. The same two-period theorem gives the required integral imaginary parts, with the minus sign displayed above. All $2n$ real lattice circles are used. For $n=0$ the torus is a point and all conditions are vacuous and true. $\square$ Lemma 10.80.3 . 5A4C95A96C6B Let $X\subset \mathbb P^ N$ be a connected compact complex submanifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, and let $\omega $ be the restricted normalized Fubini–Study form. For real closed one-forms $\gamma ,\delta $ whose classes are integral, \[  \int _ X\gamma \wedge \delta \wedge \omega ^{n-1}\in \mathbb Z.  \] This is an integral trace assertion for the displayed classes and chosen polarization; it does not presume an arbitrary integral Poincaré pairing. Proof. We first construct smooth successive hyperplane sections. If a compact complex submanifold $Y\subset \mathbb P^ N$ has dimension $d\geq 1$, the ambient linear forms generate every first jet of $L=\mathcal O(1)|_ Y$. In an affine chart one section has coefficient one and the others are the restricted affine coordinates. Their differentials span $T_ y^*Y$ because the inclusion has injective differential. Thus first-jet evaluation from the parameter space $\mathbb C^{N+1}$ is onto at every $y$. The incidence of pairs $(y,c)$ for which the corresponding section has zero first jet is a holomorphic kernel bundle over $Y$, of rank $N-d$. Indeed an invertible $(d+1)$-minor of the jet evaluation solves for that many parameters holomorphically. Its total complex dimension is $N$, smaller than the parameter dimension $N+1$. Its parameter image has measure zero: on each compact coordinate box the projection is Lipschitz, and subdividing a real $a$-dimensional box into cubes of side $r$ bounds its image volume in dimension $b>a$ by $O(r^{b-a})$. Countably many such boxes cover the incidence. Choose a parameter outside this null image. Its section is nonzero on every component and its zero set is a smooth compact complex hypersurface, possibly empty, by the local holomorphic inverse function theorem. This proves the required generic section statement without a transversality theorem as an extra input. Repeat until a smooth compact curve $C$ is reached, allowing an empty set at any stage. The single-section Poincaré–Lelong identity the line-bundle Poincaré–Lelong formula , applied at each smooth stage, gives \[  \int _ X\gamma \wedge \delta \wedge \omega ^{n-1} =\int _ C\gamma |_ C\wedge \delta |_ C.  \] At a stage of dimension $d$, pair $[Z]-\omega $ with the closed smooth form $\gamma \wedge \delta \wedge \omega ^{d-2}$; its integral is zero because $[Z]-\omega $ is an exact current and the stage is compact. Only a single integration current is paired with a smooth form at each step; no product of arbitrary currents is taken. For $n=1$ there is no cutting and $C=X$. Restrictions of the two classes to each component of $C$ are integral by naturality. We retain the precise comparison sign: the positive connecting convention obeys \[  \Psi _2([\alpha \wedge \beta ]) =-\Psi _1[\alpha ]\smile \Psi _1[\beta ]  \] in degree one, by theorem 10.58.9 . Hence the class of the displayed wedge on $C$ is the positive real image of the negative of an integral cup class. The proved lemma 10.79.7 identifies $H^2(C_0,\underline{\mathbb Z})$ on each connected component $C_0$ with $\mathbb Z$, its positive point-divisor generator having integral one. The integral is therefore an integer. Sum over the finitely many components; an empty $C$ contributes zero. $\square$ Theorem 10.80.4 . 183B8F4BFE57 For a connected projective manifold $X$, its complex tori $J(X)=\operatorname {Pic}^0(X)$ and $A(X)=\operatorname {Alb}(X)$ are abelian varieties. In particular the Jacobian of every connected compact Riemann surface is an abelian variety. Proof. The zero-dimensional case is a point. Otherwise choose a projective embedding and put $\omega =c_1(\mathcal O(1)|_ X)$ with the induced metric, so the preceding integral trace lemma applies. Write \[  W=H^{0,1}(X),\quad V=H^{1,0}(X)=H^0(X,\Omega _ X^1),\quad \Lambda =\operatorname {pr}^{0,1}H^1(X,\underline{\mathbb Z}).  \] Use harmonic representatives for $\omega $. The exact period theorem 10.79.4 , theorem 10.79.5 identify $J(X)=W/\Lambda $ and $A(X)=V^*/\Gamma $, with both lattices full. Here $\Gamma $ consists of loop-period functionals. If $W=0$ both tori are points, so suppose its dimension is positive. Define the linear-first Hermitian form \[  h(u,v)=-2\mathrm i\int _ Xu\wedge \bar v\wedge \omega ^{n-1} \qquad (u,v\in W).  \] Conjugating and interchanging the two one-forms proves Hermitian symmetry. In a coframe with $\omega =\mathrm i\sum _ j\theta _ j\wedge \bar\theta _ j$ and $u=\sum _ ju_ j\bar\theta _ j$, direct expansion gives \[  -2\mathrm i\, u\wedge \bar u\wedge \omega ^{n-1} =\frac2n\sum _ j|u_ j|^2\omega ^ n.  \] Consequently $h$ is positive definite. The norm identity is asserted only for $v=u$. For integral real harmonic one-forms $\gamma ,\delta $, write $\gamma =\gamma ^{1,0}+\gamma ^{0,1}$ and similarly for $\delta $. Their pure $(2,0)$ and $(0,2)$ wedges vanish against $\omega ^{n-1}$. Taking real parts of $\int \gamma ^{0,1}\wedge \delta ^{1,0}\wedge \omega ^{n-1}$ gives \[  \operatorname {Im}h(\gamma ^{0,1},\delta ^{0,1}) =-\int _ X\gamma \wedge \delta \wedge \omega ^{n-1}\in \mathbb Z.  \] The preceding lemma supplies the actual integer trace. Thus theorem 10.80.2 proves that $J(X)$ is projective. For the Albanese torus consider the complex-linear map \[  B:W\longrightarrow V^*,\qquad B(u)(v)=\int _ Xu\wedge v\wedge \omega ^{n-1}.  \] It is an isomorphism: $B(u)=0$ implies $h(u,u)=0$, so $u=0$, and Kähler Hodge conjugation gives equal dimensions. For an integral real class $\gamma $, the integer trace lemma makes \[  a_\gamma :\  H^1(X,\underline{\mathbb Z})\longrightarrow \mathbb Z, \qquad \delta \longmapsto \int _ X\gamma \wedge \delta \wedge \omega ^{n-1}  \] an integer homomorphism. By the actual degree-one evaluation theorem 10.79.2 , it is evaluation by a loop class modulo its torsion. Extend this equality real-linearly and then complex-linearly to de Rham cohomology. On $v\in V$ its value is $B(\gamma ^{0,1})(v)$, because the other Hodge component has out-of-range bidegree. Hence $B\Lambda \subset \Gamma $. This uses the proved character/evaluation lattice, not an identification with all integer degree-$(2n-1)$ cohomology. Both lattices are full and $B$ is an isomorphism, so this inclusion has finite index. Explicitly, in a basis of $\Gamma $, a basis of $B\Lambda $ is a nonsingular integer matrix; its determinant and adjugate give an integer $m\geq 1$ with $m\Gamma \subset B\Lambda $. Every compact curve is projective by corollary 10.41.3 ; its Jacobian is $J(X)$, also identified with $A(X)$ by the already proved theorem 10.79.13 . This proves the last assertion. For a disconnected compact projective manifold, the Picard torus is the finite product of the component Picard tori; the direct sum of their integral positive forms proves it projective as well. The Albanese assertion is applied to each connected component with its chosen base point. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.80.1
text: Corollary 10.80.1 . 167D644EB419 A compact Kähler manifold $X$ with $H^2(X,\mathcal O_ X)=0$ is projective. Proof. Work on a connected component. The zero-dimensional case is a point. In positive dimension, the sheaf/Dolbeault comparison and the Kähler Hodge decomposition give $H^{0,2}=H^{2,0}=0$. Hence all real degree-two cohomology is of type $(1,1)$. By theorem 10.64.3 , it has a finite real basis of integral-image classes. Let $\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ b$ be their real harmonic representatives for a fixed Kähler form $\omega $. They are of type $(1,1)$ by theorem 10.47.13 . The form $\omega $ itself is harmonic: its Hodge star is a constant multiple of $\omega ^{n-1}$ and is closed. Thus equality of harmonic representatives gives \[  \omega =\sum _{j=1}^ b\lambda _ j\alpha _ j,\qquad \lambda _ j\in \mathbb R.  \] If $b=0$ this contradicts positive definiteness, so that case cannot occur in positive dimension. Let $C_ j$ bound the operator norm of $\alpha _ j$ relative to $\omega $; these constants are finite by compactness. Choose rational $\mu _ j$ with $\sum _ jC_ j|\mu _ j-\lambda _ j|<1/2$. Then \[  \omega '=\sum _ j\mu _ j\alpha _ j\geq \tfrac 12\omega >0.  \] It is a closed real $(1,1)$-form. A common positive integer denominator $m$ makes $[m\omega ']$ integral. The already proved theorem 10.40.10 gives projectivity. A compact manifold has finitely many components, so these conclusions combine, including any point components. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.80.2
text: Theorem 10.80.2 . 826013CCAFEC Let $T=V/\Gamma $ be a complex torus, with $\dim _{\mathbb C}V=n$. It is projective if and only if $V$ has a positive definite Hermitian form $h$ such that \[  \operatorname {Im}h(\gamma ,\delta )\in \mathbb Z \qquad (\gamma ,\delta \in \Gamma ).  \] For such a form the associated Kähler form is $\omega =-\operatorname {Im}h$ on the underlying real vector space. For every ordered real lattice basis $a_1,\ldots ,a_{2n}$ one has \[  \int _{T_{jk}}\omega =\omega (a_ j,a_ k) =-\operatorname {Im}h(a_ j,a_ k),\qquad 1\leq j<k\leq 2n,  \] where $T_{jk}$ is the oriented lattice parallelogram torus. Proof. Let $J$ be multiplication by $\mathrm i$ on $V$. For a Hermitian $h$ linear in its first argument, $\omega =-\operatorname {Im}h$ is alternating, $J$-invariant and satisfies $\omega (v,Jv)=h(v,v)>0$ for nonzero $v$. It is constant, hence closed, and descends to a Kähler form. The displayed parallelogram formula follows by pulling back to $(s,t)\mapsto sa_ j+ta_ k$. The exact integral two-period criterion theorem 10.65.1 makes its class integral. Then theorem 10.40.10 proves projectivity. Conversely projectivity supplies an integral Kähler form. By proposition 10.65.2 , its average is a constant positive real $(1,1)$-form $\omega $ in the same integral class. Set \[  h(v,w)=\omega (v,Jw)-\mathrm i\omega (v,w).  \] $J$-invariance and alternation make its real part symmetric and its imaginary part skew. Directly $h(Jv,w)=\mathrm i h(v,w)$ and $h(v,Jw)=-\mathrm i h(v,w)$, so it is Hermitian with the specified convention; $h(v,v)=\omega (v,Jv)>0$. The same two-period theorem gives the required integral imaginary parts, with the minus sign displayed above. All $2n$ real lattice circles are used. For $n=0$ the torus is a point and all conditions are vacuous and true. $\square$

title: Lemma 10.80.3
text: Lemma 10.80.3 . 5A4C95A96C6B Let $X\subset \mathbb P^ N$ be a connected compact complex submanifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, and let $\omega $ be the restricted normalized Fubini–Study form. For real closed one-forms $\gamma ,\delta $ whose classes are integral, \[  \int _ X\gamma \wedge \delta \wedge \omega ^{n-1}\in \mathbb Z.  \] This is an integral trace assertion for the displayed classes and chosen polarization; it does not presume an arbitrary integral Poincaré pairing. Proof. We first construct smooth successive hyperplane sections. If a compact complex submanifold $Y\subset \mathbb P^ N$ has dimension $d\geq 1$, the ambient linear forms generate every first jet of $L=\mathcal O(1)|_ Y$. In an affine chart one section has coefficient one and the others are the restricted affine coordinates. Their differentials span $T_ y^*Y$ because the inclusion has injective differential. Thus first-jet evaluation from the parameter space $\mathbb C^{N+1}$ is onto at every $y$. The incidence of pairs $(y,c)$ for which the corresponding section has zero first jet is a holomorphic kernel bundle over $Y$, of rank $N-d$. Indeed an invertible $(d+1)$-minor of the jet evaluation solves for that many parameters holomorphically. Its total complex dimension is $N$, smaller than the parameter dimension $N+1$. Its parameter image has measure zero: on each compact coordinate box the projection is Lipschitz, and subdividing a real $a$-dimensional box into cubes of side $r$ bounds its image volume in dimension $b>a$ by $O(r^{b-a})$. Countably many such boxes cover the incidence. Choose a parameter outside this null image. Its section is nonzero on every component and its zero set is a smooth compact complex hypersurface, possibly empty, by the local holomorphic inverse function theorem. This proves the required generic section statement without a transversality theorem as an extra input. Repeat until a smooth compact curve $C$ is reached, allowing an empty set at any stage. The single-section Poincaré–Lelong identity the line-bundle Poincaré–Lelong formula , applied at each smooth stage, gives \[  \int _ X\gamma \wedge \delta \wedge \omega ^{n-1} =\int _ C\gamma |_ C\wedge \delta |_ C.  \] At a stage of dimension $d$, pair $[Z]-\omega $ with the closed smooth form $\gamma \wedge \delta \wedge \omega ^{d-2}$; its integral is zero because $[Z]-\omega $ is an exact current and the stage is compact. Only a single integration current is paired with a smooth form at each step; no product of arbitrary currents is taken. For $n=1$ there is no cutting and $C=X$. Restrictions of the two classes to each component of $C$ are integral by naturality. We retain the precise comparison sign: the positive connecting convention obeys \[  \Psi _2([\alpha \wedge \beta ]) =-\Psi _1[\alpha ]\smile \Psi _1[\beta ]  \] in degree one, by theorem 10.58.9 . Hence the class of the displayed wedge on $C$ is the positive real image of the negative of an integral cup class. The proved lemma 10.79.7 identifies $H^2(C_0,\underline{\mathbb Z})$ on each connected component $C_0$ with $\mathbb Z$, its positive point-divisor generator having integral one. The integral is therefore an integer. Sum over the finitely many components; an empty $C$ contributes zero. $\square$

Use $dd^ c=i\partial  ar\partial /(2\pi )$ and squared logarithmic weights. Let $T$ be closed positive of bidimension $(p,p)$ on a Stein manifold $X$. For an extended-continuous plurisubharmonic weight $\phi $ use the support-relative truncation masses \[  M_ T(\phi ,t)=\int _{\{ \phi <t\} }T\wedge (dd^ c\max \{ \phi ,s\} )^ p\quad (s<t),\qquad

Their monotonicity, collar identities and local semicontinuity will always be used with compact low sublevels on $\operatorname {Supp}T$. Definition 6.39.1 . E6495CF1E603 An extended-continuous plurisubharmonic function $\phi $ on $X	imes Y$ is support-proper at low levels if for every compact $L\subset Y$ there is $b_ L\in \mathbb R$ such that \[  \{ (x,y)\in \operatorname {Supp}T	imes L:\phi (x,y)\leq b_ L\}  \Subset X	imes Y.  \] Its exponential is locally Hölder in the parameter if, locally in parameter coordinates and uniformly on smaller product neighborhoods, \[  |e^{\phi (x,y)}-e^{\phi (x,y')}|\leq C|y-y'|^\gamma \quad 	ext{for some }0<\gamma \leq 1.  \] Lemma 6.39.2 . EA46D27C1C72 After restricting the parameter to a relatively compact coordinate ball, a support-proper weight can be replaced by $w$ with the same numbers $

Add a nonnegative smooth strictly plurisubharmonic function $q$ on $X	imes Y$, obtaining $\eta =\phi +q$. Such a $q$ is supplied by a smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion of $X$, given by theorem 9.26.1 , and $|y|^2$. It is bounded on the compact low-support set. Thus $\eta $ has the same poles and numbers by corollary 6.34.11 ; it remains support-proper. Choose $R<0$ so that its support sublevel $\{ \eta \leq R\} $ is compact in the $X$ direction. Richberg approximation on $\{ \eta >-\infty \} $ by relative Richberg smoothing gives a smooth plurisubharmonic $h$ with $\eta \leq h\leq \eta +1$. This is an approximation on the nonpolar open manifold, where $\eta $ is finite, continuous and strictly plurisubharmonic. Put \[  C=-R+10,\qquad B=R+8,\qquad v=\max \{ \eta ,2h+C\} ,\qquad w=v-B,  \] extending $v$ by $-\infty $ at the poles. For $\eta \leq R-12$ one has $v=\eta $; for $\eta >R-10$ one has $v=2h+C$. title: Definition 6.39.1
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.39 Parameter weights and analytic Lelong level sets
text: Definition 6.39.1 . E6495CF1E603 An extended-continuous plurisubharmonic function $\phi $ on $X\times Y$ is support-proper at low levels if for every compact $L\subset Y$ there is $b_ L\in \mathbb R$ such that \[  \{ (x,y)\in \operatorname {Supp}T\times L:\phi (x,y)\leq b_ L\}  \Subset X\times Y.  \] Its exponential is locally Hölder in the parameter if, locally in parameter coordinates and uniformly on smaller product neighborhoods, \[  |e^{\phi (x,y)}-e^{\phi (x,y')}|\leq C|y-y'|^\gamma \quad \text{for some }0<\gamma \leq 1.  \]

title: Lemma 6.39.2
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.39 Parameter weights and analytic Lelong level sets
text: Lemma 6.39.2 . EA46D27C1C72 After restricting the parameter to a relatively compact coordinate ball, a support-proper weight can be replaced by $w$ with the same numbers $\nu _ T(w_ y)=\nu _ T(\phi _ y)$ such that its support sublevel $\{ w\leq 0\} $ is contained in $K\times Y$ for a compact $K\subset X$, and $w$ is smooth on $\{ -1\leq w\leq 0\} $. The exponential of $w$ retains local parameter Hölder continuity when that of $\phi $ has it. Proof. Take the closure of a slightly larger parameter ball when applying support properness. Add a nonnegative smooth strictly plurisubharmonic function $q$ on $X\times Y$, obtaining $\eta =\phi +q$. Such a $q$ is supplied by a smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion of $X$, given by theorem 9.26.1 , and $|y|^2$. It is bounded on the compact low-support set. Thus $\eta $ has the same poles and numbers by corollary 6.34.11 ; it remains support-proper. Choose $R<0$ so that its support sublevel $\{ \eta \leq R\} $ is compact in the $X$ direction. Richberg approximation on $\{ \eta >-\infty \} $ by relative Richberg smoothing gives a smooth plurisubharmonic $h$ with $\eta \leq h\leq \eta +1$. This is an approximation on the nonpolar open manifold, where $\eta $ is finite, continuous and strictly plurisubharmonic. Put \[  C=-R+10,\qquad B=R+8,\qquad v=\max \{ \eta ,2h+C\} ,\qquad w=v-B,  \] extending $v$ by $-\infty $ at the poles. For $\eta \leq R-12$ one has $v=\eta $; for $\eta >R-10$ one has $v=2h+C$. These observations prove that the extension is plurisubharmonic and extended-continuous, and that $w-\phi =q-B$ near its poles. If $v\leq B$, then $2\eta +C\leq B$, hence $\eta \leq R-1$. If $B-1\leq v\leq B$, then $\eta >R-10$, so $v$ is smooth there. This proves the compactness and corona assertions, retaining $\operatorname {Supp}T$ in the compactness condition. On the open set $\{ \eta <R-12\} $ one has $e^ v=e^\eta $. Away from the poles, $e^ v=\max \{ e^\eta ,e^{2h+C}\} $ is a maximum of a locally Hölder function and a smooth function. Multiplication by the smooth factors $e^ q$ and $e^{-B}$, and taking a maximum, preserve a local Hölder estimate. Thus the replacement preserves the required estimate, including at the poles. No preservation claim for an arbitrary bounded Richberg perturbation is being made. $\square$

title: Proposition 6.39.3
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.39 Parameter weights and analytic Lelong level sets
text: Proposition 6.39.3 . 0426E4966C15 For a weight $w$ as in lemma 6.39.2 , choose a smooth nondecreasing function $\chi $ with $\chi (t)=t$ for $t\leq -1$ and $\chi (t)=0$ for $t\geq 0$. On the half-plane $H=\{ \operatorname {Re}z<-2\} $ put CC32CC117F5F 6.39.4 \begin{equation}  V(y,z)=-\int _{\operatorname {Re}z}^{0}M_ T(w_ y,t)\chi '(t)\, dt. \end{equation} There is a nonnegative smooth plurisubharmonic $\rho $ on the parameter ball such that $\rho (y)+V(y,z)$ is continuous and plurisubharmonic on $Y\times H$. These assertions do not require the Hölder hypothesis. Proof. Write $w_ z=\max \{ w,\operatorname {Re}z\} $. Fubini and the finite-level collar identity give the fiber-integral formula 46483D5C23FE 6.39.5 \begin{equation}  V(y,z)=\int _ X T\wedge \chi (w_ z)(dd^ c_ xw_ z)^ p. \end{equation} Indeed, $M_ T(w_ y,t)$ is the mass of the bounded product $T(dd^ c_ xw_ z)^ p$ on $\{ w_ y<t\} $ when $t>\operatorname {Re}z$, and integrating $-\chi '(t)$ gives $\chi (w_ z)$. All integrals are finite: on a compact parameter and $z$ set the truncations are uniformly bounded near the compact support of the integrand, and the bounded product estimate applies. Uniform continuity of the bounded potentials and the bounded Bedford–Taylor continuity theorem show that the last integral is continuous in $(y,z)$. Pull $T$ back by the product projection and use total differentiation in the following calculation. The terms of the product containing extra $x$ differentials vanish under fiber integration, so \[  dd^ cV=\operatorname {pr}_{Y\times H,*} \bigl (T\wedge dd^ c\chi (w_ z)\wedge (dd^ cw_ z)^ p\bigr ).  \] To justify integration by parts, multiply by a smooth compact parameter test form. Its integrand has compact support in the $x$ direction on $\operatorname {Supp}T$; choose an $x$ cutoff equal to one there. All derivatives of that cutoff meet a region where $\chi (w_ z)=0$. The bounded-product chain rule follows first for smooth local regularizations and then by uniform convergence; it is also the recursive integration-by-parts definition of these products. On $\{ w<-1\} $, $\chi (w_ z)=w_ z$, so its contribution to this Hessian is the positive current $T(dd^ cw_ z)^{p+1}$. On the corona, $w_ z=w$ is smooth and independent of $z$. Consequently the possible negative part has only parameter components and locally bounded coefficients, bounded by the mass of $T$ on a fixed compact $x$ set times bounds for finitely many derivatives of $w$ there. Thus \[  dd^ cV\geq -C_ L\, i\sum _ jdy_ j\wedge d\bar y_ j \quad \text{on }L\times H  \] for every compact parameter subball $L$, uniformly in $z$. A nonnegative smooth convex increasing function of $|y|^2$, with radial derivative larger than these bounds on successive compact subballs, supplies $\rho $. Its Hessian dominates the negative term. The distributional criterion for plurisubharmonicity now proves the claim for the continuous function $\rho +V$. $\square$

title: Theorem 6.39.8
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.39 Parameter weights and analytic Lelong level sets
text: Theorem 6.39.8 . E7AF0D4FB0C0 On the parameter ball let $c>0$. If $E_ c=\{ y:\nu _ T(w_ y)\geq c\} $ is proper, there is an extended-continuous plurisubharmonic $W$ whose pole set is exactly $E_ c$. Thus $E_ c$ is closed complete pluripolar. This conclusion, like proposition 6.39.3 , needs no Hölder assumption. Proof. Closedness follows from the compact-local semicontinuity theorem. Choose $a_ k\uparrow c$, $0<a_ k<c$, and a compact exhaustion $L_ k$ of the ball. For $N>2$, the finite-interval minimum \[  U_{a_ k,N}(y)=\min _{-N\leq r\leq -2} \{ \rho (y)+V(y,r)-a_ kr\}   \] is continuous by compact minimization and plurisubharmonic by the same minimum principle, applied to $(-N,-2)$ and continuity at the endpoints. It decreases to $U_{a_ k}$ as $N\to \infty $. Since $U_{a_ k}=-\infty $ on $E_ c$, compactness and decreasingness allow a choice $N_ k$ with $w_ k:=U_{a_ k,N_ k}\leq -2^ k$ on $E_ c\cap L_ k$. All these functions have the common continuous plurisubharmonic majorant $G(y)=\rho (y)+V(y,-2)+2c$. The plurisubharmonic functions \[  W_ N=\sum _{k=1}^ N2^{-k}w_ k+2^{-N}G  \] decrease. Outside $E_ c$, proposition 6.39.6 gives a common local lower bound for all sufficiently late $w_ k$; the common upper bound $G$ gives locally uniform convergence of the series there. Its limit $W$ is finite and continuous there, so it is not identically $-\infty $. It is plurisubharmonic as a decreasing limit, and $W=-\infty $ on $E_ c$ by the chosen bounds. Upper semicontinuity at a pole says precisely that $W$ tends to $-\infty $ there, proving extended continuity on the whole ball. $\square$

Theorem 6.40.1 . 6A51F1CD4D5B For every closed positive current $T$ of bidimension $(p,p)$ on a complex manifold, $E_ c(T)=\{ x:
u (T,x)\geq c\} $ is analytic and has complex dimension at most $p$. For every irreducible analytic set $A$, its generic number $m_ A(T)=\inf _{x\in A}
u (T,x)$ is attained outside a countable union of proper analytic subsets of $A$. Proof. On a small coordinate ball use $\phi (x,y)=\log |x-y|^2$ and restrict $y$ to a strictly smaller ball. The low sublevels are uniformly compact, the exponential is locally Lipschitz in $y$, and the weight gives exactly the ordinary normalized number. Apply theorem 6.39.11 . The dimension bound follows from the locally finite $\mathcal H^{2p}$ measure in theorem 6.33.13 : a complex submanifold of dimension greater than $p$ has infinite $2p$-measure on every nonempty open piece. Then \[  \mathbf1_ A T=m_ A(T)[A].  \] A closed positive current of bidimension $(p,p)$ supported on an analytic set of dimension less than $p$ is zero. Proof. Closedness says that all first derivatives of the scalar distribution vanish. At regular points of $A$, the smooth integration current has number $1$, so additivity of the density limits gives $
u (T,x)=\lambda +
u (R,x)\geq \lambda $. If $m_ A(T)>\lambda $, choose $d$ strictly between zero and their difference. Every compact piece of $A_{m reg}$ would lie in $E_ d(R)$. u ((dd^ cu)^ q,x)\geq

title: 2.17 Maximal domains and formal adjoints
text: Write $\mathcal H=\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial $ and use unscaled Chern curvature. A weakly pseudoconvex manifold here means one with a smooth PSH exhaustion, including compact manifolds. An exhaustion is finite and continuous with relatively compact strict sublevels; equivalently all its closed sublevels are compact. After a constant shift it may be taken nonnegative. A compact exhaustion means compact sets $K_ j\subset \operatorname {Int}K_{j+1}$ whose union is the manifold; every compact subset is then contained in some $K_ j$. Completeness means completeness for the Riemannian length distance, with the equivalent smooth-exhaustion characterizations of section 6.26 . Example 2.17.1 . 07CC926D8338 On $L^2(0,1)$ let $P_{\max }u=u'$ distributionally, with domain $\{ u\in L^2:u'\in L^2\} =H^1(0,1)$. Its Hilbert adjoint is \[  P_{\max }^*u=-u',\qquad \operatorname {Dom}P_{\max }^* =\{ u\in H^1(0,1):u(0)=u(1)=0\} ,  \] whereas the maximal extension of its formal adjoint $-\mathrm d/\mathrm dx$ has all of $H^1(0,1)$ as domain. Proof. If $v=u'\in L^2$, its integral $V(x)=\int _{1/2}^ xv(t)\, \mathrm dt$ is absolutely continuous on $[0,1]$. The distribution $u-V$ has zero derivative and hence is constant: every compact test function of integral zero is the derivative of a compact test function. Thus $u$ has an absolutely continuous representative on $[0,1]$. For $u,f\in H^1$, integration by parts gives \[  \int _0^1 f'\bar u =-\int _0^1f\overline{u'}+f(1)\bar u(1)-f(0)\bar u(0).  \] Testing a Hilbert-adjoint element first against compact smooth $f$ forces $u'\in L^2$ and the displayed value of the adjoint. Testing then against affine $f$, whose endpoint values are arbitrary, forces both boundary values to vanish. Conversely those values make this identity valid for every $f$ in the full maximal domain. $\square$

title: 10.52 Semipositive line-bundle vanishing on weak exhaustions

section: 10.52 Semipositive line-bundle vanishing on weak exhaustions
text: Theorem 10.52.1 . A46DE8D5D789 Let $(X,\omega )$ be a weakly pseudoconvex Kähler $n$-manifold, $n\geq 1$. Suppose a smooth Hermitian holomorphic line bundle $(L,h)$ has semipositive curvature $\theta =\mathrm i\Theta (L,h)$, with at least $n-s+1$ positive eigenvalues everywhere, where $1\leq s\leq n$. Then \[  H^{a,b}_{\bar\partial }(X,L)=0 \qquad (a+b\geq n+s).  \] These are smooth analytic Dolbeault groups; each smooth closed form in such a degree has a smooth global primitive. Proof. Fix a smooth PSH exhaustion $\psi \geq 0$ and a smooth closed datum $g$ of type $(a,b)$. The degree inequality implies $a,b\geq s$, so in particular $b\geq 1$. Let $\lambda _ s(x)>0$ be the $s$th ordered eigenvalue of $\theta $ relative to $\omega $. Fix $\delta >0$ so small that $n\delta \leq 1/4$. Compact-sublevel suprema, followed by the smooth increasing convex majorant construction, give a smooth increasing convex function $\rho $ with \[  e^{-\rho (\psi (x))}\leq \delta \lambda _ s(x).  \] For clarity a convex majorant of a continuous lower target on $[0,\infty )$ can be obtained by choosing nondecreasing slopes on successive intervals, smoothing their steps, and integrating; choose each preceding slope large enough to exceed the next compact-interval supremum. Add a constant for the initial interval. We may require $\rho ',\rho ''\geq 0$. Choose an increasing convex $\chi $, to be fixed below, and put DBD4A0002DEF 10.52.2 \begin{equation}  h_\chi =h e^{-\chi (\psi )},\quad \theta _\chi =\theta +\mathcal H(\chi (\psi )),\quad \alpha =\theta _\chi +e^{-\rho (\psi )}\omega . \end{equation} This is a positive Hermitian metric, although it need not be Kähler. If $\lambda _ j^\chi $ are the ordered $\omega $-eigenvalues of $\theta _\chi $, then $\lambda _ j^\chi \geq \lambda _ j$ by the min–max principle. The $\alpha $-eigenvalues of $\theta _\chi $ are \[  \mu _ j=\frac{\lambda _ j^\chi }{\lambda _ j^\chi +e^{-\rho (\psi )}} \in [0,1],\qquad \mu _ j\geq 1-\delta \quad (j\geq s).  \] The all-bidegree scalar curvature formula of proposition 10.33.6 therefore gives C7EBF8BB029C 10.52.3 \begin{equation}  [\theta _\chi ,\Lambda _\alpha ] \geq \left(\sum _{j=1}^ a\mu _ j-\sum _{j=b+1}^ n\mu _ j\right)I \geq \bigl ((a-s+1)(1-\delta )-(n-b)\bigr )I\geq \tfrac 34 I. \end{equation} The second sum in the first bound comprises the largest $n-b$ eigenvalues; the same expression follows by taking complements of the barred index set in the coefficient formula. We control the torsion explicitly. In a unitary exterior coframe, the norm of each elementary wedge or contraction is at most one. The exact formula for $T_\alpha $ in equation 11.48.13 consequently implies \[  \| T_\alpha \| \leq C_ n (|\partial \alpha |_\alpha ^2+ |\partial \bar\partial \alpha |_\alpha ).  \] Here the finite number of wedge and contraction terms gives a constant depending only on $n$, uniformly over all bidegrees. Since $\theta _\chi $ and $\omega $ are closed, \begin{align*}  \partial \alpha & =-\rho 'e^{-\rho }\partial \psi \wedge \omega ,\\  \partial \bar\partial \alpha & =e^{-\rho }\bigl (((\rho ')^2-\rho ”) \partial \psi \wedge \bar\partial \psi -\rho '\partial \bar\partial \psi \bigr )\wedge \omega . \end{align*} All scalar derivatives are evaluated at $\psi $. The three form inequalities \[  \alpha \geq e^{-\rho }\omega ,\quad \alpha \geq \chi '\mathcal H(\psi ),\quad \alpha \geq \chi ''\mathrm i\partial \psi \wedge \bar\partial \psi  \] give $|\omega |_\alpha \leq \sqrt n e^\rho $, $|\mathcal H(\psi )|_\alpha \leq \sqrt n/\chi '$ and $|\partial \psi |_\alpha \leq (\chi '')^{-1/2}$. Wedge multiplication is bounded in finite-dimensional exterior spaces. Hence 85351516D61A 10.52.4 \begin{equation}  \| T_\alpha \| \leq C_ n\left( \frac{(\rho ')^2+\rho ''}{\chi ''}+\frac{\rho '}{\chi '}\right). \end{equation} Choose a continuous lower bound for both $\chi '$ and $\chi ''$ so large that this is at most $1/4$, and also require $\chi ''\geq 1$. These lower bounds can be combined with integrability of $g$. There is a continuous $C(x)\geq 1$ such that \[  e^{-\rho }\omega \leq \alpha \leq C(x)(1+\chi '+\chi '')\omega .  \] Consequently \[  |g|_{\alpha ,h_\chi }^2\, \mathrm dV_\alpha \leq C(x)^ n e^{(a+b)\rho (\psi )}|g|_{\omega ,h}^2 (1+\chi '+\chi '')^ n e^{-\chi (\psi )}\, \mathrm dV_\omega .  \] The coefficient preceding the derivative factor has finite integrals over compact exhaustion bands. Choose a continuous $\ell \geq 1$ on $[0,\infty )$ dominating all the preceding derivative lower bounds, and large enough that the integral of that coefficient divided by $\ell (\psi )$ is finite. On the band $[k,k+1]$ it suffices to make $\ell $ at least $2^ k$ times its band integral plus one, and then take a continuous majorant. Apply lemma 6.27.12 with $N=n$ and lower target $\ell $. It provides a single $\chi $ satisfying every requirement and $g\in L^2(\alpha ,h_\chi )$. Since $|\mathrm d\psi |_\alpha ^2\leq 2$, the exhaustion criterion corollary 6.26.3 makes $\alpha $ complete. Equations ( 10.52.3 ) and ( 10.52.4 ) give $[\theta _\chi ,\Lambda _\alpha ]+T_\alpha \geq I/2$. title: Theorem 10.52.1
section: 10.52 Semipositive line-bundle vanishing on weak exhaustions
text: Theorem 10.52.1 . A46DE8D5D789 Let $(X,\omega )$ be a weakly pseudoconvex Kähler $n$-manifold, $n\geq 1$. Suppose a smooth Hermitian holomorphic line bundle $(L,h)$ has semipositive curvature $\theta =\mathrm i\Theta (L,h)$, with at least $n-s+1$ positive eigenvalues everywhere, where $1\leq s\leq n$. Then \[  H^{a,b}_{\bar\partial }(X,L)=0 \qquad (a+b\geq n+s).  \] These are smooth analytic Dolbeault groups; each smooth closed form in such a degree has a smooth global primitive. Proof. Fix a smooth PSH exhaustion $\psi \geq 0$ and a smooth closed datum $g$ of type $(a,b)$. The degree inequality implies $a,b\geq s$, so in particular $b\geq 1$. Let $\lambda _ s(x)>0$ be the $s$th ordered eigenvalue of $\theta $ relative to $\omega $. Fix $\delta >0$ so small that $n\delta \leq 1/4$. Compact-sublevel suprema, followed by the smooth increasing convex majorant construction, give a smooth increasing convex function $\rho $ with \[  e^{-\rho (\psi (x))}\leq \delta \lambda _ s(x).  \] For clarity a convex majorant of a continuous lower target on $[0,\infty )$ can be obtained by choosing nondecreasing slopes on successive intervals, smoothing their steps, and integrating; choose each preceding slope large enough to exceed the next compact-interval supremum. Add a constant for the initial interval. We may require $\rho ',\rho ''\geq 0$. Choose an increasing convex $\chi $, to be fixed below, and put DBD4A0002DEF 10.52.2 \begin{equation}  h_\chi =h e^{-\chi (\psi )},\quad \theta _\chi =\theta +\mathcal H(\chi (\psi )),\quad \alpha =\theta _\chi +e^{-\rho (\psi )}\omega . \end{equation} This is a positive Hermitian metric, although it need not be Kähler. If $\lambda _ j^\chi $ are the ordered $\omega $-eigenvalues of $\theta _\chi $, then $\lambda _ j^\chi \geq \lambda _ j$ by the min–max principle. The $\alpha $-eigenvalues of $\theta _\chi $ are \[  \mu _ j=\frac{\lambda _ j^\chi }{\lambda _ j^\chi +e^{-\rho (\psi )}} \in [0,1],\qquad \mu _ j\geq 1-\delta \quad (j\geq s).  \] The all-bidegree scalar curvature formula of proposition 10.33.6 therefore gives C7EBF8BB029C 10.52.3 \begin{equation}  [\theta _\chi ,\Lambda _\alpha ] \geq \left(\sum _{j=1}^ a\mu _ j-\sum _{j=b+1}^ n\mu _ j\right)I \geq \bigl ((a-s+1)(1-\delta )-(n-b)\bigr )I\geq \tfrac 34 I. \end{equation} The second sum in the first bound comprises the largest $n-b$ eigenvalues; the same expression follows by taking complements of the barred index set in the coefficient formula. We control the torsion explicitly. In a unitary exterior coframe, the norm of each elementary wedge or contraction is at most one. The exact formula for $T_\alpha $ in equation 11.48.13 consequently implies \[  \| T_\alpha \| \leq C_ n (|\partial \alpha |_\alpha ^2+ |\partial \bar\partial \alpha |_\alpha ).  \] Here the finite number of wedge and contraction terms gives a constant depending only on $n$, uniformly over all bidegrees. Since $\theta _\chi $ and $\omega $ are closed, \begin{align*}  \partial \alpha & =-\rho 'e^{-\rho }\partial \psi \wedge \omega ,\\  \partial \bar\partial \alpha & =e^{-\rho }\bigl (((\rho ')^2-\rho ”) \partial \psi \wedge \bar\partial \psi -\rho '\partial \bar\partial \psi \bigr )\wedge \omega . \end{align*} All scalar derivatives are evaluated at $\psi $. The three form inequalities \[  \alpha \geq e^{-\rho }\omega ,\quad \alpha \geq \chi '\mathcal H(\psi ),\quad \alpha \geq \chi ''\mathrm i\partial \psi \wedge \bar\partial \psi  \] give $|\omega |_\alpha \leq \sqrt n e^\rho $, $|\mathcal H(\psi )|_\alpha \leq \sqrt n/\chi '$ and $|\partial \psi |_\alpha \leq (\chi '')^{-1/2}$. Wedge multiplication is bounded in finite-dimensional exterior spaces. Hence 85351516D61A 10.52.4 \begin{equation}  \| T_\alpha \| \leq C_ n\left( \frac{(\rho ')^2+\rho ''}{\chi ''}+\frac{\rho '}{\chi '}\right). \end{equation} Choose a continuous lower bound for both $\chi '$ and $\chi ''$ so large that this is at most $1/4$, and also require $\chi ''\geq 1$. These lower bounds can be combined with integrability of $g$. There is a continuous $C(x)\geq 1$ such that \[  e^{-\rho }\omega \leq \alpha \leq C(x)(1+\chi '+\chi '')\omega .  \] Consequently \[  |g|_{\alpha ,h_\chi }^2\, \mathrm dV_\alpha \leq C(x)^ n e^{(a+b)\rho (\psi )}|g|_{\omega ,h}^2 (1+\chi '+\chi '')^ n e^{-\chi (\psi )}\, \mathrm dV_\omega .  \] The coefficient preceding the derivative factor has finite integrals over compact exhaustion bands. Choose a continuous $\ell \geq 1$ on $[0,\infty )$ dominating all the preceding derivative lower bounds, and large enough that the integral of that coefficient divided by $\ell (\psi )$ is finite. On the band $[k,k+1]$ it suffices to make $\ell $ at least $2^ k$ times its band integral plus one, and then take a continuous majorant. Apply lemma 6.27.12 with $N=n$ and lower target $\ell $. It provides a single $\chi $ satisfying every requirement and $g\in L^2(\alpha ,h_\chi )$. Since $|\mathrm d\psi |_\alpha ^2\leq 2$, the exhaustion criterion corollary 6.26.3 makes $\alpha $ complete. Equations ( 10.52.3 ) and ( 10.52.4 ) give $[\theta _\chi ,\Lambda _\alpha ]+T_\alpha \geq I/2$. For the constantly rescaled complete metric $\alpha /2$, both terms of this operator are multiplied by two, as follows directly from the contraction and torsion formulas. Thus lemma 9.50.3 applies to $g$ and $(L,h_\chi )$. Its minimum-norm solution is smooth and is a primitive of the original smooth closed datum. Modifying the metrics does not alter the differential or its smooth cohomology class. $\square$

title: 6.31 Weighted extension from neighborhood data
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text: Theorem 6.31.1 . 5C460CFF2115 Let $(X,\omega )$ be weakly pseudoconvex Kähler, $(L,h)$ a smooth Hermitian holomorphic line bundle and $(E,H)$ a smooth Hermitian holomorphic vector bundle. Let $\sigma $ be a holomorphic section of $E$, put $t=|\sigma |_ H^2$, $Y=\{ \sigma =0\} $ and $U=\{ t<1\} $. Assume first that $Y$ is proper on every component and nonempty, and let $p\geq 1$ be the largest codimension of its irreducible components. Suppose, on $X\setminus Y$, that 79352F870E30 6.31.2 \begin{equation}  \mathrm i\Theta (L,h)\geq \left(\frac pt+\frac\epsilon {1+t}\right) \langle \mathrm i\Theta (E,H)\sigma ,\sigma \rangle _ H, \qquad \epsilon >0. \end{equation} For every holomorphic $K_ X\otimes L$ section $f$ on $U$ with $I=\int _ U|f|_{\omega ,h}^2\, \mathrm dV_\omega <\infty $, there is a global holomorphic section $F$ with $F|_ Y=f|_ Y$ and C9D0B52C523C 6.31.3 \begin{equation}  \int _ X\frac{|F|_{\omega ,h}^2}{(1+t)^{p+\epsilon }}\,  \mathrm dV_\omega \leq \left(1+\frac{(p+1)^2}{\epsilon }\right)I. \end{equation} The equality on $Y$ means equality of values on the reduced set. On a component with $\sigma \equiv 0$ take $F=f$, and on a component with $Y$ empty take $F=0$. These conventions also settle the cases of an empty $Y$ or of codimension zero only, without a logarithmic weight argument. Proof. It suffices to treat components with proper nonempty $Y$; the same global integer $p$ can be used on all of them. Define on $X$ \[  h_0=(1-t^{(p+1)/2})f\quad (t<1),\qquad h_0=0\quad (t\geq 1).  \] This is locally $L^2$. It has distributional derivative 4DC1065B0573 6.31.4 \begin{equation}  g=D''h_0=-\tfrac {p+1}2 t^{(p-1)/2}\bar\eta \wedge f \quad \hbox{on }U,\qquad g=0\quad \hbox{off }U, \qquad \eta =\langle D'\sigma ,\sigma \rangle _ H. \end{equation} Here wedge order determines only an irrelevant common sign if the holomorphic top form is put first. To check the derivative without extending $f$ beyond $U$, multiply $h_0$ by a smooth cutoff equal to one for $t\leq 1-2d$ and zero for $t\geq 1-d$. On a compact set its extra derivative is bounded in norm by $C|f|\mathbf1_{\{ 1-2d<t<1\} }$: its derivative is $O(d^{-1})$ and $|1-t^{(p+1)/2}|\leq C d$ on that layer. Since $f$ is $L^2$ on $U$, this error tends to zero in local $L^2$ as $d\downarrow 0$. The other terms converge in local $L^2$ as well. The section is $C^1$ near $Y$, since $p\geq 1$ and $|\sigma |^{p+1}$ is $C^1$. Thus ( 6.31.4 ) holds globally, $g$ is locally $L^2$ and $D''g=0$. Global continuity across $t=1$ is not needed for either $h_0$ or $g$. On $X\setminus Y$ put $\Phi =p\log t+\epsilon \log (1+t)$ and equip $L$ with $h e^{-\Phi }$. Chern-normal differentiation gives \[  \mathcal H(\log t)\geq -\frac Rt,\qquad \mathcal H(\log (1+t)) =\frac{\mathrm i\langle D'\sigma ,D'\sigma \rangle _ H}{1+t} -\frac{\mathrm i\eta \wedge \bar\eta }{(1+t)^2} -\frac R{1+t}, \quad R=\langle \mathrm i\Theta (E)\sigma ,\sigma \rangle _ H.  \] The precise Cauchy–Schwarz inequality is $\mathrm i\eta \wedge \bar\eta \leq t\, \mathrm i\langle D'\sigma ,D'\sigma \rangle _ H$. It implies, using ( 6.31.2 ), B1C1A543A240 6.31.5 \begin{equation}  \mathrm i\Theta (L,h e^{-\Phi }) \geq \frac\epsilon {(1+t)^2} \mathrm i\langle D'\sigma ,D'\sigma \rangle _ H \geq \frac\epsilon {t(1+t)^2}\,  \mathrm i\eta \wedge \bar\eta \geq 0. \end{equation} The first inequality follows by replacing the negative rank-one term with at most $t$ times the derivative norm term; this leaves exactly its coefficient $(1+t)^{-2}$. In a unitary frame, the curvature operator of $\mathrm i\eta \wedge \bar\eta $ on $(n,1)$ is the positive rank-one matrix whose quadratic form is squared contraction by $\bar\eta $. Hence ( 6.31.4 ) and ( 6.31.5 ), with the semidefinite dual definition of inverse energy, give 68717EBB5263 6.31.6 \begin{equation}  |g|_{[\mathrm i\Theta (L,h e^{-\Phi }),\Lambda _\omega ]^{-1}}^2 \leq \frac{(p+1)^2}{4\epsilon }t^ p(1+t)^2|f|_{\omega ,h}^2 \leq \frac{(p+1)^2}\epsilon e^\Phi |f|_{\omega ,h}^2 \quad \hbox{on }U. \end{equation} In this display the dual coefficient energy uses $h$ for both datum and tests; multiplying it by $e^{-\Phi }$ gives the actual bundle energy density. Off $U$ the datum is zero. No ordinary global $L^2$ bound for $g$ in the singular weight is assumed. Let $X_ c=\{ \psi <c\} $ exhaust $X$ by a smooth PSH exhaustion. By lemma 6.28.11 , $X_ c\setminus Y$ admits a complete Kähler metric. Apply the original-metric clause of theorem 6.28.2 to the smooth weighted line bundle there, with its original $\omega $. The datum is locally $L^2$ and closed; ( 6.31.6 ) gives a solution $u_ c$ with \[  D''u_ c=g,\qquad \int _{X_ c\setminus Y}|u_ c|_{\omega ,h}^2t^{-p}(1+t)^{-\epsilon } \, \mathrm dV_\omega \leq (p+1)^2I/\epsilon .  \] These fixed smooth positive densities on compact subsets of $X\setminus Y$ give local weak $L^2$ bounds. A diagonal weak limit solves $D''u=g$ there; lower semicontinuity followed by exhaustion gives the same global estimate. Since $t$ is bounded above on compact sets, this estimate also implies ordinary local $L^2$ across $Y$. Extend $u$ over this measure-zero set. The analytic-removal lemma 6.28.12 applies to $u$ and the locally $L^2$, hence locally $L^1$, datum $g$, so $D''u=g$ on $X$. The locally $L^2$ section $F=h_0-u$ is distributionally holomorphic. Apply holomorphic distributions and minimal weighted solutions to its coefficient in local holomorphic coordinates and a holomorphic line frame. The resulting holomorphic representatives agree on overlaps, since they agree almost everywhere, so $F$ is a holomorphic section. Near $Y$, $h_0$ is continuous, so $u=h_0-F$ is continuous there. At a smooth point of $Y$ of codimension $d\leq p$, choose transverse coordinates $z'\in \mathbb C^ d$. Holomorphicity of $\sigma $ and its vanishing along $Y$ give $t\leq C|z'|^2$ on a smaller chart. If $u$ were nonzero at that point, continuity and a smooth local frame would force its weighted norm to dominate the divergent transverse integral $\int _{|z'|<r}|z'|^{-2p}\, \mathrm dV(z')$. Thus $u=0$ on every component's dense regular part and, by continuity, on all of $Y$. Therefore $F|_ Y=f|_ Y$. Finally weighted Cauchy–Schwarz on $U$, using $|h_0|\leq |f|$, and $1+t^ p\leq (1+t)^ p$ for the integer $p\geq 1$, gives \[  |F|^2\leq (1+t^{-p})|u|^2+(1+t^ p)|h_0|^2, \qquad \frac{|F|^2}{(1+t)^ p}\leq t^{-p}|u|^2+|f|^2.  \] Off $U$ the latter bound holds with $f=0$ since $F=-u$. Multiply by $(1+t)^{-\epsilon }$, integrate, and use the preceding bound for $u$. This proves ( 6.31.3 ). On components with $\sigma \equiv 0$ the datum is already global and the estimate for $F=f$ has constant one. Components with no zero set require no interpolation and $F=0$ suffices. $\square$ Corollary 6.31.7 . 20E76F1409EA Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be pseudoconvex, let $\varphi ,\psi $ be PSH on $\Omega $, with $\psi $ finite and continuous, and let $\sigma =(\sigma _1,\ldots ,\sigma _ r)$ be holomorphic. Put $t=\sum _ j|\sigma _ j|^2$, $Y=\{ t=0\} $, and let $p$ be the largest codimension of its proper nonempty irreducible components when such components exist. Fix $\epsilon >0$ and set $C_{p,\epsilon }=1+(p+1)^2/\epsilon $. For data holomorphic on the indicated neighborhood, there is a holomorphic $F$ on $\Omega $ with $F|_ Y=f|_ Y$ satisfying, respectively, 8135F4E6E5E2 \begin{align}  U_-& =\{ t<e^{-\psi }\} ,&  \int _\Omega \frac{|F|^2e^{-\varphi +p\psi }}{(1+t e^\psi )^{p+\epsilon }}\, \mathrm dV & \leq C_{p,\epsilon }\int _{U_-}|f|^2e^{-\varphi +p\psi }\, \mathrm dV, \tag{6.31.8}\\  U_+& =\{ t<e^\psi \} ,&  \int _\Omega \frac{|F|^2e^{-\varphi }}{(e^\psi +t)^{p+\epsilon }}\, \mathrm dV & \leq C_{p,\epsilon }\int _{U_+}|f|^2 e^{-\varphi -(p+\epsilon )\psi }\, \mathrm dV. \tag{6.31.9} \end{align} In the first case $f\in \mathcal O(U_-)$; in the second case $f\in \mathcal O(U_+)$. If $Y$ is empty take $F=0$. If its only components have codimension zero take $p=0$ and use $F=f$ on those ambient components and zero on the others. Proof. First let $\varphi ,\psi $ be smooth and assume the respective right-hand integral $I$ is finite. In the first case give the trivial rank-$r$ bundle the squared metric $e^\psi I$ and the trivial line bundle the squared metric $e^{-\varphi +p\psi }$. Its section norm is $t_-=t e^\psi $, and \[  R_ E=-\mathcal H(\psi )I,\qquad \theta _ L=\mathcal H(\varphi )-p\mathcal H(\psi ) \geq -\left(p+\frac{\epsilon t_-}{1+t_-}\right)\mathcal H(\psi ).  \] This is precisely ( 6.31.2 ). In the second case use squared metrics $e^{-\psi }I$ and $e^{-\varphi -(p+\epsilon )\psi }$ instead. Now $t_+=t e^{-\psi }$, $R_ E=\mathcal H(\psi )I$, and \[  \theta _ L=\mathcal H(\varphi )+(p+\epsilon )\mathcal H(\psi ) \geq \left(p+\frac{\epsilon t_+}{1+t_+}\right)\mathcal H(\psi ).  \] Apply theorem 6.31.1 , identifying scalar functions with coefficients of the fixed holomorphic volume form; its common norm-volume factor cancels. In the second case the identity $e^{-(p+\epsilon )\psi }(1+t e^{-\psi })^{-p-\epsilon } =(e^\psi +t)^{-p-\epsilon }$ gives the stated denominator. For the finite-integral singular case, first treat an ambient component on which $\varphi \equiv -\infty $. Finiteness forces $f=0$ on its data domain, so $F=0$ works there. Here a zero function has zero weighted density even where the weight is infinite. On all other components $\varphi $ is locally integrable. Choose pseudoconvex $\Omega _ j\Subset \Omega $ exhausting $\Omega $, by pseudoconvex products and relatively compact exhaustions , and let $d_ j\downarrow 0$. Radial convolution at sufficiently small radii on a neighborhood of $\overline\Omega _ j$ gives smooth PSH $\varphi _ j\geq \varphi $ converging pointwise to $\varphi $, as in the Levi criterion and decreasing convolution . Because $\psi $ is continuous, the same construction can give smooth PSH $v_ j$ with $\psi \leq v_ j\leq \psi +d_ j$ near $\overline\Omega _ j$. For the first case use $\psi _ j=v_ j$; for the second use $\psi _ j=v_ j-d_ j$, so $\psi -d_ j\leq \psi _ j\leq \psi $. The respective data domains on $\Omega _ j$ are thus subsets of $U_-$ and $U_+$, respectively. Their data integrals are bounded by $e^{p d_ j}I$ in the first case and $e^{(p+\epsilon )d_ j}I$ in the second. There is no need to extend $f$ across either neighborhood boundary or to have a global smooth PSH approximation on $\Omega $. Apply the smooth cases on $\Omega _ j$. If the zero set there has smaller maximal codimension, its proof still applies with the same larger integer $p$: this integer enters only as an upper bound for codimensions and in the prescribed bundle weights. Components on which it is empty or identically zero are settled directly as above. The resulting $F_ j$ have locally uniform ordinary $L^2$ bounds: $\varphi _ j$ are uniformly bounded above on each fixed compact set, $\psi _ j$ are uniformly bounded there and $t$ is bounded. Thus the positive output densities have a fixed positive lower bound on that set. Holomorphic mean-value and Cauchy estimates give locally uniform bounds on $F_ j$ and their derivatives. Diagonal compact convergence therefore gives a holomorphic $F$, with $F|_ Y=f|_ Y$. Pointwise convergence of the output densities and Fatou's lemma on each compact set, followed by exhaustion and $d_ j\to 0$, give the exact stated constant. Points with $\varphi =-\infty $ use the usual nonnegative extended-density convention and Fatou's lemma unchanged. If $I=+\infty $, only existence of the extension remains to be proved. The section $f$ on a neighborhood of $Y$ defines a section of $\mathcal O_\Omega /\mathcal I_ Y$, where the reduced analytic ideal $\mathcal I_ Y$ is coherent. The smooth strict-PSH exhaustion of Oka's boundary-distance criterion makes $\Omega $ strongly $1$-complete. The fully proved coherent vanishing theorem 9.51.13 gives $H^1(\Omega ,\mathcal I_ Y)=0$, so the quotient exact sequence lifts this section to a global holomorphic $F$. The asserted integral inequality then has right-hand side $+\infty $. This argument is used only for that vacuous-estimate case. All finite-integral estimates were proved by the explicit $L^2$ construction above. $\square$

Finally weighted Cauchy–Schwarz on $U$, using $|h_0|\leq |f|$, and $1+t^ p\leq (1+t)^ p$ for the integer $p\geq 1$, gives \[  |F|^2\leq (1+t^{-p})|u|^2+(1+t^ p)|h_0|^2, \qquad \frac{|F|^2}{(1+t)^ p}\leq t^{-p}|u|^2+|f|^2.  \] Off $U$ the latter bound holds with $f=0$ since $F=-u$. Multiply by $(1+t)^{-\epsilon }$, integrate, and use the preceding bound for $u$. This proves ( 6.31.3 ). On components with $\sigma \equiv 0$ the datum is already global and the estimate for $F=f$ has constant one. Components with no zero set require no interpolation and $F=0$ suffices. $\square$

title: Corollary 6.31.7
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text: Corollary 6.31.7 . 20E76F1409EA Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be pseudoconvex, let $\varphi ,\psi $ be PSH on $\Omega $, with $\psi $ finite and continuous, and let $\sigma =(\sigma _1,\ldots ,\sigma _ r)$ be holomorphic. Put $t=\sum _ j|\sigma _ j|^2$, $Y=\{ t=0\} $, and let $p$ be the largest codimension of its proper nonempty irreducible components when such components exist. Fix $\epsilon >0$ and set $C_{p,\epsilon }=1+(p+1)^2/\epsilon $. For data holomorphic on the indicated neighborhood, there is a holomorphic $F$ on $\Omega $ with $F|_ Y=f|_ Y$ satisfying, respectively, 8135F4E6E5E2 \begin{align}  U_-& =\{ t<e^{-\psi }\} ,&  \int _\Omega \frac{|F|^2e^{-\varphi +p\psi }}{(1+t e^\psi )^{p+\epsilon }}\, \mathrm dV & \leq C_{p,\epsilon }\int _{U_-}|f|^2e^{-\varphi +p\psi }\, \mathrm dV, \tag{6.31.8}\\  U_+& =\{ t<e^\psi \} ,&  \int _\Omega \frac{|F|^2e^{-\varphi }}{(e^\psi +t)^{p+\epsilon }}\, \mathrm dV & \leq C_{p,\epsilon }\int _{U_+}|f|^2 e^{-\varphi -(p+\epsilon )\psi }\, \mathrm dV. \tag{6.31.9} \end{align} In the first case $f\in \mathcal O(U_-)$; in the second case $f\in \mathcal O(U_+)$. If $Y$ is empty take $F=0$. If its only components have codimension zero take $p=0$ and use $F=f$ on those ambient components and zero on the others. Proof. First let $\varphi ,\psi $ be smooth and assume the respective right-hand integral $I$ is finite. In the first case give the trivial rank-$r$ bundle the squared metric $e^\psi I$ and the trivial line bundle the squared metric $e^{-\varphi +p\psi }$. Its section norm is $t_-=t e^\psi $, and \[  R_ E=-\mathcal H(\psi )I,\qquad \theta _ L=\mathcal H(\varphi )-p\mathcal H(\psi ) \geq -\left(p+\frac{\epsilon t_-}{1+t_-}\right)\mathcal H(\psi ).  \] This is precisely ( 6.31.2 ). In the second case use squared metrics $e^{-\psi }I$ and $e^{-\varphi -(p+\epsilon )\psi }$ instead. Now $t_+=t e^{-\psi }$, $R_ E=\mathcal H(\psi )I$, and \[  \theta _ L=\mathcal H(\varphi )+(p+\epsilon )\mathcal H(\psi ) \geq \left(p+\frac{\epsilon t_+}{1+t_+}\right)\mathcal H(\psi ).  \] Apply theorem 6.31.1 , identifying scalar functions with coefficients of the fixed holomorphic volume form; its common norm-volume factor cancels. In the second case the identity $e^{-(p+\epsilon )\psi }(1+t e^{-\psi })^{-p-\epsilon } =(e^\psi +t)^{-p-\epsilon }$ gives the stated denominator. For the finite-integral singular case, first treat an ambient component on which $\varphi \equiv -\infty $. Finiteness forces $f=0$ on its data domain, so $F=0$ works there. Here a zero function has zero weighted density even where the weight is infinite. On all other components $\varphi $ is locally integrable. Choose pseudoconvex $\Omega _ j\Subset \Omega $ exhausting $\Omega $, by pseudoconvex products and relatively compact exhaustions , and let $d_ j\downarrow 0$. Radial convolution at sufficiently small radii on a neighborhood of $\overline\Omega _ j$ gives smooth PSH $\varphi _ j\geq \varphi $ converging pointwise to $\varphi $, as in the Levi criterion and decreasing convolution . Because $\psi $ is continuous, the same construction can give smooth PSH $v_ j$ with $\psi \leq v_ j\leq \psi +d_ j$ near $\overline\Omega _ j$. For the first case use $\psi _ j=v_ j$; for the second use $\psi _ j=v_ j-d_ j$, so $\psi -d_ j\leq \psi _ j\leq \psi $. The respective data domains on $\Omega _ j$ are thus subsets of $U_-$ and $U_+$, respectively. Their data integrals are bounded by $e^{p d_ j}I$ in the first case and $e^{(p+\epsilon )d_ j}I$ in the second. There is no need to extend $f$ across either neighborhood boundary or to have a global smooth PSH approximation on $\Omega $. Apply the smooth cases on $\Omega _ j$. If the zero set there has smaller maximal codimension, its proof still applies with the same larger integer $p$: this integer enters only as an upper bound for codimensions and in the prescribed bundle weights. Components on which it is empty or identically zero are settled directly as above. The resulting $F_ j$ have locally uniform ordinary $L^2$ bounds: $\varphi _ j$ are uniformly bounded above on each fixed compact set, $\psi _ j$ are uniformly bounded there and $t$ is bounded. Thus the positive output densities have a fixed positive lower bound on that set. Holomorphic mean-value and Cauchy estimates give locally uniform bounds on $F_ j$ and their derivatives. Diagonal compact convergence therefore gives a holomorphic $F$, with $F|_ Y=f|_ Y$. Pointwise convergence of the output densities and Fatou's lemma on each compact set, followed by exhaustion and $d_ j\to 0$, give the exact stated constant. Points with $\varphi =-\infty $ use the usual nonnegative extended-density convention and Fatou's lemma unchanged. If $I=+\infty $, only existence of the extension remains to be proved. The section $f$ on a neighborhood of $Y$ defines a section of $\mathcal O_\Omega /\mathcal I_ Y$, where the reduced analytic ideal $\mathcal I_ Y$ is coherent. The smooth strict-PSH exhaustion of Oka's boundary-distance criterion makes $\Omega $ strongly $1$-complete. The fully proved coherent vanishing theorem 9.51.13 gives $H^1(\Omega ,\mathcal I_ Y)=0$, so the quotient exact sequence lifts this section to a global holomorphic $F$. The asserted integral inequality then has right-hand side $+\infty $. This argument is used only for that vacuous-estimate case. All finite-integral estimates were proved by the explicit $L^2$ construction above. $\square$

title: 10.37 Relative tautological lines
text: Projective spaces parametrize lines. Let $E$ be a holomorphic bundle of rank $r\geq 1$ on a complex manifold $X$. Set $\pi :\mathbb P(E^*)\to X$. All duals are complex linear, and Hermitian forms are linear in the first variable. Chern curvature $\Theta $ is unscaled, so the normalized curvature of a line is $\mathrm i\Theta /(2\pi )$. Proposition 10.37.1 . B8693F38C65B The space $\mathbb P(E^*)$ is a complex manifold, locally a product with $\mathbb P^{r-1}$. The subspaces $S_{[\xi ]}=\ker \xi \subset E_{\pi ([\xi ])}$ form a holomorphic subbundle of $\pi ^*E$, and there is an exact sequence \[  0\longrightarrow S\longrightarrow \pi ^*E \longrightarrow \mathcal O_ E(1)\longrightarrow 0.  \] The dual of $\mathcal O_ E(1)$ is canonically the tautological line subbundle of $\pi ^*E^*$. The restriction of $\mathcal O_ E(1)$ to each projective fiber is $\mathcal O(1)$ with the usual dual-tautological convention. For rank one, $\mathbb P(E^*)=X$ and $\mathcal O_ E(1)=E$. For rank two the kernel map canonically identifies $\mathbb P(E^*)$ with $\mathbb P(E)$. Proof. Trivializations of $E$ induce product charts on $\mathbb P(E^*)$; their changes act by projectivized invertible holomorphic matrices, and are holomorphic in the standard affine projective charts. These charts give the complex structure. The total space is Hausdorff: distinct projected points are separated in $X$, and points in the same fiber are separated within a product chart, whose base can be shrunk. A countable trivializing cover and the finite standard projective atlas give second countability. In a local frame $e_1,\ldots ,e_ r$, on the chart $\xi _1\ne 0$ write $\xi =e_1^*+\sum _{\lambda =2}^ r\xi _\lambda e_\lambda ^*$. The vectors $e_\lambda -\xi _\lambda e_1$, $2\leq \lambda \leq r$, are a holomorphic frame of its kernel, and the class of $e_1$ frames the quotient. The same argument in all charts proves the subbundle and exactness assertions. The evaluation pairing \[  E_ x/\ker \xi \  \longrightarrow (\mathbb C\xi )^*,\qquad [v]\longmapsto \bigl (\eta \longmapsto \eta (v)\bigr )  \] is well defined, nonzero and holomorphic in these charts; it is therefore the canonical quotient-line identification. On a fiber this is precisely the dual of the tautological line. For $r=1$ the kernel is zero and the projection has singleton fibers, so the product charts give the asserted identification. For $r=2$ the kernel itself is a line. In coordinates its map is $[\xi _1:\xi _2]\mapsto [-\xi _2:\xi _1]$, with holomorphic inverse given by taking the annihilator. The construction commutes with changes of frame. No general identification of line and hyperplane projectivizations in other ranks is asserted. $\square$ Write $\mathcal O_ E(k)=\mathcal O_ E(1)^{\otimes k}$, using dual powers for negative integers. Theorem 10.37.2 . CB738223B3E9 For every $k\geq 0$ evaluation induces a natural sheaf isomorphism \[  \mathcal O(\operatorname {Sym}^ kE) \  \cong \  \pi _*\mathcal O_ E(k).  \] If $r\geq 2$, then $\pi _*\mathcal O_ E(k)=0$ for $k<0$. If $r=1$, then $\pi _*\mathcal O_ E(k)=\mathcal O(E^{\otimes k})$ for every integer $k$. Proof. The symmetric power of the quotient map in the proposition, composed with pullback of sections, gives the displayed sheaf morphism. Its construction is intrinsic and commutes with restriction. Check it over an open trivialization $E|_ U=U\times V$. The fiber section proposition 10.51.5 , in scalar degree, identifies $H^0(\mathbb P(V^*),\mathcal O(k))$ with $\operatorname {Sym}^ kV$ for $k\geq 0$; it also proves negative vanishing when $\dim V\geq 2$. Its rank-one endpoint is separate. We check holomorphic dependence on the base, rather than infer a parameter statement from this fiberwise identification. Fix $k\geq 0$ and a basis $p_1,\ldots ,p_ M$ of the degree-$k$ homogeneous polynomials on $V^*$. There are $M$ nonzero covectors $\eta _1,\ldots ,\eta _ M$ such that $(p_ j(\eta _ l))_{l,j}$ is invertible. Indeed evaluations span the dual of the polynomial space: a polynomial annihilated by every evaluation is zero, as follows by successively viewing it as a polynomial in each coordinate. A spanning set of a finite-dimensional dual space contains a basis, proving the claim. For a holomorphic section $s$ on $U\times \mathbb P(V^*)$, evaluate its restriction at $[\eta _ l]$ against the fixed tautological tensor $\eta _ l^{\otimes k}$. The resulting scalars $f_ l(x)$ are holomorphic on $U$, because this is evaluation along a holomorphic constant projective section with a fixed nonvanishing line frame. On each fiber write its unique polynomial as $\sum _ ja_ j(x)p_ j$. The invertible constant evaluation matrix gives \[  (a_ j(x))_ j=(p_ j(\eta _ l))_{l,j}^{-1}(f_ l(x))_ l.  \] Thus all coefficients are holomorphic. Conversely holomorphic coefficients define a joint holomorphic section in each projective chart by polynomial evaluation. The two constructions are inverse. Their intrinsic description ensures compatibility with changes of trivialization, giving the asserted sheaf isomorphism. For $k<0$ and $r\geq 2$, every fiber restriction is zero, hence the original section vanishes at every point. For $r=1$ the preceding proposition identifies $\pi $ with the identity and $\mathcal O_ E(k)$ with $E^{\otimes k}$, including negative $k$. $\square$ Proposition 10.37.3 . CFED58EB29EF Give $E$ a smooth Hermitian metric and $\mathcal O_ E(1)$ its quotient metric. At $x_0$, choose holomorphic coordinates $z$ and a holomorphic frame $e_\lambda $ which is unitary and Chern-normal there. Write \[  \Theta (E)_{x_0}e_\lambda =\sum _{j,k,\mu }c_{jk\lambda \mu }\,  dz_ j\wedge d\bar z_ k\otimes e_\mu .  \] For a unit covector $a=\sum _\lambda a_\lambda e_\lambda ^*$, choose an orthonormal basis $b_1,\ldots ,b_{r-1}$ of $a^\perp $ and projective coordinates represented by $a+\sum _\alpha \zeta _\alpha b_\alpha $. Using the splitting given by this Chern-normal frame, at $(x_0,[a])$ one has \[  \Theta (\mathcal O_ E(1)) =\sum _{j,k,\lambda ,\mu }c_{jk\mu \lambda } a_\lambda \bar a_\mu \, dz_ j\wedge d\bar z_ k +\sum _{\alpha =1}^{r-1}d\zeta _\alpha \wedge d\bar\zeta _\alpha .  \] The horizontal term is equivalently $-\langle \Theta (E^*)a,a\rangle $. There is no mixed horizontal–vertical block at this point. Proof. The existing Chern-normal-frame construction the Levi form of a reciprocal bundle norm makes the first derivatives of the metric zero. We may additionally remove its pure holomorphic and antiholomorphic quadratic terms. In column-matrix notation, if the normal metric is \[  M=I+B(z)+B(z)^*+\sum _{j,k}C_{j\bar k}z_ j\bar z_ k+O(|z|^3),  \] with $B$ homogeneous holomorphic quadratic, the holomorphic frame change $g=I-B(z)$ replaces $M$ by $g^*Mg$ and removes $B+B^*$. It does not change the frame or its first jet at zero and hence does not change the displayed tangent splitting or curvature coefficients. The canonical formula $\Theta =\bar\partial (M^{-1}\partial M)$ gives $\Theta _{j\bar k}(0)=-C_{j\bar k}$. Transposing to the matrix of the linear-first products gives \[  \langle e_\lambda ,e_\mu \rangle =\delta _{\lambda \mu }-\sum _{j,k}c_{jk\lambda \mu }z_ j\bar z_ k +O(|z|^3).  \] The dual metric is the transpose of its inverse, so \[  \langle e_\lambda ^*,e_\mu ^*\rangle =\delta _{\lambda \mu }+\sum _{j,k}c_{jk\mu \lambda }z_ j\bar z_ k +O(|z|^3).  \] The tautological line $\mathcal O_ E(-1)$ has the nonzero local holomorphic section $\varepsilon (z,\zeta )=a(z)+\sum _\alpha \zeta _\alpha b_\alpha (z)$, where the coefficients in the dual frame are constant. Orthonormality of $a,b_\alpha $ at the center gives \[  |\varepsilon (z,\zeta )|^2 =1+\sum _\alpha |\zeta _\alpha |^2 +\sum _{j,k,\lambda ,\mu }c_{jk\mu \lambda }a_\lambda \bar a_\mu z_ j\bar z_ k+O(|(z,\zeta )|^3).  \] All omitted base–fiber terms have total degree at least three; the remainder is a joint remainder in both kinds of variables. The dual metric of the quotient line is exactly this restricted dual metric: the minimal-norm representative of a quotient class is orthogonal to $\ker \xi $, and evaluation by $\xi $ on that line has norm $|\xi |$. Thus its duality with the tautological line is isometric. Line curvature therefore gives \[  \Theta (\mathcal O_ E(1))=\partial \bar\partial \log |\varepsilon (z,\zeta )|^2.  \] The first derivatives at the center vanish, so its Hessian is the quadratic expression displayed in the statement. The general dual curvature identity $\Theta (E^*)=-\Theta (E)^{\mathsf T}$ follows by applying the square of the dual connection to the evaluation pairing: the two curvature actions sum to zero. It proves the invariant horizontal description, with the indicated index order. For rank one the vertical sum is empty and the formula is the ordinary line curvature. If $X$ has dimension zero only the projective-fiber Fubini–Study term remains; for rank one over a point both sums vanish. $\square$

title: 6.41 Concurrent slices of positive currents
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text:
Use $d^ c= rac{i}{4\pi }( ar\partial -\partial )$ and $ eta =dd^ c|z|^2$ on $\mathbb C^ n$. Write $\alpha =dd^ c\log |z|^2$ away from zero. A current of bidegree $(c,c)$ has bidimension $(p,p)$, where $p=n-c$. All almost-everywhere assertions on a complex manifold refer to its smooth volume class. In particular they are independent of the choice of a smooth positive volume form. Lemma 6.41.1 . CACB97220D52 A current $A$ whose coefficients and exterior derivative have locally finite measure coefficients has, locally, a representation $A=U+dV$ with $U,V$ having locally integrable coefficients. For weakly convergent closed positive currents $A_ j	o A$, these representations can be chosen with $U_ j	o U$ and $V_ j	o V$ in $L^1$ on compact subsets of a smaller coordinate domain. Proof. Work in real coordinates of dimension $m$. Let $\delta =-\sum _ l\iota _{\partial _ l}\partial _ l$ on coefficient forms. Expanding the two operators gives $d\delta +\delta d=-\Delta $ coefficientwise. With the fundamental solution $E_ m$ of fundamental solutions of the real Laplacian , put $G=-E_ m*$ on compactly supported distributions. A diagonal choice over the countable chart exhaustion proves the claimed subsequence statement for general $A_ j\to A$ in exactly the same way. No full-sequence almost-everywhere assertion is needed or made. Integration of the formula $U_{\rm vert}+d_ zV_{\rm vert}$ against $\theta $ and a compactly supported base density, followed by fiber integration by parts, proves ( 6.41.3 ). There is no base derivative term, since the wedged base volume has top degree. Partitions of unity give the global formula. Positivity then extends it from smooth scalar trace tests to Borel tests: first use increasing continuous approximations on open sets, regularity of the resulting positive measures, and then the monotone class argument. In particular the measure defined by integrating fiber trace measures is precisely the trace obtained by wedging $A$ with the smooth fiber trace form and $f^*\omega _ B$. $\square$

title: Lemma 6.41.4
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text: Lemma 6.41.4 . 0FAC162C7B65 For $0\leq j<n$, a smooth closed $(j,j)$-form on $\mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $ invariant under unitary transformations and positive real dilations is a constant multiple of $\alpha ^ j$. If it is positive, that constant is nonnegative. Proof. For $j=0$ closedness makes the function constant. For $1\leq j<n$, put $t=\log |z|^2$. At $(0,\ldots ,0,a)$, isotropy by $U(n-1)$ forces the form to be a combination of $\alpha ^ j$ and $dt\wedge d^ ct\wedge \alpha ^{j-1}$. To check this explicitly, diagonal unitary phases first annihilate coefficients with unequal holomorphic and antiholomorphic index sets. Permutations of the first $n-1$ coordinates then make the coefficients with the same normal-index choice equal. These are exactly the two displayed forms. Unitary invariance makes their coefficients radial and dilation invariance makes them constant. The derivative of the second form is $-dt\wedge \alpha ^ j$, which is nonzero because $j<n$. Its coefficient must vanish. Evaluating on a tangential complex $j$-plane gives the positivity assertion. No top-degree classification, or singular-current smoothing by radial dilation, is asserted here. $\square$

title: Proposition 6.41.5
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text:
Proposition 6.41.5 . F5E0CCA7AC78 Let $T$ be closed positive of bidegree $(c,c)$ on $B(0,R)$, $0\leq c\leq n$, and let $c\leq q\leq n$. Put \[  Y=\{ (z,S):S\in G(q,n),\  z\in S\} ,\qquad \pi (z,S)=z,\quad \sigma (z,S)=S,  \] and $E=\pi ^{-1}(0)$. The submersion pullback $\pi _0^*T$ on $Y_ R\setminus E$ has locally finite mass across $E$ and its zero extension $\widetilde{\pi _0^*T}$ is closed positive. Define 6A499DD7511C 6.41.6  egin{equation}  \widehat T=  egin{cases}  \widetilde{\pi _0^*T},& q>c,\  \widetilde{\pi _0^*T}+
u (T,0)[E],& q=c. \end{cases} \end{equation} For almost every $S$, its parallel slice under $\sigma $ is a closed positive current $T_ S$ on $S\cap B(0,R)$ of bidimension $(d,d)$, $d=q-c$. Away from zero it is the ordinary parallel restriction; if $T$ is smooth, it is the ordinary restriction everywhere. If $q>c$, the closed order-zero extension of $\pi _0^*T$ across $E$, when it exists, is unique. Proof. The endpoint $q=n$ is the identity construction. If $c=0$, closedness makes $T$ a nonnegative constant on the ball (all its first distributional derivatives vanish, as follows also by mollification); the assertion is immediate, including $q=0$. If $c=n$, only $q=n$ is allowed. We can therefore assume $1\leq c\leq q<n$ and $1\leq p=n-c<n$. The incidence set is the tautological holomorphic rank-$q$ bundle; its graph charts are those of proposition 10.35.1 . For $z
e 0$, its fibers under $\pi $ are the Grassmannians of $(q-1)$-planes in $\mathbb C^ n/\mathbb Cz$, of complex dimension $N=(q-1)(n-q)$; the same graph charts show that $\pi _0$ is a submersion. Its pullback is the closed positive current of pullback of currents by holomorphic submersions . Choose an invariant Kahler form $\omega _ G$ on the Grassmannian, for example the normalized form pulled back by its Plucker embedding. Then $\omega _ Y=\sigma ^*\omega _ G+\pi ^* eta $ is Kahler: a vector killed by the first summand is vertical for $\sigma $, and $\pi $ embeds each such vector into its plane. The complex dimension of $Y$ is $n+N$, and the lift's bidimension is $N+p$. Proper fiber integration over $\pi _0$ gives \[  (\pi _0)_*\omega _ Y^{N+p} =\sum _{k=0}^ p {N+p\choose k}\,   eta ^ k\wedge (\pi _0)_*(\sigma ^*\omega _ G^{N+p-k}).  \] Terms outside the possible degrees vanish. Each remaining last factor is smooth closed positive, unitary and dilation invariant, of bidegree $(p-k,p-k)$; smoothness follows by local smooth fiber integration over the compact Grassmann fibers. The preceding lemma makes it a nonnegative constant multiple of $\alpha ^{p-k}$. The projection formula follows in submersion coordinates from the coefficient product-measure construction and Fubini, so the lift's mass over $\pi ^{-1}(B(0,r)\setminus \{ 0\} )$ is a finite sum of nonnegative constants times \[  \int _{0<|z|<r}T\wedge  eta ^ k\wedge \alpha ^{p-k}.  \] For $k=0$ this is $D_ T(0,r)-
u (T,0)$ by theorem 6.33.1 . For $k\geq 1$, $0\leq \alpha \leq |z|^{-2} eta $ and the ball bound $\mu (B(0,s))\leq C s^{2p}$, $\mu =T\wedge  eta ^ p$, give finiteness. Explicitly the dyadic shell of outer radius $2^{-l}r$ contributes at most $C' (2^{-l}r)^{2k}$; their sum converges. No equality replacing the punctured $k=0$ integral by a full normalized ball mass is used. The zero section is a proper analytic subset. Apply theorem 5.60.3 with the just-proved local finite mass. This gives the zero extension and hence ( 6.41.6 ). Its slices exist by theorem 6.41.2 . A smooth $T$ has $
u (T,0)=0$ if $c>0$, and its smooth pullback has no coefficient mass on $E$, so it agrees with the zero extension. Finally an order-zero closed difference between two extensions is normal and supported on $E$. Its real dimension is $2(N+p)$, whereas $\dim _{\mathbb R}E=2q(n-q)$; their difference is $2d$. If $q>c$, this is positive, so theorem 5.56.3 makes the difference zero. The theorem applies to complex coefficients by linearity; no positivity of the difference is assumed. $\square$

title: Equation 6.41.6

text: 6A499DD7511C 6.41.6 \begin{equation}  \widehat T= \begin{cases}  \widetilde{\pi _0^*T},& q>c,\\  \widetilde{\pi _0^*T}+\nu (T,0)[E],& q=c. \end{cases} \end{equation}

title: Lemma 6.41.7
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text: Lemma 6.41.7 . 2A216A0952DC For $d\geq 1$, $r_0=p-d\geq 0$, and $0<a<R$, 3B4962C3AEC1 6.41.8 \begin{equation}  \int _{0<|z|<a}T\wedge \alpha ^{r_0}\wedge \beta ^ d =a^{2d}D_ T(0,a). \end{equation} Proof. Put $\rho =|z|^2$. Since $\beta =\rho \alpha +\rho ^{-1}d\rho \wedge d^ c\rho $ and the second summand has square zero, direct expansion gives \[  \alpha ^{p-d}\wedge \beta ^ d =d\bigl (\rho ^ d d^ c\log \rho \wedge \alpha ^{p-1}\bigr ).  \] For smooth $T$, Stokes on an annulus $b<|z|<a$ and the sphere identity in theorem 6.33.1 give its integral as $a^{2d}D_ T(0,a)-b^{2d}D_ T(0,b)$. For arbitrary $T$, first mollify and pass on annuli whose boundary spheres carry no trace mass. Positivity and smooth coefficient domination there justify this passage. Approximate the endpoints from below to retain the open outer endpoint and closed inner endpoint exactly as in that theorem. Now let $b\downarrow 0$. The density is bounded above at any fixed larger radius, and $d>0$, so the inner term tends to zero. This proves the formula, including every outer radius by continuity from below. $\square$

title: Equation 6.41.8
