title: Proposition 6.41.9
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text:
Proposition 6.41.9 . BAA80DBD5575 Let $T_ S$ be the slices just constructed and let $
u _ q$ be invariant probability on $G(q,n)$. For every $0<a<R$, D71CDC8687A9 6.41.10  egin{equation}  \int _{G(q,n)}D_{T_ S}(0,a)\, d
u _ q(S)=D_ T(0,a). \end{equation} In particular $\int 
u (T_ S,0)\, d
u _ q(S)\leq 
u (T,0)$. Proof. The endpoints $c=0$ or $q=n$ are immediate, so use the notation of the preceding incidence proof. The invariant probability is a smooth positive top form on the Grassmannian. Away from zero, \[  (\pi _0)_*\sigma ^*
u _ q=\alpha ^{n-q}.  \] Indeed testing a smooth compact form gives the average of its integrals on the planes by ordinary fiber integration over $\sigma $. Thus the identity is precisely the punctured restriction of theorem 5.57.11 , with the same constant. Fubini in submersion charts, or the same product-measure projection formula as above, now gives \[  \int _{G(q,n)}\int _{S\cap B(0,a)\setminus \{ 0\} } T_ S\wedge  eta _ S^ d\, d
u _ q(S) =\int _{0<|z|<a}T\wedge \alpha ^{n-q}\wedge  eta ^ d.  \] There is no missing mass on the zero section in this formula: the zero extension has no coefficient mass there, and smooth wedging preserves that property. Its integrated slice trace has no mass there by ( 6.41.3 ) applied to the Borel zero section. If $d>0$, the individual closed positive slice trace also has no atom at zero by corollary 6.33.5 ; the added section term occurs only when $d=0$. For $d>0$, divide the preceding identity by $a^{2d}$ and apply lemma 6.41.7 , since $n-q=p-d$. For $d=0$, the slices of $[E]$ are $\delta _0$ and the zero extension's slices have no atom there for almost all $S$, by the same Borel identity. Their added mass is exactly $
u (T,0)$. The punctured right side is $D_ T(0,a)-
u (T,0)$, proving the formula in that case as well. Measurability follows from the parallel slicing theorem. As $a\downarrow 0$ the densities converge to their Lelong numbers and are dominated by a fixed larger-radius density whose integral is finite. Dominated convergence in fact gives equality of their averages with $
u (T,0)$; the stated inequality alone will suffice below. $\square$

title: Lemma 6.41.11
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text: Lemma 6.41.11 . CE378B92124B Write $z=(w,v)\in \mathbb C^ q\times \mathbb C^ r$, with $r=n-q$, and let $p=r+d$, $1\leq d\leq q$. On the punctured space put \[  \phi _\varepsilon =\log (|w|^2+|v|^2/\varepsilon ),\quad \gamma _\varepsilon =dd^ c\phi _\varepsilon ,\quad \eta _\varepsilon =d^ c\phi _\varepsilon \wedge \gamma _\varepsilon ^{p-1}.  \] As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, these odd-degree currents satisfy FCD4E7278D0F 6.41.12 \begin{equation}  \eta _\varepsilon \  \longrightarrow  i_*\bigl (d^ c\log |w|^2\wedge \alpha _ S^{d-1}\bigr ) \quad \hbox{on }\mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} , \qquad S=\{ v=0\} . \end{equation} Proof. For $r=0$ this is the identity. For $r>0$, away from $S$ the limit is zero smoothly: after subtracting the irrelevant constant $-\log \varepsilon $, the potential tends smoothly to $\log |v|^2$, and its displayed boundary form of degree $2p-1$ vanishes because $p>r$. Near $S$ in the punctured space, keep $|w|$ bounded below and put $v=\sqrt\varepsilon y$, $a=|w|^2$, $\Phi =a+|y|^2$. Direct differentiation, with the square-zero $d\Phi \wedge d^ c\Phi $ term killed by the first factor, gives \[  d^ c\log \Phi \wedge (dd^ c\log \Phi )^{p-1} =\Phi ^{-p}d^ c\Phi \wedge (\beta _ w+\beta _ y)^{p-1}.  \] In its pairing with a fixed test form, a coefficient containing $k$ normal real differentials contributes a factor $\varepsilon ^{r-k/2}$ after change of variables. The remaining coefficient is bounded by a constant times $(1+|y|)(a+|y|^2)^{-p}$, integrable in $\mathbb R^{2r}$ uniformly for $a$ in a compact subset of $(0,\infty )$: at infinity its radial bound is $O(t^{-2d})$, and $d\geq 1$. Thus every term with $k<2r$ tends to zero, even with the changing compact support of the scaled test. A term with $k=2r$ must take the tangential part $d^ ca$ and exactly $r$ factors $\beta _ y$. Its integral is \[  {p-1\choose r}d^ ca\wedge \beta _ w^{d-1} \int _{\mathbb C^ r}\frac{\beta _ y^ r}{(a+|y|^2)^ p} =a^{-d}d^ ca\wedge \beta _ w^{d-1}.  \] For completeness, normalized polar coordinates give the scalar integral as \[  2r\int _0^\infty \frac{t^{2r-1}}{(a+t^2)^ p}\, dt =\frac{r!(d-1)!}{(p-1)!}a^{-d}.  \] The beta integral here follows, for integers $r,d\geq 1$, by the substitution $s=t^2/a$ and $u=s/(1+s)$, followed by $r-1$ integrations by parts in $\int _0^1 u^{r-1}(1-u)^{d-1}du$. The binomial coefficient cancels it exactly. The resulting odd form is $d^ c\log a\wedge (dd^ c\log a)^{d-1}$ by the same square-zero expansion. Dominated convergence also replaces the scaled test by its restriction to $v=0$. This proves the identity, with the complex normal orientation and with no uncomputed constant or limiting point mass on this punctured domain. $\square$

title: Equation 6.41.12

text: FCD4E7278D0F 6.41.12 \begin{equation}  \eta _\varepsilon \  \longrightarrow  i_*\bigl (d^ c\log |w|^2\wedge \alpha _ S^{d-1}\bigr ) \quad \hbox{on }\mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} , \qquad S=\{ v=0\} . \end{equation}

title: Lemma 6.41.13
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text:
Lemma 6.41.13 . A33ABBC95853 Suppose $T$ is smooth on $B(0,R)\setminus \{ 0\} $, closed positive on the whole ball, and $q>c$. For any plane $S$ for which its concurrent slice exists, \[  
u (T_ S,0)\geq 
u (T,0).  \] Proof. The trivial endpoints having already been treated, take $1\leq p<n$ and unitary coordinates with $S=\{ v=0\} $. Set $r=n-q$ and $d=p-r>0$. Use the potentials of the preceding lemma. For a fixed $\varepsilon >0$, the classical product $\Gamma _\varepsilon =T\wedge \gamma _\varepsilon ^ p$ exists on smaller balls by theorem 7.31.2 . Its atom at zero is $
u (T,0)$: the weight is $\log |z|^2+O_\varepsilon (1)$, so this is corollary 6.34.11 and equation 6.34.4 . We need its full boundary primitive, rather than a convergence assertion tested against the possibly singular $T$ at zero. The coefficient bounds $\gamma _\varepsilon \leq C_\varepsilon |z|^{-2} eta $ and $|d^ c\phi _\varepsilon |\leq C_\varepsilon |z|^{-1}$, with the ball bound for $\mu =T\wedge  eta ^ p$, show that $T\wedge \eta _\varepsilon $ has integrable coefficients near zero: its dyadic shell mass is $O_\varepsilon (s)$ at outer radius $s$. Likewise $T\wedge \gamma _\varepsilon ^{p-1}$ has shell trace mass $O_\varepsilon (s^2)$, and its multiplication by $\phi _\varepsilon $ has mass $O_\varepsilon (s^2(1+|\log s|))$. These are the actual classical products, agreeing with their smooth punctured formulas, since their positive bidimensions exclude any coefficient atom at zero. Insert cutoffs vanishing on $B(0,s)$ and equal to one outside $B(0,2s)$ in their distributional $d^ c$ identity. The error involving the derivative of the cutoff is $O_\varepsilon (s(1+|\log s|))	o 0$. Therefore the classical coefficient recursion gives, on the whole ball, \[  \Gamma _\varepsilon =d(T\wedge \eta _\varepsilon ).  \] Choose $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ smooth, equal to one near zero and supported in $B(0,a)$, $a<R$. Keeping the original pole atom yields \[  
u (T,0)\leq \Gamma _\varepsilon (\chi ) =-\int d\chi \wedge T\wedge \eta _\varepsilon .  \] On the fixed annular support of $d\chi $, $T$ is smooth, so ( 6.41.12 ) legitimately passes this boundary integral to \[  -\int _ S d\chi \wedge T_ S\wedge d^ c\log |w|^2 \wedge \alpha _ S^{d-1}.  \] Apply the same primitive argument to the closed positive current $T_ S$, smooth off zero and of positive bidimension $d$. This last integral is the full classical radial measure $T_ S\wedge \alpha _ S^ d$ evaluated on $\chi |_ S$, including its origin atom. It is at most $D_{T_ S}(0,a)$ by lemma 6.33.8 . Let $a\downarrow 0$. This proves the inequality. No modification or removal of the singularity of $T$ has occurred. $\square$

title: Theorem 6.41.14
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text:
Theorem 6.41.14 . 5BC026092C60 For a closed positive current $T$ of bidimension $(p,p)$ on $B(0,R)\subset \mathbb C^ n$, and $n-p\leq q\leq n$, the normalized concurrent slices defined by ( 6.41.6 ) satisfy \[  
u (T_ S,0)=
u (T,0)  \] for almost every $S\in G(q,n)$. Their finite-radius densities satisfy ( 6.41.10 ). Proof. For $q=c$, the zero extension's slice measure has no atom at zero for almost every $S$ and the added zero section gives exactly $
u (T,0)\delta _0$, as proved above. The identity and constant endpoints also follow from that construction. Assume $q>c$ in the remaining nontrivial range. Let $ho _ j\geq 0$ be smooth probability densities on $\operatorname {GL}_ n(\mathbb C)$ supported in shrinking neighborhoods of the identity and set \[  T_ j=\int g^*T\, ho _ j(g)\, dg.  \] On each smaller ball these are closed positive, tend weakly to $T$, and are smooth away from zero. To verify the last assertion, near $z_0
e 0$ the map $g\mapsto gz_0$ is a submersion (a matrix variation can send $z_0$ to any prescribed vector). Submersion coordinates for the action, with a finite partition on the compact support of $ho _ j$, write the averaging operator as integration against smooth kernels in the image variable. Their derivatives in $z$ remain smooth kernels with common compact support locally, so distributional input coefficients produce smooth output coefficients. This also accounts for the smooth matrix factors in pullback. All constructions are on a common smaller ball before passing to a countable exhaustion. Coordinate invariance in theorem 6.33.10 gives $
u (g^*T,0)=
u (T,0)$. This equality passes through the average: with $g$ in the fixed small compact identity neighborhood, change of variables gives \[  \int _{B(0,a)}g^*T\wedge  eta ^ p =\int _{gB(0,a)}T\wedge (g^{-1})^* eta ^ p \leq \| g^{-1}\| ^{2p}\int _{B(0,\| g\| a)}T\wedge  eta ^ p.  \] Consequently $D_{g^*T}(0,a)\leq C D_ T(0,C'a)$ uniformly for sufficiently small $a$. Thus these densities have a uniform finite bound, and dominated convergence as $a\downarrow 0$ proves $
u (T_ j,0)=
u (T,0)$, including the normalization constant one. The action lifts to the incidence bundle by $g_ Y(z,S)=(gz,gS)$. For $q>c$, the unique closed order-zero extension property proves the exact identity \[  \widehat{T_ j}=\int g_ Y^*\widehat T\, ho _ j(g)\, dg.  \] Both sides are closed positive extensions of the same punctured submersion pullback; the difference is supported on the zero section and is zero by that uniqueness. In particular $\widehat{T_ j}	o \widehat T$ weakly. The parallel slicing subsequence theorem gives $(T_ j)_ S	o T_ S$ weakly for almost every $S$, after one subsequence on all compact fiber charts. The preceding punctured-smooth inequality and upper semicontinuity in theorem 6.33.13 then imply \[  
u (T_ S,0)\geq \limsup _ j
u ((T_ j)_ S,0) \geq 
u (T,0)  \] for almost every $S$. Finally their average is at most $
u (T,0)$ by the average-density proposition. A nonnegative measurable function bounded below almost everywhere by that constant and having integral at most the same constant equals it almost everywhere. This finishes the proof. $\square$

title: 10.83 General complex cohomology and modifications
text: The manifolds in this section are Hausdorff and have a countable basis, and have no boundary. Write $\mathcal A^{p,q}$ and $\mathcal D^{p,q}$ for smooth forms and currents of bidegree $(p,q)$, respectively; their negative or out-of-range bidegrees are zero. Thus a current of bidegree $(p,q)$ acts on compactly supported forms of bidegree $(n-p,n-q)$ on an $n$-fold. Put $a=\partial $ and $b=\bar\partial $, so $a^2=b^2=ab+ba=0$. The factor relating $ab$ to $dd^ c$ is nonzero and does not change any quotient below.

title: 10.82.1 Symbols and exterior algebra
section: 10.82 Symbols, exterior algebra and bundle adjoints
text: Proposition 2.17.2 . 5AFFEC4D76E3 Let $P:C^\infty (M,E)\to C^\infty (M,F)$ be a differential operator of order at most $m$ between smooth real or complex bundles. In charts write $P=\sum _{|\alpha |\le m}A_\alpha \partial ^\alpha $ and use the symbol without Fourier factors, \[  \sigma _ m(P)(x,\xi )=\sum _{|\alpha |=m}A_\alpha (x)\xi ^\alpha .  \] This is an intrinsic homogeneous map $\operatorname {Sym}^ mT^*M \to \operatorname {Hom}(E,F)$. Symbols multiply under composition, with the indicated orders even when the top symbol vanishes. For bundle metrics and a positive smooth density there is a unique formal adjoint $P^*$, and for real covectors \[  \sigma _ m(P^*)(x,\xi )=(-1)^ m\sigma _ m(P)(x,\xi )^*.  \] Injectivity of the symbol for every nonzero real covector is the overdetermined ellipticity condition; for equal ranks it is equivalent to invertibility. This definition alone asserts no Fredholm conclusion. Proof. For a real smooth function $f$ and a local section $u$, $e^{-tf}P(e^{tf}u)$ is a polynomial in $t$ of degree at most $m$. Repeated Leibniz differentiation gives its top coefficient $\sigma _ m(P)(x,df_ x)u(x)$. That expression is invariant under coordinates and frames, and every covector is $df_ x$ for a suitable local $f$. This proves intrinsicness. Applying the same Leibniz rule to $QP$ proves $\sigma _{m+\ell }(QP)=\sigma _\ell (Q)\sigma _ m(P)$. In arbitrary frames let $H_ E,H_ F$ be the metric matrices and let $\rho \, dx$ be the density, with the inner product linear first. Then \[  P^*v=\rho ^{-1}H_ E^{-1} \sum _\alpha (-1)^{|\alpha |}\partial ^\alpha (\rho A_\alpha ^{\dagger }H_ Fv).  \] Integration by parts proves this formula for compactly intersecting supports. At each point a compactly supported test section detects every coefficient of a smooth section, proving uniqueness and hence agreement on overlapping frames. Only derivatives falling on $v$ contribute to the top symbol, proving its formula. For real bundles replace conjugate transpose by transpose. Finally an injective linear map between equal finite dimensions is bijective, proving the last equivalence without a regularity assertion. $\square$ Proposition 10.82.2 . 3765CBF9B2B4 On an oriented Riemannian $d$-manifold the complex-linear Hodge star is determined by $u\wedge *\overline v=\langle u,v\rangle dV$. It is an isometry, and $*^2=(-1)^{k(d-k)}$ on $k$-forms. For a real tangent vector $v$, contraction $\iota _ v$ is the degree $-1$ derivation with $\iota _ v\theta =\theta (v)$ on one-forms; it is adjoint to multiplication by $v^\flat $. If $D$ is a metric connection on a Hermitian bundle, acting on bundle-valued exterior forms, then on forms of degree $k$ \[  D^*=(-1)^{d(k+1)+1}*D*,\qquad \Delta _ D=DD^*+D^*D  \] has principal part $-g^{ij}\partial _ i\partial _ j I$. Flatness is required for $D$ to define a cochain complex, and is not required for these adjoint and principal-part identities. Proof. In a positively oriented real orthonormal coframe, $*e^ I=\epsilon (I,I^ c)e^{I^ c}$. The two permutation signs multiply to $(-1)^{k(d-k)}$, proving the square and isometry assertions. On a wedge of distinct basis covectors contraction deletes $e^ j$ with sign $(-1)^{r-1}$ if it occupies position $r$, and is zero otherwise. This proves the derivation and adjoint rules on a basis and hence generally. The evaluation Leibniz rule for a metric connection, integrated by Stokes against compactly supported forms, gives $D^*=(-1)^{d(k+1)+1}*D*$ on degree $k$; the exponent follows by applying the displayed square in degree $k-1$. For example on one-forms in any dimension the formula has a minus sign before $*D*$, as integration by parts requires. In a real orthonormal frame the first-order part of $D$ is $\sum _ j e^ j\wedge \partial _{e_ j}$ and that of its adjoint is $-\sum _ j\iota _{e_ j}\partial _{e_ j}$. The contraction rule gives $\iota _ v(\theta \wedge u)+\theta \wedge \iota _ vu=\theta (v)u$. Squaring the two first-order parts therefore gives the asserted scalar second-order part; connection and frame derivatives are lower order. Finally $D^2$ is curvature, so the cochain condition is exactly flatness. The complete compact flat-bundle Hodge and duality theorem is already corollary 10.46.10 ; it is not reasserted for nonflat connections. In Euclidean coordinates for the trivial bundle and connection, all lower-order coefficients vanish, so explicitly $d^*u=-\sum _ j\iota _{\partial _{x_ j}}\partial _{x_ j}u$ and $\Delta u=-\sum _{I,j}(\partial _{x_ j}^2u_ I)\, dx^ I$. $\square$

title: Proposition 2.17.2
text: Proposition 2.17.2 . 5AFFEC4D76E3 For a differential operator $P:E\to F$ of order at most $d$, with local expression $P=\sum _{|\alpha |\leq d}a_\alpha \partial ^\alpha $, the degree-$d$ principal symbol is the intrinsic map \[  \sigma _ P(x,\xi )=\sum _{|\alpha |=d}a_\alpha (x)\xi ^\alpha .  \] For a smooth real scalar $f$ and a section $u$, \[  e^{-tf}P(e^{tf}u)=t^ d\sigma _ P(df)u+\sum _{0\leq j<d}t^ jQ_ j u, \qquad \operatorname {ord}Q_ j\leq d-j.  \] Composition has symbol $\sigma _{QP}=\sigma _ Q\sigma _ P$ in the sum of the specified orders. There is a unique formal adjoint, and \[  \sigma _{P^*}(x,\xi )=(-1)^ d\sigma _ P(x,\xi )^*.  \] Injectivity of $\sigma _ P(x,\xi )$ for all real $\xi \ne 0$ is called ellipticity here. If the bundle ranks agree this is invertibility. Proof. The product rule gives the scalar-conjugation identity. The highest power has every derivative landing on the exponential, each through its first derivative. A term of power $t^ j$ leaves at most $d-j$ derivatives on $u$. The left side is intrinsic, so its highest coefficient gives the asserted coordinate and frame invariance. Taking all highest-order derivatives on the section in a composition gives the symbol product, even if that product vanishes and the actual composite order drops. Use smooth orthonormal local frames and write the density as $\rho (x)\, dx$. Integration by parts gives \[  P^*v=\rho ^{-1}\sum _{|\alpha |\leq d}(-1)^{|\alpha |} \partial ^\alpha (\rho a_\alpha ^*v).  \] This is a differential operator with the claimed leading symbol. The integration identity on compactly supported test sections proves uniqueness, hence the formulas glue on overlaps. A cutoff equal to one near a compact intersection of supports gives the same identity for arbitrary sections with that compact intersection. Derivatives of the cutoff contribute zero, since one of the two sections is then zero near each such point. This also defines the action on distributional sections by transposition. The argument uses a density and does not require orientability. $\square$ Proposition 2.17.2 . 5AFFEC4D76E3 Let $P:C^\infty (M,E)\to C^\infty (M,F)$ be a differential operator of order at most $m$ between smooth real or complex bundles. In charts write $P=\sum _{|\alpha |\le m}A_\alpha \partial ^\alpha $ and use the symbol without Fourier factors, \[  \sigma _ m(P)(x,\xi )=\sum _{|\alpha |=m}A_\alpha (x)\xi ^\alpha .  \] This is an intrinsic homogeneous map $\operatorname {Sym}^ mT^*M \to \operatorname {Hom}(E,F)$. Symbols multiply under composition, with the indicated orders even when the top symbol vanishes. For bundle metrics and a positive smooth density there is a unique formal adjoint $P^*$, and for real covectors \[  \sigma _ m(P^*)(x,\xi )=(-1)^ m\sigma _ m(P)(x,\xi )^*.  \] Injectivity of the symbol for every nonzero real covector is the overdetermined ellipticity condition; for equal ranks it is equivalent to invertibility. This definition alone asserts no Fredholm conclusion. Proof. For a real smooth function $f$ and a local section $u$, $e^{-tf}P(e^{tf}u)$ is a polynomial in $t$ of degree at most $m$. Repeated Leibniz differentiation gives its top coefficient $\sigma _ m(P)(x,df_ x)u(x)$. That expression is invariant under coordinates and frames, and every covector is $df_ x$ for a suitable local $f$. This proves intrinsicness. Applying the same Leibniz rule to $QP$ proves $\sigma _{m+\ell }(QP)=\sigma _\ell (Q)\sigma _ m(P)$. In arbitrary frames let $H_ E,H_ F$ be the metric matrices and let $\rho \, dx$ be the density, with the inner product linear first. Then \[  P^*v=\rho ^{-1}H_ E^{-1} \sum _\alpha (-1)^{|\alpha |}\partial ^\alpha (\rho A_\alpha ^{\dagger }H_ Fv).  \] Integration by parts proves this formula for compactly intersecting supports. At each point a compactly supported test section detects every coefficient of a smooth section, proving uniqueness and hence agreement on overlapping frames. Only derivatives falling on $v$ contribute to the top symbol, proving its formula. For real bundles replace conjugate transpose by transpose. Finally an injective linear map between equal finite dimensions is bijective, proving the last equivalence without a regularity assertion. $\square$

title: Proposition 10.82.2
section: 10.82 Symbols, exterior algebra and bundle adjoints
text: Proposition 10.82.2 . 3765CBF9B2B4 On an oriented Riemannian $d$-manifold the complex-linear Hodge star is determined by $u\wedge *\overline v=\langle u,v\rangle dV$. It is an isometry, and $*^2=(-1)^{k(d-k)}$ on $k$-forms. For a real tangent vector $v$, contraction $\iota _ v$ is the degree $-1$ derivation with $\iota _ v\theta =\theta (v)$ on one-forms; it is adjoint to multiplication by $v^\flat $. If $D$ is a metric connection on a Hermitian bundle, acting on bundle-valued exterior forms, then on forms of degree $k$ \[  D^*=(-1)^{d(k+1)+1}*D*,\qquad \Delta _ D=DD^*+D^*D  \] has principal part $-g^{ij}\partial _ i\partial _ j I$. Flatness is required for $D$ to define a cochain complex, and is not required for these adjoint and principal-part identities. Proof. In a positively oriented real orthonormal coframe, $*e^ I=\epsilon (I,I^ c)e^{I^ c}$. The two permutation signs multiply to $(-1)^{k(d-k)}$, proving the square and isometry assertions. On a wedge of distinct basis covectors contraction deletes $e^ j$ with sign $(-1)^{r-1}$ if it occupies position $r$, and is zero otherwise. This proves the derivation and adjoint rules on a basis and hence generally. The evaluation Leibniz rule for a metric connection, integrated by Stokes against compactly supported forms, gives $D^*=(-1)^{d(k+1)+1}*D*$ on degree $k$; the exponent follows by applying the displayed square in degree $k-1$. For example on one-forms in any dimension the formula has a minus sign before $*D*$, as integration by parts requires. In a real orthonormal frame the first-order part of $D$ is $\sum _ j e^ j\wedge \partial _{e_ j}$ and that of its adjoint is $-\sum _ j\iota _{e_ j}\partial _{e_ j}$. The contraction rule gives $\iota _ v(\theta \wedge u)+\theta \wedge \iota _ vu=\theta (v)u$. Squaring the two first-order parts therefore gives the asserted scalar second-order part; connection and frame derivatives are lower order. Finally $D^2$ is curvature, so the cochain condition is exactly flatness. The complete compact flat-bundle Hodge and duality theorem is already corollary 10.46.10 ; it is not reasserted for nonflat connections. In Euclidean coordinates for the trivial bundle and connection, all lower-order coefficients vanish, so explicitly $d^*u=-\sum _ j\iota _{\partial _{x_ j}}\partial _{x_ j}u$ and $\Delta u=-\sum _{I,j}(\partial _{x_ j}^2u_ I)\, dx^ I$. $\square$

title: 10.81 Complex lattice quotients
text: Example 10.81.1 . EA6824E4DE53 If $\Gamma \subset V=\mathbb C^ n$ is the integer span of a real basis of $V$, then $V/\Gamma $ is a compact complex manifold. Every constant positive Hermitian form on $V$ defines a Kähler metric on it. Proof. The real-linear map sending the standard basis to the generators of $\Gamma $ identifies it with $\mathbb Z^{2n}$. Hence it is discrete, closed, and meets each bounded set in finitely many points. Small balls whose pairwise lattice translates are disjoint give complex charts on the quotient, with translation transition maps. Two inequivalent points have disjoint such neighborhoods because their difference has positive distance from the closed lattice; thus the quotient is Hausdorff. It has a countable basis from rational balls. The closed fundamental parallelepiped is compact and maps onto the quotient. A constant positive Hermitian form and its associated real positive $(1,1)$-form are translation invariant; the latter is closed because its coefficients are constant. They descend to the required metric. In dimension zero these statements refer to a point. $\square$

title: 10.84 The Frölicher filtration
text: Theorem 10.84.1 . F105D4917B45 For a complex $n$-manifold the filtration \[  F^ p\mathcal A^ k(X)=\bigoplus _{r\ge p}\mathcal A^{r,k-r}(X)  \] has a natural spectral sequence $E_1^{p,q}=H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial }(X)$ converging to $\operatorname {gr}_ F^ pH^{p+q}_{\rm dR}(X,\mathbb C)$. If $X$ is compact, all its pages from $E_1$ are finite dimensional, and, writing $h^{p,q}=\dim H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial }(X)$ and $b_ k=\dim H^ k_{\rm dR}(X,\mathbb C)$, one has \[  b_ k\le \sum _{p+q=k}h^{p,q},\qquad \sum _ k(-1)^ kb_ k=\sum _{p,q}(-1)^{p+q}h^{p,q}.  \] Equality in the first inequality for every $k$ is equivalent to degeneration at $E_1$. This gives a canonical associated-graded identification, and a direct-sum isomorphism after choosing splittings of the finite filtrations; degeneration alone does not choose those splittings. Moreover \[  b_1\ge (h^{1,0}-h^{2,0})_+ +(h^{0,1}-h^{1,1}-h^{2,0})_+, \qquad t_+=\max \{ t,0\} .  \] Proof. The filtration is by subcomplexes because $\partial $ raises the first index and $\bar\partial $ preserves it. It equals the whole complex for $p\le 0$ and is zero for $p>n$. Apply the fully constructed pages and finite convergence in theorem 10.54.2 , theorem 10.54.3 . The associated-graded differential is $\bar\partial $, the next is induced by $\partial $, giving the asserted first page. This part uses no compactness. Compact Dolbeault finiteness is theorem 10.46.6 , and de Rham finiteness is corollary 10.46.10 for the trivial line. Put $e_ r^ k=\sum _{p+q=k}\dim E_ r^{p,q}$ and let $t_ r^ k$ be the sum of ranks of $d_ r$ out of total degree $k$. Since $d_ r$ raises total degree by one, page cohomology gives exactly \[  e_{r+1}^ k=e_ r^ k-t_ r^ k-t_ r^{k-1}.  \] The limiting sum is $b_ k$ by the finite associated-graded filtration. This proves the inequality. Equality for every $k$ forces every nonnegative loss $t_ r^ k$ to vanish, which is precisely degeneration; the converse is immediate. Alternating the displayed identity and summing the finitely many degrees cancels the two rank sums, proving Euler invariance and hence the Euler formula. Equivalently, for any bounded finite-dimensional complex, if $z_ k,b_ k'$ denote dimensions of cycles and boundaries, then $\dim C^ k=z_ k+b'_{k+1}$ and $\dim H^ k=z_ k-b'_ k$, giving the same cancellation. The finite filtration splits over $\mathbb C$ by choosing a linear section of each quotient successively; this explains existence of an abstract sum isomorphism. To see why this procedure is not canonical, the two-dimensional space with filtration $0\subset \mathbb Ce_1\subset \mathbb C^2$ has filtration-preserving automorphisms $e_1\mapsto e_1$, $e_2\mapsto e_2+ce_1$ inducing the identity on every graded piece. No complement to $\mathbb Ce_1$ is preserved by all of them. An assertion based only on the graded identification cannot choose a natural splitting. For the last inequality, the first-page map out of $E_1^{0,0}$ is zero: holomorphic functions on each compact connected component are constant, by the maximum principle. Hence $\dim E_2^{1,0}\ge (h^{1,0}-h^{2,0})_+$ and $\dim E_2^{0,1}\ge (h^{0,1}-h^{1,1})_+$. In the first quadrant no later differential enters or leaves $(1,0)$; the only later arrow involving $(0,1)$ is $d_2:E_2^{0,1}\to E_2^{2,0}$. Consequently \[  b_1=\dim E_2^{1,0}+\dim \ker d_2 \ge \dim E_2^{1,0} +(\dim E_2^{0,1}-\dim E_2^{2,0})_+.  \] Using $\dim E_2^{2,0}\le h^{2,0}$ proves the stated bound. All finite-dimensional and zero-index cases are included. $\square$

title: 10.85 Bott–Chern and Aeppli comparison
text: For either smooth forms or currents put \[  H^{p,q}_{\rm BC}=\frac{\ker a\cap \ker b}{ab(\mathcal A^{p-1,q-1})}, \qquad H^{p,q}_{\rm A}=\frac{\ker (ab:\mathcal A^{p,q}\to \mathcal A^{p+1,q+1})}{a\mathcal A^{p-1,q}+b\mathcal A^{p,q-1}},  \] replacing $\mathcal A$ by $\mathcal D$ for currents. Lemma 10.85.1 . D823F74394BA Let $Q^{p,q}$ be a bounded double complex of vector spaces, with anticommuting differentials $a,b$. If every row and column is exact, then its Bott–Chern and Aeppli groups are zero in every bidegree. Proof. Translate the bounded index rectangle so that its lower bounds are zero. If $ax=bx=0$, row exactness gives $x=au_1$. Successively choose $u_ j\in Q^{p-j,q+j-1}$ with $bu_ j=au_{j+1}$, using row exactness; the right-hand side is available because $a(bu_ j)=-b(au_ j)=0$. At the left boundary $bu_ p=0$, since $a$ has zero kernel there. Column exactness gives $u_ p=bv_ p$. Now $b(u_{p-1}+av_ p)=0$, so $u_{p-1}+av_ p=bv_{p-1}$. Continuing backwards gives $u_1=bv_1-av_2$ and $x=abv_1$. If the starting index is on the left boundary, $ax=0$ already implies $x=0$. If the staircase reaches the upper boundary first, the same argument stops there with $bu_ j=0$. Thus no endpoint was excluded. Finally if $abx=0$, then $bx$ is closed for both maps. The assertion just proved gives $bx=abv$, whence $b(x+av)=0$. Column exactness gives $x+av=bw$, so $x=bw-av$, proving Aeppli vanishing as well. $\square$ Theorem 10.85.2 . 72D73EDC0883 For every complex manifold and every bidegree, inclusion of smooth forms into currents induces natural isomorphisms on Bott–Chern and Aeppli cohomology. No compactness, Kähler assumption, or positivity of either index is required. Proof. Form the double complex of vector spaces $Q^{p,q}=\mathcal D^{p,q}(X)/\mathcal A^{p,q}(X)$. For each fixed $p$, the smooth/current Dolbeault comparison corollary 10.43.11 is an isomorphism in every degree. The long exact sequence of the quotient complexes therefore makes every $b$-column of $Q$ exact; conjugation gives the same for every $a$-row. This uses actual global cohomology comparison, rather than assuming global $\bar\partial $ solvability. The preceding staircase applies. For surjectivity on BC, let $T$ be a current closed for both maps. Its image in $Q$ is $abq$. Lift $q$ to a current $U$. Then $T-abU$ is smooth and closed for both maps. For injectivity, suppose the smooth closed form $\alpha $ is $abT$ for a current $T$. The image $t$ of $T$ in $Q$ is Aeppli closed, so $t=au+bv$. Lift $u,v$ to currents. Subtracting $aU+bV$ from $T$ makes it smooth without changing $abT$. Thus $\alpha $ is already smoothly BC exact. For surjectivity on Aeppli, if $abT=0$ its quotient class is $au+bv$, so subtracting current lifts $aU+bV$ makes $T$ smooth without changing its Aeppli class. For injectivity write a smooth form $\alpha =aU+bV$ with currents $U,V$. Their quotient images satisfy $au=-bv$; that common value is closed for both maps. Write $au=abq$ by BC vanishing in $Q$. Then $a(u-bq)=0$ and $b(v-aq)=0$, so row and column exactness give $u-bq=ac$ and $v-aq=be$. After lifting $q,c,e$ to currents, both $U-bQ-aC$ and $V-aQ-bE$ are smooth; their $a$- and $b$-derivatives still sum to $\alpha $, since $ab+ba=0$. This proves injectivity. Inclusion and all constructed quotient maps commute with restrictions; the isomorphisms themselves are the canonical inclusion maps, independent of the choices of lifts. $\square$

title: 10.86 Finite sheaf complexes for Bott–Chern cohomology
search_title: Finite sheaf complexes for Bott–Chern cohomology
section: 10.86 Finite sheaf complexes for Bott–Chern cohomology
text: Let $\Omega ^ j$ be holomorphic $j$-forms and $\overline\Omega ^ j$ antiholomorphic $j$-forms. Let $\mathcal Z^{j,q}=\ker b$ on smooth $(j,q)$-forms or on currents, as specified. Lemma 10.86.1 . 6C01A2D464F2 For $q=0$ the complex $(\mathcal Z^{\bullet ,0},a)$ resolves $\mathbb C$ in degree zero. For $q\ge 1$ its only cohomology sheaf is in degree zero and is naturally $b\overline\Omega ^{q-1}$. These statements hold both for smooth forms and for currents. Proof. All assertions are local. The smooth/current Dolbeault lemma and its conjugate, including holomorphic regularity at degree zero, are local Dolbeault exactness for forms and currents , corollary 10.43.11 . For $q=0$ they identify $\mathcal Z^{j,0}$ with $\Omega ^ j$; the holomorphic radial homotopy is exact except for constants. Explicitly, on a star-shaped polydisc integrate contraction with the radial vector field along $z\mapsto tz$; differentiating gives $ah+ha=I-\operatorname {ev}_0$, and holomorphic coefficients remain holomorphic under this integral. Conjugation gives the identical statement for antiholomorphic forms. For $q\ge 1$, local Dolbeault exactness gives the short exact sequence of horizontal complexes \[  0\longrightarrow \mathcal Z^{\bullet ,q-1} \longrightarrow \mathcal A^{\bullet ,q-1} \xrightarrow {\, (-1)^ j b\, }\mathcal Z^{\bullet ,q} \longrightarrow 0.  \] Use $\mathcal D$ in the middle for currents. The factor $(-1)^ j$ makes the quotient arrow commute with $a$. The middle horizontal complex has only degree-zero cohomology $\overline\Omega ^{q-1}$, by the conjugate Dolbeault lemma. Induction and the cochain long exact sequence show that the right complex has no positive-degree cohomology and has degree-zero cohomology $\overline\Omega ^{q-1}/b\overline\Omega ^{q-2}$, with constants in the denominator when $q=1$. The antiholomorphic radial homotopy identifies that quotient with $b\overline\Omega ^{q-1}$. These are actual kernel sheaves; no global primitive is asserted. $\square$ Fix $p,q\ge 1$. Put $k_0=p+q$ and define a bounded complex $L_{p,q}$ by \[  L^ k=\bigoplus _{r+s=k,\  r<p,\  s<q}\mathcal A^{r,s} \quad (k\le k_0-2),\qquad L^ k=\bigoplus _{r+s=k+1,\  r\ge p,\  s\ge q}\mathcal A^{r,s} \quad (k\ge k_0-1).  \] Its differential is the truncated $a+b$ except for the joining map $ab:\mathcal A^{p-1,q-1}\to \mathcal A^{p,q}$. The square is zero, including at the two joints, by $a^2=b^2=ab+ba=0$. Let $M_{p,q}$ be the same complex of currents. Let $S'$ be $\Omega ^ j$ in degrees $0\le j<p$, with differential $a$ truncated at the last term, and let $S''$ be $\overline\Omega ^ j$ in degrees $0\le j<q$, with differential $b$. Their sum inside $L$ is denoted $S$; in degree zero it is $\mathcal O+\overline{\mathcal O}$, with constants counted once. Proposition 10.86.2 . 6ED26B437C1C For $p,q\ge 1$ the actual inclusions $S\to L_{p,q}\to M_{p,q}$ are quasi-isomorphisms. For $p,q\ge 2$ their cohomology sheaves are $\mathbb C$ in degree zero, $a\Omega ^{p-1}$ in degree $p-1$, and $b\overline\Omega ^{q-1}$ in degree $q-1$; when $p=q$ the last two sheaves are a direct sum in their common degree. For $p=1<q$ replace the degree-zero sheaf by $\mathcal O$; for $q=1<p$ it is $\overline{\mathcal O}$; for $p=q=1$ it is $\mathcal O+\overline{\mathcal O}$ and all positive-degree sheaves vanish. The remaining terminal sheaf in the one-index cases is as in the preceding display. Proof. First assume $q\ge 2$ and filter all three complexes by the first bidegree. This is a finite filtration, so it suffices to show that the actual inclusion $S\to L$ induces an isomorphism on its second page at every stalk. For a lower column $r<p$, vertical cohomology is $\Omega ^ r$ in row zero and \[  \mathcal A^{r,q-1}/b\mathcal A^{r,q-2} \simeq \mathcal Z^{r,q}  \] in row $q-1$, by sending a class to $b$ of a representative. All other rows vanish. For an upper column $r\ge p$, the degree shift in the definition of $L$ places its sole vertical group $\mathcal Z^{r,q}$ in that same row $q-1$. Multiplying the lower identifications by $(-1)^ r$ and the upper ones by $(-1)^{p-1}$ makes the differential along this row $a$, including the join induced by $ab$. The row-zero complex is the truncated holomorphic de Rham complex $S'$. For $S$, vertical cohomology gives precisely that row-zero complex and $b\overline\Omega ^{q-1}$ in position $(0,q-1)$. The latter maps to the row $(\mathcal Z^{r,q},a)$ by its actual inclusion. It is its degree-zero cohomology and that row is otherwise exact by lemma 10.86.1 . The second pages are therefore isomorphic under the inclusion. Finite filtered comparison proves the asserted quasi-isomorphism, without suppressing the total degree $r+q-1$ of the terminal row. Exactly the same argument applies to currents: the vertical kernel in degree zero is still holomorphic by the distributional Dolbeault lemma, and the preceding resolution lemma explicitly included currents. Consequently $S\to M$ is also a quasi-isomorphism and so is $L\to M$. If $q=1<p$, interchange the two bidegrees and conjugate this proof. A fixed minus on one side of the joining map compensates for $ba=-ab$ and does not change any comparison. If $p=q=1$, the first page for $L$ is the one-row complex \[  \mathcal A^{0,0}\xrightarrow {ab}\mathcal Z^{1,1} \xrightarrow a\mathcal Z^{2,1}\xrightarrow a\cdots .  \] The horizontal resolution lemma says the positive part is exact: at its first term every kernel is $a\mathcal Z^{0,1}$, and local Dolbeault exactness makes $\mathcal Z^{0,1}=b\mathcal A^{0,0}$. Its degree-zero kernel consists of $f$ with $abf=0$. Then $bf$ is an antiholomorphic closed one-form, hence is $bg$ for an antiholomorphic function $g$ locally; $f-g$ is holomorphic. Thus the kernel is $\mathcal O+\overline{\mathcal O}$. The current proof is identical, since degree-zero $a$- or $b$-closed distributions are regular antiholomorphic or holomorphic functions. This proves the two remaining quasi-isomorphisms. title: Lemma 10.86.1

text: Lemma 10.86.1 . 6C01A2D464F2 For $q=0$ the complex $(\mathcal Z^{\bullet ,0},a)$ resolves $\mathbb C$ in degree zero. For $q\ge 1$ its only cohomology sheaf is in degree zero and is naturally $b\overline\Omega ^{q-1}$. These statements hold both for smooth forms and for currents. Proof. All assertions are local. The smooth/current Dolbeault lemma and its conjugate, including holomorphic regularity at degree zero, are local Dolbeault exactness for forms and currents , corollary 10.43.11 . For $q=0$ they identify $\mathcal Z^{j,0}$ with $\Omega ^ j$; the holomorphic radial homotopy is exact except for constants. Explicitly, on a star-shaped polydisc integrate contraction with the radial vector field along $z\mapsto tz$; differentiating gives $ah+ha=I-\operatorname {ev}_0$, and holomorphic coefficients remain holomorphic under this integral. Conjugation gives the identical statement for antiholomorphic forms. For $q\ge 1$, local Dolbeault exactness gives the short exact sequence of horizontal complexes \[  0\longrightarrow \mathcal Z^{\bullet ,q-1} \longrightarrow \mathcal A^{\bullet ,q-1} \xrightarrow {\, (-1)^ j b\, }\mathcal Z^{\bullet ,q} \longrightarrow 0.  \] Use $\mathcal D$ in the middle for currents. The factor $(-1)^ j$ makes the quotient arrow commute with $a$. The middle horizontal complex has only degree-zero cohomology $\overline\Omega ^{q-1}$, by the conjugate Dolbeault lemma. Induction and the cochain long exact sequence show that the right complex has no positive-degree cohomology and has degree-zero cohomology $\overline\Omega ^{q-1}/b\overline\Omega ^{q-2}$, with constants in the denominator when $q=1$. text: Proposition 10.86.2 . 6ED26B437C1C For $p,q\ge 1$ the actual inclusions $S\to L_{p,q}\to M_{p,q}$ are quasi-isomorphisms. title: 10.87 Strong Hodge structure under modifications
text: The natural maps used here are \[  j^{p,q}:H^{p,q}_{\rm BC}\to H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial },\qquad k^ r:\bigoplus _{p+q=r}H^{p,q}_{\rm BC} \to H^ r_{\rm dR}(X,\mathbb C),  \] induced by the same closed forms. A compact complex manifold has strong Hodge decomposition when all these maps are isomorphisms. The resulting subspaces of de Rham cohomology are canonical; conjugation exchanges types. This is stronger data than an abstract splitting of the Frölicher filtration. The Fujiki class $(\mathcal C)$ consists here of compact complex manifolds admitting a Kähler modification. Theorem 10.87.1 . C4B9BA82F24B Let $\mu :\widetilde X\to X$ be a modification of compact complex manifolds: they have equal dimension and $\mu $ is biholomorphic off a positive-codimension analytic subset and its inverse image. If $\widetilde X$ has strong Hodge decomposition, then so does $X$. More generally, proper holomorphic maps of relative complex dimension $r$ have natural pushforward maps on de Rham, Dolbeault and Bott–Chern cohomology lowering types by $(r,r)$, commuting with the displayed natural maps and satisfying the projection formula against smooth classes. Pullback is defined by smooth forms. Consequently every compact complex manifold admitting a Kähler modification has strong Hodge decomposition, Hodge symmetry and first-page Frölicher degeneration. Proof. A proper map pushes a current forward by evaluation on the pullback of a compactly supported test form; properness makes that pullback have compact support. The differential and bidegree rules and the projection formula are the current calculus manifold cutoffs, partitions and compact-support Stokes , Stokes' formula on compact domains with corners and the definition: testing against $\eta $ gives $F_*(T\wedge F^*\beta )(\eta )=T(F^*(\beta \wedge \eta ))$ with the same graded convention on both sides. Thus it commutes with $a,b$ and lowers bidegree by the relative dimension, and descends to all three current quotients. Smooth/current de Rham and Dolbeault comparison is corollary 10.43.11 ; BC comparison is theorem 10.85.2 . These actual inclusion maps transport pushforward to the smooth groups and make it independent of representatives. They commute with the natural maps $j,k$ because all of them use the same current representative. Smooth pullback commutes with $a,b$ and likewise descends. For the modification, $\mu _*\mu ^*\alpha =\alpha $ as currents for every smooth form $\alpha $. Test against a smooth form $\beta $ of complementary degree. The integral of $\mu ^*(\alpha \wedge \beta )$ equals that of $\alpha \wedge \beta $ by the biholomorphic change of variables off the exceptional sets. A proper analytic subset of a connected manifold has zero smooth volume: in a coordinate chart, a nonzero holomorphic function vanishing on it has a zero set of real measure zero, by one-variable isolated zeros and induction with Fubini on its power-series coefficients. Countably many charts suffice. Thus deleting these sets changes neither integral. If a whole connected component upstairs maps into the exceptional subset, the complex Jacobian vanishes identically on it: an invertible Jacobian at one point would give an open image by the inverse function theorem. The pulled-back top-degree form is therefore zero on that component, so it also contributes nothing. This includes that harmless extra component possibility if the definition does not require a dense biholomorphic locus upstairs. The current equality and all three comparison maps prove $\mu _*\mu ^*=I$ on the cohomology groups in question. Consider either $j^{p,q}$ or $k^ r$. Its square under $\mu ^*$ commutes, as does its square under $\mu _*$. If a class downstairs maps to zero, pull it up, use injectivity of the upper isomorphism, then apply $\mu _*$ to conclude it is zero. Given a target class downstairs, pull it up, lift through the upper isomorphism, then push that lift down. Commutativity and $\mu _*\mu ^*=I$ show that this is a preimage. Both downstairs maps are therefore isomorphisms. Compact Kähler manifolds have strong Hodge decomposition by theorem 10.47.13 . Applying the result to a Kähler modification proves the last assertion. Conjugation is well defined on BC, and the canonical pure-type de Rham sum gives Hodge symmetry; its dimensions give equality in every Frölicher inequality and hence degeneration by theorem 10.84.1 . $\square$

Proposition 6.43.1 . AD7655D0958A Let $F:(\mathbb C^ q,0)	o (\mathbb C^ N,0)$ be a holomorphic germ, where $q\geq 1$, and suppose $F^{-1}(0)=\{ 0\} $ as a germ. Then \[  d(F,0):= igl ((dd^ c\log |F|^2)^ q igr )(\{ 0\} )  \] is a positive integer. More precisely, on a proper finite representative $F:V	o B=F(V)$, let $s$ be its generic sheet number. Then \[  d(F,0)=s\operatorname {mult}_0 B.  \] For every cone-adapted linear projection $P:\mathbb C^ N	o \mathbb C^ q$ of the image germ, $PF$ is finite at zero and its local sheet number is $d(F,0)$. When $N=q$, $d(F,0)$ is simply the local sheet number of $F$. This assertion does not use integer Lelong numbers for general currents or an integer-coefficient decomposition theorem. Proof. Choose a small ball $U$ with $\overline U\cap F^{-1}(0)=\{ 0\} $ and with $F$ defined near its closure. The compact image $F(\partial U)$ misses zero. For a sufficiently small target ball $W$, the map from $V=U\cap F^{-1}(W)$ to $W$ is proper: the preimage of a compact subset cannot accumulate on $\partial U$. Its fibers are compact analytic subsets of the Euclidean domain $U$, hence finite by the maximum principle on analytic branches . Its image $B$ is analytic by Remmert's proper mapping theorem . The image germ is irreducible because the domain germ is, and its dimension is $q$: otherwise the maximum rank on the domain would be smaller than $q$ and the constant-rank theorem would give positive-dimensional fibers. Shrink to these germs' representatives. The exact proper-cycle degree argument in lemma 20.5.3 gives $F_*[V]=s[B]$ with $s\in \mathbb Z_{>0}$. Literally apply that lemma to the smooth prime hypersurface $D=V	imes \{ 0\} $ of $V	imes \mathbb C$ and the map $F\circ \operatorname {pr}_ V$. Its proof constructs the analytic critical image, the finite covering off it and the zero coefficient mass on its exceptional set; no integrality of a cycle limit is being assumed here. The weight $u=\log |F|^2$ has its sole pole at zero. Compact inner sublevels therefore meet the hypotheses of theorem 7.31.2 on $V$, so its top power includes the pole atom. The proper weighted projection identity in proposition 6.35.1 gives \[   igl ((dd^ cu)^ q igr )(\{ 0\} ) =
u ([V],u)=

u ([B],0)=s\operatorname {mult}_0B.  \] The last equality is theorem 6.38.3 . For a cone-adapted $P$ on $B$, the bound $|w|\leq C|Pw|$ on $B$ proves that $PF$ still has only the point pole and that $\log |F|^2-\log |PF|^2$ is bounded. The same projection computation and bounded-change theorem give the same atom. The two coverings compose off the union of their proper analytic exceptional images, so its sheet number is $s\operatorname {mult}_0B$. If $N=q$, the image is a neighborhood of zero, by the finite open-map theorem, and has multiplicity one. $\square$ Lemma 6.43.2 . B1AA1442D441 If $H:(\mathbb C^ q,0)	o (\mathbb C^ q,0)$ is finite at zero, then the proper divisor intersection \[  dd^ c\log |H_1|^2\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ c\log |H_ q|^2  \] is $d(H,0)[\{ 0\} ]$ as a germ. Proof. Every $j$-fold intersection of distinct coordinate divisors has codimension at least $j$. Otherwise a branch of dimension greater than $q-j$, cut by the remaining $q-j$ equations, would still have positive dimension at zero; at each step a holomorphic equation drops dimension by at most one. This contradicts the point fiber. The analytic hypersurface-dimension theorem proves this argument also on singular intermediate branches. Hence the stated symmetric classical product exists, and theorem 20.5.10 makes it $a[\{ 0\} ]$ for a positive integer $a$. Choose a proper finite representative $H:V	o W$ onto a target ball. It has $H_*[V]=d(H,0)[W]$ by the proposition. For smooth approximations $v_{j,\epsilon }=\log (|w_ j|^2+\epsilon )$, ordinary pullback, pushforward and the defining recursive product give \[  H_* igwedge _{j=1}^ q dd^ c(v_{j,\epsilon }\circ H) =d(H,0) igwedge _{j=1}^ q dd^ cv_{j,\epsilon }.  \] Both sides converge by the precise decreasing-product theorem: the coordinate zero sets have the mutual codimensions just checked on source and target. Proper pushforward commutes with this weak convergence, since the inverse image of a test support is compact. The target limit is $[\{ 0\} ]$, by ordinary coordinate Poincare–Lelong. The source limit has support at the unique preimage of zero, so its pushforward is $a[\{ 0\} ]$. Thus $a=d(H,0)$. $\square$

Lemma 6.44.1 . C6BF252FC877 Let $Z\subset (\mathbb C^ n,0)$ be an analytic germ with $\dim _0Z\leq n-p$, where $1\leq p\leq n$. There is a proper analytic subset $E\subset G(p,n)$ such that, for every $S

Lemma 6.45.1 . D72B7AE5B407 A locally pluripolar subset of a neighborhood of $\mathrm U(n)$ in $\mathrm{GL}_ n(\mathbb C)$ has Haar measure zero on $\mathrm U(n)$. Proof. First a nontrivial subharmonic function on a neighborhood of a real interval has a pole set of one-dimensional measure zero on that interval. On smaller neighborhoods its Riesz decomposition the local Riesz decomposition writes it as a harmonic function plus a finite logarithmic potential. On compact intervals $I$, \[  \sup _{a\in K}\int _ I|\log |t-a||\, dt<\infty  \] for every compact set $K\subset \mathbb C$. The positive part is bounded above uniformly, and the negative part is bounded by the integral of $-\log |t-\operatorname {Re}a|$ where this is positive. Absolute Fubini makes the potential integrable on $I$ and proves the assertion. An exhaustion handles the whole interval. It follows by induction that the pole set of a nontrivial plurisubharmonic function in a complex polydisc has real measure zero on its middle real cube. Indeed, positive real measure of the pole set gives a positive-measure set of the last $d-1$ real coordinates whose first-coordinate subharmonic slices have a positive-measure pole set. Those slices are identically $-\infty $. For every fixed complex first coordinate, induction in the remaining variables then makes the function identically $-\infty $ on their polydisc, a contradiction. Choose a real basis $A_1,\ldots ,A_{n^2}$ of skew-Hermitian matrices. It is a complex basis of all complex matrices, since every matrix is uniquely a skew-Hermitian matrix plus $i$ times one. The map \[  (z_1,\ldots ,z_{n^2})\longmapsto g_0\exp  igl (	extstyle \sum _ jz_ jA_ j igr )  \] is holomorphic with invertible derivative at zero. For real $z$ it parametrizes an open neighborhood of $g_0$ in the unitary group, with a smooth positive Haar density in those real coordinates: left-translate the trace inner product on the skew-Hermitian matrices. It is invariant under unitary conjugation, so its Riemannian metric and finite normalized volume are invariant on both sides. Uniqueness identifies this volume with Haar probability. Pull back a nontrivial local plurisubharmonic pole function and use the real-cube result. A finite chart cover of $\mathrm U(n)$ proves the assertion. $\square$ Theorem 6.45.2 . text: Lemma 6.45.1 . D72B7AE5B407 A locally pluripolar subset of a neighborhood of $\mathrm U(n)$ in $\mathrm{GL}_ n(\mathbb C)$ has Haar measure zero on $\mathrm U(n)$. Proof. First a nontrivial subharmonic function on a neighborhood of a real interval has a pole set of one-dimensional measure zero on that interval. On smaller neighborhoods its Riesz decomposition the local Riesz decomposition writes it as a harmonic function plus a finite logarithmic potential. On compact intervals $I$, \[  \sup _{a\in K}\int _ I|\log |t-a||\, dt<\infty  \] for every compact set $K\subset \mathbb C$. The positive part is bounded above uniformly, and the negative part is bounded by the integral of $-\log |t-\operatorname {Re}a|$ where this is positive. Absolute Fubini makes the potential integrable on $I$ and proves the assertion. An exhaustion handles the whole interval. It follows by induction that the pole set of a nontrivial plurisubharmonic function in a complex polydisc has real measure zero on its middle real cube. Indeed, positive real measure of the pole set gives a positive-measure set of the last $d-1$ real coordinates whose first-coordinate subharmonic slices have a positive-measure pole set. Those slices are identically $-\infty $. For every fixed complex first coordinate, induction in the remaining variables then makes the function identically $-\infty $ on their polydisc, a contradiction. Choose a real basis $A_1,\ldots ,A_{n^2}$ of skew-Hermitian matrices. It is a complex basis of all complex matrices, since every matrix is uniquely a skew-Hermitian matrix plus $i$ times one. The map \[  (z_1,\ldots ,z_{n^2})\longmapsto g_0\exp \bigl (\textstyle \sum _ jz_ jA_ j\bigr )  \] is holomorphic with invertible derivative at zero. For real $z$ it parametrizes an open neighborhood of $g_0$ in the unitary group, with a smooth positive Haar density in those real coordinates: left-translate the trace inner product on the skew-Hermitian matrices. It is invariant under unitary conjugation, so its Riemannian metric and finite normalized volume are invariant on both sides. Uniqueness identifies this volume with Haar probability. Pull back a nontrivial local plurisubharmonic pole function and use the real-cube result. A finite chart cover of $\mathrm U(n)$ proves the assertion. $\square$

Theorem 6.46.1 . 86EB492BC979 Let $F:X	o Y$ be holomorphic and proper on the support of a closed positive current $T$ of bidimension $(p,p)$. For $y\in Y$, let $I_ y$ consist of the points $x$ that are singleton connected components of $\operatorname {Supp}T\cap F^{-1}(y)$ and satisfy $\operatorname {codim}_ xF^{-1}(y)\geq p$. Then \[  
u (F_*T,y)\geq \sum _{x\in I_ y}\mu _ p(F,x)
u (T,x).  \] The sum means the supremum of all finite subsums. For $p=0$ use $\mu _0=1$ and ordinary atoms of positive measures. Proof. We first justify the neighborhoods, since a singleton connected component need not be an isolated point of the whole fiber. In a compact Hausdorff space a component is the intersection of its clopen neighborhoods. Indeed that intersection $Q$ is connected: if it split into two compact pieces, disjoint neighborhoods of those pieces, together with finitely many clopen neighborhoods excluding the remaining compact set, would split a clopen neighborhood of the chosen point into two clopen pieces and exclude one of the pieces of $Q$, a contradiction. Thus, when the component is a point, its clopen neighborhoods form a neighborhood basis, by compactness of the complement of any prescribed neighborhood. The fiber $K=\operatorname {Supp}T\cap F^{-1}(y)$ is compact. Given finitely many points $x_ j\in I_ y$, choose disjoint compact clopen neighborhoods $K_ j$ in $K$, each contained in a relatively compact coordinate neighborhood of $x_ j$. Ambient relatively compact open sets $U_ j$ can be chosen disjoint, with $K\cap U_ j=K_ j$ and $\partial U_ j\cap K=\varnothing $: separate the two compact pieces by a smooth cutoff and use an intermediate level. The compact images $F(\partial U_ j\cap \operatorname {Supp}T)$ miss $y$. Choose a target neighborhood $W$ avoiding them. The restrictions to $V_ j=U_ j\cap F^{-1}(W)$ are proper on their respective supports, and positivity gives $F_*T\geq \sum _ j(F|_{V_ j})_*(T|_{V_ j})$ on $W$. It suffices to prove the estimate for one point, now denoted zero, on one such coordinate open $V$. Put $u=\log |F-y|^2$. Its low support sublevels are compact, although its pole set on $\operatorname {Supp}T\cap V$ can include other points. For an integer $a$ set $H=(F-y,z_1^ a,\ldots ,z_ n^ a)$ and $v=\log |H|^2$. Its only pole is zero and $v\geq u$. The localized weight comparison theorem 6.34.10 applies with $P_ v\subset P_ u$ on the support and ratio at most one on low finite $u$-levels. Consequently \[  
u (T,u)\geq 
u (T,v) \geq \mu _ p(H,0)
u (T,0)=\mu _ p(F,0)
u (T,0)  \] for sufficiently large $a$. The second step is the isolated-weight theorem and the last is finite-augmentation stability. The proper weighted projection formula identifies $
u (T,u)$ with the ordinary number of this local direct image at $y$. Summing the disjoint pieces and taking the supremum of finite subsets proves the assertion. For $p=0$, pushforward of a positive measure has atom equal to the total fiber measure, which dominates every indicated finite sum directly. $\square$ Theorem 6.46.2 . 751F9003E019 Let $F:X^ n	o Y^ m$ be a proper finite holomorphic map, with $n\geq 1$, and let $T$ be closed positive of bidimension $(p,p)$. For a finite holomorphic germ $H$ at $x$, put \[  \sigma (H,x)=\inf \{ a>0:\  |H(z)|\geq c|z-x|^ a 	ext{ near }x	ext{ for some }c>0\} .  \] Define the real upper multiplicity \[  \overline\mu _ p(F,x)= \inf _ G rac{\sigma (GF,x)^ p}{\mu _ p(G,F(x))},  \] where $G:(Y,F(x))	o (\mathbb C^ n,0)$ and $GF$ is finite at $x$. For $p=0$ the ratio is one. Then \[  
u (F_*T,y)\leq \sum _{x\in \operatorname {Supp}T\cap F^{-1}(y)} \overline\mu _ p(F,x)
u (T,x).  \] The set of $G$ in this definition is nonempty, and each denominator is a positive integer. No general integrality of $\overline\mu _ p$ is asserted. Proof. A proper finite map splits over a small neighborhood of $y$ into disjoint neighborhoods of the finitely many points of its fiber; compactness of inverse images excludes additional points. It suffices to treat a single point $x=0$ of that fiber. The finite image germ $B=F(X,0)$ has dimension $n$. A cone-adapted $n$-row linear projection of $B$ supplies an admissible $G$, so the infimum is nonempty. For any admissible $G$, its zero fiber in $Y$ has codimension at least $n$. To check this assertion even for a singular image $B$, recall the local intersection inequality $\dim (A\cap B)\geq \dim A+\dim B-m$ at their common point. It follows by taking $A	imes B$ and imposing the $m$ diagonal coordinate equations, each of which lowers dimension by at most one. If a branch $A$ of $\{ G=0\} $ had codimension less than $n$, $A\cap B$ would have positive dimension. Its finite inverse image under $F$ would then have positive dimension, contradicting the point fiber of $GF$. Thus $\mu _ p(G,0)$ is defined and positive by the generic-slice theorem. The analytic Nullstellensatz applied to the isolated fiber of $H=GF$ gives powers of the source coordinates in the ideal of its components. Bounded coefficients give a finite exponent in the displayed definition of $\sigma $. The admissible exponents form an upper interval, so every $a>\sigma (H,0)$ is admissible. The lower-bound theorem applied locally to $G$ on the support of $F_*T$ gives \[  \mu _ p(G,0)
u (F_*T,0)\leq 
u (G_*F_*T,0) =
u (T,\log |GF|^2).  \] The required proper support is supplied by the finite composite and a smaller target neighborhood, as in the preceding proof. The bound $|GF(z)|\geq c|z|^ a$ and the common point pole give $
u (T,\log |GF|^2)\leq a^ p
u (T,0)$ by weight comparison. Let $a\downarrow \sigma (H,0)$, then take the infimum over $G$. All these constants are finite and the current numbers are finite; zero current numbers cause no undefined product. Sum the local pieces. For $p=0$, the finite fiber measure is exactly the sum of its atoms, proving the stated upper bound with equality. $\square$

Proposition 6.47.1 . 0A17C5BE0625 Let $F(z)=(z_1^{s_1},\ldots ,z_ n^{s_ n})$, where $1\leq s_1\leq \cdots \leq s_ n$ are integers. Then \[  \mu _ p(F,0)=s_1\cdots s_ p,\qquad \overline\mu _ p(F,0)=s_{n-p+1}\cdots s_ n.  \] Empty products, for $p=0$, equal one. Proof. Take a generic $p$-plane $S$, on which $z_1,\ldots ,z_ p$ are coordinates, and a generic $p$-row target projection $P$ whose first $p$ columns are invertible. Row operations make that block the identity, without changing the finite local degree. Writing $G=PF|_ S$, its $j$th component then has the form \[  G_ j=z_ j^{s_ j}+\sum _{k>p}c_{jk} L_ k(z_1,\ldots ,z_ p)^{s_ k}.  \] It has vanishing order at least $s_ j$. The system need not be triangular; no successive one-variable root count is inferred. By the coordinate-intersection degree lemma and corollary 6.34.13 , its finite local degree is at least $\prod _{j\leq p}s_ j$. The usual logarithmic-growth identification of the Lelong number of a holomorphic logarithm with its vanishing order, calculus and semicontinuity of potential Lelong numbers , is used here. For the reverse inequality use the coordinate plane $S_0$ and the first $p$ target coordinates. The resulting germ is $(z_1^{s_1},\ldots ,z_ p^{s_ p})$, of degree $\prod _{j\leq p}s_ j$, by independent root choices off the coordinate hyperplanes. On a fixed small ball, this special system is nonzero on its boundary. All nearby systems retain a uniform boundary lower bound, so their total pole masses in the ball are upper semicontinuous by theorem 6.34.8 . Each local degree at zero is at most that total mass, even when additional zeros move in the ball. Generic $S,P$ can be chosen arbitrarily near this pair; the generic-slice theorem identifies their degree with $\mu _ p(F,0)$. This proves the reverse inequality and the first formula. Let $s$ be a common multiple of the $s_ j$ and put $G(w)=(w_ j^{s/s_ j})_ j$. Then $GF=(z_ j^ s)_ j$ has exponent $\sigma (GF,0)=s$. The first formula, with the exponents reordered, gives $\mu _ p(G,0)=s^ p/(s_{n-p+1}\cdots s_ n)$. This choice bounds $\overline\mu _ p(F,0)$ above by the claimed product. For the reverse bound take $T$ to be integration over the last $p$ coordinate plane. Its number at zero is one and its pushforward has number $s_{n-p+1}\cdots s_ n$, by independent sheet counting on that plane. The finite-map upper theorem forces the reverse inequality. The $p=0$ convention gives both formulas. $\square$ Corollary 6.47.2 . 240191846A51 For $0<\lambda _1\leq \cdots \leq \lambda _ n$, put $ho _\lambda (z)=\max _ j\lambda _ j\log |z_ j|^2$. u (T,0) \leq 
u (T,ho _\lambda ) \leq (\lambda _{n-p+1}\cdots \lambda _ n)
u (T,0).  \] Both constants are sharp. Proof. For integer coefficients, the logarithm of the monomial tuple differs by a bounded function from $ho _\lambda $. Its proper weighted projection formula and the preceding lower and upper map bounds give the inequality. Integration over the first and last $p$ coordinate planes shows sharpness. For real coefficients choose positive integers $s_ j(k)=\lfloor k\lambda _ jfloor $ for sufficiently large $k$. Positive homogeneity and coefficientwise monotonicity are the established directional-weight comparison. If two positive coefficient vectors differ by a factor between $1-\epsilon $ and $1+\epsilon $, those same comparisons squeeze their numbers between the corresponding $(1\pm \epsilon )^ p$ multiples. Hence the directional number is continuous in positive coefficients. Divide the integer inequalities by $k^ p$ and pass to $\lambda $. For $p=0$ all numbers are the same point atom and all products are one. $\square$

section: 6.47 Monomial maps and the sharp directional comparison
text: Proposition 6.47.1 . 0A17C5BE0625 Let $F(z)=(z_1^{s_1},\ldots ,z_ n^{s_ n})$, where $1\leq s_1\leq \cdots \leq s_ n$ are integers. Then \[  \mu _ p(F,0)=s_1\cdots s_ p,\qquad \overline\mu _ p(F,0)=s_{n-p+1}\cdots s_ n.  \] Empty products, for $p=0$, equal one. Proof. Take a generic $p$-plane $S$, on which $z_1,\ldots ,z_ p$ are coordinates, and a generic $p$-row target projection $P$ whose first $p$ columns are invertible. Row operations make that block the identity, without changing the finite local degree. Writing $G=PF|_ S$, its $j$th component then has the form \[  G_ j=z_ j^{s_ j}+\sum _{k>p}c_{jk} L_ k(z_1,\ldots ,z_ p)^{s_ k}.  \] It has vanishing order at least $s_ j$. The system need not be triangular; no successive one-variable root count is inferred. By the coordinate-intersection degree lemma and corollary 6.34.13 , its finite local degree is at least $\prod _{j\leq p}s_ j$. The usual logarithmic-growth identification of the Lelong number of a holomorphic logarithm with its vanishing order, calculus and semicontinuity of potential Lelong numbers , is used here. For the reverse inequality use the coordinate plane $S_0$ and the first $p$ target coordinates. The resulting germ is $(z_1^{s_1},\ldots ,z_ p^{s_ p})$, of degree $\prod _{j\leq p}s_ j$, by independent root choices off the coordinate hyperplanes. On a fixed small ball, this special system is nonzero on its boundary. All nearby systems retain a uniform boundary lower bound, so their total pole masses in the ball are upper semicontinuous by theorem 6.34.8 . Each local degree at zero is at most that total mass, even when additional zeros move in the ball. Generic $S,P$ can be chosen arbitrarily near this pair; the generic-slice theorem identifies their degree with $\mu _ p(F,0)$. This proves the reverse inequality and the first formula. Let $s$ be a common multiple of the $s_ j$ and put $G(w)=(w_ j^{s/s_ j})_ j$. Then $GF=(z_ j^ s)_ j$ has exponent $\sigma (GF,0)=s$. The first formula, with the exponents reordered, gives $\mu _ p(G,0)=s^ p/(s_{n-p+1}\cdots s_ n)$. This choice bounds $\overline\mu _ p(F,0)$ above by the claimed product. For the reverse bound take $T$ to be integration over the last $p$ coordinate plane. Its number at zero is one and its pushforward has number $s_{n-p+1}\cdots s_ n$, by independent sheet counting on that plane. The finite-map upper theorem forces the reverse inequality. The $p=0$ convention gives both formulas. $\square$

u (T,0) \leq 
u (T,ho _\lambda ) \leq (\lambda _{n-p+1}\cdots \lambda _ n)
u (T,0).  \] Both constants are sharp. Proof. For integer coefficients, the logarithm of the monomial tuple differs by a bounded function from $ho _\lambda $. Its proper weighted projection formula and the preceding lower and upper map bounds give the inequality. Integration over the first and last $p$ coordinate planes shows sharpness. For real coefficients choose positive integers $s_ j(k)=\lfloor k\lambda _ jfloor $ for sufficiently large $k$. Positive homogeneity and coefficientwise monotonicity are the established directional-weight comparison. If two positive coefficient vectors differ by a factor between $1-\epsilon $ and $1+\epsilon $, those same comparisons squeeze their numbers between the corresponding $(1\pm \epsilon )^ p$ multiples. Hence the directional number is continuous in positive coefficients. Divide the integer inequalities by $k^ p$ and pass to $\lambda $. title: 10.75 The integer cohomology ring of projective space
search_title: The integer cohomology ring of projective space
section: 10.75 The integer cohomology ring of projective space
text: Cohomology with integer coefficients means constant-sheaf cohomology, with the previously constructed cup product. Let $\Theta $ denote the multiplicative augmentation comparison from real sheaf cohomology to de Rham cohomology, and $\Psi _ q$ the successive positive connecting comparison in the opposite direction. We retain their exact relation \[  \Theta _ q^{-1}=\epsilon _ q\Psi _ q,\qquad \epsilon _ q=(-1)^{q(q+1)/2}.  \] Thus the two conventions are distinguished even in even degree. The complex orientation is used for every projective subspace. Lemma 10.75.1 . 419BAFBD0FA6 For $n\geq 0$ the integer cohomology groups of $\mathbb P^ n$ are \[  H^ q(\mathbb P^ n,\underline{\mathbb Z})= \begin{cases}  \mathbb Z,& q=0,2,\ldots ,2n,\\  0,& \text{otherwise}. \end{cases}  \] In particular they have no torsion. For $0\leq k\leq m\leq n$, restriction to a linear $\mathbb P^ m$ is an isomorphism in degree $2k$. Proof. The assertion for $n=0$ is the cohomology of a point. Suppose $n\geq 1$ and let $H=\mathbb P^{n-1}$ be a hyperplane. Both spaces are compact Hausdorff manifolds, and the complement is the affine chart $\mathbb C^ n$. The compact closed subset $H$ is strongly paracompact in $\mathbb P^ n$: a cover near $H$ admits a finite shrinking there, which supplies the required locally finite ambient refinement. The precise relative/support comparison theorem 10.69.3 therefore gives \[  H^ q(\mathbb P^ n,H;\underline{\mathbb Z}) =H_ c^ q(\mathbb C^ n,\underline{\mathbb Z}).  \] The complement is open and has compact closure in $\mathbb P^ n$, as required for this last identification. Apply integral cap duality theorem 10.71.5 to the oriented real $2n$-manifold $\mathbb C^ n$. Radial contraction and the proved singular prism identity give its homology $\mathbb Z$ in degree zero and zero elsewhere. Consequently the displayed relative group is $\mathbb Z$ for $q=2n$ and zero in every other degree. This is an integer calculation, not a conclusion from the real groups. Use the pair long exact sequence lemma 10.69.2 . In degrees $0\leq q\leq 2n-2$ restriction to $H$ is an isomorphism, since its adjacent relative terms vanish. In degree $2n-1$ the relative term and the corresponding group of $H$ vanish, so the group of $\mathbb P^ n$ vanishes. At the top the exact segment is \[  0=H^{2n-1}(H,\underline{\mathbb Z})\longrightarrow \mathbb Z \longrightarrow H^{2n}(\mathbb P^ n,\underline{\mathbb Z}) \longrightarrow H^{2n}(H,\underline{\mathbb Z})=0.  \] Thus this top group is exactly $\mathbb Z$, with no extension or torsion ambiguity. All higher groups vanish by the same sequence. Induction proves the group calculation. Iterating the restriction isomorphisms along a linear flag proves the final assertion; any specified linear subspace can be included in such a flag by extending a vector-space basis. $\square$ Theorem 10.75.2 . 0CD4D885B4B4 Let $h=c_1^{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal O(1))$ in the exponential and frame convention of theorem 10.40.2 . Then \[  H^*(\mathbb P^ n,\underline{\mathbb Z}) =\mathbb Z[h]/(h^{n+1}),\qquad |h|=2.  \] For every $0\leq k\leq n$, $h^ k$ is a primitive generator of degree $2k$. Restriction to a linear subspace of dimension at least $k$ preserves this generator. Writing $h_{\mathbb R}$ for its coefficient image and $\omega $ for the normalized Fubini–Study form, the comparison conventions give \[  \Psi _{2k}[\omega ^ k]=h_{\mathbb R}^ k,\qquad \Theta _{2k}(h_{\mathbb R}^ k)=(-1)^ k[\omega ^ k].  \] Accordingly, on a linear $\mathbb P^ k$ the cap-normalized integer trace sends $h^ k$ to $(-1)^ k$. Equivalently the generator $-h$ has positive Fubini–Study image under $\Theta $, and its top powers have complex-orientation trace $1$. Proof. The line/frame classification defines $h$ integrally before any real comparison. By theorem 10.40.5 , with its specified positive connecting convention, \[  h_{\mathbb R}=\Psi _2[\omega ].  \] The line here and its normalized curvature are the existing projective line and Fubini–Study objects. Naturality of the exponential sequence makes $h$ restrict to the same Chern class on every linear projective subspace. The exact sign identity and multiplicativity in theorem 10.58.9 , corollary 10.58.11 give $\Theta _2(h_{\mathbb R})=-[\omega ]$, and therefore $\Theta _{2k}(h_{\mathbb R}^ k)=(-1)^ k[\omega ^ k]$. Since $\epsilon _{2k}=(-1)^ k$, the first comparison formula follows as well, including $k=0$. No unsigned interchange of the two comparison maps is made. On $\mathbb P^ k$, integral cap duality and the orientation trace corollary 10.72.4 identify top integer cohomology with $\mathbb Z$. This trace commutes with the coefficient map to $\mathbb R$. Its real version is integration in the multiplicative augmentation convention, by theorem 10.73.1 . The previously proved normalization in theorem 10.50.3 is $\int _{\mathbb P^ k}\omega ^ k=1$. Hence \[  \operatorname {tr}_{\mathbb P^ k}(h^ k)=(-1)^ k.  \] This is a unit in $\mathbb Z$, so $h^ k$ is primitive in that top integer group. The preceding lemma makes restriction from $H^{2k}(\mathbb P^ n,\underline{\mathbb Z})$ an isomorphism onto this group. It follows that $h^ k$ is primitive there also. This step uses the full integer computation, so no torsion class has been lost through a real comparison. The graded ring map $\mathbb Z[t]\to H^*(\mathbb P^ n,\underline{\mathbb Z})$ sending $t$ to $h$ is surjective, since its powers give a basis in every nonzero degree. The power $h^{n+1}$ vanishes by degree. Every lower homogeneous power generates an infinite cyclic group, so no polynomial of degree at most $n$ lies in the kernel unless all its coefficients vanish. The kernel is therefore exactly $(t^{n+1})$. For $n=0$, $h=0$ and this is the ring $\mathbb Z$ of a point. Finally $\Theta _2(-h_{\mathbb R})=[\omega ]$, and multiplying the trace formula by $(-1)^ k$ proves the positive-generator assertion. $\square$

title: Corollary 9.55.8
section: 9.55 Entire-function growth and arithmetic zero sets
text: Corollary 9.55.8 . 16B6E15BB4A5 Let $S\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be finite and nonempty, and let $\delta $ be the least degree of a nonzero polynomial vanishing on $S$. There is $C_ S\geq 2$ such that, for every nonzero entire $f$, $R\geq r\geq 1$, and $m=\min _{w\in S}\operatorname {ord}_ w f$, DAB4F1171966 9.55.9 \begin{equation}  \log M_ f(r)\leq \log M_ f(R) -m\, \frac{\delta +n(n-1)/2}{n!}\log \frac{R}{C_ Sr}. \end{equation} For $k\geq 1$ put $\omega _ k(S)=\min \{ \deg P:0\ne P,\  \operatorname {ord}_ wP\geq k \text{ for all }w\in S\} $. Then 4554B80BB7F9 9.55.10 \begin{equation}  \Omega (S)=\lim _{k\to \infty }\frac{\omega _ k(S)}k =\inf _{k\geq 1}\frac{\omega _ k(S)}k \geq \frac{\omega _1(S)+n(n-1)/2}{n!}. \end{equation} Proof. Evaluation at $S$ is injective on polynomials of degree less than $\delta $. Choose $h=\binom {\delta +n-1}n$ independent evaluation coordinates, corresponding to distinct points $w_1,\ldots ,w_ h$. For each multi-index $|\alpha |=\delta $, interpolation on those points gives a polynomial $R_\alpha $ of degree less than $\delta $ with $R_\alpha (w_ j)=w_ j^\alpha $. Set $P_\alpha =z^\alpha -R_\alpha $. Its leading forms are all the monomials of degree $\delta $, whose only common zero is $0$. The preceding theorem bounds the weighted mass below by $hm$, so, when $R>C_ Sr$, its coefficient can be replaced by the lower bound \[  \delta ^{1-n}h =\frac{\delta ^{1-n}}{n!}\prod _{j=0}^{n-1}(\delta +j) \geq \frac{\delta +n(n-1)/2}{n!}.  \] All omitted polynomial coefficients in the product are nonnegative. For $R\leq C_ Sr$ use monotonicity directly. This proves the inequality, including $m=0$. The degrees $\omega _ k$ are finite, by taking powers of a polynomial vanishing on $S$, and subadditive by multiplication. If $k=aq+b$, $0\leq b<q$, subadditivity gives $\omega _ k\leq a\omega _ q+\max _{0\leq b<q}\omega _ b$, with $\omega _0=0$. Divide by $k$ and let $k\to \infty $, then take the infimum over $q$, to prove the limit formula. Apply ( 9.55.9 ) to a degree-$\omega _ k$ polynomial with $m\geq k$, fix $r=1$, and let $R\to \infty $. A degree-$D$ polynomial has $\log M(R)=D\log R+O(1)$, by its nonzero leading homogeneous part. This proves the lower bound. $\square$

title: Example 9.55.11
section: 9.55 Entire-function growth and arithmetic zero sets
text: Example 9.55.11 . DDE636CB719F The coefficient in ( 9.55.9 ) is optimal in dimensions $1$ and $2$. In dimension $1$ take any set of $\delta $ points and its simple root polynomial. In dimension $2$ take the pairwise intersection points of $\delta +1$ affine lines in general position, for $\delta \geq 1$. Each line contains $\delta $ distinct points. A polynomial of degree less than $\delta $ vanishing at all those points must vanish identically on every line, hence be divisible by all $\delta +1$ line equations, which is impossible unless the polynomial is zero. Products of any $\delta $ line equations do vanish on every intersection, so the least degree is $\delta $. The product of all $\delta +1$ equations has order $2$ at each point and degree $\delta +1$. Letting $R\to \infty $ in any proposed stronger growth inequality shows that its coefficient is at most $(\delta +1)/2$. Powers give the same bound for $\Omega $. In dimensions $n\geq 3$ the displayed universal coarse coefficient is not always optimal: for a single point the exact coefficient is $1$, while $[1+n(n-1)/2]/n!<1$.

title: Lemma 9.55.12
section: 9.55 Entire-function growth and arithmetic zero sets
text: Lemma 9.55.12 . A9F728A9CDAA For every PSH $V$ on $\mathbb C^ n$, not identically $-\infty $, and every $\eta >0$, there is a nonzero entire $g$ with F1433CD2E7FB 9.55.13 \begin{equation}  \int _{\mathbb C^ n}|g|^2e^{-V}(1+|z|^2)^{-n-\eta }\, dV_{2n}<\infty . \end{equation} Proof. Choose a point $a$ with $V(a)>-\infty $ and a ball $B$ around it. The exact bounded-domain point-value theorem bounded-domain weighted extension from a point gives $h\in \mathcal O(B)$ with $h(a)=1$ and $\int _ B|h|^2e^{-V}<\infty $. Take a smooth cutoff $\chi $ supported in $B$ and equal to one near $a$. Its datum $\alpha =\bar\partial (\chi h)$ is closed and compactly supported away from $a$. Apply the canonical singular-weight estimate the singular-weight $L^2$ estimate with a smooth curvature lower bound to the PSH weight $p=V+n\log |z-a|^2$ and smooth strictly PSH addition $q=\eta \log (1+|z|^2)$. On the fixed support of $\alpha $, the inverse Hessian of $q$ and the factor $|z-a|^{-2n}$ are bounded. Thus its inverse energy is finite, giving $\bar\partial u=\alpha $ and \[  \int |u|^2e^{-V}|z-a|^{-2n}(1+|z|^2)^{-\eta }<\infty .  \] Here the datum is locally $L^2$ because $V$ is bounded above on compact sets and $h$ is holomorphic. The distributional holomorphic regularity theorem holomorphic distributions and minimal weighted solutions makes $u$ holomorphic near $a$. Since $e^{-V}$ is bounded below there, the singular norm forces $u(a)=0$ by the divergent $\int _0^ r s^{-1}\, ds$. Then $g=\chi h-u$ is entire and $g(a)=1$. The compactly supported $\chi h$ has finite final norm by the local weighted bound. For $u$ use $|z-a|^{2n}\leq C(1+|z|^2)^ n$. This proves the assertion. $\square$
