title: Lemma 9.55.14
section: 9.55 Entire-function growth and arithmetic zero sets
text: Lemma 9.55.14 . CE482CBDAFC5 Let $T$ be a closed positive $(1,1)$-current on $\mathbb C^ n$. If its ordinary normalized ball densities satisfy $D_ T(0,r)\leq A$ for every $r>0$, then there is a global PSH function $U$ with \[  dd^ cU=T,\qquad U(z)\leq A\log (1+|z|^2)+C.  \] Proof. Let $\omega _{\rm FS}=dd^ c\log (1+|z|^2)$ on the affine chart of $\mathbb P^ n$. The convex weight change proposition 6.34.5 , with $\rho =\log |z|^2$ and $\chi (t)=\log (1+e^ t)$, gives for $n\geq 2$ \[  \int _{|z|<r}T\wedge \omega _{\rm FS}^{n-1} =\left(\frac{r^2}{1+r^2}\right)^{n-1}D_ T(0,r)\leq A.  \] For $n=1$ it is the ordinary measure mass, with no Hessian power. Consequently $T$ has finite Fubini–Study mass. On each compact chart that metric is equivalent to the Euclidean metric. The hyperplane at infinity is locally the pole set of the negative PSH function $\log |z_1|$. The complete finite-mass theorem 5.60.3 therefore extends $T$ by zero to a closed positive current $\widehat T$ on $\mathbb P^ n$. Its coefficient measures give the hyperplane zero mass, so \[  a:=\int _{\mathbb P^ n}\widehat T\wedge \omega _{\rm FS}^{n-1} =\int _{\mathbb C^ n}T\wedge \omega _{\rm FS}^{n-1}\leq A.  \] By theorem 10.50.3 , the real degree-two cohomology is generated by $[\omega _{\rm FS}]$, with $\int \omega _{\rm FS}^ n=1$. The exact current $dd^ c$-decomposition the compact Kähler $(1,1)$-current $dd^ c$ decomposition consequently writes $\widehat T=a\omega _{\rm FS}+dd^ cv$, with a canonical quasi-PSH $v$ on the compact projective space. Indeed its harmonic part has this class, and a harmonic exact form is zero. The function $v$ is bounded above. On the affine chart $U=a\log (1+|z|^2)+v$ is PSH and has curvature $T$. Since $a\leq A$, it has the required upper bound. This argument also covers $n=1$, where extension closedness is automatic by degree. $\square$

title: Lemma 9.55.15
section: 9.55 Entire-function growth and arithmetic zero sets
text: Lemma 9.55.15 . 78667F4CB908 For a finite nonempty $S$ and $0<\epsilon <\Omega (S)$, there is $r_\epsilon \geq 1$ such that every nonzero entire $f$ vanishing to order at least $m\geq 1$ at each point of $S$ satisfies \[  D_{[Z_ f]}(0,r)\geq m(\Omega (S)-\epsilon ) \qquad (r\geq r_\epsilon ).  \] Proof. Otherwise choose integers $j\to \infty $ and functions $f_ j$, with orders at least $m_ j$ at $S$, such that $D_{T_ j}(0,j)<A:=\Omega (S)-\epsilon $, where $T_ j=m_ j^{-1}[Z_{f_ j}]$. For every fixed radius $R$ and $j\geq R$, ordinary Lelong monotonicity bounds the trace mass on $B(0,R)$ by $AR^{2n-2}$. Local positive-current compactness and a diagonal subsequence give a global closed positive weak limit $T$. The open-ball measure inequality gives $D_ T(0,R)\leq A$ for all $R$, and ordinary Lelong upper semicontinuity gives $\nu (T,s)\geq 1$ at every $s\in S$. Take the PSH potential $U$ from the preceding lemma. The potential/current Lelong comparison and the attained logarithmic bound imply $U(z)\leq \log |z-s|^2+C_ s$ near every $s$. For each integer $k\geq n$, apply lemma 9.55.12 to $V=kU$, with $\eta =1/2$, obtaining a nonzero entire $g_ k$. Near $s$ the weighted integrability forces $\operatorname {ord}_ s g_ k>k-n$: the first nonzero homogeneous term of degree $b$ has positive squared spherical mean, and its radial integral is bounded below by a constant times $\int _0^ r t^{2b-2k+2n-1}\, dt$. Thus its order is at least $k-n+1$. title: Theorem 9.55.16

text: Theorem 9.55.16 . A6707829AA5A For every finite nonempty $S\subset \mathbb C^ n$ and every $\epsilon >0$ there is $C_{S,\epsilon }\geq 1$ such that every nonzero entire $f$, $R\geq r\geq 1$, and $m=\min _{s\in S}\operatorname {ord}_ s f$ satisfy C1D876879EC5 9.55.17 \begin{equation}  \log M_ f(r)\leq \log M_ f(R) -m(\Omega (S)-\epsilon )\log \frac{R}{C_{S,\epsilon }r}. \end{equation} The largest possible coefficient in such an inequality is at most $\Omega (S)$. No bound on $C_{S,\epsilon }$ uniform over point configurations is asserted. Proof. If $m=0$, monotonicity suffices. If $\epsilon \geq \Omega (S)$, take $C_{S,\epsilon }=1$ and again use monotonicity. Thus assume $m\geq 1$ and $0<\epsilon <\Omega (S)$. Apply the preceding lemma with $\epsilon /2$. Choose a fixed $B\geq 2$ so large that $Br\geq r_{\epsilon /2}+r$ for $r\geq 1$ and \[  (1-B^{-1})^{2n-2}(\Omega (S)-\epsilon /2) \geq \Omega (S)-\epsilon .  \] For $|z_0|\leq r$ and $t\geq Br$, inclusion of balls and the translation-invariance of the Euclidean trace form give \[  D_{[Z_ f]}(z_0,t) \geq \left(\frac{t-r}{t}\right)^{2n-2}D_{[Z_ f]}(0,t-r) \geq m(\Omega (S)-\epsilon ).  \] When $R>2Br$, radial weighted Jensen about any $z_0\in B(0,r)$ with $f(z_0)\ne 0$, using outer radius $R/2$, consequently yields \[  \log M_ f(R)-\log |f(z_0)| \geq \int _{Br}^{R/2}D_{[Z_ f]}(z_0,t)\frac{dt}{t} \geq m(\Omega (S)-\epsilon )\log \frac{R}{2Br}.  \] Take the supremum of the point values. text: Lemma 9.70.2 . BAA8DAF93F9F If an integer matrix has $L$ rows, $M>L$ columns, and entries of absolute value at most $B\geq 1$, its kernel contains a nonzero integer vector $c$ with \[  \log \| c\| _\infty \leq \log 3+ \frac{L}{M-L}\log (3MB).  \] Proof. Choose an integer $H>(3MB)^{L/(M-L)}$ with $H\leq 3(3MB)^{L/(M-L)}$. The $(H+1)^ M$ integer vectors in $\{ 0,\ldots ,H\} ^ M$ have at most $(2MBH+1)^ L\leq (3MBH)^ L$ images. Since $H^{M-L}>(3MB)^ L$, two vectors have the same image. Their nonzero difference is the required kernel vector. $\square$ Lemma 9.70.3 . 08B68F4101B6 Let $K\subset \mathbb C$ be a number field of degree $D$, let $F_1,\ldots ,F_ N$ be holomorphic near finitely many points $w_1,\ldots ,w_ h$, and suppose all values $F_ i(w_ j)$ lie in $K$. Suppose every $\partial _{z_ l}F_ i$ is a fixed polynomial in the $F_ i$ with coefficients in $K$. There are an integral primitive element $\theta $ for $K$, integers $A\geq 2$, $C_0\geq 1$, and $C_1>0$ such that for every monomial $F^\alpha $ of degree $s$ and every multi-index $\kappa $ of length $k$, the number \[  A^{C_0(s+k+1)}\partial ^\kappa (F^\alpha )(w_ j)  \] is in $\mathbb Z[\theta ]$ and has coefficients in $1,\theta ,\ldots ,\theta ^{D-1}$ of size at most $\exp (C_1(s+k+1))\, [C_1(s+k+1)]^ k$. The same upper bound, with a changed $C_1$, holds at every field embedding before multiplication by this power of $A$. Proof. We recall the finite field facts being used. A finite extension of $\mathbb Q$ is separable: the derivative of an irreducible polynomial in characteristic zero has no common factor with that polynomial. Successively adjoining roots therefore gives exactly $D$ embeddings in $\mathbb C$. If two generators are combined as $a+qb$, only finitely many rational $q$ identify two distinct embedding values. Choose a rational value avoiding them. Its $D$ distinct conjugates show that it generates the field. Induction gives a primitive element, and integer scaling makes its minimal polynomial monic with integer coefficients: for a root of a rational monic polynomial, clearing denominators after the substitution $x=\theta /A$ gives such a scaling. This gives an integral primitive $\theta $. All the finitely many differential-polynomial coefficients and point values belong to $\mathbb Z[\theta ,1/A]$ after one common choice of $A$. Replace differentiation by polynomial derivations $\mathcal D_ l=\sum _ iQ_{li}(X)\partial _{X_ i}$. If the $Q_{li}$ have degrees at most $b$, $k$ applications produce polynomial degree at most $s+k\max (b-1,0)$. At the next step the coefficient sum norm is multiplied by at most $C(s+(k+1)b)$. Each multiplication uses fixed elements of $\mathbb Z[\theta ,1/A]$; multiplication in the fixed basis, with powers of $\theta $ reduced by its monic equation, costs at most a fixed factor and a fixed power of $A$. Evaluation at the fixed point values costs at most an exponential in the resulting degree and the same linear power of $A$. Induction gives exactly the stated coefficient and denominator bounds. Applying any embedding to the finitely many fixed coefficients proves the conjugate bound by the identical polynomial induction. No analytic estimate on uncontrolled derivatives is being assumed here. $\square$ Lemma 9.70.4 . 5A16550DA466 Let $F_1,\ldots ,F_ N$ be meromorphic on $\mathbb C^ n$ and suppose $F_1,\ldots ,F_ d$, $d>n$, are algebraically independent over $\mathbb Q$, with respective finite orders at most the nonnegative numbers $\rho _1,\ldots ,\rho _ d$. Let $K\subset \mathbb C$ be a number field of degree $D$. Suppose the ring $K[F_1,\ldots ,F_ N]$ is stable under coordinate derivations, and choose a nonempty finite set $\{ w_1,\ldots ,w_ h\} $ where all $F_ i$ are holomorphic and have values in $K$. For every $\epsilon >0$ there are $r\geq 1$, constants $C_1,C_2>0$, and an unbounded sequence of positive integers $t$, with nonzero entire functions $G_ t$, such that 36DC9A8C6743 \begin{align}  \operatorname {ord}_{w_ j}G_ t& \geq t\quad (1\leq j\leq h), \tag{9.70.5}\\  M_{G_ t}(r)& \geq (C_1t)^{-Dt}, \tag{9.70.6}\\  M_{G_ t}(R(t))& \leq C_2^ t,\qquad R(t)=\left(\frac{t^{d-n}}{\log t}\right)^{1/(\sum _{i=1}^ d\rho _ i+\epsilon )}. \tag{9.70.7} \end{align} Here finite order at most $\rho $ means a quotient of entire functions bounded, for every $a>\rho $, by $C_ a\exp (|z|^ a)$. Proof. Put $A_0=(\sum _ i\rho _ i+\epsilon )/(d-n)$ and choose $0<\eta <\epsilon /(2d)$. Write $a_ i=\rho _ i+\eta $. Discard indices with $a_ i\geq A_0$, and call the remaining set $J$, with $e=|J|$. Since $\sum _ i a_ i<A_0(d-n)$, fewer than $d-n$ indices were discarded; thus $e>n$. Moreover 10E6C67574C9 9.70.8 \begin{equation}  \gamma =e-A_0^{-1}\sum _{i\in J}a_ i-n>0. \end{equation} For large integers $T$ put $s_ i=\lfloor T/R(T)^{a_ i}\rfloor $, $i\in J$. Every exponent $1-a_ i/A_0$ is positive, so $s_ i\to \infty $. The monomials $X^\alpha $, $0\leq \alpha _ i\leq s_ i$, number \[  M=\prod _{i\in J}(s_ i+1)\geq cT^{n+\gamma },  \] where the logarithmic factors only increase this lower bound. Their total degrees are at most $CT$. Require a polynomial $P=\sum _\alpha c_\alpha X^\alpha $ to satisfy $\partial ^\kappa P(F)(w_ j)=0$ for $|\kappa |<T$. Expand in the fixed number-field basis and clear common $A^{CT}$ denominators, using the preceding jet lemma. This gives an integer matrix with $L\leq Dh\binom {T+n-1}n\leq CT^ n$ rows and entries $B\leq \exp (CT\log T)$. The small-kernel-vector lemma gives nonzero integer coefficients with 51C15E261502 9.70.9 \begin{equation}  \log \max _\alpha |c_\alpha | \leq C T^{-\gamma }(T\log T+\log M)+C\leq CT. \end{equation} The function $f=P(F_ i:i\in J)$ is not identically zero, by algebraic independence over $\mathbb Q$. Let $t\geq T$ be the least vanishing order of $f$ at the chosen points, and choose $w_ j$ and a coordinate derivative $\partial ^\kappa $, $|\kappa |=t$, with nonzero value $b=\partial ^\kappa f(w_ j)\in K$. The jet lemma and ( 9.70.9 ) show that $A^{Ct}b\in \mathbb Z[\theta ]$ and that every conjugate of $b$ has modulus at most $e^{Ct}(Ct)^ t$. For a nonzero $x\in \mathbb Z[\theta ]$, multiplication by $x$ on the basis $1,\theta ,\ldots ,\theta ^{D-1}$ has integer matrix and nonzero integer determinant. Evaluation at the distinct roots of the minimal polynomial diagonalizes it by the Vandermonde matrix. Its determinant is therefore the product of all conjugates. It follows that EF59C873F2EE 9.70.10 \begin{equation}  |b|\geq e^{-Ct}(Ct)^{-(D-1)t}. \end{equation} This also covers $D=1$. For $i\in J$ write $F_ i=A_ i/H_ i$ with the prescribed finite-order entire numerator and denominator, and put $G=P(F_ i:i\in J)\prod _{i\in J}H_ i^{s_ i}$. In coordinates with this last direction, choose a small last-radius circle on which all these one-variable restrictions are nonzero. Combine this with ( 9.70.10 ) and $t!\leq t^ t$ to prove the small-radius lower bound. For $t\geq T$ each function $u/R(u)^{a_ i}$ is increasing for large $u$, because its power $1-a_ i/A_0$ is positive. Thus $s_ iR(t)^{a_ i}\leq t$. Finite-order growth, the number of monomials and ( 9.70.9 ) give \[  \log M_ G(R(t))\leq CT+\log M+ C\sum _{i\in J}s_ i(1+R(t)^{a_ i})\leq Ct.  \] Since $t\geq T\to \infty $, pass to a subsequence of distinct $t$ and call these functions $G_ t$. If $S$ is empty there is nothing to prove. Henceforth assume it is nonempty, and write $D=[K:\mathbb Q]$. Let $\delta \geq 1$ be an integer such that $S$ is not contained in any zero set of degree less than $\delta $. Evaluation on $S$ is then injective on the space of polynomials of degree less than $\delta $, so finitely many distinct points of $S$ already make it injective, by choosing a basis from the spanning evaluation functionals. In particular their least vanishing degree is at least $\delta $. The finite-set Schwarz inequality therefore has coefficient at least $c_\delta =(\delta +n(n-1)/2)/n!$. Apply it to the arithmetic $G_ t$ and the fixed $r$ in that lemma: \[  -Dt\log (C_1t)\leq t\log C_2 -tc_\delta \log \frac{R(t)}{Cr}.  \] Divide by $t\log t$ and let $t\to \infty $, obtaining $c_\delta (d-n)/(\sum _ i\rho _ i+\epsilon )\leq D$. Let $\epsilon \downarrow 0$. If $S$ were not contained in any algebraic hypersurface, this would hold for every $\delta $, a contradiction. Hence if $S$ is nonempty it has a positive least vanishing degree $\delta $, and the same argument proves exactly the claimed bound. Empty $S$ requires no degree bound and is an explicit separate alternative. $\square$

text: Use $dd^ c=i\partial \bar\partial /(2\pi )$ and the full classical products. On a product chart write $(z,w)\in D\times W$, with $D\subset \mathbb C^ q$ a ball centered at zero and $W\subset \mathbb C^{n-q}$ a connected ball. The coordinate volume form on $W$ is denoted by $dV_ w$. Its pullback to the product is understood. If $q=n$, integration on the single parameter point means evaluation, with mass one. Lemma 6.48.1 . D0453276E370 Let $1\leq q\leq n$ and let $u$ be extended-continuous plurisubharmonic on $D\times W$, with pole set exactly $Z=\{ 0\} \times W$. Put \[  Q=(dd^ cu)^ q,\qquad \mu _ w=(dd^ c_ z u(\cdot ,w))^ q.  \] These classical products exist. There is a nonnegative constant $\lambda $ with $\mathbf1_ ZQ=\lambda [Z]$, and \[  \lambda =\mu _ w(\{ 0\} )\quad \text{for Lebesgue almost every }w\in W.  \] More precisely, for every continuous compactly supported function $f$ on $D\times W$, C03DD469B3DD 6.48.2 \begin{equation}  \int f\, Q\wedge dV_ w =\int _ W\left(\int _ D f(z,w)\, d\mu _ w(z)\right)dV_ w. \end{equation} Proof. The unbounded locus of $u$ is $Z$, of codimension $q$. Every intersection of $m\leq q$ repeated unbounded loci therefore has codimension at least $m$. Thus corollary 7.31.4 gives $Q$ and its decreasing continuity. On each normal fiber the pole set is the single point zero, so the same theorem gives $\mu _ w$ and the corresponding decreasing continuity there. The coefficient restriction formula proposition 6.40.2 gives $\mathbf1_ ZQ=\lambda [Z]$ with a constant $\lambda \geq 0$, since $Z$ is connected and smooth of dimension $n-q$. For $q=n$, $Q$ is the single fiber measure and all assertions follow immediately from extraction of its atom. Suppose $q<n$. Work first over a compact parameter set $L\Subset W$ and a normal ball $B(0,r)\Subset D$ containing the normal projection of the test support. Choose $r<R$ with $\overline{B(0,R)}\subset D$. Take a closed collar of the sphere $|z|=r$, still disjoint from zero, and enlarge $L$ slightly within $W$. On the product of that collar with the enlarged compact parameter set, $u$ is finite continuous and hence bounded below. Set \[  u_ m=\max \{ u,-m\} ,\qquad Q_ m=(dd^ cu_ m)^ q, \qquad \mu _{m,w}=(dd^ c_ z u_ m(\cdot ,w))^ q.  \] For every integer $m\geq m_0$ with $m_0$ sufficiently large, $u_ m=u$ on this common collar. For fixed $w\in L$, the bounded collar identity lemma 6.34.1 gives \[  \mu _{m,w}(B(0,r))=\mu _{m_0,w}(B(0,r)).  \] There is no regular-value or zero-boundary-mass requirement: the two products agree on an open collar and their distributional difference has compactly supported primitive in the ball. The functions $u_{m_0}(\cdot ,w)$ are uniformly bounded on $\overline{B(0,R)}\times L$. The bounded CLN estimate the bounded Chern–Levine–Nirenberg estimate consequently gives a constant $C_ L$ such that D82DEC261845 6.48.3 \begin{equation}  \mu _{m,w}(B(0,r))\leq C_ L \quad (w\in L,\  m\geq m_0). \end{equation} It also bounds the limiting $\mu _ w$ on every smaller compact normal set, by weak convergence. All masses used below have one fixed such buffered bound. We first prove ( 6.48.2 ) for each fixed $m$, with $Q_ m$ and $\mu _{m,w}$. Locally convolve the continuous bounded PSH function $u_ m$ in the joint $(z,w)$ coordinates. Its smooth PSH regularizations converge locally uniformly. For each regularization, wedging with the full parameter volume kills every Hessian factor containing a parameter differential. Ordinary Fubini therefore gives exactly the fiber identity with the normal Hessian power. Bounded-product uniform continuity uniform convergence of bounded Bedford–Taylor products passes the left side to $Q_ m$. On each fixed fiber it passes the right-side measures to $\mu _{m,w}$. For this fixed $m$, the regularized potentials have one common bound on buffered compact product sets, so the bounded CLN estimate bounds all their normal-fiber masses uniformly in the smoothing parameter and $w\in L$. Dominated convergence therefore passes the integrated right side to its limit as well. This proves the fixed-$m$ identity. For clarity, its parameter integrands are measurable. For the smooth approximations they are continuous in $w$ for continuous $f$, by ordinary integration on a fixed compact normal support. Their pointwise limits, supplied by the fiber uniform-continuity theorem, are measurable. The same is true for the pointwise limit as $m\to \infty $. The local test support can be covered by finitely many buffered product sets; a continuous partition of unity gives the identity for every continuous compactly supported $f$. Now let $m\to \infty $. The full classical decreasing-continuity theorem gives $Q_ m\to Q$ and $\mu _{m,w}\to \mu _ w$ on every fiber. The common estimate ( 6.48.3 ) permits dominated convergence in $w$. It proves ( 6.48.2 ) for the actual unbounded products, retaining their pole mass. Neither positivity of a weak slice limit alone nor monotonicity of the measures $Q_ m$ is being assumed. Finally take $\psi \in C_ c(W)$ nonnegative and normal radial cutoffs $0\leq \chi _ j\leq 1$ with $\chi _ j(0)=1$, decreasing pointwise to $\mathbf1_{\{ 0\} }$ and supported in a fixed buffered normal ball. Apply the formula to $f(z,w)=\chi _ j(z)\psi (w)$. Continuity from above for the fixed locally finite measures, and the same uniform bound for the parameter integral, give \[  \lambda \int _ W\psi \, dV_ w =\int _ W\psi (w)\mu _ w(\{ 0\} )\, dV_ w.  \] In particular $w\mapsto \mu _ w(\{ 0\} )$ is measurable, as a decreasing limit of the already measurable cutoff integrals. Uniqueness of locally finite measures tested against continuous compactly supported functions proves the almost-everywhere identity. This extracts the coefficient from an actual measure restriction, rather than interchanging a point mass with weak convergence. $\square$ Theorem 6.48.4 . DBE978B1362A Let $F_1,\ldots ,F_ N$ be holomorphic on an $n$-dimensional manifold, let $1\leq q\leq n$, and suppose their common zero set $Z$ has codimension at least $q$. If $\gamma _ j$ are positive integers, the coefficients $\lambda _ k$ in proposition 6.40.4 are positive integers, for both potentials \[  u=\log \sum _ j|F_ j|^{2\gamma _ j} \quad \text{and}\quad u=2\log \sum _ j|F_ j|^{\gamma _ j}.  \] Thus that decomposition, with its transverse coefficient and zero residual mass on $Z$, holds with integral coefficients. Proof. Set $G_ j=F_ j^{\gamma _ j}$ and $v=\log \sum _ j|G_ j|^2$. These are genuine holomorphic functions because the exponents are integers. Fix a codimension-$q$ component $Z_ k$. At a regular point away from the other components take a product chart where $Z=\{ z=0\} $ as in the lemma. For each $w$, the tuple $G_ w=(G_1(\cdot ,w),\ldots ,G_ N(\cdot ,w))$ has its only zero at $z=0$. The finite-map pole-degree formula proposition 6.43.1 gives \[  (dd^ c_ z v(\cdot ,w))^ q(\{ 0\} ) =\deg _0(P_ wG_ w)\in \mathbb Z_{>0},  \] where $P_ w$ is any cone-adapted generic projection from the local analytic image to $\mathbb C^ q$. This formula is the isolated-map sheet calculation and analytic Thie multiplicity; it does not assume King's formula. The projection may depend on $w$, since only the pointwise integral value is used. By lemma 6.48.1 , the coefficient of $[Z_ k]$ in $(dd^ cv)^ q$ is equal to that integer for almost every $w$ in this nonempty product chart. A nonempty parameter ball has positive Lebesgue volume; for a zero-dimensional parameter space the formula is direct. Thus the constant coefficient is a positive integer. The restriction/generic-value identity in proposition 6.40.2 identifies this local coefficient with the coefficient of the full component. For the second potential the elementary inequalities \[  \sum _ j|G_ j|^2\leq \Bigl (\sum _ j|G_ j|\Bigr )^2 \leq N\sum _ j|G_ j|^2  \] show that $u-v$ is bounded and that their pole sets agree. At any point of $Z$, apply theorem 6.34.12 in both directions to the repeated $q$-tuples and the ordinary logarithmic weight centered at that point. The codimension hypothesis gives all required classical products, all reference potentials have the specified point as pole, and the two upper ratios are one. Their ordinary product Lelong numbers are consequently equal. Taking the generic value along $Z_ k$ proves that its coefficient is the same integer. The other conclusions and the explicit transverse value were already proved in proposition 6.40.4 . $\square$

title: 9.58 Finite-type models and nilpotent structure
text: Rings are commutative with identity and morphisms preserve identity. Fix an algebraically closed field $k$. In the algebraic constructions below $\operatorname {Spm}A$ means the space of closed points , the maximal ideals of a finitely generated $k$-algebra, with its local ring sheaf. It is not the underlying all-prime topological space $\operatorname {Spec}A$. Nilpotents are retained in every structure sheaf unless a reduction is explicitly taken.

title: 9.58.1 Closed points and their localizations
text:
Theorem 9.58.2 . 36502A11961A Polynomial rings over $k$, their quotients and localizations are Noetherian. If $A$ is a finitely generated $k$-algebra, every maximal ideal has residue field $k$, and for every ideal $I\subset A$ \[   igcap _{\mathfrak m\supset I}\mathfrak m=\sqrt I.  \] In particular $I(V(J))=\sqrt J$ for a polynomial ideal $J$. The empty intersection in this formula is the unit ideal. Proof. Recall first the elementary module consequence of Noetherianity. A submodule of $R^ r$ is finitely generated: project onto the last coordinate, lift finitely many generators of that ideal, and add generators of the kernel by induction on $r$. Passing to a quotient gives the assertion for submodules of any finite module. The zero ideal is already finitely generated. If $R$ is Noetherian and $0
e I\subset R[T]$, its leading coefficients form an ideal of $R$. Choose polynomials $f_ i\in I$ realizing finitely many generators of that ideal and put $d=\max \deg f_ i$. Subtracting suitable multiples $T^{m-\deg f_ i}f_ i$ reduces the degree of any element of $I$ of degree $m\ge d$. The remainders in $I\cap R[T]_{<d}$ form a submodule of $R^ d$, hence have finitely many generators. Together with the $f_ i$ they generate $I$. This proves the polynomial assertion by induction; ideals of a quotient lift, and an ideal of a localization is generated by the images of generators of its contraction. These facts prove all the stated Noetherian assertions. Here is the needed field lemma. Suppose a field $K$ is finitely generated as a $k$-algebra, with generators $t_1,\ldots ,t_ r,u_1, \ldots ,u_ s$, where the $t_ i$ are a maximal algebraically independent subfamily. The $u_ j$ are algebraic over $k(t_1,\ldots ,t_ r)$. Clearing their finitely many monic-equation denominators makes them integral over $R=k[t_1,\ldots ,t_ r,1/f]$ for a nonzero polynomial $f$. Thus $K=R[u_1,\ldots ,u_ s]$ is a finite $R$-module, spanned by bounded powers of the $u_ j$. If a field is integral over a subring, that subring is a field: for $0
e a\in R$ the integral equation of $a^{-1}$, multiplied by $a^{m-1}$, expresses $a^{-1}$ as an element of $R$. If $r>0$, choose $c\in k$ such that $t_1-c$ does not divide $f$, possible because $k$ is infinite. It cannot be invertible in $R$, since otherwise it would divide a power of $f$ in the polynomial ring. This contradiction gives $r=0$. The finite algebraic extension $K/k$ is $k$ because $k$ is algebraically closed. Applying this to $A/\mathfrak m$ proves the residue-field assertion. If $a
otin \sqrt I$, the localization $(A/I)[1/a]$ is nonzero. It is finitely generated over $k$, so has a maximal ideal, and its residue map to $k$ restricts to a maximal ideal of $A$ containing $I$ and not $a$. Conversely a nilpotent element vanishes in every field quotient. This proves the intersection formula. Applying it to $k[T_1,\ldots ,T_ N]/J$ proves the last statement. $\square$ For $X=\operatorname {Spm}A$ put $V(I)=\{ \mathfrak m:I\subset \mathfrak m\} $ and $D(s)=X\setminus V(s)$. The identities $V(\sum I_\alpha )= igcap V(I_\alpha )$ and $V(IJ)=V(I)\cup V(J)$ define the Zariski topology. The $D(s)$ form a basis, and $D(s)\cap D(t)=D(st)$. Proposition 9.58.3 . 72F3ADBDFF9A The assignments $D(s)\mapsto A_ s=A[1/s]$ form a sheaf on this basis. Its extension $\mathcal O_ X$ to all opens has \[  \Gamma (D(s),\mathcal O_ X)=A_ s,\quad \mathcal O_{X,\mathfrak m}=A_{\mathfrak m},\quad \mathcal O_{X,\mathfrak m}/\mathfrak mA_{\mathfrak m}=k.  \] Every open of $X$ is quasi-compact. The construction is contravariantly equivalent to finitely generated $k$-algebras when its morphisms are local morphisms of $k$-ringed spaces. Passing to reduced algebras gives the usual equivalence with affine algebraic sets and polynomial maps. For $A=0$ the space and structure sheaf are empty. Proof. An increasing sequence of radical ideals stabilizes by Noetherianity, so decreasing sequences of closed sets stabilize. More generally every family of opens has the same union as a finite subfamily: otherwise successively add a member not contained in the preceding finite union to obtain a strictly increasing sequence of opens. Apply this also to covers of any open subset, proving quasi-compactness. If $D(t)\subset D(s)$, then $t\in \sqrt{(s)}$ by the preceding theorem. Thus $s$ is a unit in $A_ t$, giving the restriction $A_ s	o A_ t$. These maps obey transitivity by the localization universal property, including empty opens whose localization is zero. It remains to check the sheaf axiom on a basic open; localize first to reduce it to $X=D(1)$ and take a finite cover $D(t_ i)$. Its covering condition implies $(t_ i)=A$. Suppose $x_ i=a_ i/t_ i^{n_ i}\in A_{t_ i}$ agree in $A_{t_ it_ j}$. There is $N_{ij}$ such that \[  (t_ it_ j)^{N_{ij}}(t_ j^{n_ j}a_ i-t_ i^{n_ i}a_ j)=0.  \] Choose one $r\ge \max (n_ i+N_{ij},n_ j+N_{ij})$ for all pairs and put $b_ i=t_ i^{r-n_ i}a_ i\in A$. Then $t_ j^ rb_ i=t_ i^ rb_ j$ in $A$. The powers $t_ i^ r$ still generate the unit ideal, since no maximal ideal contains all of them. Choose $1=\sum c_ it_ i^ r$ and put $a=\sum c_ ib_ i$. In $A_{t_ j}$ the displayed compatibility gives $a=\sum c_ it_ i^ r x_ j=x_ j$. Uniqueness follows similarly: an element restricting to zero is killed by a common set of powers $t_ i^ r$, whose ideal is the unit ideal. Thus the basis sheaf axiom holds even with zero divisors; it did not replace equality after localization by equality in $A$. The sheaf on arbitrary opens is obtained by compatible local basic sections, so retains those basis sections. Its stalk is the union of the localizations $A_ s$ with $s
otin \mathfrak m$, namely $A_{\mathfrak m}$. Fractions with numerator outside $\mathfrak m$ are exactly its units, proving the local-ring and residue assertions. A homomorphism $\phi :A	o B$ sends a maximal ideal of $B$ to a maximal ideal of $A$, because the associated residue homomorphism is $A	o k$. Its inverse image of $D(s)$ is $D(\phi (s))$ and the localization maps give its local sheaf morphism. Conversely a local morphism yields $\phi $ on global sections. Locality and the residue maps show that its point map is the same inverse-image map of maximal ideals. Its sheaf map on every fraction is forced by the global numerator and the inverse of its denominator, so it is the one just constructed. These two constructions are inverse and respect composition. For a presentation $A=k[T]/J$, the residue maps identify $X$ with $V(J)$ and its polynomial functions with $A/\sqrt0$. A map of reduced coordinate rings is given by the images of the finitely many coordinates, which are polynomial functions; their equations hold exactly when the map lands in the target algebraic set. This proves the reduced equivalence. $\square$ For example the unpowered gluing formula fails already in $A=k	imes k$: take $t_1=(1,0)$, $t_2=(0,1)$, $a_1=(0,1)$, $a_2=0$ and $x_ i=a_ i/t_ i=0$. Although $1=t_1+t_2$, the proposed sum $a_1+a_2$ is nonzero. The powers-cleared proof above is the required replacement. The nilradical of a finite-type algebra is finitely generated and nilpotent: if generators $u_ i$ have $u_ i^{e_ i}=0$, its power $1+\sum (e_ i-1)$ is zero. Every maximal ideal contains it, so $\operatorname {Spm}(A/\sqrt0)$ has the same underlying space; exactness of localization identifies its sheaf with the corresponding quotient of $\mathcal O_ X$. Thus this reduction removes precisely the nilpotents, not any closed points. In the reduced case sections inject into their value functions by the Nullstellensatz in each localized algebra.

It is finitely generated over $k$, so has a maximal ideal, and its residue map to $k$ restricts to a maximal ideal of $A$ containing $I$ and not $a$. Conversely a nilpotent element vanishes in every field quotient. This proves the intersection formula. Applying it to $k[T_1,\ldots ,T_ N]/J$ proves the last statement. $\square$

title: Proposition 9.58.3
text: Proposition 9.58.3 . 72F3ADBDFF9A The assignments $D(s)\mapsto A_ s=A[1/s]$ form a sheaf on this basis. Its extension $\mathcal O_ X$ to all opens has \[  \Gamma (D(s),\mathcal O_ X)=A_ s,\quad \mathcal O_{X,\mathfrak m}=A_{\mathfrak m},\quad \mathcal O_{X,\mathfrak m}/\mathfrak mA_{\mathfrak m}=k.  \] Every open of $X$ is quasi-compact. The construction is contravariantly equivalent to finitely generated $k$-algebras when its morphisms are local morphisms of $k$-ringed spaces. Passing to reduced algebras gives the usual equivalence with affine algebraic sets and polynomial maps. For $A=0$ the space and structure sheaf are empty. Proof. An increasing sequence of radical ideals stabilizes by Noetherianity, so decreasing sequences of closed sets stabilize. More generally every family of opens has the same union as a finite subfamily: otherwise successively add a member not contained in the preceding finite union to obtain a strictly increasing sequence of opens. Apply this also to covers of any open subset, proving quasi-compactness. If $D(t)\subset D(s)$, then $t\in \sqrt{(s)}$ by the preceding theorem. Thus $s$ is a unit in $A_ t$, giving the restriction $A_ s\to A_ t$. These maps obey transitivity by the localization universal property, including empty opens whose localization is zero. It remains to check the sheaf axiom on a basic open; localize first to reduce it to $X=D(1)$ and take a finite cover $D(t_ i)$. Its covering condition implies $(t_ i)=A$. Suppose $x_ i=a_ i/t_ i^{n_ i}\in A_{t_ i}$ agree in $A_{t_ it_ j}$. There is $N_{ij}$ such that \[  (t_ it_ j)^{N_{ij}}(t_ j^{n_ j}a_ i-t_ i^{n_ i}a_ j)=0.  \] Choose one $r\ge \max (n_ i+N_{ij},n_ j+N_{ij})$ for all pairs and put $b_ i=t_ i^{r-n_ i}a_ i\in A$. In $A_{t_ j}$ the displayed compatibility gives $a=\sum c_ it_ i^ r x_ j=x_ j$. Uniqueness follows similarly: an element restricting to zero is killed by a common set of powers $t_ i^ r$, whose ideal is the unit ideal. Thus the basis sheaf axiom holds even with zero divisors; it did not replace equality after localization by equality in $A$. The sheaf on arbitrary opens is obtained by compatible local basic sections, so retains those basis sections. Its stalk is the union of the localizations $A_ s$ with $s\notin \mathfrak m$, namely $A_{\mathfrak m}$. Fractions with numerator outside $\mathfrak m$ are exactly its units, proving the local-ring and residue assertions. Locality and the residue maps show that its point map is the same inverse-image map of maximal ideals. Its sheaf map on every fraction is forced by the global numerator and the inverse of its denominator, so it is the one just constructed. These two constructions are inverse and respect composition. title: 9.59 Products, closed subspaces and projective charts

section: 9.59 Products, closed subspaces and projective charts
text: Finite unions of affine charts are glued by sheaf isomorphisms on open overlaps satisfying the cocycle rule. Gluing the underlying spaces by those identifications and defining a section to be a compatible tuple gives a sheaf whose stalks are the original local rings. We use the algebraic separation condition that its diagonal is closed in its algebraic product; the product is specified next. This is the finite-type closed-point ringed-space convention. Proposition 9.59.1 . 476B5A661E43 The algebraic product of $\operatorname {Spm}A$ and $\operatorname {Spm}B$ is $\operatorname {Spm}(A\otimes _ kB)$ with its localization sheaf. These affine products glue canonically for finite affine atlases and have the categorical product property. Closed subspaces are locally given by quotient rings, or by coherent ideal sheaves. Intersection has ideal $I+J$ and the least closed union has ideal $I\cap J$. The product ideal $IJ$ gives a possibly larger thickening of that union and has the same underlying set. Proof. The tensor algebra is finitely generated. Its maps to $k$ are exactly pairs of maps $A\to k$, $B\to k$, so its closed points are the set-theoretic product. For every finite-type affine source, the tensor universal property and the preceding full faithfulness give the required universal property for maps. Maps from a general glued source to an affine target are likewise homomorphisms to its global sections: construct them on each affine chart and use the forced fraction maps to glue. This proves the product property for general sources as well. Localizing one or both tensor factors gives the same ring as localizing their tensor product at the corresponding elements. Thus the products of overlapping affine charts are open, agree on triple overlaps, and glue independently of the chosen affine refinements. For a finite presentation matrix over $A_ s$, its kernel is a finite module, and localization is exact: if a fraction is killed by a localized map, some power of its denominator kills its image before localization, giving a localized kernel element. Consequently its kernel sheaf is locally generated by finitely many elements. This proves coherence of the localization sheaf and of kernels, images and finite quotients. A locally finitely generated ideal is therefore coherent, and its local quotient descriptions glue to closed subspaces. On $\operatorname {Spm}A$ a quotient $A/I$ has the underlying closed set $V(I)$ and local rings $(A/I)_{\mathfrak m}=A_{\mathfrak m}/I_{\mathfrak m}$. Factoring a quotient morphism is exactly containment in the reverse direction of its defining ideals. Hence $I+J$ gives the intersection and $I\cap J$ the least closed subspace containing both. Since $IJ\subset I\cap J$ and their radicals agree, the stated thickening and underlying-set assertions follow. They also hold for ideal sheaves because they can be checked on localizations. Taking $I=J=(T)\subset k[T]$ distinguishes the doubled point $k[T]/(T^2)$ from its least union with itself, $k[T]/(T)$. $\square$ The product topology generally differs from the Zariski topology just constructed. In the affine line every proper algebraic closed set is finite, so every two nonempty opens meet. In the product of two such topologies the diagonal is dense, since two cofinite sets meet, but in the algebraic plane it is the proper closed set $V(x-y)$. The local regular function $(1-x-y)^{-1}$ at $(0,0)$ also does not belong to $k[x]_{(x)}\otimes _ k k[y]_{(y)}$: an element of that tensor has a separated denominator $p(x)q(y)$, with both factors nonzero at zero. Equality would force $1-x-y$ to divide that product, impossible after substituting $y=1-x$. The line with a doubled origin, obtained by gluing two affine lines off zero, fails separation: in the product of its two different origin charts the diagonal is the punctured line $x=y\ne 0$. Its closure contains the distinct pair of origins, so the diagonal is not closed. Theorem 9.59.2 . 4D90B8C4C837 Let $B=\bigoplus _{m\ge 0}B_ m$ be a graded $k$-algebra generated by its finite-dimensional spaces $B_0,B_1$. No reducedness is assumed. For a positive-degree homogeneous $s$ let $B_{(s)}=(B[1/s])_0$. The affine spaces $U_ s=\operatorname {Spm}B_{(s)}$ glue by $U_ s\cap U_ t=U_{st}$ to a finite-type separated ringed space $\operatorname {Proj}_{\rm cl}B$. A basis $s_0,\ldots ,s_ N$ of $B_1$ gives a finite cover by the $U_{s_ i}$. One has $\operatorname {Proj}_{\rm cl}k[T_0,\ldots ,T_ N]=\mathbb P^ N_ k$, and every such $B$ gives a closed subspace of some $\mathbb P^ N_ k$. A graded homomorphism $B\to C$ gives a morphism on the open set of $\operatorname {Proj}_{\rm cl}C$ where the image of $B_1$ does not vanish simultaneously. It is a global morphism when this open is the whole space; a graded surjection gives a closed embedding. Positive Veronese subalgebras give the same projective ringed space. Proof. If $B_1=0$ all positive components vanish and the construction is empty; its finite cover is empty and it is a closed subspace of $\mathbb P^0_ k$. Assume otherwise for the following chart argument. If $s$ has degree $m$, then $B_{(s)}$ is generated over $B_0$ by the finite-dimensional space $B_ m/s$: a numerator of degree $dm$ is a sum of products of $d$ degree-$m$ monomials in $B_1$. Thus it is a finite-type algebra. For $t$ of degree $n$, \[  B_{(st)}=B_{(s)}[1/(t^ m/s^ n)].  \] Indeed the right side is the degree-zero part after both $s$ and $t$ are inverted; multiplying homogeneous numerators and denominators by powers makes their degrees agree, proving each inclusion. These canonical localizations commute on triple overlaps, so the preceding gluing construction applies, initially to the degree-one charts. For a point of $U_ s$, write $s$ as a $B_0$-linear combination of degree-$m$ monomials $s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_ m}$. The identity $s/s=1$ implies that at least one fraction $s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_ m}/s$ is nonzero there. Its nonvanishing open is $U_ s\cap U_{s_{i_1}}\cap \cdots \cap U_{s_{i_ m}}$, by the same localization equality. Thus every $U_ s$ is covered by the degree-one charts. This proves the finite-cover assertion and identifies all the charts with the originally glued space. The polynomial graded ring has $k[T_0,\ldots ,T_ N]_{(T_ i)}=k[T_ j/T_ i:j\ne i]$. Their overlaps are the usual projective coordinate changes, proving the projective-space assertion. The diagonal of projective space is closed: its equations in the product charts are $T_ iS_ j-T_ jS_ i=0$, and at a pair of points they hold exactly when their projective coordinates are proportional. To reduce general $B$ to this case, replace $B_0$ by $k1$ and keep every positive-degree component. The resulting subalgebra $B^+$ is generated by the $k$-space $B_1$: a coefficient from $B_0$ can be absorbed into the first positive-degree factor. Its degree-zero localization is unchanged, since $b_0=(b_0s)/s$. A polynomial graded algebra on a basis of $B_1$ therefore surjects onto $B^+$. In each affine projective chart it gives the quotient by the dehomogenized homogeneous relations. These quotient ideals agree on overlaps, giving a closed embedding. The diagonal of a closed subspace is closed by restriction of the ambient diagonal, proving separation even with nilpotents. A graded homomorphism gives the localization maps $B_{(s)}\to C_{(\phi (s))}$. They glue exactly on the indicated union of nonvanishing opens. In a graded surjection the images of $B_1$ generate $C$ in positive degree, so those opens cover, and the local maps are surjective, proving the closed-embedding claim. Without a covering condition a global morphism need not exist: $k[x_0,x_1]\to k[t_0,t_1,t_2]$, $x_ i\mapsto t_ i$, gives the rational projection $[t_0:t_1:t_2]\mapsto [t_0:t_1]$. At the base point $[0:0:1]$ any extension would restrict on the two lines $t_1=0$ and $t_0=0$ to the incompatible constants $[1:0]$ and $[0:1]$. These constants are forced on the whole lines by continuity, since a point is closed and the punctured line is dense. Finally $B_{(s)}=B_{(s^\ell )}$ for every positive $\ell $: multiply a fraction by enough powers of $s$ to make its denominator exponent divisible by $\ell $. The charts with degrees divisible by $\ell $ cover, since they include every $U_{s_ i^\ell }$, and their rings are those of the Veronese algebra $\bigoplus _ mB_{\ell m}$. This proves its canonical projective identification. $\square$

title: 9.60 Analytic local models and infinitesimal information

section: 9.60 Analytic local models and infinitesimal information
text: We use the ringed-space and local comorphism conventions of subsection 9.64.1 . In the analytic case the local models are $(A,(\mathcal O_\Omega /J)|_ A)$, where $J$ is a coherent ideal and $A=V(J)$, and analytic morphisms are those locally induced by ambient holomorphic maps carrying target equations into $J$. An analytic space is a Hausdorff ringed space with a countable basis admitting these local models and analytic transition isomorphisms. Compatible isomorphisms on chart overlaps glue by the same sheaf pasting construction used above; the Hausdorff and countable-basis conditions must also hold for the glued base. Their stalk rings are quotients of convergent power-series rings and have residue field $\mathbb C$. Proposition 9.60.1 . 57433F7B0D87 Such analytic local models retain their nilpotent germs. Their nilradical sheaf is coherent, locally nilpotent, and equals $\sqrt J/J$ in a model. Its quotient is the usual reduced analytic space with structure sheaf $(\mathcal O_\Omega /I_ A)|_ A$. Morphisms induce reduction morphisms, and morphisms between reduced models are determined by their point maps. For the doubled hyperplane with coordinates $(z,\epsilon )$ and $\epsilon ^2=0$, its sections are uniquely $u(z)+\epsilon v(z)$. Every analytic self-map is determined by arbitrary holomorphic $f$, a holomorphic tangent vector of coefficients $a$, and a holomorphic scalar $c$ on the reduced hyperplane, by \[  z\longmapsto f(z)+\epsilon a(z),\qquad \epsilon \longmapsto \epsilon c(z).  \] For any analytic local model its smallest ambient embedding dimension is $\dim _\mathbb C\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$. Proof. The ambient quotient $\mathcal O_\Omega /J$ is a coherent ambient module. It is also a coherent ring sheaf: lift finitely many quotient sections to ambient sections and adjoin generators of $J$; projections of their ambient relation generators generate the quotient relations. The same argument shows that coherence of a module annihilated by $J$ is equivalent before and after passage to the quotient. This argument uses the full ideal, so applies without reducedness. The analytic Nullstellensatz the analytic Nullstellensatz gives $\sqrt J=I_ A$. Coherence of the ideal of an analytic set and coherent quotient algebra, Cartan's coherence theorem for analytic ideals , kernels and exact sequences of coherent modules , therefore give coherence of the radical quotient. Locally choose finitely many nilpotent generators $u_ i$ with $u_ i^{e_ i}=0$; every monomial of total degree $1+\sum (e_ i-1)$ has a vanishing factor. This proves local nilpotence, without replacing a full section by its point values. Homomorphisms carry nilpotents to nilpotents, giving reduction maps. On reduced models a section is its actual holomorphic value function, so its pullback is forced by the point map. The same observation applies to local ringed spaces modeled on real $C^ r$ coordinate domains ($r=0,1,\ldots ,\infty $, or real analytic) or holomorphic domains. Their morphisms are exactly the usual manifold morphisms of that regularity: coordinate pullbacks have the asserted regularity, and evaluation on residue fields forces the pullback of every function to be its composition. Taylor expansion in $\epsilon $ modulo its square gives the unique section description. An ambient lift preserving the hyperplane has normal component vanishing at $\epsilon =0$; its first Taylor terms have the displayed form. Conversely those formulas are realized by the ambient holomorphic map $(z,w)\mapsto (f(z)+wa(z),wc(z))$, whose squared normal coordinate belongs to $(w^2)$. On a section its pullback is \[  u(f(z))+\epsilon \bigl (du(f(z))a(z)+c(z)v(f(z))\bigr ).  \] Thus the formulas really define the comorphism on all germs, and different coefficients can have the same reduced point map. For the embedding assertion write the local ring as $R=\mathbb C\{ z_1,\ldots ,z_ N\} /J$. The coordinate classes generate its maximal ideal, so $d=\dim \mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2 \le N$. Choose linear combinations of coordinates representing a basis of that quotient. The remaining $N-d$ independent linear relations modulo $\mathfrak m^2$ are represented by elements of $J$ with independent differentials at zero. By the holomorphic implicit function theorem their common zero set is a smooth germ of dimension $d$. Since those equations belong to $J$, the full quotient ring, including nilpotents, is a quotient of that smooth germ's ring by the remaining ideal. It is therefore a model in $\mathbb C^ d$. This proves the reverse inequality and the formula. $\square$ Example 9.60.2 . 94F2248906E2 For $N\ge 1$ the analytic curve $t\mapsto (t^ N,t^{N+1},\ldots ,t^{2N-1})$ has local ring $\mathbb C+t^ N\mathbb C\{ t\} $ at zero, dimension one and embedding dimension $N$. For $N=3$, writing $(x,y,z)=(t^3,t^4,t^5)$, its full analytic ideal sheaf is generated by \[  xz-y^2,\qquad x^3-yz,\qquad x^2y-z^2.  \] At zero this ideal requires three generators, so the codimension-two curve is not a sheaf-theoretic complete intersection there. A set-theoretic complete intersection means equality of zero sets using codimension-many equations and does not assert generation of the whole ideal sheaf. Proof. The parametrization is proper, since its first coordinate tends to infinity when $|t|$ does, and it is injective with holomorphic inverse $t=z_2/z_1$ off zero when $N\ge 2$. The proper-image theorem Remmert's proper mapping theorem makes its image analytic; it is a curve, with zero the only possible singular point. Every power $t^ j$ with $j\ge N$ is in the coordinate algebra. More precisely a convergent series with its first $N-1$ nonconstant coefficients zero has the form \[  c+t^ Ng_0(t^ N)+\sum _{r=1}^{N-1}t^{N+r}g_ r(t^ N)  \] with convergent $g_ r$, by grouping coefficients modulo $N$. Convergence follows from a coefficient bound $|a_ j|\le CR^{-j}$. This proves the local-ring assertion. Its maximal ideal and square are $t^ N\mathbb C\{ t\} $ and $t^{2N}\mathbb C\{ t\} $, so their quotient has basis $t^ N,\ldots ,t^{2N-1}$, proving the embedding dimension by the preceding proposition. For $N=3$ let $I$ be the displayed three-generator ideal. Replacing $y^2$ by $xz$, $yz$ by $x^3$ and $z^2$ by $x^2y$ reduces every monomial modulo $I$ to $x^ a$, $x^ ay$ or $x^ az$. Each replacement decreases the total number of $y,z$ factors and never decreases the ordinary total degree, so this terminates after at most the original degree many steps. The same reduction works for convergent power series: for an input coefficient bound $CR^{-d}$ in degree $d$, at most $d$ terms enter the ideal coefficients, each of degree at least $d-2$, with coefficients of absolute value one times the input. On a smaller polydisc of radius $r<\min (R,1)$ the resulting series are bounded by convergent sums of a polynomial in $d$ times $(r/R)^ d$. Thus it gives a convergent identity $f=A(x)+yB(x)+zC(x)\pmod I$ with convergent $A,B,C$. Under the parametrization the three terms have distinct exponent classes modulo three, so the resulting series vanishes identically exactly when $A=B=C=0$. This proves the full ideal assertion at zero. Away from zero the equations imply $x\ne 0$ and give $t=y/x$, $x=t^3,y=t^4,z=t^5$; two of the displayed equations have independent differentials there. The holomorphic implicit function theorem and division by smooth coordinate equations give the same ideal sheaf away from zero. Finally write $\mathfrak n=(x,y,z)$ for the maximal ideal of the ambient convergent ring. The quadratic initial terms $xz-y^2,-yz,-z^2$ are linearly independent. Every element of $\mathfrak n I$ has order at least three, so the three generators are independent modulo $\mathfrak n I$. Any generating family must span that quotient and has at least three members. This is incompatible with ideal generation by the codimension two. The argument makes no false inference from set-theoretic to ideal-theoretic complete intersection. $\square$ More generally, for a pure-dimensional analytic subset $A$ of a pure-dimensional complex space $X$, local set-theoretic complete intersection means that near every point of $A$ its underlying set is the common zero set of exactly $\operatorname {codim}_ X A$ holomorphic functions. This is a condition on the radical of the defining ideal; an ideal-theoretic complete intersection requires the ideal itself to have that many generators.

The same observation applies to local ringed spaces modeled on real $C^ r$ coordinate domains ($r=0,1,\ldots ,\infty $, or real analytic) or holomorphic domains. Their morphisms are exactly the usual manifold morphisms of that regularity: coordinate pullbacks have the asserted regularity, and evaluation on residue fields forces the pullback of every function to be its composition. Taylor expansion in $\epsilon $ modulo its square gives the unique section description. An ambient lift preserving the hyperplane has normal component vanishing at $\epsilon =0$; its first Taylor terms have the displayed form. Conversely those formulas are realized by the ambient holomorphic map $(z,w)\mapsto (f(z)+wa(z),wc(z))$, whose squared normal coordinate belongs to $(w^2)$. On a section its pullback is \[  u(f(z))+\epsilon \bigl (du(f(z))a(z)+c(z)v(f(z))\bigr ).  \] Thus the formulas really define the comorphism on all germs, and different coefficients can have the same reduced point map. For the embedding assertion write the local ring as $R=\mathbb C\{ z_1,\ldots ,z_ N\} /J$. The coordinate classes generate its maximal ideal, so $d=\dim \mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2 \le N$. Choose linear combinations of coordinates representing a basis of that quotient. The remaining $N-d$ independent linear relations modulo $\mathfrak m^2$ are represented by elements of $J$ with independent differentials at zero. By the holomorphic implicit function theorem their common zero set is a smooth germ of dimension $d$. Since those equations belong to $J$, the full quotient ring, including nilpotents, is a quotient of that smooth germ's ring by the remaining ideal. It is therefore a model in $\mathbb C^ d$. This proves the reverse inequality and the formula. $\square$

title: Example 9.60.2
section: 9.60 Analytic local models and infinitesimal information
text: Example 9.60.2 . 94F2248906E2 For $N\ge 1$ the analytic curve $t\mapsto (t^ N,t^{N+1},\ldots ,t^{2N-1})$ has local ring $\mathbb C+t^ N\mathbb C\{ t\} $ at zero, dimension one and embedding dimension $N$. For $N=3$, writing $(x,y,z)=(t^3,t^4,t^5)$, its full analytic ideal sheaf is generated by \[  xz-y^2,\qquad x^3-yz,\qquad x^2y-z^2.  \] At zero this ideal requires three generators, so the codimension-two curve is not a sheaf-theoretic complete intersection there. A set-theoretic complete intersection means equality of zero sets using codimension-many equations and does not assert generation of the whole ideal sheaf. Proof. The parametrization is proper, since its first coordinate tends to infinity when $|t|$ does, and it is injective with holomorphic inverse $t=z_2/z_1$ off zero when $N\ge 2$. The proper-image theorem Remmert's proper mapping theorem makes its image analytic; it is a curve, with zero the only possible singular point. Every power $t^ j$ with $j\ge N$ is in the coordinate algebra. More precisely a convergent series with its first $N-1$ nonconstant coefficients zero has the form \[  c+t^ Ng_0(t^ N)+\sum _{r=1}^{N-1}t^{N+r}g_ r(t^ N)  \] with convergent $g_ r$, by grouping coefficients modulo $N$. Convergence follows from a coefficient bound $|a_ j|\le CR^{-j}$. This proves the local-ring assertion. Its maximal ideal and square are $t^ N\mathbb C\{ t\} $ and $t^{2N}\mathbb C\{ t\} $, so their quotient has basis $t^ N,\ldots ,t^{2N-1}$, proving the embedding dimension by the preceding proposition. For $N=3$ let $I$ be the displayed three-generator ideal. Replacing $y^2$ by $xz$, $yz$ by $x^3$ and $z^2$ by $x^2y$ reduces every monomial modulo $I$ to $x^ a$, $x^ ay$ or $x^ az$. Each replacement decreases the total number of $y,z$ factors and never decreases the ordinary total degree, so this terminates after at most the original degree many steps. The same reduction works for convergent power series: for an input coefficient bound $CR^{-d}$ in degree $d$, at most $d$ terms enter the ideal coefficients, each of degree at least $d-2$, with coefficients of absolute value one times the input. On a smaller polydisc of radius $r<\min (R,1)$ the resulting series are bounded by convergent sums of a polynomial in $d$ times $(r/R)^ d$. Thus it gives a convergent identity $f=A(x)+yB(x)+zC(x)\pmod I$ with convergent $A,B,C$. Under the parametrization the three terms have distinct exponent classes modulo three, so the resulting series vanishes identically exactly when $A=B=C=0$. This proves the full ideal assertion at zero. Away from zero the equations imply $x\ne 0$ and give $t=y/x$, $x=t^3,y=t^4,z=t^5$; two of the displayed equations have independent differentials there. The holomorphic implicit function theorem and division by smooth coordinate equations give the same ideal sheaf away from zero. Finally write $\mathfrak n=(x,y,z)$ for the maximal ideal of the ambient convergent ring. The quadratic initial terms $xz-y^2,-yz,-z^2$ are linearly independent. Every element of $\mathfrak n I$ has order at least three, so the three generators are independent modulo $\mathfrak n I$. Any generating family must span that quotient and has at least three members. This is incompatible with ideal generation by the codimension two. The argument makes no false inference from set-theoretic to ideal-theoretic complete intersection. $\square$

title: 10.88.1 Germ spaces and regular-function coherence
section: 10.88 Local sheaf interfaces and regular-function coherence
text: Proposition 10.88.2 . 5809CC1BC6C9 If the étalé space of a sheaf is Hausdorff, two sections on a connected open set that agree on a nonempty open subset agree everywhere. The converse holds when the base is Hausdorff and locally connected. The sheaf of locally polynomial functions on $\mathbb C^ n$ is coherent, for its ordinary or Zariski topology. The regular-function localization sheaf on any finite-type algebraic model is coherent, and remains so on passage to the ordinary complex topology. Proof. The equality set of two sections is always open. In a Hausdorff étalé space it is also closed, since the diagonal is closed and sections are continuous; connectedness proves the first assertion. For the converse germs over different points are separated using the Hausdorff base. For different germs over the same point, take representatives on a common connected open neighborhood, available by local connectedness. If their étalé graph neighborhoods met, the representatives would agree near that meeting point and hence everywhere on the connected neighborhood, a contradiction. The two graphs are thus disjoint open neighborhoods of the germs. Locally polynomial functions give the constant sheaf of rings $\mathbb C[z_1,\ldots ,z_ n]$: equality on a nonempty ordinary open, or on a nonempty Zariski open, is polynomial identity. A finite matrix over this sheaf is locally a matrix over that Noetherian ring. Its algebraic kernel is finitely generated, and sheafifying those constant generators gives exactly the kernel sheaf, by its stalks. This proves coherence, including the finite-generation condition for its unit module. For the regular localization sheaf, clear a common denominator in a finite local matrix, take its kernel over the finite-type algebra, and localize. Exactness of localization and Noetherianity, already proved above, identify all nearby kernel stalks with those finitely many localized generators. This is exactly coherence. Its inverse image to the ordinary complex topology has the same local stalk rings and presentations: inverse image of sheaves is exact, and a finite family of sections is locally pulled back from a Zariski neighborhood. The same finite kernel generators therefore prove coherence there as well. This does not identify regular germs with all holomorphic germs. The sheaf inverse/direct-image adjunction for arbitrary continuous maps is already proposition 10.43.2 , with its full stalk construction; it is reused here without a second proof. $\square$

title: 9.67.1 Meromorphic functions under modifications
text: Let $\mathcal M_ X$ denote localization of the structure sheaf at its nonzerodivisors. For a reduced complex space these are exactly functions not vanishing identically on any local branch, as in universal denominators for weakly holomorphic functions . Theorem 9.67.2 . BC1BD33555B1 Let $\mu :X\to Y$ be a proper bimeromorphic map of reduced complex spaces with countable bases. Require its isomorphism locus to be dense both upstairs and downstairs, as in the bimeromorphic convention. Then pullback on the dense locus gives a sheaf isomorphism \[  \mathcal M_ Y\  \simeq \  \mu _*\mathcal M_ X.  \] It is a direct-image assertion, not an inverse-image isomorphism at an individual exceptional point. Neither arbitrary embedded nilpotents nor exceptional open components can be omitted from these qualifications. Proof. A nonzerodivisor downstairs remains one upstairs: its zero set is nowhere dense, and its inverse image is nowhere dense by nowhere-dense inverse images under bimeromorphic maps . Thus meromorphic pullback is defined. It is injective, since a numerator vanishing on the dense isomorphism locus is zero on the reduced space. To prove surjectivity it suffices to work near a fixed $y\in Y$. Let $u$ be meromorphic on $\mu ^{-1}U$ for a neighborhood $U$ of $y$, and form the coherent submodule $F=\mathcal O_ X+u\mathcal O_ X\subset \mathcal M_ X$. It is coherent: where $u=g/d$ with $d$ a nonzerodivisor, multiplication by $d$ identifies it with the coherent ideal $(d,g)$. The proper coherent direct-image theorem 9.47.2 makes $G=\mu _*F/\mu _*\mathcal O_ X$ coherent on $U$. Off the exceptional locus it is the quotient $(\mathcal O_ Y+u\mathcal O_ Y)/\mathcal O_ Y$ and is zero at generic regular points of each branch, because $u$ is meromorphic there. Hence its support contains no local irreducible component after shrinking around $y$; the support is analytic by coherence. There is $h\in \operatorname {Ann}(G_ y)$ not vanishing identically on any branch at $y$. The finitely many minimal prime ideals $P_ i$ of the reduced local ring are its branch ideals by irreducible analytic branches and prime ideals . Localization of $G_ y$ at $P_ i$ is zero; finite generation supplies an element of its annihilator outside $P_ i$. Finite prime avoidance then supplies one outside their union. Explicitly choose $a_ i$ in that ideal outside $P_ i$ and $b_ i\in \bigcap _{j\ne i}P_ j\setminus P_ i$, possible by the incomparability of the distinct minimal primes; $\sum _ i a_ ib_ i$ is outside every $P_ i$. Shrinking gives a holomorphic $h$ killing the coherent quotient, still a nonzerodivisor at nearby points after excluding no branch; the nowhere-dense zero set criterion suffices for its meromorphic germ. The section class of $u$ in $G$ is killed, so $(h\circ \mu )u$ is holomorphic upstairs over a smaller neighborhood. Here equality is sheafwise over full inverse images, the meaning of the direct image, rather than at one exceptional stalk. By properness, after shrinking to a relatively compact neighborhood of $y$, this holomorphic function is bounded on its inverse image. On the dense isomorphism locus it gives a bounded holomorphic function downstairs. Bounded holomorphic removal on the regular locus extends it across the exceptional analytic subset there; it is weakly holomorphic across the singular locus. The full universal-denominator statement universal denominators for weakly holomorphic functions therefore makes its germ at $y$ an element $v\in \mathcal M_{Y,y}$. Then $v/h$ pulls back to $u$ on the dense locus and hence everywhere as a meromorphic germ on the reduced space. This proves surjectivity on every stalk of the direct image and the claimed sheaf isomorphism. $\square$ The qualifications can be checked explicitly. The proper map $\mathbb C\coprod \{ p\} \to \mathbb C$ equal to the identity on the first component and sending $p$ to zero is an isomorphism off zero but has an exceptional open component; $1/z$ has no pullback there. On the embedded double point over a line, $R=\mathbb C\{ z,\epsilon \} /(\epsilon ^2,z\epsilon )$, every nonunit annihilates $\epsilon $, so the total fraction ring is $R$ itself. The reduction to $\mathbb C\{ z\} $ kills nonzero $\epsilon $ and has the larger meromorphic field, disproving invariance in that case. Even a reduced blowup does not have inverse-image meromorphic invariance: in its chart $(x,w)\mapsto (x,xw)$ the germ $e^ w$ cannot be $g(x,xw)/h(x,xw)$ for base holomorphic germs. Their first nonzero powers of $x$ would give polynomials $g_ a(w),h_ b(w)$; the finite nonzero limit forces $a=b$ and $e^ w=g_ a(w)/h_ a(w)$. If $Pe^ w=Q$ for nonzero polynomials, differentiating gives $Q'P-QP'=QP$, whose degrees contradict one another. Finally on the ordinary doubled line $\mathbb C\{ z,\epsilon \} /(\epsilon ^2)$, the section $\epsilon e^{1/z}$ on the punctured line has zero reduction but no meromorphic extension: every nonzerodivisor is $a(z)+\epsilon b(z)$ with $a\ne 0$, and its inverse gives only ordinary meromorphic coefficients of $1,\epsilon $. Those cannot contain the essential singularity $e^{1/z}$.

title: 2.18 Elliptic operators of arbitrary order
text: Manifolds are smooth, Hausdorff, second countable and without boundary. Bundles are real or complex and of finite rank. A positive smooth density and bundle inner products define formal adjoints; complex inner products are linear in the first variable. Fourier transforms use $e^{-2\pi i x\cdot \xi }$, and $\langle \xi \rangle =(1+|\xi |^2)^{1/2}$. Proposition 2.17.2 . 5AFFEC4D76E3 For a differential operator $P:E\to F$ of order at most $d$, with local expression $P=\sum _{|\alpha |\leq d}a_\alpha \partial ^\alpha $, the degree-$d$ principal symbol is the intrinsic map \[  \sigma _ P(x,\xi )=\sum _{|\alpha |=d}a_\alpha (x)\xi ^\alpha .  \] For a smooth real scalar $f$ and a section $u$, \[  e^{-tf}P(e^{tf}u)=t^ d\sigma _ P(df)u+\sum _{0\leq j<d}t^ jQ_ j u, \qquad \operatorname {ord}Q_ j\leq d-j.  \] Composition has symbol $\sigma _{QP}=\sigma _ Q\sigma _ P$ in the sum of the specified orders. There is a unique formal adjoint, and \[  \sigma _{P^*}(x,\xi )=(-1)^ d\sigma _ P(x,\xi )^*.  \] Injectivity of $\sigma _ P(x,\xi )$ for all real $\xi \ne 0$ is called ellipticity here. If the bundle ranks agree this is invertibility. Proof. The product rule gives the scalar-conjugation identity. The highest power has every derivative landing on the exponential, each through its first derivative. A term of power $t^ j$ leaves at most $d-j$ derivatives on $u$. The left side is intrinsic, so its highest coefficient gives the asserted coordinate and frame invariance. Taking all highest-order derivatives on the section in a composition gives the symbol product, even if that product vanishes and the actual composite order drops. Use smooth orthonormal local frames and write the density as $\rho (x)\, dx$. Integration by parts gives \[  P^*v=\rho ^{-1}\sum _{|\alpha |\leq d}(-1)^{|\alpha |} \partial ^\alpha (\rho a_\alpha ^*v).  \] This is a differential operator with the claimed leading symbol. The integration identity on compactly supported test sections proves uniqueness, hence the formulas glue on overlaps. A cutoff equal to one near a compact intersection of supports gives the same identity for arbitrary sections with that compact intersection. Derivatives of the cutoff contribute zero, since one of the two sections is then zero near each such point. This also defines the action on distributional sections by transposition. The argument uses a density and does not require orientability. $\square$ Lemma 2.18.1 . 0D76F8A1E29B On a compact smooth $m$-manifold and a smooth bundle, Sobolev spaces $H^ s$ are defined for every real $s$, locally by \[  \| u\| _{H^ s(\mathbb R^ m)}^2 =\int \langle \xi \rangle ^{2s}|\widehat u(\xi )|^2\, d\xi .  \] Finite charts, frames and cutoffs give equivalent norms independent of these choices. Their Hilbert duals under the density/metric pairing are $H^{-s}$. Smooth sections are dense; every distribution belongs to some $H^{-N}$. One has $H^ s\subset C^ l$ when $s>l+m/2$, and $H^{s+1}\hookrightarrow H^ s$ is compact for every real $s$. If $r<a$, then, for every $\varepsilon >0$, \[  \| u\| _{H^{a-1}}\leq \varepsilon \| u\| _{H^ a} +C_{\varepsilon ,a,r}\| u\| _{H^ r}.  \] Proof. If $m=0$, all these spaces are finite dimensional and the assertions are immediate. Suppose $m\geq 1$. Here are the real-order details extending the coefficient Sobolev construction in Sobolev spaces, duality and local embedding . For $0<\theta <1$, Fourier inversion and the Plancherel theorem and the change of variables $h\mapsto |\xi |^{-1}h$ give, initially for rapidly decreasing smooth functions, \[  \iint \frac{|u(x+h)-u(x)|^2}{|h|^{m+2\theta }}\, dx\, dh =c_{m,\theta }\int |\xi |^{2\theta }|\widehat u(\xi )|^2\, d\xi .  \] The constant is the integral with numerator $|e^{2\pi i h_1}-1|^2$: near zero it is $O(|h|^2)$, and at infinity it is bounded. It is finite and positive. Rotation invariance removes the direction of $\xi $. Fourier-space smooth approximation extends the identity by completion. Adding $\| u\| _2^2$ gives an equivalent $H^\theta $ norm. A bounded smooth multiplier with bounded first derivatives acts boundedly: split its difference into its bounded value times the difference of $u$ and its Lipschitz difference times $u$. The latter term is bounded by $C\| u\| _2^2$ using $\min \{ |h|^2,1\} $ in the integral. On compact coordinate pieces, a smooth change of coordinates and its inverse have bounded Jacobians and are locally bi-Lipschitz. The difference integral therefore proves boundedness on $H^\theta $. For precision, subdivide into finitely many sufficiently small convex pieces: approximation of the derivative by its invertible central value gives both Lipschitz bounds there. A partition handles these pieces. In the zero extensions, pairs leaving a larger piece have distance bounded below from the cutoff support and add only an $L^2$ term. For an integer $q\geq 0$, the Fourier norm of $H^{q+\theta }$ is equivalent to the sum of the $H^\theta $ norms of derivatives of orders at most $q$. The chain and product rules now prove the same coordinate/multiplier assertions in every nonnegative real order. Negative orders follow by transposition, including the smooth Jacobian and metric multipliers. A finite partition and its reconstruction map identify the dual global norm with the corresponding local $H^{-s}$ norms. This proves all the claimed norm and duality identifications. Fourier cutoff approximation, followed by multiplication with a fixed larger spatial cutoff, proves density locally in each order; sum the finite pieces globally. Fourier inversion and Cauchy–Schwarz give $C^ l$ bounds because $\int \langle \xi \rangle ^{2l-2s}d\xi <\infty $. A compactly supported distribution has finite order, hence is bounded on some $C^ l$ test norm. This embedding puts it in $H^{-N}$ for sufficiently large $N$. A finite partition gives the global assertion. For compactness, a bounded sequence in $H^{s+1}$ supported in one fixed compact coordinate set has $H^ s$ Fourier tail at most $C/R$ on $|\xi |>R$. On each bounded frequency ball its Fourier transforms and their first derivatives are uniformly bounded: pair the distributions with $\chi (x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot \xi }$ and $x_ j\chi (x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot \xi }$, where $\chi =1$ near that support, and use the bounded $H^{-s-1}$ norms of these test functions for bounded $\xi $. Finite frequency grids and the derivative bound give a uniformly convergent subsequence on the ball; a diagonal choice over integer $R$, together with the tail bound, is Cauchy in $H^ s$. Sum over the finite charts. This proof also covers negative $s$. Finally the pointwise weight inequality $\langle \xi \rangle ^{a-1}\leq \varepsilon \langle \xi \rangle ^ a+ C_\varepsilon \langle \xi \rangle ^ r$ follows by separating large and bounded frequencies. Integration and finite localization prove the final estimate, with an arbitrary prescribed small coefficient. $\square$ Lemma 2.18.2 . 3C443B01B6F3 Suppose a matrix symbol $a(x,\xi )$ is the sum of an $x$-independent symbol and one supported in a fixed compact $x$-set, and satisfies \[  |\partial _ x^\alpha \partial _\xi ^\beta a(x,\xi )| \leq C_{\alpha \beta }\langle \xi \rangle ^{\mu -|\beta |}.  \] Its Fourier operator $\operatorname {Op}(a)$ is bounded $H^ s\to H^{s-\mu }$ for every real $s$; its adjoint has the same order bound. On rapidly decreasing smooth functions it is defined by \[  \operatorname {Op}(a)u(x)= \int e^{2\pi ix\cdot \xi }a(x,\xi )\widehat u(\xi )\, d\xi .  \] If $P$ is elliptic of positive order $d$ in a bundle chart, there is, near any relatively compact smaller chart, an exact identity on sections supported there, \[  v=A Pv-R^*v,  \] where $A:H^ s\to H^{s+d}$ and $R^*:H^ s\to H^{s+1}$ are bounded for every real $s$. These operators need not be differential. Proof. For a compact-$x$ symbol, integration by parts in its $x$-Fourier transform gives, for every $N$, \[  |\widehat a(\eta -\xi ,\xi )| \leq C_ N\langle \eta -\xi \rangle ^{-N}\langle \xi \rangle ^\mu .  \] The weighted Fourier kernel from $H^ s$ to $H^{s-\mu }$ is thus bounded by $C_ N\langle \eta -\xi \rangle ^{-N+|s-\mu |}$. Here the elementary inequalities $\langle \eta \rangle \leq \sqrt2\langle \xi \rangle \langle \eta -\xi \rangle $ and its interchange control their ratio to any real power. Choose $N>|s-\mu |+m$. Both integrals of this kernel, in either variable, are uniformly bounded. Cauchy–Schwarz with its absolute value, followed by integration, gives its $L^2$ operator bound. The $x$-independent part is a Fourier multiplier with the asserted bound. Duality gives the adjoint bound in every order. In particular smooth bounded-coefficient differential operators, localized if necessary, have their expected Sobolev orders. Write $P^\dagger $ for the Euclidean coefficient adjoint in this chart and set $Q=P^\dagger P$. The Fourier principal symbol of $P$ is $p_ d(x,\xi )=(2\pi i)^ d\sigma _ P(x,\xi )$. The principal symbol of $Q$ is the positive matrix $q(x,\xi )=p_ d(x,\xi )^*p_ d(x,\xi )$. On a compact subchart and $|\xi |=1$ its smallest eigenvalue has a strictly positive lower bound: continuity and compactness give the minimum, and injectivity excludes zero. We construct a self-adjoint global extension. Let $Q_0$ be the constant homogeneous differential operator with Fourier symbol $q(x_0,\xi )$ at a fixed chart point. Choose $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ compactly supported in the chart and equal to one on a neighborhood of the smaller chart. On $\mathbb R^ m$ set \[  \widetilde Q=Q_0+\chi (Q-Q_0)\chi .  \] The last term is extended by zero. This operator is formally self-adjoint and agrees with $Q$ near the smaller chart. Its principal symbol $\widetilde q=\chi ^2q+(1-\chi ^2)q(x_0,\xi )$ remains positive definite, uniformly on all $x$ and the unit sphere. Outside a fixed compact set it is $q(x_0,\xi )$. Choose a smooth frequency cutoff $\rho $ equal to zero near zero and one for $|\xi |\geq 2$. The explicit matrix symbol \[  b(x,\xi )=\rho (\xi )\widetilde q(x,\xi )^{-1}  \] has order $-2d$. Differentiating the inverse matrix identity proves all its symbol estimates; homogeneity gives one extra inverse power per $\xi $ derivative. Its difference from the corresponding frozen symbol is compactly supported in $x$. Put $B=\operatorname {Op}(b)$. There is an exact, finite computation of $\widetilde Q B$: if $\widetilde Q=\sum a_\alpha (x)\partial ^\alpha $, its symbol is \[  \sum _{\alpha }\sum _{\beta \leq \alpha } \binom \alpha \beta a_\alpha (x)(2\pi i\xi )^{\alpha -\beta } \partial _ x^\beta b(x,\xi ).  \] This follows directly by differentiating the Fourier integral. The degree-$2d$, $\beta =0$ terms sum to $\rho I$. Every other term has order at most $-1$. Thus \[  \widetilde Q B=I+R,  \] where $R$ has order $-1$ in the just proved class; outside the fixed compact $x$-set its symbol is $(\rho -1)I$, a smooth low-frequency multiplier. Transposing this identity, using self-adjointness of $\widetilde Q$, gives $B^*\widetilde Q=I+R^*$. These identities initially hold on rapidly decreasing smooth functions and extend to all applicable Sobolev spaces by density and duality. For $v$ supported in the smaller chart, $\widetilde Qv=Qv$. Extend the coefficients of $P^\dagger $ smoothly with a compact cutoff equal to one there and put $A=B^*P^\dagger $ with this extension. It has order at most $-d$ by the bounds above. Hence $v=APv-R^*v$, with the required gains. The construction used one matrix inverse and a finite Leibniz formula; no asymptotic symbol sum or unproved composition theorem is being invoked. $\square$ Theorem 2.18.3 . DB125476638D Let $P:E\to F$ have smooth coefficients and injective principal symbol, of positive order $d$. If $u$ is a distributional section and $Pu\in H^ s_{\rm loc}$ for a real $s$, then $u\in H^{s+d}_{\rm loc}$. In particular $Pu$ smooth implies $u$ smooth. On a compact manifold, for every real $s$ and $r<s+d$, \[  \| u\| _{H^{s+d}}\leq C_{s,r} (\| Pu\| _{H^ s}+\| u\| _{H^ r})  \] whenever the right side is finite. In particular, if $u\in L^2$ and $Pu\in H^ k$, $k\geq 0$, then \[  u\in H^{k+d},\qquad \| u\| _{H^{k+d}}\leq C_ k(\| Pu\| _{H^ k}+\| u\| _2).  \] The constants depend on the fixed operator, norms and compact localizations, as well as the displayed orders. Proof. Localize inside a chart where the preceding identity holds. Choose cutoffs $\varphi ,\psi $ supported there, with $\psi =1$ near $\operatorname {Supp}\varphi $. Write $f=Pu$. For $v=\varphi u$, the identity gives \[  v=A\bigl (\varphi f+[P,\varphi ](\psi u)\bigr )-R^*v.  \] The commutator has order at most $d-1$. If $\psi u\in H^ t$ and $f\in H^ s$ locally, the three terms on the right belong respectively to $H^{s+d}$, $H^{t+1}$ and $H^{t+1}$. Thus $v\in H^{\min \{ s+d,t+1\} }$, with a bound by the localized $H^ s$ norm of $f$ and $H^ t$ norm of $u$. A compactly supported localization of any distribution starts in some $H^{-N}$ by the Sobolev lemma. Finitely many nested cutoffs and iteration reach $s+d$, proving the local result. If $f$ is smooth, repeat for every order and use Sobolev embedding. For a smooth global $u$ on a compact manifold, take $t=s+d-1$ in the same identity and sum over finitely many smaller charts and cutoffs. It gives \[  \| u\| _{H^{s+d}}\leq C_ s (\| Pu\| _{H^ s}+\| u\| _{H^{s+d-1}}).  \] The interpolation inequality in lemma 2.18.1 , with a sufficiently small coefficient, absorbs the intermediate norm and gives the asserted bound with any $r<s+d$.
