Then for every real $s$ the bounded operator \[  P:H^{s+d}(M,E)\longrightarrow H^ s(M,F)  \] is Fredholm. Its kernel $K$ and the distributional kernel $K^*$ of its formal adjoint are finite dimensional and smooth, independent of $s$, and its range is \[  \{ f\in H^ s(M,F):\langle f,v\rangle =0\text{ for every }v\in K^*\} .  \] Here the pairing with a smooth section is the distributional extension of the $L^2$ pairing. There are continuous direct sums \[  H^ s(M,F)=P H^{s+d}(M,E)\oplus K^*,\qquad C^\infty (M,F)=P C^\infty (M,E)\oplus K^*.  \] They are orthogonal for $s=0$ in the first identity and in the $L^2$ pairing for the smooth identity. The index is $\dim K-\dim K^*$ and does not depend on the Sobolev order. Proof. All distributional null solutions are smooth by the preceding theorem. Fix $s$, put $a=s+d$, and use its estimate with remainder $H^{a-1}$. On the kernel the $H^ a$ norm is bounded by the $H^{a-1}$ norm. Compactness of that inclusion makes the closed unit ball of the kernel compact in $H^ a$: a lower-order convergent subsequence is upgraded by the estimate on differences. An infinite orthonormal sequence would contradict compactness, so the kernel is finite dimensional. Its elements are exactly the fixed smooth space $K$. Let $\Pi _ K$ be the finite-rank projection defined using an $L^2$ orthonormal basis of $K$. Pairing with its smooth members makes $\Pi _ K$ continuous in every Sobolev order. There is a bound \[  \| u\| _{H^ a}\leq C_ s\| Pu\| _{H^ s} \qquad (\Pi _ Ku=0).  \] Otherwise choose a normalized sequence violating it, with $Pu_ j\to 0$. After a subsequence it converges in $H^{a-1}$; the general estimate on differences makes it converge in $H^ a$. Its limit has norm one, is in $K$ and has projection zero, a contradiction. If $Pu_ j$ converges in $H^ s$, subtract $\Pi _ Ku_ j$ and apply this bound to differences. The resulting sections converge in $H^ a$ and their limit maps to the target limit. The range is therefore closed. Equal ranks make the principal symbol invertible. The adjoint symbol formula makes $P^*$ elliptic as well. The same argument gives its finite-dimensional smooth distributional kernel $K^*$. The annihilator of the range in $(H^ s)^*=H^{-s}$ consists precisely of distributional solutions of $P^*v=0$: test first against smooth domain sections and then use density. Thus it is exactly $K^*$. A closed linear subspace is the intersection of the kernels of its continuous annihilators, by Hilbert projection and Riesz representation . This proves the range description and finite codimension. Its $L^2$ projection onto $K^*$ is continuous on $H^ s$, giving the first direct sum and index. For a smooth target, the Sobolev decomposition at $s=0$ writes $f=Pu+v$ with $u\in H^ d$ and $v\in K^*$. The right side $Pu=f-v$ is smooth, so regularity makes $u$ smooth. Conversely the range annihilates $K^*$ by integration by parts. Thus the smooth range is the common kernel of finitely many continuous smooth functionals, and is closed in the smooth topology. This proves the second direct sum and its orthogonality. The index formula uses the same smooth spaces for every $s$. $\square$ If $d=0$ and $\dim M>0$, ellipticity is pointwise injectivity. The smooth left inverse $(P^*P)^{-1}P^*$ gives the corresponding order-zero regularity estimates directly. With equal ranks $P$ is a smooth bundle isomorphism, its inverse acts boundedly in every Sobolev order, and its index and both kernels are zero. No compact positive-order argument is needed. A compact zero-dimensional manifold is a finite set: all section and distribution spaces are finite dimensional and smooth, and the assertions reduce to linear algebra. In that case ellipticity on nonzero cotangent vectors is vacuous, so pointwise invertibility is not inferred from it; for an endomorphism the finite-dimensional index is zero.

title: Lemma 2.18.1
text: Lemma 2.18.1 . 0D76F8A1E29B On a compact smooth $m$-manifold and a smooth bundle, Sobolev spaces $H^ s$ are defined for every real $s$, locally by \[  \| u\| _{H^ s(\mathbb R^ m)}^2 =\int \langle \xi \rangle ^{2s}|\widehat u(\xi )|^2\, d\xi .  \] Finite charts, frames and cutoffs give equivalent norms independent of these choices. Their Hilbert duals under the density/metric pairing are $H^{-s}$. Smooth sections are dense; every distribution belongs to some $H^{-N}$. One has $H^ s\subset C^ l$ when $s>l+m/2$, and $H^{s+1}\hookrightarrow H^ s$ is compact for every real $s$. If $r<a$, then, for every $\varepsilon >0$, \[  \| u\| _{H^{a-1}}\leq \varepsilon \| u\| _{H^ a} +C_{\varepsilon ,a,r}\| u\| _{H^ r}.  \] Proof. If $m=0$, all these spaces are finite dimensional and the assertions are immediate. Suppose $m\geq 1$. Here are the real-order details extending the coefficient Sobolev construction in Sobolev spaces, duality and local embedding . For $0<\theta <1$, Fourier inversion and the Plancherel theorem and the change of variables $h\mapsto |\xi |^{-1}h$ give, initially for rapidly decreasing smooth functions, \[  \iint \frac{|u(x+h)-u(x)|^2}{|h|^{m+2\theta }}\, dx\, dh =c_{m,\theta }\int |\xi |^{2\theta }|\widehat u(\xi )|^2\, d\xi .  \] The constant is the integral with numerator $|e^{2\pi i h_1}-1|^2$: near zero it is $O(|h|^2)$, and at infinity it is bounded. It is finite and positive. Rotation invariance removes the direction of $\xi $. Fourier-space smooth approximation extends the identity by completion. Adding $\| u\| _2^2$ gives an equivalent $H^\theta $ norm. A bounded smooth multiplier with bounded first derivatives acts boundedly: split its difference into its bounded value times the difference of $u$ and its Lipschitz difference times $u$. The latter term is bounded by $C\| u\| _2^2$ using $\min \{ |h|^2,1\} $ in the integral. On compact coordinate pieces, a smooth change of coordinates and its inverse have bounded Jacobians and are locally bi-Lipschitz. The difference integral therefore proves boundedness on $H^\theta $. For precision, subdivide into finitely many sufficiently small convex pieces: approximation of the derivative by its invertible central value gives both Lipschitz bounds there. A partition handles these pieces. In the zero extensions, pairs leaving a larger piece have distance bounded below from the cutoff support and add only an $L^2$ term. For an integer $q\geq 0$, the Fourier norm of $H^{q+\theta }$ is equivalent to the sum of the $H^\theta $ norms of derivatives of orders at most $q$. The chain and product rules now prove the same coordinate/multiplier assertions in every nonnegative real order. Negative orders follow by transposition, including the smooth Jacobian and metric multipliers. A finite partition and its reconstruction map identify the dual global norm with the corresponding local $H^{-s}$ norms. This proves all the claimed norm and duality identifications. Fourier cutoff approximation, followed by multiplication with a fixed larger spatial cutoff, proves density locally in each order; sum the finite pieces globally. Fourier inversion and Cauchy–Schwarz give $C^ l$ bounds because $\int \langle \xi \rangle ^{2l-2s}d\xi <\infty $. A compactly supported distribution has finite order, hence is bounded on some $C^ l$ test norm. This embedding puts it in $H^{-N}$ for sufficiently large $N$. A finite partition gives the global assertion. For compactness, a bounded sequence in $H^{s+1}$ supported in one fixed compact coordinate set has $H^ s$ Fourier tail at most $C/R$ on $|\xi |>R$. On each bounded frequency ball its Fourier transforms and their first derivatives are uniformly bounded: pair the distributions with $\chi (x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot \xi }$ and $x_ j\chi (x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot \xi }$, where $\chi =1$ near that support, and use the bounded $H^{-s-1}$ norms of these test functions for bounded $\xi $. Finite frequency grids and the derivative bound give a uniformly convergent subsequence on the ball; a diagonal choice over integer $R$, together with the tail bound, is Cauchy in $H^ s$. Sum over the finite charts. This proof also covers negative $s$. Finally the pointwise weight inequality $\langle \xi \rangle ^{a-1}\leq \varepsilon \langle \xi \rangle ^ a+ C_\varepsilon \langle \xi \rangle ^ r$ follows by separating large and bounded frequencies. Integration and finite localization prove the final estimate, with an arbitrary prescribed small coefficient. $\square$

title: Lemma 2.18.2
text: Lemma 2.18.2 . 3C443B01B6F3 Suppose a matrix symbol $a(x,\xi )$ is the sum of an $x$-independent symbol and one supported in a fixed compact $x$-set, and satisfies \[  |\partial _ x^\alpha \partial _\xi ^\beta a(x,\xi )| \leq C_{\alpha \beta }\langle \xi \rangle ^{\mu -|\beta |}.  \] Its Fourier operator $\operatorname {Op}(a)$ is bounded $H^ s\to H^{s-\mu }$ for every real $s$; its adjoint has the same order bound. On rapidly decreasing smooth functions it is defined by \[  \operatorname {Op}(a)u(x)= \int e^{2\pi ix\cdot \xi }a(x,\xi )\widehat u(\xi )\, d\xi .  \] If $P$ is elliptic of positive order $d$ in a bundle chart, there is, near any relatively compact smaller chart, an exact identity on sections supported there, \[  v=A Pv-R^*v,  \] where $A:H^ s\to H^{s+d}$ and $R^*:H^ s\to H^{s+1}$ are bounded for every real $s$. These operators need not be differential. Proof. For a compact-$x$ symbol, integration by parts in its $x$-Fourier transform gives, for every $N$, \[  |\widehat a(\eta -\xi ,\xi )| \leq C_ N\langle \eta -\xi \rangle ^{-N}\langle \xi \rangle ^\mu .  \] The weighted Fourier kernel from $H^ s$ to $H^{s-\mu }$ is thus bounded by $C_ N\langle \eta -\xi \rangle ^{-N+|s-\mu |}$. Here the elementary inequalities $\langle \eta \rangle \leq \sqrt2\langle \xi \rangle \langle \eta -\xi \rangle $ and its interchange control their ratio to any real power. Choose $N>|s-\mu |+m$. Both integrals of this kernel, in either variable, are uniformly bounded. Cauchy–Schwarz with its absolute value, followed by integration, gives its $L^2$ operator bound. The $x$-independent part is a Fourier multiplier with the asserted bound. Duality gives the adjoint bound in every order. In particular smooth bounded-coefficient differential operators, localized if necessary, have their expected Sobolev orders. Write $P^\dagger $ for the Euclidean coefficient adjoint in this chart and set $Q=P^\dagger P$. The Fourier principal symbol of $P$ is $p_ d(x,\xi )=(2\pi i)^ d\sigma _ P(x,\xi )$. The principal symbol of $Q$ is the positive matrix $q(x,\xi )=p_ d(x,\xi )^*p_ d(x,\xi )$. On a compact subchart and $|\xi |=1$ its smallest eigenvalue has a strictly positive lower bound: continuity and compactness give the minimum, and injectivity excludes zero. We construct a self-adjoint global extension. Let $Q_0$ be the constant homogeneous differential operator with Fourier symbol $q(x_0,\xi )$ at a fixed chart point. Choose $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ compactly supported in the chart and equal to one on a neighborhood of the smaller chart. On $\mathbb R^ m$ set \[  \widetilde Q=Q_0+\chi (Q-Q_0)\chi .  \] The last term is extended by zero. This operator is formally self-adjoint and agrees with $Q$ near the smaller chart. Its principal symbol $\widetilde q=\chi ^2q+(1-\chi ^2)q(x_0,\xi )$ remains positive definite, uniformly on all $x$ and the unit sphere. Outside a fixed compact set it is $q(x_0,\xi )$. Choose a smooth frequency cutoff $\rho $ equal to zero near zero and one for $|\xi |\geq 2$. The explicit matrix symbol \[  b(x,\xi )=\rho (\xi )\widetilde q(x,\xi )^{-1}  \] has order $-2d$. Differentiating the inverse matrix identity proves all its symbol estimates; homogeneity gives one extra inverse power per $\xi $ derivative. Its difference from the corresponding frozen symbol is compactly supported in $x$. Put $B=\operatorname {Op}(b)$. There is an exact, finite computation of $\widetilde Q B$: if $\widetilde Q=\sum a_\alpha (x)\partial ^\alpha $, its symbol is \[  \sum _{\alpha }\sum _{\beta \leq \alpha } \binom \alpha \beta a_\alpha (x)(2\pi i\xi )^{\alpha -\beta } \partial _ x^\beta b(x,\xi ).  \] This follows directly by differentiating the Fourier integral. The degree-$2d$, $\beta =0$ terms sum to $\rho I$. Every other term has order at most $-1$. Thus \[  \widetilde Q B=I+R,  \] where $R$ has order $-1$ in the just proved class; outside the fixed compact $x$-set its symbol is $(\rho -1)I$, a smooth low-frequency multiplier. Transposing this identity, using self-adjointness of $\widetilde Q$, gives $B^*\widetilde Q=I+R^*$. These identities initially hold on rapidly decreasing smooth functions and extend to all applicable Sobolev spaces by density and duality. For $v$ supported in the smaller chart, $\widetilde Qv=Qv$. Extend the coefficients of $P^\dagger $ smoothly with a compact cutoff equal to one there and put $A=B^*P^\dagger $ with this extension. It has order at most $-d$ by the bounds above. Hence $v=APv-R^*v$, with the required gains. The construction used one matrix inverse and a finite Leibniz formula; no asymptotic symbol sum or unproved composition theorem is being invoked. $\square$

title: 10.89.1 Complex planes and volume comparison
text: For a Hermitian metric $h$ use its Riemannian metric $g=\operatorname {Re}h$ and its associated form $\omega (v,w)=g(Jv,w)$. Thus in unitary coordinates $\omega =(i/2)\sum dz_ j\wedge d\bar z_ j$. Proposition 10.89.2 . AB0853CAC9B1 Let $L$ be an oriented real $2p$-plane in a Hermitian vector space. Then \[  \left|\frac{\omega ^ p}{p!}\bigg|_ L\right|\leq dV_ L.  \] Equality holds precisely when $JL=L$. For a complex plane the coefficient is $+1$ in its complex orientation and $-1$ in its opposite orientation. Consequently, on a real $C^1$ submanifold of dimension $2p$ the equality condition at every interior point is equivalent to being locally a complex submanifold there. In the equality case the orientation sign is a separate locally constant sign on each connected component. Proof. Let $A=P_ LJ|_ L$, with $P_ L$ the orthogonal projection. It is real skew adjoint and has norm at most one. There is an orthonormal basis of $L$ in which its alternating form is $\omega |_ L=\sum _{j=1}^ p a_ j e_{2j-1}^*\wedge e_{2j}^*$, with $|a_ j|\leq 1$. One elementary construction takes an eigenvector of the symmetric operator $-A^2$; if its eigenvalue is $a^2>0$, the vector and $Av/a$ span an invariant orthonormal two-plane. Its orthogonal complement is invariant, so induction gives the blocks; the zero eigenspace is split into orthonormal pairs. The finite-dimensional symmetric spectral theorem itself follows by maximizing its quadratic form on the unit sphere, taking the orthogonal complement of a maximizing eigenvector, and induction. A final sign change makes the whole basis positively oriented. Thus $\omega ^ p/p!=(\prod _ j a_ j)dV_ L$, proving the inequality. Equality makes every $|a_ j|=1$, so $\| Av\| =\| v\| $ for all $v\in L$. Since $J$ is an isometry and orthogonal projection cannot preserve the norm of a vector outside $L$, this is exactly $JL=L$. Conversely on a complex plane a unitary basis followed by its $J$-images gives coefficient one in the complex orientation. A reversed orientation changes the sign. For a $C^1$ submanifold, holomorphic regularity of complex tangent submanifolds proves the holomorphic regularity from the complex tangent condition. The sign of a continuous nonzero top form is constant on each connected component. $\square$ Theorem 10.89.3 . EB0F17719184 Suppose $\omega =d\gamma $ for a smooth real one-form on a complex manifold $X$. Let $1\leq p\leq \dim _\mathbb C X$, and let $Y,Z$ be compact oriented embedded real $C^1$ submanifolds of dimension $2p$, possibly with boundary. Assume that the interior of $Z$ is complex analytic and that $Z$ has its complex orientation. If $[\partial Y]=[\partial Z]$ as oriented boundary currents, then \[  \operatorname {Vol}(Y)\geq \operatorname {Vol}(Z).  \] Proof. The preceding inequality gives $\operatorname {Vol}(Y)\geq \int _ Y\omega ^ p/p!$ and $\operatorname {Vol}(Z)=\int _ Z\omega ^ p/p!$. Since $d\omega =0$ and $p\geq 1$, $\omega ^ p=d(\gamma \wedge \omega ^{p-1})$. The $C^1$ Stokes theorem of proposition 5.55.1 and equality of the oriented boundary currents make these two integrals equal. A smooth ambient cutoff equal to one near $Y\cup Z$ permits the use of the noncompactly supported primitive in this current identity. This proves the assertion. $\square$ Example 10.89.4 . 75AEF98694BC The positive-dimensional hypothesis is necessary: one point and two points have the same empty boundary but respective volumes one and two. Independent orientation reversals on the components of $Z$ must also be excluded. In Euclidean $\mathbb C^2$ take the two complex discs \[  Z_\pm =\{ |z_1|\leq R,\  z_2=\pm h\} ,\qquad 0<h<R/2,  \] with the upper disc complex oriented and the lower one oppositely oriented. The side cylinder $Y=\{ |z_1|=R,\  z_2\in [-h,h]\subset \mathbb R\} $ can be oriented with exactly their oriented boundary. Nevertheless $\operatorname {Vol}(Y)=4\pi Rh<2\pi R^2=\operatorname {Vol}(Z_+\cup Z_-)$. The standard Hermitian form is exact. Thus a componentwise mixed orientation on the comparison complex manifold does not satisfy the stated calibration conclusion. A single simultaneous global reversal is harmless, by reversing $Y$ as well.

A single simultaneous global reversal is harmless, by reversing $Y$ as well.

title: 5.62.2 Currents on CR submanifolds

For a real $C^1$ submanifold $M$ of a complex manifold put $H_ x=T_ xM\cap JT_ xM$ and $h(x)=\dim _\mathbb C H_ x$. It is a CR submanifold of CR dimension $p$ when $h(x)=p$ everywhere. A normal current and its exterior derivative have measure coefficients; we use their action on continuous forms and the $C^1$ calculus of lemma 5.56.1 . A current of bidimension $(p,p)$ has bidegree $(n-p,n-p)$. Theorem 5.62.3 . 88C601DA5D62 Let $T$ be normal of bidimension $(p,p)$ and let $\operatorname {supp}T\subset M$, where $M$ is a real $C^1$ submanifold. Then \[  \operatorname {supp}T\subset \{ x\in M:h(x)\geq p\} .  \] In particular $T=0$ when every $h(x)<p$; no constant-rank or positivity assumption is needed. On any open part of $M$ where $h(x)=p$, the dimensional coefficient vectors of $T$ are tangent to $H$, in its real dimension $2p$. Proof. Multiplication of their values with the coefficient measures gives $g_ jT=g_ jdT=0$, since both supports lie in $M$. The $C^1$ normal product rule gives $dg_ j\wedge T=0$. As $T$ has a pure bidegree, its distinct type components yield separately \[  \partial g_ j\wedge T= ar\partial g_ j\wedge T=0.  \] These are products of continuous forms with measures, not derivatives of a merely continuous moving frame. u  \] for a complex coefficient measure $
u $ on $D	imes B$. The intrinsic $C^1$ normal-current calculus permits computation of its boundary against smooth Euclidean tests in these coordinates. Testing with forms missing the factor $ds_ j$ shows $\partial _{s_ j}
u =0$. The preceding measure lemma gives $
u =ds\otimes \mu _ B$. Consequently \[  T|_\Omega =\int _ B[F_ y\cap \Omega ]\, d\mu _ B(y)  \] in this box, for an actual transverse complex Radon measure. If two boxes overlap at a point, a smaller product box in their overlap projects onto a neighborhood of its base point. A continuous leaf top form, supported in that smaller box and with fiber integral one over a still smaller buffered base neighborhood, tests both formulas and shows that their transverse measures agree there. The normalized form can be obtained in its product coordinates from a compact leaf bump of integral one times a base cutoff equal to one on that buffered neighborhood; its coefficients extend continuously to an ambient chart, which is enough for order-zero currents. A change of leaf coordinates preserves this normalization by ordinary oriented $C^1$ change of variables. Now take any two boxes over a point $y$. Choose points in their plaques. Connectedness of $F_ y$, a manifold, makes it path connected. A compact connecting path is covered by finitely many product boxes with successive overlaps along that path. Every overlap projects onto a neighborhood of $y$; shrink to their finite intersection. The preceding local agreement propagates through this chain. Thus the two transverse measures agree near $y$, even when the original boxes are disjoint. They therefore agree on their entire common base domain and glue to a unique complex Radon measure on $Y$. Surjectivity ensures that these domains cover $Y$. The finite partition argument used to define the integral then proves ( 5.62.6 ) globally. The same normalized tests prove its uniqueness. For positivity choose a Hermitian form $\omega $ on $X$. In a product box its restriction to a leaf satisfies $F_ t^*(\omega ^ p/p!)=J(s,t)ds$, with continuous $J>0$. For a nonnegative compactly supported base function $\psi $, let $\kappa \geq 0$ be a compact leaf bump of integral one. The nonnegative continuous scalar $\kappa (s)\psi (t)/J(s,t)$ extends, after a local $C^1$ graph retraction and cutoff, to a nonnegative compactly supported ambient function. Multiply it by $\omega ^ p/p!$. Positivity of $T$, extended from smooth to these continuous tests by nonnegative smooth approximation, gives $\int \psi \, d\mu _ B\geq 0$. Thus $\mu $ is positive. Conversely, if $\mu $ is positive, every weakly positive $(p,p)$-form restricts nonnegatively to each complex fiber by strong and weak positivity of differential forms . Its integral is nonnegative, which is precisely strong positivity of the current, and implies ordinary positivity. Finally, if $\mu $ vanishes near a base point, the local formula vanishes on all its plaques. If a base point is in its support, the normalized tests in any arbitrarily small product box over that point detect a nonzero measure pairing. Hence every point of that fiber is in the support of $T$. This proves the exact support formula. For $p=0$ the leaf boxes are points and the same argument is simply transport of a measure; for $p=n$ the base is discrete and it says that the coefficient on each connected complex component is a constant. F39ED1E5BACF A normal current of bidimension $(p,p)$ supported on an analytic set of dimension less than $p$ is zero, even if it is not closed or positive. Proof. On the regular locus of the analytic set its CR dimension is less than $p$, so the rank theorem annihilates the current there. Its support is consequently contained in the singular set, whose local dimension is smaller by analytic singular strata and Hausdorff dimension . Repeat on its regular locus. D73EBFFE10D2 Let $A$ be an analytic subset of $X$ of dimension at most $p$, and let $A_ j$ be its locally finite $p$-dimensional irreducible components. Every closed complex order-zero current $T$ of bidimension $(p,p)$ with support in $A$ has a unique expression \[  T=\sum _ j\lambda _ j[A_ j],\qquad \lambda _ j\in \mathbb C.  \] It is positive if and only if all $\lambda _ j\geq 0$, and then it is strongly positive. Proof. In $X\setminus A_{m sing}$ the regular locus is closed. On its components of dimension less than $p$, corollary 5.62.7 makes the current zero. title: 9.61.1 Linear growth and affine algebraicity
text:
An algebraic subset of $\mathbb C^ n$ is a common zero set of polynomials. Finite equations suffice by theorem 9.58.2 . Algebraic irreducibility refers to decompositions into algebraic subsets; analytic irreducibility refers to closed analytic subsets. Lemma 9.61.2 . D8FA405BDFAC Suppose a nonempty pure $p$-dimensional analytic subset $A\subset \mathbb C^ p	imes \mathbb C^{n-p}$ satisfies D6D620F9E57D 9.61.3  egin{equation}  |z''|\leq C(1+|z'|)\quad 	ext{on }A. \end{equation} Projection to $z'$ is proper and finite. If $p>0$, it is onto, and outside a proper analytic subset of $\mathbb C^ p$ it is a covering with a constant finite positive number of sheets. The global analytic irreducible components of $A$ are finite in number. For $p=0$, $A$ is a finite set. Proof. The inverse image of a compact base set is a closed subset of a bounded product, and hence compact. A fiber is a compact analytic subset of a Euclidean space, so it is finite by the maximum principle on analytic branches . For $p=0$ this already proves the assertion. For $p>0$, the finite-open-map theorem proper finite representatives of analytic map germs makes projection open at every point of the pure-dimensional source. Its nonempty image is also closed by properness, and therefore is all of $\mathbb C^ p$. Here are the precise exceptional-set and covering steps. The union of the singular locus with the rank-deficient regular locus is analytic: in local ambient equations, the maximal minors formed from their differentials and the $p$ base coordinate rows test surjectivity on the regular tangent space and vanish on the singular locus. This is the same analytic critical-set construction in lemma 6.38.1 . It contains no irreducible component. Otherwise on a regular open subset of that component the maximum differential rank would be less than $p$, and the constant-rank theorem would give a positive-dimensional fiber. Its dimension is thus at most $p-1$. Its proper image $E$ is analytic by Remmert's proper mapping theorem , and has dimension at most $p-1$ by dimension bounds for holomorphic images . Outside $E$ projection is a proper local biholomorphism. Finitely many inverse charts at one fiber and properness exclude extra inverse points over a smaller base neighborhood, proving that it is a covering. The complement of $E$ in $\mathbb C^ p$ is connected by bounded holomorphic removal and connected complements , so its sheet number is constant. Each global irreducible component $B$ is pure of dimension $p$, by purity and dimension of irreducible analytic sets . Projection on $B$ is again proper, finite and open, and hence onto. It meets the finite fiber over zero. There are only finitely many local branches of $A$ at the points of that fiber. Every such global component contains one of those branches, and distinct components cannot contain the same branch: it would give a nonempty regular open overlap, and the identity principle on the connected regular locus would identify the components. Thus there are only finitely many global components. $\square$ Theorem 9.61.4 . D15F5F84A74A Every pure $p$-dimensional algebraic subset of $\mathbb C^ n$ admits linear coordinates $(z',z'')$, with $z'\in \mathbb C^ p$, in which ( 9.61.3 ) holds. Conversely, a pure $p$-dimensional analytic subset satisfying that bound is algebraic. Proof. First suppose $A$ is algebraic and nonempty. Homogenize a finite set of its defining equations and let $B$ be their common zero set in $\mathbb P^ n$. Its part outside the hyperplane at infinity $H_\infty $ is exactly $A$. By analytic closure after removing an analytic subset , the ordinary closure $\overline A$ in $\mathbb P^ n$ is analytic: it is the union of the components of $B$ not contained in $H_\infty $. Only finitely many occur, since $B$ is compact and its analytic components are locally finite. Every such component meets the affine chart in a pure $p$-dimensional open subset, so it is pure of dimension $p$. title: Lemma 9.61.2
text: Lemma 9.61.2 . D8FA405BDFAC Suppose a nonempty pure $p$-dimensional analytic subset $A\subset \mathbb C^ p\times \mathbb C^{n-p}$ satisfies D6D620F9E57D 9.61.3 \begin{equation}  |z''|\leq C(1+|z'|)\quad \text{on }A. \end{equation} Projection to $z'$ is proper and finite. If $p>0$, it is onto, and outside a proper analytic subset of $\mathbb C^ p$ it is a covering with a constant finite positive number of sheets. The global analytic irreducible components of $A$ are finite in number. For $p=0$, $A$ is a finite set. Proof. The inverse image of a compact base set is a closed subset of a bounded product, and hence compact. A fiber is a compact analytic subset of a Euclidean space, so it is finite by the maximum principle on analytic branches . For $p=0$ this already proves the assertion. For $p>0$, the finite-open-map theorem proper finite representatives of analytic map germs makes projection open at every point of the pure-dimensional source. Its nonempty image is also closed by properness, and therefore is all of $\mathbb C^ p$. Here are the precise exceptional-set and covering steps. The union of the singular locus with the rank-deficient regular locus is analytic: in local ambient equations, the maximal minors formed from their differentials and the $p$ base coordinate rows test surjectivity on the regular tangent space and vanish on the singular locus. This is the same analytic critical-set construction in lemma 6.38.1 . It contains no irreducible component. Otherwise on a regular open subset of that component the maximum differential rank would be less than $p$, and the constant-rank theorem would give a positive-dimensional fiber. Its dimension is thus at most $p-1$. Its proper image $E$ is analytic by Remmert's proper mapping theorem , and has dimension at most $p-1$ by dimension bounds for holomorphic images . Outside $E$ projection is a proper local biholomorphism. Finitely many inverse charts at one fiber and properness exclude extra inverse points over a smaller base neighborhood, proving that it is a covering. The complement of $E$ in $\mathbb C^ p$ is connected by bounded holomorphic removal and connected complements , so its sheet number is constant. Each global irreducible component $B$ is pure of dimension $p$, by purity and dimension of irreducible analytic sets . Projection on $B$ is again proper, finite and open, and hence onto. It meets the finite fiber over zero. There are only finitely many local branches of $A$ at the points of that fiber. Every such global component contains one of those branches, and distinct components cannot contain the same branch: it would give a nonempty regular open overlap, and the identity principle on the connected regular locus would identify the components. Thus there are only finitely many global components. $\square$

title: 20.6.1 Analytic cycle sheaves and Cartier cycles
search_title: Analytic cycle sheaves and Cartier cycles
text:
Definition 20.6.2 . BE0C86A8DD65 For $\Lambda =\mathbb Z,\mathbb Q$ or $\mathbb R$ and $q\geq 0$, a $q$-dimensional analytic $\Lambda $-cycle on a reduced complex space is a formal sum $\sum _ A c_ A A$, where the $A$ are distinct irreducible closed analytic subsets of pure dimension $q$, $c_ A\in \Lambda $, and the family with nonzero coefficient is locally finite. Its support is their union. It is effective when every coefficient is nonnegative. On a pure-dimensional space of dimension $n$, the cycles of dimension $n-1$ are called Weil divisors. In negative dimensions set the cycle module equal to zero. Proposition 20.6.3 . FD8966432506 Restrictions, with each restricted irreducible set decomposed into its analytic components carrying the same coefficient, make these cycles a sheaf of $\Lambda $-modules. Its stalk at $x$ is the free $\Lambda $-module on irreducible $q$-dimensional analytic germs at $x$. The coefficientwise maximum and minimum are sheaf operations and give its natural lattice order. Proof. The local decomposition and global component theorem global irreducible analytic components give locally finite irreducible restrictions. Distinct irreducible global sets cannot acquire the same local branch: a common branch gives a regular open overlap, and the identity principle on the connected regular locus identifies the global sets. A locally finite cycle thus restricts unambiguously, and restrictions compose by uniqueness of analytic component decomposition. Equality can be checked locally, proving the separated sheaf axiom. For gluing, suppose cycles agree on an open cover. Their supports glue to a closed analytic set $S$: around each point a single cover member describes the same support on all overlaps, so closedness and analytic equations hold locally. It is pure of dimension $q$ where nonempty. Its global irreducible components are locally finite. On the connected regular locus of each component, outside its intersections with other components, the local coefficients agree and are locally constant. They therefore have one constant value on that component; connectedness and density follow from global irreducible analytic components and removing proper analytic subsets. These constants give a global cycle with the prescribed restrictions. Germwise equality shows uniqueness. Only finitely many local branches occur at a point, so a stalk element gives a finite formal combination of irreducible germs. Conversely finitely many such germs have representatives on one neighborhood, so every finite combination occurs. A zero germ forces all its coefficients to vanish by uniqueness of branch decomposition, proving the free-module assertion. For two cycles use the locally finite union of their component families and put missing coefficients equal to zero. Their coefficientwise maximum and minimum remain locally finite, and restrictions preserve these operations because every restricted branch retains its coefficient. This proves the stated lattice and its compatibility with the sheaf structure. $\square$ Proposition 20.6.4 . AA96C35C8290 Let $X$ be reduced and pure of dimension $n$, with singular locus of dimension at most $n-2$. A holomorphic function $f$ nonzero on every irreducible component defines an effective Weil divisor $\operatorname {div}(f)$ by its generic vanishing orders on $X_{m reg}$. These orders are well defined and \[  \operatorname {div}(fg)=\operatorname {div}(f)+\operatorname {div}(g).  \] Cycles locally given by integer combinations of these divisors form the subsheaf of Cartier cycles; locally each is $\operatorname {div}(g)-\operatorname {div}(h)$. On a complex manifold every integral Weil divisor is Cartier, and every effective integral Weil divisor is locally the divisor of one holomorphic function. Proof. The zero set of $f$ is pure of dimension $n-1$ by purity of a nontrivial holomorphic zero set , and its components are locally finite. No such component lies in $X_{m sing}$. On the smooth locus of a zero component, away from the other zero components and from $X_{m sing}$, choose its local coordinate equation $t=0$. The factorial hypersurface result local equations and currents of irreducible hypersurfaces and its factorization give $f=t^ m v$ with $v$ a unit and $m\geq 1$. The integer $m$ is locally constant on this locus. It is connected and dense in the irreducible zero component, by the global component theorem and removal of proper analytic subsets. Thus it has one value, which defines the coefficient. At a regular point of a component in the union of the zero divisors of $f,g$, their powers of the same coordinate multiply, proving additivity of the orders. A finite integer combination of principal holomorphic divisors is the difference of the divisors of the products with positive and negative exponents. Functions nonzero on every component remain so under those products. This proves the asserted local description and its sheaf compatibility. On a manifold take local prime equations for the finitely many hypersurface branches, as in local equations and currents of irreducible hypersurfaces . Their product with the prescribed nonnegative powers has the required effective divisor. Taking a quotient treats arbitrary integral coefficients. Dimension zero has no nonempty hypersurface divisors, so its assertion is immediate. $\square$ Example 20.6.5 . 0C462992AB3A On the three-dimensional quadric \[  X=\{ x_1x_2+x_3x_4=0\} \subset \mathbb C^4, \qquad A=\{ x_1=x_3=0\} ,  \] the effective Weil divisor $A$ is not a Cartier cycle at zero. Proof. The rank-one matrix parametrization \[  F:\mathbb C^4\longrightarrow X,\qquad (a,b,c,d)\longmapsto (ac,bd,ad,-bc)  \] is surjective. It is surjective as a germ at zero as well: every sufficiently small rank-one matrix factors as a column times a row with both factors small, by scaling the factors to equal norm. Thus the germ of $X$ is irreducible, since an analytic decomposition would pull back to one of the irreducible smooth germ $\mathbb C^4$. The quadric is pure of dimension three. Its nonzero points are regular, by its gradient, and its origin is singular: its lowest quadratic form has rank four, so cannot factor into two linear forms, and its reduced principal ideal has no linear term. Its tangent dimension there is four. In particular the singular set is the point zero. Suppose $A$ were Cartier as a cycle. Its local description in the proposition would give a meromorphic function $f=g/h$ with $\operatorname {div}(f)=A$, where $g,h$ are holomorphic germs nonzero on $X$. Pullback by $F$ is defined: germwise surjectivity makes $h\circ F$ nonzero. Outside \[  F^{-1}(0)=\{ a=b=0\} \cup \{ c=d=0\} ,  \] the map is a submersion onto $X_{m reg}$. Indeed, for nonzero column $u=(a,b)$ and row $v=(c,d)$, the kernel of $(\dot u,\dot v)\mapsto \dot u v+u\dot v$ consists exactly of $(t u,-t v)$ and has dimension one. There the pullback of $A$ is the reduced hypersurface $a=0$. For example where $b
e 0$ its normal coordinate is $a/b$, and where $a=0$ one has $b
e 0$ off the displayed exceptional set. Pullback of divisors by this submersion therefore gives $\operatorname {div}(f\circ F)=[a=0]$ off that set. The exceptional set has codimension two, so it cannot support any additional hypersurface in a meromorphic divisor. The required smooth local factorization follows from the already proved Noetherianity of convergent power-series modules , local equations and currents of irreducible hypersurfaces : factorization into nonunits terminates by the ascending chain condition on principal ideals; each irreducible factor is associated to the prime equation of its hypersurface branch. Such factors are therefore prime. Applying this to the numerator and denominator of $f\circ F$ cancels all factors except one $a$, giving $f\circ F=a e$ for a holomorphic unit $e$ at zero. For $t\in \mathbb C^*$ the transformation $(a,b,c,d)\mapsto (ta,tb,t^{-1}c,t^{-1}d)$ preserves $F$. For each fixed $t$ close to one, the equality of meromorphic germs $a e=t a\, e(ta,tb,t^{-1}c,t^{-1}d)$ permits cancellation of $a$. Evaluating at zero gives $e(0)=t e(0)$, impossible for $t
e 1$ because $e$ is a unit. This proves non-Cartierness as a cycle, without confusing it with nonprincipality of the reduced ideal alone. $\square$

Their product with the prescribed nonnegative powers has the required effective divisor. Taking a quotient treats arbitrary integral coefficients. Dimension zero has no nonempty hypersurface divisors, so its assertion is immediate. $\square$

title: Example 20.6.5
text:
Example 20.6.5 . 0C462992AB3A On the three-dimensional quadric \[  X=\{ x_1x_2+x_3x_4=0\} \subset \mathbb C^4, \qquad A=\{ x_1=x_3=0\} ,  \] the effective Weil divisor $A$ is not a Cartier cycle at zero. Proof. The rank-one matrix parametrization \[  F:\mathbb C^4\longrightarrow X,\qquad (a,b,c,d)\longmapsto (ac,bd,ad,-bc)  \] is surjective. It is surjective as a germ at zero as well: every sufficiently small rank-one matrix factors as a column times a row with both factors small, by scaling the factors to equal norm. Thus the germ of $X$ is irreducible, since an analytic decomposition would pull back to one of the irreducible smooth germ $\mathbb C^4$. The quadric is pure of dimension three. Its nonzero points are regular, by its gradient, and its origin is singular: its lowest quadratic form has rank four, so cannot factor into two linear forms, and its reduced principal ideal has no linear term. Its tangent dimension there is four. In particular the singular set is the point zero. Suppose $A$ were Cartier as a cycle. Its local description in the proposition would give a meromorphic function $f=g/h$ with $\operatorname {div}(f)=A$, where $g,h$ are holomorphic germs nonzero on $X$. Pullback by $F$ is defined: germwise surjectivity makes $h\circ F$ nonzero. Outside \[  F^{-1}(0)=\{ a=b=0\} \cup \{ c=d=0\} ,  \] the map is a submersion onto $X_{m reg}$. Indeed, for nonzero column $u=(a,b)$ and row $v=(c,d)$, the kernel of $(\dot u,\dot v)\mapsto \dot u v+u\dot v$ consists exactly of $(t u,-t v)$ and has dimension one. There the pullback of $A$ is the reduced hypersurface $a=0$. For example where $b
e 0$ its normal coordinate is $a/b$, and where $a=0$ one has $b
e 0$ off the displayed exceptional set. Pullback of divisors by this submersion therefore gives $\operatorname {div}(f\circ F)=[a=0]$ off that set. The exceptional set has codimension two, so it cannot support any additional hypersurface in a meromorphic divisor. The required smooth local factorization follows from the already proved Noetherianity of convergent power-series modules , local equations and currents of irreducible hypersurfaces : factorization into nonunits terminates by the ascending chain condition on principal ideals; each irreducible factor is associated to the prime equation of its hypersurface branch. Such factors are therefore prime. Applying this to the numerator and denominator of $f\circ F$ cancels all factors except one $a$, giving $f\circ F=a e$ for a holomorphic unit $e$ at zero. For $t\in \mathbb C^*$ the transformation $(a,b,c,d)\mapsto (ta,tb,t^{-1}c,t^{-1}d)$ preserves $F$. For each fixed $t$ close to one, the equality of meromorphic germs $a e=t a\, e(ta,tb,t^{-1}c,t^{-1}d)$ permits cancellation of $a$. Evaluating at zero gives $e(0)=t e(0)$, impossible for $t
e 1$ because $e$ is a unit. This proves non-Cartierness as a cycle, without confusing it with nonprincipality of the reduced ideal alone. $\square$

text: Corollary 9.56.6 . A99D1189F3F3 For finite nonempty $S\subset \mathbb P^ n$, $n\geq 2$, and all integers $t,u\geq 1$, \[  \frac{\omega _ t(S)+1}{t+n-1} \leq \Omega (S)\leq \frac{\omega _ u(S)}u.  \] If, for a fixed $t$, there is an unbounded sequence of integers $u$ admitting degree-minimizing polynomials whose fractional divisors formed with $\alpha =(t+n-1)/u$ have nonintegrability locus of dimension at most $a_0$, using zero for an empty locus, then \[  \frac{\omega _ t(S)+n-a_0-1}{t+n-1}\leq \Omega (S).  \] In particular a zero-dimensional or empty locus along such a sequence gives the numerator $\omega _ t(S)+n-1$. For $n=1$, $\omega _ t(S)=t\, \# S$ and $\Omega (S)=\# S$. Proof. In the theorem always $a\leq n-2$. Let $t_2\to \infty $ through all positive integers and use the defining limit, giving the first lower bound. The upper bound is the infimum property. title: 9.62.1 Logarithmic convexity and complete Reinhardt domains
search_title: Logarithmic convexity and complete Reinhardt domains
text:
An open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ is Reinhardt if it is invariant under separate rotations of all coordinates. Its logarithmic indicatrix is \[  D=\{ (\log |z_1|,\ldots ,\log |z_ n|): z\in \Omega \cap (\mathbb C^*)^ n\} .  \] Here logarithms are unsquared; changing to squared logarithms dilates $D$ by two and changes none of the convexity assertions. Proposition 9.62.2 . B7A5F2850576 If $\Omega $ is pseudoconvex, every connected component of $D$ is convex. Conversely, if $D$ is open and convex, the set \[  \Omega _ D^*=\{ z\in (\mathbb C^*)^ n:\log |z|\in D\}   \] is pseudoconvex, considered as an open subset of $\mathbb C^ n$. Convexity of $D$ alone does not imply pseudoconvexity of an arbitrary Reinhardt open set having indicatrix $D$. Proof. The map $E(\zeta )=(e^{\zeta _1},\ldots ,e^{\zeta _ n})$ has inverse image $E^{-1}(\Omega )=D+\mathrm i\mathbb R^ n$. If $ho \geq 0$ is a continuous PSH exhaustion of $\Omega $, then $|\zeta |^2+ho (E(\zeta ))$ exhausts this inverse image. Indeed, a sublevel lies in a bounded $\zeta $-ball and its image lies in the compact sublevel $\{ ho \leq c\} \subset \Omega $; a convergent sequence therefore has its limit in the same inverse image and sublevel. Thus the tube is pseudoconvex. For completeness the tube criterion follows from exact earlier inputs. For an open $V\subset \mathbb R^ n$, the Euclidean distance to the complement of $V+\mathrm i\mathbb R^ n$ is $d_ V(x)$, $x=\Re \zeta $. Unless $V=\mathbb R^ n$, Oka's boundary-distance criterion makes $-\log d_ V(x)$ PSH on a pseudoconvex tube. Applying translation-invariant plurisubharmonic functions on tubes on small convex real balls shows that it is locally convex in $x$. Consequently $|x|^2+\max \{ 0,-\log d_ V(x)\} $ is a finite continuous locally convex exhaustion of $V$. Its restriction exhausts every component, since components are relatively closed. The exact connected-set criterion local convexity and convex exhaustion makes each component convex. The full-space case is immediate. Apply this to $V=D$. If $D=\varnothing $, its converse assertion is immediate. Otherwise let $\chi $ be a nonnegative continuous convex exhaustion of $D$, supplied by local convexity and convex exhaustion . The function $\chi (\log |z|)$ is PSH by toric plurisubharmonic functions and logarithmic convexity , with the factor-two change of variables in its squared-log convention. It exhausts $\Omega _ D^*$: the inverse image of a compact subset of $D$ is compact, since every coordinate modulus is bounded above and bounded away from zero and the angular torus is compact. For the last assertion take $\Omega =\mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $, $n\geq 2$. Its indicatrix is $\mathbb R^ n$. If it had a PSH exhaustion $ho $, the discs $\zeta \mapsto (\zeta ,t,0,\ldots ,0)$, $|\zeta |\leq 1$, $0<|t|\leq 1$, would lie in $\Omega $. Their boundary union for $|t|\leq 1$ is compact in $\Omega $, so the maximum principle bounds $ho (0,t,0,\ldots ,0)$ uniformly. These points approach the missing origin, contradicting compactness of that sublevel. $\square$ Lemma 9.62.3 . 9179B3F88EE7 Let $D\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be nonempty, open, convex and downward closed: $x\in D$, $y_ j\leq x_ j$ imply $y\in D$. Set 591389D2112E 9.62.4  egin{equation}  \widetilde\Omega _ D =\{ z\in \mathbb C^ n: |z_ j|\leq e^{x_ j}\  (1\leq j\leq n) 	ext{ for some }x\in D\} . \end{equation} If $\chi :D	o [0,\infty )$ is finite, convex and coordinatewise nondecreasing, then $\chi (\log |z|)$ on the nonzero-coordinate locus has a unique continuous extension $u$ to $\widetilde\Omega _ D$. This extension is PSH. For a point with nonzero-coordinate set $J$ and zero-coordinate set $I$, its value is D8AC5552CA80 9.62.5  egin{equation}  u(z)=\lim _{T	o \infty }\chi (\log |z_ J|,-T\mathbf1_ I). \end{equation} The order of coordinates in this formula is the original one. Proof. Openness of $D$ permits every witnessing $x$ in ( 9.62.4 ) to be increased slightly in all coordinates. Thus the same union is obtained using strict inequalities, and it is an open union of polydiscs through zero. It is invariant under all coordinate contractions. Its intersection with $(\mathbb C^*)^ n$ is exactly $\Omega _ D^*$, by downward closure. Write $D_ J$ for the coordinate projection of $D$ to $\mathbb R^ J$. It is open and convex. A point with nonzero coordinates exactly $J$ belongs to $\widetilde\Omega _ D$ if and only if $x_ J=\log |z_ J|$ belongs to $D_ J$. To verify the reverse direction, lift $x_ J$ to a point of $D$ and then increase all coordinates slightly. The resulting radii strictly dominate the given point. The forward direction follows from downward closure after decreasing the nonzero coordinates to their logarithms. For every compact real box $K\subset D_ J$, all $(x_ J,-T\mathbf1_ I)$ with $x_ J\in K$ belong to $D$ when $T$ is sufficiently large. By local regularity of finite convex functions , a finite convex function on an open convex set is continuous. Hence convergence is uniform on compact boxes. As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, these functions decrease to the continuous extension $u$: the same sandwich handles unequal negative logarithms in the zero coordinates. They are nonnegative and locally uniformly bounded above by monotonicity and a fixed larger radius vector. Dominated convergence therefore passes every circle submean to $u$. Otherwise let $d_ D(x)=\operatorname {dist}(x,\mathbb R^ n\setminus D)$. The ball argument in local convexity and convex exhaustion makes $d_ D$ concave. Downward closure gives $d_ D(x-h)\geq d_ D(x)$ for $h\geq 0$, since translating an inner ball by $-h$ leaves it in $D$. Thus \[  \chi (x)=\sum _{j=1}^ n e^{2x_ j}+\max \{ 0,-\log d_ D(x)\}   \] is finite, nonnegative, convex and coordinatewise nondecreasing. It blows up at every finite boundary point of $D$. The previous lemma gives a continuous PSH extension $u$ on $\widetilde\Omega _ D$, with $u(z)\geq |z|^2$. We prove that this is an exhaustion even at boundary points where some coordinates vanish. Suppose a bounded sequence $z_
u \in \widetilde\Omega _ D$ converges to $b\in \partial \widetilde\Omega _ D$. Let $J=\{ j:b_ j
e 0\} $. This set is nonempty, since zero is an interior point. The vector $x^ b_ J=\log |b_ J|$ is in $\partial D_ J$: it is in the closure by projection from the approaching points, but cannot belong to $D_ J$ by the exact stratum criterion above. In particular $D_ J$ is proper. A ball in $D$ projects to a ball of the same radius in $D_ J$, so \[  d_ D(x)\leq d_{D_ J}(x_ J)\qquad (x\in D).  \] For points with every coordinate nonzero this gives $u(z)\geq \max \{ 0,-\log d_{D_ J}(\log |z_ J|)\} $. By continuity it holds also when other coordinates vanish, as long as $z_ J$ stays nonzero. Its right side tends to infinity along $z_
u $. Thus no bounded sublevel of $u$ accumulates at any boundary stratum. Since $u\geq |z|^2$, each sublevel is bounded and, by continuity and this boundary exclusion, closed in $\mathbb C^ n$. It is compact. This proves the full asserted pseudoconvexity. $\square$

title: 9.63.1 Full regularity of Levi foliations
text: Lemma 9.63.2 . 6F469AB373C2 Let $m\geq 1$, and let $H(z,t)$ be continuous on a neighborhood of $\overline{P_ r}\times I$, holomorphic in $z\in \mathbb C^ m$, where $P_ r=\{ |z_ j|<r_ j\} $ and $I$ is an open real interval. Suppose $b(\zeta ,t)=\operatorname {Im}H(\zeta ,t)$ on its distinguished torus $\zeta _ j=r_ je^{\mathrm i\theta _ j}$ is $C^ l$ in $(\theta ,t)$, and $a(t)=\operatorname {Re}H(0,t)$ is $C^ l$, for an integer $l\geq 0$. Then on the interior product $P_ r\times I$, all derivatives of $H$ with at most $l$ derivatives in $t$ and arbitrarily many derivatives in $z$ exist and are jointly continuous. Explicitly, F5B6ECCA47FD 9.63.3 \begin{equation}  H(z,t)=a(t)+\frac{\mathrm i}{(2\pi )^ m} \int _{[0,2\pi ]^ m} \left(2\prod _{j=1}^ m\frac{\zeta _ j}{\zeta _ j-z_ j}-1\right) b(\zeta ,t)\, d\theta . \end{equation} Proof. Let $K_ z(\zeta )=\prod _ j\zeta _ j/(\zeta _ j-z_ j)$ and write normalized torus integration as an average. Iterated Cauchy gives $\mathrm{avg}(K_ zH)=H(z,t)$. The normally convergent Taylor series of $H$ on this torus and the geometric series for $K_ z$ give $\mathrm{avg}(K_ z\overline H)=\overline{H(0,t)}$: their angular exponents are all nonpositive for $\overline H$ and for the kernel expansion, so only the common constant term survives. Also $\mathrm{avg}(\operatorname {Im}H)=\operatorname {Im}H(0,t)$. Substituting $b=(H-\overline H)/(2\mathrm i)$ proves the formula. On each smaller closed polydisc, every $z$ derivative of its kernel is uniformly bounded. Differentiation under this fixed compact integral therefore gives all the asserted derivatives, including the full order $l$ in $t$, with continuous dependence on the remaining variables. No derivative of the integration surface is involved. $\square$ Theorem 9.63.4 . A6B15EBA6E91 Let $M$ be a $C^ k$ real hypersurface in a complex $n$-manifold, with $2\leq k\leq \infty $. title: 9.64.1 Reduction and strong reduction of ringed spaces
search_title: Reduction and strong reduction of ringed spaces
text: Rings are commutative with identity and homomorphisms preserve identity. The zero ring is allowed; prime and maximal ideals are proper. A local ring has a unique maximal ideal, so the zero ring is not local. For an ideal $I\subset R$ put $\sqrt I=\{ a:a^ m\in I\text{ for some }m\geq 1\} $. This is an ideal: if $a^ m,b^ n\in I$, every term in $(a+b)^{m+n-1}$ belongs to $I$, and $(ra)^ m\in I$. The nilradical is $N(R)=\sqrt{(0)}$. The quotient $R/N(R)$ is reduced, since $a^ m\in N(R)$ implies some power of $a$ is zero. A ringed space is a topological space $X$ with a sheaf of rings $\mathcal R_ X$. A morphism $F:X\to Y$ consists of a continuous map $f$ and a sheaf homomorphism $F^\# :f^{-1}\mathcal R_ Y\to \mathcal R_ X$. Composition has comorphism $F^\# \circ f^{-1}G^\# $. A locally ringed space has local stalk rings, and its morphisms carry the target maximal ideal into the source maximal ideal. For a field $k$, a locally ringed space with residue field $k$ means a sheaf of $k$-algebras whose structural maps identify every residue field with $k$; its morphisms are local $k$-homomorphisms. No separation, finiteness or analytic hypothesis is imposed here. Proposition 9.64.2 . ADC46EC60E54 There is an ideal sheaf $\mathcal N_ X\subset \mathcal R_ X$ with stalk $N(\mathcal R_{X,x})$. Its sections are precisely the sections whose germs are nilpotent at every point. The ringed space \[  X_{\mathrm{red}}=(X,\mathcal R_ X/\mathcal N_ X)  \] is reduced, and the quotient defines a natural morphism $X_{\mathrm{red}}\to X$. Every ringed-space morphism induces a reduction morphism, compatibly with identities and composition. If the original spaces are locally ringed with residue field $k$, so are their reductions and these maps. Proof. The stated germ condition is local, is preserved by restrictions, and glues; the elementary radical calculation makes its sections an ideal. If a germ is nilpotent, one representative has a zero power after shrinking, so all its germs on that neighborhood are nilpotent. Conversely membership in the displayed subsheaf gives a nilpotent germ at the selected point. These observations prove the asserted stalk identity. Stalks of a quotient are the quotient stalks by proposition 10.43.1 ; the preceding ring calculation proves reducedness. The quotient comorphism has the displayed direction. Every homomorphism carries nilpotents to nilpotents, so the comorphism factors uniquely on these quotient stalks and hence on sheaves. Uniqueness proves functoriality. The nilradical of a local ring lies in its maximal ideal, because a nilpotent unit would make $1=0$. Quotienting therefore preserves locality and the residue field. The induced stalk maps are local, as their maximal ideals are the images of the original ones. $\square$ The definition is local: a section of $\mathcal N_ X$ need not have one power vanishing on its whole domain. On a countable discrete space put $\mathcal R_{X,j}=k[t]/(t^ j)$. The section with value $t$ in each stalk belongs to $\mathcal N_ X(X)$ but has no uniform vanishing exponent. Local finite generation, when available, gives additional local bounds; it is not part of this construction. Proposition 9.64.3 . 16DE5782FC00 Let $X$ be a locally ringed space with residue field $k$. Evaluation gives a sheaf homomorphism \[  e_ X:\mathcal R_ X\longrightarrow \mathcal F_ X, \qquad e_ X(s)(x)=s_ x\bmod \mathfrak m_ x,  \] where $\mathcal F_ X(U)$ is the ring of all functions $U\to k$. Let $\mathcal R_ X^{\mathrm{val}}$ be its sheaf image, not merely its presheaf image, and set $X_{\mathrm{st\text{-}red}}=(X,\mathcal R_ X^{\mathrm{val}})$. This is a reduced locally ringed space with residue field $k$, with natural morphisms \[  X_{\mathrm{st\text{-}red}}\longrightarrow X_{\mathrm{red}} \longrightarrow X.  \] Strong reduction is functorial for local $k$-morphisms. Between strongly reduced spaces such a morphism is determined by its point map: its comorphism is pullback of functions. Strong reduction is idempotent, and it agrees with ordinary reduction exactly when $\ker e_ X=\mathcal N_ X$. Proof. Evaluation commutes with restriction and the ring operations. The sheaf image consists of functions which locally are evaluations of sections; it is a subsheaf of the actual function sheaf by proposition 10.43.1 . Write $\mathcal K_ X= \ker e_ X$. A germ in $\mathcal K_{X,x}$ is represented by a section whose value function vanishes on some neighborhood of $x$. Every nilpotent germ has such a representative, so $\mathcal N_ X\subset \mathcal K_ X$, and $\mathcal R_ X^{\mathrm{val}}=\mathcal R_ X/\mathcal K_ X$. Every germ in $\mathcal K_{X,x}$ has residue zero at $x$, whence $\mathcal K_{X,x}\subset \mathfrak m_ x$. Its quotient is a local ring with residue field $k$. More explicitly, a function germ with nonzero value at $x$ locally lifts to a section whose germ is a unit in $\mathcal R_{X,x}$; its inverse germ and its representative evaluate to an inverse on a smaller neighborhood. A function germ with value zero at $x$ cannot be a unit. This describes exactly the maximal ideal of the quotient. Function sheaves are reduced: if a power of a function vanishes, the function vanishes pointwise. The same is true of their subsheaves and their stalks, by shrinking representatives. Thus the quotient is reduced. The inclusions of the two kernel sheaves give the two quotient comorphisms with the stated arrow directions. If $F:X\to Y$ is a local $k$-morphism, its stalk maps induce the identity on $k$. Consequently for a section $s$ of $\mathcal R_ Y$ one has \[  e_ X(F^\# s)=e_ Y(s)\circ f  \] on its inverse-image domain. Hence $F^\# $ carries the inverse image of $\mathcal K_ Y$ into $\mathcal K_ X$, and descends uniquely to the value sheaves. The formula persists on their locally lifted sections, proving the assertion about pullbacks, identities and composition. On a value sheaf its own residue evaluation is its inclusion into functions, by the maximal-ideal description above. It is therefore strongly reduced, proving idempotence and point-map uniqueness. Finally the natural map from ordinary to value quotient is an isomorphism precisely when its kernel $\mathcal K_ X/\mathcal N_ X$ is zero, proving the last equivalence. $\square$ Example 9.64.4 . 28539480EFD0 The one-point ringed space with local ring $k[t]_{(t)}$ is reduced with residue field $k$, but its strong reduction has ring $k$. Indeed the localization is a domain, so its nilradical is zero, whereas evaluation at its sole point is the residue map with nonzero kernel $(t)$. Thus ordinary and strong reduction differ even without any nilpotents.

section: 5.63 Positive-current coefficient bounds and support maxima
text:
Use $dd^ c=i\partial  ar\partial /(2\pi )$. All topological spaces below are Hausdorff. Norms of currents on a closed set include its boundary mass. Supremum norms on a current support mean actual pointwise suprema, not ambient Lebesgue essential suprema. Proposition 5.63.2 . 7ECC0248E832 In coordinates on an $n$-manifold write a positive current of bidimension $(p,p)$ as \[  T=i^{(n-p)^2}\sum _{|I|=|J|=n-p}T_{I,J}\, dz_ I\wedge d ar z_ J.  \] Its coefficient distributions are measures, its matrix is Hermitian, and $T_{M,M}\geq 0$. For arbitrary $\lambda _ j\geq 0$, put $\lambda _ I=\prod _{j\in I}\lambda _ j$. Then, as measures, \[  \lambda _ I\lambda _ J|T_{I,J}| \leq 2^ p\! \sum _{\substack {|M|=n-p\ I\cap J\subset M\subset I\cup J}} \lambda _ M^2 T_{M,M}.  \] Inclusions in this formula allow equality. The assertion includes $p=0$ and $p=n$. Proof. Reality, order zero and diagonal positivity are the exact earlier result coefficient measures and compactness of positive currents ; we prove only its additional quantitative refinement. Let $K=I^ c$, $L=J^ c$, and order these two $p$-element sets so their common elements occupy matching positions. Put $\alpha _ s=dz_{k_ s}$, $ eta _ s=dz_{l_ s}$. For $a\in (\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z)^ p$, the form \[  \gamma _ a= igwedge _{s=1}^ p rac{i}{4} (\alpha _ s+i^{a_ s} eta _ s)\wedge ( ar\alpha _ s+i^{-a_ s} ar eta _ s)  \] is strongly positive. Direct four-term summation in each slot gives \[  \sum _ a i^{\sum _ s a_ s}\gamma _ a = igwedge _{s=1}^ p i\alpha _ s\wedge  ar eta _ s, \qquad \sum _ a\gamma _ a = igwedge _{s=1}^ p i(\alpha _ s\wedge  ar\alpha _ s+  eta _ s\wedge  ar eta _ s).  \] The first identity extracts $T_{I,J}$, up to a constant of modulus one in the complex-oriented volume form. Each $T\wedge \gamma _ a$ is a positive measure, so the triangle inequality for variation bounds $|T_{I,J}|$ by the second displayed expression wedged with $T$. Its at most $2^ p$ terms are positive diagonal terms. Every nonzero chosen $p$-index contains $K\cap L$ and lies in $K\cup L$; its complementary index therefore satisfies the asserted conditions on $M$. Each multiplicity is at most $2^ p$. This proves the unweighted estimate, including empty wedges. For positive $\lambda _ j$, apply the constant diagonal linear change to the covector slots of $T$, at the same base point. The resulting current is positive: its dual transformation preserves every strongly positive test form. Its coefficients are $\lambda _ I\lambda _ JT_{I,J}$. The unweighted estimate for this current is the required weighted estimate. Finally replace each zero $\lambda _ j$ by $\lambda _ j+\varepsilon $ and let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, testing the measure inequality against nonnegative compactly supported continuous functions. $\square$ Lemma 5.63.3 . 192CB50CA0EA Let $X$ be locally compact, and let $\mu _ k,\mu $ be positive Radon measures with $\mu _ k	o \mu $ vaguely. Suppose $f_ k:X	o [-\infty ,\infty )$ are upper semicontinuous and decrease pointwise to $f$. Whenever the products $f_ k\mu _ k$ are locally finite signed Radon measures, every vague cluster limit $
u $ of those products satisfies \[  
u \leq f\mu .  \] Existence of such a cluster limit also implies $f\in L^1_{m loc}(\mu )$. No local boundedness of the limit and no separability assumption on $X$ is needed. Proof. We give the needed compact-set version of the upper weak inequality. In a locally compact Hausdorff space, for compact $C\subset U$ with $U$ open there is $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ in $C_ c(U)$ equal to one on $C$. Here are the topological ingredients of that assertion. Separating a point from each point of a compact set by disjoint neighborhoods and taking a finite subcover proves regularity. It gives $C\subset V\Subset U$ by a second finite subcover. The same finite separation argument proves normality of the compact Hausdorff closure of a slightly larger such neighborhood. The dyadic construction of nested open sets with $\overline{V_ r}\subset V_ s$ for dyadic $r<s$, starting with the two disjoint closed sets, gives the continuous function $x\mapsto \inf \{ r:x\in V_ r\} $; its sublevel and superlevel sets are open by these closure inclusions. Taking its complement and extending by zero gives the asserted compactly supported cutoff. Thus vague convergence gives $\limsup _ k\mu _ k(C)\leq \mu (C)$: bound $1_ C$ by those cutoffs and shrink their support to $C$. The required outer approximation of $\mu (C)$ follows from inner regularity on $L\setminus C$, where $L$ is a compact neighborhood of $C$ with finite measure. It follows also that the $\mu _ k$ masses of any fixed compact set are uniformly bounded. If $g\geq 0$ is bounded, upper semicontinuous and compactly supported, its sets $\{ g\geq t\} $ are compact for $t>0$. Layer integration and the upper Fatou inequality, with that uniform mass bound, prove \[  \limsup _ k\int g\, d\mu _ k\leq \int g\, d\mu .  \] Layer sets with $>$ or $\geq $ give the same integral; any exceptional levels have one-dimensional measure zero. Take any convergent cofinal subnet defining $
u $ and fix $0\leq \chi \in C_ c(X)$ and an index $k_0$. Apply the preceding inequality to $\chi (\max \{ f_{k_0},-m\} +m)$ and subtract the convergent continuous term $m\int \chi \, d\mu _ k$. This bound holds for the full sequence and hence for the cofinal subnet as well. Hence \[  \int \chi \, d
u \leq \int \chi \max \{ f_{k_0},-m\} \, d\mu .  \] Let $m	o \infty $ and then $k_0	o \infty $. title: Proposition 5.63.2
section: 5.63 Positive-current coefficient bounds and support maxima
text: Proposition 5.63.2 . 7ECC0248E832 In coordinates on an $n$-manifold write a positive current of bidimension $(p,p)$ as \[  T=i^{(n-p)^2}\sum _{|I|=|J|=n-p}T_{I,J}\, dz_ I\wedge d\bar z_ J.  \] Its coefficient distributions are measures, its matrix is Hermitian, and $T_{M,M}\geq 0$. For arbitrary $\lambda _ j\geq 0$, put $\lambda _ I=\prod _{j\in I}\lambda _ j$. Then, as measures, \[  \lambda _ I\lambda _ J|T_{I,J}| \leq 2^ p\! \sum _{\substack {|M|=n-p\\ I\cap J\subset M\subset I\cup J}} \lambda _ M^2 T_{M,M}.  \] Inclusions in this formula allow equality. The assertion includes $p=0$ and $p=n$. Proof. Reality, order zero and diagonal positivity are the exact earlier result coefficient measures and compactness of positive currents ; we prove only its additional quantitative refinement. Let $K=I^ c$, $L=J^ c$, and order these two $p$-element sets so their common elements occupy matching positions. Put $\alpha _ s=dz_{k_ s}$, $\beta _ s=dz_{l_ s}$. For $a\in (\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z)^ p$, the form \[  \gamma _ a=\bigwedge _{s=1}^ p\frac{i}{4} (\alpha _ s+i^{a_ s}\beta _ s)\wedge (\bar\alpha _ s+i^{-a_ s}\bar\beta _ s)  \] is strongly positive. Direct four-term summation in each slot gives \[  \sum _ a i^{\sum _ s a_ s}\gamma _ a =\bigwedge _{s=1}^ p i\alpha _ s\wedge \bar\beta _ s, \qquad \sum _ a\gamma _ a =\bigwedge _{s=1}^ p i(\alpha _ s\wedge \bar\alpha _ s+ \beta _ s\wedge \bar\beta _ s).  \] The first identity extracts $T_{I,J}$, up to a constant of modulus one in the complex-oriented volume form. Each $T\wedge \gamma _ a$ is a positive measure, so the triangle inequality for variation bounds $|T_{I,J}|$ by the second displayed expression wedged with $T$. Its at most $2^ p$ terms are positive diagonal terms. Every nonzero chosen $p$-index contains $K\cap L$ and lies in $K\cup L$; its complementary index therefore satisfies the asserted conditions on $M$. Each multiplicity is at most $2^ p$. This proves the unweighted estimate, including empty wedges. For positive $\lambda _ j$, apply the constant diagonal linear change to the covector slots of $T$, at the same base point. The resulting current is positive: its dual transformation preserves every strongly positive test form. Its coefficients are $\lambda _ I\lambda _ JT_{I,J}$. The unweighted estimate for this current is the required weighted estimate. Finally replace each zero $\lambda _ j$ by $\lambda _ j+\varepsilon $ and let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, testing the measure inequality against nonnegative compactly supported continuous functions. $\square$

Lemma 5.63.3 . 192CB50CA0EA Let $X$ be locally compact, and let $\mu _ k,\mu $ be positive Radon measures with $\mu _ k	o \mu $ vaguely. Suppose $f_ k:X	o [-\infty ,\infty )$ are upper semicontinuous and decrease pointwise to $f$. Whenever the products $f_ k\mu _ k$ are locally finite signed Radon measures, every vague cluster limit $
u $ of those products satisfies \[  
u \leq f\mu .  \] Existence of such a cluster limit also implies $f\in L^1_{m loc}(\mu )$. No local boundedness of the limit and no separability assumption on $X$ is needed. Proof. Separating a point from each point of a compact set by disjoint neighborhoods and taking a finite subcover proves regularity. It gives $C\subset V\Subset U$ by a second finite subcover. The same finite separation argument proves normality of the compact Hausdorff closure of a slightly larger such neighborhood. The dyadic construction of nested open sets with $\overline{V_ r}\subset V_ s$ for dyadic $r<s$, starting with the two disjoint closed sets, gives the continuous function $x\mapsto \inf \{ r:x\in V_ r\} $; its sublevel and superlevel sets are open by these closure inclusions. It follows also that the $\mu _ k$ masses of any fixed compact set are uniformly bounded. If $g\geq 0$ is bounded, upper semicontinuous and compactly supported, its sets $\{ g\geq t\} $ are compact for $t>0$. Layer integration and the upper Fatou inequality, with that uniform mass bound, prove \[  \limsup _ k\int g\, d\mu _ k\leq \int g\, d\mu .  \] Layer sets with $>$ or $\geq $ give the same integral; any exceptional levels have one-dimensional measure zero. Take any convergent cofinal subnet defining $
u $ and fix $0\leq \chi \in C_ c(X)$ and an index $k_0$. For $k\geq k_0$, \[  \int \chi f_ k\, d\mu _ k \leq \int \chi \max \{ f_{k_0},-m\} \, d\mu _ k.  \] The right weight is bounded on the compact support of $\chi $; upper semicontinuity gives a finite upper bound there. Apply the preceding inequality to $\chi (\max \{ f_{k_0},-m\} +m)$ and subtract the convergent continuous term $m\int \chi \, d\mu _ k$. This bound holds for the full sequence and hence for the cofinal subnet as well. Hence \[  \int \chi \, d
u \leq \int \chi \max \{ f_{k_0},-m\} \, d\mu .  \] Let $m	o \infty $ and then $k_0	o \infty $. Both passages are decreasing convergence after subtraction from a common integrable upper bound on this compact set. The right side tends to $\int \chi f\, d\mu $. It cannot be minus infinity, since the left side is finite. Choose such a $\chi $ equal to one on any prescribed compact set to obtain $f\in L^1_{m loc}(\mu )$. title: Theorem 5.63.4

text: Theorem 5.63.4 . 949B825CA873 Let $\Omega =\{ \psi <0\} \Subset X$ be a smoothly bounded domain, where $\psi $ is smooth strictly plurisubharmonic near $\overline\Omega $ and $d\psi \ne 0$ on $\partial \Omega $. Let $T$ be closed positive of bidimension $(p,p)$ near $\overline\Omega $, with $p\geq 1$. For every plurisubharmonic $u$ defined near $\overline\Omega $, \[  \sup _{\overline\Omega \cap \operatorname {Supp}T}u_+ =\sup _{\partial \Omega \cap \operatorname {Supp}T}u_+.  \] Here $u_+=\max \{ u,0\} $ and the supremum of this nonnegative function over the empty set is zero. Discontinuity of $u$ is allowed. Proof. Put $\omega =dd^ c\psi >0$. First let $u$ be smooth and fix $b>\sup _{\partial \Omega \cap \operatorname {Supp}T}u$. For $\varepsilon >0$ the bounded plurisubharmonic function \[  v=\max \{ u-b+\varepsilon \psi ,0\}   \] vanishes near $\partial \Omega \cap \operatorname {Supp}T$. Thus $vT$ has compact support in $\Omega $. The bounded recursive product locality and positivity of bounded Bedford–Taylor products is positive and gives \[  \int _\Omega dd^ c(vT)\wedge \omega ^{p-1}=0  \] by compact-support Stokes. On the open set $E=\{ u-b+\varepsilon \psi >0\} $ its integrand dominates $\varepsilon T\wedge \omega ^ p$. Consequently $E$ is disjoint from $\operatorname {Supp}T$: otherwise its positive trace measure would have positive mass on that open neighborhood. Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $u\leq b$ on $\Omega \cap \operatorname {Supp}T$. For general $u$, reuse the exact smooth-decreasing-majorant lemma 7.31.1 on $K=\overline\Omega $, whose strict function is $\psi $. It gives smooth plurisubharmonic $u_ j\downarrow u$ on a fixed neighborhood. For every real $b$ strictly above the boundary supremum, eventually $u_ j<b$ on the compact boundary support: the increasing open sets $\{ u_ j<b\} $ cover it. Apply the smooth conclusion to such $u_ j$ and then let $j\to \infty $ and $b$ decrease to the boundary supremum. If that supremum is minus infinity, use every real $b$. Taking positive parts gives the stated equality, because the closed domain contains its boundary. Empty support is harmless. If the boundary support is empty but interior support were nonempty, the same compact-support Stokes argument with the strictly positive form $\omega ^ p$ would give $T=0$ inside, a contradiction. $\square$

title: 7.32.1 Collar estimates for plurisubharmonic potentials
text: Corollary 7.32.2 . EAB247B80433 Under the preceding geometric hypotheses, fix $\delta _0>0$ and set $\Omega _\delta =\{ \psi <-\delta \} $, $0<\delta \leq \delta _0$. If $L(u)\cap \operatorname {Supp}T\subset \Omega _\delta $, put \[  M=\sup _{(\overline\Omega \setminus \Omega _\delta ) \cap \operatorname {Supp}T}|u|.  \] Then $M<\infty $, $uT$ is coefficient-integrable, and \[  \| uT\| _{\overline\Omega ,\omega } \leq \frac{C}{\delta }M\| T\| _{\overline\Omega ,\omega }, \qquad C=4\delta _0+8\| \psi \| _{L^\infty (\Omega )}.  \] Here $\| uT\| _{A,\omega }=\int _ A|u|T\wedge \omega ^ p$. For any fixed smooth Hermitian norm the same assertion holds with a constant depending only on the fixed geometric data and $p$. It has no dependence on $u$, $T$ or $\delta $. Proof. The closed collar support is compact and misses $L(u)$, so $u$ is bounded on a neighborhood of each of its points; a finite subcover makes $M$ finite. Empty collar support forces $T=0$ inside by the preceding theorem. We may otherwise use the same decreasing smooth majorants $u_ j$. For each $\eta >0$, eventually $-M\leq u_ j\leq M+\eta $ on that compact collar support. The lower bound follows from $u_ j\geq u$, and the upper bound from compactness and decreasing convergence, as above. The support maximum theorem gives $u_ j\leq M+\eta $ on the whole closed domain support. Set \[  v_ j=u_ j-M-2\eta ,\qquad N=2M+3\eta ,\qquad A=4N/\delta .  \] Thus $v_ j\leq -\eta $ on the closed domain support, and $v_ j>-N$ on the collar support. Continuity makes these strict inequalities valid on suitable neighborhoods. Modify $v_ j$ only near that support: leave it unchanged for $\psi <-\delta /2$, and use $\max \{ v_ j,A\psi \} $ on the outer collar. These formulas glue on a support neighborhood. Indeed, choose the outer neighborhood with $\psi >-3\delta /4$; on the overlap $-3\delta /4<\psi <-\delta /2$ one has $A\psi \leq -2N<v_ j$. Near the boundary the maximum is exactly $A\psi $. Call the resulting locally bounded plurisubharmonic function $w_ j$. It is defined near $\overline\Omega \cap \operatorname {Supp}T$, is nonpositive on that support and equals $A\psi $ on its boundary collar. Its currents extend unambiguously across the complementary region where $T=0$; no values of $w_ j$ away from the support are needed. Write $m_ T=\int _\Omega T\wedge \omega ^ p$ and $B=\| \psi \| _{L^\infty (\Omega )}$. The two common-collar identities in lemma 7.29.1 apply here with precisely the same compact-difference proof, which does not use the spherical shape of its original ball. Namely $(w_ j-A\psi )T$ has compact support in $\Omega $; integration by parts with a cutoff equal to one near that support gives \[  \int _\Omega dd^ cw_ j\wedge T\wedge \omega ^{p-1}=A m_ T, \quad \int _\Omega (-w_ j)T\wedge \omega ^ p =\int _\Omega (-\psi )dd^ cw_ j\wedge T\wedge \omega ^{p-1} \leq BA m_ T.  \] The functions $w_ j$ and $v_ j$ agree on the inner region, and $-v_ j\leq N$ on the rest of the support. Therefore \[  \int _\Omega |u_ j|T\wedge \omega ^ p \leq (N+M+2\eta +4BN/\delta )m_ T.  \] Fatou as $j\to \infty $, followed by $\eta \downarrow 0$, bounds the open-domain integral by $(3+8B/\delta )Mm_ T$. The boundary integral is at most $M\int _{\partial \Omega }T\wedge \omega ^ p$ because the boundary belongs to the closed collar. This proves the claimed closed-domain estimate, also when $M=0$. Coefficient integrability follows by the existing trace domination theorem. On the fixed compact closed domain any fixed Hermitian metric is uniformly comparable with $\omega $, giving the final assertion. $\square$ The strictly plurisubharmonic defining-function convention entails no loss for a smoothly strongly pseudoconvex Stein domain. For completeness, first take any smooth defining function $r$ on a boundary collar. Replacing it by $r+Cr^2$ makes it strictly plurisubharmonic on a smaller collar: on the compact boundary its Levi form is already positive on the complex tangent space, and $2C\, \partial r\otimes \bar\partial r$ makes the remaining normal direction positive for one sufficiently large $C$, by the Schur complement. Continuity preserves positivity on a smaller collar; the sign and zero set remain unchanged. Now use this strict defining function and the strict exhaustion given by theorem 9.32.12 . Choose two negative levels inside the collar. A sufficiently small positive multiple of the exhaustion plus a negative constant lies above the defining function near the inner level and below it near the outer level; all relevant inner sets are compact, so both strict inequalities can be imposed at once. The normalized smooth maximum Euclidean Richberg smoothing glues these two functions, with exact branches near the two levels. It stays negative inside, agrees with the original defining function near the boundary, and is strictly plurisubharmonic throughout a neighborhood of the closed domain. Thus the support maximum and collar bound hold throughout the stated smooth strongly pseudoconvex Stein scope, including discontinuous potentials and boundary mass. The case $p=0$ is excluded here: a point mass and a logarithmic pole already violate integrability.
