title: 9.65 Projective models and Kähler modifications
text: Manifolds are connected unless otherwise stated. A modification is proper, bimeromorphic and an isomorphism away from nowhere dense analytic subsets upstairs and downstairs. Curvature below is $\mathrm i\Theta $, without division by $2\pi $. Lemma 9.65.1 . 24EDDE45E392 A closed analytic subset of projective space is algebraic. Proof. The cone argument in the proof of theorem 10.40.10 applies to singular analytic subsets as well. Here are its precise hypotheses in that case. For a nonempty closed analytic $B\subset \mathbb P^ N$, its inverse image in $\mathbb C^{N+1}\setminus \{ 0\} $ is an analytic cone, all of whose branches have dimension at least one. The theorem the Remmert–Stein extension theorem extends its closure across zero as an analytic cone $C$. Take finite holomorphic equations $f_ j=\sum _ m P_{jm}$ near zero, where the $P_{jm}$ are homogeneous. Scaling in $C$ shows that every $P_{jm}$ vanishes on it. Conversely their simultaneous vanishing implies that of the convergent sums $f_ j$. By Noetherianity of convergent power-series modules , the germ ideal generated by all the $P_{jm}$ is generated by a finite subfamily. If that subfamily vanishes at $z$, evaluate every other germ relation at $tz$ for sufficiently small nonzero $t$; homogeneity gives $P_{jm}(z)=0$. Scaling back from the local equations puts $z$ in $C$. Thus the finite homogeneous polynomials define $C$ globally. Projectivizing proves the claim. The empty subset uses the equation $1$. $\square$ Lemma 9.65.2 . 5174706A0D80 Let $f:M\to \mathbb P^ n$ be a holomorphic map from a compact connected complex $n$-manifold, with rank $n$ somewhere, $n\geq 1$. There is a homogeneous polynomial $P$ of positive degree $d$, divisible by $Z_0$, such that, for $D=\{ P=0\} $, \[  M^\circ =M\setminus f^{-1}D\longrightarrow U=\mathbb P^ n\setminus D  \] is a finite unbranched covering. It has a fixed positive degree $e$. On $M^\circ $ the function \[  \psi =-\log |P\circ f|_{\rm FS}^2  \] can be normalized to be nonnegative and is a proper smooth strictly PSH exhaustion. In fact $\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial \psi =d f^*\omega _{\rm FS}^{\rm un}$, where $\omega _{\rm FS}^{\rm un}=\mathrm i\Theta (\mathcal O(1))$. Proof. The image is analytic by Remmert's proper mapping theorem and contains an open subset, so it is all of $\mathbb P^ n$. The critical locus $C=\{ \det df=0\} $ is analytic of dimension at most $n-1$. Its proper image is analytic and has dimension at most $n-1$ by dimension bounds for holomorphic images . By the preceding lemma it is algebraic. A nonzero homogeneous polynomial vanishes on it; multiply it by $Z_0$ and use $P=Z_0$ if $C$ is empty. Off $D$ there are no critical points. Properness makes every discrete fiber finite, and inverse charts plus properness give a covering: finitely many disjoint inverse charts cover a fiber, and the complement cannot acquire new points over a sufficiently small base neighborhood. The complements of proper analytic subsets of connected manifolds are connected, by the bounded-holomorphic-removal argument; hence the covering degree is constant and positive. The asserted Hessian is the local Chern formula, since $P$ is holomorphic and nonzero off $D$. The pullback is positive because $df$ is invertible there. The function tends to $+\infty $ at $f^{-1}D$. Compactness of $M$ proves properness; multiplying $P$ by a constant makes its squared norm at most one. $\square$ Lemma 9.65.3 . 4F31DD82134A Under the preceding hypotheses, fix $b\in U$ and enumerate $f^{-1}(b)=\{ x_1,\ldots ,x_ e\} $. There are global meromorphic functions $g_1,\ldots ,g_ e$ on $M$, holomorphic on $M^\circ $, such that $g_ i(x_ j)=\delta _{ij}$. Proof. Use affine coordinates $z=(Z_1/Z_0,\ldots ,Z_ n/Z_0)$ on $U$ and put $\Omega =f^*(dz_1\wedge \cdots \wedge dz_ n)$. It is a nowhere zero holomorphic top form on $M^\circ $ and a meromorphic top form on $M$. The original metric $\omega _0=f^*(\mathrm i\sum dz_ j\wedge d\bar z_ j)$ is Kähler on $M^\circ $. Choose a smooth cutoff $\chi _ i$ supported in a small coordinate ball about $x_ i$, equal to one near $x_ i$, with support disjoint from all other $x_ j$. Its top-form datum \[  \eta _ i=\bar\partial (\chi _ i\Omega )  \] is closed, smooth, compactly supported and zero near the whole fiber. For any fixed $A>0$ put, off that fiber, \[  \Phi =A\psi +n\log |z\circ f-b|^2.  \] This is smooth PSH there and its complex Hessian is at least $A d f^*\omega _{\rm FS}^{\rm un}>0$. Thus the inverse-curvature energy of $\eta _ i$ for the trivial line metric $e^{-\Phi }$ and the metric $\omega _0$ is finite: every quantity is smooth on the fixed compact support, with strictly positive curvature there. Apply theorem 6.28.2 on the increasing sublevels of $\psi $, with the finite fiber removed. Each admits a complete Kähler background by lemma 6.28.11 , applied to the holomorphic tuple $z\circ f-b$. The original-metric top-degree clause applies with line rank one and barred degree one. Its inverse energy bound is independent of the sublevel once the datum is included. The fixed weights give local weak $L^2$ bounds on the complement of the fiber. A diagonal weak limit and lower semicontinuity give \[  \bar\partial u_ i=\eta _ i,\qquad \int _{M^\circ \setminus f^{-1}(b)} |u_ i|^2e^{-A\psi }|z\circ f-b|^{-2n}<\infty .  \] Top-form norms and volume use $\omega _0$; their product is the intrinsic top-form density, independent of that choice. Near the omitted fiber the weight is bounded below, so $u_ i$ is ordinarily locally $L^2$ across it. The analytic removal lemma 6.28.12 extends the equation over it. The coefficient of $u_ i$ in the frame $\Omega $ is holomorphic near every $x_ j$, by holomorphic distributions and minimal weighted solutions . Since $f$ is a local biholomorphism there, the nonintegrable radial weight $|z-b|^{-2n}$ forces that coefficient to vanish at each $x_ j$. Consequently \[  g_ i=\chi _ i-u_ i/\Omega  \] is holomorphic on $M^\circ $ and has the claimed fiber values. The compact cutoff term and the preceding estimate give the weaker but nonsingular-at-the-fiber global bound 1D8298271C51 9.65.4 \begin{equation}  \int _{M^\circ }|g_ i\Omega |^2 e^{-A\psi } (1+|z\circ f-b|^2)^{-n}<\infty . \end{equation} We do not claim integrability of $g_ i$ itself against the point-pole weight; its nonzero prescribed value forbids that assertion. It remains to prove meromorphic extension at the boundary. In a relatively compact coordinate neighborhood of a point of $f^{-1}D$, write $\tau $ for a holomorphic coefficient of $f^*P$ in a line frame, and $\Omega =(a/c)\, dw_1\wedge \cdots \wedge dw_ n$, with $a,c$ holomorphic and not identically zero. Smooth frame factors give $e^{-A\psi }\geq C|\tau |^{2A}$. Because $P$ is divisible by $Z_0$ and its remaining factor has bounded Fubini–Study norm, \[  1+|z\circ f-b|^2\leq C'|\tau |^{-2}  \] on this neighborhood off the boundary. Since $c$ is bounded above, the top-form density is bounded below by a positive constant times $|g_ i a|^2$. Equation ( 9.65.4 ) therefore implies \[  \int |g_ i a|^2|\tau |^{2(A+n)}\, dV<\infty .  \] Choose an integer $N\geq A+n$. The holomorphic function $g_ i a\tau ^ N$ off $f^{-1}D$ is locally $L^2$ across it and extends holomorphically by the same analytic removal theorem. title: Lemma 9.65.1
text: Lemma 9.65.1 . 24EDDE45E392 A closed analytic subset of projective space is algebraic. Proof. The cone argument in the proof of theorem 10.40.10 applies to singular analytic subsets as well. Here are its precise hypotheses in that case. For a nonempty closed analytic $B\subset \mathbb P^ N$, its inverse image in $\mathbb C^{N+1}\setminus \{ 0\} $ is an analytic cone, all of whose branches have dimension at least one. The theorem the Remmert–Stein extension theorem extends its closure across zero as an analytic cone $C$. Take finite holomorphic equations $f_ j=\sum _ m P_{jm}$ near zero, where the $P_{jm}$ are homogeneous. Scaling in $C$ shows that every $P_{jm}$ vanishes on it. Conversely their simultaneous vanishing implies that of the convergent sums $f_ j$. By Noetherianity of convergent power-series modules , the germ ideal generated by all the $P_{jm}$ is generated by a finite subfamily. If that subfamily vanishes at $z$, evaluate every other germ relation at $tz$ for sufficiently small nonzero $t$; homogeneity gives $P_{jm}(z)=0$. Scaling back from the local equations puts $z$ in $C$. Thus the finite homogeneous polynomials define $C$ globally. Projectivizing proves the claim. The empty subset uses the equation $1$. $\square$

title: Lemma 9.65.2
text: Lemma 9.65.2 . 5174706A0D80 Let $f:M\to \mathbb P^ n$ be a holomorphic map from a compact connected complex $n$-manifold, with rank $n$ somewhere, $n\geq 1$. There is a homogeneous polynomial $P$ of positive degree $d$, divisible by $Z_0$, such that, for $D=\{ P=0\} $, \[  M^\circ =M\setminus f^{-1}D\longrightarrow U=\mathbb P^ n\setminus D  \] is a finite unbranched covering. It has a fixed positive degree $e$. On $M^\circ $ the function \[  \psi =-\log |P\circ f|_{\rm FS}^2  \] can be normalized to be nonnegative and is a proper smooth strictly PSH exhaustion. In fact $\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial \psi =d f^*\omega _{\rm FS}^{\rm un}$, where $\omega _{\rm FS}^{\rm un}=\mathrm i\Theta (\mathcal O(1))$. Proof. The image is analytic by Remmert's proper mapping theorem and contains an open subset, so it is all of $\mathbb P^ n$. The critical locus $C=\{ \det df=0\} $ is analytic of dimension at most $n-1$. Its proper image is analytic and has dimension at most $n-1$ by dimension bounds for holomorphic images . By the preceding lemma it is algebraic. A nonzero homogeneous polynomial vanishes on it; multiply it by $Z_0$ and use $P=Z_0$ if $C$ is empty. Off $D$ there are no critical points. Properness makes every discrete fiber finite, and inverse charts plus properness give a covering: finitely many disjoint inverse charts cover a fiber, and the complement cannot acquire new points over a sufficiently small base neighborhood. The complements of proper analytic subsets of connected manifolds are connected, by the bounded-holomorphic-removal argument; hence the covering degree is constant and positive. The asserted Hessian is the local Chern formula, since $P$ is holomorphic and nonzero off $D$. The pullback is positive because $df$ is invertible there. The function tends to $+\infty $ at $f^{-1}D$. Compactness of $M$ proves properness; multiplying $P$ by a constant makes its squared norm at most one. $\square$

title: Lemma 9.65.3
text: Lemma 9.65.3 . 4F31DD82134A Under the preceding hypotheses, fix $b\in U$ and enumerate $f^{-1}(b)=\{ x_1,\ldots ,x_ e\} $. There are global meromorphic functions $g_1,\ldots ,g_ e$ on $M$, holomorphic on $M^\circ $, such that $g_ i(x_ j)=\delta _{ij}$. Proof. Use affine coordinates $z=(Z_1/Z_0,\ldots ,Z_ n/Z_0)$ on $U$ and put $\Omega =f^*(dz_1\wedge \cdots \wedge dz_ n)$. It is a nowhere zero holomorphic top form on $M^\circ $ and a meromorphic top form on $M$. The original metric $\omega _0=f^*(\mathrm i\sum dz_ j\wedge d\bar z_ j)$ is Kähler on $M^\circ $. Choose a smooth cutoff $\chi _ i$ supported in a small coordinate ball about $x_ i$, equal to one near $x_ i$, with support disjoint from all other $x_ j$. Its top-form datum \[  \eta _ i=\bar\partial (\chi _ i\Omega )  \] is closed, smooth, compactly supported and zero near the whole fiber. For any fixed $A>0$ put, off that fiber, \[  \Phi =A\psi +n\log |z\circ f-b|^2.  \] This is smooth PSH there and its complex Hessian is at least $A d f^*\omega _{\rm FS}^{\rm un}>0$. Thus the inverse-curvature energy of $\eta _ i$ for the trivial line metric $e^{-\Phi }$ and the metric $\omega _0$ is finite: every quantity is smooth on the fixed compact support, with strictly positive curvature there. Apply theorem 6.28.2 on the increasing sublevels of $\psi $, with the finite fiber removed. Each admits a complete Kähler background by lemma 6.28.11 , applied to the holomorphic tuple $z\circ f-b$. The original-metric top-degree clause applies with line rank one and barred degree one. Its inverse energy bound is independent of the sublevel once the datum is included. The fixed weights give local weak $L^2$ bounds on the complement of the fiber. A diagonal weak limit and lower semicontinuity give \[  \bar\partial u_ i=\eta _ i,\qquad \int _{M^\circ \setminus f^{-1}(b)} |u_ i|^2e^{-A\psi }|z\circ f-b|^{-2n}<\infty .  \] Top-form norms and volume use $\omega _0$; their product is the intrinsic top-form density, independent of that choice. Near the omitted fiber the weight is bounded below, so $u_ i$ is ordinarily locally $L^2$ across it. The analytic removal lemma 6.28.12 extends the equation over it. The coefficient of $u_ i$ in the frame $\Omega $ is holomorphic near every $x_ j$, by holomorphic distributions and minimal weighted solutions . Since $f$ is a local biholomorphism there, the nonintegrable radial weight $|z-b|^{-2n}$ forces that coefficient to vanish at each $x_ j$. Consequently \[  g_ i=\chi _ i-u_ i/\Omega  \] is holomorphic on $M^\circ $ and has the claimed fiber values. The compact cutoff term and the preceding estimate give the weaker but nonsingular-at-the-fiber global bound 1D8298271C51 9.65.4 \begin{equation}  \int _{M^\circ }|g_ i\Omega |^2 e^{-A\psi } (1+|z\circ f-b|^2)^{-n}<\infty . \end{equation} We do not claim integrability of $g_ i$ itself against the point-pole weight; its nonzero prescribed value forbids that assertion. It remains to prove meromorphic extension at the boundary. In a relatively compact coordinate neighborhood of a point of $f^{-1}D$, write $\tau $ for a holomorphic coefficient of $f^*P$ in a line frame, and $\Omega =(a/c)\, dw_1\wedge \cdots \wedge dw_ n$, with $a,c$ holomorphic and not identically zero. Smooth frame factors give $e^{-A\psi }\geq C|\tau |^{2A}$. Because $P$ is divisible by $Z_0$ and its remaining factor has bounded Fubini–Study norm, \[  1+|z\circ f-b|^2\leq C'|\tau |^{-2}  \] on this neighborhood off the boundary. Since $c$ is bounded above, the top-form density is bounded below by a positive constant times $|g_ i a|^2$. Equation ( 9.65.4 ) therefore implies \[  \int |g_ i a|^2|\tau |^{2(A+n)}\, dV<\infty .  \] Choose an integer $N\geq A+n$. The holomorphic function $g_ i a\tau ^ N$ off $f^{-1}D$ is locally $L^2$ across it and extends holomorphically by the same analytic removal theorem. Its extension divided by $a\tau ^ N$ is a meromorphic extension of $g_ i$. The denominator is not the zero germ, since $df$ has full rank on a dense set. The local extensions agree on the dense open part, and hence glue globally. This proves the assertion. $\square$

We use the Riemannian volume of a Hermitian metric $\omega $, normalized so that $\omega =(\mathrm i/2)\sum dz_ j\wedge d ar z_ j$ has the standard Euclidean metric. The curvature of a Hermitian holomorphic line bundle $L$ is its Chern curvature $\Theta _ L$; thus its real first Chern form is $\Omega _ L=\mathrm i\Theta _ L/(2\pi )$. Curvature eigenvalues below refer to $\mathrm i\Theta _ L$ relative to $\omega $. Lemma 2.24.2 . 3E8E852DB903 A densely defined, nonnegative closed quadratic form $Q$ on a Hilbert space, whose form-domain unit ball for $Q+\| \cdot \| ^2$ is compact in that space, has an orthonormal eigenbasis with eigenvalues $0\leq e_1\leq e_2\leq \cdots 	o \infty $, counted with multiplicity. In finite dimension the list terminates; the zero-dimensional case has an empty list. Its counting function and first Riesz mean are \[  N_ Q(t)=\# \{ j:e_ j\leq t\} ,\qquad R_ Q(t)=\sum _ j(t-e_ j)_+.  \] The count is the largest dimension of a subspace on which $Q\leq t\| \cdot \| ^2$. Moreover, for a positive trace-class contraction $0\leq \gamma \leq I$ with finite form trace, 89116945DA7D 2.24.3  egin{equation}  \operatorname {Tr}\gamma (t-Q)\leq R_ Q(t), \end{equation} where the left side means $t\operatorname {Tr}\gamma $ minus its form trace. Equality is obtained by the spectral projection onto $e_ j<t$. Proof. Hilbert representation for the form inner product gives the bounded inverse $T=(Q+I)^{-1}$; its image is form-norm bounded on bounded sets, so it is compact, positive and self-adjoint. title: 10.95.1 Dolbeault spectral asymptotics on a Hermitian manifold

text:
Let $X$ be a compact Hermitian complex $n$-manifold, $n\geq 1$, let $L$ be a smooth Hermitian holomorphic line bundle, and let $F$ be a fixed Hermitian holomorphic vector bundle of rank $r$. No curvature sign or Kähler hypothesis is imposed in this section. Put \[  Q_{k,q}(u)= rac2k igl (\|  ar\partial u\| ^2+ \|  ar\partial ^*u\| ^2 igr ), \qquad u\in \mathcal A^{0,q}(X,L^ k\otimes F).  \] Let $\alpha _1(x),\ldots ,\alpha _ n(x)$ be the ordered real curvature eigenvalues, $b_ j=|\alpha _ j|$, and, for $|J|=q$, put \[  V_ J=\sum _{j=1}^ n\alpha _ j-2\sum _{j\in J}\alpha _ j, \qquad \mathcal R_ q(t)=r\int _ X\sum _{|J|=q}r_{b(x)}(t+V_ J(x))\, dV_\omega .  \] The integrand is continuous, including at zero curvature eigenvalues. Lemma 10.95.2 . 0EAC1C0027AB In a finite collection of relatively compact coordinate and unitary bundle charts, let $P_ k$ be a coordinate cube of side $l_ k=k^{-1/3}$, centered at $a$. Freeze the base metric at $a$ and the line curvature at $a$, and use the corresponding constant magnetic connection. The flat Dirichlet Dolbeault form $Q^0_{k,q,a}$ is the orthogonal direct sum, with multiplicity $r$, of the forms 3EC3FF64BA96 10.95.3  egin{equation}  k^{-1}\| 
abla _{k,b(a)}v\| ^2-V_ J(a)\| v\| ^2, \qquad |J|=q. \end{equation} There are $\epsilon _ k\downarrow 0$, uniform in the centers, such that the actual and frozen squared $L^2$ norms differ by factors $1\pm \epsilon _ k$, and on $H^1_0(P_ k)$ B3E87C118A60 10.95.4  egin{equation}  (1-\epsilon _ k)Q^0_{k,q,a}(u)-\epsilon _ k\| u\| _0^2 \leq Q_{k,q}(u) \leq (1+\epsilon _ k)Q^0_{k,q,a}(u)+\epsilon _ k\| u\| _0^2. \end{equation} The same assertions hold on cubes enlarged by a factor tending to one. Proof. In a unitary line frame its connection is $d+\mathrm i A$, $A$ real. Remove the constant and symmetric linear Taylor terms of $A$ by the phase given by their linear and quadratic primitive. The remaining linear part $A^0$ has constant curvature $dA(a)$, and $|A-A^0|\leq C l_ k^2$. Derivatives through order two on the finitely many chart closures give one uniform constant. The tensor-power connection is $d+\mathrm i kA$, and this phase change is unitary. Choose complex linear coordinates unitary for the frozen metric and diagonalizing its real $(1,1)$-curvature. There $\omega _ a=(\mathrm i/2)\sum dz_ j\wedge d ar z_ j$ and $\mathrm i\Theta _ L(a)=(\mathrm i/2)\sum \alpha _ j dz_ j\wedge d ar z_ j$. The real magnetic field is $dA=-\mathrm i\Theta _ L$. An additional quadratic phase gives the following gauge without changing the $O(l_ k^2)$ remainder: $A^0=-\sum \alpha _ j x_ jdy_ j$. Write $T_ j=(
abla _{x_ j}+\mathrm i
abla _{y_ j})/2$. Its adjoint is $T_ j^*=(-
abla _{x_ j}+\mathrm i
abla _{y_ j})/2$, and \[  [T_ j,T_ j^*]=k\alpha _ j/2,\qquad 4T_ j^*T_ j=-
abla _{x_ j}^2-
abla _{y_ j}^2-k\alpha _ j.  \] In the fixed orthonormal exterior basis $d ar z_ J/\sqrt{2^{|J|}}$, creation and contraction give, on the $J$ coefficient, \[  \square _{0,q}=2\sum _ j T_ j^*T_ j+2\sum _{j\in J}[T_ j,T_ j^*].  \] Thus $2\square _{0,q}/k$ is exactly ( 10.95.3 ), with field magnitudes $|\alpha _ j|$. Real coordinate reflections change any negative magnetic field sign to its magnitude; their images of the cubes remain parallelepipeds with the same bounded shape constants. This also proves that every frozen form is nonnegative. The fixed bundle $F$ contributes $r$ identical coefficients at this stage. Here is the error estimate on the actual non-Kähler chart. In fixed coordinate form frames, $ ar\partial $ is exterior multiplication by $d ar z_ j$ followed by the covariant barred derivative, plus the fixed bundle's bounded zero-order coefficients. Its formal adjoint is minus the corresponding unbarred covariant derivative and contraction with the metric coefficients, plus bounded zero-order terms. This follows by integration by parts with the smooth Gram matrices and volume density: derivatives of those matrices and of the density are bounded independently of $k$; the unitary line potential remains in the covariant derivative. The actual Gram matrices differ from their frozen values by $O(l_ k)$. Consequently the differences of these two first-order operators from the frozen ones satisfy \[  k^{-1}\| \mathrm{error}(u)\| _0^2 \leq C l_ k^2 igl (Q^0_{k,q,a}(u)+C\| u\| _0^2 igr ) +C(kl_ k^4+k^{-1})\| u\| _0^2.  \] Indeed the derivative part is $O(l_ k)
abla _{k,A^0}u$ and the remaining part is $O(kl_ k^2+1)u$; the displayed flat identity bounds $k^{-1}\| 
abla _{k,A^0}u\| _0^2$ by $Q^0+C\| u\| _0^2$. Apply $2ab\leq \delta a^2+\delta ^{-1}b^2$ with $\delta =k^{-1/12}$ to the two squared operator norms. Since $kl_ k^4=k^{-1/3}$, all additive and relative errors tend uniformly to zero. Norm and volume comparison give ( 10.95.4 ); smooth approximation gives it on $H^1_0$. This explicit coefficient estimate includes all torsion and fixed-bundle terms, without assuming that the base is Kähler. $\square$ Theorem 10.95.5 . 151C621E620C Let $R_{k,q}$ be the first Riesz mean of $2\square _{L^ k\otimes F}/k$ in bidegree $(0,q)$. For every real $t$, 2144B8649BC8 10.95.6  egin{equation}  \lim _{k	o \infty }k^{-n}R_{k,q}(t)=\mathcal R_ q(t). \end{equation} Except at a countable set of $t$, its eigenvalue count satisfies B86B26574A5C 10.95.7  egin{equation}  \lim _{k	o \infty }k^{-n}N_{k,q}(t) =r\int _ X\sum _{|J|=q}
u _{b(x)}(t+V_ J(x))\, dV_\omega . \end{equation} One common exceptional countable set can be used for all $q$. Proof. The compact resolvent, smooth eigensections and positive scalar principal part are those of lemma 10.46.1 , theorem 10.46.6 . The form eigenbasis and variational principles above therefore apply. The same applies to local Dirichlet forms by zero extension, local Sobolev compactness and Hilbert representation, as in the constant model. On each cube of side $l_ k$, the transformation $y=\sqrt k(x-a)$ turns the frozen magnetic form into $H_{b(a)}-V_ J(a)$ on a parallelepiped whose size is comparable to $\sqrt k l_ k=k^{1/6}$. Its shape and inverse shape matrices are uniformly bounded. The constant-field Riesz limit, including its uniformity in the field, and the form/norm comparisons consequently give 287B591FF910 10.95.8  egin{equation}  R_{Q_{k,q},P_ k}(t) =k^ n\operatorname {Vol}_\omega (P_ k) \left(r\sum _{|J|=q}r_{b(a)}(t+V_ J(a))+o(1)ight). \end{equation} This error is uniform in all centers. To justify passage through the form comparison explicitly, minmax places its eigenvalues between $(1-\delta _ k)e_ j^0-\delta _ k$ and $(1+\delta _ k)e_ j^0+\delta _ k$, after folding in norm errors. Their Riesz sums lie between $(1+\delta _ k)R^0((t-\delta _ k)/(1+\delta _ k))$ and $(1-\delta _ k)R^0((t+\delta _ k)/(1-\delta _ k))$. Frozen and actual volume densities differ by $1+O(l_ k)$. We give the covering and localization details needed to sum it. Choose finitely many relatively compact coordinate boxes $W_ j$ whose interiors cover $X$, with smooth faces inside larger charts. Assign successive disjoint open pieces $U_ j=W_ j\setminus  igcup _{i<j}\overline W_ i$. They cover outside the finite union $S$ of box boundaries, which has measure zero; their closures cover $X$. A coordinate layer of thickness $l$ around $S$ has volume $O(l)$: in finitely many smooth face charts this follows by integrating the bounded graph thickness. Use a lattice of cubes of side $l_ k$ in each assigned chart. The cubes compactly contained in $U_ j$ are mutually disjoint and miss volume $O(l_ k)$. Cubes meeting $\overline U_ j$, enlarged by the factor $1+\eta _ k$, $\eta _ k=k^{-1/24}$, cover $X$. Their total volume tends to $\operatorname {Vol}(X)$: overlap across the fixed faces occupies $O(l_ k)$ volume and enlargement costs $O(\eta _ k)$. Their overlap multiplicity is bounded by the fixed number of charts and a dimensional lattice constant. All cubes lie in their larger charts for sufficiently large $k$. There is a real partition $\sum \chi _{j,k}^2=1$ subordinate to these enlarged cubes, with $\sum |d\chi _{j,k}|^2\leq C(\eta _ k l_ k)^{-2}$. To construct it, take a bump equal to one on each un-enlarged cube, with compact support in its enlargement and derivative $O((\eta _ k l_ k)^{-1})$, then divide by the square root of the sum of all squared bumps. title: 10.96 Holomorphic Morse inequalities
text: For $0\leq q\leq n$ let $X(q)$ be the open set where $\mathrm i\Theta _ L$ is nondegenerate with exactly $q$ negative eigenvalues, and set \[  I_ q=\frac r{n!}\int _{X(q)}(-1)^ q\Omega _ L^ n, \qquad h_ k^ q=\dim H^{0,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,L^ k\otimes F).  \] By corollary 10.43.11 these are also the holomorphic sheaf-cohomology dimensions. Theorem 10.96.1 . 778548FB8A37 For every compact Hermitian complex manifold and bundles as above, 6B15B5C74219 \begin{align}  \limsup _{k\to \infty }k^{-n}h_ k^ q& \leq I_ q, \tag{10.96.2}\\  \limsup _{k\to \infty }k^{-n} \sum _{j=0}^ q(-1)^{q-j}h_ k^ j & \leq \sum _{j=0}^ q(-1)^{q-j}I_ j, \tag{10.96.3}\\  \lim _{k\to \infty }k^{-n}\sum _{q=0}^ n(-1)^ q h_ k^ q & =\frac r{n!}\int _ X\Omega _ L^ n. \tag{10.96.4} \end{align} No Riemann–Roch or index asymptotic is assumed in these conclusions. Proof. For fixed $t>0$, let $C_ k^ q(t)$ be the span of eigensections of $2\square /k$ with eigenvalue at most $t$. The identities $\bar\partial \square =\square \bar\partial $ and $\bar\partial ^*\square =\square \bar\partial ^*$ follow by expanding $\square =\bar\partial \bar\partial ^*+\bar\partial ^*\bar\partial $ and using $\bar\partial ^2=0$. Thus these finite spaces form a complex. On each positive eigenspace of $\square $, the operator $\bar\partial ^*/\lambda $ is a contracting homotopy, since $\bar\partial \bar\partial ^*/\lambda + \bar\partial ^*\bar\partial /\lambda =I$. The zero eigenspaces give the actual Dolbeault cohomology by theorem 10.46.6 . Hence this finite complex has dimensions $c_ k^ q=N_{k,q}(t)$ and cohomology dimensions $h_ k^ q$. If $b_ j$ is the rank of its differential into degree $j$, then $c_ k^ j=h_ k^ j+b_ j+b_{j+1}$, with $b_0=b_{n+1}=0$. It follows directly that $h_ k^ q\leq c_ k^ q$, \[  \sum _{j=0}^ q(-1)^{q-j}h_ k^ j =\sum _{j=0}^ q(-1)^{q-j}c_ k^ j-b_{q+1} \leq \sum _{j=0}^ q(-1)^{q-j}c_ k^ j,  \] and the alternating Euler sums are equal for $q=n$. This is the entire finite-dimensional cancellation used here. Choose $t\downarrow 0$ outside the common exceptional countable set in the spectral theorem. At a point with no zero eigenvalues the model measure is discrete with lowest energy $\sum |\alpha _ j|$ and mass $(2\pi )^{-n}\prod |\alpha _ j|$ there. Always $V_ J\leq \sum |\alpha _ j|$, with equality precisely when $J$ is the set of negative indices. Thus the limit of $\nu _{|\alpha |}(t+V_ J)$ is this mass for that $J$ and zero for the others. If at least one $\alpha _ j$ is zero, the corresponding factor $dt/(4\pi )$ makes the convolution diffuse; it has no atom at its lowest energy. Every such limit is therefore zero. The uniform density bound permits dominated convergence on $X$. In coordinates unitary for $\omega $ one has $\Omega _ L^ n/n!=(2\pi )^{-n}\prod \alpha _ j\, dV_\omega $. Consequently the limiting integral of the $q$th small-eigen density is exactly $I_ q$. For each fixed admissible $t$, take $k\to \infty $ in the preceding finite-dimensional inequalities, then let $t$ decrease to zero. This proves the two inequalities. For the Euler sum its exact equality with the finite-complex sum gives both normalized limsup and liminf the same limit. Finally the top curvature form is zero on the degenerate locus and the nondegenerate loci partition its complement; hence $\sum (-1)^ qI_ q=r\int _ X\Omega _ L^ n/n!$. This proves the equality as well. $\square$

section: 19.10 Section growth of semipositive line bundles
text: Corollary 19.10.1 . F31884F26A29 Let $L$ be a smooth Hermitian holomorphic line bundle on a compact Hermitian complex $n$-manifold. If $\mathrm i\Theta _ L\geq 0$, then 2B3916324C79 19.10.2 \begin{equation}  h^0(X,L^ k)=\frac{k^ n}{n!}\int _ X\Omega _ L^ n+o(k^ n). \end{equation} If its curvature is positive definite at one point, the coefficient is positive, so $h^0(X,L^ k)\geq c k^ n$ for one $c>0$ and all sufficiently large integers $k$. The base is not assumed Kähler. Proof. Take $F$ trivial. Semipositivity makes $I_ q=0$ for $q\geq 1$ and $I_0=\int _ X\Omega _ L^ n/n!$. The weak degree-zero inequality gives the upper bound. The strong inequality for $q=1$ gives $\liminf k^{-n}h_ k^0\geq I_0$, since $h_ k^1\geq 0$. For $n=1$ the same inequality is the Euler equality, so it applies also in that endpoint. Thus the limit is $I_0$. Strict positivity at one point persists on a nonempty open set and its top form has positive density there; the integral is positive. Taking any $0<c<I_0$ proves the stated eventual lower bound. $\square$

title: 10.91 One-point positivity and modification descent
text: Proposition 10.91.1 . 35E27213FA56 Let $\mu :Y\to X$ be a modification of compact complex manifolds of the same dimension $n$, and let $F$ be a holomorphic vector bundle on $X$. For every $0\leq p,q\leq n$, smooth pullback induces an injection \[  \mu ^*:H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,F) \longrightarrow H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial }(Y,\mu ^*F).  \] It has a left inverse obtained by proper pushforward of bundle-valued currents and the canonical smooth/current Dolbeault comparison. Proof. An $F$-valued current of type $(p,q)$ pairs with compactly supported smooth $F^*$-valued forms of type $(n-p,n-q)$ by contraction of the coefficient bundles and exterior multiplication. For a $\mu ^*F$-valued current $T$ on $Y$, define \[  (\mu _*T)(\eta )=T(\mu ^*\eta ).  \] Properness gives compact support of the pulled-back test. In local holomorphic frames of $F$ this is scalar current pushforward in each coefficient. On overlaps the transition matrices pull back by $\mu $, so the scalar projection formula shows that the definitions agree. Those matrices are holomorphic; thus the coefficientwise operators $\bar\partial _ F$ agree and \[  \bar\partial _ F\mu _*T=\mu _*\bar\partial _{\mu ^*F}T.  \] There is no relative-dimension sign, since the real relative dimension is zero. Smooth pullback also commutes with these operators, by the chain rule in those same frames. For any smooth $F$-valued form $a$, one has $\mu _*\mu ^*a=a$ as bundle-valued currents. Indeed testing gives \[  \int _ Y\mu ^*(a\wedge \eta )=\int _ X a\wedge \eta .  \] The contraction $a\wedge \eta $ is an ordinary scalar top form. The scalar modification identity and change-of-variables proof in theorem 10.87.1 apply exactly to it: proper analytic exceptional subsets have zero smooth volume, and the map is biholomorphic on their complements. title: 9.66 Section growth and Kähler modifications
text: Lemma 9.66.1 . ABF5E7654F82 Let $X$ be a compact connected complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$ and $L$ a holomorphic line bundle. Put $V_ k=H^0(X,L^ k)$. If \[  \limsup _{k\to \infty } k^{-n}\dim V_ k>0,  \] then for some $k\geq 1$ the meromorphic map to $\mathbb P(V_ k^*)$ defined by the complete linear system has complex differential rank $n$ at some point outside its base set. In particular $X$ has $n$ algebraically independent meromorphic functions, given by ratios of sections of this one tensor power. Proof. Choose finitely many coordinate balls $B_ j$ of radius $R_ j$, with holomorphic frames of $L$ near their closures, so their concentric balls $B'_ j$ of radius $R_ j/4$ cover $X$. Fix a smooth Hermitian metric on $L$ and write it as $e^{-\phi _ j}$ in those frames. Let $A\geq 0$ bound half the oscillation of every $\phi _ j$ on $B_ j$. If $s\in V_ k$ vanishes to order at least $p$ at $x_ j\in B'_ j$, the scalar representative $f_ j$ satisfies \[  \sup _{B'_ j}|s| \leq e^{Ak}(2/3)^ p\sup _ X|s|.  \] Indeed $B'_ j\subset B(x_ j,R_ j/2)$ and $B(x_ j,3R_ j/4)\subset B_ j$. A holomorphic function vanishing to order $p$ at the center of a ball satisfies the radius-ratio Schwarz bound: restrict to each complex line through that center and apply the maximum principle to $f(\zeta )/\zeta ^ p$. The metric weights introduce at most the displayed factor $e^{Ak}$. Choose an integer $p=p_ k\leq C(k+1)$ such that $e^{Ak}(2/3)^ p<1$. Consequently a section vanishing to order $p$ at one chosen point in every $B'_ j$ is zero: take the maximum of these inequalities over the finite covering. Taking all ambient coordinate derivatives of order less than $p$ at any fixed choices of the points $x_ j$ gives an injective linear map from $V_ k$ into a finite-dimensional jet space, by the same Schwarz argument. Thus $V_ k$ is finite-dimensional, without any cohomology or elliptic input. For a nonzero $V_ k$, choose a basis and let $Z_ k$ be its common zero set. This is a proper analytic subset; off it the section coordinates define a holomorphic map $\Phi _ k$. Let $d_ k\leq n$ be its maximum differential rank. The locus of this rank is open and dense: the lower-rank locus is defined by homogeneous Jacobian minors of the section coordinates, and a nonzero maximal minor cannot vanish on an open set of connected $X$. The same holds for $X\setminus Z_ k$, since a nonzero section cannot vanish on an open set. Thus for each $j$ choose $x_ j\in B'_ j\setminus Z_ k$ at which the rank is $d_ k$. Choose $s_0\in V_ k$ nonzero at all these finitely many points; the forbidden sections form a finite union of proper linear hyperplanes, which cannot cover a complex vector space. Near $x_ j$ all ratios $s/s_0$ are holomorphic and factor through $\Phi _ k$. The holomorphic constant-rank theorem the holomorphic constant rank theorem gives coordinates $(w',w'')$ there with $w'$ of dimension $d_ k$, in which all these ratios depend only on $w'$. Hence their $w'$ derivatives of total order less than $p$ at $x_ j$ determine whether $s$ vanishes to order at least $p$. This equivalence is invariant under invertible holomorphic coordinate changes and multiplication by the nonzero local section $s_0$. The resulting linear jet map on $V_ k$ is injective by the preceding Schwarz bound. If there are $N$ balls, it follows that \[  \dim V_ k\leq N\binom {p+d_ k-1}{d_ k}.  \] The bound holds also when $d_ k=0$, with the binomial equal to one; zero spaces require no argument. If every $d_ k\leq n-1$, its right side is $O((k+1)^{n-1})$, with a constant independent of $k$ and of the varying transverse coordinates. This contradicts the assumed limsup. Thus some $d_ k=n$. At that point choose $n$ section ratios with independent differentials. Their local holomorphic map has open image by the inverse function theorem. A polynomial relation among them would vanish on that open image and hence be the zero polynomial. The ratios are meromorphic on all of $X$ by their local frame quotients, proving algebraic independence. $\square$ Theorem 9.66.2 . DC74B9CCEB47 Let $X$ be a compact connected complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$. Suppose a holomorphic line bundle $L$ has a smooth Hermitian metric with semipositive curvature everywhere and positive definite curvature at one point. Then $X$ admits a modification from a compact connected Kähler manifold. This conclusion uses the explicitly declared external geometric existence input theorem 9.65.8 . Proof. Choose any smooth Hermitian metric on $X$. The fully proved analytic corollary 19.10.1 gives \[  \lim _{k\to \infty }k^{-n}h^0(X,L^ k) =\frac1{n!}\int _ X \left(\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\Theta _ L\right)^ n>0.  \] The top form is nonnegative everywhere and strictly positive on a nonempty open neighborhood of the specified point, so its integral is positive. The preceding section-growth lemma therefore supplies a complete linear system with maximum differential rank $n$. Apply theorem 9.65.9 . Its proof constructs a bimeromorphic projective model, a compact Kähler resolution and, using exactly the declared external elimination input, an actual holomorphic modification to $X$. This gives the asserted map. No Kähler assumption on $X$ is used. $\square$

text: Corollary 10.92.1 . B3500F172230 The conclusions of theorem 10.91.2 hold on every compact connected complex manifold $X$, under its stated curvature hypotheses, without assuming a Kähler modification in advance. In particular, an everywhere $m$-semipositive rank-$r$ bundle $F$ that is strictly $m$-positive at one point satisfies \[  H^{n,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,F)=0 \quad \left(1\leq q\leq n,\quad m\geq \min (n-q+1,r)\right).  \] An everywhere $m$-seminegative $F$, strictly $m$-negative at one point, satisfies \[  H^{p,0}_{\bar\partial }(X,F)=0 \quad \left(0\leq p<n,\quad m\geq \min (p+1,r)\right).  \] A seminegative line bundle, strictly negative at one point, also satisfies $H^{0,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,L)=0$ for $0\leq q<n$. These are statements on arbitrary compact complex $X$; Kählerness of $X$ is not a hypothesis. Proof. In each nonzero-rank case the given positivity of $E$ makes $\det E$ semipositive everywhere and positive at the strict point, by the preceding trace calculation. The line criterion supplies a compact Kähler modification. All conclusions now follow from corollary 10.91.3 . Its pointwise determinant and subbundle calculations preserve semipositivity at critical points of that modification; strictness survives at a point of the biholomorphic locus. The Dolbeault injection descends the vanishing. The zero subbundle has no sections or cohomology. $\square$

title: 10.93.2 Vector bundles and holomorphic jets
text: Proposition 10.93.1 . 24324B70E319 Let $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $X$ be a topological space, and let $\mathcal A$ be a subsheaf of the sheaf of continuous $\mathbb K$-valued functions containing the locally constant functions. Locally free $\mathcal A$-modules of rank $r$ correspond to topological vector bundles with an $\mathcal A$-atlas, meaning trivializations whose transition matrices and their inverses have entries in $\mathcal A$. The correspondence identifies the module with the sections whose coefficient functions belong to $\mathcal A$, and identifies module morphisms with bundle morphisms having such coefficient matrices. No locality assumption on the rings $\mathcal A_ x$ is necessary. Proof. Evaluation $\mathcal A_ x\to \mathbb K$ is onto, since constants are present; denote its maximal kernel by $\mathfrak m_ x$. For a locally free module $\mathcal M$ put $E_ x=\mathcal M_ x/\mathfrak m_ x\mathcal M_ x$ and $E=\coprod _ xE_ x$. A local module basis identifies these fibers with $\mathbb K^ r$. Between two bases the coefficient columns obey $v_ i=g_{ij}v_ j$, where $g_{ij}$ and $g_{ji}$ are matrices of $\mathcal A$-sections and $g_{ij}g_{jk}=g_{ik}$. Their evaluated matrices are continuous and invertible. Give $E$ the topology of the glued charts $U_ i\times \mathbb K^ r$ with these identifications. Every product chart is open and homeomorphic to its corresponding part of $E$, so this is a topological vector bundle. If $X$ is Hausdorff, so is $E$: different base points are separated on $X$, and points in a common fiber are separated in one product chart. Local module sections give exactly the coefficient functions just specified. This description is injective, since a section with all fiber values zero has all its local coefficient functions zero. It is surjective by the sheaf gluing axiom. Conversely an $\mathcal A$-atlas glues copies of $\mathcal A^ r$ with the same matrices, giving a locally free module and recovering the original bundle and atlas. A module morphism is locally multiplication by the matrix of the images of its basis sections. These matrices obey the bundle transition rules, and conversely such matrices give a module morphism. This proves both constructions are inverse on objects and morphisms. With continuous, $C^ k$ or holomorphic coefficient sheaves the same charts give respectively continuous, $C^ k$ or holomorphic bundles and morphisms; in the latter two cases their coordinate changes have exactly that regularity. Taking smooth or holomorphic coefficient sheaves gives the corresponding smooth or holomorphic equivalence as a special case. $\square$ Proposition 10.93.3 . 79E5312B02F1 Let $E$ be a holomorphic bundle of rank $r$ on a complex manifold $X$ of dimension $n$. For every integer $k\geq 0$, the vector spaces \[  (J^ kE)_ x=\mathcal O(E)_ x/ \mathfrak m_ x^{k+1}\mathcal O(E)_ x  \] form a holomorphic vector bundle of rank $r\binom {n+k}{n}$. The map $s\mapsto j^ ks$ sends holomorphic local sections to holomorphic sections of this bundle and is $\mathbb C$-linear. For $k\geq 1$, the forgetful maps $J^ kE\to J^{k-1}E$ are surjective holomorphic bundle maps; $J^0E=E$. Proof. Choose holomorphic coordinates $z$ and a frame $e_1,\ldots ,e_ r$. At $x$ each class has a unique representative of the form \[  \sum _{\lambda =1}^ r\sum _{|\alpha |\leq k} c_{\lambda ,\alpha }(z-z(x))^\alpha e_\lambda (z).  \] Existence and uniqueness follow from the convergent Taylor series: the ideal $\mathfrak m_ x^{k+1}$ consists exactly of series whose terms of total degree at most $k$ vanish. For the nontrivial inclusion, assign each higher-degree monomial to a degree-$(k+1)$ monomial dividing it, using any fixed rule. The finitely many remaining coefficient subseries are convergent on a smaller polydisc by absolute convergence. They express the series as a sum of those degree-$(k+1)$ monomials times convergent germs. Use the displayed coefficients as fiber coordinates. On changing coordinates and frame, substitute the inverse coordinate map and the frame-change matrix and retain Taylor terms through $k$. The new coefficients are linear combinations of the old ones, with coefficients holomorphic in $x$: they involve only finitely many derivatives through order $k$ of those holomorphic maps at $x$. Reversing the change gives its inverse, and composing changes gives the cocycle identity because all represent the same germ modulo $\mathfrak m_ x^{k+1}$. Hence these are invertible holomorphic bundle transitions. The number of multi-indices of length at most $k$ is $\binom {n+k}{n}$: adjoining $\alpha _0=k-|\alpha |$ identifies them with the nonnegative $(n+1)$-tuples of sum $k$, counted by $k$ stars and $n$ separators. This proves the rank formula, including $n=0$ and rank zero. The coefficients of $j^ ks$ are the holomorphic derivatives of the coefficient functions of $s$, divided by $\alpha !$, proving the asserted holomorphicity and linearity. Dropping the terms of degree $k$ commutes with all changes and is onto on each fiber, proving the last assertion. For $k\geq 1$ no $\mathcal O_ X$-linearity of $j^ k$ is asserted. $\square$ Definition 10.93.4 . 1AEDB3FDC003 For a positive-rank holomorphic vector bundle $E$ on a complex manifold, global generation means that every evaluation $H^0(X,E)\to E_ x$ is onto. Very ampleness in the sense of first jets and pairs means that every map $H^0(X,E)\to (J^1E)_ x$ and every distinct-pair evaluation $H^0(X,E)\to E_ x\oplus E_ y$, $x\ne y$, is onto. The symmetric-power convention for semiampleness is that $\operatorname {Sym}^ kE$ is globally generated for every integer $k\geq k_0$, for some $k_0\geq 1$. In the same convention ampleness means that $\operatorname {Sym}^ kE$ is very ample for every $k\geq k_0$. These are the precise eventual quantifiers used here; they are not replaced by a condition on just one symmetric power. For a line bundle $\operatorname {Sym}^ kE=E^{\otimes k}$. These are generation conditions. No equivalence with a convention defined through a tautological line bundle or an embedding on an arbitrary noncompact base is part of this definition.

title: 9.67 Meromorphic maps and analytic graphs
text: Proposition 9.67.3 . 33B246500570 Let $F:U\to Y$ be an analytic morphism of complex analytic spaces, possibly nonreduced. Its graph is a closed analytic subspace of $U\times Y$, isomorphic to $U$ by the first projection. It retains the full comorphism of $F$ and may be nonreduced. Proof. Use the nonreduced analytic products of proposition 9.43.1 . In local ambient coordinates $z,w$, let $J(z)$ define $U$ and choose holomorphic lifts $w=\Phi (z)$ of the map into a target model defined by $K(w)$. The morphism condition says $K(\Phi (z))\subset J(z)$. The graph is defined by $J(z)$ together with $w-\Phi (z)$. Substitution identifies its quotient ring with $\mathcal O_ z/J$, retaining every nilpotent. Indeed subtracting the substituted function from a convergent $H(z,w)$ expresses the difference as $\sum _ j(w_ j-\Phi _ j(z))H_ j(z,w)$, by successive one-variable Taylor division. The target equations already vanish in this quotient. Different lifts and coordinates give the same graph because its first projection is the inverse of $(\mathrm{id},F)$. These local ideals thus glue. The support is closed in $U\times Y$ since the target is Hausdorff and $F$ is continuous; off the graph one uses the unit ideal. This proves the assertion. $\square$ Definition 9.67.4 . 97D17B3FB015 Let $X,Y$ be complex analytic spaces, with nilpotents allowed. A meromorphic-map representative $F:X\dashrightarrow Y$ consists of an analytic morphism $F:X\setminus A\to Y$, including its comorphism, where $A$ is a closed nowhere dense analytic subset of the reduced space $X_{\mathrm{red}}$, such that the ordinary closure of the support of its graph in $X\times Y$ is analytic in $(X\times Y)_{\mathrm{red}}$. This is a condition on the reduced closure, not a claim of existence of a canonical full nonreduced graph closure over $A$. No properness of its projection to $X$ is imposed by this definition. Representatives may be identified after a common such restriction, requiring equality as analytic morphisms, including the comorphism. Shrinking the domain by another closed nowhere dense analytic subset does not change that reduced graph closure: the smaller domain is dense in the old one, and its graph is dense in the old graph by continuity. The full map cannot be replaced by its point map. On the nonreduced point with ring $\mathbb C[\epsilon ]/ (\epsilon ^2)$, the endomorphisms $\epsilon \mapsto 0$ and $\epsilon \mapsto \epsilon $ have the same point map and the same reduced graph closure, but different graph ideals $(\eta )$ and $(\eta -\epsilon )$ in $\mathbb C[\epsilon ,\eta ]/(\epsilon ^2,\eta ^2)$. There is no smaller dense open subset of a point on which these full morphisms agree.

title: 2.19 Concrete completed tensor products
text: All locally convex spaces are Hausdorff and complex. Completed projective and injective tensors use the exact seminorm conventions of section 2.13 . The compact spaces in the continuous-function assertion need not be Hausdorff. Proposition 2.19.1 . 84C71E271314 For arbitrary discrete index sets $I,J$, coefficient multiplication induces an isometric isomorphism \[  \ell ^1(I)\widehat\otimes _\pi \ell ^1(J) \simeq \ell ^1(I\times J),\qquad x\otimes y\longmapsto (x_ i y_ j)_{i,j}.  \] Empty index sets give the zero space. Proof. For $t=\sum _ r x_ r\otimes y_ r$, its coefficient matrix $a$ satisfies \[  \| a\| _{\ell ^1(I\times J)}\leq \sum _ r\| x_ r\| _1\| y_ r\| _1.  \] Conversely the coordinate-basis decomposition of a finite matrix has projective cost $\sum _{i,j}|a_{ij}|$. Every algebraic tensor is approximated in projective norm by tensors with finite coefficient matrices: truncate each of its finitely many $\ell ^1$ vectors. Thus the two norms agree on the algebraic tensor product. Its completion maps isometrically onto a closed subspace containing every finite matrix; these are dense in $\ell ^1(I\times J)$, proving surjectivity. An $\ell ^1$ family has countable support, since each set where its modulus is at least $1/m$ is finite. Hence these truncations and sums are valid also for uncountable index sets. $\square$ Proposition 2.19.2 . 96A052277244 For Banach spaces $E,F$, the unit ball of $E\widehat\otimes _\varepsilon F$ is the polar, under the canonical pairing, of the unit ball of $E'\widehat\otimes _\pi F'$. This is a statement about polar sets, not an identification of the whole continuous dual with a projective tensor product. For arbitrary discrete $I,J$ there is an isometric isomorphism \[  c_0(I)\widehat\otimes _\varepsilon c_0(J) \simeq c_0(I\times J).  \] Here a family belongs to $c_0(I)$ if only finitely many entries have modulus at least $\eta $, for every $\eta >0$. Proof. For algebraic tensors the injective norm is exactly the supremum of $|(\xi \otimes \eta )(t)|$ over unit $\xi \in E'$, $\eta \in F'$. Its pairing with $E'\otimes _\pi F'$ is therefore bounded by the product of these two norms and extends to the completions. The closed projective unit ball is the closed convex hull of simple unit tensors: the projective infimum gives finite decompositions of cost at most $1+\epsilon $, and completion and rescaling give the closed-ball assertion. Conversely simple unit tensors already test the injective norm. The same supremum formula persists in the completion, by uniform convergence of their bounded test functions. These observations prove the polar assertion. For clarity, $c_0(I)'=\ell ^1(I)$ with its exact norm. If $L$ is a bounded functional, put $a_ i=L(e_ i)$. Testing on finitely many coordinates with suitable phases gives $\sum _{i\in A}|a_ i|\leq \| L\| $ for every finite $A$. Thus $a\in \ell ^1(I)$ and finite-coordinate approximation gives $L(x)=\sum _ i a_ i x_ i$; its norm is $\sum _ i|a_ i|$ by the same finite phase tests. For the coefficient matrix of an algebraic tensor in $c_0(I)\otimes c_0(J)$ this dual description gives \[  \| t\| _\varepsilon =\sup _{i,j}|a_{ij}|.  \] The upper bound follows by summing two unit $\ell ^1$ families, and the reverse bound by coordinate evaluations. A product matrix $x_ i y_ j$ vanishes at infinity: outside finite coordinate sets one factor is arbitrarily small and the other is bounded. The same holds for finite sums. Finite matrices are dense in $c_0(I\times J)$, so the isometric map of completions is onto, including empty sets. $\square$ Proposition 2.19.3 . C9CDFE118A86 For arbitrary compact spaces $K,L$, multiplication of separated functions gives an isometric isomorphism \[  C(K)\widehat\otimes _\varepsilon C(L)\simeq C(K\times L).  \] Proof. Let $a(x,y)=\sum _ r f_ r(x)g_ r(y)$. For unit $\xi \in C(K)'$ the function $h_\xi (y)=\xi (\sum _ r f_ r g_ r(y))$ has sup norm at most $\| a\| _\infty $. A second unit functional on $C(L)$ therefore gives $\| t\| _\varepsilon \leq \| a\| _\infty $; two Dirac evaluations give the reverse inequality. No measure-representation theorem for these duals is required. We prove density directly, retaining the full compact-space scope. Given $a\in C(K\times L)$, the map $x\mapsto a_ x=a(x,\cdot )$ is continuous from $K$ into the Banach space $C(L)$: each $x\in K$ has a neighborhood $U_ x$ with \[  \sup _{y\in L}|a(x',y)-a(x,y)|<\epsilon \qquad (x'\in U_ x).  \] Indeed continuity gives product neighborhoods at each $(x,y)$, and a finite subcover of the $y$-factor gives one common $U_ x$. The image $Q=\{ a_ x:x\in K\} $ is therefore compact in $C(L)$. Choose finitely many $a_{x_ i}$ whose open $\epsilon $-balls cover $Q$ and put \[  b_ i(x)=\max \{ \epsilon -\| a_ x-a_{x_ i}\| _\infty ,0\} ,\qquad \theta _ i(x)=\frac{b_ i(x)}{\sum _ j b_ j(x)}.  \] These are continuous, their sum is one, and $\theta _ i(x)>0$ implies $\| a_ x-a_{x_ i}\| _\infty <\epsilon $. The tensor $\sum _ i\theta _ i\otimes a_{x_ i}$ therefore approximates $a$ uniformly within $\epsilon $. The algebraic tensor image is dense. Completing its already proved norm equality gives the asserted isomorphism. Empty compact spaces again give zero. $\square$

title: 9.68 Relative nuclear maps and composition
text: Let $A$ be a unital commutative Fréchet algebra. Modules are Fréchet with jointly continuous action. Use the existing relative definitions: an $A$-nuclear map has a summable scalar series with equicontinuous $A$-linear coefficient maps into $A$ and bounded target vectors. A map $f:E\to F$ is $A$-subnuclear if there is a continuous open surjective module map $p:M\to E$ such that $fp$ is $A$-nuclear. When $E$ is nuclear, the covering module $M$ is required to be nuclear. These are the definitions preceding proposition 9.46.1 ; that earlier proposition proves the ideal property within nuclear modules. Proposition 9.68.1 . DB4C2E622157 $A$-nuclear maps are preserved by arbitrary continuous module precomposition and postcomposition. $A$-subnuclear maps are always preserved by postcomposition. For $f:E\to F$ subnuclear and $u:S\to E$, precomposition is valid if $S$ is not nuclear, or if $f$ has a witnessing nuclear covering module. In particular it is valid whenever $E$ is nuclear, and throughout the nuclear-module category. No nuclearity of $A$ is needed for these assertions. Proof. In a nuclear series, precomposition preserves equicontinuity of the coefficient family and postcomposition preserves boundedness of the vector family. This proves the first assertion directly. For subnuclear postcomposition keep the identical witness $p$; its domain requirement depends on $E$, which has not changed. For precomposition form the closed module \[  P=\{ (s,m)\in S\times M:u(s)=p(m)\} .  \] It is Fréchet, and $q:P\to S$ is onto and open. Explicitly, the image of $(U\times V)\cap P$, for open zero neighborhoods $U,V$, is $U\cap u^{-1}(p(V))$, which is open since $p$ is open; translations give the full assertion. Moreover $(fu)q=(fp)\operatorname {pr}_ M$ is $A$-nuclear by the first assertion. If $S$ is not nuclear, this is all the definition asks. If $S$ and $M$ are nuclear, their product and its closed subspace $P$ are nuclear by theorem 2.13.3 . This supplies the additional covering requirement. When $E$ is nuclear, the original witness already requires $M$ nuclear. These are actual closed products and open quotients; no nuclearity is assigned to an arbitrary Fréchet pullback. $\square$ Example 9.68.2 . FECBDA82D7CC The preceding precomposition statement cannot be extended to arbitrary Fréchet modules with the same definition. There is a commutative unital Banach algebra $A$, an $A$-subnuclear map $f:E\to \mathbb C$ and a continuous module map $u:\mathbb C\to E$ for which $fu=\operatorname {Id}_{\mathbb C}$ is not $A$-subnuclear. The scalar module is nuclear, while $E$ is not nuclear. Proof. Let $B=\ell ^2(\mathbb N)$ and give \[  A=\mathbb C\oplus B,\qquad (c,b)(d,e)=(cd,ce+db),\qquad \| (c,b)\| =|c|+\| b\| _2  \] its square-zero Banach algebra structure. The norm is submultiplicative, and $(1,0)$ is its unit. Let $q(c,b)=c$ and make $\mathbb C$ an $A$-module through this character. This scalar space is nuclear: its identity is the one-term finite-dimensional nuclear series. We recall explicitly why $B$ is not nuclear. For a Banach space with a nuclear Fréchet defining family, its Banach norm is bounded by one defining seminorm, and every defining seminorm is bounded by the norm. Sufficiently late seminorms are therefore equivalent to the norm. A nuclear link between two of their Banach completions would make its identity a nuclear Banach operator. Such an operator is compact by lemma 2.13.1 ; the orthonormal unit vectors in $\ell ^2$ have mutual distance $\sqrt2$, a contradiction. Closed subspaces and finite products of nuclear Fréchet spaces are nuclear by the fully proved theorem 2.13.3 . Thus $A$, and $E=A\oplus \mathbb C$, are not nuclear: each contains the closed subspace $B$. The module surjection \[  p:A^2\longrightarrow E,\qquad p(a,b)=(a,q(b))  \] is continuous and open. It has the continuous linear right inverse $(a,c)\mapsto (a,(c,0))$, which suffices for openness and need not be $A$-linear. Define $f(a,c)=c$. Its composite $fp(a,b)=q(b)=b\cdot 1$ is a one-term $A$-nuclear series with coefficient map $(a,b)\mapsto b$ and vector $1\in \mathbb C$. Since $E$ is not nuclear, the definition permits the nonnuclear cover $A^2$. Hence $f$ is $A$-subnuclear. For every nuclear Fréchet $A$-module $N$ and continuous $A$-linear $\xi :N\to A$ one has $q\xi =0$. Otherwise choose $v\in N$ with $q\xi (v)=c\ne 0$, and consider the continuous map \[  L:B\to N,\qquad L(b)=(0,b)v.  \] $A$-linearity gives $\xi L(b)=(0,cb)$. Therefore $R=c^{-1}\operatorname {pr}_ B\xi :N\to B$ is a continuous left inverse to $L$. In particular $L(B)$ is topologically isomorphic to $B$ and is closed: $LR$ is a continuous projection and its range is $\ker (\operatorname {Id}-LR)$. This contradicts the closed-subspace nuclear permanence just recalled. Thus $q\xi =0$. It follows that every $A$-nuclear map from such an $N$ to the character module $\mathbb C$ is zero, term by term in its defining series. If its identity were subnuclear, its nuclear source $\mathbb C$ would require a nuclear cover $N\to \mathbb C$; that cover itself would then be $A$-nuclear, an impossible nonzero surjection. Finally $u(c)=(0,c)\in E$ is a continuous $A$-linear inclusion and $fu=\operatorname {Id}_{\mathbb C}$. All stated maps and actions lie in the literal Fréchet category. $\square$

title: Proposition 9.68.1
text: Proposition 9.68.1 . DB4C2E622157 $A$-nuclear maps are preserved by arbitrary continuous module precomposition and postcomposition. $A$-subnuclear maps are always preserved by postcomposition. For $f:E\to F$ subnuclear and $u:S\to E$, precomposition is valid if $S$ is not nuclear, or if $f$ has a witnessing nuclear covering module. In particular it is valid whenever $E$ is nuclear, and throughout the nuclear-module category. No nuclearity of $A$ is needed for these assertions. Proof. In a nuclear series, precomposition preserves equicontinuity of the coefficient family and postcomposition preserves boundedness of the vector family. This proves the first assertion directly. For subnuclear postcomposition keep the identical witness $p$; its domain requirement depends on $E$, which has not changed. For precomposition form the closed module \[  P=\{ (s,m)\in S\times M:u(s)=p(m)\} .  \] It is Fréchet, and $q:P\to S$ is onto and open. Explicitly, the image of $(U\times V)\cap P$, for open zero neighborhoods $U,V$, is $U\cap u^{-1}(p(V))$, which is open since $p$ is open; translations give the full assertion. Moreover $(fu)q=(fp)\operatorname {pr}_ M$ is $A$-nuclear by the first assertion. If $S$ is not nuclear, this is all the definition asks. If $S$ and $M$ are nuclear, their product and its closed subspace $P$ are nuclear by theorem 2.13.3 . This supplies the additional covering requirement. When $E$ is nuclear, the original witness already requires $M$ nuclear. These are actual closed products and open quotients; no nuclearity is assigned to an arbitrary Fréchet pullback. $\square$

title: Example 9.68.2
text: Example 9.68.2 . FECBDA82D7CC The preceding precomposition statement cannot be extended to arbitrary Fréchet modules with the same definition. There is a commutative unital Banach algebra $A$, an $A$-subnuclear map $f:E\to \mathbb C$ and a continuous module map $u:\mathbb C\to E$ for which $fu=\operatorname {Id}_{\mathbb C}$ is not $A$-subnuclear. The scalar module is nuclear, while $E$ is not nuclear. Proof. Let $B=\ell ^2(\mathbb N)$ and give \[  A=\mathbb C\oplus B,\qquad (c,b)(d,e)=(cd,ce+db),\qquad \| (c,b)\| =|c|+\| b\| _2  \] its square-zero Banach algebra structure. The norm is submultiplicative, and $(1,0)$ is its unit. Let $q(c,b)=c$ and make $\mathbb C$ an $A$-module through this character. This scalar space is nuclear: its identity is the one-term finite-dimensional nuclear series. We recall explicitly why $B$ is not nuclear. For a Banach space with a nuclear Fréchet defining family, its Banach norm is bounded by one defining seminorm, and every defining seminorm is bounded by the norm. Sufficiently late seminorms are therefore equivalent to the norm. A nuclear link between two of their Banach completions would make its identity a nuclear Banach operator. Such an operator is compact by lemma 2.13.1 ; the orthonormal unit vectors in $\ell ^2$ have mutual distance $\sqrt2$, a contradiction. Closed subspaces and finite products of nuclear Fréchet spaces are nuclear by the fully proved theorem 2.13.3 . Thus $A$, and $E=A\oplus \mathbb C$, are not nuclear: each contains the closed subspace $B$. The module surjection \[  p:A^2\longrightarrow E,\qquad p(a,b)=(a,q(b))  \] is continuous and open. It has the continuous linear right inverse $(a,c)\mapsto (a,(c,0))$, which suffices for openness and need not be $A$-linear. Define $f(a,c)=c$. Its composite $fp(a,b)=q(b)=b\cdot 1$ is a one-term $A$-nuclear series with coefficient map $(a,b)\mapsto b$ and vector $1\in \mathbb C$. Since $E$ is not nuclear, the definition permits the nonnuclear cover $A^2$. Hence $f$ is $A$-subnuclear. For every nuclear Fréchet $A$-module $N$ and continuous $A$-linear $\xi :N\to A$ one has $q\xi =0$. Otherwise choose $v\in N$ with $q\xi (v)=c\ne 0$, and consider the continuous map \[  L:B\to N,\qquad L(b)=(0,b)v.  \] $A$-linearity gives $\xi L(b)=(0,cb)$. Therefore $R=c^{-1}\operatorname {pr}_ B\xi :N\to B$ is a continuous left inverse to $L$. In particular $L(B)$ is topologically isomorphic to $B$ and is closed: $LR$ is a continuous projection and its range is $\ker (\operatorname {Id}-LR)$. This contradicts the closed-subspace nuclear permanence just recalled. Thus $q\xi =0$. It follows that every $A$-nuclear map from such an $N$ to the character module $\mathbb C$ is zero, term by term in its defining series. If its identity were subnuclear, its nuclear source $\mathbb C$ would require a nuclear cover $N\to \mathbb C$; that cover itself would then be $A$-nuclear, an impossible nonzero surjection. Finally $u(c)=(0,c)\in E$ is a continuous $A$-linear inclusion and $fu=\operatorname {Id}_{\mathbb C}$. All stated maps and actions lie in the literal Fréchet category. $\square$

title: 2.20 Elliptic systems and unique continuation
text:
Lemma 2.20.1 (Positive fourth-order modes) . CB1875F07408 Let $z\geq 2$, $0<a<1$, and $\lambda _ z(t)=z^3-z^4t^4\geq 0$ for $0\leq t\leq a$. There is a positive nondecreasing solution $w$ of \[  (\partial _ t-z)^4w=\lambda _ z(t)w  \] with any prescribed positive value at any $s\in [0,a]$. For every integer $m\geq 0$ there are constants $C_ m,A_ m$ independent of $z,a,s$ and that prescribed value such that 9F264158A115 2.20.2 \begin{equation}  |w^{(m)}(t)|\leq C_ m z^{A_ m}w(t)\qquad (0\leq t\leq a). \end{equation} There are absolute constants $c,C>0$ such that, whenever $0\leq T\leq t\leq a$ and $0\leq l\leq \lambda _ z\leq L$ on $[T,t]$, F83983317719 2.20.3 \begin{equation}  c z^{-3}e^{(z+l^{1/4})(t-T)} \leq \frac{w(t)}{w(T)} \leq C z^3e^{(z+L^{1/4})(t-T)}. \end{equation} Proof. Solve $y^{(4)}=\lambda _ z y$ with $y^{(j)}(0)=1$ for $0\leq j\leq 3$. Here existence and the needed comparison principle have an elementary integral proof. The first-order state $Y=(y,y',y'',y''')$ satisfies $Y'=M(t)Y$, where $M$ has three superdiagonal entries equal to one and its bottom-left entry equal to $\lambda _ z(t)$, all other entries being zero. Successive substitution in $Y=Y(0)+\int _0^ t M(v)Y(v)\, dv$ converges uniformly on $[0,a]$: its $j$th iterated-integral term is bounded by $\| Y(0)\| (a\sup \| M\| )^ j/j!$. Differentiating the integral equation gives a smooth solution. The same series on $[T,t]$, including a nonnegative inhomogeneous term, proves componentwise comparison, since every matrix entry is nonnegative. In particular all four state components are at least one and are nondecreasing. For $0\leq j\leq 2$, integration gives $y^{(j)}\leq 1+a y^{(j+1)}\leq 2y^{(j+1)}$. Also $y'''\leq 1+a z^3y\leq 2z^3y$. Thus \[  2^{-j}y\leq y^{(j)}\leq 8z^3y\qquad (0\leq j\leq 3).  \] All derivatives of $\lambda _ z$ are bounded by a fixed power of $z$ on this interval, with constants depending only on their order. Differentiating $y^{(4)}=\lambda _ z y$ and inducting therefore bounds every $|y^{(m)}|$ by $C_ m z^{A_ m}y$. Multiplication by $e^{zt}$, and a positive constant to set $w(s)$, proves the equation, positivity, monotonicity and ( 2.20.2 ). For the upper growth bound compare $y$ on $[T,t]$ with \[  q(v)=8z^3y(T)e^{(L^{1/4}+1)(v-T)}.  \] Its first four state values dominate those of $y$ at $T$, and $q^{(4)}\geq \lambda _ z q$. For the lower bound use \[  p(v)=\frac{y(T)}{8(1+l)}e^{l^{1/4}(v-T)}.  \] Its state at $T$ is dominated by that of $y$, because $l^{j/4}/(1+l)\leq 1$ for $0\leq j\leq 3$; also $p^{(4)}\leq \lambda _ zp$. The componentwise comparison just proved applies to both. Since $t-T<1$ and $l\leq z^3$, their prefactors give the stated bounds after multiplication by $e^{z(t-T)}$. $\square$ Theorem 2.20.4 (A smooth fourth-order weak-continuation counterexample) . 2D8A7E49E474 For some $a\in (0,1)$ there are $f,u\in C^\infty ((-a,a)\times \mathbb R,\mathbb C)$ such that A5DFFD00C673 2.20.5 \begin{equation}  \big ((\partial _ t-i\partial _ x)^4+t^4\partial _ x^4 +i\partial _ x^3\big )u=f u. \end{equation} Both functions vanish for $t\leq 0$, whereas $u$ is not identically zero in any neighborhood of any point $(0,x)$. Proof. The construction uses only the preceding positive modes and two separated cutoff transitions. Write $\mathcal L$ for the operator on the left of ( 2.20.5 ). Set \[  \begin{aligned}  z_ n& =n^{11/4},& a_ n& =n^{-11/16}=z_ n^{-1/4},&  \Delta _ n& =a_ n-a_{n+1},\\  r_ n& =\Delta _ n/10^4,& b_ n& =a_ n-4r_ n,& s_ n& =a_ n-2r_ n. \end{aligned}  \] The functions $\lambda _ n(t)=z_ n^3-z_ n^4t^4$ are nonnegative on $[0,a_ n]$. Define also \[  G_ n=z_ na_ n^{3/4}\Delta _ n^{1/4}.  \] The mean value theorem for powers of $n$ gives D652D0FDF2A4 2.20.6 \begin{equation}  \begin{aligned}  \Delta _ n& \sim \tfrac {11}{16}n^{-27/16},&  G_ n& \sim (\tfrac {11}{16})^{1/4}n^{29/16},\\  r_ nG_ n& \sim 10^{-4}(\tfrac {11}{16})^{5/4}n^{1/8},&  z_ n-z_{n-1}& \sim \tfrac {11}{4}n^{28/16}. \end{aligned} \end{equation} In particular the last difference is $o(G_ n)$. On $[b_ n,a_ n]$, factoring $a_ n^4-t^4$ gives \[  0\leq \lambda _ n(t) \leq 16z_ n^4a_ n^3r_ n=(16/10^4)G_ n^4.  \] Put $l_ n=\lambda _{n-1}(a_ n)$. Since $\lambda _{n-1}$ decreases, it is at least $l_ n$ on this interval, and \[  \frac{l_ n}{G_ n^4} =\frac{z_{n-1}^4(a_{n-1}^4-a_ n^4)}{z_ n^4a_ n^3\Delta _ n}\longrightarrow 4.  \] Here $(a_{n-1}-a_ n)/\Delta _ n\to 1$ and the factored cubic sum, divided by $a_ n^3$, tends to four. Thus for sufficiently large $n$ one has $l_ n^{1/4}\geq G_ n$, whereas the upper fourth root for $\lambda _ n$ is at most $G_ n/5$. Increasing the starting integer if necessary gives the uniform growth-rate gap 55589EE4444A 2.20.7 \begin{equation}  (z_{n-1}+l_ n^{1/4})-(z_ n+G_ n/5)\geq G_ n/2. \end{equation} Fix such an integer $N\geq 2$. Use the preceding lemma to choose $w_ N$ on $[0,a_ N]$ with $w_ N(s_ N)=1$, and successively $w_ n$ on $[0,a_ n]$, $n>N$, with 8296A62C8BD3 2.20.8 \begin{equation}  w_ n(s_ n)=w_{n-1}(s_ n). \end{equation} The arguments $s_ n$ belong to both intervals. All these functions are positive and nondecreasing, and their relative derivatives have polynomial bounds in $n$, independent of their normalization. Their complex modes \[  u_ n(t,x)=w_ n(t)e^{-iz_ nx}  \] satisfy $\mathcal L u_ n=0$: indeed $(\partial _ t-i\partial _ x)$ becomes $(\partial _ t-z_ n)$, $\partial _ x^4$ becomes $z_ n^4$, and $i\partial _ x^3$ becomes $-z_ n^3$. Every mixed derivative of $u_ n$ is bounded in absolute value by $C_ m n^{A_ m}w_ n(t)$, for total order at most $m$. Compare the two modes about their equal value at $s_ n$. For $s_ n\leq t\leq a_ n$, the upper growth bound for $w_ n$ and the lower one for $w_{n-1}$, together with ( 2.20.7 ), give \[  \frac{w_ n(t)}{w_{n-1}(t)} \leq C n^ A e^{-G_ n(t-s_ n)/2}.  \] For $b_ n\leq t\leq s_ n$, apply the same two growth bounds on $[t,s_ n]$ and invert the lower bound. This gives \[  \frac{w_{n-1}(t)}{w_ n(t)} \leq C n^ A e^{-G_ n(s_ n-t)/2}.  \] By ( 2.20.6 ), after increasing $N$ there is $c>0$ such that, for $n>N$, $\epsilon _ n=e^{-c n^{1/8}}<1/2$ and 4B3C0F159C1D 2.20.9 \begin{equation}  \begin{aligned}  |u_ n/u_{n-1}|& \leq \epsilon _ n& &  (a_ n-r_ n\leq t\leq a_ n),\\  |u_{n-1}/u_ n|& \leq \epsilon _ n& &  (b_ n\leq t\leq b_ n+r_ n). \end{aligned} \end{equation} The polynomial prefactor is absorbed because $n^{1/8}/\log n\to \infty $. All comparisons are uniform in $x$. Choose a smooth $\rho :\mathbb R\to [0,1]$ equal to zero for $v\leq 1/4$ and to one for $v\geq 3/4$, with bounded derivatives of each order. For example normalize the integral of $e^{-1/(v(1-v))}$ on $(0,1)$, extend it constantly, and compose with $v\mapsto 2v-1/2$. These constant collars will make the adjacent strip definitions agree on neighborhoods of their endpoints. On $I_ n=[a_{n+1},a_ n]$, $n>N$, put \[  A_ n(t)=\rho ((t-b_ n)/r_ n),\qquad B_ n(t)=1-\rho ((t-a_ n+r_ n)/r_ n),\qquad u=A_ nu_{n-1}+B_ nu_ n.  \] On the lower transition $[b_ n,b_ n+r_ n]$ one has $B_ n=1$ and $|u|\geq (1-\epsilon _ n)|u_ n|$. On the upper transition $[a_ n-r_ n,a_ n]$ one has $A_ n=1$ and $|u|\geq (1-\epsilon _ n)|u_{n-1}|$. Between them both cutoffs are one; outside them in $I_ n$ they are constant as well. Consequently $\mathcal L u=0$ outside the two transition bands, even if the two modes cancel in the middle. Define $f=\mathcal L u/u$ on the bands and $f=0$ elsewhere. The displayed lower bounds give nonvanishing neighborhoods of every band endpoint. There the residual is identically zero on the adjacent constant-cutoff side. Thus this definition is smooth at every endpoint; it never divides by a possible middle zero. For clarity we check all derivatives of this quotient. On the upper band, $\mathcal L u=[\mathcal L,B_ n]u_ n$. Each derivative of this commutator is bounded by $C_ m n^{A_ m}|u_ n|$: it is a finite sum of derivatives of the cutoffs, the polynomial coefficients of $\mathcal L$, and derivatives of $u_ n$. Here $r_ n^{-1}$ is bounded by a power of $n$. On the same band, every derivative of $u$ is bounded by a power of $n$ times $|u_{n-1}|$, and $|u|\geq |u_{n-1}|/2$. Repeated differentiation of $u^{-1}$, using the product rule on $u u^{-1}=1$, therefore bounds its derivatives by a power of $n$ times $|u_{n-1}|^{-1}$. The quotient rule and ( 2.20.9 ) give 8B718C586209 2.20.10 \begin{equation}  \sup _{I_ n\times \mathbb R}|D^\alpha f| \leq C_ m n^{A_ m}\epsilon _ n, \qquad |\alpha |\leq m. \end{equation} On the lower band use $[\mathcal L,A_ n]u_{n-1}$ and the dominant mode $u_ n$ instead. Outside the bands the derivatives of $f$ are zero, completing the proof of this estimate. Near the upper endpoint of $I_ n$ the resulting $u$ is $u_{n-1}$; near its lower endpoint it is $u_ n$. These formulas agree with the neighboring strip, and $f=0$ near every $a_ n$. On $a_{N+1}<t<a_ N$ put $u=u_ N$ and $f=0$. Thus both functions are smooth on $(0,a_ N)\times \mathbb R$ and satisfy the equation there. Finally these functions extend smoothly and flatly by zero to $t\leq 0$. To verify this rather than assuming it, note $s_ n<s_{n-1}$ and ( 2.20.8 ); monotonicity gives $w_ n(s_ n)\leq w_{n-1}(s_{n-1})\leq 1$. Since $a_ n<s_{n-1}$, the upper-band estimate at $a_ n$ also gives \[  w_ n(t)\leq w_ n(a_ n) \leq \epsilon _ n w_{n-1}(a_ n)\leq \epsilon _ n \qquad (0\leq t\leq a_ n).  \] For $n\geq N+2$, both modes used on $I_ n$ therefore have size at most $\epsilon _{n-1}$, after decreasing $c$ if needed. The relative derivative and cutoff estimates imply \[  \sup _{I_ n\times \mathbb R}|D^\alpha u| \leq C_ m n^{A_ m}\epsilon _{n-1},\qquad |\alpha |\leq m.  \] Together with ( 2.20.10 ), these bounds decay faster than any power of $t$, since $t$ on $I_ n$ is comparable to $n^{-11/16}$. Every derivative thus tends uniformly to zero as $t\downarrow 0$. The zero extensions are smooth: induct on derivative order, using the zero boundary values for tangential derivatives and the fundamental theorem of calculus for the transverse derivative. All their derivatives vanish on $t=0$, so the differential equation also holds there and on $t<0$. Take $a=a_ N$. At each $t=a_ n$, $n>N$, the constructed function is $u_{n-1}(a_ n,x)$, which is nonzero for every $x$. As $a_ n\downarrow 0$, this proves the required nontriviality in every neighborhood of each $(0,x)$, and completes the construction. $\square$ Proposition 2.20.11 (An ordinary second-order prolongation) . CE8EC0706B26 Let $\Omega $ be an open subset of $\{ (t,x)\in \mathbb R^2:|t|<1\} $, and let $f\in C^\infty (\Omega ,\mathbb C)$. Put \[  D=\partial _ t-i\partial _ x,\qquad A=D^2+it^2\partial _ x^2,\qquad B=D^2-it^2\partial _ x^2, \qquad P_ f=D^4+t^4\partial _ x^4+i\partial _ x^3-f.  \] There is a smooth second-order elliptic differential operator $\mathcal P_ f$ on the trivial complex bundle $\Omega \times \mathbb C^3$ such that every smooth solution $u$ of $P_ fu=0$ gives a solution \[  U=(u,\partial _ xu,Bu),\qquad \mathcal P_ fU=0.  \] The section $U$ is zero on every open set on which $u$ is zero, and $U$ is nonzero whenever $u$ is nonzero. The realification of $\mathcal P_ f$ is also an ordinary second-order elliptic operator on a trivial real bundle of rank six. Proof. The coefficients $t^2$ commute with $\partial _ x$, and $D(t^2)=2t$, $D^2(t^2)=2$. Applying the product rule to a test function gives the exact differential-operator identity \[  AB=D^4+t^4\partial _ x^4-4it\partial _ x^2D-2i\partial _ x^2.  \] Consequently \[  P_ f=AB+Q\partial _ x-f,\qquad Q=4it\partial _ t\partial _ x+(4t+i)\partial _ x^2+2i\partial _ x.  \] Here the term $4t\partial _ x^3$ comes from $4it\partial _ x^2(-i\partial _ x)$; in particular it has positive sign. Define, for arbitrary smooth triples $(u,w,v)$, \[  \mathcal P_ f \begin{pmatrix} u

\\ w

\\ v

\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}  Bu-v

\\  Bw-\partial _ xv

\\  Av+Qw-fu 

\end{pmatrix}.  \] This is a differential operator of order two in every component. Since $B$ commutes with $\partial _ x$, substitution of $w=\partial _ xu$, $v=Bu$ makes its first two components zero, and the third component is exactly $P_ fu$. This proves the asserted solution map. Derivatives of a function that is identically zero on an open set are identically zero there; the first component also proves the nontriviality assertion. For ellipticity, take the principal-symbol convention that replaces $\partial _ t,\partial _ x$ by real variables $\tau ,\xi $; the alternative convention with $i\tau ,i\xi $ changes the entire second-order matrix by a nonzero scalar and gives the same invertibility test. The principal matrix is \[  \sigma _2(\mathcal P_ f)(t,x;\tau ,\xi )= \begin{pmatrix}  b

& 0

& 0

\\  0

& b

& 0

\\  0

& q

& a 

\end{pmatrix}, \quad \begin{aligned}  a& =(\tau -i\xi )^2+it^2\xi ^2,\\  b& =(\tau -i\xi )^2-it^2\xi ^2,\\  q& =4it\tau \xi +(4t+i)\xi ^2. \end{aligned}  \] Its determinant is $b^2a$. If $\xi =0$ and $(\tau ,\xi )\ne 0$, then $a=b=\tau ^2\ne 0$. If $\xi \ne 0$, the vanishing of either $a$ or $b$ would require, on putting $r=\tau /\xi \in \mathbb R$, \[  r^2-1=0,\qquad -2r\pm t^2=0.  \] The first equation gives $r=1$ or $r=-1$, whereas the second is impossible for $|t|<1$. Thus the symbol is invertible at every nonzero real covector. This proves ordinary ellipticity, without a Douglis–Nirenberg weighting or an unasserted positivity of the symbol. Write complex coefficients and components in real and imaginary parts. The real principal matrix is the realification of the displayed complex matrix. Its determinant is $|b^2a|^2$, so it is invertible as a real matrix at the same covectors. The real and imaginary parts of $U$ give the corresponding real solution and preserve its zero set and nontriviality. $\square$ Corollary 2.20.12 (Failure of unrestricted elliptic-system continuation) . 1ADDDDB90B14 There is a connected smooth real surface carrying a smooth ordinary second-order elliptic operator on a rank-three complex vector bundle with a nonzero smooth kernel section vanishing on a nonempty open set. The same assertion holds for a rank-six real vector bundle. Proof. Take $\Omega =(-a,a)\times \mathbb R$ and the functions from Theorem 2.20.4 , with $a<1$. Apply Proposition 2.20.11 . Its section $U$ solves the homogeneous second-order elliptic system, is nonzero because its first component is $u$, and vanishes on $(-a,0)\times \mathbb R$. The realification has the same properties. $\square$ Remark 2.20.13 (Scalar and matrix principal symbols) . ED67DD231FDF The preceding corollary disproves weak continuation for arbitrary smooth matrix-principal elliptic systems under ordinary symbol invertibility. For harmonic forms the relevant hypothesis is more restrictive: a single real elliptic second-order principal operator acts on every component, with smooth coupled lower-order terms. The weak-continuation theorem 2.16.7 applies to that class. The constructed system instead has distinct principal symbols $a,b$ and the second-order off-diagonal term $q$, so it does not belong to that class.
