title: Theorem 2.20.4 (A smooth fourth-order weak-continuation counterexample)
text: Theorem 2.20.4 (A smooth fourth-order weak-continuation counterexample) . 2D8A7E49E474 For some $a\in (0,1)$ there are $f,u\in C^\infty ((-a,a)\times \mathbb R,\mathbb C)$ such that A5DFFD00C673 2.20.5 \begin{equation}  \big ((\partial _ t-i\partial _ x)^4+t^4\partial _ x^4 +i\partial _ x^3\big )u=f u. \end{equation} Both functions vanish for $t\leq 0$, whereas $u$ is not identically zero in any neighborhood of any point $(0,x)$. Proof. The construction uses only the preceding positive modes and two separated cutoff transitions. Write $\mathcal L$ for the operator on the left of ( 2.20.5 ). Set \[  \begin{aligned}  z_ n& =n^{11/4},& a_ n& =n^{-11/16}=z_ n^{-1/4},&  \Delta _ n& =a_ n-a_{n+1},\\  r_ n& =\Delta _ n/10^4,& b_ n& =a_ n-4r_ n,& s_ n& =a_ n-2r_ n. \end{aligned}  \] The functions $\lambda _ n(t)=z_ n^3-z_ n^4t^4$ are nonnegative on $[0,a_ n]$. Define also \[  G_ n=z_ na_ n^{3/4}\Delta _ n^{1/4}.  \] The mean value theorem for powers of $n$ gives D652D0FDF2A4 2.20.6 \begin{equation}  \begin{aligned}  \Delta _ n& \sim \tfrac {11}{16}n^{-27/16},&  G_ n& \sim (\tfrac {11}{16})^{1/4}n^{29/16},\\  r_ nG_ n& \sim 10^{-4}(\tfrac {11}{16})^{5/4}n^{1/8},&  z_ n-z_{n-1}& \sim \tfrac {11}{4}n^{28/16}. \end{aligned} \end{equation} In particular the last difference is $o(G_ n)$. On $[b_ n,a_ n]$, factoring $a_ n^4-t^4$ gives \[  0\leq \lambda _ n(t) \leq 16z_ n^4a_ n^3r_ n=(16/10^4)G_ n^4.  \] Put $l_ n=\lambda _{n-1}(a_ n)$. Since $\lambda _{n-1}$ decreases, it is at least $l_ n$ on this interval, and \[  \frac{l_ n}{G_ n^4} =\frac{z_{n-1}^4(a_{n-1}^4-a_ n^4)}{z_ n^4a_ n^3\Delta _ n}\longrightarrow 4.  \] Here $(a_{n-1}-a_ n)/\Delta _ n\to 1$ and the factored cubic sum, divided by $a_ n^3$, tends to four. Thus for sufficiently large $n$ one has $l_ n^{1/4}\geq G_ n$, whereas the upper fourth root for $\lambda _ n$ is at most $G_ n/5$. Increasing the starting integer if necessary gives the uniform growth-rate gap 55589EE4444A 2.20.7 \begin{equation}  (z_{n-1}+l_ n^{1/4})-(z_ n+G_ n/5)\geq G_ n/2. \end{equation} Fix such an integer $N\geq 2$. Use the preceding lemma to choose $w_ N$ on $[0,a_ N]$ with $w_ N(s_ N)=1$, and successively $w_ n$ on $[0,a_ n]$, $n>N$, with 8296A62C8BD3 2.20.8 \begin{equation}  w_ n(s_ n)=w_{n-1}(s_ n). \end{equation} The arguments $s_ n$ belong to both intervals. All these functions are positive and nondecreasing, and their relative derivatives have polynomial bounds in $n$, independent of their normalization. Their complex modes \[  u_ n(t,x)=w_ n(t)e^{-iz_ nx}  \] satisfy $\mathcal L u_ n=0$: indeed $(\partial _ t-i\partial _ x)$ becomes $(\partial _ t-z_ n)$, $\partial _ x^4$ becomes $z_ n^4$, and $i\partial _ x^3$ becomes $-z_ n^3$. Every mixed derivative of $u_ n$ is bounded in absolute value by $C_ m n^{A_ m}w_ n(t)$, for total order at most $m$. Compare the two modes about their equal value at $s_ n$. For $s_ n\leq t\leq a_ n$, the upper growth bound for $w_ n$ and the lower one for $w_{n-1}$, together with ( 2.20.7 ), give \[  \frac{w_ n(t)}{w_{n-1}(t)} \leq C n^ A e^{-G_ n(t-s_ n)/2}.  \] For $b_ n\leq t\leq s_ n$, apply the same two growth bounds on $[t,s_ n]$ and invert the lower bound. This gives \[  \frac{w_{n-1}(t)}{w_ n(t)} \leq C n^ A e^{-G_ n(s_ n-t)/2}.  \] By ( 2.20.6 ), after increasing $N$ there is $c>0$ such that, for $n>N$, $\epsilon _ n=e^{-c n^{1/8}}<1/2$ and 4B3C0F159C1D 2.20.9 \begin{equation}  \begin{aligned}  |u_ n/u_{n-1}|& \leq \epsilon _ n& &  (a_ n-r_ n\leq t\leq a_ n),\\  |u_{n-1}/u_ n|& \leq \epsilon _ n& &  (b_ n\leq t\leq b_ n+r_ n). \end{aligned} \end{equation} The polynomial prefactor is absorbed because $n^{1/8}/\log n\to \infty $. All comparisons are uniform in $x$. Choose a smooth $\rho :\mathbb R\to [0,1]$ equal to zero for $v\leq 1/4$ and to one for $v\geq 3/4$, with bounded derivatives of each order. For example normalize the integral of $e^{-1/(v(1-v))}$ on $(0,1)$, extend it constantly, and compose with $v\mapsto 2v-1/2$. These constant collars will make the adjacent strip definitions agree on neighborhoods of their endpoints. On $I_ n=[a_{n+1},a_ n]$, $n>N$, put \[  A_ n(t)=\rho ((t-b_ n)/r_ n),\qquad B_ n(t)=1-\rho ((t-a_ n+r_ n)/r_ n),\qquad u=A_ nu_{n-1}+B_ nu_ n.  \] On the lower transition $[b_ n,b_ n+r_ n]$ one has $B_ n=1$ and $|u|\geq (1-\epsilon _ n)|u_ n|$. On the upper transition $[a_ n-r_ n,a_ n]$ one has $A_ n=1$ and $|u|\geq (1-\epsilon _ n)|u_{n-1}|$. Between them both cutoffs are one; outside them in $I_ n$ they are constant as well. Consequently $\mathcal L u=0$ outside the two transition bands, even if the two modes cancel in the middle. Define $f=\mathcal L u/u$ on the bands and $f=0$ elsewhere. The displayed lower bounds give nonvanishing neighborhoods of every band endpoint. There the residual is identically zero on the adjacent constant-cutoff side. Thus this definition is smooth at every endpoint; it never divides by a possible middle zero. For clarity we check all derivatives of this quotient. On the upper band, $\mathcal L u=[\mathcal L,B_ n]u_ n$. Each derivative of this commutator is bounded by $C_ m n^{A_ m}|u_ n|$: it is a finite sum of derivatives of the cutoffs, the polynomial coefficients of $\mathcal L$, and derivatives of $u_ n$. Here $r_ n^{-1}$ is bounded by a power of $n$. On the same band, every derivative of $u$ is bounded by a power of $n$ times $|u_{n-1}|$, and $|u|\geq |u_{n-1}|/2$. Repeated differentiation of $u^{-1}$, using the product rule on $u u^{-1}=1$, therefore bounds its derivatives by a power of $n$ times $|u_{n-1}|^{-1}$. The quotient rule and ( 2.20.9 ) give 8B718C586209 2.20.10 \begin{equation}  \sup _{I_ n\times \mathbb R}|D^\alpha f| \leq C_ m n^{A_ m}\epsilon _ n, \qquad |\alpha |\leq m. \end{equation} On the lower band use $[\mathcal L,A_ n]u_{n-1}$ and the dominant mode $u_ n$ instead. Outside the bands the derivatives of $f$ are zero, completing the proof of this estimate. Near the upper endpoint of $I_ n$ the resulting $u$ is $u_{n-1}$; near its lower endpoint it is $u_ n$. These formulas agree with the neighboring strip, and $f=0$ near every $a_ n$. On $a_{N+1}<t<a_ N$ put $u=u_ N$ and $f=0$. Thus both functions are smooth on $(0,a_ N)\times \mathbb R$ and satisfy the equation there. Finally these functions extend smoothly and flatly by zero to $t\leq 0$. To verify this rather than assuming it, note $s_ n<s_{n-1}$ and ( 2.20.8 ); monotonicity gives $w_ n(s_ n)\leq w_{n-1}(s_{n-1})\leq 1$. Since $a_ n<s_{n-1}$, the upper-band estimate at $a_ n$ also gives \[  w_ n(t)\leq w_ n(a_ n) \leq \epsilon _ n w_{n-1}(a_ n)\leq \epsilon _ n \qquad (0\leq t\leq a_ n).  \] For $n\geq N+2$, both modes used on $I_ n$ therefore have size at most $\epsilon _{n-1}$, after decreasing $c$ if needed. The relative derivative and cutoff estimates imply \[  \sup _{I_ n\times \mathbb R}|D^\alpha u| \leq C_ m n^{A_ m}\epsilon _{n-1},\qquad |\alpha |\leq m.  \] Together with ( 2.20.10 ), these bounds decay faster than any power of $t$, since $t$ on $I_ n$ is comparable to $n^{-11/16}$. Every derivative thus tends uniformly to zero as $t\downarrow 0$. The zero extensions are smooth: induct on derivative order, using the zero boundary values for tangential derivatives and the fundamental theorem of calculus for the transverse derivative. All their derivatives vanish on $t=0$, so the differential equation also holds there and on $t<0$. Take $a=a_ N$. At each $t=a_ n$, $n>N$, the constructed function is $u_{n-1}(a_ n,x)$, which is nonzero for every $x$. As $a_ n\downarrow 0$, this proves the required nontriviality in every neighborhood of each $(0,x)$, and completes the construction. $\square$

title: Proposition 2.20.11 (An ordinary second-order prolongation)
text:
Proposition 2.20.11 (An ordinary second-order prolongation) . CE8EC0706B26 Let $\Omega $ be an open subset of $\{ (t,x)\in \mathbb R^2:|t|<1\} $, and let $f\in C^\infty (\Omega ,\mathbb C)$. Put \[  D=\partial _ t-i\partial _ x,\qquad A=D^2+it^2\partial _ x^2,\qquad B=D^2-it^2\partial _ x^2, \qquad P_ f=D^4+t^4\partial _ x^4+i\partial _ x^3-f.  \] There is a smooth second-order elliptic differential operator $\mathcal P_ f$ on the trivial complex bundle $\Omega \times \mathbb C^3$ such that every smooth solution $u$ of $P_ fu=0$ gives a solution \[  U=(u,\partial _ xu,Bu),\qquad \mathcal P_ fU=0.  \] The section $U$ is zero on every open set on which $u$ is zero, and $U$ is nonzero whenever $u$ is nonzero. The realification of $\mathcal P_ f$ is also an ordinary second-order elliptic operator on a trivial real bundle of rank six. Proof. The coefficients $t^2$ commute with $\partial _ x$, and $D(t^2)=2t$, $D^2(t^2)=2$. Applying the product rule to a test function gives the exact differential-operator identity \[  AB=D^4+t^4\partial _ x^4-4it\partial _ x^2D-2i\partial _ x^2.  \] Consequently \[  P_ f=AB+Q\partial _ x-f,\qquad Q=4it\partial _ t\partial _ x+(4t+i)\partial _ x^2+2i\partial _ x.  \] Here the term $4t\partial _ x^3$ comes from $4it\partial _ x^2(-i\partial _ x)$; in particular it has positive sign. Define, for arbitrary smooth triples $(u,w,v)$, \[  \mathcal P_ f \begin{pmatrix} u

\\ w

\\ v

\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}  Bu-v

\\  Bw-\partial _ xv

\\  Av+Qw-fu 

\end{pmatrix}.  \] This is a differential operator of order two in every component. Since $B$ commutes with $\partial _ x$, substitution of $w=\partial _ xu$, $v=Bu$ makes its first two components zero, and the third component is exactly $P_ fu$. This proves the asserted solution map. Derivatives of a function that is identically zero on an open set are identically zero there; the first component also proves the nontriviality assertion. For ellipticity, take the principal-symbol convention that replaces $\partial _ t,\partial _ x$ by real variables $\tau ,\xi $; the alternative convention with $i\tau ,i\xi $ changes the entire second-order matrix by a nonzero scalar and gives the same invertibility test. The principal matrix is \[  \sigma _2(\mathcal P_ f)(t,x;\tau ,\xi )= \begin{pmatrix}  b

& 0

& 0

\\  0

& b

& 0

\\  0

& q

& a 

\end{pmatrix}, \quad \begin{aligned}  a& =(\tau -i\xi )^2+it^2\xi ^2,\\  b& =(\tau -i\xi )^2-it^2\xi ^2,\\  q& =4it\tau \xi +(4t+i)\xi ^2. \end{aligned}  \] Its determinant is $b^2a$. If $\xi =0$ and $(\tau ,\xi )\ne 0$, then $a=b=\tau ^2\ne 0$. If $\xi \ne 0$, the vanishing of either $a$ or $b$ would require, on putting $r=\tau /\xi \in \mathbb R$, \[  r^2-1=0,\qquad -2r\pm t^2=0.  \] The first equation gives $r=1$ or $r=-1$, whereas the second is impossible for $|t|<1$. Thus the symbol is invertible at every nonzero real covector. This proves ordinary ellipticity, without a Douglis–Nirenberg weighting or an unasserted positivity of the symbol. Write complex coefficients and components in real and imaginary parts. The real principal matrix is the realification of the displayed complex matrix. Its determinant is $|b^2a|^2$, so it is invertible as a real matrix at the same covectors. The real and imaginary parts of $U$ give the corresponding real solution and preserve its zero set and nontriviality. $\square$

title: Corollary 2.20.12 (Failure of unrestricted elliptic-system continuation)
text: Corollary 2.20.12 (Failure of unrestricted elliptic-system continuation) . 1ADDDDB90B14 There is a connected smooth real surface carrying a smooth ordinary second-order elliptic operator on a rank-three complex vector bundle with a nonzero smooth kernel section vanishing on a nonempty open set. The same assertion holds for a rank-six real vector bundle. Proof. Take $\Omega =(-a,a)\times \mathbb R$ and the functions from Theorem 2.20.4 , with $a<1$. Apply Proposition 2.20.11 . Its section $U$ solves the homogeneous second-order elliptic system, is nonzero because its first component is $u$, and vanishes on $(-a,0)\times \mathbb R$. The realification has the same properties. $\square$

title: Remark 2.20.13 (Scalar and matrix principal symbols)
text: Remark 2.20.13 (Scalar and matrix principal symbols) . ED67DD231FDF The preceding corollary disproves weak continuation for arbitrary smooth matrix-principal elliptic systems under ordinary symbol invertibility. For harmonic forms the relevant hypothesis is more restrictive: a single real elliptic second-order principal operator acts on every component, with smooth coupled lower-order terms. The weak-continuation theorem 2.16.7 applies to that class. The constructed system instead has distinct principal symbols $a,b$ and the second-order off-diagonal term $q$, so it does not belong to that class.

title: 23.3.1 Hopf quotients
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry

title: 23.3.2 Diagonal and triangular contractions
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Theorem 23.3.3 . D81E3145A1B4 Let $F:\mathbb C^2\to \mathbb C^2$ be either \[  F(z_1,z_2)=(\lambda _1z_1,\lambda _2z_2), \qquad 0<|\lambda _1|\leq |\lambda _2|<1,  \] or \[  F(z_1,z_2)=(\lambda z_1,\lambda z_2+z_1^ p), \qquad 0<|\lambda |<1,\quad p\in \mathbb Z_{\geq 1}.  \] Its integer iterates act freely and properly discontinuously on $U=\mathbb C^2\setminus \{ 0\} $. The quotient $X_ F=U/\langle F\rangle $ is a connected compact complex surface with \[  \pi _1(X_ F)\simeq \mathbb Z,\qquad H^1_{\rm dR}(X_ F;\mathbb R)\simeq \mathbb R.  \] Consequently $X_ F$ admits no Kähler metric. Proof. Both maps are polynomial automorphisms fixing zero. In the triangular case the inverse is obtained first from $z_1=\lambda ^{-1}w_1$ and then from $z_2=\lambda ^{-1}(w_2-z_1^ p)$. For $k\geq 1$ direct iteration gives 436562DE848D 23.3.4 \begin{equation}  F^ k(z)=\left(\lambda ^ kz_1, \lambda ^ kz_2+\lambda ^{k-1}z_1^ p \sum _{j=0}^{k-1}\lambda ^{(p-1)j}\right). \end{equation} For $p=1$ the sum is $k$; for $p>1$ it is bounded uniformly in $k$. Thus $F^ k\to 0$ uniformly on compact subsets of $\mathbb C^2$. The same assertion for the diagonal map follows immediately from its coordinate formula. If $F^ kz=z$ for $k>0$, the first coordinate forces $z_1=0$, and the second then forces $z_2=0$. A negative fixed iterate gives a positive one by applying its inverse. This proves freeness on $U$. There is a bounded neighborhood $B$ of zero with $F(\overline B)\subset B$. For the diagonal map take an ordinary Euclidean ball. For the triangular map with $p>1$, its derivative at zero is $\lambda I$, so a sufficiently small Euclidean ball has this property. For $p=1$ use the norm \[  \| (z_1,z_2)\| _ a=a|z_1|+|z_2|, \qquad a>(1-|\lambda |)^{-1}.  \] Indeed $\| Fz\| _ a\leq (|\lambda |+a^{-1})\| z\| _ a$. The closed balls for each of these norms are compact. For compact $K\subset U$, uniform convergence to zero shows that $F^ k(K)\cap K=\varnothing $ for all sufficiently large positive $k$. For negative $k$ the same follows by applying $F^{-k}$ to an intersection. Thus only finitely many translates of any compact set meet it. Freeness and this property provide, about each point, a neighborhood whose distinct translates are disjoint: start with a relatively compact neighborhood, exclude its finitely many possible nontrivial intersecting translates by shrinking about the point, and use freeness for each such translate. These neighborhoods give quotient complex charts. The same compact-neighborhood argument separates two distinct orbits, so the quotient is Hausdorff; a countable basis upstairs projects to one downstairs. The quotient map is therefore a holomorphic covering map and $X_ F$ is a connected complex surface. The compact set $K_0=\overline B\setminus F(B)$ is disjoint from zero. Every orbit meets $K_0$. In fact its forward iterates eventually belong to $B$, whereas its backward iterates cannot all belong to $B$: otherwise, writing $z=F^ k(F^{-k}z)$ with $F^{-k}z\in \overline B$ would force $z=0$ by uniform convergence on $\overline B$. The integers $j$ for which $F^ jz\in B$ consequently have a least member, since $F(B)\subset B$. The corresponding iterate belongs to $B\setminus F(B)$. Thus $K_0$ surjects onto $X_ F$, proving compactness. Radial deformation retracts $U$ onto $S^3$, which is simply connected. Here this last assertion needs only an elementary loop argument: subdivide a continuous loop into arcs in coordinate balls and replace them, by straight-coordinate homotopies fixing endpoints, by piecewise smooth arcs. A finite union of such arcs misses some point of $S^3$; for example its three-dimensional measure is zero, as follows by covering each bounded-derivative arc with $O(\epsilon ^{-1})$ balls of radius $O(\epsilon )$. Stereographic projection identifies the complement of that point with $\mathbb R^3$, where the loop contracts by linear homotopy. Hence $U$ is simply connected. Lift a based loop of $X_ F$ to $U$. Its endpoint is a unique $F^ kz_0$; concatenation adds $k$. Every integer occurs by projecting a path from $z_0$ to $F^ kz_0$. A loop with $k=0$ lifts to a closed loop, contracts upstairs and hence contracts downstairs. Path and homotopy lifting follow by finite subdivisions into the quotient charts just constructed. This proves $\pi _1(X_ F)=\mathbb Z$. The exact period comparison theorem 10.79.2 now gives $H^1_{\rm dR}(X_ F;\mathbb R)=\operatorname {Hom}(\mathbb Z,\mathbb R)$. For a compact Kähler manifold, conjugation exchanges the two summands $H^{1,0}$ and $H^{0,1}$ in theorem 10.47.13 , so its first real Betti number is even. The value one just obtained is a contradiction. $\square$

title: 10.94.1 Cubic Kähler normal-coordinate jets
text: Write a Hermitian metric, linear in its first argument, as $h(\partial _ l,\partial _ m)=g_{l\bar m}$ and associate the form $\omega =\mathrm i\sum _{l,m}g_{l\bar m}\, dz_ l\wedge d\bar z_ m$. A constant scalar convention for the associated real metric does not change its Chern connection. Here $\Theta (T^{1,0}X)$ denotes the unscaled curvature, without a factor $\mathrm i/(2\pi )$. Theorem 10.94.2 . 64B6971EF741 A smooth positive Hermitian metric is Kähler if and only if at every point there are holomorphic coordinates centered there in which \[  g_{l\bar m}(z)=\delta _{lm}+O(|z|^2).  \] If it is Kähler, the coordinates can moreover be chosen so that F8EFB833957C 10.94.3 \begin{equation}  g_{l\bar m}(z)=\delta _{lm} -\sum _{j,k}C_{j\bar k l\bar m}\, z_ j\bar z_ k+O(|z|^3), \end{equation} where the coefficients at the center are defined by \[  \Theta (T^{1,0}X)(0)\partial _ l =\sum _{j,k,m}C_{j\bar k l\bar m}\,  dz_ j\wedge d\bar z_ k\otimes \partial _ m.  \] They satisfy 89C5EDFA346C 10.94.4 \begin{equation}  C_{j\bar k l\bar m}=C_{l\bar k j\bar m} =C_{j\bar m l\bar k},\qquad \overline{C_{j\bar k l\bar m}}=C_{k\bar j m\bar l}. \end{equation} Proof. The displayed first-order vanishing at every point gives $d\omega =0$ pointwise and hence everywhere. Conversely the existing normal-coordinate lemma Kähler normal coordinates , with a constant rescaling to the displayed convention, gives holomorphic coordinates $x$ with $g(0)=I$ and $dg(0)=0$. We refine these coordinates, not merely the holomorphic frame of the tangent bundle. Write their second-order Taylor expansion as E855089CB081 10.94.5 \begin{equation}  g_{l\bar m}(x)=\delta _{lm}+\sum _{j,k} \left(A_{jklm}x_ j\bar x_ k+B_{jklm}x_ jx_ k +\overline{B_{jkml}}\bar x_ j\bar x_ k\right) +O(|x|^3). \end{equation} Here $A_{jklm}=\partial _ j\partial _{\bar k}g_{l\bar m}(0)$ and $B_{jklm}=\tfrac 12\partial _ j\partial _ kg_{l\bar m}(0)$. Hermitian symmetry gives the stated antiholomorphic coefficients. The Kähler equations are \[  \partial _ jg_{l\bar m}=\partial _ lg_{j\bar m},\qquad \partial _{\bar k}g_{l\bar m}=\partial _{\bar m}g_{l\bar k}.  \] Differentiating the first shows that $B_{jklm}$ is invariant under all permutations of $j,k,l$. Define holomorphic functions 9F6B4FD758C3 10.94.6 \begin{equation}  z_ m=x_ m+\frac13\sum _{j,k,l}B_{jklm}x_ jx_ kx_ l. \end{equation} Their Jacobian at zero is the identity, so the holomorphic inverse and submersion theorems makes them local coordinates. The three equal terms on differentiation give exactly \[  dz_ m=dx_ m+\sum _{j,k,l}B_{jklm}x_ jx_ k\, dx_ l.  \] Consequently the coefficients of $\mathrm i\sum _ m dz_ m\wedge d\bar z_ m$ in the $x$ coordinates are precisely the constant, purely holomorphic quadratic and purely antiholomorphic quadratic terms of ( 10.94.5 ), up to terms of order four. Subtracting them, and using $x=z+O(|z|^3)$ and $dx=dz+O(|z|^2)dz$, leaves \[  g_{l\bar m}(z)=\delta _{lm} +\sum _{j,k}A_{jklm}z_ j\bar z_ k+O(|z|^3).  \] This is a coordinate change, so the remaining mixed coefficients have the same coordinate-frame meaning as the original metric. For completeness compute their curvature sign and index order. For column vectors of coefficients the matrix $H$ of the metric $h(v,w)=w^*Hv$ is $H_{ml}=g_{l\bar m}$. Its Chern connection matrix and curvature are $H^{-1}\partial H$ and $\bar\partial (H^{-1}\partial H)$, respectively, as in ( 10.33.1 ). At the center $H=I$ and $dH=0$. Since $\bar\partial (\bar z_ k\, dz_ j) =-dz_ j\wedge d\bar z_ k$, the coefficient carrying $\partial _ l$ to $\partial _ m$ is \[  C_{j\bar k l\bar m}=-\partial _ j\partial _{\bar k} g_{l\bar m}(0)=-A_{jklm}.  \] This proves ( 10.94.3 ). Differentiating the two Kähler equations gives symmetry in $j,l$ and in $k,m$. Finally $\overline{g_{l\bar m}}=g_{m\bar l}$ gives the conjugation identity in ( 10.94.4 ). This also identifies explicitly every symmetry used to integrate the cubic coordinate correction. In complex dimension zero the assertions are vacuous and require no inverse function theorem. $\square$

title: 9.69.1 Star configurations of projective hyperplanes
text: Theorem 9.69.2 . FB7CD3CDDE23 Let $n\geq 1$ and $N\geq n$, and choose $N$ hyperplanes in $\mathbb P^ n$ in general position: every at most $n$ of their linear equations are independent and every $n+1$ have no common point. Let $S$ be the set of their $n$-fold intersection points. With the vanishing degrees of definition 9.56.1 , one has \[  \omega _1(S)=N-n+1,\qquad \omega _ t(S)\geq \frac{Nt}{n}\quad (t\geq 1),\qquad \Omega (S)=\frac Nn.  \] In particular \[  \Omega (S)=\frac{\omega _1(S)+n-1}{n}.  \] Thus the proposed general lower bound has equality on these configurations in every dimension, and its universal right side cannot be increased. Proof. Write the distinct hyperplane equations as $\ell _1,\ldots ,\ell _ N$. For $n=1$, these are $N$ distinct points; counting roots gives $\omega _ t=Nt$ and all assertions. Suppose $n>1$. On each $H_ i=\{ \ell _ i=0\} \simeq \mathbb P^{n-1}$, its intersections with the other hyperplanes are $N-1$ hyperplanes in general position, and their $(n-1)$-fold intersection set is exactly $S\cap H_ i$. First prove the simple vanishing degree by induction on $n$. A product of any $N-n+1$ of the $\ell _ i$ vanishes on every point of $S$: a set of $n$ incident hyperplanes cannot be contained among the $n-1$ omitted hyperplanes. Conversely if $F$ has degree less than $N-n+1$ and vanishes on $S$, then its restriction to every $H_ i$ is zero by the induction hypothesis, whose lower degree is $(N-1)-(n-1)+1=N-n+1$. Hence all $\ell _ i$ divide $F$, so their product divides it. To justify the last implication, each linear polynomial generates a prime ideal, since its quotient polynomial ring is again a polynomial ring; distinct linear factors do not divide one another. Induction on the factors therefore proves product divisibility. This contradicts $\deg F<N-n+1\leq N$ for nonzero $F$, proving the first equality. Prove the multiplicity lower bound by induction on $n$, and within a fixed $n$ by induction on the positive integer $t$. Let a nonzero homogeneous $F$ of degree $D$ have order at least $t$ at every point of $S$. If some $\ell _ i$ does not divide $F$, its nonzero restriction to $H_ i$ has order at least $t$ at every point of $S\cap H_ i$. The dimension induction hypothesis gives \[  D\geq \frac{(N-1)t}{n-1}\geq \frac{Nt}{n},  \] since $N\geq n$. Otherwise $P=\prod _ i\ell _ i$ divides $F$. It has degree $N$ and order exactly $n$ at each point of $S$, because precisely $n$ hyperplanes pass through that point. If $t\leq n$, then $D\geq N\geq Nt/n$. If $t>n$, the nonzero quotient $F/P$ has degree $D-N$ and order at least $t-n$ at all those points. The induction on $t$ gives \[  D-N\geq \frac{N(t-n)}n,  \] which proves the same bound. These alternatives also handle $N=n$, where $S$ has a single point. Finally $P$ has degree $N$ and order $n$ at every point, so $\omega _ n\leq N$. The proved lower bound and the definition $\Omega =\inf _{t\geq 1}\omega _ t/t$ now give $\Omega =N/n$. The formula for $\omega _1$ gives the last displayed equality. There is no appeal here to the conjecture for arbitrary finite sets. $\square$

title: 2.21.1 Complete metric-connection Laplacians
text: All manifolds are smooth, Hausdorff, second countable and without boundary. Completeness is for the Riemannian length distance on each component. Bundles have finite rank and smooth positive metrics. We integrate with the Riemannian density; an orientation is unnecessary. Inner products are linear in the first variable. Every differential operator mentioned below initially acts on compactly supported smooth sections, and its maximal domain consists of the $L^2$ sections whose distributional image is $L^2$. Proposition 2.21.2 . E40060D5FC24 Let $D$ be the exterior covariant derivative of a metric connection on a real or complex metric bundle over a complete Riemannian manifold. Let $\delta $ denote its formal adjoint. Their maximal realizations are closed and densely defined, and \[  D^*=\delta ,\qquad \delta ^*=D.  \] Compactly supported smooth forms are dense in each individual domain and in $\operatorname {Dom}D\cap \operatorname {Dom}\delta $ for the corresponding graph norms. Flatness is not assumed. Proof. Local $L^2$ convergence implies distributional convergence, which proves closedness of every maximal differential operator. Cutoffs, local frames and coefficient mollification prove density of compactly supported smooth forms in $L^2$, and hence dense domains. Take the complete gradient cutoffs of lemma 6.26.1 . The product rules are \[  D(\chi _ Ru)=\chi _ RDu+d\chi _ R\wedge u,\qquad \delta (\chi _ Ru)=\chi _ R\delta u- \iota _{\nabla \chi _ R}u.  \] Wedge and its adjoint contraction by a covector have norm at most the norm of that covector, by the exterior calculation in proposition 10.82.2 . Thus the error terms are bounded by $C\| u\| _2/R$. Dominated convergence reduces each graph approximation, simultaneously for the joint graph, to compact support. A finite local partition then reduces to smooth matrix first-order operators on one compact coordinate set. The complete matrix commutator calculation in the proof of graph-norm density by cutoffs and mollification proves \[  P(u*\rho _\varepsilon )-(Pu)*\rho _\varepsilon \longrightarrow 0 \quad \hbox{in }L^2  \] for every such operator $P$. That calculation is on real coordinates with arbitrary smooth matrix coefficients; it applies unchanged to $D$, $\delta $, or their joint vector. Local metric/density norms are uniformly equivalent on these compact sets. This gives the claimed smooth graph cores, without assuming constant principal coefficients for $\delta $. In fact the same local commutator conclusion holds with $C^1$ principal coefficients and continuous zeroth-order coefficients: the mean-value kernel bound needs only bounded first derivatives, the zeroth-order commutator tends to zero by continuity, and the uniform $L^2$ bound passes convergence from smooth vectors to all $L^2$ vectors by density. Testing a Hilbert-adjoint-domain element on compactly supported smooth forms identifies its adjoint with the distributional formal adjoint. Conversely the compact formal integration identity extends to the maximal domain by the graph density just proved. This shows $D^*=\delta $ and, interchanging the operators, $\delta ^*=D$. The density-based argument uses only local densities and so also applies without a global orientation. $\square$ Theorem 2.21.3 . CE09CDC33E77 In the preceding setting let $\Delta =D\delta +\delta D$ as a differential expression, and let $\Delta _{\max }$ be its maximal distributional $L^2$ realization. Put \[  V=\operatorname {Dom}D\cap \operatorname {Dom}\delta , \qquad Q(u,v)=\langle Du,Dv\rangle +\langle \delta u,\delta v\rangle .  \] Then $\Delta _{\max }$ is nonnegative and self-adjoint, and its domain has the exact weak-energy description F4319A4DE391 2.21.4 \begin{equation}  \begin{aligned}  \operatorname {Dom}\Delta _{\max }=\{ u\in V:\  & \exists f\in L^2 \text{ such that}\\ & Q(u,v)=\langle f,v\rangle \text{ for every }v\in V\} . \end{aligned} \end{equation} For such $u$ the vector $f$ is $\Delta u$, and \[  \langle \Delta u,u\rangle =\| Du\| _2^2+\| \delta u\| _2^2, \qquad \ker \Delta _{\max }=\ker D\cap \ker \delta .  \] Its kernel consists of smooth forms. The compactly supported smooth realization of $\Delta $ is essentially self-adjoint, with closure $\Delta _{\max }$. No flatness or global curvature bound is needed. Proof. The local principal part is $-g^{ij}\partial _ i\partial _ j I$ by proposition 10.82.2 . Thus if $u,\Delta u=f\in L^2$, elliptic distributional regularity theorem 2.18.3 gives $u\in H^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$. This permits the following compactly supported integrations by parts; local $H^2$ approximation justifies them before smoothness is known. Write $\chi =\chi _ R$ for the gradient cutoffs, and set $E_ R=\| \chi Du\| _2^2+\| \chi \delta u\| _2^2$. The product rules and the formal adjoint identity give \[  \langle f,\chi ^2u\rangle =E_ R+2\langle Du,\chi \, d\chi \wedge u\rangle -2\langle \delta u,\chi \, \iota _{\nabla \chi }u\rangle .  \] Taking real parts and applying Cauchy–Schwarz yields \[  E_ R\leq \| f\| _2\| u\| _2+ (C/R)\| u\| _2\sqrt{E_ R}.  \] This quadratic inequality uniformly bounds $E_ R$. Since $\chi _ R\to 1$ pointwise, Fatou proves $Du,\delta u\in L^2$, hence $u\in V$. The two error terms now tend to zero; passing to the complex identity itself proves the asserted real energy equality, including vanishing of its imaginary part. For a compactly supported smooth $v$, distributional integration gives $Q(u,v)=\langle f,v\rangle $. The preceding proposition's joint graph density extends it to every $v\in V$. Conversely any $u,f$ satisfying this identity satisfy $\Delta u=f$ distributionally by compact tests. This proves ( 2.21.4 ). In particular the maximal operator is symmetric and nonnegative. Here is the adjoint-domain argument needed for self-adjointness. If $v\in \operatorname {Dom}(\Delta _{\max })^*$, testing its adjoint identity against compactly supported smooth forms gives $\Delta v=(\Delta _{\max })^*v\in L^2$ distributionally. Thus $v\in \operatorname {Dom}\Delta _{\max }$. Symmetry supplies the reverse inclusion and equality of operators. This proves self-adjointness, not merely symmetry. If $\Delta _ c$ denotes the compactly supported smooth operator, the same distributional test shows $\Delta _ c^*=\Delta _{\max }$. Its adjoint is densely defined, and the graph-perpendicular calculation in closed operators, Hilbert adjoints and graph orthogonals identifies its graph closure with its double adjoint. Hence that closure is $\Delta _{\max }^*=\Delta _{\max }$. The energy equality identifies the kernel; in the converse direction $Du=\delta u=0$ makes $\Delta u=0$ distributionally, so the maximal domain condition holds. Local elliptic regularity makes its elements smooth. In dimension zero all differential expressions are zero, the maximal domains are all $L^2$, and finite-support approximation on the countable discrete manifold proves the same assertions directly. $\square$ Corollary 2.21.5 . A76DD53006C1 If the metric connection is flat, its $L^2$ complex has orthogonal decompositions in every degree \[  L^2=\mathcal H\  \widehat\oplus  \overline{\operatorname {Ran}D}\  \widehat\oplus  \overline{\operatorname {Ran}\delta }, \qquad \ker D=\mathcal H\  \widehat\oplus  \overline{\operatorname {Ran}D},  \] where $\mathcal H=\ker \Delta _{\max }$ consists of smooth $L^2$ harmonic forms. Consequently the reduced $L^2$ cohomology $\ker D/\overline{\operatorname {Ran}D}$ is canonically isometric to $\mathcal H$. The ranges need not be closed. Proof. Flatness gives $D^2=0$ on distributions, hence $\operatorname {Ran}D\subset \ker D$. The adjoint/range identities of closed operators, Hilbert adjoints and graph orthogonals give \[  (\operatorname {Ran}D)^\perp =\ker \delta , \qquad (\ker D)^\perp =\overline{\operatorname {Ran}\delta }.  \] Since $\overline{\operatorname {Ran}D}\subset \ker D$, orthogonal projection inside the closed space $\ker D$ leaves as its complement exactly $\ker D\cap \ker \delta =\mathcal H$. The two decompositions and the quotient statement follow. This argument makes no closed-range assertion and does not identify unreduced cohomology with harmonic forms when a range is not closed. $\square$

Thus if $u,\Delta u=f\in L^2$, elliptic distributional regularity theorem 2.18.3 gives $u\in H^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$. This permits the following compactly supported integrations by parts; local $H^2$ approximation justifies them before smoothness is known. Write $\chi =\chi _ R$ for the gradient cutoffs, and set $E_ R=\| \chi Du\| _2^2+\| \chi \delta u\| _2^2$. The product rules and the formal adjoint identity give \[  \langle f,\chi ^2u\rangle =E_ R+2\langle Du,\chi \, d\chi \wedge u\rangle -2\langle \delta u,\chi \, \iota _{\nabla \chi }u\rangle .  \] Taking real parts and applying Cauchy–Schwarz yields \[  E_ R\leq \| f\| _2\| u\| _2+ (C/R)\| u\| _2\sqrt{E_ R}.  \] This quadratic inequality uniformly bounds $E_ R$. Since $\chi _ R\to 1$ pointwise, Fatou proves $Du,\delta u\in L^2$, hence $u\in V$. The two error terms now tend to zero; passing to the complex identity itself proves the asserted real energy equality, including vanishing of its imaginary part. For a compactly supported smooth $v$, distributional integration gives $Q(u,v)=\langle f,v\rangle $. The preceding proposition's joint graph density extends it to every $v\in V$. Conversely any $u,f$ satisfying this identity satisfy $\Delta u=f$ distributionally by compact tests. This proves ( 2.21.4 ). In particular the maximal operator is symmetric and nonnegative. Here is the adjoint-domain argument needed for self-adjointness. If $v\in \operatorname {Dom}(\Delta _{\max })^*$, testing its adjoint identity against compactly supported smooth forms gives $\Delta v=(\Delta _{\max })^*v\in L^2$ distributionally. Thus $v\in \operatorname {Dom}\Delta _{\max }$. Symmetry supplies the reverse inclusion and equality of operators. This proves self-adjointness, not merely symmetry. If $\Delta _ c$ denotes the compactly supported smooth operator, the same distributional test shows $\Delta _ c^*=\Delta _{\max }$. Its adjoint is densely defined, and the graph-perpendicular calculation in closed operators, Hilbert adjoints and graph orthogonals identifies its graph closure with its double adjoint. Hence that closure is $\Delta _{\max }^*=\Delta _{\max }$. The energy equality identifies the kernel; in the converse direction $Du=\delta u=0$ makes $\Delta u=0$ distributionally, so the maximal domain condition holds. Local elliptic regularity makes its elements smooth. In dimension zero all differential expressions are zero, the maximal domains are all $L^2$, and finite-support approximation on the countable discrete manifold proves the same assertions directly. $\square$

title: Corollary 2.21.5
text: Corollary 2.21.5 . A76DD53006C1 If the metric connection is flat, its $L^2$ complex has orthogonal decompositions in every degree \[  L^2=\mathcal H\  \widehat\oplus  \overline{\operatorname {Ran}D}\  \widehat\oplus  \overline{\operatorname {Ran}\delta }, \qquad \ker D=\mathcal H\  \widehat\oplus  \overline{\operatorname {Ran}D},  \] where $\mathcal H=\ker \Delta _{\max }$ consists of smooth $L^2$ harmonic forms. Consequently the reduced $L^2$ cohomology $\ker D/\overline{\operatorname {Ran}D}$ is canonically isometric to $\mathcal H$. The ranges need not be closed. Proof. Flatness gives $D^2=0$ on distributions, hence $\operatorname {Ran}D\subset \ker D$. The adjoint/range identities of closed operators, Hilbert adjoints and graph orthogonals give \[  (\operatorname {Ran}D)^\perp =\ker \delta , \qquad (\ker D)^\perp =\overline{\operatorname {Ran}\delta }.  \] Since $\overline{\operatorname {Ran}D}\subset \ker D$, orthogonal projection inside the closed space $\ker D$ leaves as its complement exactly $\ker D\cap \ker \delta =\mathcal H$. The two decompositions and the quotient statement follow. text: Corollary 11.49.2 . 28AC2C7FBC2B On a complete Hermitian manifold with a smooth Hermitian holomorphic bundle, the preceding graph-core, adjoint, maximal-Laplacian and reduced $L^2$ Hodge assertions hold separately for $(D',\delta ',\Delta ')$ and $(D'',\delta '',\Delta '')$ in their respective type complexes. No Kähler assumption is imposed. Proof. The local first-order symbols are exterior multiplication by the $(1,0)$ or $(0,1)$ part of a covector; their adjoints are contractions. Thus the cutoff commutators have the same $C|d\chi |$ bound, and the full matrix mollifier argument proves the individual and joint graph cores and adjoint identities. Their Laplacians have scalar positive principal symbol $|\xi |^2I/2$, the creation/contraction identity of the same exterior calculation. All steps of the maximal Laplacian proof, including the complex cutoff identity, local $H^2$ regularity and the adjoint-domain test, therefore apply unchanged. In a holomorphic frame $D''=\bar\partial $ and $D'=\partial +H^{-1}\partial H$. Hence $(D'')^2=0$, and $\partial (H^{-1}\partial H)+(H^{-1}\partial H)^2=0$ gives $(D')^2=0$. Their maximal distributional realizations are therefore Hilbert complexes. The preceding projection argument gives both typewise reduced Hodge decompositions. Smooth harmonic representatives follow from the corresponding elliptic regularity. The full connection $D'+D''$ need not be flat; no cochain Hodge decomposition for that nonflat total connection is asserted. $\square$ For a positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphism $A$ of a coefficient fiber define \[  |g|_{A^{-1}}^2 =\sup _{v\ne 0}\frac{|\langle g,v\rangle |^2}{\langle Av,v\rangle }.  \] A zero denominator gives zero if the numerator is zero, and infinity otherwise. Diagonalization shows that this is $\sum _{\lambda _ j>0}|g_ j|^2/\lambda _ j$ when $g\perp \ker A$, and infinity otherwise. Equivalently it is the increasing limit $\lim _{\varepsilon \downarrow 0}\langle (A+\varepsilon I)^{-1}g,g\rangle $, so it is measurable for a smooth $A$ and measurable $g$. Theorem 11.49.3 . D6CB928B58CE Let $(X,\omega )$ be complete Hermitian of dimension $n\geq 1$, and let $E$ be a smooth Hermitian holomorphic vector bundle. Fix $0\leq p\leq n$ and $1\leq q\leq n$, and suppose \[  A=[\mathrm i\Theta (E),\Lambda _\omega ]+T_\omega \geq 0 \quad \hbox{on }\Lambda ^{p,q}T^*X\otimes E,  \] with the exact Hermitian torsion operator of theorem 11.48.15 . For every $g\in L^2_{p,q}(X,E)$ with $D''g=0$ distributionally and \[  M=\int _ X|g|_{A^{-1}}^2\, dV_\omega <\infty ,  \] there is $u\in L^2_{p,q-1}(X,E)$ such that \[  D''u=g,\qquad \| u\| _2^2\leq M.  \] The unique solution of smallest norm satisfies $\delta ''u=0$ distributionally, and is smooth when $g$ is smooth. If $A\geq \lambda (x)I$ for a positive function $\lambda $, the right side is at most $\int _ X|g|^2/\lambda \, dV_\omega $; no uniform positive lower bound for $\lambda $ is needed. Proof. For compactly supported smooth $v$ the exact energy identity equation 11.48.19 gives \[  \int _ X\langle Av,v\rangle \, dV_\omega \leq \| D''v\| _2^2+\| \delta ''v\| _2^2.  \] This inequality also holds on the full joint graph domain. Indeed the complete-Hermitian graph core in lemma 6.26.4 , or the preceding corollary, gives graph-convergent smooth approximations. A subsequence converges pointwise almost everywhere in local frames; positivity and Fatou pass the left integral to the limit, while graph convergence passes the energy on the right. This also handles an unbounded pointwise operator $A$. Pointwise dual Cauchy–Schwarz, followed by integral Cauchy–Schwarz, gives on compact smooth tests \[  |\langle g,v\rangle |^2 \leq M\bigl (\| \delta ''v\| _2^2+\| D''v\| _2^2\bigr ).  \] Since $g$ is globally $L^2$, both sides are continuous in the joint graph norm, so this holds on the full joint domain as well. Put $T=D''$ from type $(p,q-1)$ to $(p,q)$ and $S=D''$ to $(p,q+1)$, with $S=0$ when $q=n$. These maximal operators are closed, $T^*=\delta ''$, and $\operatorname {Ran}T\subset \ker S$. The exact Hilbert-complex solvability from the dual energy estimate therefore gives the asserted solution and constant one. The affine solution set is $u+\ker T$ with closed kernel; its orthogonal projection gives the unique minimum-norm solution with no larger norm. The range of the preceding $D''$ operator lies in $\ker T$, so the Hilbert adjoint identity gives $\delta ''u=0$. For $q=1$ this equation is vacuous. Distributionally, $\Delta ''u=\delta ''g$. If $g$ is smooth this right side is smooth, and local elliptic regularity makes $u$ smooth. Finally diagonalizing $A$ gives the stated inverse-energy bound when $A\geq \lambda I$. In particular its smallest eigenvalue, when positive, is a continuous choice of $\lambda $: Rayleigh minima change by at most the operator norm of a matrix perturbation. Zero eigenvalues throughout the theorem use the finite-energy convention already stated, not an inverse of a singular endomorphism. $\square$

title: 2.22.1 Approximate midpoints and compact metric balls
search_title: Approximate midpoints and compact metric balls
text: All distances in this section are finite. A metric space $(E,d)$ has approximate midpoints if D0F673E1134B 2.22.2 \begin{equation}  \inf _{z\in E}\max \{ d(x,z),d(y,z)\} =\frac{d(x,y)}2 \qquad (x,y\in E). \end{equation} The triangle inequality always gives the lower bound. Thus the axiom means that, for each $\eta >0$, one can choose $z$ with both distances less than $d(x,y)/2+\eta $. No exact midpoint is required. The length of a continuous curve is the supremum, over its finite ordered partitions, of the sums of the distances of consecutive values. A length metric is a metric equal to the infimum of these lengths over connecting continuous curves. Lemma 2.22.3 . 3B383470A6A3 Suppose that $(E,d)$ has approximate midpoints. For $x,y\in E$ and $L>d(x,y)$, there is a compatible assignment $a$ on the dyadic numbers in $[0,1]$, with $a(0)=x$, $a(1)=y$, such that \[  d(a(s),a(t))\leq L|s-t|.  \] Consequently, for every $\varepsilon >0$ there is a finite chain $x=x_0,\ldots ,x_ N=y$ whose individual steps are less than $\varepsilon $ and whose total step length is less than $d(x,y)+\varepsilon $. Completeness is not needed for this conclusion. Proof. Put $d_0=d(x,y)$ and $\eta _ n=(L-d_0)2^{-2n-2}$ for $n\geq 0$. Starting with the endpoints, at stage $n$ insert an approximate midpoint in every interval of length $2^{-n}$, with error $\eta _ n$. Keep all previously assigned values. If $M_ n$ is the maximum distance between successive assigned values at stage $n$, then \[  M_0=d_0,\qquad M_{n+1}\leq \tfrac 12M_ n+\eta _ n, \qquad 2^ nM_ n\leq d_0+\sum _{j=0}^{n-1}2^{j+1}\eta _ j<L.  \] The final strict inequality follows from $\sum _{j\geq 0}2^{j+1}\eta _ j=L-d_0$; it also holds at $n=0$. For two dyadic numbers choose a common stage. Summing its consecutive edges gives the asserted Lipschitz bound. With $L=d_0+\varepsilon $, choose $n$ so large that $L2^{-n}<\varepsilon $. The stage-$n$ values are the required chain: its total step length is at most $2^ nM_ n<L$. $\square$ Proposition 2.22.4 . EB12C0B326CA Every length metric has approximate midpoints. Conversely, a complete metric space with approximate midpoints is a length metric. More precisely, for every $L>d(x,y)$ in the latter space there is an $L$-Lipschitz connecting curve on $[0,1]$ with length at most $L$. Proof. For a length metric and $x\ne y$, take a connecting curve $\gamma $ of length less than $d(x,y)+2\eta $. The continuous real function \[  t\longmapsto d(x,\gamma (t))-d(y,\gamma (t))  \] is negative at the starting point and positive at the endpoint. At a zero, put $z=\gamma (t)$. The partition using that parameter gives $2d(x,z)=d(x,z)+d(y,z)\leq \operatorname {length}(\gamma )$. This proves the upper bound in the midpoint axiom by letting $\eta \downarrow 0$. If $x=y$, take $z=x$. Conversely use lemma 2.22.3 . For $t\in [0,1]$, choose dyadic $s_ j\to t$. The sequence $a(s_ j)$ is Cauchy by its Lipschitz bound, hence has a limit $\gamma (t)$ by completeness. Interlacing two such sequences shows independence of the choice. Passing to limits in the bound gives $d(\gamma (s),\gamma (t))\leq L|s-t|$. The curve has the prescribed endpoints, and each finite partition has total distance at most $L$. Thus its length is at most $L$. Every connecting curve has length at least $d(x,y)$, so letting $L\downarrow d(x,y)$ proves the length metric identity. For equal endpoints the constant curve suffices. $\square$ Theorem 2.22.5 . 883E85712A41 Let $(E,d)$ be a metric space with approximate midpoints. The following conditions are equivalent: $E$ is complete and locally compact; every closed ball of finite radius is compact. Proof. Under the first condition, proposition 2.22.4 makes the metric a length metric. The complete, locally compact length-space lemma 9.28.1 therefore proves compactness of all closed bounded balls. Its proof uses the supremum of compact radii, finite nets, completeness and finite local compact ball coverings; no existence of a minimizing curve is a premise. Conversely each closed ball of radius $1$ is a compact neighborhood of its center, proving local compactness. Every Cauchy sequence is bounded, hence lies in a single closed ball. Compactness gives a convergent subsequence; the Cauchy property then makes the whole sequence converge to the same limit. This proves completeness. The converse implication itself requires no midpoint assumption. $\square$ For a Riemannian manifold, its length distance has the midpoint property: choose a piecewise smooth path with length arbitrarily close to the distance, and use its continuous accumulated length to cut it into equal lengths. The finite distance and induced topology on a connected component were established in the discussion preceding lemma 9.28.1 . The preceding theorem therefore applies to each connected component. Distances between distinct components may be assigned $+\infty $; the finite metric statements are understood componentwise. The approximate-midpoint axiom by itself asserts neither the existence of an exact midpoint nor the existence of a curve that attains the distance.

title: 2.23 Completions and locally convex quotients
text: An epimorphism here is an open surjective continuous linear map of Hausdorff locally convex spaces. Completeness alone does not replace the countable neighborhood basis in successive-correction arguments. We give explicit counterexamples and retain the Fréchet conclusion. Lemma 2.23.1 . 0628F713D150 Every vector space with its finest locally convex topology is complete. Proof. Choose a Hamel basis $(e_ i)_{i\in I}$. Its vectors have finite support. The seminorms \[  q_ w\left(\sum _ i a_ ie_ i\right)=\sum _ iw_ i|a_ i|, \qquad w_ i>0\quad (i\in I),  \] generate the finest locally convex topology: every seminorm $p$ is bounded by $q_ w$ with $w_ i=p(e_ i)+1$. Let $(a_\alpha )$ be a Cauchy net. Each coordinate has a scalar limit $c_ i$. For a fixed $w$ and $\varepsilon >0$, choose a tail on which $q_ w(a_\alpha -a_\beta )<\varepsilon $. For any finite $J\subset I$, letting $\beta $ tend to the limit in those coordinates gives \[  \sum _{i\in J}w_ i|(a_\alpha )_ i-c_ i|\leq \varepsilon  \] for every $\alpha $ in that tail. Taking the supremum over finite $J$ shows both that $\sum _ iw_ i|c_ i|<\infty $ and that the formal difference has weighted sum at most $\varepsilon $. If infinitely many $c_ i$ were nonzero, choose distinct $i_ n$ with $c_{i_ n}\ne 0$ and set $w_{i_ n}=1/|c_{i_ n}|$, extending these to positive weights. This contradicts finiteness of the weighted sum. Hence $c$ has finite support and is a vector of the original space. The same estimate for every $w$ proves $a_\alpha \to c$, establishing completeness. $\square$ Example 2.23.2 . D7A9E3E20E73 There is a continuous linear bijection $u:E\to F$ between complete Hausdorff locally convex spaces such that $\overline{u(V)}$ is a zero neighborhood for every zero neighborhood $V\subset E$, but $u$ is not open. Proof. Take the vector space $\mathbb C^{\mathbb N}$ with its finest locally convex topology for $E$ and its product topology for $F$; let $u$ be the identity. It is continuous, and $E$ is complete by lemma 2.23.1 . The product is complete for the metric $D(x,y)=\sum _{n\geq 1}2^{-n}\min \{ 1,|x_ n-y_ n|\} $: Cauchy sequences converge coordinatewise, and a finite-head/tail estimate gives convergence for $D$. The same coordinate argument proves completeness for Cauchy nets in the product topology. For a convex balanced zero neighborhood $V$ in $E$, the set $B=\overline{u(V)}$ is closed, convex, balanced and absorbing in $F$. Thus $F=\bigcup _{m\geq 1}mB$. The complete-metric Baire argument gives interior to some $mB$: otherwise one constructs nested closed balls of radii tending to zero, avoiding the first $m$ closed sets at stage $m$, and their Cauchy centers give a limit outside their union. Consequently $B$ has interior; convexity and balance imply that $(B-B)/2\subset B$ contains a zero neighborhood. Every neighborhood in $E$ contains such a $V$, proving the asserted closure condition. To see that $u$ is not open, extend the functional $\ell (\sum _{n\in J}a_ ne_ n)=\sum _{n\in J}a_ n$ from the finite-support sequences to the whole vector space using a Hamel basis. It is continuous on $E$. A product-continuous linear functional depends on finitely many coordinates: a zero neighborhood restricts only finitely many coordinates, and arbitrary scalar multiples of all other coordinate vectors belong to it. Since $\ell (e_ n)=1$ for every $n$, $\ell $ is not product-continuous. Hence the two topologies are different and their identity bijection is not open. $\square$ Lemma 2.23.3 . 5F1410BEA2F7 There is a complete Hausdorff locally convex space $E$ and an open continuous linear surjection $r:E\to F$ onto an incomplete Hausdorff locally convex space $F$. Proof. Let $\omega $ be the first infinite ordinal and $\omega _1$ the first uncountable ordinal, with their order topologies, and set \[  P=[0,\omega _1]\times [0,\omega ],\qquad X=P\setminus \{ (\omega _1,\omega )\} ,  \] \[  H=[0,\omega _1)\times \{ \omega \} ,\qquad V=\{ \omega _1\} \times [0,\omega ),\qquad A=H\cup V.  \] We record the elementary topology needed for the construction. Every ordinal interval $[0,\kappa ]$ is compact and Hausdorff. For compactness, given an open cover, a least ordinal $\beta $ for which $[0,\beta ]$ has no finite subcover cannot exist: it is not zero, and a covering neighborhood of $\beta $ contains a final interval $(\alpha ,\beta ]$, leaving the earlier compact interval $[0,\alpha ]$. Order intervals separate distinct points, proving Hausdorffness. Intervals $(\alpha ,\beta ]$ and the singleton $\{ 0\} $ form a clopen neighborhood basis (with the endpoint convention at $\kappa $). The product of two compact spaces is compact: an open cover of the product gives finitely many rectangles covering each vertical fiber; the common horizontal neighborhood for those finitely many rectangles then permits a finite horizontal subcover. Thus $P$ is compact Hausdorff and has a clopen rectangle basis. Every point of $X$ has such a rectangle excluding the deleted corner. That rectangle is compact, since it is closed in $P$. Hence $X$ has a basis of compact clopen sets and is locally compact Hausdorff. The two edges $H,V$ are disjoint closed subsets of $X$, so $A$ is closed and locally compact; each edge is clopen in $A$. Every compact subset of $H$ is bounded below $\omega _1$: the open initial intervals $[0,\alpha )$, $\alpha <\omega _1$, cover $[0,\omega _1)$ and any finite subcover has bounded union. Every compact subset of $V$ is finite, since $[0,\omega )$ is discrete. For a locally compact Hausdorff space $Y$, write $C_ k(Y)$ for its continuous complex functions with seminorms $p_ K(h)=\sup _ K|h|$, $K\subset Y$ compact. This is a complete Hausdorff locally convex space. Indeed a Cauchy net has scalar pointwise limits and converges uniformly on each compact set, by passing to pointwise limits in its uniform Cauchy estimates. The limit is continuous on each compact neighborhood, hence on $Y$, and the same estimates prove convergence in every $p_ K$. Set $E=C_ k(X)$, let $r$ be restriction to $A$, and equip its image $F=r(E)\subset C_ k(A)$ with the subspace topology. Restriction is continuous and surjective onto $F$. It is also open, as follows. The balls $U_ K=\{ h:p_ K(h)<1\} $, with positive rescalings, form a cofinal family of zero neighborhoods: finite intersections contain the ball for the union of the compacts and the smallest radius. Fix $g\in F$ with $\sup _{K\cap A}|g|<1$, and choose $h\in E$ with $r(h)=g$. If $K\cap A=\varnothing $ interpret that supremum as zero. Choose $c<1$ strictly larger than it. The closed set $D=A\cap \{ |h|\geq c\} $ misses $K$. A finite union $W$ of compact clopen neighborhoods separates $K$ from $D$. Its characteristic function $\chi $ is continuous. With continuous radial truncation \[  T_ c(z)=\begin{cases} z,& |z|\leq c,\\ cz/|z|,& |z|>c,\end{cases} \qquad h'=\chi T_ c(h)+(1-\chi )h,  \] we have $p_ K(h')\leq c<1$. On $A\cap W$ we have $|h|<c$, so $h'=h$ there; on $A\setminus W$ the same equality holds because $\chi =0$. Thus $r(h')=g$. Consequently $r(U_ K)$ contains the zero neighborhood $\{ g\in F:p_{K\cap A}(g)<1\} $, proving openness. Define $b\in C_ k(A)$ to be $1$ on $H$ and $0$ on $V$. It has no continuous extension to $X$. If $h$ were such an extension, continuity at $(\omega _1,n)$ would give $\alpha _ n<\omega _1$ such that $|h(\alpha ,n)|<1/3$ for $\alpha _ n<\alpha \leq \omega _1$. The countable supremum of the countable ordinals $\alpha _ n$ is countable; choose $\alpha _*<\omega _1$ larger than all of them. Then $|h(\alpha _*,n)|<1/3$ for every finite $n$, contradicting continuity at $(\alpha _*,\omega )$, where $h$ must equal $1$. Nevertheless $b$ belongs to the closure of $F$. For $\beta <\omega _1$, the clopen-step function \[  h_\beta (\alpha ,n)=\mathbf1_{[0,\beta ]}(\alpha )  \] is continuous on $X$. For each compact $K\subset A$, its horizontal part is bounded below $\omega _1$, and $h_\beta |_ K=b|_ K$ for all sufficiently large $\beta $; the vertical equality always holds. Thus $r(h_\beta )\to b$ in $C_ k(A)$, and this net is Cauchy in $F$. It cannot converge in $F$, since continuous evaluations would force its limit to be $b\notin F$. This proves incompleteness. $\square$ Example 2.23.4 . B0973308F142 Completed projective tensor products need not preserve epimorphisms of arbitrary Hausdorff locally convex spaces. This fails even when the source of one epimorphism is complete and the other map is the identity of the scalar field. Proof. Use $r:E\to F$ of lemma 2.23.3 and $\operatorname {Id}:\mathbb C\to \mathbb C$. For any Hausdorff locally convex space $G$, the algebraic map $G\otimes \mathbb C\to G$, $x\otimes \lambda \mapsto \lambda x$, identifies the projective seminorm for $p$ and absolute value with $p$: the one-term expression gives one inequality and the triangle inequality gives the other. Therefore $G\widehat\otimes _\pi \mathbb C=\widehat G$ canonically. Since $E$ is complete, the induced tensor map is precisely $r:E\to \widehat F$. Identify $\widehat F$ with the closure of $F$ in the complete space $C_ k(A)$: the subspace uniformity and the completion construction give this identification. Its image is $F$, and the preceding explicit function $b$ belongs to $\widehat F\setminus F$. Thus the tensor map is not surjective. The target factor $F$ in this example is incomplete. No assertion about the separate variant with all four factors complete follows from this example. $\square$ Proposition 2.23.5 . 6118C797DA34 If $f:E_1\to E_2$ and $g:F_1\to F_2$ are epimorphisms between Fréchet spaces, then \[  f\widehat\otimes _\pi g: E_1\widehat\otimes _\pi F_1\longrightarrow E_2\widehat\otimes _\pi F_2  \] is an epimorphism. No nuclearity assumption is needed here. Proof. The projective-quotient part of the proof of theorem 2.13.5 proves that $Q\widehat\otimes _\pi \operatorname {Id}_ G$ is open and surjective for a Fréchet quotient $Q$ and a Fréchet space $G$, before any nuclearity is invoked. Its algebraic lifts control one seminorm at a time; the countable successive-correction construction in proposition 2.12.1 then proves the assertion on completions. The kernels of $f,g$ are closed, and their quotient identifications are topological because the maps are open. Apply this checked quotient assertion first to $f$ with factor $F_1$, and then to $g$ with factor $E_2$, interchanging the two tensor factors. Their composition is the displayed map. All intermediate completed tensors are Fréchet by section 2.13 ; compositions of open surjections are open surjections. $\square$

title: Lemma 2.23.1
text: Lemma 2.23.1 . 0628F713D150 Every vector space with its finest locally convex topology is complete. Proof. Choose a Hamel basis $(e_ i)_{i\in I}$. Its vectors have finite support. The seminorms \[  q_ w\left(\sum _ i a_ ie_ i\right)=\sum _ iw_ i|a_ i|, \qquad w_ i>0\quad (i\in I),  \] generate the finest locally convex topology: every seminorm $p$ is bounded by $q_ w$ with $w_ i=p(e_ i)+1$. Let $(a_\alpha )$ be a Cauchy net. Each coordinate has a scalar limit $c_ i$. For a fixed $w$ and $\varepsilon >0$, choose a tail on which $q_ w(a_\alpha -a_\beta )<\varepsilon $. For any finite $J\subset I$, letting $\beta $ tend to the limit in those coordinates gives \[  \sum _{i\in J}w_ i|(a_\alpha )_ i-c_ i|\leq \varepsilon  \] for every $\alpha $ in that tail. Taking the supremum over finite $J$ shows both that $\sum _ iw_ i|c_ i|<\infty $ and that the formal difference has weighted sum at most $\varepsilon $. If infinitely many $c_ i$ were nonzero, choose distinct $i_ n$ with $c_{i_ n}\ne 0$ and set $w_{i_ n}=1/|c_{i_ n}|$, extending these to positive weights. This contradicts finiteness of the weighted sum. Hence $c$ has finite support and is a vector of the original space. The same estimate for every $w$ proves $a_\alpha \to c$, establishing completeness. $\square$

title: Example 2.23.2
text: Example 2.23.2 . D7A9E3E20E73 There is a continuous linear bijection $u:E\to F$ between complete Hausdorff locally convex spaces such that $\overline{u(V)}$ is a zero neighborhood for every zero neighborhood $V\subset E$, but $u$ is not open. Proof. Take the vector space $\mathbb C^{\mathbb N}$ with its finest locally convex topology for $E$ and its product topology for $F$; let $u$ be the identity. It is continuous, and $E$ is complete by lemma 2.23.1 . The product is complete for the metric $D(x,y)=\sum _{n\geq 1}2^{-n}\min \{ 1,|x_ n-y_ n|\} $: Cauchy sequences converge coordinatewise, and a finite-head/tail estimate gives convergence for $D$. The same coordinate argument proves completeness for Cauchy nets in the product topology. For a convex balanced zero neighborhood $V$ in $E$, the set $B=\overline{u(V)}$ is closed, convex, balanced and absorbing in $F$. Thus $F=\bigcup _{m\geq 1}mB$. The complete-metric Baire argument gives interior to some $mB$: otherwise one constructs nested closed balls of radii tending to zero, avoiding the first $m$ closed sets at stage $m$, and their Cauchy centers give a limit outside their union. Consequently $B$ has interior; convexity and balance imply that $(B-B)/2\subset B$ contains a zero neighborhood. Every neighborhood in $E$ contains such a $V$, proving the asserted closure condition. To see that $u$ is not open, extend the functional $\ell (\sum _{n\in J}a_ ne_ n)=\sum _{n\in J}a_ n$ from the finite-support sequences to the whole vector space using a Hamel basis. It is continuous on $E$. A product-continuous linear functional depends on finitely many coordinates: a zero neighborhood restricts only finitely many coordinates, and arbitrary scalar multiples of all other coordinate vectors belong to it. Since $\ell (e_ n)=1$ for every $n$, $\ell $ is not product-continuous. Hence the two topologies are different and their identity bijection is not open. $\square$

title: 5.64 Null-supported Kähler currents
text:
We use $dd^ c= rac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial  ar\partial $. A set in a complex manifold is called null if it has Lebesgue measure zero in local real coordinates; this is equivalent to having measure zero for any smooth positive volume form. Lemma 5.64.1 . 0B34D9269CEA Let $V\subset \mathbb R^ m$, $m\geq 1$, be connected and open. The zero set of a nonzero real-analytic function on $V$ is null. Proof. Let $h$ be such a function. No point of $V$ has all derivatives of $h$ equal to zero. Indeed, the set of points with this property is closed, by continuity of every derivative, and open, by the convergent Taylor expansion. If nonempty, it would therefore be all of $V$. For $x\in \{ h=0\} $ choose a multi-index $\alpha $ of least total degree such that $D^\alpha h(x)
e 0$. Its degree is positive. Choose $j$ with $\alpha _ j>0$ and put $ eta =\alpha -e_ j$. Then $D^ eta h(x)=0$ and $\partial _ jD^ eta h(x)
e 0$. Consequently \[  \{ h=0\} \subset  igcup _{ eta ,j}\{ D^ eta h=0,\  \partial _ jD^ eta h
e 0\} .  \] Each set on the right is locally the graph of a smooth function of $m-1$ variables, by the implicit function theorem. Such a graph is null by Fubini's theorem. A countable subcover of these graph charts exists because $V$ is second countable. There are only countably many pairs $( eta ,j)$, so their union is null. $\square$ Theorem 5.64.2 . E682ACE02BAF Let $(X,\omega )$ be a compact Kähler manifold of complex dimension $n\geq 0$. There are a continuous function $u\in \operatorname {PSH}(X,\omega )$, with $u>0$, and a closed null set $\Sigma \subset X$ such that \[  T=\omega +dd^ cu\geq 0,\qquad \operatorname {Supp}T\subset \Sigma .  \] Thus $T$ belongs to the Kähler class $[\omega ]$. For $n\geq 1$ and $X
e \varnothing $ it is nonzero. Its coefficient measures are singular with respect to Lebesgue measure. The set $\Sigma $ can be chosen locally contained in countably many proper real-analytic level sets of pluriharmonic functions. Proof. If $X=\varnothing $, all assertions are vacuous with $\Sigma =\varnothing $. In dimension zero $X$ is a finite discrete set and every $(1,1)$-form or current is zero. Take $u=1$, $T=0$ and $\Sigma =\varnothing $. We may henceforth assume $n\geq 1$. Local functions with a strict minimum. Fix $x\in X$. By local smooth differential primitives , there is a smooth real potential $ho $ for $\omega $ in coordinates centered at $x$. The Taylor expansion has the form \[  ho (z)=ho (0)+\operatorname {Re}P(z) +\sum _{j,k}a_{j ar k}z_ j ar z_ k+o(|z|^2),  \] where $P$ is a holomorphic polynomial of degrees one and two and $(a_{j ar k})$ is positive definite. Subtracting $\operatorname {Re}P$ changes neither $dd^ cho $ nor strict plurisubharmonicity. Thus, after decreasing the coordinate ball, $ho $ has a strict minimum at its center, with $ho (z)>ho (0)$ for $z
e 0$ in that ball. Choose a smaller ball $U_ x$ whose closure lies in this potential chart, and choose numbers \[  ho (x)<\ell _ x<h_ x<\min _{\partial U_ x}ho .  \] The open set $V_ x=\{ z\in U_ x:ho (z)<\ell _ x\} $ contains $x$. Moreover $\{ z\in U_ x:ho (z)\leq h_ x\} $ is relatively compact in $U_ x$: the strict boundary inequality gives an open collar of $\partial U_ x$ on which $ho >h_ x$. Choose finitely many of these sets $V_ x$ covering $X$ and denote the corresponding data by $V_ i,U_ i,ho _ i,\ell _ i,h_ i$, $1\leq i\leq N$. For any choice $c_ i\in (\ell _ i,h_ i)$ define \[  b_ i= egin{cases}  \max \{ c_ i-ho _ i,0\} & 	ext{on }U_ i,\  0& 	ext{on }X\setminus U_ i. \end{cases}  \] This is continuous, is zero in a collar of $\partial U_ i$, and is $\omega $-psh. Indeed, on $U_ i$ its local potential is $ho _ i+b_ i=\max \{ ho _ i,c_ i\} $, which is plurisubharmonic by maxima and gluing of plurisubharmonic functions ; near the boundary and outside $U_ i$ the function $b_ i$ is zero. Also $b_ i>0$ on $V_ i$, for every permitted choice of $c_ i$. Thus these positivity sets cover $X$ independently of all subsequent choices of constants. Choosing constants. For each $i<j$, the open set $U_ i\cap U_ j$ has at most countably many connected components. Indeed, each component is open and contains an element of a fixed countable basis not contained in any other component. On any such component $W$, the smooth function $ho _ i-ho _ j$ is pluriharmonic, since its $dd^ c$ is zero. It is real analytic: on small coordinate balls a real pluriharmonic function is the real part of a holomorphic function, by smooth complex Hessian potentials on balls . If $(ho _ i-ho _ j)|_ W$ is constant, say $A_{ijW}$, impose \[  c_ i-c_ j
e A_{ijW}.  \] There are only countably many forbidden affine hyperplanes in the parameter box $B=\prod _ i(\ell _ i,h_ i)\subset \mathbb R^ N$. Each is null by Fubini's theorem, while $B$ has positive finite Lebesgue measure. Their union cannot exhaust $B$. Fix a choice of constants outside this union and define \[  u=\max _{1\leq i\leq N}b_ i.  \] It is continuous and $\omega $-psh by quasi-plurisubharmonic representatives and maxima (3), and $u>0$ because the $V_ i$ cover $X$. The tie set and the support. Put \[  \Sigma _{ij}=\{ b_ i=b_ j=u\} ,\qquad \Sigma = igcup _{i<j}\Sigma _{ij}.  \] These are closed sets because all functions involved are continuous. A point of $\Sigma _{ij}$ has $b_ i=b_ j=u>0$, so lies in $U_ i\cap U_ j$, and there \[  ho _ i-ho _ j=c_ i-c_ j.  \] On a component where $ho _ i-ho _ j$ is constant this level set is empty, by our choice. On every other component it is a proper real-analytic zero set, hence null by lemma 5.64.1 . This lemma applies in countably many real coordinate balls; on each ball the function cannot vanish identically, by real-analytic continuation on the connected component. Countably many components and finitely many pairs $(i,j)$ show that $\Sigma $ is null and give the asserted local containment in proper real-analytic level sets. At a point outside $\Sigma $ exactly one $b_ i$ realizes the maximum. The strict inequalities and $u>0$ persist on a neighborhood. On a possibly smaller neighborhood $u=b_ i=c_ i-ho _ i$, and therefore $\omega +dd^ cu=0$. This proves the support inclusion. Positivity and closedness follow from $u\in \operatorname {PSH}(X,\omega )$ and $\mathrm d\omega =0$. The formula $T-\omega =dd^ cu$ identifies their classes directly. Finally, for $n\geq 1$, distributional integration by parts gives \[  \int _ XT\wedge \omega ^{n-1}=\int _ X\omega ^ n>0,  \] since $dd^ c(\omega ^{n-1})=0$. Hence $T
e 0$. Positive currents have measure coefficients, and all those measures are supported on the null set $\Sigma $, so they are singular. $\square$ The tie set is not asserted to be a complex analytic or pluripolar set. Its defining equalities are real analytic on overlaps, together with the inequalities selecting the maximizing branches. In particular, the construction allows real hypersurfaces in the support. Lemma 5.64.3 . 7D6EE0FC8776 Let $(X,\omega )$ be a compact Kähler manifold and let $u$ be a continuous $\omega $-psh function on $X$. There are smooth functions $v_ j,w_ j$ on $X$ such that \[  v_ j\downarrow u,\qquad w_ j\downarrow u \quad 	ext{uniformly on }X,  \] and \[  \omega +dd^ cv_ j\geq 0,\qquad \omega +dd^ cw_ j\geq  rac1{j+1}\omega .  \] In particular the Kähler forms $\omega +dd^ cw_ j$ all belong to $[\omega ]$ and converge weakly to $\omega +dd^ cu$. Proof. If $X=\varnothing $ there is nothing to prove. For a zero-dimensional component take $v_ j=w_ j=u$; all forms vanish and the assertions about positivity are vacuous there. On the positive-dimensional components apply gentle quasi-equisingular approximation with $	heta =\omega $ and with $\omega $ also the Kähler reference form. It gives $\Phi _ j\downarrow u$ pointwise, with \[  \omega +dd^ c\Phi _ j\geq -\varepsilon _ j\omega , \qquad \varepsilon _ j=c'2^{-j}\downarrow 0.  \] The functions $\Phi _ j$ have gentle analytic singularities of type $(2^{-j},\mathcal I(2^ ju))$. Since $u$ is bounded, $\mathcal I(2^ ju)=\mathcal O_ X$: every holomorphic germ is square integrable against the locally bounded positive weight $\exp (-2^ ju)$ after shrinking its domain. Equivalently, the local ideal generators in these analytic presentations have no common zero. Thus $\Phi _ j$ is everywhere finite. By gentle analytic singularities , $\exp (2^ j\Phi _ j)$ is smooth, and, being positive everywhere, has a smooth logarithm. Hence every $\Phi _ j$ is smooth. This is the same smoothness argument as in smooth approximation of bounded Kähler potentials . Choose a constant $C\geq \sup _ X\Phi _1$ and put \[  v_ j=C+ rac{\Phi _ j-C}{1+\varepsilon _ j}.  \] Since $\Phi _ j-C\leq 0$, $\Phi _{j+1}\leq \Phi _ j$ and $\varepsilon _{j+1}\leq \varepsilon _ j$, we have \[   rac{\Phi _{j+1}-C}{1+\varepsilon _{j+1}} \leq  rac{\Phi _ j-C}{1+\varepsilon _{j+1}} \leq  rac{\Phi _ j-C}{1+\varepsilon _ j}.  \] Thus $v_ j$ decreases. Its pointwise limit is $u$, and \[  \omega +dd^ cv_ j = rac{\omega +dd^ c\Phi _ j+\varepsilon _ j\omega }{1+\varepsilon _ j}\geq 0.  \] Also $v_ j-C\leq 0$. Consequently the functions \[  w_ j=C+ rac{j}{j+1}(v_ j-C)  \] decrease to $u$, by the same sign argument, and \[  \omega +dd^ cw_ j = rac{j}{j+1}(\omega +dd^ cv_ j)+ rac1{j+1}\omega \geq  rac1{j+1}\omega .  \] Both convergences are uniform by Dini's theorem. Explicitly, for a decreasing continuous sequence $f_ j$ with continuous limit $u$ on compact $X$, the closed sets $\{ f_ j-u\geq \delta \} $ decrease and have empty intersection for every $\delta >0$; compactness makes one of them empty. This applies to $v_ j$ and $w_ j$. Finally uniform convergence implies distributional convergence of $dd^ cw_ j$ to $dd^ cu$, by pairing with $dd^ c$ of a smooth test form. The displayed formulas also show equality of the classes. $\square$ Corollary 5.64.4 . 3149285306C2 Every Kähler class on a compact Kähler manifold contains a closed positive current with a continuous global potential and null support, which is a weak limit of Kähler forms in that class whose global potentials converge uniformly and monotonically. Proof. Apply lemma 5.64.3 to the continuous potential supplied by theorem 5.64.2 . $\square$

title: Theorem 5.64.2

Theorem 5.64.2 . E682ACE02BAF Let $(X,\omega )$ be a compact Kähler manifold of complex dimension $n\geq 0$. There are a continuous function $u\in \operatorname {PSH}(X,\omega )$, with $u>0$, and a closed null set $\Sigma \subset X$ such that \[  T=\omega +dd^ cu\geq 0,\qquad \operatorname {Supp}T\subset \Sigma .  \] Thus $T$ belongs to the Kähler class $[\omega ]$. For $n\geq 1$ and $X
e \varnothing $ it is nonzero. Its coefficient measures are singular with respect to Lebesgue measure. The set $\Sigma $ can be chosen locally contained in countably many proper real-analytic level sets of pluriharmonic functions. Proof. If $X=\varnothing $, all assertions are vacuous with $\Sigma =\varnothing $. In dimension zero $X$ is a finite discrete set and every $(1,1)$-form or current is zero. Take $u=1$, $T=0$ and $\Sigma =\varnothing $. We may henceforth assume $n\geq 1$. Local functions with a strict minimum. Fix $x\in X$. By local smooth differential primitives , there is a smooth real potential $ho $ for $\omega $ in coordinates centered at $x$. The Taylor expansion has the form \[  ho (z)=ho (0)+\operatorname {Re}P(z) +\sum _{j,k}a_{j ar k}z_ j ar z_ k+o(|z|^2),  \] where $P$ is a holomorphic polynomial of degrees one and two and $(a_{j ar k})$ is positive definite. Subtracting $\operatorname {Re}P$ changes neither $dd^ cho $ nor strict plurisubharmonicity. Thus, after decreasing the coordinate ball, $ho $ has a strict minimum at its center, with $ho (z)>ho (0)$ for $z
e 0$ in that ball. Choose a smaller ball $U_ x$ whose closure lies in this potential chart, and choose numbers \[  ho (x)<\ell _ x<h_ x<\min _{\partial U_ x}ho .  \] The open set $V_ x=\{ z\in U_ x:ho (z)<\ell _ x\} $ contains $x$. Moreover $\{ z\in U_ x:ho (z)\leq h_ x\} $ is relatively compact in $U_ x$: the strict boundary inequality gives an open collar of $\partial U_ x$ on which $ho >h_ x$. Choose finitely many of these sets $V_ x$ covering $X$ and denote the corresponding data by $V_ i,U_ i,ho _ i,\ell _ i,h_ i$, $1\leq i\leq N$. For any choice $c_ i\in (\ell _ i,h_ i)$ define \[  b_ i= egin{cases}  \max \{ c_ i-ho _ i,0\} & 	ext{on }U_ i,\  0& 	ext{on }X\setminus U_ i. \end{cases}  \] This is continuous, is zero in a collar of $\partial U_ i$, and is $\omega $-psh. Indeed, on $U_ i$ its local potential is $ho _ i+b_ i=\max \{ ho _ i,c_ i\} $, which is plurisubharmonic by maxima and gluing of plurisubharmonic functions ; near the boundary and outside $U_ i$ the function $b_ i$ is zero. Also $b_ i>0$ on $V_ i$, for every permitted choice of $c_ i$. Thus these positivity sets cover $X$ independently of all subsequent choices of constants. Choosing constants. For each $i<j$, the open set $U_ i\cap U_ j$ has at most countably many connected components. Indeed, each component is open and contains an element of a fixed countable basis not contained in any other component. On any such component $W$, the smooth function $ho _ i-ho _ j$ is pluriharmonic, since its $dd^ c$ is zero. It is real analytic: on small coordinate balls a real pluriharmonic function is the real part of a holomorphic function, by smooth complex Hessian potentials on balls . If $(ho _ i-ho _ j)|_ W$ is constant, say $A_{ijW}$, impose \[  c_ i-c_ j
e A_{ijW}.  \] There are only countably many forbidden affine hyperplanes in the parameter box $B=\prod _ i(\ell _ i,h_ i)\subset \mathbb R^ N$. Each is null by Fubini's theorem, while $B$ has positive finite Lebesgue measure. Their union cannot exhaust $B$. Fix a choice of constants outside this union and define \[  u=\max _{1\leq i\leq N}b_ i.  \] It is continuous and $\omega $-psh by quasi-plurisubharmonic representatives and maxima (3), and $u>0$ because the $V_ i$ cover $X$. The tie set and the support. Put \[  \Sigma _{ij}=\{ b_ i=b_ j=u\} ,\qquad \Sigma = igcup _{i<j}\Sigma _{ij}.  \] These are closed sets because all functions involved are continuous. A point of $\Sigma _{ij}$ has $b_ i=b_ j=u>0$, so lies in $U_ i\cap U_ j$, and there \[  ho _ i-ho _ j=c_ i-c_ j.  \] On a component where $ho _ i-ho _ j$ is constant this level set is empty, by our choice. On every other component it is a proper real-analytic zero set, hence null by lemma 5.64.1 . This lemma applies in countably many real coordinate balls; on each ball the function cannot vanish identically, by real-analytic continuation on the connected component. Countably many components and finitely many pairs $(i,j)$ show that $\Sigma $ is null and give the asserted local containment in proper real-analytic level sets. At a point outside $\Sigma $ exactly one $b_ i$ realizes the maximum. The strict inequalities and $u>0$ persist on a neighborhood. On a possibly smaller neighborhood $u=b_ i=c_ i-ho _ i$, and therefore $\omega +dd^ cu=0$. This proves the support inclusion. Positivity and closedness follow from $u\in \operatorname {PSH}(X,\omega )$ and $\mathrm d\omega =0$. The formula $T-\omega =dd^ cu$ identifies their classes directly. Finally, for $n\geq 1$, distributional integration by parts gives \[  \int _ XT\wedge \omega ^{n-1}=\int _ X\omega ^ n>0,  \] since $dd^ c(\omega ^{n-1})=0$. Hence $T
e 0$. Positive currents have measure coefficients, and all those measures are supported on the null set $\Sigma $, so they are singular. $\square$

title: Lemma 5.64.3
text: Lemma 5.64.3 . 7D6EE0FC8776 Let $(X,\omega )$ be a compact Kähler manifold and let $u$ be a continuous $\omega $-psh function on $X$. There are smooth functions $v_ j,w_ j$ on $X$ such that \[  v_ j\downarrow u,\qquad w_ j\downarrow u \quad \text{uniformly on }X,  \] and \[  \omega +dd^ cv_ j\geq 0,\qquad \omega +dd^ cw_ j\geq \frac1{j+1}\omega .  \] In particular the Kähler forms $\omega +dd^ cw_ j$ all belong to $[\omega ]$ and converge weakly to $\omega +dd^ cu$. Proof. If $X=\varnothing $ there is nothing to prove. For a zero-dimensional component take $v_ j=w_ j=u$; all forms vanish and the assertions about positivity are vacuous there. On the positive-dimensional components apply gentle quasi-equisingular approximation with $\theta =\omega $ and with $\omega $ also the Kähler reference form. It gives $\Phi _ j\downarrow u$ pointwise, with \[  \omega +dd^ c\Phi _ j\geq -\varepsilon _ j\omega , \qquad \varepsilon _ j=c'2^{-j}\downarrow 0.  \] The functions $\Phi _ j$ have gentle analytic singularities of type $(2^{-j},\mathcal I(2^ ju))$. Since $u$ is bounded, $\mathcal I(2^ ju)=\mathcal O_ X$: every holomorphic germ is square integrable against the locally bounded positive weight $\exp (-2^ ju)$ after shrinking its domain. Equivalently, the local ideal generators in these analytic presentations have no common zero. Thus $\Phi _ j$ is everywhere finite. By gentle analytic singularities , $\exp (2^ j\Phi _ j)$ is smooth, and, being positive everywhere, has a smooth logarithm. Hence every $\Phi _ j$ is smooth. This is the same smoothness argument as in smooth approximation of bounded Kähler potentials . Choose a constant $C\geq \sup _ X\Phi _1$ and put \[  v_ j=C+\frac{\Phi _ j-C}{1+\varepsilon _ j}.  \] Since $\Phi _ j-C\leq 0$, $\Phi _{j+1}\leq \Phi _ j$ and $\varepsilon _{j+1}\leq \varepsilon _ j$, we have \[  \frac{\Phi _{j+1}-C}{1+\varepsilon _{j+1}} \leq \frac{\Phi _ j-C}{1+\varepsilon _{j+1}} \leq \frac{\Phi _ j-C}{1+\varepsilon _ j}.  \] Thus $v_ j$ decreases. Its pointwise limit is $u$, and \[  \omega +dd^ cv_ j =\frac{\omega +dd^ c\Phi _ j+\varepsilon _ j\omega }{1+\varepsilon _ j}\geq 0.  \] Also $v_ j-C\leq 0$. Consequently the functions \[  w_ j=C+\frac{j}{j+1}(v_ j-C)  \] decrease to $u$, by the same sign argument, and \[  \omega +dd^ cw_ j =\frac{j}{j+1}(\omega +dd^ cv_ j)+\frac1{j+1}\omega \geq \frac1{j+1}\omega .  \] Both convergences are uniform by Dini's theorem. Explicitly, for a decreasing continuous sequence $f_ j$ with continuous limit $u$ on compact $X$, the closed sets $\{ f_ j-u\geq \delta \} $ decrease and have empty intersection for every $\delta >0$; compactness makes one of them empty. This applies to $v_ j$ and $w_ j$. Finally uniform convergence implies distributional convergence of $dd^ cw_ j$ to $dd^ cu$, by pairing with $dd^ c$ of a smooth test form. The displayed formulas also show equality of the classes. $\square$

title: Corollary 5.64.4
text: Corollary 5.64.4 . 3149285306C2 Every Kähler class on a compact Kähler manifold contains a closed positive current with a continuous global potential and null support, which is a weak limit of Kähler forms in that class whose global potentials converge uniformly and monotonically. Proof. Apply lemma 5.64.3 to the continuous potential supplied by theorem 5.64.2 . $\square$

title: 10.97 Determinant bounds and Gauduchon separation
